units.la: COMMENTATIONUM quæ interpretandis scriptis adhiberi solent, vir nobilissime, duo genera esse non ignoras: unum contractum & pressum, fusum & latum alterum. Quorum illud accurationem iudicij maximè desiderat, hoc inventionis copiam, & orationis flumen. Utrumque verò ad οἰκοδομὴν quæ est in Christo pertinere, auctoritate, ratione, exemplis confirmamur. Nam (ut de rebus sanctis scribentes in argumento earum commoremur) pressum in sermonibus suis scriptionibusque servavit Deus, & pro commoditate eumdem ad institutionem suorum dilatavit. Quid pressius lege, quid repetitione legis, quam δευτέρωσιν legis sive Deuteronomium dixerunt Patres, copiosius? quid pressius illis Prophetarum propositionibus quæ ubique exstant, quid multiplice rerum nervorumque processu aut verborum copia, velut sanguine & colore, abundantius quam expositiones illorum? Hæc auctoritas nobis qui servimus lux est quam videamus, via quam teneamus, quam sequamur regula. Quod si rationem eius cum animis nostris expedimus, utrumque genus suas rationes habet, suasque utilitates, luce natura & communi usu experientiaque manifestissimas. Est quidem utrumque genus his necessariis constrictum legibus, ut rerum veritas insit, & cum argumento convenientia, ut sermoni perspicuitas. ut denique re & sermone iusta omnium commoditas, quæ tum in se ordinem habeant ipsa, tum pro ratione eorum quibus tradenda sunt commodè ad illam ædificationem & institutionem, propter quā suscipitur labor, ordinentur. Sed fuso scribendi ac dicendi modo sua est ratio, est & contrario[?] sua. Huius breuitas intelligentes recreat, occupatos leuat, studiosos iuuat, si bene argumento rerum & personarum modo contemperata est: illius autem vbertas imperitiores perducit manu, delectat attendentes: segnescentes, torpescentes, & aliud agentes permouet. Ad summam, hic popularitatis est, ille doctrinæ grauioris: hic vsum præbet lactis, ille solidioris cibi. In vtroque genere prout mihi concesserit Dominus versatus aliquamdiu, statueram postulanti iuuentuti gratificari, & Scripturæ sacræ breuem analysin (nam doctissimorum commentariorum ad copiam iudicio meo popularitatémque satis) in statione hac percurrere σὺν Θεοῦ[?], nisi me alio Dei voluntas rapuisset. Feci in Genesin quod potui, facturus in alios alibi, si constare sibi iuuentutis optatum, & hoc commodum publico fore animaduertero. Hoc autem quicquid est, vir nobilissime, quia per salutantium oportunos importunosque concursus non licet coram tibi aliisque valedicere vt velle, tibi visum est inscribere: à re hoc officiu vicissim postulans, vt discessum meum à loco accipias pro tua humanitate & sapientia velut à Deo imperatu, fructu vero hunc quamuis tenuem laboris mei, apud te eo loco habeas quo viri boni (in quorum numero es) dona & sigillaria amicorum (in quorum numero apud te censeri cupio) ad omne officium paratissimorum habere solent, quum alter ab altero per voluntatem Dei & rerum instantium occasiones auelluntur. Vale.
units.tr: You know, most noble sir, that there are two kinds of commentaries usually employed in interpreting writings: one compressed and close, the other full and expansive. The first chiefly demands accuracy of judgment; the second, abundance of invention and a flowing style. Both, however, we maintain by authority, reason and example to pertain to edification [οἰκοδομήν] in Christ. For (to dwell for a moment on the subject of writers on sacred matters) God has himself kept to the compressed style in his speeches and writings, and has expanded it as convenience required for the instruction of his people. What is more compressed than the law, or what is fuller than the repetition of the law, which the Fathers called Deuteronomy [δευτέρωσιν]? What is more compressed than those brief pronouncements of the prophets which are found everywhere, or what is more abundant, with its many-sided development of matters and arguments and its wealth of words, as it were with blood and colour, than their expositions? This authority is for us who serve a light to see, a way to hold, and a rule to follow. And if we weigh its reasoning against our own minds, each kind has its own reasons and its own uses, most clear by the light of nature, common practice and experience. Each kind is indeed bound by these necessary laws: that the truth of the matter be present and agree with the subject, and that the speech be clear; and finally that, in both matter and speech, there be a just arrangement of everything, so that the parts are ordered in themselves and fitted to the capacities of those to whom they are to be delivered, for the sake of that edification and instruction for which the labour is undertaken. But the diffuse manner of writing and speaking has its own reasoning, and so does its opposite. The brevity of the one refreshes those who understand, relieves the busy and helps the studious, if it is well tempered to the subject matter and the persons; the abundance of the other leads the less skilled by the hand and delights those who attend, while it stirs the sluggish, the drowsy and the inattentive. In short, the one serves popular needs, the other a weightier learning: the one offers the use of milk, the other of more solid food. Having for some time been occupied in both kinds, as far as the Lord has granted me, I had resolved to gratify the young men who asked for it, and to run through in this post a brief analysis of Holy Scripture (since, in my judgment, the very learned commentaries are sufficient in fullness but not in popular usefulness) with God's help [σὺν Θεῷ], had not the will of God drawn me elsewhere. I have done in Genesis what I could, and shall do the same for others elsewhere, if I perceive that the young men's wish is consistent and that this will prove of public benefit. Whatever this work is, most noble sir, since by reason of the opportune and inopportune crowds of well-wishers it is not allowed me to bid you and others farewell in person, I have seen fit to dedicate it to you, asking in return that you accept my departure from this place, in your kindness and wisdom, as commanded by God, and that you hold this small fruit of my labour in that place where good men (among whom you are numbered) are accustomed to keep the gifts and keepsakes of friends, who are most ready for every service, when one is torn from another by the will of God and the pressing circumstances of affairs (in whose number I wish to be counted by you). Farewell.

units.la: SYNOPSIS LIBRI GENESEOS.
units.tr: SYNOPSIS OF THE BOOK OF GENESIS.

units.la: TABVLA I.
units.tr: TABLE I.

units.la: Libro Geneseos narrantur generatio universitatis huius,cap.1. generis humani & Ecclesiæ,cap.2. peccati & maledictionum ex eo,cap.3. constitutio mundi prisci,ante diluuium, secundū propagatione peccati maledictionumque,cap.4. conseruationem Ecclesiæ in mundo peccatore,cap.5. iudicia Dei prænūtiatione & significatione,c.6. exsequutione, c.7. sequētis,à diluuio
units.tr: In the book of Genesis are narrated: the generation of this universe and of the human race and the Church, chap. 1; the origin of the human race and of the Church, chap. 2; sin and the curses arising from it, chap. 3; the constitution of the ancient world before the flood, according to the spread of sin and curses, chap. 4; the preservation of the Church in a sinful world, chap. 5; the judgements of God, in their foretelling and signification, chap. 6; in their execution, chap. 7; of the world that follows, from the flood.

units.la: TABVLA II.
units.tr: TABLE II.

units.la: Constitutio mundi sequentis à diluuio exponitur. quà instauratus est, secundum naturam communem universitatis,cap.8. ius cōmune universitatis, particulare Ecclesiæ, cap.9. post instaurationem, secundum tempora à diluuio ad Abrahamū vsq; communis, mūdi cap.10. singularis, Ecclesiæ, cap.11. Abrahami,B. Isaaci,C. Iacobi,D.
units.tr: The constitution of the world following the flood is set forth: by which it was restored, according to the common nature of the universe, chap. 8; the common law of the universe and the particular law of the Church, chap. 9; after the restoration, according to the times from the flood to Abraham, the common history of the world, chap. 10; the particular history of the Church, chap. 11; of Abraham, B; of Isaac, C; of Jacob, D.

units.la: TABVLA III.
units.tr: TABLE III.

units.la: Abrahami tempora distincta sunt vocatione, cuius propositio summa promissionibus coniuncta, fine[?] cap.11. exponitur. sermone,c. 12. & 13. opere, cap. 14. expositio promissionum de hæreditate demonstratur de hæredibus c. 15.&16. sedere cap.17. usu effectisque sederis promissionum ex vocatione Dei à Deo, communicatione consiliorum, 18. beneficiorum,19. salutis,20. prolis & gloriæ,21. à fidelib. obsequio fidei,22. officiis humanitatis,23. pietate,24.
units.tr: The times of Abraham are distinguished by his calling, the sum of which, joined with the promises, is set out in chap. 11; by speech, chap. 12 and 13; by work, chap. 14. The exposition of the promises concerning the inheritance is demonstrated with respect to the heirs, chap. 15 and 16; the covenant, chap. 17; the use and effects of the covenant of promises: from God's calling by God, the communication of counsels, 18; of benefits, 19; of salvation, 20; of offspring and glory, 21; from the faithful, the obedience of faith, 22; the offices of humanity, 23; piety, 24.

units.la: TABVLA III.
units.tr: TABLE III.

units.la: Isaaci narrantur pietas in paretem, proles, cap.25. vitæ sanctimonia diuinarum promissionum veritate confirmata, cap.26. prophetica diuinarum promissionum in Iacobū translatio, ca.27.
units.tr: The piety of Isaac towards his parent is related, and his offspring, chapter 25; the holiness of his life, confirmed by the truth of the divine promises, chapter 26; the transfer of the divine promises to Jacob by prophecy, chapter 27.

units.la: TABVLA IIII.
units.tr: TABLE IV.

units.la: Iacobi historiae narrantur in peregrinationibus Mesopotamiensi: ad quā pertinent profectio coniuncta Dei promissionibus, 28. aduentus, coniugia, liberi iusti, 29. multiplicatio liberorum bonorum 30. Cenahanea: ad quam pertinent profectio in Cenah. 31. Ægyptiaca commoratio: in qua cogressus cū Esau præparatio 32. modus 33. progressus Chebrone vsq;35 Iosephi venditio.37. Iudæ coniugium, incestus, posteri.38.
units.tr: The histories of Jacob are narrated in his sojourn in Mesopotamia, to which belong his departure, joined with God's promises (28); his arrival, marriages, and righteous children (29); and the multiplication of his good children (30). Then in Canaan, to which belongs his departure into Canaan (31). Then his sojourn in Egypt, in which are his meeting with Esau and the preparation for it (32), the manner of it (33), the progress from Hebron as far as (35), the sale of Joseph (37), and Judah's marriage, incest, and posterity (38).

units.la: TABVLA V.
units.tr: TABLE V.

units.la: Ad peregrinationē Iacobi in Ægypto pertinet antecedentia migrationis patefactio Iosephi gradatim facta Ægyptiis in carcere per officia commentariensi, & custodibus.39. per interpretationē somniorum administris Regis, 40. extra carcerem Regi populoque, 41. suis, quum aduentu priore agnouit fratres 42. posteriore excepit,43. dimisit reuocauitque 44. docuit res & consiliū suū. 45. aduocatio patris, 45. migratio,46. commoratio tempore famis,47. post tamen benedicentis Iosepho & posteris,48. proximè morte vaticinantis in omneis posteros, 49. consequentia obitum Iacobi, cap.50.
units.tr: Belonging to Jacob's sojourn in Egypt are the preceding disclosure of the migration and Joseph's gradual self-revelation: to the Egyptians in prison, through the duties of the chief jailer and the keepers (chap. 39); through the interpretation of dreams, to the king's servants (chap. 40); beyond the prison, to the king and the people (chap. 41); to his own family, when at the first coming he recognised his brothers and at the second received them (chap. 42); he sent them away and called them back (chap. 43); he taught the matter and his purpose (chap. 44). The summons of the father (chap. 45); the migration (chap. 46); the stay during the time of famine (chap. 47); yet afterwards Jacob blessing Joseph and his sons (chap. 48); shortly before death, prophesying to all his sons (chap. 49); the events following Jacob's death (chap. 50).

units.la: ΠΡΟΛΕΓΟΜΕΝΑ.
units.tr: Prolegomena [Προλεγόμενα]

units.la: RIsca illa scriptura Iudæis tradita, in nouo Testamento passim vocatur scriptura sacra: Atque etiam Scriptura κατ᾽ ἐξοχὴν [?]. Eadem quoque appellatur Lex communi appellatione, quia scriptura illa in prisca Hebræorum Ecclesia, certa lex fuit & Canon doctrinæ morum fideíque à Deo traditæ, quemadmodum appellatur à Christo Matt.5.17. & 18. Luc.16.17. Ioh.10.24.& 12.34.& 15.25. Act.23.29. Dicitur etiā à Paulo Metonymicos, Testamentū Vetus, pro eo quod est liber Veteris Testamenti 2.Cor.3.14. Huius scripturæ, quam Testamentū Vetus appellamus, partes variis modis proponuntur: Nā aliæ distribuuntur latius, aliæ angustius. Diuisio latissima est, qua Testamentum Vetus duabus partibus definitur, Lege & Prophetis, quemadmodum fit Matt.5.17.& 7.12.& 11.13.& alibi passim. Nam Lex, id est libri Mosis, singulari quadā auctoritate & testificatione, à Deo fuit cōfirmata; propterea q; fuit omnium Prophetiarū canon: & Prophetæ legis interpretes. Hinc autē Legi variæ appellationes in sacris libris tribuuntur. Nā aut proprie appellatur liber Mosis, Dan.9.11,Aut liber legis Domini, Iof.29.25. Aut liber legis Mosis Iosuæ 8.21. & 23.6. Aut Metonymicos appellatur Lex Iehouæ, Leuit. 4.22.27. Aut Lex Dei cæli, Esr.7.12.21. Aut Lex Mosis, Iof. 8.31. & 1. Reg.2.3. & Luc. 2. 22. aut denique maximè figuratè ab auctore scriptionis,vel potius instrumento, appellatur Moses,vt Lucæ 16. 29. 31. & 24. 17. & Act. 21. 21. & 2. Cor 3.15. Reliquorum librorum appella-tio cōmunis est,quâ ante diximus. Sed quia Prophetarū libri rursum in classes varias sunt distributi, fuerunt quoq; partitiones librorum Vet. Testamenti varię cōstitutę. Nā ex ratione vel modo scriptionis in duas aut tres classes distingui solent. In duas classes distinxit Chri-stus Luc.24.44. cū diceret, Hi sunt sermones quos dixi vobis cū adhuc essem apud vos, oportere impleri omnia quę scripta sunt in lege Mosis,Prophetis & Psalmis de me,&c. Nā Prophetarū alij soluta oratione scripti sunt,alij verò structa atq; numerosa,ad quā distributionem respicies Christus, tres partes dixit Vet. Testamenti,Lege,Prophetas & Psalmos. Rursūm verò quia Prophetarū qui oratione soluta scripserunt alij res ante gestas scriptis tradiderunt,alij etiā futuras cū præsentib. ex singulari Dei reuelatione coniunxerūt : propterea factū est vt horū quoque Prophetarū classes instituerentur duę:Prophetarum priorū,qui res ante gestas;& posteriorū qui post-futuras scriptis cōsignarunt:sic quadripartitū est T. Vetus in Lege,Prophetas priores, &posteriores,&Psalmos. Et sic cōmoditatis causa Hebræi[?] seorsum cū libris Psalmorū maximā parte eorū scriptorū coniūxerūt quę post trā sportatione Babylonicā fuerunt exarata. Reliquę diuisiones siunt,sed in partes,i. secundum libros singulos,aut librorum corpora. Quapropter alij,in quibus Hebræi, libros xxii Test. Veteris. Alij, in quibus Hieronymus,xxiv. Alij,quorū etiam in synopsi meminit Athanasius, xxvii. Alij denique xxxvi partes statuerunt,i. singulares libros.
units.tr: That writing delivered to the Jews is called Holy Scripture throughout the New Testament, and also Scripture by eminence [?]. It is also called, by its common name, the Law, because that writing was in the ancient Hebrew Church a fixed law and canon of doctrine concerning morals and faith, delivered by God, as Christ calls it at Matt. 5:17, 18; Luke 16:17; John 10:34, 12:34, 15:25; Acts 23:29. Paul also calls it, by metonymy, the Old Testament, meaning the book of the Old Testament, at 2 Cor. 3:14. The parts of this Scripture, which we call the Old Testament, are set out in various ways, for some divisions are broader and others narrower. The broadest division is that by which the Old Testament is defined in two parts, the Law and the Prophets, as at Matt. 5:17, 7:12, 11:13, and everywhere else. For the Law, that is the books of Moses, was confirmed by God with a singular authority and attestation; for this reason it was the canon of all the prophecies, and the prophets were the interpreters of the Law. Hence various names are given to the Law in the sacred books. It is called properly the book of Moses, Dan. 9:11; or the book of the Law of the Lord, Josh. 29:25; or the book of the Law of Moses, Josh. 8:21, 23:6; or, by metonymy, the Law of Jehovah, Lev. 4:22, 27; or the Law of the God of heaven, Ezra 7:12, 21; or the Law of Moses, Josh. 8:31, 1 Kings 2:3, Luke 2:22; and lastly, most often by a figure, it is called Moses, the author of the writing, or rather its instrument, as at Luke 16:29, 31, 24:27, Acts 21:21, and 2 Cor. 3:15. The common name of the remaining books is the one we mentioned above. But because the books of the prophets were again distributed into various classes, various divisions of the books of the Old Testament were also made. They are commonly distinguished by the manner or method of writing into two or three classes. Christ distinguished them into two classes at Luke 24:44, when he said: "These are the words which I spoke to you while I was still with you, that all things must be fulfilled which are written concerning me in the Law of Moses, in the Prophets and in the Psalms," and so on. For some of the prophets wrote in prose, others in verse and measured composition; looking to this distribution, Christ named three parts of the Old Testament: the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms. Again, because of those prophets who wrote in prose, some committed to writing events that had already happened, while others, by a singular revelation of God, joined future events with present ones; for this reason two classes of these prophets were also set up: the earlier prophets, who recorded past events, and the later prophets, who recorded events yet to come. Thus the Old Testament is fourfold: the Law, the former Prophets, the latter Prophets, and the Psalms. And so, for convenience, the Hebrews set apart the books of the Psalms together with most of those writings which were composed after the Babylonian transportation. The other divisions are made into parts, that is, according to the individual books or the bodies of books. Accordingly, some, as the Hebrews do, count twenty-two books of the Old Testament; others, as Jerome does, twenty-four; others, whom Athanasius also mentions in his synopsis, twenty-seven; and finally others set thirty-six parts, that is, the individual books.

units.la: Ordo autē in horū librorū coagmentatione, partim ex argumento partimque ex temporum consequentia,& seric[?] confectus est,si libros solum exceperis qui Psalmorum appellatione à Christo donati sunt. Sed de hoc ordine facile quisque iudicaturus est. Tamen viden-dum est nobis vt ex docendi modo libros Testamenti Veteris in tria genera distinguamus. Cū enim triplex sit docendi modus,Auctoritas cui credendum est, Ratio & Exemplum, similiter libros Testamenti Veteris in tria genera distinguimus commodissimē. Nam auctoritas est Legis:Ratio ,librorum dogmaticorum est,vt sunt Prophetæ po-steriores: Exempla , Historicorum. quæ omnia genera & si hic illic fusa sunt,omnia simul in Psalmis emicant.
units.tr: The order in joining these books together has been made partly from the subject matter and partly from the sequence of times, and from their succession, if you except the books which Christ gave the name of Psalms. But anyone will easily be able to judge about this order. Nevertheless, we must see how to distinguish the books of the Old Testament into three kinds by the mode of teaching. For since the mode of teaching is threefold, authority, which must be believed, reason, and example, we likewise distinguish the books of the Old Testament most conveniently into three kinds. For authority belongs to the Law; reason belongs to the doctrinal books, such as the later Prophets; examples belong to the historical books. And although all these kinds are poured out here and there, all of them shine forth together in the Psalms.

units.la: Horum interpretationem (vt vulgo dicunt) Analyticam institui-mus tradere veram,perspicuam & breuem. Veritatem spiritus Veri-tatis & Scriptura sacra(vt oramus à Deo) docturus est, nos propone-mus fide ac diligentia: perspicuitatem Arte procurabimus: breuita-tem,studio. Sed quia breuitatis fere comes est obscuritas,& in Analytico docendi genere non expedit singula minutatim percurrere, neque est instituti nostri: tantum id constituimus curare, vt quae obscuriora in singulis capitibus esse videbuntur, tamquam per quaestiones, exposita, communi singulorum capitum Analysi explicentur.
units.tr: We have undertaken to deliver the interpretation of these books, which is commonly called analytic, as true, clear and brief. The Spirit of truth and Holy Scripture (as we pray from God) will be the teacher of the truth; we shall set it forth with faith and diligence; we shall secure clarity by method; brevity by zeal. But since obscurity is almost always the companion of brevity, and in the analytic mode of teaching it is not expedient to run through single matters minutely, nor is that part of our purpose, we have resolved only to take care that those things which seem more obscure in individual chapters are explained, set out as questions, within the general analysis of each chapter.

units.la: Libri Mosis, qui κατ' ἐξοχὴν[?] obtinent Legis appellationem, numero sunt quinque, pro ratione temporis, quo scripti sunt, & ea quae narrantur gesta, distributi.
units.tr: The books of Moses, which hold the name of the Law by preeminence, are five in number, distributed according to the order of time in which they were written and the events which are narrated.

units.la: Primus est Geneseos[?], qui a creatione mundi ad mortem vsque Iosephi pertinet.
units.tr: The first is Genesis, which runs from the creation of the world to the death of Joseph.

units.la: Secundus est Exodi, qui a morte Iosephi pertinet ad ineuntem vsque annum secundum exitus Israelitarum ex Ægypto.
units.tr: The second is Exodus, which runs from the death of Joseph to the beginning of the second year after the departure of the Israelites from Egypt.

units.la: Tertius est Leuitici, qui mensis primi historiam complectitur, secundo anno gestam, cuius proximè meminimus.
units.tr: The third is Leviticus, which embraces the history of the first month, of the second year, which we have just mentioned.

units.la: Quartus, qui Numerorum a principio secundi mensis secundo anno, quum Israelitae ex Ægypto migrauerunt ad principium vsque mensis vndecimi anno 40. pertendit.
units.tr: The fourth, Numbers, runs from the beginning of the second month of the second year, when the Israelites migrated from Egypt, to the beginning of the eleventh month of the fortieth year.

units.la: Postremus denique Deuteronomij res mensium duorum continet ad principium anni vsque 41. ex quo Israelitae ex Ægypto discesserant.
units.tr: Lastly, Deuteronomy contains the events of two months, from the beginning of the year to the beginning of the forty-first year, from which the Israelites had departed from Egypt.

units.la: DE LIBRO GE-NESEOS.
units.tr: ON THE BOOK OF GENESIS.

units.la: LIBRI Geneseos finis aut communiter cum caeteris S. S. libris consideradus est, aut singulariter. Finis communis est, Dei creatoris gloria, & Ecclesiae inter homines aedificatio. Singularis est, vt tum ex principiis naturae & gratiae, tū ex progressu aliquot annorum gloria Dei ostendatur & aedificetur Ecclesia. Summa est, Deum tum in ratione vniuersitatis huius, tum in administratione secundum naturam & gratiam & progressu sapientissimo, summe variam sapientiam suam & gloriam in hoc mundo, in primis autem in Ecclesia sua explicasse. Partes itaque huius libri duae in vniuersum constitui possunt, vna de generatione & Principiis vniuersitatis huius, in primis autem Ecclesiae, propter quam Deus hanc vniuersitatem & Ecclesiam propter se condidit. Atque hāc[?] partem trib. capitibus possumus definire. Altera est de progressu & administratione, secundum naturam & gratiam couenientissima reliquo toto libro, cuius quidem gubernationis etsi hoc tempore partes possumus exponere, commodius tamen futurum est si in principio cap. 4. vbi loci illius quasi vestibulum statuimus, reiiciamus. De principiis autem vniuersitatis huius ordo hic a Mose seruatur, ut primùm ortus totius vniuersitatis communiter, cap.1. Tum etiam Ecclesię singulariter, cap.2. Postremò ortus corruptionis & depraua-tionis illius cap.3. exponatur.
units.tr: The end of the book of Genesis may be considered either in common with the other books of Holy Scripture, or in its own particular respect. The common end is the glory of God the Creator and the building up of the Church among men. The particular end is that the glory of God may be shown and the Church built up, both from the principles of nature and grace and from the progress of some years. The sum is that God, both in the design of this universe and in its governance according to nature and grace and in its most wise progress, has set forth his most varied wisdom and glory in this world, and above all in his Church. The parts of this book may therefore be set out in general as two. One concerns the generation and principles of this universe, and above all of the Church, for whose sake God founded this universe, and the Church for his own sake. We may define this part by three chapters. The other concerns the progress and administration according to nature and grace, which is most suitable to the whole remainder of the book. Although we could set out the parts of this government at present, it will be more convenient to defer them to the beginning of chapter 4, where we have placed that section as a kind of vestibule. As for the principles of this universe, the order followed here is Moses': first the origin of the whole universe in general, chapter 1; then also that of the Church in particular, chapter 2; and finally the origin of corruption and depravation, chapter 3, is set out.

units.la: ANALYSIS CAPITIS PRIMI.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF THE FIRST CHAPTER.

units.la: HUIUS capitis summa est, Deum ex nihilo omnia sex dicerum[?] opere condidisse quę in rerū vniuersitate sunt. Finis autē, ut Dei gloria in isto admirabili cōditu vniuersitatis & principiis Ecclesiæ recognoscatur. Partes cap.omnino sunt tres. Prima est de Principiis ad vniuersitatē condendam pertinentib.duob.vers.Secunda,de elemētis velut simplicibus corporib.quæ ex illis principiis cōstituta sunt & ordine, usu,ac effectione illorū, inde ad versum usq; io. Tertia,de corporib. ex materia elementari constitutis,eorumq; ordinatione,ad finē usque capitis. De principiis (ut paucis dicamus, ) hoc Moses statuit quod Plato etiam fecit. Principiorum duo sunt genera: vnum externum, alterum internum.Principium externum est Deus (ut optimè Plato) ut qui causa est efficiens,agens,mouens,exemplaris ( ut vocat & finalis rerum omnium quæ in hac vniuersitate sunt.Internum vero prin-cipium, ut à Physicis, ita etiam à Mose triplex constituitur: materia, priuatio, & forma,e quibus materia & forma in rei cōstitutione permanet.Priuatio pertinet ad rei cōstituedæ generationē. De his Principiis coniūctim loquitur Moses duobus versibus, duāsq; circumstā-tias adiungit inseparabiles: vnam fluxam, quæ est temporis, quum dicit In Principio, id est in primo termino pūctóque temporis & rerum omnium temporalium: alteram permanentem, nimirum communis loci ad totam vniuersitatem hanc communiter pertinentis: quem locū definit Moses duorū extremorū (ut vocant) terminorū circum-scriptione, nimirū circumferentiæ & centri. nam circumferentia vniuersitatis appellatur cœlum: Centrum, in quo tota hæc vniuersitas quasi adunata est, à Mose Terra dicitur. Secundum has circumstantias Deus Pater, filius & S. S. essentia vnus, personis trinus ( nam hoc appellatione Elohim ostenditur) tamquam principium externum huius vniuersitatis & seculi, tum præsentis, tum futuri & eorum quæ supra vniuersitatē hanc sunt, dicitur principium etiam omnium principiorum, ac proinde rerum quæ ex principiis externis constitutæ sunt: quæ magnifica operatio & plane diuina verbo Hebraeo Bara, (quod vulgo exponunt creauit) exprimitur. Cū autem dicitur Deus creauisse cælū & terram, i. peripheriā & centrū vniuersitatis huius synecdochicè, non solum locus ille communis (quē ante diximus) intelligendus est, verùm etiam materia reb. istis creādis & constituendis præbita. Atque hoc est primū principiū Physicum ad rei generationē & constitutionē pertinens. Nam his cancellis Physicę quū circumcludimur, verum est illud Principium Physicę, Ex nihilo nihil fieri: Quod Principiū de ordine naturali verū est in natura constituta; in constitueda, minimè, quia omnia Principia ad constitutionē, vniuersitatis huius sola sua potentia effecit Deus propter bonitatē suam. Alterum Principium quod Physici priuatione vocant, id est (vt ita loquamur) caretiam formæ, sed habilem capiendæ formæ & appetentem illius, describit Moses priore membro vers. 2. cum ait, Terra autem erat res informis & inanis, tenebræque in superficie abyssi. sensus enim est; Neque in centro, neque in circumferentia, neque in vlla parte à centro ad circumferentiam posita formam vllam infuisse, sed tantum fuisse rude & indigestum chaos, cui postea Deus ipse veluti Principium externum indidit formam eadem bonitate sua. Hanc priuationem Deus curauisse dicitur altera parte 2. versus, his verbis, Spiritus Dei incubabat superficiei aquarum. Quod autem Spiritus Dei appellatur, non eò adducitur vt aliud esse Spiritum Dei; aliud Deum intelligamus, sed tantum vt alium esse Spiritum, id est aliam personam credamus quàm sit persona Dei, quæ spirat illum. Cum autem ille ipse Deus spirans vel emittens Spiritum suum, dicatur Elohim, vt primo quoque versu Deus appellatus est, ex eo concludimus Spiritum non esse vnius personæ, hoc est, ab vna solum persona spiratum atque procedentem, sed spirari atque emitti à Deo Patre & filio in vnitate essentiæ. Hoc igitur Principium quod Deum appellamus, dicitur causa efficiens fuisse tertij interni Principij quod formam appellamus. Neque verò cogitandum est solam personam spiritus, tertij huius principij auctorem esse, sed eo ipso quod Pater & filius spirant hunc Spiritum æterna spiratione, ex eo concludimus communem esse in rebus omnibus exteris sanctæ trinitatis operatione, etsi actus proximus sanctæ trinitatis in rebus exteris pro ratione operationis modò patri, interdum filio, interdum vero Spiritui sancto tribuitur. Nam Patri operationes ad Principium spectantes tribuuntur, quia potentissimè in persona Patris terminantur: Filio, opera redemptionis, quia in Filio terminum habet suum redemptio. Spiritui sancto similiter sanctificatio, & hoc loco in creatione rerum opus formæ,qua res ad suum esse(vt loquun tur,)productæ sunt. Huius Spiritus sancti opus per metaphoram exponitur a Mose, cum dicit, eum incubuisse his rebus creatis inferioribus, quas res inferiores Moses appellauit aquas syneedochicè, quia tota facies istius materiæ quasi fermentata aquis confusis esse videbatur. Atque hac ratione viam sternit Moses ad narrationem, vel historiam elementorum, quam secundam esse huius cap. partem ostendimus.
units.tr: The sum of this chapter is that God created from nothing all the things that are in the universe, by the work of six days. Its end is that God's glory may be acknowledged in the wondrous construction of the universe and in the beginnings of the Church. The chapter has three parts in all. The first concerns the principles that belong to the making of the universe, and runs through the first two verses. The second concerns the elements, as simple bodies, which were constituted from those principles, and their order, use and effects, and runs from there to verse 10. The third concerns the bodies made from elemental matter and their arrangement, and runs to the end of the chapter. To speak briefly about principles: Moses lays down what Plato also laid down. There are two kinds of principle, one external and the other internal. The external principle is God (as Plato rightly says), who is the efficient, acting, moving and exemplary cause, and, as he calls it, the final cause of all the things that are in this universe. The internal principle, however, is, as the natural philosophers hold, and as Moses also holds, threefold: matter, privation and form, of which matter and form remain in the constitution of a thing. Privation pertains to the generation of the thing to be made. Moses speaks of these principles together in two verses, and he adds two inseparable circumstances: one fleeting, which belongs to time, when he says In the beginning, that is, at the first term and point of time and of all temporal things; the other permanent, namely of the common place pertaining to this whole universe in common. Moses defines this place by the circumscription of two extremes (as they are called), namely the circumference and the centre. For the circumference of the universe is called heaven; the centre, in which this whole universe is as it were gathered together, is called earth by Moses. In accordance with these circumstances, God the Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one in essence and three in persons (for this is shown by the name Elohim), is called the external principle of this universe and of the age, both present and future, and of those things which are above this universe; he is also called the principle even of all principles, and therefore of the things which are constituted from external principles. This magnificent and altogether divine operation is expressed by the Hebrew word bara [ברא], which the common version renders "created." When it is said that God created heaven and earth, that is, by synecdoche the periphery and centre of this universe, we must understand not only that common place (of which we spoke before) but also the matter supplied for the making and constituting of these things. And this is the first physical principle pertaining to the generation and constitution of a thing. For when we are enclosed within these bounds of physics, that physical principle is true: out of nothing, nothing comes. This principle is true of the natural order in a constituted nature, but not in the making of nature, because God alone, by his own power and for his own goodness, brought about all the principles of this universe in its constitution. The second principle, which the natural philosophers call privation, that is (so to speak) the lack of form but a capacity for receiving form and a desire for it, Moses describes in the first part of verse 2, when he says: Now the earth was without form and void, and darkness was on the face of the deep. The sense is that neither in the centre, nor in the circumference, nor in any part placed between the centre and the circumference was any form present, but only a rude and undigested chaos, into which God himself afterwards, as the external principle, infused form by the same goodness. God is said to have taken care of this privation in the second part of verse 2, in these words: The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. Now, that he is called the Spirit of God is not adduced so that we should understand one thing to be the Spirit of God and another to be God, but only so that we should believe that there is another Spirit, that is, another person than the person of God who breathes him. But since that same God, breathing or sending forth his Spirit, is called Elohim, just as God was named in the first verse, we conclude from this that the Spirit is not of one person alone, that is, not breathed and proceeding from one person only, but is breathed and sent forth by God the Father and the Son in the unity of essence. This principle, which we call God, is therefore said to have been the efficient cause of the third internal principle, which we call form. Nor should we think that the person of the Spirit alone is the author of this third principle; rather, from the fact that the Father and the Son breathe this Spirit by an eternal breathing, we conclude that the operation of the Holy Trinity in all external things is common, although the proximate act of the Holy Trinity in external things is attributed, according to the manner of the operation, sometimes to the Father, sometimes to the Son, and sometimes to the Holy Spirit. For operations relating to the principle are attributed to the Father, because they terminate most powerfully in the person of the Father; operations of redemption to the Son, because redemption has its term in the Son; sanctification similarly to the Holy Spirit; and in this place, in the creation of things, the work of form, by which things were produced into their being (as they say). Moses expresses the work of this Holy Spirit by a metaphor, when he says that he moved upon these created lower things, which Moses called by synecdoche waters, because the whole surface of that matter seemed as if fermented with confused waters. And in this way Moses prepares the way for the narrative, or history, of the elements, which we have shown to be the second part of this chapter.

units.la: Sequitur ergo secundus locus de constitutione elementorum, quam triduo distinxit Deus, idque iure optimo. Nam cum elementorum ea sit ratio, vt superiora quæque agant in inferioribus, & inferiora agantur a superioribus, ex eo sequitur elementum ignis,quod summum est, agere non agi, elementum vero terræ, quod infimum, agi non autem agere. Cum autem ad vocem elementorum illud pertinuerit, vt ipsorum natura,potentia,actio, & passio distinctè a Deo determinarentur, ex eo consequitur primum historiæ de Elementis membrum agere de igne operante in aere: secundum de aere operante in aquis: tertium, de aquis in terra. Locum de igne agente in aere ad historiam diei primi; alterum de aere agente in aquis,diei secundi: tertium denique de aquis agentibus in terram ad historiam diei tertij pertinere. Ac primum quidem de igne. De his elementis duo communiter breuitatis causa præmittimus. Vnû, de modo efficientis causæ ad generationem ipsorum : Alterum, de ordine quem Deus obseruauit in elemetis constituendis. Efficiente causam Deum esse iam ante ostendimus. Huic efficienti causæ modus vnicus efficiendi tribuitur, sermo: Et dixit. Verbo autem dicendi non est intelligendus hoc loco sermo ille προφορικός siue enuntiatiuus quo alij apud alios vti solent, non item sermo ille ἐνδιάθετος siue ingenitus aut innatus Christus; non sermo ἐνδιάθετος qui nulla ratione potest Deo competere: sed tantum intelligendus est actus mandantis & puro suo mandato rem ad esse (vt loquuntur) producentis. Alter locus quem rationem esse diximus a Deo & ordinem quem Deus in rebus creatis obseruauit, quatuor speciatim continet: Nam primum productio ad esse ( vt loquuntur ) ponitur; secundo approbatio, tertio ordinatio rei creatæ ac probatæ: postremo autem sanctio ordinationis illius in natura rerum. Exempli causa in primo loco de luce, productio narratur his verbis, Fiat lux. approbatio, Vidit Deus lucè esse bonam. Ordinatio, & distinxit Deus inter lucem & tenebras. Sanctio denique illius, & vocauit diem lucem, &c. Hactenus communia. De singularibus videamus. Ignis in aere actio, & aeris ab igne affectio mandata est à Deo his verbis, Esto lux: nec refert quod Moses his verbis neque ignis agentis, neque patientis aeris meminit: Nam Mosi consilium fuit,non vt subiecta ipsa minutatim Philosophico studio declararet, sed tantū vt à posteriore (quæ popularis est docendi ratio) res ipsas ostenderet. Cùm autem dixit Deus,esto lux, constitutionem ignis cum aere eam mandauit existere. Est autem lux nihil aliud nisi qualitas quædam corporis luminosi, id est, ignis aërem sua præsentia illustrans. Cum autem dixit Deus, Esto lux, mandauit vt accidens illud siue qualitas potentiáque naturalis (Physica) ignis in aere(qui per se αὐτοφυὴς[?] est,) operatione suam exerceret. Atque hoc pacto & lux primi dici consti-tuta est, & modus approbationis, ordinationis, sanctionisque in rerum natura exhibitus, quo lux suo ordine ad hunc vsque diem per-seuerat. Quod autem hîc nonnulli obiiciūt de luminaribus die quar-to ad afferendam lucem cōstitutis, id quàm bene cum hoc loco con-ueniat, postea demonstrabimus. Atque hoc quidem opus diei primi; prout concludit Moses verf.5. dicens, Sic fuit vespera, fuitque ma-ne diei primi. Diem enim Moses intelligit ex spatio noctis & lucis constantem, & opus vtroque spatio distingui docet oportere: Nempe,creationem Principiorum fuisse in prima illa nocte: di-stinctionem verò leuiorum elementorum prima luce constitu-tam esse.
units.tr: There follows, therefore, the second topic, concerning the constitution of the elements, which God distinguished over three days, and rightly so. For since the nature of the elements is such that the higher always act upon the lower, and the lower are acted upon by the higher, it follows that the element of fire, being the highest, acts and is not acted upon, while the element of earth, being the lowest, is acted upon and does not act. Since it has pertained to the description of the elements that their nature, power, action and passion should be distinctly determined by God, it follows that the first member of the history of the elements treats of fire acting in air, the second of air acting in waters, and the third of waters in earth. The passage about fire acting in air belongs to the history of the first day; the second, about air acting in waters, to the second day; and the third, finally, about waters acting upon earth, to the history of the third day. And first, indeed, concerning fire. Before these elements we set down two things in common, for the sake of brevity. One is the manner of the efficient cause in their generation; the other is the order which God observed in constituting the elements. That God is the efficient cause we have already shown. To this efficient cause is attributed one single mode of efficiency, speech: And he said. By the word of saying, however, we must not understand here that speech which is uttered [προφορικός], which others are accustomed to use with one another, nor again that inward speech [ἐνδιάθετος] which is innate or inborn; nor the inward speech [ἐνδιάθετος] which cannot in any way belong to God. Rather it must be understood only as the act of one commanding, which by his mere command brings a thing into being (as they say). The other point, which we said concerns the reason and the order that God observed in created things, contains four things specifically. For first, production into being (as they say) is set down; second, approval; third, the ordering of the created and approved thing; and last, the sanctioning of that ordering in the nature of things. To give an example in the first case, concerning light: its production is narrated in these words, Let there be light. Approval: God saw that the light was good. Ordering: and God divided the light from the darkness. Finally its sanction: and God called the light day, and so on. So much for what is common. Let us now look at the particulars. The action of fire in air, and the affection of air by fire, is commanded by God in these words, Let there be light; nor does it matter that Moses in these words mentions neither the acting fire nor the air that is acted upon. For it was Moses' intention not to explain the subjects themselves in minute detail with philosophical study, but only to show the things themselves from their effects, which is the popular method of teaching. When God said, Let there be light, he commanded that the constitution of fire together with air should come into existence. Light, moreover, is nothing other than a quality of a luminous body, that is, fire illuminating the air by its presence. When God said, Let there be light, he commanded that this accident, or quality, and natural (physical) power of fire in the air, which is self-existent [αὐτοφυής], should exercise its operation. In this way both the light of the first day was constituted, and the mode of approval, ordering and sanction was displayed in the nature of things, by which light has persisted in its order down to this day. Now, that some here object concerning the luminaries constituted on the fourth day to bring light, how well that agrees with this passage, we shall demonstrate afterwards. This is the work of the first day, as Moses concludes in verse 5, saying: So there was evening and there was morning, the first day. For Moses understands the day to consist of the space of night and of light, and teaches that the work must be distinguished by both spaces: namely, that the creation of the principles took place in that first night, and that the distinction of the lighter elements was constituted by the first light.

units.la: Secundus locus,De elemento aeris in aquis agente, proponitur in verf. 6. & sequentib. Ac primum quidem de modo efficiendi & rebus effectum consequentibus nihil iam dicturi sumus, quia communiter ad opus dierum singulorum pertinet, quod ante perstrinximus. Tantum obseruanda est actio aeris in aquis, & aquarum ab aere affectio mandata, & effecta mandato Dei. Mandata verf.6. Effecta, verf. 7. Mandati partes sunt duæ. Prima est de aeris inter aquas collocatione ad actum ipsius: Secunda,de actu vel operatione aeris aquas superiores ab inferioribus disparantis. Locus aeris, vbi collocatus est, expansum appellatur: quo nomine significatur totum illud spatium quod inani simile vitalem hunc spiritum fundit, vt verbis Plinij vtar. Nam quod de firmamento, non tam ex incommoda Græcorum interpretatione quàm ex ignoratione vocis, plerique interpretati sunt, id à Mosis sententia alienum esse versu sequente ostenditur, cum dicit Moses, Deum fecisse expansum illud (nimirum verbo) & ita distinctionem statuisse ac dissepimentum inter aquas inferiores, & superiores. Inferiores autem quæ sub expanso illo suo. Superiores vero quæ huic expanso imminent. Quòd si quis mirabitur huic regioni, quæ sub nubibus est, nomé quoq; expāsi tri-bui:iniquū[?] esse totius appellatione parti, nō vsq; adeò magnæ, applicari: meminerit eā esse naturā rerū ὁμοιομερῶν[?], i. quæ similares appellantur, ut pars vel minima earum obtineat totius appellatione: ut siquis aërem, aquā, sanguinem, carnem, & similia nominauerit. Eadem quoque ratione illud accipiendum est quod dicit Moses versu 8. Deum vocauisse expansum illud cælum. qua ratione non Hebræi solum aut Orientales, sed Græci quoque & Latini usi sunt. hoc cælum parte illam inani similem, ubi crassus aër est, appellantes.
units.tr: The second point, concerning the element of air acting in the waters, is set out in verse 6 and the verses following. As to the manner of effecting and the results that follow, we will say nothing further now, since that belongs in common to the work of each day, which we have already touched on. Only the action of the air in the waters is to be observed, and the affecting of the waters by the air, commanded and accomplished by the command of God. The command is in verse 6, the accomplishment in verse 7. The command has two parts. The first concerns the placing of the air among the waters in relation to its action; the second concerns the action or operation of the air in separating the upper waters from the lower. The place where the air is set is called expansum (the expanse), a name that signifies the whole space which, resembling a void, pours out this vital spirit, to use the words of Pliny. That the expanse is the firmament, as most have explained, comes not so much from the unfortunate Greek translation as from ignorance of the word, and this is shown to be foreign to Moses' meaning by the following verse, where Moses says that God made that expanse (namely by the word) "and so established a distinction and partition between the lower waters and the upper." The lower waters are those under that expanse of his; the upper are those that hang over it. But if anyone wonders why the name of expanse is also given to the region under the clouds, and thinks it unfair to apply the name of the whole to a part not so large, let him remember that this is the nature of homogeneous things [ὁμοιομερῶν], that is, things called similar, so that even the smallest part of them takes the name of the whole: as when one names air, water, blood, flesh, and the like. By the same reasoning must be understood what Moses says in verse 8, that God called that expanse heaven. Not only Hebrews and Orientals, but also Greeks and Latins used this way of speaking, calling by the name heaven that part, like a void, where the thick air is.

units.la: Sequitur locus Tertius, Nempe de aquis terram variatibus, & dis-iungentibus partes illius, Quam rem Moses vers.9. & 10. explicauit. Continet autē narratio mandatum Dei & effectum mandati, ut ante, cæteraque his cōiuncta, de quibus ante dicebamus. Cōstituitur ergo efficitúrque opus duplex: nam de aquis dicitur, Confluant aquæ quæ sub cælo sunt. i. proximè cōiunctæ terræ, in locum unū: de Terra verò dicitur, & conspicua sit arida, nimirū cedente aqua in suos alueos, mādato Dei. Id solum obseruandum est, utroque in versu syllepsin esse Hebraicam: quòd aquæ iubentur in locum unum confluere, id est, singulæ in suum locum prout unicuique mandato Dei attributus est. Hæc de dispositione elementorum.
units.tr: There follows the third point, namely the waters gathering the earth and separating its parts, which Moses explained in verses 9 and 10. The narrative contains God's command and the effect of the command, as before, together with the other things joined to these, of which we spoke earlier. The work is therefore established and carried out in a twofold way. For of the waters it is said, "Let the waters that are under heaven be gathered together," that is, those lying close to the earth, "into one place"; and of the earth it is said, "and let the dry land appear," namely with the water withdrawing into its channels by the command of God. This only is to be observed: in both verses there is a Hebrew syllepsis. That the waters are commanded to gather into one place means that each goes to its own place, as assigned to each by the command of God. These things concern the arrangement of the elements.

units.la: Earum rerum quæ ex elementorum compage aut affectione compositæ sunt, locum tertium esse oftedimus à versu 11. ad finem usque capitis. In hac autē historiæ parte hic ordo obseruādus est. Quod primùm res ad commoditatem incolarum in hoc domicilio terræ pertinentes creatæ esse dicuntur. Secundò animātes tanquā in domicilio parato constitutæ. Rerum ad domicilij huius constitutionem pertinentium duo sunt genera. Nā primū infrà, terræ fructus ad commoditatē incolarum, postquā ex aquis emersit terra, ortæ dicūtur v.11. & sequente ad consummationē operis in die tertio; secundò autē suprà, ornatus stellarum, syderum, planetarúmque ad res istas inferiores illustrādas & modificandas appositus ver.14. & seqq. De reb. è terra prodeuntib. mādatum est v. 11. Effectus & consequentia, 12. Rerū è terra prodeuntium genera ponuntur tria, primum herbarum tenellarum terram vestientium. Secundū herbarum caulescentium vel fruticātium, quæ panguntur quocunq; semine. Tertium denique arborum arbustorūmque, tum potētia fructum editurarū ex naturę ordine, tum re ipsa fructum habētium iam eo tempore, ad commoditatem hominis proximè venturi: Nam propterea vocatur à Mose arbor fructuosa edens fructū. Deinde verò his plantarū generibus duo creationis lege indicūtur: unum, vt singulæ plantæ in speciem suam sint, id est, non ea ipsa indiuidua quæ in ipsa creatione effecit Deus, sed eorum indiuiduorum quasi posteritas in reliquum tempus existeret.¶[?] Alterum, vt ad conseruationem speciei, quamuis pereuntibus successiue indiuiduis, semen exstaret in illis primi generis plantis,& deinceps naturæ ordine propagaretur. Seminis autem appellatione non est simpliciter intelligendum illud quod vulgò semen appellatur, sed omnino omnis substantia ex qua indiuidua secundum speciem suâ propagari solent, vt sunt taleæ, propagines, surculi,& quæcunque sunt eiusmodi. Huic mandato Dei effectus respondisse à Mose dicitur, cum generatim in fine verf. II.(& ita fuit) tum vero speciatim,ver.12. Cui narrationi subiiciuntur synecdochicas illa quæ ante diximus, de approbatione, ordinatione, & sanctione in natura rerum,quum dicitur, & vidit Deus &c. Ita clauditur historia diei tertij, cum de nocte aquæ diffugissent, matutino plantæ emersissent,ex quo terra aquis leuata esset.
units.tr: We have shown that the third point, concerning things composed from the joining or affecting of the elements, runs from verse 11 to the end of the chapter. In this part of the history the following order is to be observed. First, things pertaining to the convenience of the inhabitants of this dwelling, the earth, are said to be created; second, living creatures are established as in a prepared dwelling. There are two kinds of things pertaining to the furnishing of this dwelling. The first, below, is the fruits of the earth, for the convenience of the inhabitants, which are said to have sprung up after the earth emerged from the waters, in verse 11 and following, completing the work on the third day. The second, above, is the adornment of the stars, constellations and planets, set to illuminate and regulate these lower things, in verse 14 and following. A command concerning things coming forth from the earth is given in verse 11, and its effect and consequences in verse 12. Three kinds of things coming forth from the earth are set down: (1) the tender herbs clothing the earth; (2) the stemmed or bushy herbs, which are propagated by any seed; (3) finally, trees and shrubs, both those able by the order of nature to bear fruit and those already bearing fruit at that time and close to human use. For this reason Moses calls it "a fruit tree bearing fruit." Then, by the law of creation, two things are laid down for these kinds of plants. One is that each plant should be after its kind, that is, not the very individuals that God made in the act of creation, but as it were the posterity of those individuals, existing for the remaining time. The other is that, for the preservation of the species, although the individuals perish one after another, seed should remain in those plants of the first kind and be propagated thereafter in the order of nature. By the name of seed, however, is not to be understood simply what is commonly called seed, but altogether any substance from which individuals of a kind are customarily propagated, such as cuttings, layerings, shoots, and whatever is of this sort. To this command of God the effect is said by Moses to have corresponded: generally at the end of verse 11 ("and so it was"), and then specifically in verse 12. To this narrative are subjoined those synecdochical expressions we mentioned before, concerning approval, ordering and sanction in the nature of things, when it is said "and God saw," and so on. Thus the history of the third day is closed: the waters had withdrawn by night, and in the morning the plants had sprung up, since the earth had been lifted above the waters.

units.la: Sequitur alterum membrum ad commoditatem domicilij pertinens & ornatum eius, de corporum cælestium creatione à Domino, & illorum vsu. Hæc historia duobus membris consimiliter distincta est, mandato verf. 14. & 15. & effectu mandati, seqq. In mandato primum res, secundò vsus & ordinatio earū rerum cælestiū à Deo præstituitur. Res quidé his verbis,Sunto luminaria in expānso cæ-li. Vsus vero & ordinatio, verbis seqq.ad distinctionem faciendâ inter diê & noctê,&c.De rebus quas mādato suo iubet Deus existere,duo pronuntiat Deus.Nam res imperat esse,& definit sedé. Res generali nomine exprimuntur,luminaria: sedes similiter vniuersè, in expanso cœlorum.Luminaria cum dicūtur,non tam eorum substantia quàm vsus respicitur: Et si cum vsus à potentia sit & in relatione versetur, necessario aliquam substantiam poni oportet. De substantia variant Philosophi:Nam alij igneâ esse voluerunt:alij ex eadem materia cœli, sed nodosa solidáque, & minimè transparente præter reliquum cæli corpus.quam sententiam ego quidem facilè concesserim : maximè cū hoc loco videatur Moses repetere eundem ordinem quem in tridui præcedêtis historia vidimus. Nam die quarto de rebus æthereis agitur & cælestibus. Die quinto de rebus aereis & aquatilibus : sexto de terrestribus.Huic substantiæ,qua solidam esse statuimus, accedit illa affectio quòd obtutu ignis illius elementaris,qui antecedente triduo creationis sine commutatione obibat vires cum tenebris, nunc demum ita constituitur vt illud corpus solidum, tamquam speculū,lucem,calorem, cæteraque affecta pro natura vniusquiusq; planetæ aut syderis & coniunctione aut oppositione ipsorum inter se suam in his rebus inferioribus naturalem habeant influentiam. Hic transimus ad locu alterum de vsu ipsorū. Vsus autē à Deo exponitur his verbis, vt sint in signa &c. Atq; hic vsus (vt ex scq.verfib. perspicuē colligitur) proprie est triplex: lucis, præfecturæ in effectis suis, & distinctionis: quorū omniū genus à Mose ponitur his verbis, Sunt in signa: species vero officiorū huic generi subiectæ diuersō ordine proponuntur: nam primùm dominatus siue præfectura ipsorū designatur, hoc verbo In stata tempora: Secundo distinctiones notantur illis, in dies & annos: Tertio beneficium lucis ponitur, decimoquinto versu. At primùm quidē notandum illud est, ea non causas aut principia sed signa appellari: nā principiū est Deus agens in natura; Causa per se est ignis hæc signa afficiens; sydera verò sunt instrumēta significatia simpliciter & efficientia instrumentaliter: quo respectu signa appellantur. Signa sunt autē siue præfecta dispensationi & vicissitudini rerū annuarū per stata anni tempora; quemadmodū duobus locis Iobi, & apud Prophetam Amos, quatuor anni tempestates signis ceelestibus distinctæ sunt, & affectiones naturales illarū: Secundo signa sunt dierum & annorū, quibus & dies siue tempora, & anni ex diebus assurgetes distingui solent: Postremo signa sunt lucetia, lucémq; aëri & nobis per aërem fœnerantia. Quod autē aliis curiosis placet signa esse, non tantum affectionum ad res elementares communiter pertinentium, verum etiam rerum singularium extra ordinem contingentium, & ad animos motúsque voluntarios, ac non naturales solum pertinere, in primis autem qui in rebus humanis accidunt; ij ne vnum quidem iota ex Mose aut Prophetis afferre possunt ad sententiā illā iudiciariam confirmandam. Sunt enim signa instrumentalia solum communia ac naturalia: propterea non possunt res particulares, voluntarias, aut alias eiusmodi sua significatione efficere. Horum signorum constitutio ex mandato Dei tribuitur, ver. 16. & vsus per ὑσὶ ψαν demonstratur duobus scq. Id tamen est obseruandum cuius nomine Physici Matheologi Mosen iam olim traduxerunt; Signorum duas classes ponit: nam duo statuit Maxima in suo genere, & reliquas stellas seorsum: Maxima autem esse negant, ac proinde Mosen scientia rerum naturalium statuunt caruisse. Non vident autem res maximas appellari, nō secundū substantiam, verūm etiam secundū speciem ipsarum vel opinione nostram, & secundū efficacitatem. Qui ergo solem & lunam Maxima luminaria Moses appellauit, non respexit ad substantiam & quantitatem ipsorum in se, sed tum ad speciem illam secundum quam nobis talia videntur esse, tu ad actionem efficacitatemq; ipsorum. Nam vt alij planetæ sint maiores aliæque stellæ, tum sol respectu spectu omniū nobis, quamuis non in sese,luminare est maximū præ-sectum diei,& luna eadem ratione luminare maximum prefectum no-cti,sed minus tamē & quantitate substantiæ,& specie, & efficacitate, quàm sol.quapropter inique fallunt qui harū vocum praua interpre-tatione cupiunt Prophetæ Mosi illudere. His tandem rebus subiici-tur sua approbatio, confirmatio, & sanctio(vt ante diximus) v.18. & opus diei quarti ver.19.concluditur. Constitutis rebus superioribus Deus reliquo biduo animantes creauisse dicitur, legesque naturales eis indidisse:ac primùm quidē aëreas & aquaticas, die quinto;Dein-de verò terrenas,sexto.rerū aëriarū aquatiliūmque mandatum habe-tur v.20. effectus,21.probatio,confirmatio,& sanctio, v.21. extrema parte,& seq.ver.Animatium aquatilium species exponitur genere & differetia. Genere,quia appellatur anima viuens,i.animal:differentia, quia appellantur reptile siue natatile:Quibus addendum est proprium secundū ortū & sedem ipsorum:nempe quod ex aquis,in aquis,exun-dauerunt,& in eisdem versantur.Aëriarū similiter genus, differentiá-que specifica & proprium exponitur paucis, Genus est animal, quod ex præcedente membro [illegible, ~5 letters] repeti necesse est;differentia specifica est,volucris,appellatione coprehensa & determinata;proprii actione illius, cum iubetur volare supra terra , propriaq; circumscriptione se-dis quod versata sit in superficie expansi cæli. Atque hoc pacto facile soluuntur quæstiones illæ quæ vulgo adducuntur. Primùm vtrū sin-gulæ animantes istæ ex elemetis singulis constitutę sint, quod voluit Moses : Secundo vtrū volucres ex aquis,quod non dicit Moses,quā-uis plerique ante hæc tempora sic intellexerint. Nam horum corpo-ra ex compage elementari constant;sed ita tamē vt certa quædā ele-menta principatū in actu & in vita ipsorū obtineant.Quapropter etiā volucres,vt aereę,sunt omniū leuissimæ & minimo corpore:Aquati-lia verò propter lentorē elementi sui,etsi pro sua proportione leuissi-ma sunt,tum luxuriant maximè, & in varietate & valtitate illorū (vt verbis vtamur Plinij)natura quasi videtur ludere. Huius mandati ef-sectus sic ver.21.exponitur vt certo consilio Moses marinas illas bel-luas,quæ nobis portentosæ videntur esse,in creaturarū numeru retu-lerit: nequid forte tam magnū aut tam paruū dicatur esse quod nō sit opus creatoris Dei.His subiicitur approbatio,in fine ver.21.& ordina-tio,& sanctio de propaganda specie,ver. 22. Sanctione probati illius operis narrat Moses ver.22. Tu generatim, tu verò speciatim , prout animatib.aëriis & aquatilibus indicta est.Sactio summatim indicatur his verbis , Benedixit eis Deus dicendo. Speciatim verò exponitur, & tum aquatilibus tum etiā aëriis accōmodatur, verbis sequetibus cum Deus propagatione speciei per indiuidua fieri iubet. Propagationis autē causa est Dei benedictio, sine qua nullū indiuiduū possit subsistere, nedū similis procreatione propagationis. Propagationis autē ratio tribus modis exponitur: Primum quidem actione, vt animantes naturali ratione fœtificent: secundo effectu, vt fœtificatione illa per benedictionem Dei multiplicentur: Tertia consequente, vt aquatilia impleant aquas, non quidem omnes, sed eas quæ in suis alueis & conceptaculis sunt: quæ attributa etsi de piscibus solum enuntiatur, tamē etiam de volucribus intelligenda sunt synecdochicōs[?] secundum analogiam in sacris Scripturis frequentissimā: vt Moses indicat his verbis, Volucris multiplicetur in terra. Sic diei quinti historia concluditur noctis & lucis circumscriptione: Nempe quod de nocte aquatilia, de die aerea extiterint.
units.tr: The second part follows, concerning the creation by the Lord of the heavenly bodies, which pertain to the convenience of the dwelling and to its adornment, and concerning their use. This account is divided similarly into two parts: the command, at verses 14 and 15, and the effect of the command, from verse 16 onward. In the command, first the thing is set forth, and second the use and ordering of those heavenly things by God. The thing is stated in these words: Let there be lights in the expanse of the heavens. The use and ordering are stated in the following words: to make a distinction between day and night, and so on. Concerning the things which God commands by his command to exist, God pronounces two things. For he commands the thing to exist, and he fixes its place. The things are named in a general term, lights; the place is likewise named in general, in the expanse of the heavens. When they are called lights, it is less their substance that is regarded than their use. And although use arises from a power and consists in a relation, some substance must necessarily be posited. The philosophers differ about the substance. For some have wished them to be fiery; others, of the same matter as the heavens, but knotty and solid and not at all transparent, apart from the rest of the body of the heavens. I would readily concede this opinion, especially since in this place Moses seems to repeat the same order that we saw in the history of the preceding three days. For on the fourth day the ethereal and heavenly things are treated; on the fifth day the airy and aquatic things; on the sixth the terrestrial. To this substance, which we have established as solid, is added that affection by which, in view of that elementary fire which, during the preceding three days of creation, went about its powers without change together with the darkness, now at last it is so constituted that that solid body, like a mirror, reflects light, heat, and the other affections proper to the nature of each planet or star; and by their conjunction or opposition with one another they have their natural influence upon these lower things. Here we pass to the second point, concerning their use. Their use is set forth by God in these words: that they may be for signs, and so on. And this use (as is clearly gathered from the following verses) is properly threefold: of light, of rule over their effects, and of distinction. Moses sets down all of these under the general heading of these words, they are for signs; but the specific kinds of office placed under this genus are set out in a different order. For first their dominion or rule is designated by the phrase for fixed seasons; second, distinctions are noted by the phrases for days and years; third, the benefit of light is set down in the fifteenth verse. Now, first of all, it must be noted that these things are called not causes or principles but signs. For the principle is God acting in nature; the proximate cause is fire affecting these signs; the stars, however, are instruments that signify simply and effect instrumentally, and in this respect they are called signs. They are signs, moreover, both of the ordering and succession of annual things through the fixed seasons of the year, just as in two places of Job, and in the prophet Amos, the four seasons of the year are distinguished by heavenly signs, and their natural affections. Second, they are signs of days and years, by which both days or seasons and years, arising out of days, are customarily distinguished. Lastly, they are signs that shine and lend light to the air and, through the air, to us. As for the claim, which some curious persons like to make, that they are signs not only of affections common to elementary things, but also of particular things that happen outside the ordinary course, and that they pertain to voluntary and non-natural movements of minds, and especially to those things that happen in human affairs: these men cannot bring forward even one iota from Moses or the Prophets to confirm that judgment. For the instrumental signs are only common and natural; therefore they cannot by their signification bring about particular and voluntary things, or others of that kind. The establishment of these signs is attributed to God's command, at verse 16, and their use is demonstrated by the word [ὑσὶ ψαν] in the two following verses. Yet this must be observed, a point on which the physicists and mathematicians have long since criticized Moses: he sets up two classes of signs, for he establishes two greatest in their kind, and the remaining stars apart. But they deny that these are the greatest, and therefore they claim that Moses lacked knowledge of natural things. They do not see, however, that things are called greatest not only according to their substance, but also according to their appearance to us, which is our opinion, and according to their efficacy. Therefore, when Moses called the sun and moon the greatest lights, he did not regard their substance and quantity in themselves, but both that appearance according to which such things seem to us to be, and their action and efficacy. For although other planets are larger and other stars, yet the sun, with respect to the view of all of us, although not in itself, is the greatest light to rule the day; and the moon, by the same reasoning, is the greatest light to rule the night, but less in quantity of substance, in appearance, and in efficacy than the sun. Wherefore those men act unjustly who, by a perverse interpretation of these words, desire to mock the prophet Moses. Finally, these things are followed by their approval, confirmation, and sanction (as we said before) at verse 18, and the work of the fourth day, verse 19, is concluded. With the higher things established, God is said to have created living creatures in the remaining two days, and to have implanted in them natural laws; and first, indeed, the airy and aquatic ones, on the fifth day; then, however, the terrestrial, on the sixth. The command concerning the airy and aquatic creatures is found at verse 20; the effect, at verse 21; the approval, confirmation, and sanction, at the end of verse 21 and the following verse. The species of aquatic creatures is set forth by genus and difference. By genus, because they are called a living soul, that is, animal; by difference, because they are called creeping or swimming things. To these must be added their proper character according to origin and dwelling: namely, that they have come forth out of the waters, in the waters, and live in them. Similarly, the genus, specific difference, and proper character of the airy creatures are set forth briefly. The genus is animal, which must be repeated from the preceding member [illegible, about five letters]; the specific difference is bird, a name which comprehends and determines it; their proper action is when they are commanded to fly above the earth; and their proper circumscription of place is that they move on the surface of the expanse of heaven. And in this way those questions which are commonly raised are easily resolved. First, whether these living creatures were each constituted from the individual elements, which Moses intended; second, whether birds were made from the waters, which Moses does not say, although many before this time have so understood it. For their bodies consist of an elementary composition; but in such a way that certain elements hold the principal place in their activity and life. For this reason birds, as airy creatures, are the lightest of all and of the smallest body; while aquatic creatures, on account of the viscosity of their element, although in their proportion they are very light, nevertheless flourish most, and in the variety and bulk of them (to use the words of Pliny) nature seems as it were to play. The effect of this command is set forth at verse 21 in such a way that Moses, by deliberate design, has counted among the number of creatures those sea monsters which seem to us portentous, lest anything perhaps be said to be so great or so small that it is not a work of the Creator God. To this is added the approval at the end of verse 21, and the ordering and sanction concerning the propagation of the species, at verse 22. Moses relates the sanction of that approved work at verse 22: both generally and specially, as it was declared to the airy and aquatic creatures. The sanction is indicated in summary by these words: God blessed them, saying. It is set forth specifically, and is adapted both to the aquatic and to the airy creatures, in the following words, when God commands the propagation of the species through individuals. The cause of propagation is God's blessing, without which no individual could subsist, much less the like generation of propagation. The manner of propagation is set forth in three ways: first, by the action, that the creatures may be fruitful by natural means; second, by the effect, that through that fruitfulness, by God's blessing, they may be multiplied; third, as a consequence, that the aquatic creatures may fill the waters, not indeed all waters, but those which are in their channels and receptacles. Although this attribute is stated only of fish, it must nevertheless be understood also of birds, by synecdoche, according to the most frequent analogy in the Holy Scriptures, as Moses indicates in these words: Let the bird be multiplied on the earth. Thus the history of the fifth day is concluded with the circumscription of night and light: namely, that the aquatic creatures came forth by night, and the airy by day.

units.la: Sequitur historia diei sexti à ver.25.ad 28. Nam reliquos versus ad finem capitis, appendiculam esse omnibus animantibus communem suo loco demonstrabimus. Est autem diei sexti historia de creatione terrestrium animantiū: primum quidem earum quæ rationis expertes sunt, ver.24. & seq. Deinde verò hominis ratione præditi, ver.26. & seqq. In brutorum creatione similiter mandatum & exsecquutio ponitur singulis versibus: Nam primum mandato iubetur terra pro-ducere tamquam ex vtero suo animantes, quod genus est, secundo species animantium distinguuntur in tres classes: quarum prima est in-mentorum siue mansuetorum & cicurum animatium, secunda serpentiū humiliūmque, tertia denique ferarum bestiarum quæ non domos no-stras sed agrum liberum solent incolere: Quapropter bestiæ agri hic & in scripturis passim appellantur. Quod autē has animantes iubetur terra producere, id eodem modo intelligendum est quem supra in ver.20. expositum. Huius mandati effectus primum in genere sub finem ver.24. Deinde in specie ponitur ver.25. suaq; approbatio, & confirmatio, & sanctio adiicitur: quę omnia iam ante satis explicauimus.
units.tr: The history of the sixth day follows, from verse 25 to 28. For we will show in its proper place that the remaining verses, to the end of the chapter, are an appendix common to all living creatures. The history of the sixth day concerns the creation of land animals: first of those that lack reason (verse 24 and following), then of man, who is endowed with reason (verse 26 and following). In the creation of the beasts, command and execution are set out in individual verses. First, by command, the earth is bidden to bring forth the living creatures as from its womb; this is the genus. Second, the species of living creatures are distinguished into three classes. The first is of cattle, that is, tame and domesticated animals; the second of creeping things and low-lying animals; the third, finally, of wild beasts, which are accustomed to inhabit not our homes but the open field. Therefore they are called beasts of the field here and throughout the Scriptures. As for the fact that the earth is bidden to bring forth these creatures, this is to be understood in the same way as explained above at verse 20. The effect of this command is set out first in general at the end of verse 24, and then in particular at verse 25; and his approval, confirmation and sanction are added. All of this we have already sufficiently explained.

units.la: Sequitur alterius membri historia, de creatione hominis: in qua primum consilium ver.26. Secundo opus & effectus, 27. Postremo autē sanctio v.28. exponitur. In consilio primū videndū est quis apud quē consiliū capiat atque deliberet, secundo quodnam sit consilij huius argumentum. De priore quæstione dicit Moses, Et dixit Elohim. Cuius loquutionis triplex est potissimum interpretatio. Prima est quā Iudæi defendunt appellatione Elohim significari [illegible, ~4 letters] Deū (vt loquitur) essentialiter, citra contemplationē personarū in vnitate essentiæ. Itaq; alij Deū cum Angelis, alij cū elementis, alij cum vniuersita-te mundi loquutū putant: alij ipsum secum; qua etiā ratione Cyrillus contra Iulianum loquutus est, sed non euersa propterea distinctione personarum in vnitate essentiæ Dei. Sed hæc interpretatio, quia implicatam habet tacitè aduersariorū sententiā, iamdiu explosa est. Secunda interpretatio eorū est qui interpretantur, dixit Elohim, dixerūt sin gulæ personæ inter se, i. Pater Filio & S.S. vicissimq; Filius Patri & S.S. & illis S.S. quæ interpretatio minimè est mala, & nititur propria vocis Elohim significatione, vt ante docuimus. Tertia deniq; interpretatio eorū est, qui propter verbū Dixit sing. numeri iudicat hic proprie Deū Patrem intelligi oportere, tamquā principiū omnis sapientiæ, sermonis & consilij: itaque personam Patris hæc verba Filio & Sp. sancto enuntiauisse: quam interpretationem Sirmiensis Synodus maximè probauit omniū. Re vera tamen hę duæ postremæ, etsi in modo interpretationis diuersæ sunt, re ipsa vnum sunt. Nam & Pater hoc consilium cepit tamquam principium & Filium, & S. sanctum vnā cum Patre hoc idem dixisse, id est, decretum hoc enuntiauisse nemo pius potest dubitare: atque ita secundam interpretationem à Cyrillo probatam esse in eo loco quem ante dicebamus res ipsa loquitur.
units.tr: Next follows the history of the other member, the creation of man. In it, first the counsel is set out (verse 26), second the work and its effect (27), and finally the sanction (28). In the counsel, we must first see who takes counsel and deliberates, and second what is the subject of this counsel. On the first question Moses says, "And Elohim said." There are chiefly three interpretations of this utterance. The first is that which the Jews defend: by the name Elohim is signified God (as they put it) essentially, without regard to the persons, in the unity of essence. Hence some think God spoke with the angels, others with the elements, others with the whole universe, and others with himself. Cyril spoke in this sense against Julian, but without thereby overturning the distinction of persons in the unity of the essence of God. However, since this interpretation tacitly contains the opinion of the adversaries, it has long since been exploded. The second interpretation is that of those who read "Elohim said" as: the persons said these things to one another, that is, the Father to the Son and Holy Spirit, and in turn the Son to the Father and Holy Spirit, and they to the Holy Spirit. This interpretation is by no means bad, and rests on the proper signification of the word Elohim, as we taught above. The third interpretation is that of those who, on account of the singular verb "said," judge that here God the Father must properly be understood, as the principle of all wisdom, speech and counsel; so that the Person of the Father uttered these words to the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Synod of Sirmium most of all approved this interpretation. In truth, however, these last two, though different in manner of interpretation, are in fact one. That the Father took this counsel as the principle, and that the Son and the Holy Spirit together with the Father said the same thing, that is, pronounced this decree, no pious person can doubt. Thus the second interpretation, approved by Cyril in the passage we mentioned above, is borne out by the matter itself.

units.la: Sequitur iam argumentum huius consilij: in quo tres illæ personæ in vnitate essentiæ Dei proponūt sibi faciedum[?] hominem, & de eo prædicant primum quidem nomen speciei: secundò differentiam specificam illius: tertio proprium, quod homini propter singularem ipsius dignitatem à Deo creatore fuit attributum.
units.tr: There follows now the subject of this counsel.
