In it, those three persons, in the unity of the essence of God, propose to make man, and predicate of him: first, the name of the species; second, his specific difference; third, the property which God the Creator attributed to man on account of his singular dignity.

units.la: Specie enuntiauit Deus hominis appellatione, quę species sub animante comprehenditur. Speciem autem hoc nomine intelligi oportere ipse Moses oftedit hoc & sequentib. verf. cum hoc versu dicat, dominentur, & seq. dicat marem & fœminam creauit illos: ex quo sequitur hanc hominis appellationem syllepticam esse, vel speciei ac non indiuidui vnius appellationem: Differētia specifica hominis duabus vocibus exprimitur, In imagine nostra & secundum similitudinem nostram: quæ voces aliis numero tantum differre videntur, aliis & numero & ratione simul. Qui numero & ratione differre putant, alij in homine putant distingui res spirituales à corporalibus quæ in homine sunt: alij res spirituales solùm, nempe facultates animæ inter se, & qualitates intellectus voluntatisque nostræ: alij deniq; nomine imaginis typum siue idæam (platonici) Nomine verò similitudinis τὴν ἐκτύπον[?], id est, similitudinem quam typus expresserit. Nobis differre videntur hæ voces tantum numero, quod cum seq. versu Moses videtur confirmare, cum dicit ad imaginem Dei creauit illum, tum principio cap.5. & cap.9. verf.7. Significatur autem hæc vtraque appellatione specifica hominis differētia cū subiecto singulari ipsius, id est, anima humana praedita diuinis qualitatibus, quae in veritate, sanctitate, iustitiaque positae sunt, vt loquitur Apostolus ad Eph.4. Nam veritas simplicitatem, sanctitas pietate, iustitia humanitatis officia complectitur, quorum principiis, feminibusque ab omni macula & labe alienis homo ille a creatione est instructus in intellectu & voluntate ipsius: etsi hę perfectiones hominis, prout inde a principio fuerat conditus, si cum iustitia, sanctitate & veritate Dei comparentur, non merentur eam appellationem, sed tantum eam obtinent analogica aequiuocatione. Hoc autem subiectum adeo praecellente differentia in creatione a Deo exornatum, etiam proprio suo singulari fuit accumulatum diuinitus, cum non solum corpus praestante forma praeceteris animatibus huic animae aptatum est, verumetiam dignitas, ius, atque auctoritas supra has res omnes creatas attributa. Hoc proprium altera parte versus definitur, dicendo, Et dominentur in piscesq, &c. Nam prout a natura praestantiora quaeque dominium obtinent, ita praestantiae hominis inter has res creatas dominatu tribui oportuit; qui dominatus duas partes continet. Primum enim dominatus est in animantes caeteras: Secundo in sedem & domicilium commune omnium.
units.tr: God named man with the appellation of man, which species is comprehended under animal. That Moses himself means the species by this name he shows in this and the following verses: he says "let them have dominion," and so on, and then says "male and female he created them." From this it follows that this appellation of man is a syllepsis, or the name of the species and not of one individual. The specific difference of man is expressed by two words: "in our image and according to our likeness." Some think these words differ only in number, others both in number and in meaning. Those who think they differ in number and meaning hold various views. Some think that in man spiritual things are distinguished from the corporeal things that are in him. Others think only spiritual things are meant, namely the faculties of the soul among themselves, and the qualities of our intellect and will. Others finally understand by the name image the type or idea (the Platonists), and by the name likeness the impression [τὴν ἐκτύπωσιν], that is, the likeness which the type has impressed. To us these words seem to differ only in number, as Moses seems to confirm with the following verse, where he says "he created him in the image of God," and at the beginning of chapter 5 and in chapter 9, verse 7. Both appellations signify the specific difference of man together with his singular subject, that is, the human soul endowed with divine qualities, which are placed in truth, holiness and righteousness, as the Apostle says in Ephesians 4. For truth embraces simplicity, holiness embraces piety, and righteousness the duties of humanity. In the principles and seeds of these, free from all stain and blemish, that man was furnished from creation in his intellect and will. Yet these perfections of man, as he had been formed from the beginning, do not deserve that name when compared with the righteousness, holiness and truth of God; they hold it only by analogical equivocation. This subject, adorned by God in creation with such an excelling difference, was also heaped with his own proper singular gift from God. For not only was a body fitted to this soul with a form surpassing the other animals, but dignity, right and authority were also attributed above all these created things. This property is defined in the second part of the verse, by saying "and let them have dominion over the fish," and so on. For as the more excellent things by nature hold dominion, so the pre-eminence of man among these created things ought to be given dominion. This dominion contains two parts. First, it is dominion over the other animals; second, over the seat and dwelling common to all.

units.la: Dominatus in animates caeteras ab enumeratione partium ostenditur his verbis, in pisces maris, & in volucres caeli, & in bestias. In sedem vero & domicilium dominatus traditur illis verbis, & in vniuersam terram. Quibus subiicitur generalis quaedam attributio, & in omne reptile quod reptat super terram, id est, deniq; in ea omnia siue magna siue parua quae sidunt aut pedem ponunt in hominis habitatione. Proprium appellamus istud, ne quis forte cum Chrysostomo iudicet imaginem similitudinemque Dei in eo fuisse positam. Nam imago illa intus in anima est. Illius imaginis autem proprium attributum hominis competens est dominatus ille coniunctus diuina imagine. Huius instituti effectus ponitur verf. 27. cum dicitur, creauit Deus hominem ad imaginem ipsius. quia vero in hac locutione duo queri poterant: Vnum ad cuius imaginem Dei aut hominis; alterum, quem? virumne solum? an virum & foeminam coniunctim? propterea vtrumque ambiguu seqq. verbis dissoluit Moses, non τα ντολης sed ἑξηγηματικως. Nam ad quaestionem priore subiicit, ad imaginem Dei creauit ipsum. qua solutione opus fuit propter ambiguitate Hebraei relatiui, quod promiscue relatiuum aut reciprocum est: Ad alteram subiicit illa, Marem & foeminam creauit eos, quia vox Ada dicitur aequiuoce, potuitque solum de protoplaste homine accipi, cui nome fuit Ada, aut de specie συνθετικως, id est, de viro & foemina. Hic vero duo tenenda sunt: vnum, Trinitatem personarum in vnitate essentiae demonstrari: Alterum, hoc ipso die virum & fœminam creatos esse, etsi cap. seq. res fusius traditur ἐξηγητικῶς[?]. Vnitatem essentiæ demonstrant ista verf.26. dixit Elohim,& 27. creauit Elohim ad imaginem ipsius. Trinitatem vero personarum ostendunt ista, dixit Elohim faciamus, deinde, Ad imaginem nostram, & secundum similitudinem nostram. Nam quod Hebræi putant vocē Na-hasse, faciamus, non futuri esse, sed participij, ludunt in re seria, maximè cum videant subsequi voces plurales proximè. Quod autem alij hunc sermonem ad Angelos, alij ad elementa, alij ad alia haberi putant, id iam ante refellimus, nec vllo pacto cum Dei creatoris gloria conuenit. quod denique pluralem numerū honoris causa confirmat adhiberi, id Hebræi quidē in secūda & tertia persona receperunt: sed in prima persona nullum vsquā exemplū legitur, vbi singulare aliquid indiuiduum de se loquatur in prima persona plurali numero, prout Aben Ezra in Genes. 1. & 30. obseruauit doctissimè. Huic creationi sua sanctio & confirmatio subiicitur, ver.28. quā Moses vniuersè benedicendi verbo complexus est. Postea reliqua minutatim reliquo versu explicauit. Eius autem benedictionis ad conseruationem propagationemq; speciei pertinentis loci duo sunt à Deo indicati; prior de incolarum propagatione, posterior de vsu domicilij, & rerum in domicilio eodē commorantium. Propagatione designant hęc verba, fœtificate & multiplicate & implete terram, Auctoritate vsumque tum domicilij expressit Moses his verbis, & subigite eam, Tum rerum in eodem domicilio agentium, illis, & dominamini in pisces maris.
units.tr: Dominion over the other animals is shown from the enumeration of the parts by these words: "over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heaven, and over the beasts." Dominion over the seat and dwelling is given in these words: "and over the whole earth." To these is added a general attribution: "and over every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth." That is, finally, over all those things, great or small, that sit or set foot in the habitation of man. We call this a property, lest anyone perhaps judge with Chrysostom that the image and likeness of God was placed in it. For that image is within, in the soul. The proper attribute of that image belonging to man is this dominion, joined to the divine image. The effect of this institution is set out in verse 27, where it is said: "God created man in his own image." But since two questions could arise from this expression, first, in whose image, God's or man's; and second, which man, the male only or male and female together, Moses resolves both ambiguities in the following words, not by command [ἐπιταγῇ] but by explanation [ἐξηγηματικῶς]. To the first question he adds, "in the image of God he created him." This solution was needed because of the ambiguity of the Hebrew relative, which is used indiscriminately as relative or reciprocal. To the second he adds, "male and female he created them," because the word Adam is used equivocally: it could be taken of the first man alone, to whom the name Adam was given, or of the species compositively, that is, of man and woman. Here, however, two things are to be held. One is that the Trinity of persons in the unity of essence is demonstrated; the other is that male and female were created on this same day, although the next chapter sets the matter out more fully by explanation [ἐξηγητικῶς]. The unity of essence is shown by verse 26, "Elohim said," and verse 27, "Elohim created in his own image." The Trinity of persons is shown by "Elohim said, let us make," and then "in our image, and according to our likeness." For the Hebrews think that the word Na-hasse [נַעֲשֶׂה], "let us make," is not future but participial. This is trifling in a serious matter, especially since they see plural words following immediately. As for others who think this speech is addressed to the angels, or to the elements, or to other things, we have already refuted this, and it in no way agrees with the glory of God the Creator. Finally, the plural is used to confirm honour. The Hebrews indeed accept this in the second and third persons, but no example is anywhere read in the first person where a single individual speaks of himself in the first person plural, as Aben Ezra very learnedly observed on Genesis 1 and 30. To this creation its sanction and confirmation is added in verse 28, which Moses embraced generally in the word of blessing. Afterwards, in the remaining verse, he explained the rest in detail. Two places of that blessing, pertaining to the conservation and propagation of the species, were indicated by God: the first concerns the propagation of the inhabitants, the second the use of the dwelling and of the things dwelling in the same habitation. The propagation is designated by these words: "be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth." Moses expressed the authority and use of the dwelling by the words "and subdue it," and of the things acting in the same dwelling by those, "and have dominion over the fish of the sea."

units.la: Hactenus creatio rerum omnium: sequitur loco appendicis constitutio earum rerum quæ ad conseruationem indiuiduorum inde à Principio pertinent. Earum duo sunt genera; nam aliæ sunt quasi mediantes, id est, instrumetales & secundariæ: aliæ verò summæ, summę, sum-múmque gradum in rerum conseruatione obtinentes. Mediates sunt (vt ita loquamur) alimeta de quib. ver.29. & sequentibus. post sequitur Dei approbatio, confirmatio, & sanctio, in verf. vltimo. Alimentorū duplex ordo constituitur, quę omnia die tertio iam fuerant prouisa, antequam homo & animantes cæteræ conderentur. Primus ordo alimentorum est homini attributus, ver.29. quem præsente vocabulo ecce quasi iam ante prouisum præbitúmque homini tradit Deus, dicendo dedi vobis: Alimenti humani duo constituuntur genera: vnum herbarum, alterum fructuum qui ex arboribus colliguntur. Alimēti verò quod animatibus cæteris præbetur à Domino ordo est vnicus, nempe viriditas herba, siue gramen terram vestiens, quo pabulo acquiescebant animantes brutæ & innocente victu vtebantur, ver.30. Summa verò conseruationis causa in versu vltimo adhibetur, nimirum approbatio, confirmatio, & sanctiǫ[?] naturæ rerum, qualem in singulis fermè singulorum dierum historiis meminimus ante adhiberi, tamen eo discrimen est, quòd in locis superioribus de approbatione,confirmatione,&sanctione vnius alicuius generis agebatur; hic verò de omnibus simul in tota rerū vniuersitate. Itaque vt hos locos euidētius distinguamus,sic paucis statuimus, res omnes à Deo creatas in hac rerum vniuersitate singulariter,atque communiter respectu ipsarū in se, & inter se bonas tripliciter appellari, specie,modo, & ordine: in se quidem specie, quatenus sunt: modo , quatenus sunt vt sunt: inter se verò, quatenus ordine naturæ aliæ ad alias referuntur & suam habent conuenientiam. Quæcunque autem res ante fuerunt appellatæ bonæ, sic fuerunt appellatæ respectu ipsarum in se,nempe quòd specie modóque bonę essent, quâ subsistunt in natura rerum & sunt eiusmodi: Quæ autem hîc de approbatione, confirmatione,& sanctione rerum omniū in vniuersitate hac prædicantur, ea non solùm de specie & modo dici, verùm etiā de ordine , quo res singulæ aliæ ad alias relationem suam,& aliæ ex aliis affectionem habent: deniq; sapientissimè inter se ordinatę sunt. Atq; hanc esse loci istius sententiam verba Mosis demonstrat luculentissimè, qui pro eo quod dixerat ante, vidit Deus esse bonum, nimirū hoc aut illud de quo proximè agebatur supra, nunc demum propositione vniuersalem efficit, Vidit Deus omne quod fecerat, & affirmationem vehementiorem adhibet, Ecce bonum erat valde.
units.tr: Thus far the creation of all things. In the place of an appendix follows the establishment of those things which, from the beginning, pertain to the preservation of individual creatures. These are of two kinds. Some are, as it were, intermediate, that is, instrumental and secondary. Others are the highest, holding the highest rank in the preservation of things. The intermediate ones are (so to speak) the foods, concerning which he speaks in verse 29 and following. After them comes God's approval, confirmation, and sanction, in the last verse. Two orders of food are set out, all of which had already been provided on the third day, before man and the other animals were created. The first order of food is assigned to man, in verse 29. God hands it over to him as already provided and ready, using the word behold, and saying I have given you. Two kinds of human food are established: one of herbs, the other of fruits gathered from trees. The food given by the Lord to the other animals is of a single order, namely the green herb, or the grass covering the earth, on which the animals that graze were content and lived on innocent fare, verse 30. The highest cause of preservation is introduced in the last verse, namely the approval, confirmation, and sanction of the nature of things. We recall that something similar was introduced in the histories of almost each of the individual days. Yet there is this difference: in the earlier places the approval, confirmation, and sanction concerned one particular kind of thing, whereas here it concerns all things together in the whole universe of things. Therefore, to distinguish these passages more clearly, we lay down briefly that all things created by God in this universe are called good in three ways, both singly and collectively, with respect to themselves and to one another: in species, in mode, and in order. In species they are good insofar as they exist; in mode, insofar as they exist as they do; and among themselves, insofar as by the order of nature some are referred to others and have their own fitting relation. Whatever things were called good before were so called with respect to themselves, namely because they were good in species and mode, by which they subsist in the nature of things and are of such a kind. But what is here affirmed of approval, confirmation, and sanction of all things in this universe is said not only of species and mode, but also of the order by which individual things have their relation to others and receive their affection from one another; and finally, they are most wisely arranged among themselves. That this is the meaning of this passage is shown most clearly by the words of Moses. In place of what he had said before, God saw that it was good, namely this or that thing of which he had just been speaking above, he now at last makes a universal statement, God saw everything that he had made, and adds a stronger affirmation, Behold, it was very good.

units.la: CAPITIS II. ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER II. ANALYSIS.

units.la: EXPOSITA rerum omnium , ac in primis Ecclesiæ generatione,quam visum est Deo ex humano genere colligere,sequitur constitutio illius,primum quidē prout integra fuit constituta à Domino cap.2. Deinde verò prout facto suo corrupta est,capite 3. Finis itaque 2.ca. est vt Ecclesiæ integræ,ex qua defecimus,conditionem recordemur. Summa verò,Deum facto exemploque suo Ecclesiam integram con-stituisse , atque docuisse vt in sua vocatione temporali ac spirituali, secundum ordinem à Deo constitutum, permaneret in hac sociabili vita. Huius itaque capitis partes omnino duę sunt: Nam primum sex versus in narratione exempli & facti à Domino cōsumuntur. Dein-de vero reliquum caput in Ecclesiæ constitutione exponenda, quam Deus exemplo factoque suo statuerat. Prior locus per modum con-clusionis clufionis à Mose proponitur,cum diei septimi quies, benedictio & sanctificatio narratur, tribus versibus: deinde creatarum modus, tribus alteris. prior illa pars de quiete ac sanctificatione diei septimi primū occasionem continet verf. 1. quod cæli & terra cum toto exercitu vel instrumento ipsorum absoluti effent, eáque Deus omnia haberet absoluta in die septimo,principio 2. versus : Secundo quietem vel cessatione ab operatione creationis,altera parte fecūdi versus: Postremo autem benedictionem diei illius septimi, quo Deus tamquā in suo opere acquiescens benedixit diei illi præ cæteris eúmque sanctificauit in Ecclesia sua,ut sanctus ab ea haberetur coleretūrq;ex instituto ipsius:quod institutum Deus partim exeplo suo ac cessatione , partimque institutione in Ecclesia comprobauit, ut Adam & Eua (qui tunc viuebant) eum diem sanctum ex institutione Dei agnoscerent. Vnum lectores obseruent, optimè Mosen opus fuftentationis & conseruationis , id est,prouidétię,ab opere creationis distinguere 2.verf. Nam prouidétiam sustentantem ac regentem omnes res creatas,testatur Moses illis verbis,Cum itaque absolutum haberet Deus die septimo opus fuū quod fecerat: creationem vero & cessationem à creando tradit fequētibus, cessauit die septimo ab omni opere suo quod fecit, vel, quod faceret. Posterior locus est summa ἀνακεφαλαίωσις [?] illius creationis,quam Moses præcedente capite proposuerat ad institutā narratione de Ecclesia μετάβασις [?]: nam in hac summa ἐπανακεφαλαιώσει [?] primum ordinem creationis; fecūdò, modum summatim Moses explicauit.Ordinem creationis quem tripartitum esse præcedente capite docuimus,Moses perstringit paucis: nam primum creationem principiorum naturalium primo die facta perstringit his verbis, Hæ sunt generationes, id est, ortus,ac velut cunabula cæli & terra,id est circumferetię & centri, & omniū quę sunt in eis. Secundo dispositionem istorum principiorum ex elementari ordine, quem die primo, fecundo & tertio creationis demonstrauimus,percurrit Moses illis verbis,quo die fecit Iehoua Deus terram & cælum. Vbi obseruandum est ordine præpostero terrā & cælum nominari, tantū iudicio meo,causa ἀτοπίας [?]. Tertiò creatione rerum elementarium fynecdochicæs percurrit Moses,destringes solùm opus corporū elementariū diei tertij quæ terra progenuit: tū quia ex hoc principio de cæteris cōpofitis facilè iudicaturi fuerūt boni,tū quia huius generis creaturarū recefio maximè ad sequentę hiftoriapertinebat, fiue de modo creationis quæsiueris , quē Deus fermè immediate seruari per omnia voluit,fiue deEcclefię inter homines domicilio,ut postea exponitur inde à v. 7. Modū verò creationis quē Deus non solū in principiorū & elementorū constitutione, verū etiam in compositorum corporū
units.tr: Having set out the generation of all things, and especially of the Church, which God was pleased to gather from the human race, there follows its constitution. This is first, as it was established whole by the Lord, in chapter 2, and then as it was corrupted by man's act, in chapter 3. The aim of chapter 2 is therefore that we should recall the condition of the whole Church, from which we have fallen. Its summary is that God, by his example and deed, constituted the Church whole, and taught it to remain in this sociable life in its temporal and spiritual calling, according to the order established by God. The parts of this chapter are therefore wholly two. First, six verses are spent on the narrative of the example and deed of the Lord. Second, the rest of the chapter sets out the constitution of the Church, which God had established by his example and deed. The first passage is put forward by Moses in the manner of a conclusion, when in three verses he narrates the rest, blessing and sanctification of the seventh day. Then, in three further verses, he describes the manner of creation. The first part, on the rest and sanctification of the seventh day, contains first the occasion, in verse 1: that heaven and earth were finished with all their host or equipment, and that God had all these things finished on the seventh day. Second, at the beginning of verse 2, comes the rest or cessation from the work of creation. Last, in the other part of verse 2, comes the blessing of that seventh day, on which God, as resting in his work, blessed that day above the others and sanctified it in his Church, so that it should be regarded as holy by the Church and kept according to his own ordinance. God confirmed this ordinance partly by his example and cessation, and partly by an institution in the Church, so that Adam and Eve, who were then living, would acknowledge that day as holy by the institution of God. Readers should note that Moses, in verse 2, rightly distinguishes the work of sustaining and preserving, that is, providence, from the work of creation. For Moses bears witness to providence, which sustains and governs all created things, in the words, "Therefore, when God had finished on the seventh day his work which he had made." He delivers creation and the cessation from creating in the following words: "He ceased on the seventh day from all his work which he had made, or which he was to make." The second passage is a summary recapitulation [ἀνακεφαλαίωσις] of that creation, which Moses had set out in the preceding chapter, and a transition [μετάβασις] to the narrative about the Church. For in this summary recapitulation [ἐπανακεφαλαιώσει] Moses explains, first, the order of creation, and second, its manner, in brief. He touches briefly on the order of creation, which we showed in the preceding chapter to be threefold. First, he touches on the creation of the natural principles, made on the first day, in these words: "These are the generations," that is, the origins, and as it were the cradles, "of heaven and earth," that is, of the circumference and the centre, and of all that is in them. Second, he runs through the disposition of these principles according to the elemental order, which we showed in the first, second and third days of creation, in the words, "On the day when Iehovah God made earth and heaven." Here it must be observed that earth and heaven are named in a reversed order, in my judgment only for the sake of an unusual effect [ἀτοπίας]. Third, he runs through the creation of the elemental things by synecdoche, touching only on the work of the elemental bodies of the third day, which the earth brought forth. This is both because the good readers would easily judge the other composite things from this principle, and because the account of this kind of creature pertained especially to the following history, whether you ask about the manner of creation, which God willed to be preserved almost immediately in all things, or about the dwelling of the Church among men, as is explained afterwards from verse 7 onwards. The manner of creation which God willed to preserve not only in the constitution of principles and elements, but also in the case of composite bodies, Moses describes by the removal [περιώρισεν], or, as they call it, the removal of all those things which pertain in this universe to the generation of elemental bodies.

units.la: ratione seruare voluit, describit Moses περιώρισεν siue remotione (vt vocant) eorū omnium quę ad genituram corporum elementarium in hac vniuersitate pertinent. Remotio autem mediorū est duplex. nam primum terræ tamquam matri ex vtero suo profundenti facultas profundendi adimitur his verbis, Nondum fuisset futurus in terra frutex, nondum effloruisset. secundò, remouetur omnia foris accedentia ad commoditatem genituræ illius. Nimirum pluuię quam Deus in terrā solet defundere: culturæ quam homo adhibere, & roris siue vaporis e terra prorumpentis, quo irrigaretur superficies terræ. Ac proinde remotis omnibus illis internis externisq; mediis quibus gignentia terræ producuntur, ostendit Moses solam vim creatoris Dei fuisse auctorem cur tum arbores, herbæ, fruticesque die tertio crearentur, cū reliqua dierum sequentiū opera, quæ nunc secundum naturæ ordinē à Deo constitutū interuenientibus mediis proferuntur. Alterius partis, qua Ecclesiæ integræ exponitur status, duo sunt omnino loci. Vnus est de natura hominis, ex quo Ecclesia constat; Alter de vocatione: Nam hominis pro ratione ortus describit Moses v.7. Cui adiunctū perpetuum est locus, quem locū singulare prisce illi integræque Ecclesiæ Deus tribuerat, quèadmodū inde ad v.15. exponitur. Vocationis locus à Mose traditur inde à v.15.ad finem vsq; capitis. Naturale igitur hominis cōstitutione demōstrat ortus, modus, & partes illius. Ortum attribuit Moses formationi Iehoua, qua voce singulare ortus humani modū præ creaturis reliquis declarauit, respicies ad copiosiorem illā historiā quæ cap.1.v.26.& seq. fuit expositā. Partes verò essentiales hominis, ex quibus persona humana est constituta, ponuntur duę; primū materia, puluis e terra: quā materiā coagmentauit fermentauitq; Dominus ad creationē viri. Deinde formam ἀνθρώπου, i. immateriatā, nimirū mentem siue animam hominis vitalem, quā Deus in nares illius inspiravit. Atque hac ratione animam hominis ab animantium cæterarū anima discreuit Deus, cum subsistere humanam, reliquarū animantiū qualitatiuam (vt Scholastici loquuntur) animam esse ostenderit: Humanam subiectum per se, cæterarum animantium in subiecto. Ex hac compositione illud consequitur quod postea adiecit Moses, hominem fuisse in animam viuentem. i. corpus illius ab anima fuisse hac lege animatum vt anima viuens esset, sed quæ mori posset. Non autem viuificans, quæ morte ipsa per se depelleret, prout commodissime Apostolus interpretatur 1. Cor.15. Huic subiecto suus locus deinde tribui tur versibus seqq. ex cuius tamquā domicilij dignitate, hominis tamquā incolæ dignitas colligenda est. Nam etsi homo posset communis illius domicilij fuit quod animantibus omnibus attribuit Deus, tamen particulare domicilium ipsi amplius voluit attribuere, tamquā regi in res creatas cæteras dominanti palatium suū. Huius palatij cōditio primum generatim v. 8: deinde speciatim, sequentibus explicatur. Describitur autē primum a forma, quōd hortus circumclusus & circumseptus fuerit; Secundo a loco & situ, quōd fuerit in Hedene, i. regione deliciarum, quam Ptolemæus vocat Audanitida siue Auranitida in Babylonia & quidem in Orientali vel anteriore parte illius, quæ amœnissima fuit totius Orientis, ut Plinij utamur verbis; Tertiō, Instrumento illius horti, quod Deus hortum illum plantis conseuerit singulari ratione præ terra reliqua, ubi hominem quem finxerat collocaret. Hæc tria Moses sequetibus versibus exponit ὑστέρῳ[?] ὑπερῷῳ[?]; Ornatum, v. 9. Loci commoditatem v. 10. & tribus seqq. Formam denique v. 14. Instrumentum horti describit Moses his verbis, fecit itaque Iehoua Deus ut efflorescceret; cuius instrumenti duo sunt genera; commune, ad communem usum; singulare, ad singularem destinatum. Communis est omnis arbor desiderabilis ad aspectum & bona ad cibum, id est arbor tam voluptaria quam ad fructum vitæ necessarium pertinens. Singulare instrumentū est duplex: arbor vitæ in horto, & arbor scientiæ boni & mali. Singulare est, non natura sua, sed instituto Dei. Instituit autem hæc Deus, tum ut hominem præsentis suæ conditionis admoneret, tum ut de futura ex hypothesi faceret certiorē. Præsens hominis conditio fuit libertas (ut vocant) arbitrij, siue potentia naturalis adhærendi bono, cuius symbolum arbor vitæ fuit, siue declinandi ad malū, cuius symbolum arbor scientiæ, &c. Atque hæc symbola sic hominem excitauerunt ad præsentis status conscientiam, ut de futuro quoque præmonerent, prout homo illa naturali potentia & libertate arbitrij usurus esset: Nempe bene futurum homini, si arborem vitæ obseruaret: Male, si de arbore scientiæ boni & mali esset gustaturus. Loci & situs conditio a commoditate fluvij & rebus circumstantibus optimè describitur. Nam primum fluvius unus procedere ex ea regione dicitur qui irrigaret hortum; secundo in fluenta quatuor dividi, ver. 10. Atque hic fluvius communi appellatione Euphrates a geographis nū-cupari solet. Fluenta tum propriis nominibus, tū finibus distinguntur. Primi nomen est Pifon. finis regio Chauilæ, id est Sufianes, quæ trium præstantissimarum rerum nomine commendatur: auri, versic. 11. Bdellij arboris, & gemmæ sardonychis, versu 12. Secundi fluenti nomen est Gihon, Geographi Maharfares vocant vel potius Naharfares: fines, terra Cus regio Arabiæ desertæ, ad quam dispe-rit fluvius in paludes Babylonicas mersus. Tertij nomē dicitur Chiddekel, i. Tygris cursus ad Assyriam orientem versus: hoc autē Euphratis membrum Chaldaeis dictū est Nahar Melcha, Graecis ποταμός regium flumen interpretatur Ammianus. Quarti nomen est commune Euphrates, nempe quod Babylonem & Otrin permeat reliquis praecellens, vt Ammiani verbis.
units.tr: Now the removal of means is twofold. First, the earth, as a mother bringing forth from her womb, is deprived of the power of bringing forth, in these words: "There was not yet a shrub to be in the earth, nor had any plant yet sprung up." Second, all things that come from outside to help that generation are removed: namely the rains, which God is accustomed to pour upon the earth; the cultivation which man applies; and the dew or vapour rising from the earth, by which the surface of the earth would be watered. Accordingly, with all those internal and external means removed, by which growing things are produced from the earth, Moses shows that the power of God the Creator alone was the cause why trees, herbs and shrubs were then created on the third day, whereas the other works of the following days are now brought forth, with intervening means, according to the order of nature established by God. There are wholly two passages on the other part, which sets out the condition of the whole Church. One concerns the nature of man, of which the Church consists; the other concerns the calling. Moses describes the origin of man in verse 7, according to his nature. To this is joined the perpetual place, which God had given to that singular and whole ancient Church, as is explained from verse 15 onwards. Moses delivers the place of calling from verse 15 to the end of the chapter. The constitution of man's nature is therefore shown by his origin, his manner, and his parts. Moses attributes the origin to "the formation of Iehovah," a word which declares the singular manner of human origin in preference to the other creatures, looking back to the fuller history set out in chapter 1, verses 26 and following. The essential parts of man, of which the human person is constituted, are said to be two: first the matter, "dust from the earth," which the Lord gathered together and fashioned for the creation of the man. Second, the form of man, that is, the immaterial part, namely the mind or the vital soul of man, which God "breathed into his nostrils." By this arrangement God distinguished the soul of man from the souls of the other living creatures, since he showed that the human soul subsists, while the souls of the other living creatures are qualitative (as the Scholastics speak), the human being being a subject in itself, and the others being in a subject. From this composition there follows what Moses added afterwards, that man became "a living soul," that is, his body was animated by the soul under this law, that he should be a living soul but one able to die, not a quickening soul, which by death itself would drive death away, as the Apostle interprets most fittingly in 1 Corinthians 15. Afterwards a place is assigned to this subject in the following verses, and from the dignity of this dwelling the dignity of the man as its inhabitant is to be gathered. For although man might share in the common dwelling which God assigned to all living creatures, nevertheless he willed to assign to him a particular dwelling, as a king ruling over the other created things has his palace. The condition of this palace is explained first in general, in verse 8, and then in particular, in what follows. It is described first from its form, in that it was a garden enclosed and fenced round; second, from its place and situation, in that it was in Eden, that is, the region of delights, which Ptolemy calls Audanitis or Auranitis, in Babylonia, and indeed in the eastern or front part of it, which, to use the words of Pliny, was the most pleasant part of the whole East. Third, from the instrument of that garden, namely that God "planted that garden," in a singular manner above the rest of the earth, where "he placed the man whom he had formed." Moses sets out these three in the following verses, in reverse order [ὑστέρῳ ὑπερῷῳ]: the adornment in verse 9; the convenience of the place in verse 10 and the three following; and finally the form in verse 14. Moses describes the instrument of the garden in these words: "So Iehovah God caused to grow" ... This instrument is of two kinds: common, for common use, and singular, for a singular purpose. The common kind is every "tree desirable to the sight and good for food," that is, a tree as pleasing as it is necessary for the fruit of life. The singular instrument is twofold: "the tree of life in the garden" and "the tree of the knowledge of good and evil." It is singular not by its nature but by the institution of God. God instituted these trees both to remind man of his present condition, and to make him more certain of the future on a condition. The present condition of man was freedom (as they call it) of choice, or the natural power of cleaving to the good, of which the symbol was the tree of life, or of turning aside to evil, of which the symbol was the tree of the knowledge, and so on. And these symbols so stirred man to awareness of his present state that they also forewarned him of the future, according as man would use that natural power and freedom of choice: namely, that it would go well for man if he kept the tree of life, and ill if he were to taste of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The condition of the place and situation is best described from the convenience of the river and the surrounding things. For first, "a river is said to proceed out of that region, which would water the garden"; second, that it is "divided into four streams," verse 10. This river is commonly called the Euphrates by the geographers. The streams are distinguished both by their proper names and by their regions. The name of the first is Pishon, whose region is Havilah, that is, Susiana, which is commended for three most excellent things: gold, verse 11; the bdellium tree, and the sardonyx gem, verse 12. The name of the second stream is Gihon, which the geographers call Maharsares, or rather Naharsares; its region is the land of Cush, the region of the Arabian desert, into which the river, lost in the Babylonian marshes, sinks. The name of the third is Hiddekel, that is, the Tigris, flowing towards the east to Assyria. This branch of the Euphrates was called by the Chaldeans Nahar Melcha, and to the Greeks [ποταμός], which Ammianus translates as the royal river. The name of the fourth is the common name Euphrates, which passes through Babylon and Orthin and surpasses the rest, as Ammianus says.

units.la: Sequitur modus; ad cuius explicationem Moses ingreditur alterum locum de vocatione hominis, & Ecclesiae illius integrae. Vocationem igitur hominis (qui secundus locus est ad constitutionem Ecclesiae pertinens) triplicem fuisse tradit Moses: Vnam temporariā, ad singulorum indiuiduorum occupationem; alteram spiritualem, ad Dei gloriam atque obsequium: Tertiam denique sociale. Temporariā ad alimentū singulorum pertinente exponit Moses v.15. Spirituale, v.16. & seq. Socialem, reliquis versibus ad vltimū vsque. Temporaria his verbis ostenditur, Iehoua Deus accipiens hominē nempe de terra extra hortum ex qua creatus fuerat, collocauit eum in horto Hedenis ad colendum ipsum & ad seruandum, nempe curadas species ab omni labe, prout gigni & interire ex natura poterant. Hac autē specie omnis homo neftus labor ad huius vitae commoditatem pertinens nostrāmq; occupatione intelligedus est: Nam homine ad otium nō creauit Deus.
units.tr: Next comes the manner. To explain it, Moses turns to a second topic, the calling of man and of the whole Church. Moses teaches that the calling of man, which is the second point belonging to the constitution of the Church, was threefold. The first was temporal, concerning the occupation of individuals; the second was spiritual, concerning God's glory and obedience; the third, finally, was social. Moses sets out the temporal calling, which concerns the sustenance of individuals, in v.15; the spiritual, in v.16 and following; and the social, in the remaining verses to the end. The temporal calling is shown by these words: the LORD God took the man, namely from the earth outside the garden, from which he had been created, and put him in the garden of Eden to till it and to keep it, namely to keep the kinds free from every blemish, so far as they could be generated and perish by nature. Under this heading must be understood every honest labour that pertains to the convenience of this life and to our occupation, for God did not create man for idleness.

units.la: Vocationis spiritualis in fide & obsequio positae ratio ostenditur singulari mandato Dei, v.16. & seq. cū primum quidē liberū vsum ad res singulas permittit Deus, vt supra cap.1.v.29. Deinde vero singulari instituto arborē illam excipit de qua in v.9. dicebamus, v.17. Nā interdicto suo Deus fidem & obsequium hominis probaturus, primum cauet ipsi a maleficio: secundo poenam maleficij, si commiserit, denuntiat, dicens, Nam quo die comederis de ea, morte moriturus es.
units.tr: The reason for the spiritual calling, founded on faith and obedience, is shown by a special command of God, v.16 and following. At first God indeed grants free use of individual things, as above in chapter 1, v.29. Then, by a special ordinance, he excepts that tree of which we spoke in v.9, v.17. For by his prohibition God, about to test the faith and obedience of man, first guards him against wrongdoing; and second, he announces the penalty for wrongdoing, should he commit it, saying: For in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.

units.la: Interdicti de gustando arboris illius fructu ad exercendū hominis obsequium & probandum pertinebat: vt qui vitam a Deo habeat & vitae symbolum in arbore vitae propositum, Deo creatori obsequi teneretur: huic vero interdicto poena subiicitur, & homini (si more non gereret) denuntiatur his verbis, Nam quo die comederis de illa, moriendo moriturus es, i. vitam quam a Deo habes amissurus: quemadmodum autē vita hominis erat duplex: vna qua homo secundum animā viuebat in Deo, coniunctus illi: altera qua secundū corpus viuebat ex anima: sic e diuerso duplicem mortem intelligi hac denuntiatione necesse est: vnā mortem animae, i. separationem illius a Deo, quam peccatū efficit; Altera morte corporis, i. separationem ab anima siue dissolutione animae a corpore quam vanitas nostra efficit ex peccato: quapropter etiā in hominis restitutione huic vtriq;, morti priori, qua anima moritur a Deo separata, & posteriori, qua corpus ab anima, duplex resurrectio opponitur. Apoc.19. & 20. prior qua anima ante in peccatis mortua a tua à peccatis resurgit ad iustitiā in Christo: altera & secunda, qua corpus in se mortuum redintegratur viuenti animæ, prout futurū est secundo aduentu Christi. Nunc ad tertium vocationis genus veniamus, quod sociale, siue coniugale, docendi causa, appellabimus. Eius narratio tribus membris continetur: nam primū consilium & causa exponitur ver.18. Secundo narratur factum, uerfib. sequetibus. Postremo cuenta, tribus uerfib. vltimis. Primi loci ver.18. mébra sunt duo: nam primum causa proponitur, priore mébro versus: deinde consilium posteriore. Causam declarant hæc verba, Non est bonū hominem esse solum. Bona autē quoties dicuntur, aut respectu speciei secundum esse; aut respectu modi secūdum esse, vel qualitates essentiæ; cum denique respectu ordinis ad aliud appellantur. Hic autem nō agitur de bono secundum speciem, aut modum, sed secūdum ordinem & relationem ad aliud. Cum itaque Deus res omnes creatas, quę quidem animatæ sunt, coniugatas instituisset, Hominem vero principio marem duntaxat edidisset; commoditatem illius ordinationis defuisse illi principio illo pronuntiat, cuius commoditatis respectu dicit non esse bonum vt homo solus sit. Sed quamuis homo secundū speciem modumque sit bonus, tamē melius ei fore atque cōmodius si sua quoque homini, vt cæteris animātibus, suppeditetur coniugatio. Huic causæ consilium subiicitur, his verbis, Faciam illi auxilium secundum rationē ipsius. Auxilium autē, id est, personam auxiliarem siue adiutricem ad commoditatē ipsius in omni vocatione, siue temporaria ad vitā hāc, siue spiritali ad vitam æternam, siue denique cōmuni ad speciei propagationem & liberorum educationem institutionémque in Domino. In narratione facti cūm Deus viro creauit adiumentum, tria sunt obseruanda. Primūm antecedens quasi occasio, vt homo ad expetendum consortium & percipiendam vtilitatem eius adduceretur, ver. 19. & 20. Secundò modus subministrandæ illius consortis, vers.21. & sequentis parte. Postremo autem legitima consociatio ac velut dedūctio in domum viri, secunda parte vers.21. Occasio antecedens hæc fuisse dicitur, quòd cūm Iehoua formauisset omnes animantes terrestres atque aerias eásque coniugas, omnes ad hominem adduxerat eásque sliterat coram ipso, vt nouo principi, secundum verba institutionis supra, i.v.26. Huius dominatus tria signa hoc loco adferuntur: primūm quòd Deus animantes adduxit ad hominem, vt videret quo nomine ipsas appellaret: nam impositio nominis eorum est proprie qui auctoritate præualent. Secundo cum finis hic à Mose adfertur, vt quocūque nomine homo bestias appellasset, id nomen ipsorum esset, & tāquam ex auctoritate sui principis inditum obtineret, ver.19. Tertiò cūm ex hac inftitutione & consilio Dei homo dicitur animantes nominibus suis ap-pellasse, v.20. Ex hac igitur occasione dicitur homo comperisse sibi no adesse auxilium quod esset viro commodu, cum tamen animantes omnes, quæ imperio ipsius suberant, suis coniugibus instructæ essent. Ex hac ergo occasione consequutus est modus, quo Deus coniugem viro suppeditauit. Primùm quòd dormienti, id est nihil tale cogitanti aut iuuanti: nam propterea soporem altum iniecisse Deus dicitur, quum vxorem fabricaturus esset Deus. Secundò, quòd materiam sumpsit ex ipso viro, nempe costam, velut laboris consortem, & fulcrum viro accommodum. Tertio quòd carnem occlusit costæ illius loco, ne quid secundum carnem etiam experrectus homo de eo mysterio cognosceret: Postremò quod ex ea costa de viro sumpta ædifi-cauit fœminam, id est, constituit corpus laxius virili, quod tamquam ædificium esset capiendo fœtui atque alendo percommodum. His subiicitur deductio in domum viri legitimáque à Deo consociatio, his verbis, adduxit eam ad Adamum. Ex his euenta consequuntur tria, singulis versibus exposita. Primùm particularis conscientia & gratulatio coniugij, vers. 23. Secundo communis institutio, vers. 24. Postremò vsus in illa integra Ecclesiæ constitutione, vers. vltimo. In singulari agnitione duo ab Adamo prædicantur; Ortus fœminæ, & natura. Ortus, cum dicit, hac vice adest os ex ossibus meis, & caro ex carne mea. Sic enim naturalis corporum animorúmque coniunctionis ratio optime exprimitur. Natura verò, quòd homo velut caput vxoris illi imponit nomen, & quidem consortij coniunctissimi, cum à viro appellaret Viram, tamquam si diceret se alterum. Huius appellationis atque consortij vinculum pernececssarium est, non solùm à singulari Dei institutione, verùm etiam à natura ipsa, quia de viro sumpta est: ex quo sequitur coniugium & natura & singulari Dei instituto sanctissimum habendum esse, quemadmodum versu sequente concluditur de coniugio humano vniuersé. Nam illius institutionis tria membra accuratè conscripta sunt: Primùm tantum esse ius coniugij, vt causa illius vir relinquat patrem suum & matrem suam: Secundo vinculum esse arctissimum quo agglutinati coniuges interse hæreant: Tertio ius illius esse, vt caro vna sint in Domino, ex quo ab ipso coagmentati sunt. Hinc autè vsus ille in Ecclesia integra consequutus est, qui versu vltimo dicitur: quòd cum ambo nudi essent, tum ea integritate animorum corporúmque fuerunt præditi vt eos non puderet nuditatis suæ, quæ iam ex vitiofitate nostra probrosa effecta est. Hîc duæ quæstiones incidunt ad rationem temporis pertinentes: vna, de tempore quo hortus tus in Hedene consitus & constitutus est : Altera, de tempore quo creata est fœmina,& loco illius. Prioris quæstionis ratio facilis est, si ad secundum opus dici tertij respexeris, de quo supra primo cap. verf. 11. quo enim tempore terram circumuestiuit Deus sua viri-ditate, floribus, & fructibus, eodem quoque tempore hortum in Hedene fuisse constitutum satis aperte declarat Moses ; quia Deus eodem tempore & universitatem hanc exornauit, & partem illius ornatissimam : quam rem universe propositam in verf. octauo, non obscure confirmat Moses verf. nono. Altera quæstio de creatione fœminæ , & tempore ac loco ipsius , plus videtur habere ob-scuritatis , propterea quod antea narrauit Moses hominem in horto collocatum, verf. decimoquinto, bestias ad ipsum adductas , & alia consimilia. Verum hoc in narrationibus sacris opus est observari, eas interdum pro ratione temporum , interdum pro ratio-ne argumentorum citra temporis observationem solere collocari: quam rem Hebraei confirmant vulgari dicto in commentariis , di-centes , non esse prius aut posterius in scripturis , id est , non semper rationem temporis accurate in historiis observari. Muta-tur autem ratio temporis ad commoditatem historiæ , sive me-moriam juvari legentium oporteat , ( ut sit in Genealogiis , in quibus nomina ὕστερον πρότερον[?] percurruntur, ) sive causas , quamvis antecedentes , post factorum historiam explicari , ( quæ ratio in scripturis est frequentissima, ) sive ordinem argumentorum, ut hoc loco factum est , observari. Nam vocationes hominis distinctè percurruntur , non secundum earum tempus , sed secundum argu-mentum. Primum quidem vocationes particulares , vel potius sin-gulares unius cuiusque in se , corporalis & spiritualis, deinde vero socialis & coniugata vocatio, quam velut compositam sim-plicibus vocationibus postponi oportuit. quamobrem quod an-te narratum est hominem fuisse in horto collocatum,& significatum interdictum , id creationem fœminæ subsequutum est: quam extra hortum cum Adamo creatam esse , & communiter cum illo interdi-ctum Dei percepisse, argumentis duobus demonstrabimus. Primùm quòd omnes animantes terrestres & aeriæ ad hominem adductæ sunt cùm fœminam Deus creaturus esset : non autem in hortum esse adductas ratio ipsa peruincit, sed potiùs (si forte) ante hortum,tam-quam hominis,qui princeps datus erat animantibus,palatium & do-miciliu[?]. Alterum argumetum est quòd disertis verbis fœmina cap.3. 2.ver. & seq. interdictū sibi æquè ac viro fatetur divinitus fuisse pro-nuntiatum : quod tum in narratione huius capitis antecedit ordine. Ex hac quæstione & solutione illius aliæ nonnullæ quas breuitatis causa omittimus facilè soluuntur. Sic enim statuimus virum creatum primùm, tum animantes ad ipsum adductas, post creatam fœminam extra hortum, inde coniuges in hortum introductos esse, ibi denique interdictum à Deo significatum Arbores coram demonstrante, quas Deus discretione singulari ab aliis distinxerat.
units.tr: The prohibition against eating the fruit of that tree served to exercise and test man's obedience: since he had life from God and the symbol of life was set before him in the tree of life, he was bound to obey God his Creator. A penalty is attached to this prohibition, and it is announced to man (should he not comply) in these words: For on the day you eat of it, dying you shall die, that is, you will lose the life you have from God. Just as man's life was twofold, one by which he lived in God according to the soul, joined to him, and another by which he lived in the body from the soul, so conversely this announcement necessarily points to a twofold death: one death of the soul, that is, its separation from God, which sin brings about; the other death of the body, that is, its separation from the soul, or the dissolution of the soul from the body, which our vanity brings about through sin. For this reason also, in the restoration of man, a twofold resurrection is set against these two deaths, the former death, by which the soul dies separated from God, and the latter, by which the body is separated from the soul. Revelation 19 and 20. The first, by which the soul, once dead in sins, rises from sins to righteousness in Christ; the second, by which the body, dead in itself, is restored to the living soul, as will happen at the second coming of Christ. Now let us come to the third kind of calling, which we shall call social, or conjugal, for the sake of teaching. Its account is contained in three parts: for first the counsel and cause are set out in verse 18; second, the deed is related in the following verses; last, the conclusion, in the three final verses. The first part, verse 18, has two members: for first the cause is put forward in the first member of the verse, then the counsel in the second. The cause is declared by these words: It is not good for man to be alone. Now, things are called good either with respect to their species, according to their being; or with respect to their mode, according to their being or the qualities of their essence; or finally they are called good with respect to order and relation to something else. Here, however, the discussion is not about good according to species or mode, but according to order and relation to another. Since God had established all created things that are living in pairs, and had produced man as male alone at the beginning, he declares that the advantage of that ordering was lacking to him at the beginning; and with respect to this advantage he says it is not good for man to be alone. But although man is good according to his species and mode, it would nonetheless be better and more convenient for him if a partnership, as with the other living creatures, were also supplied to him. To this cause a counsel is added, in these words: I will make him a helper according to his own kind. By "helper" is meant a helping or assisting person, for his convenience in every calling: whether temporal, for this life; or spiritual, for eternal life; or finally common, for the propagation of the species and the upbringing and instruction of children in the Lord. In relating the deed, when God created a helper for the man, three things are to be observed. First, the preceding occasion, as it were, by which man was led to desire companionship and to perceive its usefulness, verses 19 and 20. Second, the manner of supplying that companionship, verse 21 and the first part of the following verse. Last, the lawful union and, as it were, the leading of her into the man's house, the second part of verse 21. The preceding occasion is said to have been this: when Jehovah had formed all the living creatures of the earth and of the air, and had brought them to him, he had them pass before him, as to a new prince, according to the words of the institution above, verse 26. Three signs of this dominion are cited in this passage. First, that God brought the living creatures to man, to see what name he would call them; for the imposition of a name is properly the act of one who holds authority. Second, the purpose is given by Moses: that whatever name man called the beasts, that would be their name, and it would hold as if imposed by the authority of its prince, verse 19. Third, when from this institution and counsel of God man is said to have called the living creatures by their names, verse 20. From this occasion, then, it is said that man came to see that no help fitting for him was at hand, although all the creatures that were subject to his command were furnished with their mates. From this occasion, therefore, followed the manner in which God supplied a wife to the man. First, that he was asleep, that is, not thinking of or assisting in any such thing; for God is said to have cast a deep sleep upon him, since God was about to fashion a wife. Second, that he took the material from the man himself, namely a rib, as a companion in labour and a support suited to the man. Third, that he closed up the flesh in place of that rib, so that the man, even when awake, should know nothing in the flesh of that mystery. Last, that from that rib, taken from the man, he built a woman, that is, he constituted a body looser than the male's, which, like a building, was very well suited for holding and nourishing the foetus. To these is added the leading of her into the man's house and the lawful union by God, in these words: he brought her to Adam. Three events follow from these, each set out in its own verse. First, the particular recognition and rejoicing of the marriage, verse 23. Second, the common institution, verse 24. Last, the use of it within the whole constitution of the Church, the final verse. In the particular recognition, two things are attributed to Adam: the origin of the woman, and her nature. Her origin, when he says this time there is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. For in this way the natural reason of the joining of bodies and souls is most aptly expressed. Her nature, however, is shown in that the man, as head, imposes a name on his wife, and indeed the name of a most intimate partnership, since he calls her Virago, as if to say she is another himself. The bond of this naming and partnership is most necessary, not only from God's particular institution but also from nature itself, because she was taken out of man. From this it follows that marriage is to be held most holy both by nature and by God's particular institution, as is concluded in the following verse concerning human marriage in general. For three parts of that institution are accurately written down: first, that the right of marriage is such that for its sake a man shall leave his father and his mother; second, that the bond by which the spouses are joined is most close, so that they cleave to one another; third, that it is their right to be one flesh in the Lord, since they were joined together by him. From this arises that use of marriage within the whole Church which is mentioned in the last verse: that since both were naked, they were endowed with such integrity of soul and body that they were not ashamed of their nakedness, which has now, through our corruption, been made shameful. Here two questions arise concerning the reckoning of time: one, about the time at which the garden was planted and established in Eden; the other, about the time at which the woman was created, and about her place. The reasoning for the first question is easy, if you look back to the second deed of the third day, of which above in the first chapter, verse 11. For at the time when God clothed the earth with its greenness, flowers, and fruits, Moses declares quite plainly that at the same time the garden in Eden was also established; because God at the same time adorned this whole universe and its most splendid part. Moses, in verse 9, does not obscurely confirm this matter, which was set forth generally in verse 8. The second question, about the creation of the woman and the time and place of her, seems to have more obscurity, because Moses had earlier related that the man was placed in the garden, verse 15, that the beasts were brought to him, and other similar things. But in sacred narratives this must be observed: that they are sometimes arranged according to the reason of time, and sometimes according to the reason of the subject matter, without regard to the order of time. The Hebrews confirm this by a common saying in the commentaries, saying that there is no before or after in the Scriptures, that is, that the order of time is not always strictly observed in the histories. The order of time, however, is altered for the convenience of the narrative, whether it is needful to help the memory of the readers (as is the case in the genealogies, in which names are run through hysteron proteron [ὕστερον πρότερον]), or to explain after the account of the deeds causes that are nonetheless antecedent (a practice most frequent in the Scriptures), or to observe the order of the subject matter, as has been done in this place. For the callings of man are set forth distinctly, not according to their time but according to their subject: first the particular callings, or rather the single callings of each person in himself, bodily and spiritual; then the social and conjugal calling, which, as compounded from the simple callings, had to be placed after them. For this reason, what was related earlier, that man had been placed in the garden and the prohibition was announced, was followed by the creation of the woman. We shall prove by two arguments that she was created outside the garden with Adam, and received God's prohibition in common with him. First, that all the living creatures of the earth and air were brought to man when God was about to create the woman; but reason itself shows that they were not brought into the garden, but rather (if at all) before the garden, as the palace and dwelling-place of the man, who was set as prince over the creatures. The second argument is that the woman herself, in plain words in chapter 3, verses 2 and following, confesses that the prohibition was pronounced to her as much as to her husband by God's command; which in the narrative of this chapter comes earlier in order. From this question and its solution, several other matters, which we omit for the sake of brevity, are easily resolved. For thus we hold: the man was created first, then the living creatures were brought to him, after the woman was created outside the garden, and then the pair were brought into the garden, where at last the prohibition was signified by God, the tree being pointed out, which God had distinguished from the others by a singular separation.

units.la: CAPITIS III ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER III.

units.la: E[?]xposita creatione integraque Ecclesiæ, prout creata fuerat, constitutione, sequitur postremus locus de constitutione Ecclesiæ corruptæ: quam hoc in cap. Moses breuissimè demonstrauit, ut quasi fundamentum reliquæ historiæ suæ & doctrinæ commune subsisterneret. Ad constitutionem autem corruptæ huius Ecclesiæ, & mundi ex corruptione hominis inquinati, duo distinctè ponenda sunt; Primũ enim actus corruptionis exponitur, siue constitutio corruptionis in fieri (ut loquuntur vulgò,) secundò status corruptionis ex quo facta est in humano genere corruptio. Priorem locũ Moses 6.primis vers. explicauit; posteriorem verò, reliquo capite. Ad instantem corruptionis actum pertinent hæc duo membra; Tentatio, versibus quinque; & tentationis assensus, in 6.ver. Tentationum duo ponuntur genera; vnum externum & foris proritans, alterum internū, & intus, paulatim provocanti occasioni acquiescens. Has duas tentationis formas, quia secundum mutuum respectum ipsarum vna agit, irritas, altera agitur, irritata; coniunctim modum tentationis vtriusque per διαλογισμὸν[?] summámque narrationem sermonum vltro ac citro habitorum, describit Moses. Ac primę quidem partes sunt provocantis, in versu primo: secundæ, provocatæ creaturæ, ver.2. & 3. In provocante primum causa efficiens obseruatur; secundò, modus. Causa efficiens duplex est: vna principalis; altera adiuuans, quam instrumentalem vocant. Principalis est diabolus, qui non perstiterat in veritate, ut Christus loquitur Ioan.8. Instrumentalis verò est serpens, in quem diabolus ingressus est, aut certè cui insedit, ut illius specie operaque ad circumueniendum fœminam abuteretur. Nec refert quod à Mose diabolus hoc in loco minimè nominatur. Nam ex signo atque instrumento res significata & causa principalis agens necessario intelligenda est: quod cum ex natura spirituum tum ex natura serpentis brutarumque animantium debemus colligere: Nam Spiritus est iustum atque iniustum cognoscere scere & de eo ratiocinari: Ac proinde neque serpentis, neque bruti animalis cuiusquam est de iusto,iniusto,virtute, vitio, legitimo obsequio, aut peccato cognoscere intellectu, aut ratiocinatione diffe-rere. De hoc autem instrumento dicit Moses, serpentem fuisse astutum præ omnibus bestiis agrestibus, quas fecerat Iehova Deus. Non quòd significari hoc pacto voluerit eam fuisse astutiā, aut prudentiam serpentis secundum naturam ipsius, vt ipse de bono aut malo, virtute aut vitio cognosceret,aliósque informaret per se;sed quia hoc pacto obseruata naturali serpentis constitutione diabolus animal vidit esse ad suas artes commodissimum,siue latenter ingredi hortum oporteret, siue in horto versari, siue ex eo effugere & a conspectu Adami discedere.
units.tr: Having set out the creation and the whole constitution of the Church as it was created, there follows the last topic: the constitution of the corrupted Church. Moses demonstrates this very briefly in this chapter, so that it might stand as a common foundation for the rest of his history and doctrine. To understand the constitution of this corrupted Church, and of the world made corrupt by the defilement of man, two things must be set out separately. First, the act of corruption is explained, or the constitution of corruption in process (as they commonly say, in fieri). Second, the state of corruption is explained, from which corruption came upon the human race. Moses explained the first in the first six verses, and the second in the rest of the chapter. Two parts belong to the present act of corruption: the temptation, in five verses, and the assent to the temptation, in the sixth verse. Two kinds of temptation are set down: one external, which urges from without, and the other internal, which yields from within to an opportunity that gradually invites it. These two forms of temptation act upon each other, the one being made ineffective and the other made effective. Moses describes the manner of both together, by means of a dialogue and a full account of the words exchanged on both sides. The first parts belong to the one who tempts, in verse 1; the second to the creature who is tempted, in verses 2 and 3. In the one who tempts, the efficient cause is noted first; second, the manner. The efficient cause is twofold: one principal, the other assisting, which they call instrumental. The principal is the devil, who did not stand in the truth, as Christ says in John 8. The instrumental cause is the serpent, into which the devil entered, or at least upon which he sat, so that he might abuse the serpent's form and work to beguile the woman. Nor does it matter that the devil is not named by Moses in this place. For from the sign and the instrument the thing signified and the principal acting cause must necessarily be understood. We must gather this both from the nature of spirits and from the nature of the serpent and of the brute animals. For a spirit is able to know what is just and unjust and to reason about it. Accordingly, it is not the business of a serpent or of any brute animal to know by understanding, or to distinguish by reasoning, what is just or unjust, virtue or vice, lawful obedience or sin. Moses says of this instrument that the serpent was more subtle than all the beasts of the field which Jehovah God had made. He did not mean by this that the serpent had such cunning or prudence according to its own nature, so that it could itself know good and evil, virtue and vice, and instruct others of its own accord. Rather, he meant that, given the natural constitution of the serpent, the devil saw that this animal was most suitable for his arts, whether it was necessary to enter the garden secretly, to remain in the garden, or to escape from it and withdraw from the sight of Adam.

units.la: Modus tentationis quo diabolus vsus est, altera parte versus exponitur: nempe quòd in dubium vocauerit, tamquam sciscitando, interdictum illud Dei, de quo supra cap.2.16. audiuimus. Etsi fortasse per ambiguitatem sermonis amplius fœminæ illuserit, cum ei dicit, non comedetis de omni fructu arborum huius horti.Id bifariam secundū phrasin Hebraeam exponi potest. Primum tamquam si dixisset,nō comedetis de quouis fructu, & aliquem excepisset: aut etiam tamquam si dixisset,nō comedetis de vllo fructu: sic enim Hebraea phrasis potest variari, tamquam si negatiua particula aut cum v.6. proximo,comedetis,aut cum nomine,omnis,coniungenda esset. hoc autem diabolus non sensit. Huic tētationi, qua diabolus fœminam inuasit,respondise dicitur fœmina v.2.& 3. Ac primū quidem cur fœmina primum inuaserit,ratio est euidēs;quia vas à natura est;etiā citra conteplatione peccati,infirmius.Respōdet autē diabolo tum cōtraria affirmatio-ne 2.verf. de fructu arboris huius horti comedemus. Tum singulari exceptione,ver.3. de fructu autem arboris istius, &c. Exceptionémque graviter amplificat dicens,non comedetis ac ne attingetis quidem,id est,nec libabitis tantillum siue gustabitis primoribus labiis.Deinde vero interminationem à Deo denuntiatam subiicit, sed cum quadam dubitationis specie.Ac proinde in hac ipsa cōfabulatione fœminę multi-plex ad peccatum aditus videtur esse:primus quòd cum diabolo con-tulit, quacumque specie; nam non potest cuiquam citra vocationem Dei vtilis esse cum diabolo communicatio. Secundus,quòd ad propositionē illam blasphemia non exhorruit vt aures obturaret.Tertius quòd fine viri communicatione, id est capitis sui in eodem horto versantis contulit. postremus quòd his ipsis modis videtur quædam dubitatio de veritate diuinarum interminationum in metem ipsius irrepsisse. Infirmæ illi responsioni qua fœmina vsa est, succedit alter aggressionis locus,quo nutantem quodammodo fœminam pertraxit Satan, vt in tentatione mali acquiesceret. Itaque duobus modis aggreditur,labefactaturus fidem illius,& obsequium subuersurus. Nam primum artificiose denuntiationem poenarum leuat, ver.4. Deinde vero promissione contrariam adfert, vel potius prædictionem mendacem, blasphemia in Deum contumelia iunctam,ver.5. Quibus tentationis argumentis non sermone respondisse foemina dicitur, sed re & facto acquieuisse,versu 6.Certitudine poenarum quas Deus denuntiauerat leuauit Satan his verbis, Non moriedo moriemini quemadmodum phrasi Hebraea significari in Grammatica syntaxi docuimus. Huic vero negationi opponitur contraria affirmatio in specie,sed re ambigua;qua Satan primū accusat Deum inuidentię,secūdo homines Deo similes fore pronuntiat.Inuidentiæ accusat dicens,non propterea interdixisse Deū quod morituri essent si de eo fructu gustarent; sed potius quòd nō esset ignarus boni ad hominē euenturi ex gustato cibo,nēpe quòd aperturi se essent oculi ipsorū quo die comedissent. Egregiè autē fefellit loquutionis huius ambiguitate.Nā aperire oculos in se quidē bonū est,sed aperire ad videndum & percipiendū malū, quemadmodū homini ex peccato factū est,id vero nulla ratione bonū appellari potest. Quapropter vt amplius foemina exstimularet,magnifica promissione adiecit ἔσεσθε ὡς[?] Nam eritis tamquā Dij scientes boni & mali. Cuius promissionis amplitudo duobus modis animū foeminæ irritauit:primum persuasione similitudinis vel adæquationis cū Deo:secūdo varietatis scientia,quæ varietas humano generi fuit dānosissima.Hactenus tentatio a principio externo adueniens. sequitur postea modus interni principij acquiescentis in tentatione illa quæ foris aduenerat. Huius tetationis internę instrumeta fuerunt,auditus,verf.antecedetibus, & visus,hoc versu.Quibus instrumetis foemina adducta est,primū vt ad obiectū tentationis concupiscētia sua oculos adiiceret: secūdo vt capies comederet: tertio vt viro quoque ministraret. Cōcupiscentia autē excitauit partim obiectū,partimq; promissum;obiectū, quòd fructus arboris illius ad cibū bonus videretur & ad aspectū gratus: promissum vero,quòd desiderabilis ad assequenda intelligentia, cuius spe magnifica Satan excitauerat.Sic eadem opera intellectu & voluntate foeminæ siue appetitu corrupto,tū ipsa eo deuenit vt capies de fructu comederet: tū etiā vt viro suo comedendū daret:qui ineptè,cū caput esset foeminę,auscultauit voci illius & comedit de fructu quo Deus interdixerat,prout nomi-natim Deus exprobrat v.17. Hactenus prior locus:nūc ad posteriorē veniamus,qui est de statu corrupto Ecclesię Dei,ex quo nimirū corruptio facta est.Eius status,loci in vniuersū tres sūt:Primus est de cognitione,ad verf. vsq; 14.Secūdus de sentētia ex cognitione,ad vers. vsq; 19: Tertius de executione, ad finé vsq; capitis. Cognitionis loci duo sunt, cómunis, & singularis. Cōmunis, siue naturalis, & internus est cō- sciētiæ: singularis, siue supernaturalis, & foris adueniēns est cognitio qua cognoscit Deus de peccatoribus. Internæ cognitionis locus est in v.7. Diuinæ verò foris adueniētis, vers.seqq. Cognitione conscien tię qua primi parētes affecti sunt, Moses narrat his verbis, tum aperuerunt se amborū illorū oculi, i. reliqua illa lux quæ in funesta illa paretum corruptione mansit, præluxit illis quantū opus fuit vt antecedētis suę lucis recordati se tenebras esse animaduerteret. Hanc verò cognitionem naturalem conscientiæ demonstrat Moses infuisse illis adiuncto & consequente necessario: Adiuncto, quia prælucente conscientia viderunt se nudos esse & pudore ex nuditate affecti sunt: prout hęc loquutio [illegible, ~8 letters] est, & suppleda ex v. vlt. cap. precedentis. Nam integrā natura non fuit pudenda nuditas, corrupta verò pudorem iniecit vehe- mentissimū. Consequens itaque fuit quod frondes ficus consuerunt & subligacula siue præcinctoria fecerunt sibi tegendis iis partibus salte quę omniū videbantur inhonestissimæ. Alterum genus cognitionis, quà Deus in homine peccatorem adhibet, necessario præter conscientiæ cognitionem fuit adiungendū, quia conscientia apud nos partes agit testiū, Deus verò iudicis. Sic hominem testimonio euictū conscien- tiæ & [illegible, ~10 letters] coram se sistit, vt versibus seqq. exponitur. Huius autem cognitionis partes humanitus describuntur secundū rationē forensis iudicij, vt Dei Op. Max. sapientia & patientia semper ante oculos habeamus sese accōmodātis rationi nostræ. Nam primū reus peruestigari dicitur, v. 8. Secundò nominatim vocari in ius, v.9. Tertiò examinari, v. 11. & seqq. In singulis autē membris binæ partes obseruandæ sunt, iudicis, & rei: Nam primū in peruestigatione Iehoua iudex dicitur ambulauisse per hortū ad ventum diei illius, i. cū ventus diei illius sese confirmaret: cum autē naturale fit illud quod à Philosophis traditur à sole augeri & coprimi flatus, augeri ascendente, comprimi occidente, mihi videtur probabile hæres[?] matutino fuisse gestas: sic autē aduentante iudice reus primum inaudiuisse dicitur aduentantis sonū, prout Deus adueniens, precursore veto vti solitus est, Exodi 34. & 1. Reg. 19. Iechezk. 1. & Act. 2. & aliis locis. Deinde verò vterq; reus sese abdidisse inter arbores illius horti metu iudicis & sui peccati conscientia. Quemadmodum autē in peruestigatione iudicis & sapientia videmus & patientia lenitatemq; maximam, sic contra in reorum fuga cernimus & insipientiam, quōd fugerint ad arbores à conspectu iudicis, cui omnia sunt præsentissima, & vim conscientiæ, quæ ad solam auditionem venti reos perterrefecerit. Citationis in ius partes item duæ sunt; vocatio à Deo, vers. 9. & comparitio reo-rum, 10. Citationem iuste Deus quidem adhibuit; sed quæstione sibi non necessariam, cùm sciret omnia, causa reorum vsurpauit, dicendo, vbi es, & virum qui caput est fœminæ appellando. Comparentis rei verba in v. 10. exponuntur, & fugam suam excusantis, idque ea ratione ut sese peccati sui accusaret: nam fugam suam excusaturus tres causas coniunctè adfert: primam Deum aduentantem quem à se auditum dicit: Secundam metum suum[?]: Tertiam occasionem metus, quod nudus esset, occasionem dico, quia hæc non vera causa metus exstiterat, sed occasio quæsita excusationi: Non enim metuebat homo proprie à Deo, quòd nudus esset simpliciter, (prius enim fuerat nudus ac non metuerat c. 2.) sed vera causa est quam dissimulauit, peccatum hominis, cuius causa res omnes creatas pudebat hominis, & hominem sui: adeo ut illa ipsa externa hominis species qua tamen animantes cæteræ facilè superantur, horrida homini effecta sit. Ex his ergo causis confitetur homo seipsum se abdidisse, tamquam si culpam partim in grauitatem præsentiæ Dei, partimque in corporis sui quod creauerat Deus constitutionem reiecisset. Ex hac autem qualicumque hominis confessione Deus occasionem arripit, v. 11. & tertium locum cognitionis, id est examen aggreditur. Examinis autem partes duæ sunt; nam primum narratur examen viri, v. 11. & 12: deinde fœminæ, v. 13. Examen viri instituit Deus argumentatione à signo sumpta: signum enim proponitur his verbis, Quis indicauit tibi te nudum esse? Ex eo signo conficitur hominem peccauisse, illis verbis, An de fructu illius arboris, &c. Nam huius argumentationis axioma est, Peccati signum esse nuditatem & nuditatis conscientiam. Huic examini respondet Adam per translationem criminis, ut vulgò appellatur. Itaque non inficiatur jam peccatum, sed leuare tentat, v. 12: tamquam si diceret se quidem peccauisse, sed non fuisse auctorem peccati. Etsi exceptio hæc tribus maximè nominibus indigna fuit: Primum quòd in fœminam peccatum transfertur, cuius vir caput est: Secundò quòd Deus obliquè incusatur dicedo, fœmina quam collocauisti mecum: Tertiò quòd ipse interdictum à Deo amplius cognouisset beneficiaque ampliora expertus esset quàm fœmina. Huic confessioni peccati cum translatione criminis Deus utcumque acquiescens, transit ad secundum examen, nimirum fœminæ, v. 13. Et pro confesso habet illam comedisse, ut quæ porrexisset viro, tantum de causa percontatur, cur fecisset illud! Respondet fœmina eadem arte: Nam primum peccatum in serpentem träsfert, eúmque fraude in causa fuisse dicit: Deinde ut amplius peccatum suum leuet, comedisse quidem se agnoscit: viro autem porrexisse reticet: quæ vera est ars naturalis hominum se & malefacta sua excusantium. Atque hactenus cognitio: nam serpentem Deus non examinat, vt qui in eo solùm causam peccati sui inesse sciret, cum in homine contrà causa duplex fuerit, externa à serpente, & interna ab hominis voluntate in peccatum prolabente. Sententiæ verò quam Deus dixit, pro numero reorum tres loci distinguendi sunt: Primus locus est in serpentem v.14.&15. Secundus in fœminam, v.16. Tertius in virum. v. 17. & duobus seqq. Nempe gradatim sententiam suam proferens in reos pro ratione malefacti: in reum grauissimum primam, & sic ex ordine.
units.tr: The manner of the temptation that the devil used is explained from the other side. He called into question, as if by asking a question, that prohibition of God which we heard about above in chapter 2:16. Perhaps through the ambiguity of his words he also deceived the woman further, when he said to her, you shall not eat of every fruit of the trees of this garden. This can be explained in two ways according to Hebrew idiom. First, it may be taken as if he had said, you shall not eat of any fruit, with one exception; or else as if he had said, you shall not eat of any fruit at all. For the Hebrew phrase can be read either way, if the negative particle is joined with the following verb, you shall eat, or with the word every. The devil, however, did not intend this. The woman is said to have answered this temptation, by which the devil attacked her, in verses 2 and 3. First, the reason why the woman was attacked first is plain: she is the weaker vessel by nature, even apart from any consideration of sin. She answers the devil, first, with a contrary affirmation in verse 2: we shall eat of the fruit of the trees of this garden. Then, with a particular exception in verse 3: but of the fruit of the tree that is in the midst of the garden, etc. And she greatly enlarges the exception, saying you shall not eat of it, neither shall you touch it, that is, you shall not so much as taste it or sip it with the tip of your lips. Then she adds the threat declared by God, but with a certain show of doubt. Accordingly, in this very conversation the woman's way into sin seems to have been opened in several respects. The first is that she conversed with the devil in any manner whatever; for communication with the devil can never be profitable to anyone apart from the calling of God. The second is that she did not shudder at his blasphemous proposition so as to stop her ears. The third is that she conversed without the fellowship of her husband, that is, of her head, who was living in the same garden. The last is that by these very means some doubt about the truth of the divine threats seems to have crept into her mind. To that weak answer of the woman there follows a second point of attack, by which Satan drew the woman, who was in some sense wavering, into consenting to the evil of temptation. Thus he attacks in two ways, intending to weaken her faith and to overthrow her obedience. For first he cleverly lightens the denunciation of punishments, in verse 4. Then, indeed, he brings a promise contrary to it, or rather a lying prediction, joined with insult to God in blasphemy, in verse 5. To these arguments of temptation the woman is said not to have replied in words, but to have assented in deed and in act, in verse 6.
