Satan weakened the certainty of the punishments that God had threatened with these words, you shall not surely die, as we have shown in the grammatical syntax, the Hebrew idiom signifies. To this denial there is opposed a contrary affirmation, in form, but ambiguous in substance; by which Satan first accuses God of jealousy, and secondly declares that men will become like God. He accuses him of jealousy, saying that God had forbidden them, not because they would die if they tasted of that fruit, but rather because he was not ignorant that good would come to man from eating the food, namely that their eyes would be opened on the day they ate it. He deceived her very skilfully by the ambiguity of this expression. For to have one's eyes opened is in itself a good thing; but to have them opened to see and perceive evil, as happened to man through sin, can by no reasoning be called good. Therefore, in order to stir the woman further, he added a magnificent promise: you shall be [ἔσεσθε ὡς] for you will be as gods, knowing good and evil. The greatness of this promise excited the woman's mind in two ways: first by the persuasion of likeness or equality with God; second, by the knowledge of variety, which variety proved most harmful to the human race. So far the temptation has come from an external principle. Next follows the manner of the internal principle, which assented to that temptation which had come from outside. The instruments of this internal temptation were hearing, in the preceding verses, and sight, in this verse. By these instruments the woman was led, first, to fix her eyes with desire on the object of the temptation; second, to take and eat; third, to give to her husband also. Desire was excited partly by the object, and partly by the promise: by the object, because the fruit of that tree looked good for food and pleasant to the sight; but by the promise, because it was desirable for gaining understanding, with the hope of which Satan had aroused her. Thus by the same act the woman's understanding and will, or corrupt appetite, were brought to this: on the one hand she came to take the fruit and eat it; on the other hand, to give it to her husband to eat as well. He, foolishly, since he was the head of the woman, listened to her voice, and ate of the fruit that God had forbidden, as God rebukes him by name in verse 17. So far the first point; now let us come to the second, which concerns the corrupt state of the Church of God, from which indeed the corruption arose. The points concerning this state are three in general. The first concerns knowledge, verses to 14. The second concerns the sentence arising from knowledge, verses to 19. The third concerns execution, to the end of the chapter. There are two kinds of knowledge in these points, common and particular. Common, or natural, knowledge is internal, and is that of conscience; particular, or supernatural, knowledge comes from outside, and is the knowledge by which God knows about sinners. The place of internal knowledge is in verse 7; that of divine knowledge coming from outside is in the following verses. Moses relates the knowledge of conscience with which the first parents were affected in these words: then the eyes of both of them were opened, that is, that remaining light which persisted in the deadly corruption of our parents shone upon them as much as was needful, so that, remembering their former light, they perceived that they were in darkness. Moses shows that this natural knowledge of conscience was in them as an accompaniment and as a necessary consequence. As accompaniment, because, with conscience shining upon them, they saw that they were naked, and were affected with shame arising from their nakedness; as this expression is, and must be supplied from the last verse of the preceding chapter. For nakedness was not shameful in their integrity; but corruption brought in a most vehement shame. The consequence, therefore, was that they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves aprons or girdles, to cover at least those parts that were seen as the most dishonourable of all. The second kind of knowledge, by which God deals with man as a sinner, necessarily had to be added beside the knowledge of conscience, because conscience among us plays the part of witnesses, but God that of judge. So he brings the man, convicted by the testimony of conscience, and [illegible] before himself, as is set out in the following verses. The parts of this knowledge are described in human terms according to the manner of a court of law, so that we may always keep before our eyes the wisdom and patience of God, the Best and Greatest, adapting them to our understanding. For first the guilty party is said to be searched out, verse 8. Secondly, he is summoned by name into court, verse 9. Thirdly, he is examined, verse 11 and following. In each of these parts two sides must be observed, that of the judge and that of the accused. For first, in the searching out, Jehovah is called the judge who walked in the garden at the cool of the day, that is, when the wind of that day was gathering strength. Since it is a natural matter, as the philosophers teach, that the wind is increased by the sun and reduced by it, increasing as the sun rises and decreasing as it sets, it seems to me probable that this happened in the morning. Thus, as the judge drew near, the accused is said first to have heard the sound of his approach, just as God, when he comes, is accustomed to use a forerunner, Exodus 34, 1 Kings 19, Ezekiel 1, Acts 2, and in other places. Then both guilty parties hid themselves among the trees of that garden, through fear of the judge and the consciousness of their sin. Just as in the searching out we see the wisdom and patience and very great gentleness of the judge, so on the other hand in the flight of the guilty we see folly, in that they fled among the trees from the sight of the judge, to whom all things are most present, and we see the power of conscience, which terrified the guilty by the mere hearing of the wind. The parts of the summons to court are likewise two: the calling by God, verse 9, and the appearance of the guilty, verse 10. God indeed summoned them justly, but, though he knew all things, he asked a question unnecessary for himself, assuming the role of the accused, saying where are you?, and addressing the man, who is the head, as the woman's head. The words of the accused in verse 10 are set forth, excusing his flight, and in such a way as to accuse himself of his sin. For in excusing his flight he brings three causes together: the first is God approaching, whom he says he heard; the second is his fear; the third is the occasion of his fear, that he was naked. I say occasion, because this was not the true cause of his fear, but an occasion sought for an excuse. For man did not properly fear God because he was simply naked (for he had been naked before and had not feared, chapter 2), but the true cause, which he concealed, was the sin of man, on account of which all created things were ashamed of man and man of himself; so much so that that very outward appearance of man, in which the other animals are nonetheless easily surpassed, became horrible to man. From these causes, then, man confesses that he hid himself, as though he had cast the blame partly upon the weight of God's presence, and partly upon the constitution of his own body, which God had created. From this confession of man, however it may be described, God seizes the occasion, verse 11, and approaches the third point of knowledge, that is, the examination. The parts of the examination are two: for first the examination of the man is related, verses 11 and 12; then that of the woman, verse 13. God conducts the examination of the man by an argument drawn from a sign: for the sign is put forward in these words, who told you that you were naked? From that sign it is inferred that man has sinned, in these words, have you eaten of the fruit of that tree? etc. For the axiom of this argument is that nakedness and the consciousness of nakedness are a sign of sin. To this examination Adam answers by the transfer of the crime, as it is commonly called. Accordingly he no longer denies sin, but tries to lighten it, verse 12, as if he were to say that he had indeed sinned, but had not been the author of the sin. Yet this excuse was unworthy in three especially notable respects. First, because the sin is transferred to the woman, whose husband is her head. Second, because God is indirectly accused in saying, the woman whom you placed with me. Third, because he himself had known the prohibition from God more fully and had experienced greater benefits than the woman. God, somewhat acquiescing in this confession of sin with transfer of blame, passes on to the second examination, namely of the woman, verse 13. And taking it as admitted that she had eaten, since she had handed it to the man, he asks only the reason, why did you do this? The woman answers with the same art. For first she transfers the sin to the serpent, and says that he was the cause through deceit; then, to lighten her sin still further, she acknowledges that she did eat, but keeps quiet that she gave it to the man; which is the natural art of men who excuse themselves and their misdeeds. So far the knowledge; for God does not examine the serpent, since he knew that the cause of sin lay in it alone, whereas in man the cause was twofold: external, from the serpent, and internal, from the man's will falling into sin. But as for the sentence that God pronounced, three places are to be distinguished according to the number of the guilty: the first place is concerning the serpent, verses 14 and 15; the second concerning the woman, verse 16; the third concerning the man, verse 17 and the two following. Namely, in pronouncing his sentence step by step on the guilty, in proportion to the wrong done: first on the most grievous offender, and so in order.

units.la: Primę sententiæ quam Deus in serpentem enuntiat, duæ sunt partes: peccatum, & pœna: peccatum Deus his verbis exprimit sermone ad serpentem conuerso, Quia fecisti hoc, id est fuisti in transgressionem, vt Paulus loquitur. Pœna vero causæ efficienti peccati denuntiata duo membra continet: vnum est pœnæ serpenti, tamquam instrumento tentationis, impositæ, v.14. Alterum membrum est pœnæ quam Deus satanæ tamquam principali causæ efficienti peccati denuntiauit, v.15. Atque hæ pœnæ propterea coniunctæ sunt, quòd actus tentationis fuit coniunctus, Diabolo serpentem in instrumentum ad eam assumente: quapropter etiam cùm Moses Deum serpenti hæc dixisse pronuntiat, serpetem synecdochicè opus est accipi: nempe tum pro naturali serpente, qui fuit instrumentum peccati, tum pro serpente illo magno & inuisibili, qui homicida fuisse dicitur à principio, Ioh.8. Serpenti visibili pœna triplex indicitur; Prima quòd præ omnibus aliis iumentis & bestiis agrestibus maledictione cumulandus est, omniáque mala præ aliis animantibus experturus: Secunda quòd super ventrem suum sit ambulaturus, id est nihil nisi latitaturus coram hominibus & aliis animantibus: Tertia, quòd puluerem comesturus omnibus diebus vitæ suæ, id est, non ita commodè vt aliæ animantes sibi quæsiturus victum, sed ad leuandam inediam etiam puluere terræ vbi delitescit abusurus. Neque tamen propterea cogitandum est, quod Iudæi temere statuerunt, ante fuisse serpeti pedes, eúmque erectiorem ambulauisse, sed tantum sic accipienda hæc vtraque maledictio, vt intelligamus quod ante serpenti fuit non incommodum, illud poltea maledictione factum fuisse incommodissimum. Reptauit igitur prius, sed non ea molestia, aut metu, vel latitandi studio: Simi- litérq; puluerè ponitur labere, sed nō ea necessitate præmebatur quę postea ex maledictione Dei oppressit ipsum. Quapropter Iefchahiæ 65.in descriptione regni Christi, vt ostenderetur animantes quasi uis noxias nemini esse nociturasm futurum dicitur vt serpens comedat de puluere terræ, vt antea. Alter pœnarum locus, v. 15. duo membra continet: vnum, de inimicitiis perpetuis inter genus humanum & Satanam Angelósque illius: Alterum, de effectis inimicitiarum. Ini-micitiarum auctor Deus futurus dicitur pro sua misericordia: primum quidem inter serpentem & fœminam, quam serpens ille seduxerat, secundo interfemen illius serpentis, id est, eos qui corruptionis illius à diabolo importatæ hæredes forent voluntarij & fe-men illius fœmina, id est, Primum quidem Christum, qui caput est Ecclesiæ factus ex fœmina: Deinde eos omnes qui ad Christum in Ecclesia pertinent, quæ corpus est ipsius. Itaque Christum quidem proprie; ad corpus verò & membra ipsius κατ' ἐφαρμογὴν [?] per accommodationem pertinent hæc, analogiæ sequentis membri de euentis inimicitiarum eadem ratio. Nam euentus in partem vtramque prædicitur, agentis, & patientis. Prior quòd Christus per se & Ecclesiam per Christum caput illius contriturus est, id est, vim omnem vitámque serpenti tandem adempturus. Posterior, quòd ille Christo in persona & corpore, Ecclesia scilicet, ipsius contriturus est calcaneum, id est, grauiter quidem admorsurus, sed tum citra periculum, quia Christus vi diuina personæ suæ tum humanitatem suam, tum Ecclesiam sibi adunatam sustentat potentissimé.
units.tr: The first sentence that God pronounces against the serpent has two parts: the sin and the punishment. God states the sin in these words, spoken to the serpent: Because you have done this, that is, you have become a transgressor, as Paul puts it. The punishment, announced against the efficient cause of the sin, has two members. One is the punishment imposed on the serpent as the instrument of the temptation (v. 14). The other is the punishment God declared against Satan, the principal efficient cause of the sin (v. 15). These punishments are joined because the act of temptation was joined, the devil taking the serpent as his instrument. Therefore, when Moses reports that God said these things to the serpent, "serpent" must be taken by synecdoche: both the natural serpent, which was the instrument of sin, and that great and invisible serpent who is said to have been a murderer from the beginning (John 8). The visible serpent receives a threefold punishment. First, it is to be cursed above all cattle and wild beasts, and to suffer every evil more than other animals. Second, it is to go upon its belly, that is, to lurk unseen before humans and other animals. Third, it is to eat dust all the days of its life, that is, it is not to seek its food as comfortably as other animals do, but to relieve its hunger by feeding on the dust of the earth where it hides. Yet we should not therefore think, as the Jews rashly held, that the serpent once had feet and walked more upright. These two curses must be understood only in this way: what was not inconvenient to the serpent before became most inconvenient after the curse. So it crept before, but not with that trouble, fear, or need to hide; likewise it was placed to lick dust, but not under that necessity which afterwards pressed upon it through God's curse. Hence in Isaiah 65, in the description of Christ's kingdom, to show that the noxious animals will harm no one, it is said that the serpent shall eat the dust of the earth, as before. The second punishment, v. 15, has two parts: one concerning the perpetual enmity between the human race and Satan and his angels, the other concerning the effects of that enmity. God is said to be the author of the enmity, in his mercy: first between the serpent and the woman, whom that serpent had seduced; second, between the seed of the serpent, that is, those who became voluntary heirs of that corruption brought in by the devil, and the seed of the woman, that is, first Christ, who was made the head of the Church born of a woman, and then all those who belong to Christ in the Church, which is his body. Thus these things pertain to Christ properly, but to his body and members by application [κατ' ἐφαρμογήν]; the same reasoning applies to the analogous member that follows, concerning the outcome of the enmity. For the outcome is predicted in both respects, of the agent and of the patient. The first: that Christ himself, and the Church through Christ its head, will crush the serpent's head, that is, will at last strip it of all its power and life. The second: that the serpent will bruise the heel of Christ in his person and body, that is, the Church. It will indeed bite severely, but without danger, because Christ by divine power most powerfully sustains both his humanity and the Church joined to him.

units.la: Secundus pœnarum locus est in mulierem, verf. 16. Eius partes sunt quatuor. Nam primùm denuntiantur dolores molestiæque grauissimæ in conceptu & gestatione fœtus muliebri. Secundò quod partui & educationi liberorum laboriosi quoque dolores adiunguntur. Nam hæc synecdochicè opus est intelligi in locutione ista, in do-lore parties liberos, vt 1. Timot. 2. Tertiò quòd fœmina quamuis antea ex lege naturæ subiectæ viro, tum ex peccato amplius conscia infirmitatis suæ, & meticulosa facta cum maiore animi sollicitudine virum suum appetitura est, & ab eo dependebit studiosissimé. Quarto, quòd vir dominabitur in ipsam, id est etiam exercebit ipsam dominatu suo, non sine molestia & cruciatu fœminæ, quia peccato supponit Dominus omnem ordinem interuersum esse: atque hæc pœna sexus muliebris particularis est. Restat tertius pœnarum locus verf. 17. & duobus seqq. in virum quidem proprius, sed fœminæ quoque communis secundum speciei analogiam. Huius denuntiationis partes similiter duæ sunt: Peccatum tamquam suppliciorum causa, & pœna ex peccato consequens. Peccatum viro duplex obiicitur: vnum particulariter, quòd obedierit [?] voci vxoris suæ: alterum com-mune, mune, quod comederit homo de fructu, &c. Hic enim peccatum fuit in Adamo duplex; unum, quòd præposterè obediuit ei cui non fuerat obediendum: Alterum, quòd non obediuit cui obedire & religione & natura debuerat. Pœnarum, quas Deus homini denuntiat, duo sunt genera: unum, earum molestiarum quæ antecedunt mortem & præsentem vitam condiunt miseriis: alterum, mortis ipsius quam Deus ante denuntiauerat, & distulit quidem, sed non plane sustulit dilatione sua. Pœnarum antecedentium mortem genus est maledictio Dei, species verò hæ à Deo indictæ sunt: Maledictio domicilij ipsius propter peccatum hominis, maledicta terra, &c. tum maledictus usus quem homo inde percepturus est, in dolore comedes. Tertium maledictus fructus, quòd pro bono malum, pro utili damnosum terra allatura est, verf. 18. Quartò priuatio horti Hedenis, & collocatio in sede communi cum animantibus reliquis: comedes herbam agri. Postremo violentus labor & sudores grauissimi ab homine occupandi ut cibum suum, quasi extorqueat ingemiscenti propter maledictionem terræ. verf. 19. in sudore vultus tui comedes, Et quidem indesinenter dum vivet: quod grauissima periphrasi denotauit Deus his verbis, usque dum reverteris in terram, quia inde sumptus es: qua periphrasi fit transitus ad alterum pœnarum genus quod posteriore membro exponitur: quia pulvis es, etiam in pulverem reverteris, id est, peribis mala morte. Atque hæ quidem sententiæ cum in fœminam, tum in virum pronuntiatæ sunt, ut pœnam peccati sui tum in sese, quia personæ singulares erant; tum in suis posteris, quia principia erant generis sui ac velut radices, experirentur. verum tamen in ea ipsa pœna, quam sanciuit Dominus, testimonia misericordiæ extiterunt peccatores ad resipiscentiam à malo suo & fiduciam bonitatis divinæ reuocantis: cuiusmodi illud est, quod etsi absolutè Deus pronunciauerat cap. 2. homines morte morituros, tamen illis indulsit tempus per quod conscientia vanitatis & mortis suæ affecti & horrore peccati illam Dei benignitatem in sese agnoscerent. Ac propterea quamuis reos mortis præsentissimæ, tamen Deus in hac vita degere permisit, & spem fecit melioris vitæ resipiscentibus dum in via essent. Sententiæ itaque partes duæ ponendæ sunt: quarum una expressa est, pœnæ denunciatio; altera tacita, conditionis implicatio de liberatione à pœna, & vitæ æternæ communicatione, victa carne, peccato, morte, & principe mortis diabolo in semine promisso mulieris, breui Satanam sub nostris pedibus contri-turo. Ac proinde exsequutionis, qui ultimus est capitis locus,
units.tr: The second place of punishments is on the woman, v. 16. It has four parts. First, the most grievous pains and troubles are announced for the conception and bearing of the child. Second, laborious pains are also joined to the birth and the rearing of children. For this must be understood by synecdoche in the phrase in pain you shall bring forth children, as in 1 Timothy 2. Third, although the woman was before subject to her husband by the law of nature, now, made more conscious of her weakness through sin and become timid, she shall desire her husband with greater anxiety of mind, and shall depend on him most eagerly. Fourth, the husband shall rule over her, that is, he will also exercise his lordship over her, not without trouble and torment to the woman, because sin, as the Lord counts it, overturns all order. This punishment is peculiar to the female sex. There remains the third place of punishments, v. 17 and the two following, proper to the man, but common to the woman as well, according to the analogy of the species. The parts of this announcement are likewise two: the sin, as the cause of the punishments, and the punishment that follows from the sin. The man is charged with a twofold sin: one particular, that he obeyed the voice of his wife; the other common to all, that man ate of the fruit, and so on. For in Adam the sin was twofold: first, that he obeyed out of order the one to whom he should not have been obedient; second, that he did not obey the one to whom he owed obedience by both religion and nature. Of the punishments which God announces to man there are two kinds: one of the troubles that precede death and season the present life with miseries; the other of death itself, which God had announced before, and which he indeed deferred, but did not altogether remove by his delay. The kind of punishments preceding death is the curse of God, and its species are those pronounced by God: the curse on his very dwelling because of man's sin, cursed is the earth, and so on; then the cursed use which man will derive from it, in pain you shall eat. Third, cursed fruit, because the earth will bring forth evil instead of good and harm instead of profit (v. 18). Fourth, the deprivation of the garden of Eden, and his placing in a common state with the other animals: you shall eat the herb of the field. Last, violent labour and the heaviest sweats, by which man must wrest his food, as it were, groaning, from the cursed earth (v. 19): in the sweat of your face you shall eat, and indeed without ceasing for as long as he lives. God expressed this in a most weighty periphrasis in these words: until you return to the earth, because from it you were taken. By this periphrasis there is a transition to the other kind of punishment, which is set out in the last member: because you are dust, to dust you shall return as well, that is, you shall perish by an evil death. These sentences were pronounced on both the woman and the man, so that they might experience the punishment of their sin both in themselves, because they were single persons, and in their posterity, because they were the beginnings of their race and, as it were, its roots. Yet even in that punishment which the Lord ordained, there were testimonies of mercy, calling sinners back to repentance from their evil and to confidence in the goodness of God. Such is this: although God had absolutely declared in chapter 2 that men would die, he granted them a time in which, struck by awareness of their own vanity and mortality and by horror of sin, they might recognise that kindness of God within themselves. Therefore, although they were guilty of immediate death, God allowed them to remain in this life and gave hope of a better life to those who repented while they were still on the way. So the sentence has two parts to be set down: one expressed, the announcement of punishment; the other tacit, the implied condition of deliverance from punishment and the bestowal of eternal life, through the promised seed of the woman, who will crush Satan under our feet shortly, after flesh, sin, death, and the devil, the prince of death, have been conquered. And so the execution, which is the last place of the chapter,

units.la: duæ partes ordine à Mosè proponuntur: vna, testimoniorum bonitatis Dei, dum in hac vita senescimus, verf. 20. & seq.: altera iudiciorum, reliquis. Testimonia diuinæ bonitatis erga indignos atque ingratos peccatores duo sunt; vnum est indulgentia vitæ, quod vita homini, quamuis reo præsentissimæ mortis, permittitur, v.20: alterum commoditatum ad tolerandam hanc vitam pertinentium, v.21. Præsentis vitæ concessio indulgentiaque duobus modis testata est, professione Adami, & causa illius. Professio Adami hæc fuit, quòd conscius peccati & mortis acquisitæ peccato, agnouit tamen & testatus est vxoris suæ appellatione acceptum Dei beneficium in immerentes collatum: nam propterea vxorem suam appellauit Chauam: Cuius nominis interpretatio secundum formam ipsius non est proprie Vita aut viuens, sed conseruans in vita (habet enim formam 2. coniug.) Sic duplex Dei beneficium Adam professus est: vitæ suæ conseruationem in vtroque indiuiduo, & speciei conseruationem in propagatione naturali. Huius verò nominis causam sequitur verbis exponit Moses dicens, eo quòd ipsa fit Mater cuiusque viuentis, nimirum hominis, cui ζωῆς tribuitur hæc appellatio. Alter miseri-cordiæ diuinæ locus exponitur, v.21. quâuis synecdochicè, quòd Deus homini de commodis ad vitæ huius necessitate honestatémque pertinentibus prospexerit: huc enim spectabat Moses, cùm Iehouam fecisse scribit Adamo & vxori eius vestes pelliceas & eas induisse. Sequitur alter locus, de exsequutione suppliciorum, quæ Deus proximè præcedentibus versibus indixerat. In narratione illius duo habentur membra, consilij, v.22. & facti, duobus vltimis. Consilij auctor dicitur Iehoua Deus, quam appellationem ante cap.1. sumus interpretati. Consilium autem capere dicitur humanitus in deturbando homine, prouit in faciendo homine cepisse dictus est supra 1.26. Propter rei gravitatem & ad summum quasi tædium in exequendo isto iudicio demonstrandum. In Consilio tres partes sunt obseruandæ; subiectum fiue materia de qua consilium capiendum fuit ex præsente facto; summa consilij vel deliberationis, & finis illius. Subiectum Deus proponit Ecce, inquit Deus, homo iste fuerit factus sicut vnus ex nobis cognoscendo bono & malo? quam loquutionem Latinè infinito modo expresseris, Hominem factum esse? &c. Sunt enim verba non ridentis, aut illudentis homini misero; sed indignantis proteruiam illius, qui tantam insaniam animo suo indiderit, vt se Deo parem fore consideret, scietiam boni & mali assequutum. duplex itaque hic testimonium habetur sanctæ trinitatis. Primum quòd Iehoua Elohim appellatur: secundo quòd dicitur, sicut vnus è nobis. Deliberationis vel rei consilio capto faciendæ, hoc quidem in versu mentio nulla est. Sed subintelligi demonstratur duobus modis: Primum ellipsi ordinaria apud Hebræos ante particulam, ne forte: secundo autem sequentium versuum historia. Nam ex his rebus inter se comparatis facile quiuis intelligat id Deū cepisse consilij, vt homine ex horto eiiceret, & ingressum in hortum occluderet. Huius consilij institutum à Deo demonstratur hac sola particula, nunc igitur, nempe postquam homo tentauit vt sibi hanc æqualitatem assumeret, oportet semel iudicium fieri. cuius consilij finis, (quem tertium esse locum monuimus) demonstratur his verbis, ne immittat manum suam, &c. Quo in fine duo distinctè sunt observanda: vnum, quem finem sibi proponat Deus: alterum, quem homo peccator. Finis Deo propositus hic fuisse dicitur, vt impediret hominem ne immittens manum accipe ret de fructu arboris vitæ. Finis autem homini propositus fuit, si de fructu illo caperet vt comederet victurus in seculum. Ac suum quidem finem Deus assequutus est, ne homo iniecta manu caperet de fructu illius arboris: suum vero finem homo non fuisset assequuturus, etiam si cepisset de illo fructu atque comedisset. Spondet enim sibi peccator hypocrita fore, vt percepto sacramento tamquam ex opere operato finem adipiscatur veritatemque sacramenti: Deus vero infinita sua prouidentia prospectum voluit, ne hypocrita vel attingendi sacramenti fiduciam conciperet, multo minus veritatis ex operato opere assequendæ. Ex hoc consilio sequitur exsequutio duobus membris comprehensa. Prius est quod homo ex horto Hedenis, id est, summa illa amœnitate est dimissus imò etiam eiectus, vt principio versus vltimi exponitur. Et relegatus ad colendam terram vnde sumptus fuerat. Alterum est, quod eo eiecto aditus præpeditus est, vers. vltimo. Eiectionem hominis quæ narratur vers.22. duæ res acerbiorem effecerunt; vna, quod eijceretur ex horto Hedenis, id est, delitiarum amœnitatumque, quem Deus omnibus vitæ commodis instruxerat locupletissimè, vt cum reliquis animatibus sedes sibi quæreret. Altera est quod iniectus est in labore culturæ molestissimum, & quidem illius terræ vnde sumptus fuerat, supra quam Deus hortum Hedenis omni benedictionum genere cumulauerat. Alter locus de exilio vers. vltimo proponitur duobus modis: Primum quod homo fugatus est turpissimè ex amplissima illa & principali statione quam prius obtinuerat: deinde quod Deus regiam illam stationem hominis ita circumsepiuit, vt nullus homini aditus ad eum locum patesceret, sed in perpetuitatem homo sua Basilica priuatus permaneret. Huius autem exilij perpetuitatem Deus signo aspectabili dicitur ostendisse, in secunda parte versus. Nam primum administri iudiciorum Dei ad perpetuitatem exsilij ponuntur duo: Cherubim, id est, angeli e coelo: & flam-ma gladÿ, id est, gladius flammans, per ὑπάγω[?]: tum actio illius gladij quod sese versaret, id est, huc illuc differretur flamma, prout a natura mobilis est & sequax: tum circumstantias adhibet Moses quod Deus fecit ut habitarent, id est, in diuturnitate sedes fixas eo in loco obtinerent, & quidem ab interiore parte horti Hedenis, id est quacumque aditus patere homini posset: postremo autem narratur finis ut observarent viam ad arborem vitæ, id est, homini iter praecluderent, ne forte de fructu arboris illius perciperet, quemadmodum antecedente consilio Deus pronuntiauerat. Hic autem variae quastiones oriri solent, prima de Cherubinis & natura ipsorum, quos cum vulgo interpretum pro Angelis accipimus. Altera de habitatione ipsorum in loco, quam alij commorationem fuisse putant: Nos habitationem vertimus ad ostenden-dam diuturnitatem exsilij. Nam quod alij paulo post haec fi-gna a Deo sublata esse: alij per diluuium putant: alij alio modo, cogitationes sunt mihi quidem incertae, utcumque aliis certæ videantur. Neque enim Moses de circumscriptione loci tam adcurate fuisset laboraturus, nisi etiam per ea tempora vestigium aliquod iudicij istius permansisset. Postrema quastio est de flamma gladij sese circumuersantis, id est, flamma velut gladio circumlambente totam illam sedem in quam tam honorificè fuerat homo a Deo collocatus. Fortasse locus ille fuerit in Babylonia, cuius mentionem alibi nusquam extare memini quam apud Plinium lib. 2. Nat. hist. scribentem his verbis, campus Babyloniæ flagrat quadam velut piscina iugeri magnitudine.
units.tr: Moses sets out two parts in order: first, the testimonies of God's goodness while we grow old in this life (v. 20 ff.), and second, the judgments that follow. There are two testimonies of the divine goodness towards unworthy and ungrateful sinners. The first is the indulgence of life, in that life is granted to a man who is guilty of immediate death, v. 20. The second is the provision of things pertaining to bearing this life, v. 21. The grant and indulgence of present life was attested in two ways, by Adam's profession and by its cause. Adam's profession was this: although he was conscious of sin and of the death gained through sin, he nevertheless acknowledged and attested, by the name of his wife, the benefit of God bestowed on undeserving men. For this reason he named his wife Chauam. The interpretation of this name, according to its form, is not properly "life" or "living," but "preserving in life" (for it has the form of the second conjugation). Thus Adam professed a twofold benefit of God: the preservation of his own life in each individual, and the preservation of the species by natural propagation. Moses gives the cause of this name in the words that follow: because she is the mother of every living thing, namely of man, to whom this appellation of life [ζωῆς] is given. The other place of divine mercy is set out in v. 21, though by synecdoche, in that God provided man with the things pertaining to the necessity and decency of this life. Moses was looking to this when he wrote that Jehovah made garments of skins for Adam and his wife and clothed them. There follows the second part, concerning the execution of the punishments that God had decreed in the preceding verses. In its narrative there are two members: the counsel, v. 22, and the deed, in the last two verses. The author of the counsel is called Jehovah God, a name which we explained before chapter 1. Now, to take counsel is said of God in a human manner, in expelling man; in making man, he is said to have taken counsel above, at 1:26. This is on account of the gravity of the matter, and to show, as it were, his supreme displeasure in carrying out this judgment. In the counsel three parts are to be observed: the subject, or matter, about which counsel was to be taken from the present fact; the sum of the counsel or deliberation; and its end. God sets forth the subject with Behold, says God, this man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil? Which phrase, if you render it in Latin with an infinitive, would be "that man has been made," etc. For these are not the words of one who mocks or makes sport of a wretched man, but of one who is indignant at his insolence, who had put into his mind such madness that he thought he would be equal to God, having attained the knowledge of good and evil. Thus there is a twofold testimony here of the holy Trinity: first, that he is called Jehovah Elohim; second, that it is said, like one of us. Of the deliberation, or the matter to be done after counsel was taken, there is indeed no mention in this verse. But it is shown to be understood in two ways: first, by the ordinary ellipsis among the Hebrews before the particle lest perhaps; second, by the history of the verses that follow. For anyone who compares these things with one another will easily understand that God took counsel to cast man out of the garden and to shut the way into the garden. The institution of this counsel by God is shown by this single particle, now therefore, namely, after man tried to assume this equality for himself, it is necessary that judgment be made once. The end of this counsel (which we noted as the third place) is shown by these words, lest he put forth his hand, etc. In this end two things are to be observed distinctly: one, what end God proposed to himself; the other, what end the sinner proposed. The end proposed by God was, as is said, to hinder man lest, putting forth his hand, he take of the fruit of the tree of life. The end proposed to man was that, if he took of that fruit, he would eat and live for ever. God indeed attained his end, that man should not put forth his hand and take of the fruit of that tree; but man would not have attained his end, even if he had taken of that fruit and eaten it. For the hypocritical sinner promises himself that, having received the sacrament, he will obtain its end and the truth of the sacrament as if by the work worked (ex opere operato). But God, by his infinite providence, willed that provision be made lest the hypocrite should conceive confidence either of touching the sacrament, much less of attaining the truth of it by the work worked. From this counsel follows the execution, comprised in two members. The first is that man was sent out, indeed even cast out, from the garden of Eden, that is, from that supreme pleasantness, as is explained at the beginning of the last verse; and he was banished to till the ground from which he had been taken. The second is that, once he was cast out, access was blocked, in the last verse. Two things made the casting out of man, which is related in v. 22, more bitter: one, that he was cast out of the garden of Eden, that is, of delights and pleasantnesses, which God had most richly furnished with all the conveniences of life, so that he might seek a dwelling for himself with the other animals; the other, that he was thrown into the most troublesome labour of cultivation, and that of the very land from which he had been taken, above which God had heaped the garden of Eden with every kind of blessing. The other place, concerning exile, is set forth in the last verse in two ways. First, that man was driven out most shamefully from that ample and principal station which he had held before; then, that God so fenced around that royal station of man that no access to that place lay open to man, but man remained deprived of his court for ever. Now God is said to have shown the perpetuity of this exile by a visible sign, in the second part of the verse. For the first agents of God's judgments, appointed for the perpetuity of the exile, are two: the cherubim, that is, angels from heaven; and the flame of a sword, that is, a flaming sword, by a figure of speech. Then the action of that sword is given, that it turned itself, that is, the flame was moved hither and thither, as it is by nature mobile and changeable. Then Moses adds the circumstances: God did it that they might dwell, that is, that they should hold fixed seats in that place for a long time, and indeed on the east side of the garden of Eden, that is, wherever access might lie open to man. Lastly, the end is related: that they might keep the way to the tree of life, that is, that they should block man's path, lest perhaps he should take of the fruit of that tree, as God had pronounced in the preceding counsel. Here various questions are wont to arise. The first is about the cherubim and their nature, whom we take, with the common run of interpreters, as angels. The second is about their dwelling in the place, which others think was a sojourn; we have rendered it a dwelling, to show the perpetuity of the exile. For as to what others think, that these signs were taken away by God shortly afterwards, and others think it was by the flood, and others in another way: these are indeed uncertain thoughts to me, however they may seem certain to others. For Moses would not have troubled so exactly about the circumscription of the place, unless some trace of that judgment had remained even in those times. The last question is about the flame of the revolving sword, that is, a flame as if a sword were licking all round that whole seat in which man had been so honourably placed by God. Perhaps that place was in Babylonia, of which I remember no mention anywhere else than in Pliny, Natural History book 2, writing in these words: the plain of Babylon blazes with a certain pool, as it were, the size of an acre.

units.la: HACTENUS subiectum historiæ sacræ fuit expositum, nimirum creatio mundi & Ecclesiæ a Domino, constitutióque integra & corrupta illius. Sequitur deinceps historia rerum in Ecclesia gestarum, ad illud usque tempus quo Ia-cob & Ioseph in Ægypto exsularunt. Huius autem historiæ partes summas hoc in libro duas poni necesse est; Unam, historiam veteris mundi, pro ut a Petro appellatur, ad caput usque 8. Alteram vero, historiam mundi ex diluuio illo funesto re-creati, reliquo in libro. Ad historiam veteris mundi duo sum-matim pertinent. Primum narratio peccatorum illius & constantis Dei erga suos misericordiae in tanta peccatorum fæce, cap. quarto & quinto. Alterum, iudicia Dei seuerissima in rebellem mundum cap. sexto & septimo. In priore membro duo distincte pronuntur, auctore Mose; narratio mundi & peccatorum quibus se miser ille mundus contaminauerat, cap. 4. & narratio Ecclesiae ac misericordiae, qua Deus propter Christum semen electum prosequutus est, cap. 5. peccatorum quae in hoc cap. exponuntur, duo sunt gradus: Unus est, Caini in fratre suo persequentis Ecclesiam Dei, ad vers. usque 17: Alter est posterorum Caini impietatem & iniustitiam certatim aemulantium, ad vers. usque 25. quibus postremo tamquam μετάβασις[?] conclusio capitis subiicitur de nouo Adami filio, ut commodius ad historiam capitis sequentis transeatur. Id autem communiter in huiusmodi narrationibus opus est obseruari, Deum singula singulorum peccata, aut etiam multa, non solere perse-qui in narratione; sed pauca tantum, ex uno aut altero docens iudicium de reliqua instituta illorum vita fieri oportere. Antequam vero historia illa exponatur, ortus duorum fratrum, vers. 1. & 2. describitur, Caini & Hebeli. utriusque ortus antecedentia duo sunt, concubitus naturalis, & conceptus gestatioque in utero: Hinc enim sequitur partus, & partui coniuncta denominatio. Prioris partus nomen fuisse dicitur Cain: causa nominis impositi, sancta, quod se mulier virum acquisiuisse à Iehoua agnosceret, cum alioquin Adam & uxor ipsius malefacto suo omnem gratiam benedictionem-que Domini à se abalienauissent. Hanc enim interpretatione omnibus modis illi anteposuerim[?] quae a multis hoc tempore defenditur, {†}Acquisiui virum Iehouam: Nam etsi speciosa videtur ratio, quod Eua respexerit ad semen illud promissum supra 3.15. Tamen mihi dubium videri non potest, quin Eua probe memincrit semen fœminæ non autem viri & mulieris promissum esse: sibi vero hunc filium non ex pro-missione singulari, sed ex naturali ordine & congressu viri fuisse datum.
units.tr: Hitherto the subject of sacred history has been set out, namely the creation of the world and of the Church by the Lord, and its constitution, both whole and corrupted. There follows next the history of the things done in the Church, down to the time when Jacob and Joseph went into exile in Egypt. Of this history two main parts must be laid down in this book. The first is the history of the old world, as Peter calls it, to chapter 8. The second is the history of the world re-created after that deadly flood, in the rest of the book. Two things pertain in summary to the history of the old world. The first is the narration of that world's sins and of God's constant mercy towards his own amid so great a dregs of sinners, chapters 4 and 5. The second is the most severe judgments of God against the rebellious world, chapters 6 and 7. In the former part two things are set forth distinctly, Moses being the author: the account of the world and of the sins with which that wretched world had defiled itself, chapter 4; and the account of the Church and of the mercy by which God, for the sake of Christ the chosen seed, pursued it, chapter 5. The sins set out in this chapter are of two degrees. One is that of Cain persecuting the Church of God in his brother, to verse 17. The other is that of the posterity of Cain vying eagerly with one another in impiety and injustice, to verse 25. To these, last, as a transition [μετάβασις], is added the conclusion of the chapter concerning the new son of Adam, so that one may pass more conveniently to the history of the following chapter. Now in narratives of this kind it is commonly necessary to observe that God does not usually pursue in the narrative each single sin of each person, or even many; but only a few, teaching from one or another instance that a judgment about the rest of their life ought to be made. Before that history is expounded, the birth of the two brothers, Cain and Abel, is described in verses 1 and 2. Antecedent to the birth of each are two things: natural intercourse, and conception and carrying in the womb; for from these follows the birth, and with the birth the naming. The name of the first birth is said to have been Cain, and the cause of the name given is a holy one: that the woman recognised she had gotten a man from Jehovah. Otherwise Adam and his wife, by their wrongdoing, had alienated from themselves all grace and the blessing of the Lord. For I would prefer this interpretation in every way to that other one, which is defended by many at this time, I have gotten a man, Jehovah. For although the reason seems specious, that Eve looked to that promised seed mentioned above at 3:15, yet it cannot seem doubtful to me that Eve knew well that the seed of the woman, not of the man and woman, had been promised; and that this son was given to her not by a special promise but by the natural order and union of man and wife.

units.la: Incœptam Dei benedictionem in propagatione humani generis Deus porrexisse dicitur 2. v. cum filius alter primis parentibus dicitur fuisse datus: & parentum quoque pietas eo ostenditur, quod filio nomen imposuerunt Hebel, ad vanitatis nostrae testificationem. de his ergo duobus subiectis duarū Ecclesiarum, verae & falsae, siue duarum ciuitatū[?], nempe ciuitatis Dei & ciuitatis diaboli, typis, narratio post instituitur.Huius narrationis partes tres statuedę sunt. Prima de occasionibus,à v.2.ad 7.vsque : secunda de facto, versu, 8: postrema de rebus ex facto consequuutis,ver.9. & seqq. Summa est Ecclesiam Dei cum Ecclesia Satanæ in terris promiscuè versari, ab eáque affligi & persecquutionibus infestari,donec cumulata iniquitate sua iudiciū si- bi accersiuerit. Occasionū loci duo sunt;vnus cōmunis, ab instituto vitæ,secunda parte2.vers. Alter particularis,ex facto duorum fratrū, institutum Hebeli fuisse dicitur vita pastoritia; Caini, agricolatio; vtrumque sanctum per se ,sed hominum vitio facilè inquinatum,vt ex Caini exemplo ostenditur. Ex illo vitæ instituto genera oblatio- num diuersa orta sunt, quòd Cain munus obtulit de fructu terræ, id est, incruentum : qua ratione videtur vtcumque Deo satisfacere potius quàm effusione sanguinis profiteri se remissionem peccato- rum in sacrificio Christi percipere.Huic vero ex opposito Hebel sa- crificium dicitur obtulisse de grege suo,& adipem adoleuisse Domi- no,fide professus se vtrumque à Deo in Christo exspectare cum re- missionem peccatorum in sanguine, tum nouitatem sui in spiritu & igne. Huic facto duorum fratrum duo adiuncta narrantur à Domi- no; primùm testificatio quam perhibuit muneribus, vers. 4. & 5. Deinde verò reprehensio & reuocatio Caini, vers. 6.& 7. Testifi- catio vna est comprobationis secunda parte, vers. 4. altera impro- bationis, vers. 5. Comprobationem Moses à Deo factam scri- bit humanitus respexit Iehoua ad Hebelem. Cuius comprobationis duo sunt membra ; prius, quòd persona grata est & accepta Domino: posterius quòd ex persona grata oblationes quoque censentur gra- tæ:etsi vtrumque gratum est non propter dignitatem suam ,sed propter gra- tiam paternam Dei. Improbationem similiter describit Moses fuisse duplicem; primùm personæ Caini, secundò autem muneris, quia(vt ait sapiens) sacrificium impij abominationi est Iehouæ. Quæritur quo modo sit testificatus Deus? Responsio est, modo aspectabili, quo & pium Hebelem confirmauit & impium Cainum grauius assi- ceret.Nondum satis est. Quæritur quis ille modus aspectabilis, quem Apostolus ad Heb.11.confirmaret.Responsio est,nobis certò ex scri- pturis (si bene memini) constare non posse. verum tamen consensus ferme omnium Hebræorum est, aliorúmque præterea interpretum, ignem cælitus demissum esse : quapropter vertebat Aquila ἐνπῦρ. Qua testificatione immissa in sacrificiū Hebeli, & ad sacrificiū Cai- ni omissa,facilè fuit Caino recognoscere voluntateDei.Etsi autē cæ- leste illud testimoniū ad frangendū Caini fuit animū potentissimum, tamen,quod solet hypocrisis,id fecit Cain: Non enim succensuit sibi ipsi, vt sibi suaeque vitiositati renuntiaret; sed contra animo percepit & vultu tcstificatus est impium fastidium, & quidem vehemens, aduersus illam testificationem Dei: quapropter alterū quoque adiumentum adhibuit Deus, & quemadmodum signo Cainum commonefecerat, sic etiam verbo monuisse dicitur, v.6. & 7. Moniti partes duae sunt; prior, reprehensio constitutionis malae, v.6: posterior, revocatio ad bonum, v. 7. Malam constitutionem vtramque, de qua modo dicebamus, reprehendit Deus communicatione dicens, Quare exarsit tibi ira? & quare cecidit vultus tuus? Reuocationem ad bonum Deus adhibet sequente vers. duobus modis: Primum ab euentu futuro hypotheticēs: secundo a dignitatis praesentis contemplatione. Prioris loci hypothesis est haec; Aut bene facturus es ô Caine & emendaturus viam tuam, aut malefacturus: iam vero (nam Deus vtitur eadem communicatione,) appello conscientiam tuam, quis huius rei euentus futurus sit. Nonne si benefeceris condonatio tibi futura est, videlicet peccatorum tuorum? siue, vt interpretantur alij, Elatio faciei tuae quae concidit? quemadmodum Dauid in Psalm. 3. dicit Domino, Tu es gloria mea & efferens caput meum. Sin autem non benefeceris, nonne peccatum & supplicium illius condonationi oppositum iamiam prae foribus excubat vt poenas des vindice Domino? A contemplatione dignitatis praesentis Deus Cainum reuocat hoc argumento, indignum est inuidere quemquam ei qui totus ab ipso pendet & in quem dominatur. Hebeli autem fratris tui appetitus totus fertur ad te, & tu dominaris in illum puta fratrem tuum vt minorem natu; te itaque inuidere illi & succensere indignum est, quem potius memorem beneficiorum, auctoritatis, & gratiae a Deo acceptae oportuit fratri vt maiorem minori consulere, maxime cum inde a principio primogenitam dignitatem maximam eo habuerint, quod adumbrarent primogenitorum Christi seruatoris nostri. Hactenus occasiones: sequitur factum, quod ex his occasionibus Cain instituit duplex: prius est, strenua dissimulatio maleuolentiae, & quasi fraterna communicatio in tantis odiis, priore membro: posterius est cruenta caedes quam perpetrauit Cain, posteriore membro 8.v. Dissimulatio his verbis significatur: Alloquutus est Cain Hebelum fratrem suum, id est, nec vultu nec sermone odium quod intus coquebat declarauit. Caedem apertis verbis Moses narrat, & captatam occasionem illius, cum essent in agro. Hinc sequitur locus tertius de rebus ex maleficio isto consequutis. Eae sunt, primum cognitio, v.9. & 10: secundo, sententiae dictio, v.11. & 12: tertio, scelerati expostulatio & Dei responsio, appendix antecedentis sententiæ ver.13. & duobus sequentibus. postremo exsequutio verf.16. & 17.
units.tr: God is said to have extended the blessing begun in the propagation of the human race in verse 2, when a second son is said to have been given to the first parents. The piety of the parents is also shown by this, that they gave the son the name Abel, as a testimony to our vanity. Therefore, from these two subjects, the two Churches, true and false, or the two cities, namely the city of God and the city of the devil, figured in them, the narrative is next instituted. Three parts of this narrative must be established. The first concerns the occasions, from verse 2 to 7; the second the deed, verse 8; the last the things that followed from the deed, verse 9 and following. The summary is that the Church of God and the Church of Satan dwell promiscuously together on earth, and that the former is assailed and harassed with persecutions by the latter, until the latter, having piled up its iniquity, summons judgment upon itself. There are two places of occasions: one common, from the manner of life, in the second part of verse 2; the other particular, from the deed of the two brothers. It is said that the manner of life of Abel was pastoral and that of Cain agricultural; each is holy in itself, but easily polluted by the fault of men, as the example of Cain shows. From that manner of life there arose different kinds of offerings, because Cain offered a gift from the fruit of the earth, that is, a bloodless one. By this means he seems somehow to satisfy God, rather than to profess by the shedding of blood that he receives the remission of sins in the sacrifice of Christ. Abel, on the contrary, is said to have offered a sacrifice from his flock and to have burned its fat to the Lord, professing in faith that he expected from God in Christ both the remission of sins in blood and the newness of himself in spirit and fire. Two things joined to this deed of the two brothers are related by the Lord: first, the testimony he gave to the gifts, verses 4 and 5; then the rebuke and recall of Cain, verses 6 and 7. The testimony is one of approval in the second part, verse 4, and another of disapproval, verse 5. Moses writes that the approval was made by God in the manner of men: Jehovah looked upon Abel. Of this approval there are two parts: the first, that the person is pleasing and acceptable to the Lord; the second, that from the acceptable person the offerings also are judged acceptable. Yet both are pleasing not because of their own worth, but because of the fatherly grace of God. Likewise Moses describes the disapproval as twofold: first of the person of Cain, and second of his gift, because (as the wise man says) the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to Jehovah. The question is in what way God gave testimony. The answer is, in a visible way, by which he both confirmed pious Abel and more gravely afflicted impious Cain. This is not yet enough. The question is what that visible manner was, which the Apostle confirms at Heb. 11. The answer is that it cannot certainly be established for us from the Scriptures (if I remember rightly). Yet there is almost universal agreement of the Hebrews, and of other interpreters besides, that fire was sent down from heaven; wherefore Aquila rendered it [ἐν πυρί], in fire. With this testimony sent upon Abel's sacrifice, and withheld from Cain's, it was easy for Cain to recognise the will of God. And although that heavenly testimony was most powerful for breaking Cain's spirit, nevertheless Cain did what hypocrisy customarily does. He did not become angry with himself so as to renounce himself and his own wickedness; on the contrary, he showed in his mind and countenance an impious disdain, and indeed a vehement one, against that testimony of God. Wherefore God applied a second help, and as he had admonished Cain by sign, so he is said to have admonished him also by word, verses 6 and 7. The admonition has two parts: the first, a rebuke of the wrong disposition, verse 6; the second, a recall to good, verse 7. God rebukes that wrong disposition, of both kinds of which we were just speaking, by a question, saying, Why has anger flared up for you? and why has your countenance fallen? God applies the recall to good in the following verse in two ways: first from a future outcome, hypothetically; second from the contemplation of present dignity. The hypothesis of the first is this: either you will do well, O Cain, and amend your way, or you will do evil. Now (for God uses the same figure) I call upon your conscience to say what the outcome of this matter will be. Will not forgiveness be given you, if you do well, namely of your sins? Or, as others interpret, the lifting up of your face which has fallen? Just as David in Psalm 3 says to the Lord, You are my glory and the lifter of my head. But if you do not do well, does not sin, and its punishment opposed to forgiveness, already lie in wait at the doors, so that you will pay the penalties with the Lord as avenger? From the contemplation of present dignity God recalls Cain with this argument: it is unworthy to envy anyone who depends wholly on you and over whom you rule. Your brother Abel's desire is wholly directed to you, and you rule over him. Suppose him your brother as younger by birth: it is therefore unworthy for you to envy him and be angry with him. Rather, mindful of the benefits, authority and grace received from God, you ought, as the elder, to care for your younger brother; especially since from the beginning they had the greatest dignity of the firstborn, because they foreshadowed Christ our Saviour, the firstborn. Thus far the occasions. There follows the deed, which Cain made from these occasions in a twofold way: the first is a vigorous dissimulation of ill will, and a kind of brotherly fellowship amid such hatreds, in the former member; the second is the bloody slaughter that Cain perpetrated, in the latter member, verse 8. The dissimulation is signified by these words: Cain spoke to Abel his brother, that is, he declared by neither countenance nor speech the hatred he was boiling within. Moses narrates the slaughter in plain words, and the opportunity seized for it: when they were in the field. Hence follows the third place, concerning the things that followed from this wickedness. These are, first, the inquiry, verses 9 and 10; second, the pronouncing of sentence, verses 11 and 12; third, the wicked man's expostulation and God's response, an appendix to the preceding sentence, verse 13 and the two following; last, the execution, verses 16 and 17.

units.la: Cognitione Deus forensi modo instituit: primo, quæstione, versu nono, deinde vero, euictione, versu decimo. Quæstionem Deus instituit his verbis compellans reum, Vbi est Hebel frater tuus? Qua quæstione Deus vtitur non sciscitandi animo (noverat enim) sed potius excitandi: & adiecta blanda fratris appellatione Caini confscientiam amplius verberat. Ad quæstionem Reus ferociter respondisse dicitur duobus modis: Primum quidem mendacio, quo inficiatur crimen: secundo exceptione, qua negat suum fuisse officium vt custos fratris esset: ac proinde custodiam illius à se præstari non oportere. Hanc ferocem responsionem sequitur alter inquisitionis locus, euictio, verf. decimo. qua primum confscientiam Caini appellat testem, dicens, quid fecisti? Secundo producit testimonia tum sanguinis fraterni indigne fusi, tum etiam terræ quæ sanguinem illum exceperat.
units.tr: God conducted the examination in the manner of a court of law: first by a question, in verse nine, and then by refutation, in verse ten. He put the question to the accused in these words: Where is Abel your brother? God uses this question not to find out (for he knew), but to provoke Cain, and by adding the gentle name of brother he strikes Cain's conscience more sharply. It is said that the accused answered defiantly in two ways: first by a lie, denying the crime; second by an excuse, saying that it was not his duty to be his brother's keeper, and that he therefore ought not to be bound to guard him. This defiant answer is followed by the second part of the inquiry, the refutation, in verse ten. In it God first calls Cain's conscience as a witness, saying, What have you done? Second, he produces as witnesses both the blood of his brother unjustly shed and the earth which had received that blood.

units.la: Tamquam si Deus diceret, quandoquidem Cain testibus euincei cupit, & per illud tempus non fuerunt qui aut testarentur, aut maleficium eiusmodi perpetrarent, rem præsentem satis esse ad fratricidam euincendum, nempe tum sanguinem ipsius cruentantem terram ac velut clamantem iniuriam & vltionem poscentem à Domino, (quo spectauit Apostolus ad Hebræos, dicens sanguinem Christi proferre longe meliora quam sanguis Hebeli fecerit) tum vero terram sanguine illo cruentatam. Sic ergo Cainum euincit Deus. Nemo fuit qui fratrem occidere potuerit præter te. Occisum autem esse sanguis ipsius & terra cruentata clamant: Clamant igitur maleficium tuum. Ex cognitione sententia sequitur v. 11. & 12. cuius partes duæ sunt: prior, qua maledictio; posterior, qua maledictionis adiuncta in Cainum pronuntiantur.
units.tr: It is as if God were saying: since Cain wishes to be refuted by witnesses, and at that time there were no one who could either bear witness or commit such a crime, the present fact is enough to convict the fratricide, namely the blood itself staining the earth and, as it were, crying out an injury and demanding vengeance from the Lord (to which the Apostle looked when he wrote to the Hebrews, saying that the blood of Christ speaks better things than the blood of Abel); and then the earth itself, stained with that blood. So God convicts Cain. No one was able to kill his brother except you. But that they have been killed, the blood itself and the stained earth cry out. They therefore cry out your crime. From the examination follows the sentence, in verses eleven and twelve, the parts of which are two: the first, the curse; the second, in which the additions to the curse are pronounced against Cain.

units.la: Maledictio pronuntiatur, verf. primo duobus modis: simpliciter, cum dicit Deus, nunc itaque maledictus es; & comparatè cum dicitur, Maledicta propter te terra quæ aperuit os suum ad recipiendum sanguinem fratris tui de manu tua. Nam de maledictione terræ sententia prius lata fuerat communiter cap. tertio verf. decimo-tertio: iam vero singularis maledictio communi superadditur propter singulare maleficium quod Cain volens perpetrauerat, & terra inuita pertulerat. Quod humana loquutione Deus indicauit dicens, quæ aperuit os suum ad recipiendum, &c. Maledictionis adiuncta duo sunt, verf. duodecimo: Vnum, in rebus exteris: alterum in persona ipsa Caini. In rebus exteris, quod res omnes illi quamuis labore & cultura maxima vtenti non sunt inseruiturae ad commoditatem vitae. In persona vero, quòd cum ita oppressurus est Deus & conscientiam exagitaturus, vt nullo loco figere possit pedem, sed vagus & errabundus incertis sedibus, fit Deum fugiturus prae terroribus conscientiae.Atque haec quidem sententia est à Deo lata. Sed cum grauitatem illius sententiae, siue ex horrore & consternatione animi, siue ex alia causa non satis Cain perciperet, ex eo factum est vt Cain extorta confessione vtens per modum expostulationis peteret interpretamentum illius, verf. 13. & seq. Cuius dubitationem Deus eximit responsione sua, verf. 15. Sermo autem Caini duabus ex partibus constat. Nam primum confessione quadam vtitur, verf. 13: Deinde expostulat, sequente. Confessio haec est, non proprie quidem explicata, sed implicita verbis illius: Maior est poena iniquitatis mea quam vt ferre possim. Nam primum quasi in transcursu coactus agnoscit iniquitatem suam, deinde vero certo consilio amplificat poenam iniquitatis suae, & obliquè accusat Deum iniustitiae, tamquam si poenae modum ex modo peccati nesciret Deus expendere. Nam lex naturalis est qua Tullius vtitur lib. de legibus 3. NOXIAE POENA PAR ESTO.
units.tr: The curse is pronounced in verse eleven in two ways: simply, when God says, now therefore you are cursed; and comparatively, when it is said, Cursed because of you is the earth which opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand. For the sentence of a curse upon the earth had been pronounced earlier in general terms, in chapter three, verses thirteen and fourteen; but now a particular curse is added to the general one, on account of the particular crime which Cain had willingly committed and which the earth had unwillingly endured. God indicated this in human speech when he said, which opened its mouth to receive, etc. There are two additions to the curse, in verse twelve: one in external things, the other in Cain's own person. In external things, because all the things which he will use, however much labour and cultivation he applies, will not serve him for the comfort of life. In his person, because God will so oppress him and so trouble his conscience that he can plant his foot in no place, but will be a wanderer and a vagabond without a fixed dwelling, and so will flee from God for fear of the terrors of conscience. This is indeed the sentence pronounced by God. But since Cain did not sufficiently perceive the gravity of that sentence, whether from the horror and dismay of his mind or from some other cause, it came about that, extracting a confession, he asked by way of protest for an explanation of it, in verse thirteen and following. God removes his doubt by his answer, in verse fifteen. Cain's speech consists of two parts. For first he makes a certain confession, in verse thirteen; then he protests, in what follows. This confession is not properly expressed, but implied in his words: My punishment for iniquity is greater than I can bear. For at first, as if in passing and under compulsion, he acknowledges his iniquity; then, with deliberate purpose, he magnifies the punishment for his iniquity, and obliquely accuses God of injustice, as if God did not know how to weigh the measure of punishment against the measure of sin. For this is the natural law which Cicero uses in the third book of De legibus: LET THE PUNISHMENT BE EQUAL TO THE HARM.

units.la: Hic vero aliquid impar obscurè criminatur inesse sententiae Dei, cum par quidem fuerit Caini maleficio perpetrando, sed impar sit supplicio perferendo. Atque hoc illud est quod exponit seq. versu, adiunctas maledictioni poenas aggrauans: de maledictione vero non faciens vllum verbum: & quidem ordine praepostero sententiae antecedentis partes resumens, prout carnalis homo magis rebus propinquis quàm longinquis afficitur. Nam primum dicit: En expellis me hodie à superficie terrae, id est, quod me vagum & errantem pronuntias fore, eo satis ostendis iam nullo esse loco apud te vitam meam: Secundo, à facie tua sum absconsurus me, id est nunquam compariturus coram te aut Ecclesia tua, quae adhuc in domo Adami permanebat. Ex his autem duobus concludit in hunc modum: Quod si neque in terra, neque in Ecclesia apud te mihi receptus vllus est, vae misero mihi. Quid amplius restat quàm vt obuiae cuiusque creaturae iniuriis sim expositus, & à prima occursante enecer? Sic ergo praesentia mala quae Deus sententia indixerat expendit Cain, vt tantum de misera illa vita conseruanda sollicitus permaneat. Huic postulato respondit Dominus, v.15. sermone, & signo. Nam cum de aliis rebus minimè, sed de vita solùm proroganda Cain laboraret; Deus caeteris omissis de eo ipso postulato agit, sed per paralepsin Hebraeis frequentissimam, qua ex consequentibus intelliguntur antecedentia. Antecedens est quod hic reticetur, nolo te occidi. Neque hoc dixi sententia mea; consequens est quod exprimitur, Propterea fi vllus occiderit Cainum, septuplo vindicabitur, id est, grauissime: Placuit enim Deo vt Cain quàm diutissimè terrores conscientiæ experiretur & aliis exemplo esset. Deinde verò quod sermone Deus promiserat, signo confirmauisse dicitur his verbis, & imposuit Iehoua Caino signum ne caderet eum vllus qui ipsum inuenturus esset. De signo quæritur: scriptura non exprimit illius modum. Interpretum alij in ipso Caino, alij extra Cainum fuisse putant. Qui extra Cainum, vt Iudæi quidam, putant vbicunque locorum fuit Cain ibi aliquod spacium circūstantis terræ tremuisse: Qui in ipso signum fuisse putant, nituntur verbis Mosis, sed signi modum amplius nō possunt exponere: quorum sententiam & modestiam sequor. Nisi quis forte statuerit ita fuisse horrendum aspectu Cainum ex terroribus illis conscientiæ, & aliqua patibili (vt vocant) qualitate sic affectum in se, vt omnes quoque aspicientes, itidem affeccrit.
units.tr: Here, however, he obscurely charges that there is something unequal in God's sentence, since the crime, as Cain committed it, was equal, but the punishment, as he must bear it, is unequal. And this is what he sets out in the following verse, enlarging the punishments joined to the curse, but making no mention of the curse itself; and indeed, resuming the parts of the preceding sentence in reverse order, as carnal man is more affected by near things than by distant ones. For first he says: Behold, you drive me out today from the surface of the earth, that is, by pronouncing that I shall be a wanderer and a vagabond you show clearly enough that my life now has no place with you. Second: I shall be hidden from your face, that is, I shall never appear before you or before your Church, which still remained in the house of Adam. From these two things he concludes in this way: If neither on earth nor in the Church is there any place for me with you, woe is me. What remains except that I be exposed to the injuries of every creature that meets me, and be slain by the first who comes upon me? Thus Cain weighs the present evils which God had decreed by his sentence, so that he remains anxious only about preserving that wretched life. The Lord answered this plea, in verse fifteen, by word and by sign. For since Cain was concerned not at all about other things, but only about prolonging his life, God, leaving the rest aside, deals with that very plea, but by paralepsis [παράλειψις], which the Hebrews use very frequently, whereby the preceding things are understood from the following. The preceding thing is what is here left unsaid: I do not wish you to be killed. Nor have I said this as my sentence; the following is what is expressed: Therefore whoever kills Cain shall be avenged sevenfold, that is, most severely. For it pleased God that Cain should experience the terrors of conscience for as long as possible and be an example to others. Then, indeed, what God had promised by word he is said to have confirmed by a sign, in these words: and the Lord set a sign upon Cain, lest anyone who found him should strike him down. Concerning the sign there is a question: Scripture does not express its manner. Some of the interpreters think it was in Cain himself, others outside Cain. Those who think it was outside Cain, as certain Jews do, hold that wherever Cain was, some space of the surrounding land trembled. Those who think the sign was in him rely on the words of Moses, but cannot explain further the manner of the sign; I follow their opinion and its moderation. Unless someone perhaps should hold that Cain was so horrible in appearance from those terrors of conscience, and affected by some passible quality (as they call it), that he affected all who looked upon him in the same way.

units.la: Dicta à Deo sententia proximè sequitur exsequutio, v.16. & seq. Cuius exsequutionis tria à Mose membra proponuntur. Primum est separatio à Deo & Ecclesia eius: secundum, habitatio instabilis, v.16. Tertium denique irritum & laboriosum studium comparandæ stationis certæ aduersus sententiam à Deo latam, v.17. separationem à Deo Ecclesiáque eius Moses indicauit his verbis, egressus est (Cain à conspectu Iehouæ, ac proinde parentum quoque suorum & Ecclesiæ apud illos permanentis. Sedis vel habitationis instabilitatem demonstrant ista consedit vel commoratus est (Cain in terra Nodi. Nam etsi hoc tempore ex scriptis Geographorum non ita commodè ôstendi potest quæ terra hac appellatione donata sit, id tamen sufficeret ad præsentem causam, si ex notatione vocis Nod (quæ errare siue erro-rem significat, siue errabundum) intelligamus Deum re vera sententiam suam exsequutum esse, atque effecisse vt totam vitam Cain incertis sedibus transigeret in errore. Verum tamen cum in illo tractu qui subest Babyloniæ, gentes feræ sint in tuguriis & mapalibus habitantes, tum in Arabia deserta, tum in extrema Babylonia ad sinum Persicum, tum in Susiane contermina, quæ gentes Nomades appellantur, totum illum tractum appellari terram Nod ex eo iudicauerim. Sed quia latè patebat ille tractus quem Nomades coluerũt, propterea distinctionis ergo circumstantia altera adiicitur: nempe Cainũ se in eam terram Nod recepisse quæ ex aduerso Hedenis orientem versus sita est: ac proinde ex eo concludimus sedem Caini fuisse in vna Susiane, vbi Characeni & Eulei à Geographis dicuntur habitasse, vt sequentibus Mosis verbis, 17.verf.mox confirmabitur.
units.tr: The sentence pronounced by God is followed immediately by its execution, in verse sixteen and following. Moses sets out three parts of this execution. The first is separation from God and his Church; the second, an unstable dwelling, verse sixteen; the third, finally, the vain and laborious effort to secure a firm station against the sentence pronounced by God, verse seventeen. Moses indicated the separation from God and his Church in these words: Cain went out from the presence of the Lord, and therefore from his parents also and from the Church which remained with them. The instability of his seat or dwelling is shown by these words: Cain settled or dwelt in the land of Nod. For although at this time it cannot be shown very conveniently from the writings of the geographers which region was called by this name, it would nevertheless be sufficient for the present purpose if, from the meaning of the word Nod (which signifies to wander or to err, or a wanderer), we understand that God really carried out his sentence and brought it about that Cain spent his whole life in uncertain dwellings, in wandering. Yet, since in that tract which lies beneath Babylonia the peoples are wild, living in huts and tents, and since in the Arabian desert, in the farthest part of Babylonia on the Persian Gulf, and in the region bordering on Susiana, peoples called nomads live, I should judge that the whole of that tract was called the land of Nod for this reason. But because the tract which the nomads inhabited extended widely, for the sake of distinction another circumstance is added: namely, that Cain withdrew into that land of Nod which lies to the east, opposite Eden. From this we conclude that Cain's seat was in Susiana alone, where the Characeni and Eulaeans are said by the geographers to have lived, as will be confirmed shortly by the following words of Moses, in verse seventeen.

units.la: Restat locus tertius, de studio quo misèr ille Cain, quamuis acerbissimo Dei iudicio pressus, tum laborauit vt se & nomen suum aduersus Dei sententiâ quodâmodo confirmaret. Eius rei assequendæ duos adhibuit modos: vnum, quòd generationi posterorum dedit operam homo maledictus; alterum, quòd se generationémque suam tentauit structura vrbis & munitionis, quæ tum adhuc inaudita fuerat, confirmare. Generationis studium Moses narrat his verbis, cognouit Cainus, &c. studium verò confirmandi sui maximis operibus, aduersus iudicium Dei, demonstratur illis, fuitque ædificans ciuitatem, &c. In generatione obseruandum est nomen filio impositum Chanoc, tamquâ si dicatum vel conseruatù dixeris. Nam hac appellatione videtur Cain voluisse, vt à Deo eiectus erat, tamen Dei cultum præ se ferre, & apud suos instituere: ac propterea filium suum primogenitum nomine Chanocum sacrauisse vt impurum illius familiæ sacerdotium à primogenito coleretur.In munitione verò comparanda duo opus est obseruari; primùm quidem studium illius non successisse, sed (vt verax Deus est in minis & promissionibus) quo amplius tentauit institutum opus perficere, eo amplius vexatum à Domino fuisse ne illud perficeret. Alterum quòd inchoatæ illius vrbis munitionisque nomen constituit de nomine filij sui, vt gloriam sibi assumeret, quam Deus iudicio suo in ignominiam maximâ commutauit. Nam videtur illius impij instituti vestigium apud Geographos nostros etiam remansisse, qui in ima Sufiane secundum mare Persicum opidum tradunt exstitisse nomine Anuctam vt à Ptolemæo in Geographicis nominatur. Atque hæc de principio Ecclesiæ impiorum, quæ à consortio piorum est eiecta, maximo piorum bono: sequitur pars secunda capitis, progressum illius explicas duobus modis: Primùm Ecclesiæ illius impiorum propagatione, verf. 18. Tum singulari exemplo, v.19.& seqq. Ecclesiæ impiorum propagationem describit Moses secundum seriem ipsorum: Etsi non obseruata ratione annorum, quia hæc ratio ad historiam Ecclesiæ Dei potissimum visa est pertinere. Exemplum verò singulare, quod in Lemeco & familia ipsius statuitur, eo positum est, vt corruptionem illius Ecclesiæ, Dei tolerantiam, hominúmque obstinationem in impietate & iniustitia sua, quæ ad diluuium vsque perdurauit, probè recognoscamus.Illius exempli ad impietatem spectantis partes hæ sunt:primùm impietas Lemeci ius diuinum & naturale coniugij auctoritate sua perfringentis,verf.19.Secundò institutum totius familiæ illius,v. 20.& duobus sequentibus. Postremò inhumanitas & iniustitia pu-
units.tr: There remains a third point, concerning the zeal with which that wretched Cain, although pressed by God's most bitter judgment, nevertheless laboured to confirm himself and his name, as it were, against God's sentence. He used two means to achieve this: first, the accursed man devoted himself to the begetting of posterity; second, he tried to secure himself and his line by the building of a city and a fortification, which was still unheard of at that time. Moses narrates the zeal for begetting in these words, "Cain knew," etc. The zeal for securing himself by great works, against God's judgment, is shown by those words, "and he was building a city," etc. In the begetting, it must be observed that the son was named Chanoc, as if you were to say dedicated or preserved. For by this name Cain seems to have wished, although cast out by God, to display the worship of God before his own people and to establish it among them; and therefore he consecrated his firstborn son by the name Chanoc, so that the priesthood of that impure family might be maintained from the firstborn. In the construction of the fortification, two things must be observed. First, his undertaking did not succeed; rather (as God is true in his threats and promises), the more he tried to complete the work he had begun, the more the Lord harassed him so that he would not complete it. Second, he gave the name of his son to the city and fortification he had begun, in order to assume glory for himself, which God by his judgment turned into the greatest shame. For a trace of that impious undertaking seems to have remained even among our geographers, who report that in the lowest part of Susiana, along the Persian Sea, there existed a town named Anuctam, as Ptolemy names it in his Geography. And this is said of the beginning of the Church of the impious, which was cast out from the fellowship of the pious, to the great good of the pious. There follows the second part of the chapter, which explains its progress in two ways: first by the propagation of that impious Church, verse 18; then by a singular example, verse 19 and following. Moses describes the propagation of the Church of the impious by the sequence of their names, though without observing the reckoning of years, because that reckoning seemed to pertain chiefly to the history of God's Church. The singular example, which is set forth in Lamech and his family, is placed there so that we may properly recognise the corruption of that Church, God's forbearance, and the obstinacy of men in their impiety and injustice, which lasted until the flood. The parts of this example that bear on impiety are these: first, the impiety of Lamech, who by his own authority breaks the divine and natural law of marriage, verse 19; second, the practice of his whole family, verse 20 and the two following; lastly, the inhumanity and injustice of public life.

units.la: F. j. blica, verf.23. & 24. Impietatis hoc documentum est, quòd sibi duxit vxores duas, eásque (si rationem nominum spectemus) specie & forma commendabiles. Nam prioris nomen Hada ab ornatu dicitur. posterioris Tsilla a colore grato quem sol minimè infuscauerit. Id enim fuit impietatis, quòd contra institutum Dei (qui vnam vni viro coniugauerat) & contra naturæ legem (quam Adam pronuntiauerat) duas vxores libidini seruiens adiùxit sibi. Studia verò familiæ tribus sequentib. versibus ita exponuntur, vt intelligamus in ea singulos dedisse operam rebus quidem diuinis & sacris nullam: humanis verò ac profanis maximam.
