Quandoquidem quæcunque hîc à posteris Lemeci dicûtur facta, ea aut ad commoditatem opum videntur pertinere, vt cum tentoria, caulæ, pecuaria, instituta sunt sin gulari modo; alia ad voluptatè, vt cum instrumenta Musica, tum quæ pulsantur, tum quę impelluntur vento dicûtur excogitata, siue ad artè & ornatum commoditatémque operum, vt cum politura rebus fa- brilibus dicitur accessisse & omnium corollarium, formæ venustatis- que muliebris ratio, propter quam soror Tubalcain Nahama, id est, amœna siue delicata dicebatur. Inhumanitatem & iniustitiam illius seculi demonstrat singularis Lemeci inhumanitas & Thrasonica præsidentia, qua in Deũ & homines videtur insultare, vers. 23. & seq. In huius autem sceleris interpretatione duo nobis ordine viden- da sunt: Primò qua occasione Lemecad verba ista proruperit: secun- dò quod crimen his verbis inesse comperiatur. Occasionem alij fer- me nullam esse putant quàm animi præsidentis insolentiam: cuius- modi fuit Sancheribi & aliorum inimicorum Dei: hæc autem oc- casio etsi plausibilis est, tamen altera quædam ωεψκατα ρκτικὼ videtur adhibenda, quæ præsidentiam illam hominis irritauerit. Eam verò ex hac ipsa historia exprimentes, statuimus occasionem à duabus vxoribus, quas impiè duxerat, oblatam esse. Nam vxores duas simul dućtas, propter rixas illarum perpetuas, scriptura angentes vocat 1. Samuel. 1. & ostendunt alij scripturæ loci Genef. 30. Leuitic. 18. & his consimiles. Has igitur vxores duas amaras fuisse tum viro rixis indefinentibus, tum inter se, statuimus, suás- que rixas fiducia posterorum, studiorūmque, & artium pluri- mum acuisse. Ex hac igitur occasione verba ista Lemeci non a- pud omnes, sed apud vxores suas (quibus coniugali fide obstri- ctus erat) dicitur pronuntiauisse, quòd longè grauius est quàm si exteros homines aut minus coniunctos his modis compellasset.
units.tr: ...verses 23 and 24. This is the evidence of impiety: that he took for himself two wives, and these (if we consider the meaning of their names) attractive in appearance and beauty. For the name of the first, Adah, comes from her adornment; that of the second, Zillah, from a pleasing colour which the sun had not darkened. For this was impiety: that, against God's institution (who had joined one wife to one husband) and against the law of nature (which Adam had declared), he took two wives, serving his lust. The occupations of the family are set out in the three following verses, so that we understand that in it each one devoted himself to things not divine and sacred at all, but to human and profane things in the highest degree. For whatever is said here to have been done by the posterity of Lamech, these things seem to pertain either to the convenience of wealth, as when tents, sheepfolds and herds are said to have been established in a singular way; or to pleasure, as when musical instruments are said to have been invented, both those that are struck and those that are moved by the wind; or to the art, ornament and convenience of works, as when polish is said to have been added to metalwork, and, as a crown of all, the care of feminine beauty and grace, on account of which the sister of Tubal-cain was called Naamah, that is, pleasant or delicate. The inhumanity and injustice of that age is shown by Lamech's singular inhumanity and boastful arrogance, by which he seems to insult God and men, verses 23 and following. In interpreting this crime, two things must be considered in order: first, on what occasion Lamech burst out with those words; second, what crime is found to be contained in them. Almost everyone else thinks there was no occasion except the insolence of a proud spirit, such as that of Sennacherib and other enemies of God; but although this occasion is plausible, some other cause [ωεψκατα ρκτικὼ] seems to be applied, which provoked that arrogance of the man. Drawing this from the history itself, we determine that the occasion was offered by the two wives whom he had impiously taken. For two wives taken together, on account of their constant quarrels, Scripture calls rivals (1 Samuel 1), and other passages of Scripture show it, Genesis 30, Leviticus 18, and similar ones. We therefore determine that these two wives were bitter, both to their husband with unceasing quarrels and to one another, and that their quarrels were greatly sharpened by the confidence placed in their children and their pursuits and arts. From this occasion, then, those words of Lamech are said to have been uttered not before everyone, but before his wives (to whom he was bound by marital faith), which is far graver than if he had addressed outsiders or less closely related persons in such terms.

units.la: Sermonis autem illius duæ sunt partes: Mandatum, & minarum denundenuntiatio in immorigeros. Mandatum his verbis continetur, Hada & Tfilla audite, &c. sensus enim est,iam plus fatis vocem vestram audiui obstrepentem, & aurem aduerti ad rixas æmulationesque vestras: Ego vero non statui deinceps me præbere facilem istis querimoniis: vos potius deinceps ad meū sermonem attentæ efote, & a me conturbando vestris querimoniis abstinete. Huic mandato denuntiatio subiicitur altera parte versus, Nam virum occidero ad vulnus; sensus est, id vos oportet reputare, meum animum deinceps non posse ferre exacerbationes & vlcera ista. Si quis me porro his nugis obtuderit, sciat me pro eo factum illius habiturum ac si me percussisset. Nunc vero hac conditione mea vsque adeo meum animum impotentem esse, vt nemini qui mihi molestus esse voluerit sim parciturus. Neque mihi vires filiorum vestrorum(vt vt viri sint) neque gratiam pucrulorū (vtcumque pueruli sint)opponite: Nec viro,ac ne puero quidem parciturus sum,qui me hoc modo offenderit, tam enim odiosum mihi futurum illius factum, quàm si vulnus infli-xisset aut intulisset corpori meo. Hæc autē per gradationem dicūtur: Nam incrementum est inhumanitatis si quis non solum viro, sed etiam puero; non solum pro vulnere, sed etiam pro tumice mortem denuntiauerit. Huius vero denuntiationis amplificatio blasphema additur verf. 24. Qua iste Thrafo illudit Deo, & sibi vires ampliores diuinis arrogat, cum dicit, Nam septuplo vindicandus est Cain, vt Deus denuntiauit verf. 15. Sed siquis mihi negotium facesserit, vindex longe atrocior futurus sum, neque impune quemquam tanta lenitate abire sinam. Lemec enim pro malo vel minimo quod acceperit,septuagies septies tantum malum auctori repensurus est. Atque hæc vera imago est Thrasonum istorum, qui elata manu in Deum atque homines insolescunt. Sequitur progressus Ecclesiæ piorum ad sequens caput μεταβατικὸς [?]: verf. 25. & seq. quo in progressu primum instauratio exponitur Ecclesiæ Dei, verf. 25. & seq. parte. Deinde occupatio, in fine capitis instauratio & continuatio Ecclesiæ genitura Sethi ostenditur, quia hurus posteros in Ecclesia genitos & coftantes fuisse primo appellationibus ipsorum,deinde occupatione ostenditur. Appellationibus, nam Seth,repositum sonat; quod nomen recens nato imposuit mater pia recognitione misericordiæ Dei; nam reposuit, inquiebat, mihi s men alteru &c. Filio vero illius nomē est impositū Enoc, quasi mortalem aut doloribus fractum pressūm ve significaeris, quia per illud tempus Ecclesia piorum intumescere & ingrauescere impiorum iniquitatem videns, quasi exedebatur zelo domus Dei, iustúmque cor suum affligebat. Atque hæc causa fuit occupationis illius, quæ postremis verbis huius capitis exponitur: tunc cœptum est inuocari nomen Iehoua siue inclamari in nomine Iehoua, siue vocari de nomine Iehoua: nam hæ tres interpretationes (vtcunque aliæ aliis allubescant) vnius sunt argumenti, & id sibi volunt synecdochicos[?], Ecclesiam piorum, quum prius ordinariè in familia Adami constiterit, tunc temporis nouam quandam rationem in continuando cultu Dei iniuisse propter singularem impietatem seculi illius. Noua autem & singularis videtur fuisse: primùm, quia tum ex vna Ecclesia quæ apud Adamum constiterat plures Ecclesiæ factæ sunt, & à singulis piis patribus familiâs constitutę: Secundò, quia occupatio illa increscēte malitia seculi similiter increuit in Ecclesia aduersus malitiam seculi sui omnibus piis exercitationibus, in primis verò nominis diuini inuocatione in tantis malis, decertante. Alteram interpretationem de profanato nomine Iehouę communem fermè Hebræorum omnium, nos certo consilio omittimus: quia etsi re & argumento coniuncta est, tamen non satis Hebrææ phrasi conuenit. Alioquin dubium non est quin prout irrumpebat malitia hominum in Ecclesiam, eò amplius necesse habuerit Ecclesia de inuocando nomine Iehouæ, & recolligendis piis atque defendendis à technis Satanæ & mundi laborare.
units.tr: There are two parts to his speech: a command, and a declaration of threats against the disobedient. The command is contained in these words, "Adah and Zillah, hear," etc. For the sense is: I have already heard your voice grumbling more than enough, and have turned my ear to your quarrels and rivalries. But I have decided that from now on I will not show myself easy towards these complaints; rather, from now on be attentive to my words, and refrain from disturbing me with your complaints. To this command a declaration is added in the second part of the verse: "For I have slain a man for a wound." The sense is: you ought to consider this, that my mind can no longer bear these irritations and sores. If anyone further pesters me with these trifles, let him know that I will count his deed as if he had struck me. Now, given this condition of mine, my spirit is so ungovernable that I will spare no one who has chosen to be troublesome to me. Do not set against me the strength of your sons (so that they may be men), nor the favour of the boys (whatever their age); I will not spare even a man or a boy who offends me in this way, for his deed will be as hateful to me as if he had inflicted a wound on my body. These things are said by gradation: for it is an increase of inhumanity if someone threatens death not only to a man but also to a boy, and not only for a wound but also for a bruise. A blasphemous amplification of this threat is added in verse 24, by which that braggart mocks God and arrogates to himself powers greater than God's, when he says, "For Cain shall be avenged sevenfold," as God declared in verse 15. "But if anyone causes me trouble, I will be a far more savage avenger, nor will I let anyone go unpunished with such leniency. For Lamech will repay the author seventy-seven times as much evil for the smallest evil he has received." And this is the true image of those braggarts who, with raised hand, grow insolent against God and men. There follows the progress of the Church of the pious into the following chapter, [transitional]: verse 25 and following, in which progress the restoration of God's Church is first set out, verse 25 and the following part. Then, at the end of the chapter, the restoration and continuation of the Church is shown in the birth of Seth, because his posterity, born and steadfast in the Church, is shown first by their names and then by their occupation. By names: Seth means "appointed"; the pious mother gave this name to the newborn in acknowledgment of God's mercy, "for God has appointed me another seed," she said, etc. To his son was given the name Enosh, as if you would signify mortal, or broken by sorrows, because at that time the Church of the pious, seeing the iniquity of the impious swelling and growing heavier, was as it were consumed with zeal for the house of God and afflicted its righteous heart. And this was the cause of that occupation, which is set out in the last words of this chapter: "then men began to call upon the name of Jehovah," or "to be called by the name of Jehovah." For these three interpretations (however different ones please different people) have one meaning, and they point to a synecdoche: that the Church of the pious, although previously it had ordinarily stood within the family of Adam, at that time entered upon a new manner of continuing the worship of God, because of the singular impiety of that age. This seems to have been new and singular: first, because from the one Church that had stood with Adam many churches were made, each established by individual pious fathers with their households; second, because that occupation, as the wickedness of the age increased, increased in the same way in the Church, with all pious exercises contending against the wickedness of its own age, and above all with the invocation of the divine name in such great evils. We deliberately omit the other interpretation, of a profaned name of Jehovah, which is nearly common to all the Hebrews: although it is connected in substance and argument, it does not fit the Hebrew idiom well enough. Otherwise there is no doubt that, as the wickedness of men broke into the Church, the Church had the more need to labour at invoking the name of Jehovah, gathering the pious and defending them against the snares of Satan and the world.

units.la: CAPITIS V ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER V.

units.la: EXPOSITA constitutione cœtus impiorum præcedente capite, & quibusdam exemplis demonstrata cruce quam mali bonis solent importare, sequitur in hoc capite demonstratio constantiæ Dei in suis promissionibus, & stabilitatis Ecclesiæ in Deo suo, pro-posita historia de successione piorum, & continuatione Ecclesiæ in electo semine: itaque finis huius capitis est, vt demonstretur fides Dei in gignenda, alenda, conseruandáque Ecclesia contra omnes portas inferorum. Summa verò, Deum inde à principio, quamuis furente Satana, Ecclesiam suam indesinenter curauisse: gignendo, propagando, alendo, docendo, atque conseruando, prout ad Dei ipsius gloriam vtsum est pertinere. Huius ergo capitis partes omnino duæ sunt. Prior est antecedentis creationis summa repetitio, inscriptione huius cap. comprehensa, v. 1. & 2. Secunda est narratio illius ortus atque illius progressus Ecclesiæ, secundum tempora & annos singulorum patrum distincta luculentissimè usque ad historiam diluvij. Inscriptionis hæc verba sunt: Hic liber, siue libellus, Generationis hominis: siue Adami: Etsi appellatiuè potius quàm proprie exponi oportere ex secundo versu constat euidentissimè. De hoc autem quatuor in hac inscriptione prædicantur: Primum creatio hominis, & conditio illius ex creatione: nempe ad imaginem Dei fuisse factum, vt expositimus supra, i. 26. & seqq. Secundum speciem in sexus distinxisse ad commoditatem propagandæ illius, supra c. 1. & 2. Tertiò benedixisse illis & propagationem instituisse benedictione sua: Quarto commune nomen indidisse, ad communionem naturæ & vitæ inter utrumque sexum testificandam nomine. Atque hæc inscriptionis membra singulariter ad creationem respicientia. Sequitur continuatio eiusdem speciei per benedictionem diuinam propagatæ morientibus indiuiduis: ac proinde opus habentib. propagatione ad speciei suæ conseruationem. Itaq; enumerantur capita omnia primogenitorū siue benedictorū patrū, qui inde ab Adamo ad diluvij vsq; pertenderunt[?], eorumq; nomina describuntur. In hac verò descriptione triplex ratio temporum ponitur, ex qua facilè confirmatur totius chronicę huius rationis fides: Nam primùm duę partes ętatis in Patres singulos tribuuntur: deinde summa conficitur vniuersi temporis quo illi vixerunt ex duarum partium coagmentatione. Prior pars est numerus annorum quo vixerunt Patres vsque dum suos illos primogenitos genuissent: Posterior pars est numerus annorum quo iidem vixerunt posteaquam illos genuissent. Hinc assurgit annorum summa quibus vixerunt illi vsque dum morte vitam commutarent: quemadmodum à Deo cap. 2. & 3. fuerat pronuntiatum. Quapropter ex hac supputatione adeò accurata facile tū rationem temporum communium totius mundi, tum singularium Ecclesiæ cognoscimus, cuius maximè causa hic labor institutus est. Pietatem verò istorum patrum etsi minutatim nō percurrit Moses, tamè non dubium est quin ex præcedentis capitis fine communiter intelligi eamdem voluerit, cū dixit temporibus Sethi & Enoschi cœptum fuisse inuocari nomen Iehouæ. Nam ex eo sequitur eamdè inuocatione in benedicto genere illo perstitisse: quemadmodum è diuerso impietatem gentis Cainicæ ex illis pauculis exemplis, quæ superiore capite extant, Spiritus sanctus voluit intelligi. His adde argumentationem à sanctis nominibus, quę liberis suis imposuerunt Patres, vt intelligentibus Hebreę linguæ est euidentissimum: In tempore geniturâ antecedente, aut etiam coniuncto, duæ sunt obseruationes: vna de spatio temporis: altera de conditione genitorum. Spatium temporis plurimùm fuisse longum dicitur,ut Adam Sethū genuisse 130.anno,Seth genuisse 105. & sic deinceps, ut ea ratione sides sanctorum Patrum probaretur, qui lente gignere videbantur, cum e diuerso Cainitæ liberos quasi funditarent, eáque ratione demonstraret Deus illos non solùm naturæ esse, verum etiam promissionis filios. Conditio liberorum qui fuerunt geniti,semel quidem proponitur in v.3. Sed communiter in sequentium omnium genitura intelligeda est. Eam his verbis descripsit Moses: Adam genuit in imagine sua in similitudine sua. Nam imago Adami imagini Dei quę v.1. dicta est, opponitur, ut corrupta integrę: genuisse autem homo dicitur hac conditione liberos, quia Adam nobis considerandus est tamquā principiū humani generis, vel tamquā radix, in qua omnes propterea homines dicuntur peccauisse, Rom.5. Habet enim genitura hominis,primū quidē à natura integra vel creatione quòd homo est; à natura verò corrupta vel peccati labe, quòd homo corruptus est in principio suo. In tempore quòd genitura consequutū est duo similiter opus est observari,longęuitate,& aliorum procreationem.Longęuitatis causę fuerunt hę,rerū diuinarū diuturna comprehensio, earumdē cum posteris communicatio, & auctoritas ad Ecclesiæ conseruationē.quapropter etiā legimus in Epistola Iudę memoriam Prophetiæ Enoci, qui septimus ab Adamo fuit, fuisse in Ecclesia conseruatam. Aliorum verò liberorum generatio eò pertinuit, ut sancti Patres agnoscerent non humana virtute, sed diuina promissione & viribus è cælo inditis eos posteritatem adeptos esse: quemadmodum Abrahamo centenario vires sunt inditæ ad generationem, quibus ætate illa fuerat cariturus, Geneseos 25. In tertio numerandi genere duo similiter observationis loci sunt: Vnus, de spatio totius vitæ: alter, de exitu. Spatium vitæ si cum æternitate Dei comparetur, nihil est: sin autem cum vitæ nostræ breuitate,plurimum. Quarum observationum illa admirabilitatem essentiæ Dei, vanitatémque nostram communem docet:Hæc verò nostrā præ illis sanctis Patribus longè maiorem vanitatem & corruptionem seculi. Exitus autem vitæ in omnibus fermè hoc verbo demonstratur, mortuus est: eóque pacto veritas minarum iudiciorúmque Dei ostenditur, ut promissionum veritas in illa hominum sustentatione, quæ prius dicta est. Excipitur singularis Chanoci historia,qui septimus ab Adamo fuit,prout verf.21. & seqq.docet Moses.In ea historia primùm,ut in cęteris,tempus ad geniturnam Methuselaci vsq; v.21. Secūdò tempus à genitura ad discessum vsque ab hac vita,v.22. Tertiò summa vitæ,quam apud homines duxit, verf.23. Postremò vitæ modus & exitus, v. 24. describitur.Ac vitæ quidem modus,verf.22. expressus iisdem verbis in vers. 24. repetitus est: cuius modi summa hæc est, Chanocū hic fuisse viatorem; vitam esse actum, mundumesse viam, Deum esse lucem & scopum huius vitæ, ad quem quicunque contendunt, ij seruant iustum vitæ suæ modum: quemadmodum hic de Chanoco dicitur. Exitus vero huius vitæ diuersus huic quàm aliis contigisse dicitur. Nam primum dicitur non amplius exstitisse. Deinde adfertur causa, quod Deus illum receperit. Cùm non exstitisse amplius dicitur, id ἐξ τῆ[?] ac non ἁπλῶς[?] accipi oportet. Non enim putandum est eum ex eo tempore plane non exstitisse, sed tantum non exstitisse in hac via & vita mortali: causa vero, quod Deus eum receperit, varie exponitur: nam recipiendi verbum in hunc modum de Deo enunciatum, aut euectionem extra mundum hunc significat, ut in raptu Eliae 2. Reg. 2. aut vitæ cum morte commutationem, ut Iechezk.24. & Ionæ 4. Quapropter non defuerunt qui hæc verba de præpropera Chanoci morte acciperent, ut qui non ita diu vixisset ac patres cæteri; qua in sententia videtur fuisse auctor libri Sapientiæ cap. 4. Nobis tamen magis probatur in Ecclesia Dei recepta sententia & tradita ad Heb. 11. vers. 5. quam etiam Siracides duobus locis Ecclesiastici amplexus est: nempe hunc translatum à Domino, ut non videret mortem. Sic duobus modis seculum illud contumax à Deo fuit reprehensum, vita Enoci, & discessu. Vita, quia in-definenter ambulauit secundum Dominum, recedens à malo quo exū dabat mundus, & faciens bonum docensq; invitum mundum. Morte verò, quia insolitum illud gratiæ & gloriæ diuinæ testimonium non potuit miseros illos & obfirmatos peccatores non commouere. Re-stat vltimus locus de historia Noachi, ad cuius narrationem sequentia capita maxime pertinent. In ea duo singularia sunt, ut de cōmu-nibus taceamus. Prius est nominis impositio, v.29. Posterius genitu-ra liberorum, v.vlt. Nominis impositio est hæc, quòd à pio patre pie dictus Noach fuisse dicitur, ac proprie quidem Noach quietum siue tranquillum significat. Notationem verò retulit alio pater, respiciens ad coniunctam alterius verbi significationem, quia pius ille senex magis ad sensum quàm ad verba ipsa respexerat. Prophetice igitur Noach fuisse nominatus dicitur, & occasione illa pater Prophetiam sibi revelatam promissionemque Dei enuntiauisse: Nempe fore tum ut Deus in illo filio acquiesceret, unde est Noachi nomen, tum ut ille humanum genus consolaretur. Argumenta quibus necessaria videbatur esse consolatio, duum sunt generum: nam primum effecta ponuntur duo: opus nostrum, i. misera & peccatrix vita, & dolor manuum nostrarum, i. vita laboriosissima ex peccato, in hac terra: deinde verò ponitur causa istorum omnium, Iehouæ maledictio, quam pius ille senex in veterem illum mundum exundantibus peccatis videbat incumbere.
units.tr: Having set out, in the preceding chapter, the gathering of the wicked, and shown by some examples the cross that the wicked are wont to bring upon the good, this chapter goes on to demonstrate God's constancy in his promises and the stability of the Church in its God. It does so by setting forth the history of the succession of the pious and the continuation of the Church in the chosen seed. The aim of the chapter, therefore, is to show God's faithfulness in begetting, nourishing and preserving his Church against all the gates of hell. The sum is that God, from the beginning, though Satan raged, has unceasingly cared for his Church: begetting, propagating, nourishing, teaching and preserving it, as far as it pertains to the glory of God himself. The chapter has two parts. The first is a brief restatement of the preceding creation, contained in the inscription of this chapter, verses 1 and 2. The second is the narrative of the origin and progress of the Church, distinguished according to the times and years of the individual fathers and set out most clearly as far as the history of the flood. The words of the inscription are: "This is the book," or little book, "of the generation of man," or of Adam. It is evident from the second verse that these words ought to be explained appellatively rather than properly. Four things are predicated of man in this inscription. First, his creation and his condition arising from creation, namely that he was made "in the image of God," as we explained above at Gen. 1:26 and following. Second, that he distinguished the species into sexes for the convenience of propagating it, as in chapters 1 and 2. Third, that he blessed them and instituted propagation by his blessing. Fourth, that he gave them a common name, to attest by the name the communion of nature and life between the two sexes. These members of the inscription refer singly to creation. There follows the continuation of the same species, propagated by divine blessing while individuals die, and so in need of propagation to preserve the species. Thus all the firstborn, or blessed, fathers are enumerated, from Adam down to the flood, and their names are described. In this description a threefold reckoning of time is given, by which the reliability of the whole chronology is easily confirmed. First, two parts of age are assigned to each father, and then the sum of the whole time he lived is made up by joining the two parts together. The first part is the number of years the father lived until he begot that firstborn son; the second is the number of years he lived after he had begotten him. Hence arises the sum of years in which they lived until they changed life by death, as God had pronounced in chapters 2 and 3. From this so accurate a reckoning we easily learn both the common chronology of the whole world and the particular chronology of the Church, which is the chief reason this labour has been undertaken. Moses does not run through the piety of those fathers one by one, yet there is no doubt that, from the close of the preceding chapter, he meant the same to be understood in general, when he said that in the times of Seth and Enosh men began to call upon the name of Jehovah. For it follows that this invocation persisted in that blessed line, just as, conversely, the Holy Spirit wished the impiety of the Cainite race to be understood from the few examples found in the preceding chapter. To this add the argument from the holy names which the fathers gave their children, which is most evident to those who understand the Hebrew language. In the time preceding or accompanying the begetting there are two observations: one concerning the span of time, the other concerning the condition of the begotten. The span of time is said to have been very long: Adam is said to have begotten Seth in his 130th year, Seth to have begotten a son at 105, and so on in turn. By this reckoning the faith of the holy fathers, who seemed to beget slowly while the Cainites almost poured out children, is proved, and God shows that they were sons not only of nature but of promise. The condition of the begotten is set out once, in verse 3, but is to be understood as common to the begetting of all who follow. Moses describes it in these words: "Adam begot in his image, in his likeness." For the image of Adam is set against the image of God mentioned in verse 1, as corrupted against entire; and man is said to have begotten children under this condition because Adam must be considered as the beginning of the human race, or as its root, in which all men are therefore said to have sinned, Rom. 5. For the begetting of man has, on the one hand, from nature entire or creation, that he is man; on the other, from nature corrupted or the stain of sin, that he is corrupt in his beginning. In the time following the begetting, two things likewise must be observed: longevity, and the procreation of others. The causes of longevity were these: the long-continued grasp of divine things, the communication of these to posterity, and authority for the preservation of the Church. So too we read in the Epistle of Jude that the memory of the prophecy of Enoch, who was seventh from Adam, was preserved in the Church. The begetting of the other children tended to this end: that the holy fathers might acknowledge that they obtained posterity not by human strength but by divine promise and by vigour infused from heaven. Just so, vigour was infused into Abraham at a hundred years old for begetting, which at that age he would otherwise have lacked, Gen. 25. In the third kind of reckoning there are likewise two points of observation: one concerning the span of the whole life, the other concerning its end. The span of life, compared with the eternity of God, is nothing; compared with the brevity of our life, it is much. Of these observations, the former teaches the admirable essence of God and our common vanity; the latter teaches the far greater vanity and corruption of this age compared with those holy fathers. The end of life is shown in almost every case by this word: "he died." Thus the truth of God's threats and judgments is displayed, just as the truth of his promises is displayed in that sustaining of men mentioned earlier. The history of Enoch, the seventh from Adam, is an exception, as Moses teaches in verses 21 and following. In that history, first, as in the others, the time up to the begetting of Methuselah is given, verse 21; second, the time from the begetting to his departure from this life, verse 22; third, the sum of the life he led among men, verse 23; last, the manner and end of his life are described, verse 24. The manner of his life, expressed in verse 22, is repeated in verse 24 in the same words. Its sum is this: Enoch here was a wayfarer; life is a journey, the world is a road, God is the light and goal of this life, and whoever strive towards him keep the just measure of their life, as is said here of Enoch. The end of this life is said to have come to him otherwise than to others. For first it is said, "he was no more." Then the cause is added, that "God took him." When it is said that he was no more, this must be understood as relative, not absolute. For it is not to be thought that from that time he altogether ceased to exist, but only that he no longer existed in this way, in mortal life. The cause, "that God took him," is variously explained, for the word "take," used of God in this way, signifies either removal outside this world, as in the rapture of Elijah, 2 Kings 2, or a change of life into death, as in Ezekiel 24 and Jonah 4. Hence there were not lacking those who took these words to mean an untimely death for Enoch, as one who had not lived as long as the other fathers; the author of the Book of Wisdom, chapter 4, seems to have been of this opinion. Yet the view received and handed down in the Church of God, set out at Heb. 11, verse 5, is more approved by us, and Siracides too embraced it in two places of Ecclesiasticus: namely, that he was translated by the Lord so that he should not see death. Thus that stubborn age was rebuked by God in two ways: by the life of Enoch, and by his departure. By his life, because he walked constantly with the Lord, withdrawing from the evil that the world poured out, and doing good and teaching the unwilling world. By his death, because that unusual testimony of divine grace and glory could not move those wretched and hardened sinners. There remains a last passage, concerning the history of Noah, to whose narrative the following chapters chiefly pertain. In it two things are singular, if we set aside what is common. The first is the imposition of the name, verse 29; the second, the begetting of children, in the last verse. The imposition of the name is this: Noah is said to have been named piously by a pious father, and properly the name Noah signifies rest or quiet. But the father gave a different etymology, looking to the joined meaning of another verb, because that pious old man had regarded the sense rather than the words themselves. Noah is therefore said to have been named prophetically, and on that occasion the father uttered the prophecy revealed to him and the promise of God: namely, that God would then "be pleased" (acquiesce) in that son, whence the name Noah comes, and that he would "comfort" the human race. The arguments for which comfort seemed necessary are of two kinds. First, two effects are set down: our work, that is, a miserable and sinful life, and the sorrow of our hands, that is, a most laborious life in this land because of sin. Then the cause of all these is set down: the curse of Jehovah, which that pious old man saw hanging over the old world as its sins overflowed.

units.la: Postremus locus est de generatione Noachi in vers. ultimo: in qua primum illud obseruari necesse est, non proprie aut speciatim denotari annum unicum quo tres filios tamquam ex partu uno genuerit; sed tantum primum terminum ostendi quo coepit gignere, puta quingentesimum ætatis annum. Nam diuersis annis tres filios fuisse genitos sacra historia deinde ostendit v.9.& 10. & 11. Hic vero duo notanda sunt. Primnm [?] quòd anno demum quingentesimo Noach genuisse dicitur, eo demonstrari tum sapientiam Dei suos exercentis & probantis eorum fidem, tum virtutem benedictionis eius, qua emortua corpora habilia ad gignendum effecta sunt. Sic denique ostenditur hoc pacto Noachi patientia & præmium fidei, cum ante annos 2o. Prophetiam de excidio mundi Noach à Deo audiuisset.
units.tr: The last passage is the account of Noah's begetting in the last verse. Here it must first be observed that it is not properly or specifically denoted that he begot the three sons in a single year, as if from one birth; rather only the first point is indicated at which he began to beget, namely the five-hundredth year of his life. For sacred history then shows that the three sons were born in different years, at v. 9, 10 and 11. Two things are to be noted here. First, that Noah is said to have begotten them only in the five-hundredth year: by this is shown both the wisdom of God, who exercises and tests the faith of his people, and the power of his blessing, by which bodies already dead were made fit for begetting. Thus at last is shown, by this means, the patience of Noah and the reward of faith, since he had heard from God the prophecy of the destruction of the world twenty years before.

units.la: Altera obseruatio est, Nomina filiorum Noachi non esse hoc loco naturali ordine disposita. Nam in sacris historiis triplex ordo nominum recensendorum tenendus est; Naturalis, secundum tempus; personalis, secundum dignitatem; & Historicus secundum commoditatem historiæ. Naturalis est, cum eo ordine recensentur nomina quo personæ exstiterunt. Personalis est, cum dignissimi nomen primo loco ponitur & sic ex ordine, ut hoc loco factum est: Cui generi ordo quoque ille accensendus est, quo auctor rei quæ narratur, primo loco ponitur, ut Numerorum 12.1. Historicus vero est, cum plane ordine præposteros nomina perscribuntur, siue [illegible, ~8 letters], quia historia proximè subsequens recto ordine historias perscriptura est, ut infra cap. 11. v.26. & 1.Chronic.3.5. Atque hoc modo veteres memoriam iuuari maximè putauerunt.
units.tr: The second observation is that the names of Noah's sons are not arranged here in their natural order. For in sacred histories a threefold order of recounting names is to be observed: the natural, according to time; the personal, according to dignity; and the historical, according to the convenience of the history. The natural order is when names are recounted in the order in which the persons came into being. The personal order is when the name of the most worthy is placed first, and so out of sequence, as has been done in this place. To this kind is also to be assigned that order by which the author of the thing narrated is placed in the first place, as at Numbers 12.1. The historical order is when names are written down in a plainly reversed sequence, because the history that immediately follows is going to be written in proper order, as below in chapter 11, v. 26, and 1 Chronicles 3.5. And in this way the ancients especially thought that memory was aided.

units.la: CAPITIS VI ANALYSIS.
units.tr: Analysis of Chapter 6.

units.la: EXpositis duobus hominum generibus qui prisco illo seculo vixerūt, eorumque instituto & administratione vitæ, duobus capite, Iam sequitur utriusque generis euentus à Deo institutus duobus alteris 6. & 7. in narratione autem euentus, duo ordine proponuntur, causa, & effectus ex causa consequens: quorum primum capite sexto, posterius septimo demonstratur. Causarum quæ Deum adduxerunt ut hunc euentum prisco illi seculo tribueret, duo sunt genera: Unum innatum in ipsis hominibus atque intestinum, puta peccatum ipsorum: alterum foris adueniens, puta iustitia Dei in peccatores, & gratia in electos, qui propterea in scripturis vasa gratiae & misericor-diae appellantur. Atque haec duo in singulis huius capitis partib. con-iuncta sunt sapientissimè. Huius ergo capitis finis est, ut sapientia, iu-stitia, misericordiaque Dei in praedicedis iudiciis suis elucescat. Sum-ma vero Deum sapientissimè tum iudicia suae iustitiae peccatoribus praenuntiauisse ut euincerentur: tum gratiam & misericordiam suam Ecclesiae suae ostendisse. Partes autem huius capitis sunt tres: pro-ut Deus gradatim succedente tempore iudicia sua in Ecclesia expo-ni voluit, antequam ad exsequenda & perficienda transgrederetur. Prima pars est primae denuntiationis, quae diluuium antecessit 120. annis, versibus 1. 2. 3. Secunda est denuntiatio altera, eaque praecisa, non autem (ut prior) hypothetica, inde à v. 4. ad 10. vsque. Tertia est vltima denuntiatio quae exsequutionem antecessit proximè, sermo-ne & signo à verf. 11. ad finem vsque capitis. Ad primam denun-tiationem quòd attinet, causa interna illius in hominibus verf. 1. & 2. Causa externa à Deo verf. 3. proponitur, & denuntiationis argumen-tum. Causae internae duo sunt loci, occasionum v. 1. & malefactorum, quae oblatis occasionibus homines perpetrarunt. Occasiones duae fuerunt: Una, hominum multiplicatio in superficie terrae, hominū inquam, id est, eorum qui aut à Caino erant, aut ad Ecclesiam illius pertine-bant, ut 2. v. Filiae hominum Filiis Dei opponuntur. Altera occasio est genitura filiarum hominum, id est, earum foeminarum quę nihil cum Deo aut Ecclesia eius habetes commune, tantum laborabant ut ho-minibus & mundo placerent. Malefactorum genera ponuntur duo, secundo versu; Unum, aspectus adulter, siue concupiscentia oculorum: alterum, coniunctio promiscua ex concupiscentia. Etsi autem hoc v-trumque malum est coram Deo grauissimum, tamē atrocitatem ad-fert crimini ratio personarum: quod nō viri mundani foeminas mun-danas appetiuisse atq; adiunxisse dicuntur sibi, sed potius Filij Dei, id est, homines ad Deum ex foedere & ad Ecclesiam Dei ex professio-ne pertinentes dicuntur scortati post oculos suos, illecti foeminarum specie externa: Ex quo priore malo alterum consequutum est, quod ceperunt sibi siue coiugio, siue extra coniugium adulterio & scorta-tione promiscua foeminas de omni genere quascunque delegissent oculorū aspectu. Atque hoc pacto non solum se ipsi peccatis implicarunt, ve-rumetiam Dei Ecclesiam contagione infecerunt, de qua Deus con-queritur sequente versu. Quod autem alij filios Dei pro angelis, alij pro potentioribus accipiunt: illud adeo alienum est à consilio Mosis. & proxima Dei sententia, ut non videatur opus habere confutatione. Ex his igitur internis causis, id est, peccato in genus hominum exundante, occasionem cepit Deus denuntiandi ea quae habentur in vers. 3. Denuntiationis autem duae sunt partes: una, qua Deus denuntiat se non passurum semper ut genus humanum abutatur patientia ipsius: altera praefinit tempus hypothetice ad resipiscentiam. Non semper laturum esse, denuntiat his verbis: non disceptabit Spiritus meus pro homine in seculum. Deinde causam adfert, eo quod etiam iste (fylleptice dictum, pro illis hominibus quos filios Dei appellauit) iste inquam caro est, id est, tam filij Dei ad Ecclesiam ipsius pertinentes, quam filij hominum quorum portio est in malo iacent, & ipsi etiam caro sunt, carnisque opera faciunt, renuntiantes Deo & exacerbantes Spiritum ipsius. Nam propterea dixit, non disceptabit Spiritus meus. Altera pars denuntiationis, definitio temporis hypothetica, continetur his verbis, sed erunt dies illius 120. anni. Tamquam si diceret, hoc spatium hominibus indulgetur, quo spatio per Noachum & Ecclesiam piorum reuocentur a peccatis suis, & intra quod nisi resipuerint a Deo profligentur. Quapropter non dubitamus quin haec ipsa denuntiatio primum quidem Noacho significata sit, quemadmodum iudicia sua seruis suis reuelat Deus, & quin imperatum eidem fuerit, ut Dei verbis hoc ipsum secretum denuntiaret seculo illi immorigero, tamquam praeco iustitiae, ut a Petro in Epistola utraque appellatur.
units.tr: Having set out the two kinds of men who lived in that ancient age, with their way of life and their government in the two preceding chapters, there now follows the outcome of each kind as instituted by God, in the two following chapters, 6 and 7. In the narrative of an outcome, two things are set out in order: the cause, and the effect that follows from the cause. The first is shown in chapter six, the second in chapter seven. There are two kinds of causes that moved God to bring this outcome upon that ancient age. One is innate in men themselves and internal, namely their own sin. The other comes from outside, namely the justice of God against sinners and his grace towards the elect, who for this reason are called in the Scriptures vessels of grace and mercy. These two are most wisely joined together in each part of this chapter. The aim of this chapter, then, is that the wisdom, justice and mercy of God may shine forth in the judgments he foretold. The sum is that God most wisely announced his judgments of justice to sinners in advance, so that they might be convicted, and at the same time showed his grace and mercy to his Church. There are three parts to this chapter, according as God chose to set forth his judgments in the Church step by step, as time went on, before he proceeded to carry them out and complete them. The first part is the first announcement, which preceded the flood by 120 years, verses 1, 2 and 3. The second is a second announcement, and this one is definite, not conditional as the first was, running from verse 4 to verse 10. The third is the final announcement, which immediately preceded the execution, by word and by sign, from verse 11 to the end of the chapter. As for the first announcement, its internal cause in men is set out in verses 1 and 2, its external cause from God in verse 3, together with the subject of the announcement. The internal causes are two: the occasions, verse 1, and the wrongs that men committed when the occasions were offered. There were two occasions. The first was the multiplication of men on the face of the earth, men, I say, that is, those who either descended from Cain or belonged to his Church, as in verse 2 the daughters of men are set against the sons of God. The second occasion was the bearing of daughters of men, that is, of those women who had nothing in common with God or his Church, and who laboured only to please men and the world. Two kinds of wrongdoing are set out in the second verse. One is adulterous looking, or the lust of the eyes; the other is promiscuous union arising from that lust. Although each of these evils is most grievous before God, the standing of the persons adds to the atrocity of the crime. For it is not said that worldly men desired and took to themselves worldly women. Rather, the sons of God, that is, men who belonged to God by covenant and to the Church of God by profession, are said to have gone whoring after their eyes, enticed by the outward beauty of the women. From this first evil another followed: they chose for themselves, whether in marriage or outside marriage in adultery and promiscuous whoredom, women of every kind whom they had picked out by the sight of their eyes. In this way they not only entangled themselves in sins, but also infected the Church of God with contagion, about which God complains in the following verse. As for others who take the sons of God to be angels, and others who take them to be the more powerful men, that is so far from the plan of Moses and from God's immediately following sentence that it does not seem to need refutation. So from these internal causes, that is, from sin overflowing into the human race, God took occasion to announce what is contained in verse 3. The announcement has two parts. In one, God declares that he will not always allow the human race to abuse his patience. The other sets a time, conditionally, for repentance. He declares that he will not always bear it in these words: my Spirit shall not strive with man for ever. Then he gives the reason, because he also is flesh (a figure of speech, referring to those men whom he had called the sons of God). He, I say, is flesh: both the sons of God who belonged to his Church and the sons of men who lie in wickedness are flesh, and they do the works of the flesh, renouncing God and provoking his Spirit. For this reason he said, my Spirit shall not strive. The second part of the announcement, the conditional fixing of a time, is contained in these words: but his days shall be 120 years. It is as if he said: this space of time is granted to men, within which through Noah and the Church of the godly they may be called back from their sins, and beyond which, unless they repent, they will be destroyed by God. Wherefore we do not doubt that this very announcement was first made known to Noah, just as God reveals his judgments to his servants, and that he was commanded to proclaim this same secret, by God's word, to that disobedient age, as a herald of righteousness, as Peter calls him in both of his epistles.

units.la: Secundo loco huius cap. decretum Dei exponitur sublata hypothesi vel conditione praecedente, quo Deus absolute statuit seculum illud perdere. In hoc autem loco, ut in praecedente, partes duae ponendae sunt: una causarum, altera decreti quod Deus constituit ex causis iustissimis. Causarum aliae sunt internae in hominibus ipsis perdendis, vers. 4. Aliae foris a Deo advenientes, vers. 5. & 6. Internarum causarum duo sunt genera: Unum, eadem licentia quam ante vers. 2. exposuimus, nempe confusio populi Dei cum alienis, & propagatio: Alterum, obfirmatio & peruicacia Gigantea, quae vulgo in scripturis violentiae nomine appellatur.
units.tr: Second, in this chapter God's decree is set out, with the conditional hypothesis or preceding condition removed, by which God absolutely determined to destroy that age. In this place, as in the one before, two parts must be set out: one of the causes, and the other of the decree that God established for most just causes. Some of the causes are internal, lying in the men who are to be destroyed, verse 4. Others come from God from outside, verses 5 and 6. There are two kinds of internal causes. One is the same licence that we set out before at verse 2, namely the mixing of God's people with outsiders, and its spread. The other is the hardening and obstinacy of the giants, which in the Scriptures is commonly called violence.

units.la: Cuius peruicaciae meminit his verbis Moses, Gigantes fuerant in terra diebus illis, nempe quibus decretum suum primum exposuit Deus, atque etiam postea, id est, neque monitis salutaribus Dei unquam adducti sunt ut resipiscerent, sed post illa monita amplius ad scelera exarserunt, prout in hominibus impiis peccatum piis monitis inardescit & irritatur. Licentiam vero demonstrant illa, quibus congressi sunt filij Dei cum filiabus hominum, & pepererunt ipsis. Sed quia vocis novitas fortasse lectoré fuisset remoratura, [illegible, ~8 letters] adhibuit Moses, ut vocē Nephi-lim, i. gigantium explicaret: illi (inquit) sunt potentiores ipsi, qui iam olim fuerunt facinorum suorum ac violentiae nemine celebrati. Externae causae a Deo advenientes duae sunt: cognitio iudicialis Dei sive scientia, & voluntas iusta sive iustitia ipsius: quarum prior, verf. 5. posterior, 6. proponitur. Cognitionis qua Deus omnia peruidet, duo membra fuisse dicuntur: Unum, quod Deus opera seculi illius cognovit; alterū, quod fontes operum. De operibus haec dicuntur a Mose, Vidit Iehoua plurimum esse malum hominis in terra, i. maleficium: fontes operū quae cognovit Deus, describuntur illis, omne figmentum cogitationum humani cordis, tantummodo malum esse quotidie: Ac proinde cogitatione ipsam & intelligentia hominis tota esse addicta malo. Ex quibus verbis intelligimus cor esse malū, cogitationes eius esse malas; singula cogitationū figmenta mala; & quidē sic mala, ut neq; ulla boni parte, neq; ullo tempore per se habere possint. Iustę volūtatis, qua Deus iustos homines prosequitur, gradus similiter ponuntur duo, in v. 6. Unus, tædij sive poenitentiae quae humanitus de Deo praedicatur: alter doloris intus prementis ex tædio. Tædiū vel poenitentia figurate Deo tribuitur, quod poenituerit ipsum fecisse hominem in terra, humano loquendi modo: Nam homines tum demum res mutant, cum antecedentis consilij factive poenitet: Deus vero cum factum mutat videtur consilium mutare, sed reuera permanet immutabilis. Doloris eadem ratio. Etsi dolor duobus nominibus hic Deo tribuitur; primum propter odium iniustitiae, quia iustus est; secundo commiseratione creaturae, quae iniustitia sua oppugnat misericordiam Dei. Hinc ergo sequitur decretum, in verf. 7. idque absolutum, cuius tempus quando fuerit pronuntiatum non ausimus definire. alioquin nobis id constat, sufficiens aliquod temporis spatium inter denuntiationem antegressam, quae est hypothetica, & hanc, quae absoluta vel categorica, interveniisse. Huius decreti partes sunt duae, Argumentum, & causa. Argumentum decreti est de hominibus & animantibus cateris, quae in terra degunt, delendis de superficie terrae. Hominibus, quia peccatores sunt, impietati & iniustitiae mancipati. Bestiis, quia mancipia sunt hominum peccatorum atque instrumenta. Nam propterea Deus bestias quoque exscindi voluit, tum ut gravitatem peccati nostri ostenderet, tum ut homini fomites suae nequitiae eriperet, quibus fretus non dubitaret in Deū insolescere: Postremo ad exemplū illud non parum pertinebat. Non est tamē silentio praetereunda in hoc decreto illa commiserationis particula, qua Deus dolore animi sui testificatus est dicens, homine quē creavi. His enim verbis docet se iusto studio creaturam prosequi, sed malum creaturæ interuertere locum Misericordiæ ipsius causam decreti comprehensam his verbis, pœnitet me quod fecerim eam, præcedente versu exposuimus. Sequitur tertius locus, quo Deus appropinquante exfequutionis tempore decretum suum amplius explicat, & omnia cóparat ad exfequutionem ipsius. Hoc autem in loco similiter partes sunt duæ: Vna, causarum, à v.8.ad 12: altera verò decreti singularis, à v.13.ad finè vsque capitis.
units.tr: Moses mentions this obstinacy in these words: There were giants in the earth in those days, namely the days in which God first set out his decree, and also afterwards, that is, they were never brought by God's wholesome warnings to repent, but after those warnings they burned all the more to commit crimes, just as in impious men sin is inflamed and provoked by pious warnings. The licence is shown by those words, when the sons of God went in to the daughters of men, and they bore children to them. But because the novelty of the word might perhaps have held up the reader, Moses added a gloss to explain the word Nephilim, that is, giants: those, he says, are the mighty men, who were of old men of renown, celebrated for their crimes and violence. The external causes that come from God are two: God's judicial knowledge or science, and his just will or justice. Of these, the former is set out in verse 5, the latter in verse 6. Of the knowledge by which God sees all things, two parts are said to exist: one, that God knew the works of that age; the other, that he knew the sources of the works. Concerning the works, Moses says: the LORD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, that is, the doing of evil. The sources of the works that God knew are described by these words: every imagination of the thoughts of the human heart was only evil continually. Thus the very thought and understanding of man is wholly given over to evil. From these words we understand that the heart is evil, its thoughts are evil, and each imagining of the thoughts is evil, and evil in such a way that it can have no part of good in itself, nor at any time. The degrees of God's just will, by which he pursues just men, are similarly set out as two in verse 6. One is grief or repentance, which is predicated of God in human terms. The other is the pain that presses inwardly from that grief. Grief or repentance is attributed to God figuratively, in that it repented him that he had made man on the earth, in human manner of speaking. For men change their course when they repent of a previous plan or deed; God, however, when he changes his deed, seems to change his plan, but in truth he remains unchangeable. The reasoning about pain is the same. Although pain is here attributed to God under two names: first, on account of his hatred of injustice, since he is just; second, from compassion for the creature, which by its injustice assails the mercy of God. Hence there follows the decree in verse 7, and it is absolute. The time at which it was pronounced we dare not define; yet it is clear to us that some sufficient interval of time came between the earlier announcement, which was conditional, and this one, which is absolute or categorical. This decree has two parts: its subject, and its cause. The subject of the decree is the destruction from the face of the earth of men and the other living creatures that dwell in the earth. Men, because they are sinners, given over to impiety and injustice. Beasts, because they are the servants and instruments of sinful men. For this reason God wished the beasts too to be cut off, partly to show the gravity of our sin, and partly to take from man the fuel of his wickedness, relying on which he would not hesitate to grow insolent against God; and finally, that example was of no small importance. Yet in this decree that particle of compassion must not be passed over in silence, by which God, testifying to the grief of his mind, says, the man whom I created. For by these words he teaches that he pursues the creature with just zeal, but that the creature's wickedness overturns the place of his mercy. The cause of the decree, contained in the words it repents me that I have made them, we set out in the preceding verse. There follows the third place, in which God, as the time of execution draws near, explains his decree more fully, and compares everything with its execution. In this place too there are two parts: one of the causes, from verse 8 to 12; the other of the particular decree, from verse 13 to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Tertij ergo loci partes eædem sunt quas in antecedentibus ostendimus: primum occasiones, v. 8. & feqq. quatuor: Deinde verò decreti sententia exponitur, v.13. & reliquo capite. Cum autem decreti partes duæ sint, pro ratione duplicis Ecclesiæ quam Moses duobus antecedentibus capitibus exposuerat: propterea in occasionibus narrandis pro ratione duplicis subiecti duæ partes sunt distinguendæ. Nam primum occasio Misericordiæ in vasa misericordiæ, v.8.& duobus sequentibus: deinde occasio iudicij in vasa iræ, verf.11. & 12. proponitur. Occasionem misericordiæ duobus modis describit Moses, causa, & adiunctis. Causa misericordiæ est vnica Dei gratia, qui non propter nostram, sed propter suam bonitatem etiam immerentibus benefacit. Hanc causam, v. 8. expressit Moses,dicens, Noach innuenit gratiam in oculis Iehoua. Nam, vt verbis vtamur Apostoli, fi gratia, non ergo ex operibus. Alter occasionum locus, nimirum ab adiunctis, in v.9.exponitur: Nempe quod idé[?] ille vir qui in gratia Dei fuisse dicitur in eadem gratia constiterit, iustitia coram hominibus, integritate coram Deo, & pietate vel obsequio fidei quod probauit Deus. Nam horum trium respectu vir iustus, integer & coram Deo ambulans Noach fuisse dicitur. Atque hæ virtutes Noachi circumstantia temporum personarumque amplificantur, cum ita fuisse dicitur, non ætate vna, sed multis, non conuersione cum bonis solum, sed cum hominibus corruptissimis & seculo corruptissimo. Nam propterea idem à Petro præco iustitiæ appellatur. Illius verò diuinæ gratiæ amplificatur locus à subiecto. Quod non solum ad Noachum peruenerit, sed etiam ad familiam ipsius secundum promissionem Dei postea Abrahamo factam, capite (vt vulgo distinguitur) xii. Atque hæc causa est cur generationum Noachi, id est, liberorum mentio iniicitur: generatim quidem v. 9: postea vero speciatim. 10. Altera pars de causa iræ diuinæ in vasa iræ duobus modis, vt ante, distinguitur: factis hominum, v. 11. & cognitione Dei, quæ falli non potest, v.12. Maleficia duobus modis ostenduntur, cum tota terra, id est, incolæ terræ metonymicè, se corrupisse dicitur coram Deo, id est, sine vlla numinis aut maiestatis diuinæ reuerentia in peccata sese proie-cisse: cisse: deinde, quod ista proteruia effectum est vt terra impleretur violentia,& quasi pressa peccatorum pondere fatisceret. Quae duo in cognitionem Dei peruenisse [illegible, ~6 letters] affirmat Moses verf.12. Ex his ergo occasionibus decretum à Deo factum est, & Noacho praesignificatum vt reliquo capite exponitur ad v.vsque vlt.quo haec narratio tota concluditur. Decreti autem duae sunt singulares partes, quas no ita luculenter Deus in praecedentibus expresserat: Prior est denuntiatio irę in vasa irae, v.13. Posterior modus Misericordiae & gratiae faciendae Noacho significatus atque imperatus, verf. 14. & duobus seqq. Quibus subiicitur sua enarratio v.17. & reliquis. Priorem partem decreti secundum substantiam, & causam ipsius,& modum Noacho exposuit Deus. Substantia haec est, finis vniuersæ carnis aduenit coram me. Causa subiicitur illis verbis, quia plena est terra violentia ab iis. Modus denique illis, & ecce me perditurum illos e terra, vel potius, cum ipsa terra, id est, animantibus quae calcant terram, vt supra v.7, Deus expresserat. Secunda pars decreti de Misericordia in vasa misericordiae explicanda duobus membris continetur, Mandato, & promissione. Mandatum est de instrumento ad conseruationem Ecclesiae fabricando, tribus versibus: promissio de salute in eo instrumento quod Deus imperauerat exhibenda. Instrumetum a Deo imperatur arca, secundum materiam & formam illius a Deo circumscripta diligentissimé. Postquam enim Deus communiter imperauit, dicendo, fac tibi arcam, materia illius describitur, nimirum ligna Gopher, quod nomen cedrebates, inter cedros praestantissimae arboris, putamus esse: quo ex ligno etiam nidi, id est, secluforia fuerunt facienda, nequid intus occasione sordium putresceret: deinde vero pix, qua arcam intus & foris oblini oportuit, ne qua forte rima aquae perrumperent, v. 14. Forma vero tum secundum quantitatem partium v. 15. tum secundum qualitatem dispositionemque traditur, verf.16.
units.tr: So the parts of the third section are the same as those I showed in the earlier ones: first the occasions, vv. 8 and following, of which there are four; then the sense of the decree is set out, from v. 13 to the end of the chapter. Since the decree has two parts, corresponding to the twofold Church that Moses described in the two preceding chapters, the occasions too must be divided into two parts according to the twofold subject. The first occasion, that of mercy towards the vessels of mercy, is put forward in v. 8 and the two following verses; the second, that of judgment against the vessels of wrath, in vv. 11 and 12. Moses describes the occasion of mercy in two ways, by its cause and by its accompanying circumstances. The sole cause of mercy is the grace of God, who does good to the undeserving not for our sake but for his own goodness. Moses expressed this cause in v. 8, saying, "Noah found grace in the eyes of Jehovah." For, to use the words of the Apostle, "if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works." The other place for occasions, namely that from circumstances, is set out in v. 9: that this same man, who is said to have been in the grace of God, persevered in that same grace, in righteousness before men, in integrity before God, and in piety or the obedience of faith, which God approved. For in respect of these three things Noah is said to have been "a righteous man, blameless and walking with God." These virtues of Noah are magnified by the circumstances of time and persons, since it is said that he was so, not for one age but for many, not only in the company of good men but among the most corrupt men and in the most corrupt age. For this reason Peter also calls him a preacher of righteousness. The place of God's grace is magnified by its subject: it reached not only Noah but also his family, according to the promise of God later made to Abraham, in chapter 12 (as it is commonly divided). And this is the reason why the mention of Noah's "generations," that is, of his children, is introduced: in general in v. 9, and afterwards in particular in v. 10. The other part concerns the cause of God's wrath against the vessels of wrath, which, as before, is divided in two ways: the deeds of men, v. 11, and the knowledge of God, which cannot be deceived, v. 12. Wickedness is shown in two ways: when "all the earth," that is, the inhabitants of the earth, by a metonymy, is said to have "corrupted itself before God," that is, to have thrown itself into sin without any reverence for the divine majesty or power; and then, because of this insolence, the earth was "filled with violence" and, as if pressed down by the weight of sins, was ready to collapse. Moses affirms in v. 12 that these two things [illegible] came to the knowledge of God. From these occasions, then, the decree was made by God and was signified to Noah in advance, as is set out in the rest of the chapter down to the last verse, with which this whole narrative is concluded. There are two distinct parts of the decree, which God had not so clearly expressed earlier. The first is the declaration of wrath against the vessels of wrath, v. 13. The second is the manner of mercy and of grace to be shown, signified and commanded to Noah, in v. 14 and the two following verses, to which is added its explanation from v. 17 onward. God set out the first part of the decree according to its substance, its cause and its manner, to Noah. The substance is this: "the end of all flesh has come before me." The cause is added in these words: "because the earth is full of violence through them." Finally, the manner is given in these words: "and behold, I will destroy them from the earth," or rather, "together with the earth," that is, with the living things that tread the earth, as God had stated above in v. 7. The second part of the decree, concerning mercy towards the vessels of mercy, is contained in two members: a command and a promise. The command concerns the building of the instrument for preserving the Church, in three verses; the promise concerns the salvation to be given in that instrument which God had ordered. The instrument commanded by God is the ark, its material and form being precisely laid out by God. For after God had commanded in general terms, saying, "make yourself an ark," its material is described, namely "gopher wood," which name we think denotes the cedar-like, among the cedars, a most excellent tree. Of this wood the "nests," that is, the compartments, were also to be made, lest anything rot within through the accumulation of filth; then there is the "pitch," with which the ark had to be smeared inside and out, lest any crack let the water through, v. 14. The form is given both according to the measurement of its parts, v. 15, and according to its quality and arrangement, v. 16.

units.la: Quantitatis loci tres sunt pro natura solidorum corporum, vel soli-dam speciem obtinentium: longitudo, latitudo, atque altitudo: e quibus longitudo trecentorum cubitorum: latitudo, quinquaginta: altitudo, triginta imperatur. Ac proinde longitudo sex spatia latitudinis & decem altitudinis obtinebat, quem naturalem esse corporis humani commensum veteres tradiderunt. Qualitatem dispositionemque partium quatuor distinctè imperauit Deus verf. 16. Primum fenestrarum his verbis, claram lucem, vel meridianam, facies arcae, id est, fenestratum opus luculentissimum. Secundo tectum imperatur (quod ego quidem cameratum esse ad formam thori putauerim) his verbis, ad cubitum consummabis eam superne, pro eo quod est eiusmodi aptabis tectū quod in omnes partes in longitudine cubiti proiiciatur supra mensurā arcæ, adeò vt subgrūdę tecti cubito promine-tes arcæ latera defendant ab imbriū iniuria in omnes partes. Tertiò portæ dispositione imperauit Deus his verbis, Porta facies arcæ ad latus illius. Postremò cōtignationes arcæ distinguūtur his verbis, infimas, secundanas, & tertianas nimirū stationes facies, siue nidos, vt v.14. appellauerat, i.totidē contignationes quarū infima solo iuncta, secūdana vulgò mediana, tertiana verò summa appellatur. Hic variæ quæ-stiones oboriri solent, quarū parte ipsa interpretatione dissoluimus: duæ nobis restare videtur: vna, de veritate facti; altera, de significatio-ne. Veritate facti controuertūt imperiti, eo quòd existimāt fieri nūqua potuisse, vt tā angusto in spatio tātus numerus tantorū animaliū cū reb. cæteris quas Deus imperauit cōprehēderetur. quapropter apud veteres excogitata fuit hæc ratio, vt cubitorum mensura distinguē-retur. Nam alij cubitū hunc non communē sed regiū esse putauerūt, i. (vt docet Herodotus) qui communē minore palmo superauerit. Alij sacrum dixerunt esse, i. duplarem, quēadmodū siclus sacer communē duplo superabat. Alij deniq; (quorū princeps fuisse videtur Origenes) cubitum Geometricum hunc definiuerunt, qui senos cōmunes cubitos sit cōplexus, vt illud taceamus, quod fermè omnes adiecerunt, etiā priscos illos cubitos quāuis cōmunes communibus nostris maiores extitisse, pro ratione priscorū corporū, secundū quā stadiū Herculis maius fuisse cōmunib³ stadiis legimus apud Agelliū Principio Noct. Att. Atq; hoc quidē postremū facile acceperim. Cæteras determina-tiones vsq; adeò probare non possum, quia notantur plurimū in scri-pturis differentiæ eiusmodi cū a mesura aut ratione cōmuni discedi-tur. Manet igitur quæstio, quomodo illa omnia in arcā ingredi Deus præceperit, quæ contineri ea nō potuisse videatur. Respōsio est, facile hunc nodū explicari, si amplitudine arcę cū animantiū numero cō paraueris. Amplitudine arcæ eā fuisse, si vniuscuiusq; contignationis solū metiaris, vt quindecies millenos cubitos in planū habuerit: quā ré facile deprehensuri sunt quicunq; trecenta per quinquaginta multi-plicauerint. Quod si tria sola contignationum simul coniunxeris, comperies fuisse quadragies quinquies mille cubitos. Quæ autem in hoc cubitorū numero fuerint comprehensa facile quiuis hoc modo subduxerit. Primum aquatilia non venerunt in arcam. Restant ter-restres & aeriæ animantes: aeriarum maximam vulgus esse aquilam aut otum nouit. Harum spatium non vsque adeò fuisse magnum oportuit. De terrestribus plus laboris videtur esse; sed frustra. Nam etiamsi trecenta animalium terrestrium genera daremus esse, eáq; in vnica cōtignatione versata poneremus, tamē vnicuiq; generi capiendo quinquaginta cubiti superessent[?] in vnica solum contignatione. Iam vero si omnia genera in vnum contraxeris eorum animalium quæ insistunt pedibus (nam reptilia vix quicquam capiunt loci) vix quinquaginta genera, aut ad summum sexaginta deprehenderis; quorum maximum & capacissimum est elephas, secundum ab eo rhinoceros, & bos: nam equus & camelus etsi proceritate excedunt tamē corporis gracilitate boui cedunt plurimum. cæteras animantes longè minores esse constat. Quid ergo impedimento est, cum quinquageni cubiti generi vnicuique tribui possint, si trecenta animalium genera statueris, quo minus iste numerus animalium, qui à Deo imperatus est, in vnam contignationem non possit conuenire? Facile itaque immundæ animantes binæ, mas & fœmina; mundæ septenæ in arcam à Noacho intromissæ sunt. Atque hæc de veritate facti. Alter locus de significatione primùm commotus est à Petro 1. Epist. cap.3. sub finem. Dicit enim diluuio illi vel aquis illis diluuij, per quas arca fluitauit & Noach seruatus est, fuisse Baptismum, quo seruamur, ἀντίτυπος: Baptismo autem mortificantur vetera ac sepeliuntur, & noua omnia in Christo excitantur. Hoc putant homines præsidetes nō satis appositè à Petro accōmodari historiæ diluuij: inepti, qui nesciunt distinguere inter rerum veritatem, & signorum cum rebus signatis analogiam, maximè verò eorum signorum quæ ab institutione sunt. res igitur explicatu facilis est in hunc modum, vt vetus ille mundus olim, ita est semper vetus homo: veteri mundo maledixit Deus, & eadem iustitia veteri homini maledicit. veterem mundum perdidit Deus & sepeliuit aquis, reliquias gratiæ, id est semen sanctum in aquis seruauit eluendo peccata antecedentia veteris mundi. Sic ergo Deus in Christo veterem hominem mortificat, sepelitque peccatum illius, & a peccato abluens iisdem aquis excitat nouum ad imaginem suam in Christo Iesu:cuius rei olim fuit typus in aquis diluuij, quemadmodum hoc tempore typus est in aqua Baptismi. quapropter diluuium & Baptismus inter se comparata, optimè à Petro dicuntur ἀντίτυπα, vt Nazianzenus ferm. de Bapt. annotauit. Dixerit fortasse quispiam, At non dicitur à Mose fuisse huius rei typus. Respondeo, At dicitur à Paulo 1. Cor.10. quæ ante gesta sunt fuerunt typi: siue communes typi illi fuerint, siue proprij atque destinati ad certam rem aliquam adumbrandam. Cum autem Deus per Apostolum hunc fuisse typum nostræ mortificationis, sepulturæ, & resurrectionis in Christo docuerit, quam eandem rem docemur Baptismo nostro; illud sanctè cū Petro affirmamus, quatenus aquæ diluuij in familiam Noachi operatæ sunt, eas typū fuisse proprium atque destinatū beneficiorum quæ in Christo obtinemus, quemadmodum in Testamento nouo typus earundem rerum Baptismus est, & hic typus illius ἀντίτυπος.
units.tr: The dimensions are three, as belongs to the nature of solid bodies, or those having a solid form: length, breadth and height. Of these, a length of three hundred cubits, a breadth of fifty and a height of thirty is commanded. Accordingly the length was six times the breadth and ten times the height, a proportion which the ancients taught was the natural measure of the human body. God gave the quality and arrangement of the parts in four distinct commands, v. 16. First, concerning the windows, in these words: "a clear light," or midday light, "you shall make for the ark," that is, a most splendid work with windows. Secondly, the roof is commanded (which I myself would think was vaulted, in the form of a bed-chamber), in these words: "you shall finish it above to a cubit," that is, you shall fit a roof which projects on every side by a cubit in length beyond the measure of the ark, so that the eaves projecting a cubit defend the sides of the ark from the harm of rain on every side. Thirdly, God commanded the arrangement of the door in these words: "you shall make the door of the ark at its side." Lastly, the storeys of the ark are distinguished in these words: "lower, second and third" you shall make, namely the "stations," or nests, as he called them in v. 14, that is, as many storeys, of which the lowest is joined to the ground, the second is commonly called the middle, and the third is called the uppermost. Here various questions usually arise, some of which I have already resolved in the interpretation itself; two seem to remain: one concerning the truth of the fact, the other concerning its meaning. Unskilled people dispute the truth of the fact, because they think it could never have happened that so great a number of such great animals, together with the other things which God commanded, could be contained in so narrow a space. For this reason the ancients devised the explanation that the measure of the cubit must be distinguished. For some thought that this cubit was not the common one but "royal," that is, (as Herodotus teaches) one that exceeded the common cubit by a smaller palm. Others said it was "sacred," that is, double, just as the sacred shekel was double the common one. Others finally (of whom Origen seems to have been the leader) defined this as a geometrical cubit, which contained six common cubits; to say nothing of what almost all added, that even those ancient cubits, although common, were larger than our common ones, in proportion to the bodies of the ancients, according to which we read that the stadium of Hercules was larger than common stadia, in Aulus Gellius, at the beginning of the Attic Nights. And this last point I could readily accept. The other determinations I cannot approve to that extent, because such differences are very often noted in the Scriptures when we depart from common measure or reckoning. The question therefore remains, how God could have commanded that all those things be brought into the ark, which seem not to have been able to be contained in it. The answer is that this knot is easily untied, if you compare the size of the ark with the number of animals. The area of the ark, if you measure the floor of each storey alone, will be found to have been fifteen thousand cubits in plan; a thing which whoever multiplies three hundred by fifty will easily discover. And if you add together the three storeys, you will find that the area was four times five thousand cubits. Anyone can easily work out for himself what was contained in this number of cubits. First, the creatures of the water did not come into the ark. There remain land animals and creatures of the air. The common people know that the largest of the winged creatures are the eagle and the ostrich. The space needed for these need not have been very great. The land animals seem to involve more labour; but in vain. For even if we were to grant three hundred kinds of land animals, and place them in a single storey, still, for each kind there would remain fifty cubits of room in that one storey. Now if you gather all the kinds of animals that walk on feet into one (for reptiles hardly take up any room), you will find scarcely fifty kinds, or at most sixty; of which the largest and most capacious is the elephant, next to it the rhinoceros and the ox; for the horse and the camel, though they exceed in height, yield for the most part to the ox in the slenderness of their bodies. It is agreed that the other animals are far smaller. What then stands in the way, since fifty cubits can be assigned to each kind, if you posit three hundred kinds of animals, why that number of animals which was commanded by God could not be accommodated in a single storey? So the unclean animals, two of each, male and female, and the clean, seven each, were easily brought into the ark by Noah. And so much for the truth of the fact. The second question about the meaning was first raised by Peter, 1 Epistle, chapter 3, near the end. For he says that the flood, or those waters of the flood through which the ark floated and Noah was saved, were a baptism, by which we are saved, [ἀντίτυπος] (an antitype): by baptism the old things are mortified and buried, and all things are raised anew in Christ. Some men, who are not wise, think that Peter has applied this too loosely to the history of the flood: they do not know how to distinguish between the truth of the things and the analogy of signs with the things signified, especially those signs which are of divine institution. The matter is therefore easily explained in this way: as the old world once was, so the old man always is. God cursed the old world, and by the same righteousness he curses the old man. God destroyed the old world and buried it in the waters; he preserved the remnants of grace, that is, the holy seed, in the waters, by washing away the sins of the old world that went before. So in Christ God mortifies the old man, and buries his sin; and by washing him from sin with the same waters he raises up the new man in the image of himself in Christ Jesus. Of this thing the flood's waters were once a type, just as at this time the water of baptism is a type. Therefore the flood and baptism, compared with one another, are rightly called [ἀντίτυπα] (antitypes) by Peter, as Nazianzen noted in his sermon on baptism. Someone may perhaps say: but Moses does not say that they were a type of this thing. I answer: but Paul says, in 1 Corinthians 10, that the things which happened before were types; whether these were common types, or proper and destined to shadow forth some particular thing. Since God, through the Apostle, has taught that the flood was a type of our mortification, burial and resurrection in Christ, which is the same thing we are taught by our baptism, we affirm with Peter, and rightly, that the waters of the flood, insofar as they operated upon the family of Noah, were a proper and destined type of the benefits which we obtain in Christ; just as in the New Testament baptism is a type of the same things, and this type is the antitype of that one.

units.la: Antecedentis mandati causa in promissionibus & vsu rerum imperatarum ostenditur, ad v.vsque 20. Deinde vero appendix attexitur, v.21. promissionis quam Deus mandato subiicit. Summa est, Deũ post diluuium ex fœdere gratioso Noacho, familiæ eius & animantibus quæ in arca futuræ erant, parciturum, ac propterea arcam fuisse ab ipso imperatam. Promissionis antecedens est, fore diluuium, v.17. subsistantia est, seruatum iri Noachum & familiam resque ipsius ex fœdere v.19. & sequentibus. Adiunctum denique est, Noacho ipsi de commeatu videndum esse, v.21. de diluuio eadem pronuntiantur quæ ante. Primum Deum auctore fore illius, omnésq; animantes eo perdi-tum iri: sed restrictio adhibetur, quicquid in terra est, expirabit, vt no-minatim ex opposito aquatilia excipi intelligamus. Promissionis partes duæ sunt: Vna, Deum fœdus suum cum Noacho initum, esse præstiturum: altera ex fœdere ipsum familiamque in arca seruaturum, v. 18. & propter ipsum animantes binas siue coniugas ex omni genere in eadem arca conseruaturum esse. Ratio vero animantium introducendarum duobus modis exponitur: nempe studium Noachi, verf. 19. Ex omnibus, &c. & voluntarium illarum obsequium v.20. quia singularis fuit instinctus à Deo inditus, vt exspoliata natura sua animantes se ad Noachum reciperent, & innocentem vitam inter se in arca viuerent. Adiunctum de commeatu v.21. facile à quouis intelligitur. Ita concluditur caput breui narratione v.22. cuius partes duæ sunt: Vna de re, id fecisse Noachum quod Deus mandauerat: altera de mandato, omnino prout mandauerat sic fecisse. Nam hoc v-trumque caput in omni piorum obedientia est necesse.
units.tr: The reason for the preceding command is shown in the promises and in the carrying out of the things commanded, down to verse 20. Then an appendix is added, verse 21, concerning the promise which God attaches to the command. The sum is this: after the flood God, by a gracious covenant, will spare Noah, his family, and the living creatures that were to be in the ark; and for this reason the ark was commanded by him. The antecedent of the promise is that there will be a flood (verse 17); its substance is that Noah and his family and belongings will be preserved by covenant (verse 19 and following). Finally, something is added: that provision of food must be made for Noah himself (verse 21). Concerning the flood the same things are declared as before: first, that by God's doing it will come, and that all living creatures will perish in it; but a restriction is added, "whatever is on the earth shall expire," so that we understand the water creatures to be excepted by name by way of contrast. The promise has two parts: one, that God will fulfil the covenant he made with Noah; the other, that by the covenant he will keep him and his family in the ark, and for his sake will preserve two of every kind of living creature, that is, a pair, in the same ark (verse 18). The reason for bringing in the living creatures is set out in two ways: namely, Noah's diligence (verse 19, "Of all," etc.) and their willing obedience (verse 20), since it was a singular instinct implanted by God, so that the creatures, stripped of their own nature, would betake themselves to Noah and live a harmless life together in the ark. The addition about food (verse 21) is easily understood by anyone.
