So the chapter is concluded with a brief narrative (verse 22), whose parts are two: one concerning the thing, that Noah did what God had commanded; the other concerning the command, that he did everything just as he had been commanded. For each of these two points is necessary in all the obedience of the godly.

units.la: CAPITIS VII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: THE ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 7.

units.la: DOST decretum quod præcedente cap. proposuit Moses, nunc sequitur exsequutionis historia: Cum autem decreti duæ singulares partes sint: vna, de per-dendo seculo; altera de Ecclesia conseruanda: vtriusq; partis historia coniuncta est hoc capite. Nam prima vocatio singularis Dei ad præsentem salutem Ecclesiæ proponitur versibus quatuor. Deinde vero Noachi obsequium ad præparationem eiusdem salutis pertinens, ad verf. vsque 10. Postremo autem exsequuexsequutio ipsa describitur, adfinem usque cap. Vocationis Dei ad rem præsentem argumentū idem est quod v.18.& seqq. proximi cap. Exposuit Deus, nempe ut sine mora Noach cum familia ingrediatur arcam & animantes intromittat. Ingrediendi mandatum continetur, v.1.& causam coniunctam habet, quia te vidi iustum coram me in generatione ista. quasi dicat tota hæc generatio coram me corrupta est, te unum deprehendi alienum a corruptione illius: quapropter effecturus sum ut iustitiæ tuæ testificatio beneficij diuini respondeat. Causam autem dicimus, non quòd Noach per se iustus fuerit, sed quòd Deus illum iustum viderit, id est iustificatum per fidem in sanguine Christi,& amplexum promissiones ipsius animaduertit operam dedisse sanctificationi, ut illam iustitiam, quæ coram Deo est iustitia, & sanctimoniam vitæ, quæ coram hominibus iustitia est, testificaretur. Nam iustitia quæ coram Deo est, ea re iustificat: iustitia vero quę coram hominibus, ea iustificatos sequitur & probat, ut fructus arboré. Alter locus de intromittendis animalibus aliquid amplius enuntiat quàm præcedente cap. expressum est: nempe quot ex quibus animalibus intromittenda sint per se duo & tria: nempe ex mundis animalibus septena, id est, tria paria, & unum ad sacrificium. Ex immundis animalibus bina, id est par coniugalium unum. Cur autem mundorum numerus maior quàm aliorum fuerit intromissus, ratio est evidens: quia hæc adhiberi oportuit præ immundis tū ad sacrificia, tum ad vitæ præsentis vsum, vt seq. cap. demonstrabimus. Vnum vero nō coniugatum ex mundis amplius imperatum est, quia hoc pertinuit ad illud sacrificium cuius post meminit Moses cap.8.v.20. Vtriusque mandati causa est, v.4. salus Ecclesiæ ab vniuersali diluuio liberandæ. Huius diluuij principium, progressus, & exitus paucis exponitur: Principium, quod die 7 : progressus, quod 40. dies & noctes: exitus quod ad internecionem excidiumque eorum animalium quæ in terra sunt futurum esset. Huic singulari mandato & vocationi Dei, antequam diluuium aduentaret, Noach obsequutus dicitur, primò quidem vniuersè in verf. 5: deinde vero speciatim, verfib.sequentibus. nam ætate Noachi annotata verf.6. dicitur ipse cum familia arcam ingressus esse v.7.& animalia intromisisse, v. 8. Eáque coniuga, v.9. quæ animalia Deus præceperat. His ita comparatis narratur exsequutio, primò quidem generatim, v. 10 : deinde minutatim, v. seqq. Generatim his verbis, Fuit septimo die, &c. Minutatim vero in obsequutione narrantur ista: primò tempus, & modus orti diluuij, v. 11. tum spatium quo modus ille continuatus est, v.12. & seqq. Postremò autem effecta à v.16. ad finem. Tempus orti diluuij circumscribitur secundum annum & diem definitū.Nam annus fuisse dicitur 600. vitæ Noachi,qui fuit mundi 1656. Deinde mensis numeratur secūdus: postremò dies 17. illius mensis. Quæritur qui annus fuerit, vtrum lunaris an solaris : vtrum ciuilis an Ecclesiasticus, vt Hebræi solent distinguere. Lunarem esse ostendit ipsafupputatio & historicorum veterum auctoritas. supputatio ; nam si à die 17. secundi mensis inceperis numerare illos 150. dies, quorum mentio est vers.vlt. huius cap. & tertio sequentis ad 17. vsque mensis septimi, qui refertur à Mose c.seq. v. 4. omnino comperies hos menses non lunares, sed magis solares extitisse. Nam quinque menses efficiunt præcisè 150. dies,secundum rationem annorum Babylonicam & Ægyptiacam. Apud hos enim menses tricenûm dierum erant: proinde menses duodecim effecerunt 360. dies, quibus ad supplementum solaris cursus adhibebantur in sine cuiusque anni festi dies quinque , quos illi ἡμέρας ἐπαγομένας appellabant. Idem quoque aliis numeris in hoc & seq. cap. demonstrari posset,quos diligentiæ lectorum permittimus. Accedit historicorum veterum auctoritas, Herodoti lib. 1. Diodori Siculi, Plutarchi, & aliorum optimæ notæ, qui hanc rationem annorum à Chaldæis & Ægyptiis iam olim seruatam & per manus fuisse traditam posteris vno consensu docuerunt.Altera quæstio est,Vtrum ciuilis sit annus, an Ecclesiasticus, id est vtrum huius anni principium ab eo tempore quo sol ingreditur signum Arietis duci oporteat,an verò quo in Libram venit.Plerósque Hebrǝorum,& alios adstipulantes ipsis, non sum nescius ista de anno ciuili accepisse, qui autumno inceperit. Mihi verò,bona ipsorum & omnium pace, annus videtur fuisse is quem postea Hebræi dixerunt Ecclesiasticum, id est qui ineunte vere inceperit. Nam quod illi putât annum Ecclesiasticum tempore demùm Mosis Exod.12. institutum esse,non est simpliciter accipiendum in eum modū,vt si primùm eo tempore institutus esset, sed potiùs restitutum esse intelligimus, cùm apud Israëlitas in Ægypto in obliuionem abiisset. Neque refert quod ipsi quoque Ægyptij eandem rationem annorum similiter obliuione inuoluerint: Nam id eo factum est apud Ægyptios, quòd inde à temporibus illius famis, qua Ægyptios pauit Ioseph , & illi omnes regi suo addicti sunt, annos inceperunt numerare à singulari obligatione & pensitatione anniuersaria , qua quintam suorum prouentuum regi pendere tenebantur Genef.46.
units.tr: Now that Moses has set out the decree in the preceding chapter, the history of its execution follows. The decree has two distinct parts: one concerning the destruction of the world, and the other concerning the preservation of the Church. The history of both parts is joined together in this chapter. The first, the singular call of God to the present salvation of the Church, is set out in four verses. Then Noah's obedience, which pertains to the preparation of that same salvation, is given to verse 10. Finally, the execution itself is described, to the end of the chapter. The subject of God's call to the present matter is the same as in verses 18 and following of the preceding chapter, where God set forth that Noah, without delay, should enter the ark with his family and bring in the animals. The command to enter is given in verse 1, and it has a connected reason: because I have seen you to be righteous before me in this generation. It is as if he said: this whole generation is corrupt before me; I have found you alone to be free of that corruption; therefore I will bring it about that the witness of your righteousness corresponds to the blessing of God. We call this a reason not because Noah was righteous in himself, but because God saw him as righteous, that is, justified through faith in the blood of Christ, and because God noticed that he had embraced the promises and had devoted himself to sanctification, so that he bore witness to that righteousness which is righteousness before God, and to that holiness of life which is righteousness before men. For the righteousness which is before God justifies by that very fact, whereas the righteousness which is before men follows the justified and proves them, as fruit proves the tree. The other passage, on bringing in the animals, states something more than was expressed in the preceding chapter: namely, how many of each kind are to be brought in, namely, of clean animals seven pairs, that is, three pairs and one for sacrifice; of unclean animals two, that is, one pair of mates. The reason why more of the clean animals were brought in than of the others is plain: these were needed both for sacrifices and for the use of this present life, as we shall show in the following chapter. Moreover, one unmated clean animal was commanded in addition, because this pertained to that sacrifice which Moses mentions afterwards in chapter 8, verse 20. The cause of both commands is, in verse 4, the salvation of the Church, which was to be freed from the universal flood. The beginning, the course and the end of this flood are set out briefly: the beginning, that it was on the day 7; the course, that it lasted 40 days and nights; the end, that it would bring about the destruction and ruin of those animals that are on the earth. Noah is said to have obeyed this singular command and this call of God before the flood came: first in general terms, in verse 5, and then in particular, in the following verses. For after Noah's age is noted in verse 6, it is said that he himself with his family entered the ark (verse 7), and brought in the animals (verse 8), and that they came in pairs (verse 9), as God had commanded. Having thus set these things in order, the execution is narrated: first in general, in verse 10, It was on the seventh day, etc.; then in detail, in the verses that follow. In detail, the obedience is recounted thus: first the time and the manner of the beginning of the flood (verse 11); then the length of time over which that state continued (verse 12 and following); and finally the things accomplished from verse 16 to the end. The time of the beginning of the flood is fixed by the year and the day specified. The year is said to be the 600th of Noah's life, which was the 1656th year of the world. Then the second month is numbered, and finally the 17th day of that month. The question arises what kind of year this was, whether lunar or solar, and whether civil or ecclesiastical, as the Hebrews are accustomed to distinguish. That it was lunar is shown by the reckoning itself and by the authority of the ancient historians. As to the reckoning: if you begin counting from the 17th day of the second month those 150 days, of which mention is made at the end of verse 3 of this chapter and in verse 3 of the following chapter, down to the 17th day of the seventh month, which Moses mentions in verse 4 of the next chapter, you will find that these months were not lunar but rather solar. For five months make exactly 150 days, according to the Babylonian and Egyptian reckoning of years. For among these peoples the months had thirty days each; therefore twelve months made 360 days, and to complete the solar course, five extra days were added at the end of each year, which they called ἡμέρας ἐπαγομένας [added days]. The same could also be demonstrated from other numbers in this and the following chapter, which we leave to the diligence of the reader. To this comes the authority of the ancient historians: Herodotus, book 1; Diodorus Siculus; Plutarch; and others of the best repute, who with one voice have taught that this reckoning of years was observed by the Chaldeans and Egyptians from of old and handed down to posterity. The other question is whether the year was civil or ecclesiastical, that is, whether the beginning of this year should be taken from the time when the sun enters the sign of Aries, or rather when it enters Libra. I am not unaware that most of the Hebrews, and others who agree with them, have understood these things of the civil year, which began in autumn. But to me, with all due respect to them and to everyone, the year seems to have been that which the Hebrews later called ecclesiastical, that is, the one that began in early spring. For the view that the ecclesiastical year was instituted only at the time of Moses (Exod. 12) is not to be taken simply in the sense that it was first established at that time; rather, we understand that it was restored, since among the Israelites in Egypt it had fallen into oblivion. Nor does it matter that the Egyptians themselves likewise let the same reckoning of years fall into oblivion. For this happened among the Egyptians because, from the time of that famine in which Joseph fed the Egyptians, and they all became bound to their king, they began to count the years from a single obligation and an annual payment, by which they were bound to pay the king a fifth of their produce (Gen. 46).

units.la: Modus verò illius ortus de quo Moses instituit dicere,in v.10. duplex est, his verbis comprehensus, hoc eodem die diffiderunt se omnes fontes abyssi magnæ & cataractæ cæli apertæ siue solutæ sunt: pro eo quod est inferne & superne omnia exundauerunt iudicio Dei. Cui narrationi e diuerso opponitur illa 2.v.cap.seq. obturati sunt fontes abyssi, & cataractæ cæli, fuitque cohibitus imber e cælo. Sensus igitur est, omnia naturæ vincula soluta fuisse, vt aquæ in mundum inundarent. Nam cùm aquæ e fontibus in terra eructentur tamquam e suis conceptaculis, & pluuiæ e spécubus nubium deorsum immittantur secundum naturæ ordinem, non potuit melius naturæ huius conturbatio significari, quàm vt conceptacula illa disrupta dicerentur; fontes e rupibus tamquam dissilientibus & fissis, & nubes tamquam e spécubus (quibus claustris continentur) erumpentes. Atque hic ortus diluuij: cuius modus similiter vniuersè describitur seq.v.quod ex illis fontibus & spécubus aquæ dies 40.& noctes totidem in terras irruperint,v.11. atque hæc vniuersè dicta minutatim exponuntur duobus modis.
units.tr: The manner of that beginning, of which Moses undertook to speak in verse 10, is twofold, comprehended in these words: on this same day all the fountains of the great deep were broken up and the windows of heaven were opened, so that all things below and above were flooded by the judgment of God. Opposed to this account, on the other hand, is that of verse 2 of the following chapter: the fountains of the deep and the windows of heaven were stopped, and the rain from heaven was restrained. The sense, therefore, is that all the bonds of nature were loosed, so that the waters poured into the world. For since waters well up from the fountains in the earth as from their own reservoirs, and rains are sent down from the hollows of the clouds according to the order of nature, the disturbance of this nature could not have been signified better than by saying that those reservoirs were broken: the fountains bursting from the rocks as from things that split and cracked, and the clouds breaking forth as from hollows (by which they are enclosed like barred doors). And this is the beginning of the flood. Its course is similarly described in general in the following verse: that from those fountains and hollows the waters poured down upon the lands for forty days and as many nights, verse 11. These general statements are then set out in detail in two ways.

units.la: Nam primùm antecedens Dei erga Ecclesiam studium confirmatur, tamquam per [illegible, ~7 letters] versibus quatuor. Deinde verò modus progressionis diluuij copiosè exponitur, ad finem vsque capitis. Studiu Dei in Ecclesiam veritásque promissionum eius demonstratur primùm salute Noachi & familiæ eius, cui oportunissimo velut momento prospexit Deus, v. 12. secundo accessione omnium animantium ad commoditatem venturi mundi & Ecclesiæ,pertinentium,v. 13.Præterea ductu vel instinctu singulari Dei quo animantes cæteræ actæ sunt, vt sine graui labore humano ad Noachum in arcam aduentarent ad salutem suam, v.14.& ad propagationem, coniugatæ, v. 15. Postremò quòd illis omnibus ingressis Deus illis ianuam occlusit arcæ,eámque stipauit ne quâ forte rimâ aquæ diluuij perrumperent intro,v.16.His positis, pertexitur progressionis modus: primùm quòd aquæ inualescentes arcam paulatim extulerunt e terra,v.17. Secundò quòd illis amplius inualescentibus incepit arca fluitare,v.17. cum adhuc extarent montium cacumina. Tertiò quòd tandem ipsa montium cacumina aquis immersa sunt, v.18. & quidem vsq; adeo immersa vt aquæ tandem montes altissimos quindecim cubitis superauerint,v. 19. Huius diluuij effectus postea consequutus dicitur, quòd omnes animantes quæ in terra degunt expirauerunt & mortuæ atque deletæ sunt,v. 20.& duobus seqq.Ex quo iudicio Noach solus cum suis in arca euaserit per gratiam Dei secundum promissionem eius, v.23. Postremò quòd aquæ illæ obtinuerunt dies 150.id est,menses quinque(vt heri exposuimus) vsque dum arca fluitans coepit consistere, prout seq. cap. narrat Moses.
units.tr: For first the earlier care of God for the Church is confirmed, as by [illegible] in four verses. Then, however, the manner of the progress of the flood is fully set out, to the end of the chapter. God's care for the Church, and the truth of his promises, is shown first by the salvation of Noah and his family, for which God provided at the most opportune moment, verse 12; second, by the coming of all the animals pertaining to the convenience of the coming world and the Church, verse 13. Moreover, by the singular guidance or impulse of God by which the other animals were led, so that without heavy human labour they came to Noah into the ark for their own safety, verse 14, and for propagation, in pairs, verse 15. Lastly, when all of them had entered, God closed the door of the ark for them and stopped it up, lest by chance the waters of the flood should break in through some crack, verse 16. With these things laid down, the manner of the progress is set out: first, the waters, growing stronger, gradually lifted the ark from the earth, verse 17. Second, when they grew stronger still, the ark began to float, verse 17, while the peaks of the mountains still stood out. Third, at last the very peaks of the mountains were submerged under the waters, verse 18; and indeed they were so completely submerged that the waters at last rose fifteen cubits above the highest mountains, verse 19. The effect of this flood is afterwards said to have followed: all the animals that move on the earth breathed their last and were dead and destroyed, verse 20, and in the two following verses. From this judgment Noah alone escaped with his own in the ark, by the grace of God according to his promise, verse 23. Lastly, those waters prevailed for 150 days, that is, five months (as we explained yesterday), until the floating ark began to settle, as the following chapter relates in Moses's account.

units.la: CAPITIS VIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 8 ANALYSIS.

units.la: ALTERAM partem libri Genefeos diximus esse de historia seculi posterioris à Deo gratiose instaurati, postquam horrendo iudicio prius illud seculum deleuerat. In hac autem parte altera similiter duo capita summa instituì necesse est: quo-rum unum est, Historia instaurationis, cap. 7. & 8: alterum, Historia instaurati mundi & Ecclesiae, us-que ad illud tempus quo Ioseph in Ægypto vita defunctus est. In-staurationis historia duabus partibus conclusa est: nam primum nostrae ipsius vel rerum quae in natura sunt instauratio ponitur cap. 8. Deinde vero leges & iura ad mundum Ecclesiamque, dum in mundo est, pertinentia, cap. 9. in naturae rerum instauratione, quae hoc capite exponitur, ortus instaurationis obseruandus est: Primum quidem facto, ad v. 14. capitis: deinde vero sermone, v. 14. & duobus seqq. Postremo universali constitutione rerum ex promisso Dei, ad finem usque capitis. In ortu tria opus est obseruari; primum causas, v. 1. & 2: deinde facta v. 3. & seqq: postremo autem cuenta, v. 13.
units.tr: We said that the second part of the book of Genesis concerns the history of the later age, which God graciously restored after he had destroyed the former age by a dreadful judgment. In this second part we must likewise set out two main heads: one is the History of the Restoration, chapters 7 and 8; the other is the History of the Restored World and Church, down to the time when Joseph died in Egypt. The history of the restoration is divided into two parts. First, the restoration of our own world, or of the things that exist in nature, is set out in chapter 8. Then, in chapter 9, come the laws and rights pertaining to the world and to the Church while it remains in the world. In the restoration of the natural order, which is explained in this chapter, the origin of the restoration must be observed: first in the deed, down to verse 14 of the chapter; then in the word, verse 14 and the two that follow; and finally in the general arrangement of things, in accordance with God's promise, to the end of the chapter. In the origin three things must be observed: first the causes, verses 1 and 2; then the deeds, verse 3 and following; and finally the outcome, verse 13.

units.la: Causarum duo sunt genera. nam primum causa efficiens ponitur per se principaliter, deinde vero causae secundariae. Efficiens est Deus: qui non alio argumento ad hanc instaurationem adductus dicitur quàm quòd recordatus fit Noachi, & caterorum, id est, promissionis factae per gratiam Noacho, foederisque initi, supra 6. v. 19. & seqq. quo in foedere non solum Noach cum familia, verum etiam animantes propter Noachum fuerunt comprehensae. In secundariis causis, quas Deus coordinauit ad hoc opus instaurationis, numerantur ista; Ventus a Deo transmissus, nempe post illam pluuiam dierum 40. quo nubes depulsae sunt, & sedatus aquarum impetus qui praeceps in terras ferebatur; Secundo conceptaculorum interclusio, quorum alia superne fuerunt, alia inferne, quemadmodum supra cap. 7. v. 10. fuit expositum. nam aquae inferne erumpentes cohibita sunt occlusis fontibus abyssi, siue omnibus ad tempus, siue iis ex quibus insolenter aqua eruperat: similiterque specus nubium dicuntur a Deo coercitae pluuiaque cohibita e calo. Hinc autem sequuntur facta: quorum alia sunt ab aquis ipsis, alia à Noacho, res singulas obseruante. Ab aquis est progressus deminutionis ipsarum: quem progressum duobus temporibus distinxit Moses, antequam ad facta Noachi narranda veniat. Prior locus est v. 3. & 4: quòd aquae fluitantes[?] defecerunt plurimum post dies centum quinquaginta quàm coeperat esse diluvium in terra.Hi au-tem dies nominatim ab eo tempore incipiendi sunt, prout in caput septimum ante ostendimus. Huius verò deminutionis signum, v.4. exponitur quod arca conquieverit mense septimo , die decimo septimo mensis in montanis Armeniæ, quæ ad illud usque tempus instabilis flui-tauerat. Montosam autem esse Armeniam nemo ignorat qui histo-rias delibauerit. In ea communi omnium consensu mötes statuütur, quos Onkelos Chaldæus paraphraftes appellat Carda,alij Gordiæos, alij Gorduæos affini appellatione: & in iis dicitur esse eminentissi-mus,quem Armeni vocabant Lupar, ut apud Epiphanium legimus, id est, (ut Iosephus ex Nicolao Damascene exponit) [illegible, ~12 letters]
units.tr: There are two kinds of causes. For the first cause is set down as the efficient cause, principal in itself, and then the secondary causes. The efficient cause is God, who is said to have been moved to this restoration by no other reason than that he remembered Noah, and all the rest, that is, the promise made to Noah by grace and the covenant entered into, above at chapter 6, verse 19 and following. In this covenant not only Noah with his family but also the animals were included on account of Noah. Among the secondary causes, which God appointed for this work of restoration, these are counted: a wind sent by God, namely after that rain of forty days, by which the clouds were driven off and the violence of the waters, which had rushed headlong upon the lands, was calmed. Second, the closing of the receptacles, some of which were above and some below, as was explained above in chapter 7, verse 10. For the waters breaking out from below were restrained, the fountains of the deep being shut, whether all of them for a time, or those from which the water had unusually burst forth. Likewise the cavities of the clouds are said to have been restrained by God, and the rain withheld from heaven. From these causes the deeds follow: some are done by the waters themselves, others by Noah, who observes each thing. The waters proceed to diminish, and Moses distinguishes this progress in two stages before he comes to relate the deeds of Noah. The first passage is verses 3 and 4: that the waters [were] floating[?] and decreased much after the hundred and fifty days from when the flood began on the earth. These days are to be reckoned from that time, as we showed before in the seventh chapter. As a sign of this diminishing, verse 4 sets out that the ark rested in the seventh month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on the mountains of Armenia, which until that time had been floating unsteadily. Anyone who has tasted histories knows that Armenia is mountainous. In it, by the common consent of all, mountains are named, which Onkelos the Chaldee paraphrast calls Carda, others Gordiaei, others by a similar name Gorduaei. Among these is said to be the highest, which the Armenians called Lupar, as we read in Epiphanius, that is (as Josephus explains from Nicolaus of Damascus) [illegible, ~12 letters].

units.la: Alter gradus deminutionis, v.5.exponitur.Nempe quod inde à me-se septimo ad ineunte usq; decimum itafunt minuta aquæ ut principio mensis illius apparuerint montium cacumina.Ex hac occasione Noach adductus fuisse dicitur,ut ipse quoque opus Dei exploraret,tum oculis prospectans, v.6. tum emittens animalia per quæ de statu terræ cognosceret versibus seqq.Huius rei principium statuitur dies quadragesimus ab illo conspectu montium,id est,decimus dies mensis undecimi quo Noach fenestram apertuisse dicitur & oculis omnia circumluistrauisse.Sed quia ne sic quidem rerum quæ in terra erant commoditatem poterat Noach pernoscere, propterea animalium opera usus fuisse dicitur,quæ & leviora essent,ac proinde terram uliginosam non ita grauiter pressura videbantur, & semina terræ esitarent. Primùm itaque coruum ablegauisse dicitur,v. 7:sed frustra, quia coruus & lon-giore volatu utitur & pascitur cadaueribus,ac proinde nihil habebat quod ipsum in arcam magnopere retraheret: postea verò columbam misisse dicitur, quæ innocente victu utitur, semina terræ perquirit: & vitam socialem colit, ac proinde non ita facile in terra extra arcam videbatur emansura. Hanc igitur primò misisse dicitur post dies octo quàm coruum emiserat, v. 8. & illa revertisse atque à Noacho recepta esse, v.9.Nempe quia aquæ erant in superficie totius illius terræ quæ proximè circum arcam erat.Deinde iterum remisisse, v. 10. & illa revertisse, v. 11. cum fronde oleaginea, qua cognovit Noach levari aquis superficiem terræ:Postremò autem remisisse tertio, & illa non amplius ad Noachum revertisse, v. 12. tum quia tædebat ipsam quasi carceris diuturni arcæ, tum quia commoditate rerum in terra oblatarum detinebatur: ac proinde Noacho eam ipsam commoditatem significabat sua absentia.
units.tr: The second stage of the diminishing is set out in verse 5. Namely, that from the seventh month until the beginning of the tenth, the waters so decreased that, at the beginning of that month, the tops of the mountains appeared. On this occasion Noah is said to have been moved to examine God's work himself, first looking out with his eyes, verse 6, and then sending forth animals by which he might learn the state of the earth, in the verses that follow. The beginning of this is placed on the fortieth day from that sight of the mountains, that is, on the tenth day of the eleventh month, when Noah is said to have opened the window and to have looked round on everything with his eyes. But because not even so could Noah learn the convenience of the things that were on the earth, he is said to have made use of the work of animals, which were both lighter and therefore seemed not to press down the muddy earth so heavily, and which would eat the seeds of the earth. First, then, he is said to have sent out a raven, verse 7, but in vain, because the raven uses a longer flight and feeds on carcasses, and therefore had nothing that might greatly draw it back into the ark. Afterwards, however, he is said to have sent a dove, which lives on harmless food, seeks out the seeds of the earth, and cultivates social life, and therefore did not seem likely to remain easily on the earth outside the ark. He is said to have sent this dove first after eight days, after he had let out the raven, verse 8; and she returned and was received by Noah, verse 9. Namely, because the waters were on the surface of the whole land that lay closest around the ark. Then he sent her again, verse 10, and she returned, verse 11, with an olive leaf, by which Noah knew that the surface of the earth had been lifted from the waters. Finally he sent her a third time, and she did not return again to Noah, verse 12: partly because she was weary of the ark, as of a long confinement, and partly because she was detained by the abundance of things offered on the earth. Accordingly her absence signified to Noah that very abundance.

units.la: Illius ordinis quem Deus in efficienda instauratione servavit effectus ostenditur v.13.Nempe quòd ineunte[?] anno 61.vita Noachi aquæ illa diluuij aruerant, quibus terra fuerat obruta: cuius rei explora-tionem Deus per Noachum fieri voluit exempto arca illius tecto ut terrae constitutionem in omnes partes perlustraret. Hactenus igitur modus praestandae instaurationis, & ordo perscriptus est. Sequitur locus alter, nimirum decretum vel sermo Dei,quo homo vocatus est ut ex arca prodiret in terram, & Deo vocanti paruit; utriusque tem-pus definitur, v.14. atque occasio. Tempus, dies 27.fecundi mensis: Oc-casio cum terra exaruisset. Hoc igitur tempore Deus mandauisse Noa-cho dicitur exitum, v. 15. & duobus sequentibus, & Noach obtem-perauisse v. 18. & 19. Primum itaque illud obseruandum est non vo-luntate sola Noachi, sed vocatione Dei Noachum ex arca exiuisse: ut posteris suis ostenderet nihil citra testimonium vocationemque diuinam, quamuis optatissimum, instituti ab vllo oportere. Vocationis autem institutum duo complectitur, nempe vocationem ipsam, & promissionem coniunctam: Vocationem, qua & homi-nibus mandatur ut exeant, v. 16. & ut animalia qua in arcam recepta fuerant ministratura homini educerent, verf. 17. Quibus adiuncta est promissio haec, fore ut quantulocumque numero sint, tamen abunde progignant, foetificent, & multiplicentur in terra, quas res capit. I. exposuimus. Huic vocationi consequens fuit obsequium, vocationi diuinae conformatum, verf.18. & 19. Restat locus de inftau-ratione uniuersi, ad finem vsque cap. In quo primum occasio describitur, verf.20. Deinde causa atque institutum, duobus versibus vltimis. Occasio fuit gratus Noachi animus: Causa, Dei acceptantis gratia: gratum animum Noach exhibuit Domino structura altaris & sacrificio legitimo, verf. 20. Nam etsi his externis non mouetur Deus, tamen cum ex institutione illius altaria & sacrificia Patrum veritatem suam in Christo habuerint, (qui idem est, sacerdos, altare, & sacrificium nostrum) atque ad hos typos olim patres sancte respexerint, gratum illorum animum non in altari, aut materiali sacrificio, sed in Christo (qui corpus est & veritas) probauit Deus, verf.19. Illam vero probationem qua Patres sibi acceptos & actiones sacras ipsorum testatur Deus, allegorice respiciens ad sacrificiorum modum Moses describit his verbis, verf. 21. Odoratus est Iehova odorem quietis, id est in quo acquieuit, quia bonus odor fumus Deo in Christo, in quo velut Filio dilectionis suae acquiescit Pater. Hac igitur cum occasione nostra, tum causa diuina, nempe gratia vnica & bonitate sua, Deus adductus est ad instaurationem vniuersitatis faciendam; cuius instaurationis loci duo sunt. Prior, Deum non esse deinceps huic vniuersitati importaturum exitium, verf. 21. Posterior, naturae ordinem in hac universitate gratiose conservaturum esse, verf. 22. Prius amplificat Deus, cum etiam causam adhibet propter quam mundum illum priorem perdiderat; cum dicit, propter hominem, quia figmentum cordis eius malum, &c. quasi dicat nec causa hominum, nec causa peccatorum quae ab hominibus perpetrantur, sic unquam exarsurum Deum ut hanc universitatem deleat. Posterius, de conservando naturae ordine partim actionibus ordinariis, cum nominantur sementis & messis; partim constitutionibus temporum, cum frigus & aestus; partim tempestatibus cum aestas & hyems; partimque minutis partibus temporum ac velut momentis circumscribitur, cum dies & nox nominantur. Nam his modis Deus complexus est quaecumque in rerum natura esse fierive possunt.
units.tr: The effect of that order which God observed in bringing about the restoration is shown in verse 13. Namely, that in the beginning of the 601st year of Noah's life the waters of that flood, by which the earth had been overwhelmed, had dried up. God wished this to be explored through Noah, the covering of the ark having been removed, so that he might survey the condition of the earth in every part. Thus far, therefore, the manner of effecting the restoration and its order have been set down. There follows a second passage, namely the decree or word of God, by which man was called to come out of the ark onto the earth, and he obeyed God calling him. The time of each is defined, verse 14, and the occasion. The time is the twenty-seventh day of the second month; the occasion is when the earth had dried up. At this time God is said to have commanded Noah to go out, verse 15 and the two following, and Noah is said to have obeyed, verses 18 and 19. The first thing, then, to be observed is that Noah came out of the ark not by his own will alone but by the calling of God: so that he might show to his posterity that nothing ought to be undertaken by anyone apart from the testimony and divine calling, however much desired. The institution of the calling, moreover, comprises two things: the calling itself and the promise joined to it. The calling is that by which men are commanded to go out, verse 16, and to lead out the animals that had been received into the ark, so that they might serve man, verse 17. To this calling is added a promise: that, however small their number, they will nonetheless produce abundantly, be fruitful, and multiply on the earth, which things we explained in chapter 1. To this calling there followed an obedience conformed to the divine calling, verses 18 and 19. There remains the passage concerning the restoration of the universe, to the end of the chapter. In it the occasion is first described, verse 20; then the cause and the purpose, in the last two verses. The occasion was Noah's grateful mind; the cause was God's grace in accepting it. Noah showed his grateful mind to the Lord by building an altar and a lawful sacrifice, verse 20. For although God is not moved by these outward things, yet since the altars and sacrifices of the Fathers, by their institution, had their truth in Christ (who is himself the priest, altar and sacrifice for us), and since the holy Fathers of old looked to these types, God approved their grateful mind, not in the altar or the material sacrifice, but in Christ (who is the body and the truth), verse 19. That approval, by which God bears witness to the Fathers' acceptance and their sacred actions, Moses describes in these words, verse 21, looking allegorically to the manner of sacrifice: Jehovah smelled a sweet savour of rest, that is, one in which he rested, because the sweet smell is a fume pleasing to God in Christ, in whom the Father rests as in his beloved Son. Thus by this occasion on our part and this cause on God's part, namely his unique grace and goodness, God was moved to make the restoration of the universe; and there are two points to this restoration. The first is that God would not henceforth bring destruction upon this universe, verse 21. The second is that he would graciously preserve the order of nature in this universe, verse 22. God amplifies the first, when he also adds the cause on account of which he had destroyed that former world, saying on account of man, because the imagination of his heart is evil, and so on, as if to say that neither on account of men nor on account of the sins committed by men would God ever so burn with anger as to destroy this universe. The second, concerning the preservation of the order of nature, is described partly by ordinary actions, when seedtime and harvest are named; partly by the arrangements of the seasons, when cold and heat are named; partly by the tempests, when summer and winter are named; and partly by the small divisions of time, and as it were moments, when day and night are named. For by these means God has embraced whatever can be or come to be in the order of nature.

units.la: CAPITIS IX ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 9 ANALYSIS.

units.la: INSTAURATIONIS, quam Deus a diluvio fecit, altera pars in hoc capite exponitur: Nimirum particularis ad animantes, in primis vero ad Ecclesiam illius pertinens. utriusque fons principio huius cap. ponitur, Dei benedictio erga Noachum & filios ipsius, id est, erga Ecclesiam, cuius causa mundus restitutus est. Ac huius quidem instaurationis duae omnino sunt partes: quarum prior ad animantes omnes pertinet communiter, aut etiam ad humanum genus secundum naturalem constitutionem ipsius, versibus septem: Deinde vero locus gratiae, ad instaurationem eandem necessarius, exponitur ad finem usque capitis. Ad naturae ordinem in animantibus instaurandum pertinent ista; propagatio animantium, verf. 1. & ordo inter animales institutio Dei positus, versibus sequentibus: huius ordinis leges aliae naturales sunt, ut quae primum de metu & subiectione animantium reliquarum fertur, verf. 3. ut pareant homini; & quia cibum hominis ex eis instituit, ad humani generis conservationem, verf. 3. Aliae ceremoniales, ut cum esus carnis coniunctae sanguini, prohibetur, verf. 4. Aliae denique civiles atque politicae, v. 5. & 6. ut cum Deus pronuntiat se homicidia ultarum esse, manumque sui magistratus instruit gladio ad ulciscendum ea: quas leges tandem concludit Deus v. 7. generali institutione officii illius naturalis, ut omnes ad conservationem, propagationem, & multiplicationem sui generis spectent quam fidelissime. Hic variae quæstiones oriuntur, quas nos dissoluemus paucis. Prima in vers. 28. an ad illud vsque tempus homo carnibus animantium pastus non fuerit: responsio est, primùm non legi; secundo institutione cibarij humani aliter videri, ex Gen. 1.29. Tertio ex hac ipsa institutione sic vno consensu à Iudæis confirmari, quia dicit Deus, vt viriditatem herbæ, dedi vobis omnia, nimirum vtenda eodem iure quo ante vsi estis viridi herba secundum illud creationis institutum: postremò idem confirmari huius instaurationis argumento, quia animates reliquæ humano generi secundum Deum acceptam ferebant vitam, æquum fuisse vt Deo auctore etiam hunc fructum homo ex animantibus perciperet, propter vitam ab ipso acceptam atque conseruatam. Vnum maximè videtur obseruare, quod ante homines vsi sunt sacrificiis supra cap. 4. De sacrificiis autem sacrificantes videntur comedisse. Mihi vtrumque videtur verum, patres in sacrificiis comedisse extra ordinem; sed ordinariam vitam suam instituisse quàm frugalissimè, & victu parcissimo sine carnium esu fuisse contentos.
units.tr: The second part of the restoration that God made after the flood is set out in this chapter. It is the particular restoration that concerns living creatures and, above all, the Church. The beginning of this chapter presents both: God's blessing towards Noah and his sons, that is, towards the Church, for whose sake the world was restored. This restoration has two parts altogether. The first, which concerns all living creatures in general, and also the human race in respect of its natural constitution, is set out in seven verses. Then the place of grace, which is necessary for the same restoration, is explained to the end of the chapter. The following belong to the restoration of the natural order among living creatures: the propagation of animals (v. 1), and the order God established among the animals (the verses that follow). Of this order some laws are natural. The first is that the fear and subjection of the other animals are given to man, so that they obey him (v. 2), and because God appointed them as food for man, for the preservation of the human race (v. 3). Others are ceremonial, such as the prohibition of eating flesh joined with blood (v. 4). Others, finally, are civil and political (vv. 5 and 6): God declares that he will avenge murders and arms the hand of the magistrate with the sword to punish them. God concludes these laws in v. 7 with a general appointment of that natural duty: that all should, as faithfully as possible, look to the preservation, propagation and multiplication of their own kind. Here various questions arise, which we shall resolve briefly. The first, on v. 28, is whether man had not fed on the flesh of animals up to that time. The answer is: first, it is not so stated in the law; second, the institution of human food seems otherwise, from Gen. 1.29; third, the Jews all agree that this very institution is confirmed by it, because God says, As the green herb, I have given you all things, that is, they are to be used under the same right by which you formerly used the green herb under the institution of creation. Lastly, the same thing is confirmed by the argument of this restoration: since the other animals had their life from God for the human race, it was fitting that, by God's authority, man should also receive this fruit from the animals, on account of the life he had received from God and that was preserved. One thing in particular seems to need observing: before the flood men offered sacrifices (see above, ch. 4). Now it seems that those who offered sacrifices also ate of them. To me both seem true: the fathers ate of the sacrifices outside the ordinary course, but they ordered their ordinary life as frugally as possible, and were content with the scantiest diet and without eating meat.

units.la: Altera quæstio est ad legem ceremonialem pertinens, quomodo sanguis animantium anima dicatur esse. Responsio est, attributione illam secundum quam sanguis anima appellatur, non propriam, sed figuratam esse. Nam cum sanguis per se (vt natura indicat) substantia sit; anima verò brutarum animantium (de quibus hoc loco agitur) non substantia sit, sed facultas siue qualitas, quapropter etiam scholastici animam hominis substantiuam esse, pecudis qualitatiuam dixerunt; ex eo conficitur neque animam proprie sanguinem esse, neque è conuerso, sed brutorum sanguinem censeri animam atque appellari, quia facultas illa potissimùm in sanguine sedem habet, tamquam instrumento vitæ quæ inést animantibus. Quòd autem de brutis animantibus hoc loco dicitur, non est de hominibus temere accipiendum. nam si bene obseruauimus, nusquam in scripturis loquutio hæc de anima humana dicitur, & animam humanam etiam sine corpore & sanguine subsistere pie credimus atque profitemur. Tertia quæstio est, cur sanguinem humanum se Deus à bestia reposcitarum pronùtiet: sed huius dicti rationem iam ante in serpentis exèplo exposuimus c. 3. Nunc ad secundum capitis locum veniamus: in quo rerum instauratarum historia quædam exponitur duobus modis. Primum quidem conseruatio virtute diuini fœderis in hac vniuersitate perstitura, v. 8. & seqq. Deinde verò singularis ductus hominum, & in primis Ecclesiæ Dei, prædiction, v. 17. & sequentib. Fœdus diuinum ad conseruationem vniuersitatis istius tribus modis à Deo propositum fuisse dicitur: Primum generali propositione, tribus versibus, 9. 10.&11. 10.& 11.Secundò speciali sederis significatione, verf.12.& sequentib. Postremò signi ipsius ad fedus pertinentis exhibitione, v.16. Generalis constitutio sederis exponit, quibuscū, & quod fedus inire Deus statuerit. Nam federatorum circumscriptio, v.9. & 10. Federis substantia, v. 11. Singularis verò determinatio sederis eáque copiosior, quatuor seqq. hoc ordine proponitur, quòd primū constatia sederis cum sederatis idti, verf.12. Deinde signum, v.13. Postremò vsus, seqq. verfib. ostenditur, quòd eo signo fit recordaturus Dominus illius sederis quod cum rebus creatis iniuerit. Signi traditio est evidens. Unica hîc quæstio imperitiores videtur morari posse: nempe de iride vel cælesti arcu, vtrū ante fuerit: si fuit, vtrum signū sederis appellari possit. Ante fuisse, non dubitauerim. Nam cùm eædé naturales causæ liberæ ac non impeditæ inde ab orbis conditu fuerint, ex quibus iris post diluuium creari solet, non est dubium, quin ex concursu eodem earundem causarum iris ante diluuium exstiterit. Quod autè signum sederis à Deo datum est, id non rem nouam, sed institutionem nouam docet à Deo processisse, nempe institutionem rei, quæ res ante fuerat, ad vsum & significationem nouam.
units.tr: The second question concerns the ceremonial law: in what sense the blood of animals is the soul. The answer is that the attribution by which blood is called the soul is not proper but figurative. For blood in itself (as nature shows) is a substance, whereas the soul of brute animals (the subject here) is not a substance but a faculty or quality. That is why the Schoolmen also said that the soul of man is substantial, but the soul of a beast is qualitative. It follows that the soul is not properly the blood, nor conversely, but the blood of brutes is counted and called the soul because that faculty has its seat chiefly in the blood, as in the instrument of life that is in animals. But what is said here of brute animals must not be rashly applied to men. For if we have observed well, this way of speaking is nowhere in Scripture applied to the human soul, and we devoutly believe and profess that the human soul subsists even without body and blood. The third question is why God demands the blood of man from a beast. But the reason for this saying we have already explained above, in the example of the serpent (ch. 3). Now let us come to the second part of the chapter, in which the history of the restored things is set out in two ways. First, the preservation of this universe by the power of the divine covenant, which will endure (vv. 8ff.). Then the particular guidance of men, and above all of the Church of God, is foretold (v. 17ff.). The divine covenant for the preservation of this universe is said to have been proposed by God in three ways: first, by a general statement in three verses (9, 10 and 11); second, by a particular explanation of the covenant (v. 12ff.); lastly, by the showing of the sign belonging to the covenant (v. 16). The general constitution of the covenant sets out with whom, and what covenant, God decided to make. For the description of the parties to the covenant is in vv. 9 and 10; the substance of the covenant is in v. 11. The particular determination of the covenant, which is fuller, is set out in the four following verses in this order: first the constitution of the covenant with those who are party to it (v. 12); then the sign (v. 13); lastly, its use is shown in the following verses, that the Lord, by that sign, will be mindful of the covenant he made with created things. The giving of the sign is clear. Only one question here seems likely to detain the less learned: concerning the rainbow or heavenly bow, whether it existed before. If it did, can it be called a sign of the covenant? I should not hesitate to say that it existed before. For since the same natural causes, free and unhindered, have been at work from the foundation of the world, from which the rainbow is usually produced after the flood, there is no doubt that by the same concurrence of those same causes the rainbow existed before the flood. And what God gave as a sign of the covenant does not teach that something new was brought about by God, but a new institution, namely the appointment of a thing that existed before to a new use and signification.

units.la: Quemadmodum etiam omnia sacramentorum signa in Testamento vetere & nouo duobus modis considerandā sunt, si à miraculosis discesseris: vnum quòd res sunt in natura, tum quòd res illæ efficiuntur signa. Prius autē res absolutè oportet existere, quàm relationem illam vel significationem assequantur. Alter locus ad constitutionem futuram mundi, ex quo instauratus est, pertinens à Mose traditur à v.17.ad finem vsque. Huius autē loci partes omnino duæ ponendæ sunt: vna est [illegible, ~10 letters] siue eorum quæ Prophetiam illam antecesserunt, ad v. vsque 25. Posterior autem est de illa ipsa Prophetia, quam Deus olim praesignificatā voluit Ecclesiæ suæ ad veritatis suæ confirmationē. [illegible, ~10 letters] autē duo sunt genera: alia communia, alia verò singularia huius historiæ; communia sunt quæ verf.17. & 18. exponuntur. Nam duo illi versus certo consilio à Mose fuerunt adhibiti, vt ad sequentem historiā huius & proximi capitis essent [illegible, ~6 letters]. Etenim priore versu, Filij Noachi (quorum res gesta hoc reliquo capite proponitur) à Mose enumerati sunt. posteriore versu respersa ab illis fuisse terra suis habitatoribus dicitur. quod autem priore versu hæ voces à Mose insertæ sunt, Cham autè is est Pater, &c. eæ ad institutionem Israëlitarum maximè pertinebant, vt eo pacto fierent certiores, neque promissionem terræ neque ius illius à Deo recens fuisse datum, sed iam olim à Deo definitum ac praenuntiatum; ac proinde hoc illud tempus esse quo Israëlitæ velut manu ducendi erant in possessione illius. Restant antecedētia, quæ singulari quadam ratione ad Propheticam Ecclesiæ historiam pertinent: ea versibus quatuor continētur, in quibus accuratissi-me occasio exponitur, quam arripuit Deus sapientissimus, vt Prophetiam hanc denuntiaret in futurum, ex præsente hominum facto. Eo-rum antecedentium loci sunt quatuor, totidem versibus distincti.
units.tr: In the same way, all the signs of the sacraments in the Old and New Testaments are to be considered in two respects, if one sets aside the miraculous: first, that the things exist in nature; second, that those things are made into signs. The former must exist absolutely before that relation or signification is attained. The other part, concerning the future constitution of the world from which it was restored, is delivered by Moses from v. 17 to the end. Two parts of this passage must altogether be distinguished. The one is the account of the things that preceded that prophecy, to v. 25. The latter is of that very prophecy, which God long ago willed to be foreshadowed to his Church for the confirmation of his truth. The things preceding are of two kinds: some common, others particular to this history. The common ones are those set out in vv. 17 and 18. For those two verses were introduced by Moses with a definite purpose, so that they would serve for the following history of this and the next chapter. For in the first verse Moses enumerates the sons of Noah, whose deeds are set out in the rest of this chapter. In the later verse it is said that the earth was scattered by them over its inhabitants. And as to the fact that in the first verse Moses inserted these words, Ham is the father of Canaan, etc., these chiefly pertained to the instruction of the Israelites, so that by this means they might be more certain that neither the promise of the land nor the right to it had been newly given by God, but had long before been determined and foretold by him; and therefore that this was the time when the Israelites were to be led, as it were by the hand, into possession of it. There remain the things preceding, which pertain in a particular way to the prophetic history of the Church. These are contained in four verses, in which the occasion is set out with the greatest accuracy, which God, the most wise, seized upon in order to announce this prophecy for the future from a present deed of men. The places of these preceding things are four, distinguished by as many verses.

units.la: Nam primum vocatio humana & occupatio Noachi describitur, v. 19. deinde factum imprudens illius, verf. 20. tum impium Chami factum, v. 21. Præterea pium & modestum Semi ac Iepheti factum, verf. 22. quibus occasionibus tandem Noach ad prædictionem illam diuinitus prænuntiandum adductus est, vt narratur v. 23. Vocatio Noachi ex creationis & naturæ lege est, vt colat terram, Genes. 2. & 3. ac proinde vt vites conferat, quæ species est culturæ à Deo data atque benedicta. Imprudens boni senis factū, exemplum est ad cautionem nostram, non ad imitationem propositum, quòd bibens de vino illo inebriatus est. Cum autem vini præter modum hausti ea natura fit, vt illudat suis potoribus, quemadmodum Prouerb. 20. & 23. dicitur, effectus ille inde consequutus est, quòd temulentus Noach & sui ipsius impos retexit sese in medio sui tentorij, id est, destitutus cognitione sui ipsius & honestatis pudorisque illius naturalis quem omnes, in primis autem senes in graui ætate illa, coram omnibus præsertim domesticis, sed ante omnia liberis, præ se ferre debent, suam turpitudinem illudendam suis imprudens exposuit.
units.tr: For first there is described the calling and occupation of Noah, v. 19; then his unwitting deed, v. 20; then the wicked deed of Ham, v. 21. Besides these, there is the pious and modest deed of Shem and Japheth, v. 22. By these occasions Noah was at last led, as v. 23 relates, to pronounce that prediction under divine guidance. Noah's calling belongs to the law of creation and nature, that he should till the ground, Gen. 2 and 3, and therefore should plant vines, which is a kind of cultivation given and blessed by God. The unwitting deed of the good old man is an example set before us for caution, not for imitation, in that he drank of that wine and became drunk. Since wine drunk beyond measure is by its nature such that it mocks its drinkers, as Prov. 20 and 23 say, the result that followed was that Noah, drunk and no longer master of himself, uncovered himself within his tent. That is, bereft of self-knowledge and of that natural sense of decency and shame which all men, and especially the old in their advanced years, ought to display, above all before their household and, most of all, before their children, he unwittingly exposed his own shame to be mocked by his sons.

units.la: Sic enim Hebræum verbum quarta coniugatione accipimus. Neque putamus alieno facto, sed suo ipsius crimine Noachum retectum esse: vt ex eo intelligamus quàm verè Basilius dixerit, ebrietatem breuem mortem esse; sed vtcumque breuis sit, tamē eò deteriorem morte naturali esse, quòd hæc voluntaria, illa inuoluntaria est: hæc corpus & animam occidit simul, destituitque singulis facultatibus, illa solum corpus destituit anima.
units.tr: For this is how we take the Hebrew verb in the fourth conjugation. And we do not think Noah was exposed by another's deed, but by his own fault. From this we understand how truly Basil said that drunkenness is a brief death. However brief it may be, it is nonetheless worse than natural death, because the one is voluntary and the other involuntary: the latter destroys body and soul together and strips a man of all his faculties, whereas drunkenness strips only the body, and the soul remains.

units.la: Tertium factum Chami duobus modis reprehendendum est: Primò, quòd vidit & aspexit quasi iocabundus pudenda patris sui: deinde quòd ad eundem aspectum fratrem suum vtrumque prouocauerit: quæ res impietatem coniunctam habuit: cum iste miser pudore naturali abiecto, nec senem nec patrem reuereretur.
units.tr: Ham's third deed must be censured in two respects. First, because he looked upon and saw his father's nakedness, as if in jest. Second, because by that same look he provoked both his brothers. That deed involved impiety, since this wretched man, having cast off natural shame, showed reverence neither to the old man nor to his father.

units.la: Nam quòd nonnulli putant Chamum retexisse pudenda patris, mihi religio est dicere, quia scriptura non dicit: sed potius Noacho factum videtur tribuere, vt præcedente diximus versu.
units.tr: For as for those who think Ham uncovered his father's nakedness, I am reluctant to say so, because Scripture does not say it. Rather, it seems to ascribe the deed to Noah, as we said in the preceding verse.

units.la: Accedit quoque ad hunc versum Aben-Ezrae interpretatio, qui per Chenaanem puerum rem Chamo patri indicatam putat, adductus illis Noachi verbis, maledictus Cenaam. Sed hoc utrum verum sit, necne, non possumus confirmare. Pium Sethi & Jepheti factum tum re ipsa, tum etiam modo ipsius est commendabile. Re,quod neque per ludibrium & impietatem vereda patris respexerunt; neque retecta diutius fuerunt esse;sed uno eodemque facto verecundiam germanis filiis dignam, prudentiam, & pietatem coluerunt: verecundiam quod accepta patris fui veste suisque am-borum humeris imposita, patris verenda minime respexerunt; ne forte illius apud se auctoritas aut reverentia minuta esset. Prudentiam: quod retrogrado passu ad patrem accesserunt quem veste contegerent: pietatem, quod obtexerunt senem: atque hanc ipsam virtutem natura iam olim docuit. Nec absimile est ab honestate hac quod a Cicer.libro 1.de Officiis, & Ambrosio itidem scribitur, Eam fuisse apud veteres etiam Romanos honestatem, ut ne in balneo quidem gener nudum soceri corpus auderet aspicere. Restat po-stremum antecedens, nimirum quod Noach, postquam edormiuisset vinum suum, expergefactus est & factum minimi fui filij in se cognouit, id est postquam inaudiuisset, justam cognitionem in-stituit, & rebus probe cognitis ad sententiam pronuntiandam Deo auctore adductus est. Sic enim Metaleptice loqui scriptura solet, & verbo cognoscendi, audiendi, similibusque complecti omnia quae ad legitimam rei cognitionem pertinent, ut Genes. 31. Alter locus, prophetia historica a Noacho pronuntiata, tribus versibus exponitur. Nam primum Chamo maledictio, deinde Semo bene-dictio praesens, postremo Jepheto benedictio olim ventura praedicitur. Quaeritur autem utrum hanc sententiam hac occasione Noach saltem in filium Chamum jure pronuntiare potuerit, quia plerisque visum est hanc sententiam aut ab ebrio Noacho, aut ab exacerbato pronuntiatam fuisse:Respō. Neque ebrius pronuntiauit, (Nam edormiuerat vinum suum, & de facto quaesiuit cognouitque sobrius) neque ex perturbata animi exacerbatione. nam ut per-turbatus fuerit ad primam rei cognitionem, tum sedato & tranquillato animo non dubium est cognouisse. Neque igitur ex vino, neque ex perturbatione pronuntiata fuerunt ista; sed ex divina auctoritate & inspiratione, quia auctoritatem ut Pater in filios habuit, inspirationem ut Propheta & Doctor in Ecclesia datus: utramque; vero vocatio-nem hanc Deus singulari Spiritus praesentia regit, & exemplis multis in scriptura confirmauit, quum patres etiam iniquos & prophetas sal-sos propter vocationem, non propter ipsos, persæpe adhibuerit ad fi-gnificandā voluntate suā. Hæc igitur divinitus pronuntiauit Noach: in Cham, maledictionem & seruitutem acerbissimam maledictionis consectariam. In seruum benedictionem praesentem ex Dei sedere & dominatum in Chamu posteritatemque illius benedictionis fructum. In Iephetum denique futuram vocationem illius ad participandam benedictionem Semi, eumdemque benedictionis fructum, nempe dominationem in fratres a Deo attributam. Quae res aduentu Christi plene est effecta, cum diruto interiecto pariete effecti fumus vnum oui-le cum Iudaeis. Quaeritur cur ergo pro Chamo Noach Chenahanem dixerit? Resp. Haec vox, maledictus Cenahan, aut Noachi dictum est, aut Mosis interpretamentum: Si a Noacho dictum statuimus, aut probanda est AbenHezrae sententia, nempe puerum Chenahanem primum fuisse indicem qui Chamum Patrem ad spectanda aui verenda prouocauerit: aut statuendum hoc a Noacho dictum Prophetice, vt complementum olim ad Israelitas prouenturum amplius designaret. Sin Mosis interpretamentum est (quod ego quidem facile probauerim) Moses nempe hoc versu atque seqq. certo consilio Cenahanem substituisse dicendus est, vt tum primogenitum notaret Chami, tum vero maxime Israelitas, qui versabantur in itinere Cenahanem possessuri, de iure atque veritate promissionum diuinarum iam olim a seruis Dei pronuntiatarum confirmarent. Nam communis fuit in Chamum & posteros maledictio; quod autem commune est ad singulos pertinet communiter, ac proinde verissime de singulis pronuntiatur. Huius vero in fortem communis illa maledictio per hoc tempus particulariter praestanda fuit, quam ad rem Israelitae ex Aegypto educti sunt.
units.tr: To this verse there is also added the interpretation of Aben Ezra, who thinks that by the boy Canaan the matter was reported to his father Ham, led by those words of Noah, cursed be Canaan. But whether this is true or not, we cannot confirm. The pious deed of Shem and Japheth is commendable both in its substance and in its manner. In substance, because they neither looked upon their father's nakedness in mockery and impiety, nor did they leave it uncovered any longer; rather, by one and the same act they showed a modesty worthy of brothers, prudence, and piety. Modesty, in that, taking their father's garment and laying it upon both their shoulders, they did not look at their father's nakedness, lest perhaps his authority or reverence in their eyes should be diminished. Prudence, in that they came to their father walking backwards so that they might cover him with the garment. Piety, in that they covered the old man. Nature itself taught this very virtue long ago. Nor is it unlike this propriety which Cicero, in book 1 of On Duties, and Ambrose likewise write: that among the ancient Romans too such decency prevailed that a son-in-law would not dare to look upon his father-in-law's naked body even in the bath. There remains the last preceding matter, namely that Noah, after he had slept off his wine, awoke and knew what his youngest son had done to him. That is, after he had heard the matter, he conducted a just inquiry, and when the facts were properly known, he was brought, with God as author, to pronounce sentence. For Scripture is accustomed to speak in this metaleptic manner, embracing by the words to know, to hear, and the like, everything that pertains to lawful knowledge of a matter, as in Gen. 31. The second passage, a historical prophecy pronounced by Noah, is set out in three verses. For first a curse is foretold for Ham, then a present blessing for Shem, and lastly a future blessing for Japheth. But it is asked whether Noah could rightly have pronounced this sentence, on this occasion at least, against his son Ham, since it seemed to most that this sentence was pronounced either by Noah while drunk or by Noah in a fit of anger. Answer: He did not pronounce it drunk, for he had slept off his wine and inquired into the deed and knew it when sober; nor did he pronounce it from a disturbed and angry mind. For even if he was disturbed at the first knowledge of the matter, there is no doubt that once his mind was calmed and quieted he understood it. Therefore these words were pronounced neither from wine nor from disturbance, but from divine authority and inspiration: authority, because he had it as a father over his sons; inspiration, because he was given it as a prophet and teacher in the Church. Now God governs both this calling by a singular presence of his Spirit, and has confirmed it by many examples in Scripture, since he has very often employed even wicked fathers and false prophets, on account of their calling and not on account of themselves, to signify his will. Therefore Noah pronounced these things by divine inspiration: upon Ham, a curse and the most bitter servitude that follows from the curse. Upon the servant, a present blessing from the seat of God, and dominion over Ham and his posterity as the fruit of the blessing. Finally, upon Japheth, his future calling to share in the blessing of Shem, and the same fruit of the blessing, namely dominion over his brothers, bestowed by God. This was fully accomplished at the coming of Christ, when the dividing wall was broken down and we were made one fold with the Jews. But why then did Noah say Canaan instead of Ham? Answer: These words, cursed be Canaan, were either spoken by Noah or are Moses' own interpretation. If we hold that they were spoken by Noah, then either the opinion of Aben Ezra must be accepted, namely that the boy Canaan was the first informer who provoked his father Ham to look upon the shameful parts, or it must be held that Noah spoke these words prophetically, to designate further the fulfilment that was to come in time upon the Israelites. But if it is Moses' interpretation (which I would readily approve), then Moses must be said to have deliberately put Canaan in place of Ham in this verse and those that follow, so that he might both mark out the firstborn of Ham and, above all, so that the Israelites, who were on their journey to possess the land of Canaan, might be confirmed in the right and truth of the divine promises already long before pronounced by the servants of God. For the curse was common to Ham and his posterity; and what is common pertains to each individually in common, and therefore is most truly pronounced of each. And that common curse was to be carried out in particular at this time upon the one portion of the descendants, for which purpose the Israelites were led out of Egypt.

units.la: Concluditur tandem hoc caput narratione chronica vitae Noachi, primum quidem post diluuium, vers.penult. Deinde vero vniuersae, versu vltimo.
units.tr: This chapter is finally concluded with the chronological account of the life of Noah, first indeed after the flood, in the penultimate verse, and then of his whole life, in the last verse.

units.la: CAPITIS X ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER X.

units.la: NTE docuimus historiam Mosis a diluuio duabus partibus contineri: Vnam esse historiam instaurationis ex diluuio: alteram, historiam mundi ex quo instauratus est, ad illud vsque tempus quo Iosephi in Aegypto vita defunctus est. Historiam instaurationis duobus cap. proximis explicauimus. Historiam vero instaurati mundi, in quatuor partes commode pro ratione temporum distinguimus: primus locus est historia rerum à Noacho ad Abrahamum & vocationem illius, his duobus capitibus. Secundus locus est historia Abrahami; ex quo vocatus est in fedus à Domino ad mortem vsq;, nimirum à fine cap. 11.ad principium vsque 25.Tertius est historia Isaaci, à cap.25.ad 28. vsque,quartus denique Iahakobi inde ad finem vsque libri Gen.Primus locus à diluuio ad Abrahamum vsque pertinens duplicem historiam continet: Vnam, communem humani generis hoc cap. & principio sequentis: Alteram, particularem Ecclesiæ & Gentis benedictæ,cap. sequente à v. 19.ad finem.In communi historia rursum duæ partes constituendæ sunt: Vna est historia habitationum mundi,id est,de facto eorum per quos variæ mundi habitationes suis habitatoribus respersæ sunt, cap. 10: Altera de causa cur isti incolæ & habitatores mundi in tam varias habitationes repente disiecti sint, principio cap. sequentis. Hic enim plurimum Scripturæ sacræ ordo est,vt facta priore loco, posteriore causæ enarrentur, quamuis antegressæ tempore.
units.tr: We have already taught that the history of Moses from the Flood is contained in two parts. One is the history of the restoration after the Flood; the other is the history of the world from the time it was restored, down to the death of Joseph in Egypt. We explained the history of the restoration in the two preceding chapters. The history of the restored world we conveniently divide, according to the order of time, into four parts. The first part is the history of things from Noah to Abraham and his calling, covered by these two chapters. The second is the history of Abraham, from the time he was called into covenant by the Lord until his death, that is, from the end of chapter 11 to the beginning of chapter 25. The third is the history of Isaac, from chapter 25 to chapter 28. The fourth, finally, is that of Jacob, from there to the end of the book of Genesis. The first part, reaching from the Flood to Abraham, contains a twofold history. One is the common history of mankind, found in this chapter and at the beginning of the next. The other is the particular history of the Church and of the blessed nation, found in the following chapter from verse 19 to the end. Within the common history two parts must again be distinguished. One is the history of the dwelling-places of the world, that is, of the deeds of those through whom the various habitations of the world were scattered among their inhabitants, which is chapter 10. The other is the account of why these inhabitants and dwellers of the world were suddenly scattered into so many different habitations, which is at the beginning of the next chapter. For it is the greatest part of the order of Holy Scripture that the deeds are related first and their causes afterwards, although the causes came earlier in time.

units.la: Huius capitis propositio summa v.1. comprehenditur: Enarratio propositionis, ad versum vsque penultimum: conclusio denique, in v. vlt. Propositionis, etsi verbis differentibus, sententia eadem est quam proxime præcedente capite v.18. & 19,Moses expresserat,nepe primum qui filij Noachi fuerint, priore membro; deinde qui posteri ex eis post diluuium profluxerint. Itaque filiorum Noachi posteri in narratione ordine recensentur: Primum quidem Iephethi,vt natu maximi,v.2.& tribus seqq. Deinde Chami,vt natu minimi, à v.6.ad 20.vsque: postremo autem Semi (quia ad illum maxime reliqua historia pertinet) Gens vltimo loco exponitur ad compagem commodam historiæ: prout apud Hebræos fieri in finem capitis quinti annotauimus. De horum autem posteris eorumque explicatione, quia sententiæ variant, ad resecandas quæstiones innumeras quæ in hoc caput solent adferri, primum finem Mosis in hoc capite perscribendo, deinde summam, postremo terminos αντ declarabimus, singularem circumscriptionem in alium locum reiecturi. Finis ergo Mosi videtur huic fuisse propositus, non vt communem historiam de habitatoribus vniuersi mundi curiosis proponeret: nam spiritus Dei ea demum in scripturis exponi voluit quæ pertinent ad ædificationem in fide: non item vt amplissimos fines generis ex Noacho orti demonstraret; sed vt tum fines ad Ecclesiam decreto Dei pertinentes, tum vero ad alios, prout ad historiam Ecclesiæ intelligendam visum est pertinere, hoc capite circumscriberet: nam absque hoc capite esset, multa quæ spiritus Dei per Mosen aliósque Prophetas consignauit scripto, neque illo tempore fuissent ab Ecclesia percepta, neque hoc nostro perciperentur.Summa igitur est ; ex tribus Noachi filiis ante annos fermè centum tantum examen liberorum prodiisse, ut regiones amplissimæ uno quasi momento suis incolis & habitatoribus respersæ sint, tum iis qui ad Ecclesiam Dei pertinuerunt, tum aliis qui sua infidelitate & iniustitia proteruissima à Deo & Ecclesia ipsius abiuerunt ; quorum illos discreuit Dei misericordia, & ad participationem beneficentiæ suæ adoptauit,hos permisit impietati & iniustitiæ suæ, ac propterea segregatos voluit ab Ecclesia sua : qui tamen postea indesinenter Ecclesiam ,infestauerunt & fines illius,pietatémque,iustitiam,ac sanctimoniam tentauerunt omnibus modis euertere : quæ res ut intelligeretur, aliquo saltem modo circumscribi primas illas maiorum sedes oportuit. Numeratur autem in hac recensione tota ( ut olim observauerunt Patres)septuaginta duo [illegible, ~6 letters] i.prisci auctores suarum Gentium,quos illi præter omnem historiæ fidem veritatémq; totidem linguis,quot regionibus,familiis,& Gentibus fuisse distinctos putauerunt.Sed etsi numerus ille patribus arrisit plurimùm,non solum in hoc argumento , sed etiam aliis multis ; non dubium est tamen quin certis rationibus aut plures, aut pauciores in hoc capite constitui possent.Ut ut sit, non potest constare illud quod plerique crediderunt, totidem fuisse differentes linguas : hoc enim tum recensione Gentis Cenahanæorum, tum etiam Ioktanis reuincitur. Quorum posteri,Cenahanis quidem omnes plurimùm fuerunt ἐμόγλωσσοι[?], & communem linguam etiam post dispersionem Babylonicam habuerunt. Horum autem singulares terminos non est huius temporis definire. Tantum ita statuendum est, Iepheti posteros eas maximè regiones incoluisse, quæ supra Mesopotamiam, Syriámque, & citra Syriam habitauerunt.Posteris Chami proprie attribuendæ sunt regiones illæ, quæ inde à Babylonia Mesopotamiáque Meridiem versus protenduntur, ut omnium appellationem comparatio docet.Sed quia non potuit impium illud genus se suis finibus ita continere quin adducente ambitione in alienos fines perrumperet: propterea narratur extra ordinem de primo illo publico prædone נִמְרוֹד[?], quòd primus cœperit potens esse venatione, id est, vicinos perinde infestare ut venator feras, adeò ut ipsius impotens factum in prouerbium abierit. Cuius facti principium exponitur versus 10. quòd primùm tyrannidem suam in Mesopotamia constabiliuerit positis ad fines regni munitionibus: deinde verò progressus eiusdem tyrannidis, quòd confirmatus in regno non acquicuerit, sed in Assy-riam riam[?] quoque inuolaucrit[?], ibidémque suæ tyrannidis sedes constitue-rit.
units.tr: The proposition of this chapter is summed up in verse 1. The explanation of the proposition runs to the penultimate verse, and the conclusion is in the last verse. The proposition, although in different words, has the same sense as that which Moses expressed in the immediately preceding chapter, verses 18 and 19: first, who the sons of Noah were, which is the first member; then, who were the descendants that sprang from them after the Flood. Accordingly, the descendants of Noah's sons are listed in the narrative in order. First comes Japheth, as the eldest, at verse 2 and the three following verses. Then Ham, as the youngest, from verse 6 to verse 20. Last, Shem (because the rest of the history pertains chiefly to him) is set out last, to give a convenient connection to the history, as we noted at the end of chapter 5 is the practice among the Hebrews. Now, since opinions vary about these descendants and their explanation, and in order to cut away the countless questions that are usually raised about this chapter, we shall first set out the purpose of Moses in this chapter, then its summary, and last declare the boundaries, reserving the particular delimitation for another place. The purpose of Moses therefore seems to have been this: not to set forth for the curious a general history of the inhabitants of the whole world, for the Spirit of God willed that in the Scriptures only those things be expounded which pertain to building up in faith. Nor was it to demonstrate the very wide boundaries of the race sprung from Noah; but rather to delimit in this chapter the boundaries which pertain to the Church by the decree of God, and also those of others, as far as seemed to pertain to understanding the history of the Church. For without this chapter, many things which the Spirit of God committed to writing through Moses and the other prophets would neither have been perceived by the Church at that time, nor would they be perceived in our own. The summary, then, is this: from the three sons of Noah, about one hundred years before, so small a multitude of descendants came forth that the most extensive regions were, as it were in a single moment, scattered with their inhabitants and dwellers. These were partly those who belonged to the Church of God, and partly others who, by their unbelief and most shameless injustice, had departed from God and His Church. Of these, God's mercy set the former apart and adopted them into a share of His goodness, while He permitted the latter to their impiety and injustice, and therefore willed them to be separated from His Church. Yet these latter afterwards ceaselessly harassed the Church and tried in every way to overthrow its borders, its piety, its justice, and its holiness. So that this might be understood, those first seats of the peoples had to be circumscribed at least in some way. In this enumeration, moreover, the whole number (as the Fathers observed long ago) is seventy-two [illegible] the ancient founders of their nations, whom they believed, quite apart from all faithfulness and truth of history, to have been distinguished into as many languages as regions, families and nations. But although that number pleased the Fathers very much, not only in this matter but in many others, there is no doubt that, on sound grounds, either more or fewer could be counted in this chapter. However that may be, it cannot be established what most have believed, that there were as many different languages; for this is refuted both by the enumeration of the nation of the Canaanites and also by that of Joktan. Of these, the descendants of the Canaanites were all very largely of one tongue [ἐμόγλωσσοι], and they kept a common language even after the dispersion at Babel. But it is not the business of this present discussion to define their particular boundaries. Only this must be laid down: the descendants of Japheth inhabited chiefly those regions which lay beyond Mesopotamia and Syria, and on this side of Syria. The regions which stretch from Babylonia and Mesopotamia southwards properly belong to the descendants of Ham, as the comparison of their names shows. But since that impious race could not keep itself within its own bounds without bursting, driven by ambition, into the territories of others, therefore a narrative is given out of order about that first public robber, Nimrod [נִמְרוֹד], who first began to be powerful in hunting, that is, to harass his neighbours just as a hunter does wild beasts, so that his lawless deeds passed into a proverb. The beginning of this action is set out in verse 10: he first established his tyranny in Mesopotamia, placing fortifications on the borders of his kingdom. Then the progress of the same tyranny is set out: once confirmed in his kingdom, he was not content, but also broke into Assyria and there established the seats of his tyranny.

units.la: In eadem vero narratione illud singulare est quod Moses Cenahanis posteros & sedes illorum circumscribit accuratissimè: nempe vt populus Israelis, qui iam in præsente expeditione erat, certò cognosceret quam quorum hæreditatem breui habiturus esset. Ad Schemi genus transiturus Moses duas adhibet singulares commen-dationes illius, antequam genus recenseat; Nam primùm ostendit gentem sanctam ab hoc processisse, deinde verò ad hunc primo-genita pertinuisse, tamquam à Iephetho natu maximo ad ipsum deriuata. Gentem sanctam ex hoc profluxisse hæc verba indicant, Patri omnium filiorum Heberi, id autem est, Hebræorum, quemadmodum etiam à Bilehamo appellantur Heber, proprio nomine ex consuetudine Hebræorum sumpto in locum Gentilitij, Numer. 24. 24. Primogenita verò ad Schemum pertinuisse hæc verba denotant, Fratrem Iepheti natu maximi, id est ascitum in iuris eiusdem communicationem, adeóque antepositum occasione illius beneficij quod in Noachum contulerat, cùm auctor illius obtegendi primus fuisse dicitur, supra 9. verf. 22. Terminus verò possessionis quam huius posteri obtinuerunt, non ita late fusus est vt fratrum præcedentium: tum quia pars à consilio impiæ illius ædificationis abstinens, de qua capite seq. in Ecclesia Dei apud Noachum & maiores conquieuit, tum quia non fuit pars generis huius dispersa maledictione Dei, vt quæ à consilio illo impio abstinuisset; quapropter etiam factum est (vt optimè Augusti. de ci-uit.
