Dei obseruauit) vt non tantùm suis sedibus consisterent ij, sed etiam integram priscam & à maioribus acceptam linguam conseruarent in familia Heberi, ex quo Hebræa fuit appellata. huius autem rei certissimum documentum est verf. 25. in nominis im-positione quo primogenitus Heberi filius vocatus est. cùm enim Peleg à parentibus diceretur, id est, diuisio, tum horrendi iudicij monimentum extare voluit Heber quòd tempore ortus illius terra di-uisa esset, vt familiæ suæ integritatem ab impio illo consilio testa-tam faceret, hos autem in Chaldæa substitisse apud Arpacshadum (de cuius nomine mutilato Chaldæi dicti) tum ex hoc cap. tum ex sequente manifestum est. Reliquam Gentem his terminis cir-cumclusam fuisse ex scripturis deprehendimus. Ecclesiam quidem in Mesopotamia & Chaldæa substitisse; sed reliquos illius Gentis, qui Babylonis ædificandæ consilio cum aliis communicauerant, in regiones non ita longinquas abiisse: putà in Assyriam proximam, quam postea inuasit Nimrod, in Syriam, & propinquum Siliciæ. tractum à Septemtrione, & in Arabiam desertam petreámque à Meridie, adeò ut isti cum aliorum posteris quodammodo permixti hæserint à Tauro monte & Masio ad mare rubrum & Montana Arabiæ usque. His narrationibus tribus sua conclusio particularis in singula capita tribuitur eiusdem modi: una verò communis omnium, ultimo versu huius capitis, quarum evidens est interpretatio.
units.tr: In this same narrative there is one singular feature: Moses marks out with the greatest precision the descendants of Shem and their seats, namely, so that the people of Israel, who were already on this expedition, might know for certain what inheritance of these they were soon to possess. Before he lists the race of Shem, Moses, about to pass to it, gives two singular commendations of it. For first he shows that the holy nation came forth from this man, and then that the firstborn right belonged to him, as derived to him from Japheth, the eldest. That the holy nation sprang from him is indicated by these words, to the father of all the sons of Heber; that is, of the Hebrews, just as they are also called Heber by Balaam, the proper name taken, according to Hebrew custom, in place of the gentilic name, Numbers 24:24. That the firstborn right belonged to Shem is shown by these words, the brother of Japheth the eldest; that is, one taken into the same right of communication, and therefore placed before the others, on account of that benefit which he had conferred on Noah, since he is said to have been the first to cover him, above 9:22. The boundary of the possession which his descendants obtained is not so widely spread as that of the preceding brothers: partly because a part of the race, abstaining from the counsel of that impious building (which is treated in the next chapter), rested in the Church of God with Noah and his forebears; and partly because this part of the race was not scattered by the curse of God, since it had abstained from that impious counsel. Hence it also came about (as Augustine rightly observed in De civitate Dei) that those descendants not only remained in their own seats, but also kept the whole ancient language, received from their forebears, in the family of Heber, from whom it was called Hebrew. The most certain proof of this matter is in verse 25, in the naming of Heber's firstborn son. For when Peleg was called by his parents, that is, "division," Heber wished to leave a memorial of that dreadful judgment, that in the days of his birth the earth was divided, so as to bear witness to the integrity of his family against that impious counsel. That these settled in Chaldaea, near Arpachshad (from whose corrupted name the Chaldeans are called), is clear both from this chapter and from the following one. We find from the Scriptures that the rest of the nation was enclosed within these boundaries. The Church indeed settled in Mesopotamia and Chaldaea; but the remaining members of that nation, who had joined others in the plan to build Babylon, departed into regions not so distant: for example, into neighbouring Assyria, which Nimrod later invaded, into Syria, and into the neighbouring stretch of Cilicia on the north, and into the desert and stony Arabia on the south. So these men, mixed in some measure with the descendants of others, remained settled from Mount Taurus and Masius to the Red Sea and the mountains of Arabia. To these three narratives a particular conclusion is assigned for each separate section, of the same kind; but there is one common conclusion for all, in the last verse of this chapter, whose meaning is evident.

units.la: EXPOSITA propagatione familiæ Noachi in capita, Gentes, regiones, familias & linguas, cap.10.nunc demum in hoc capite primùm causa illius propagationis exponitur, versibus novem: deinde continuatio generis sancti in Ecclesia (quam secundam partem sermonis huius esse diximus) reliquo cap. exponitur ad Abrahami vocationem usque. In Historia autem illius propagationis per gentes & linguas, narratio partes illas ordine continet quas in principio huius instituti à Tullio desiderari diximus lib.1.de Orat. Nam primū causa illius facti exponitur ad v.4. Secundò consilium, v.5. & duobus seqq. Tertiò factum, v.8. Postremò autem eventus, v.9. Causa fuit impium atque iniustum humani generis institutum; ad cuius instituti explicationem versus 1.est [illegible, ~12 letters], cum omnes homines terra, sermone uno iisdemque verbis ante illud tempus dicuntur usi, & una fuisse lingua communis omnium. In facti autem illorum impij atque iniusti historia, primùm occasio 2.v. deinde consilium, 3.& 4. exponitur. factum reticetur, quia tum ex consilio capto, tum ex seqq. intelligitur. Occasionem dedit loci commoditas, quod illo ex Armenia post diluvium profecti ad capiendas sedes, locum specie amoenissimum, re fertilissimum totius Orientis delegerunt ubi habitarent. Is locus est in terra Schinharis, id est Mesopotamiæ, & Babyloniæ, supra quàm est mons quem Geographi appellant Singaram, & oppidum Singara Euphrati impositum, nempe qua in regione primùm fuerat homo collocatus in creatione, ibi sedem homines in mundi instauratione fixuri sibi videbantur. Consilij membra sunt duo: nam primum instrumenta o-peris constituuntur, v.3. deinde opus & finis illius, v.4. Instrumenta (quia locus ipse negabat) sive materiam ædificationi commodam, arte curaverunt, cùm lateres pro lapidibus faciendos & percoquendos ad durationem contra omnes iniurias: bituménque pro intrita censuerunt adhiberi: quemadmodum impietas ad perficienda consilia im-pia est. pia est folertissima. Operis vero consilium vers. 4. duplex ostendi-tur, urbis, & turris aedificanda, eiusque altissimae. Finis duplex; unus vanitatis, ut nomen sibi compararent ipsi: alter impietatis, ac non vanitatis solum, ne dispergerentur deinceps in superficiem terrae, tamquam si aduersus caelestia tela cauere sibi hoc modo possent. Hanc ne-sariam causam ab hominibus oblatam sequitur secundus locus, nimirum consilij quod Deus cepit contra istud nefarium hominum institutum. Huius consilij necessarium apud homines [illegible, ~10 letters] vers.5. Modus vero consilij, v.6. & 7. ostenditur. [illegible, ~10 letters] est, accurata dispositio ad quaestionem de materia proposita habendam, remque certo & legitime cognoscendam: quae res praedicatur de Deo hu-manitus, dicete Mose, descendit Iehoua ad videndum, &c. Neque enim ascendit aut descendit Deus, qui infinitus est; sed perinde nobis proponitur ac summus iudex ex arce ius dicens; & quando ius dicturus est, descendens vltro & demittens se ad captum suorum popularium, ut ex singulis & ex re praesente peruestiget facti & consequatur co-gnitionem absolutam illius: quam rationem aliquot in locis scriptura seruauit, ut Dei moderationem in peccatis nostris cognoscendis, iudiciis dissimulandis, tandemque, quasi si coactus esset, profun-dendis in reos ostenderet: praesertim quum generale aliquod iudicium agitur, ut optime Basilius ex hoc loco & cap.18. in Psalm.13. (qui nobis est14.) obseruauit. Atque hoc pacto omnibus iis qui iuri dicun-do praesunt exemplum Dei pro lege habendum est, ut nihil nisi cer-tissima cognitione ausint statuere. Consilij autem quod Deus ex co-gnitione cepit pro ut verbis ipsius a Mose exprimitur, partes duae sunt totidem versibus distinctae. Nam primum contentio ponitur [illegible, ~8 letters] in verf. 6. Deinde vero sententia iudiciumque definitum il-lius, v.7. In contetione [illegible, ~8 letters] comparatio instituitur iudicati cum Dei consilio consiliis hominum repugnante. In iudicato duae partes exponuntur: vna, de operariis; altera, de opere illorum. In operariis duae maxime commoditates obseruantur; vna consensio & conspira-tio animorum in tantum sceleus, quam Deus ostendit [illegible, ~8 letters], Ecce populus vnus (consensione) est: altera, linguę conuenientia, tamquam instrumenti ad perficiendam conspirationem pernecessarij. Operis modum his verbis proponit Deus, atque hoc inceptum illorum est in faciendo opere. Huic malo consilium Dei per indignationem opponitur: quapropter etiam alterum versus membrum tamquam indigna-bundi verba cum interrogatione accipimus, nunc ergo (inquit Deus) id est, cum isti in hoc tempore animis, linguis, opere conueniant & conspirent aduersus voluntatem Dei Gigantea quadam audacia, nunc inquam, non interciperetur istis quicquid cogitauerunt facere? Tamquam fi diceret, omnino impedimentum experturi sunt. Itaque in hac contetionis parte, duo maximè opus est obseruari: unū, impiam hominum præsidentiam, qua putát fieri non posse vt sua consilia affabrefacta vnquam nec à Deo quidem euertantur: alterum, nihil esse impedimento Deo, quominus & cosultores ipsos, quū videtur, vindemiet (vt etiam psaltes loquutus est) aut etiam consilia ipsorum exsecet tamquam funes ductarios peccati; vt Iefchahiæ 5. appellantur. Sententia quâ Deus fert contra istorum scelus, primùm iudiciū Dei, deinde finem illius exponit in verf.7. iudicium Dei his verbis enuntiatur à Deo Patre Filium & S. Sanctum ad commune opus iudicij istius appellante: agite, descendamus, &c. Nā hoc opus indiuisum Sanctæ trinitatis est, quòd Deus non descendit quidem fecundum essentiam (id enim dicitur humanitus) sed tamquā fi descendisset qui priùs aderat, singulari operatione testificatus est præsentiam suam: cofufio autem ista linguarum per differentiam earum repentè à Deo inditam effecta est: quapropter optimè Paulus 1.Cor.14.Ex Iefchahia confirmauit linguas signa esse infidelibus, non autè fidelibus, fiue ad poenā, fiue ad exercitametum illorum, quod exercitamentū fidelium & infidelium comune est. Finis iudicij huius duplex fuit: unus, quę Moses exprimit, dicens, vt non intelligant alter alterum linguam. Alter, quę reticet in consilio, nempe vt ex ista linguarum ignoratione dispergantur ij qui ad opus vnum vno consensu consurrexisse videbantur. Sed videant lectores hic breuitatem Mosis, qui priorem finè in consilio exprimes reticet in narratione facti, feq.v. Posteriore in cofilio dissimulans diserte proponit in narratione facti, feq.v. ne idè subinde repeti oporteret. Ex consilio igitur sequitur factū, v.8. nēpe quòd Deus confudit linguas illorū, ne alter ab altero intelligeretur, vt modò dixi-mus: & quòd dispersit eos inde in superficie vniuersa terra, cū sese præpeditos ignoratione linguarū animaduerterent: qua in re singularis fuit Dei misericordia non pessumdantis homines pro merito ipsorū, sed instrumentum coniunctionis subtrahentis pro misericordia sua, vt ab impio consilio desisterent. Atque hoc fecundum factum est quod v. 8. exprimitur. Ita destiterunt edificare ciuitatem illam quam cogitauerant. Postremus locus euentorum est in v.9. duo autem euenta à Mose exponuntur: quorum euétus prior in loco, posterior in toto orbe documentum exhibuit iustitiæ Dei hominum impietatem oppugnantis. In loco, quòd ex eo iudicio vrbs nominata est Babel, propter superuenientem confusionem: in orbe, quòd inde dispersit eos Iehoua in &c. Hactenus prior narrationis pars, siue historia communis toti humano generi inde à diluuio. Nunc ad singularem historiā venien-dū est, quæ est de rebus Ecclesiæ Dei, & electi feminis, in quo Deus continuari veritatem suarum promiffionū voluit. Huius narrationis modus est duplex: vnus crassior ac nō æque accuratus; alter verō accuratior. molliore fiue leuiore (vt loquuntur) brachio pertexitur narratio capitum quæ in sanćta hac gente à Noacho ad Theracū vfq; pertenderūt, i.ad versum vsque 25. accuratius verò historia perscribitur de familia Therachi, ad finem vsque cap. Communis horum infcri-ptio his verbis continetur, v.10. hæ generationes Schemi. Deinde verò prior narrationis locus de geteSchemi proponitur; & oćto perfonarū (vt loquuntur) nomina binis versibus ordine recensentur. In recefione fingulorū capitū, primum ætas qua filiū genuerūt in quo promissiones Dei constaret exponitur, priore versu: deinde verò reliquū vitę tepus ostenditur quo illi vixerunt, poftquā primogenitos suos genuissent: ex quib. numeris inter fe collectis facile de toto vitę cuiufq; tepore constare potest. Tepus autē ad certitudinē historiæ, tum communis mūdo, tū singularis Ecclesiæ pertinet. Vnica hic incidit quæstio quæ piū lectorem possit remorari: nēpe, quomodo à lxx. interpretibus, & iis omnib. qui hæferūt illorū interpretationi, interseratur Kenan, tāquā Arpafchadi filius, cū tamē à Mose aut alio auctore vllo teftameti veteris nulla metio illius confirmari possit. Hāc quæstione vt soluamus, paucis ita habedū est. lxx. interp. fide olim quidē in pretio fuisse habitā, præsertim addućta commendatione miraculi ꝗ apud auctores nō paucos legitur: sed tamen etiam olim nō fine causa fuisse cōtrouerfam, & ab Hieronymo in locis aliquot desiderari: etsi postea cū à Ruffino ea de causa reprehenderetur, sententiā suā quāmaxime potuit dissimulauit, ne in odia & exagitationes multorū (quas iā plus fatis erat expertus) incurreret. In hoc autem ipso argumento duo esse potiffimū, in quibus lxx. illi à Mose difceffierint: Vnū, quōd Kenane interposuerunt: alterū, quōd ratione annorum mirifice adauxerunt, queadmodū etiā supra in caput 5. docuimus. Vtriufq; facti causa hæc videtur exstitisse, quōd existimauerint nō esse geti Ægyptiorū aut illi alteri cedendū in laudatiffimo antiquitatis argumento, quia antiquitatis nomē dignitatē rebus venerandā adferre solet. Quapropter derunt illi opera (vt ante alibi monuimus) vt certis scripturę locis infercirent nomina personarum, & rationem temporum adaugerent; nō eo consilio vt de veritate derogarent, sed eo potius vt de exterarū gentiū gloriatione (quā adhibebant illæ antiquitatis specie) detrahe-rent: maximē cū putarent in reb. eiusmodi nō laborare aut infirmari piorū fidē, quę in dogmatis pietatis fundata est, nō autē narrationib. historicis. Hanc cogitationem probare quidē nō possumus: quia fine
units.tr: Having set out in chapter 10 the spread of Noah's family into its heads, nations, regions, families and languages, the text now, in these nine verses, explains the cause of that spread. Then the rest of the chapter, down to the calling of Abraham, sets out the continuation of the holy stock in the Church, which we said is the second part of this discourse. In the history of that dispersion through nations and languages, the narrative contains those parts which, at the start of this undertaking, we said Cicero requires in De Oratore, book 1. First, the cause of the event is set out, to verse 4. Second, the counsel, verse 5 and the two following. Third, the deed, verse 8. Last, the outcome, verse 9. The cause was an impious and unjust plan of the human race. To explain this plan, verse 1 says that all men on earth used one speech and the same words before that time, and that there was one common language for all. In the account of their impious and unjust deed, first the occasion is set out in verse 2, then the counsel in verses 3 and 4. The deed itself is passed over, because it is understood both from the counsel taken and from what follows. The convenience of the place gave the occasion. After the flood they had set out from Armenia to take up dwellings, and they chose a place most pleasant in appearance and most fertile in fact, in all the East, in which to live. That place is in the land of Shinar, that is, of Mesopotamia and Babylonia, above the mountain the geographers call Singara, and the town of Singara set on the Euphrates. In that region, where man had first been placed at creation, they seemed to themselves likely to fix their home at the restoration of the world. The counsel has two parts. First the instruments of the work are set up, verse 3; then the work and its purpose, verse 4. Since the place itself lacked them, they took care by art to make suitable material for building: they decided that bricks should be made instead of stones and baked thoroughly so as to last against every injury, and that bitumen should be used instead of mortar. So impiety is most clever at carrying out impious plans. The counsel for the work is shown in verse 4 to be twofold: a city is to be built, and a tower, and that tower very high. The purpose is twofold. One is vanity: that they might make a name for themselves. The other is impiety, and not vanity only: lest they be scattered afterwards over the face of the earth, as if in this way they could guard themselves against the weapons of heaven. The second point follows this wicked cause put forward by men, namely the counsel which God took against this impious plan of men. The need for this counsel among men is [...] verse 5. The manner of the counsel is shown in verses 6 and 7. [...] is a careful arrangement for holding an inquiry into the matter proposed, and for knowing the fact with certainty and by due process. This is said of God in human terms, Moses saying, Jehovah came down to see, etc. For God, who is infinite, neither ascends nor descends. But he is set before us as a supreme judge who pronounces judgment from his seat, and who, when he is about to give judgment, comes down of his own accord and lowers himself to the level of his people, so that he may investigate the deed on the spot from individuals and from the matter before him, and reach an absolute knowledge of it. Scripture has kept this manner of speaking in several places, to show God's restraint in inquiring into our sins, in deferring judgment, and at last, as if compelled, pouring out punishment on the guilty. This is especially so when some general judgment is being carried out, as Basil well observed from this passage and from chapter 18 on Psalm 13 (which is Psalm 14 for us). In this way all who preside over the giving of judgment ought to take God's example as a rule, so that they dare to decide nothing except on the most certain knowledge. The counsel which God took from this knowledge, as it is expressed by Moses in God's own words, has two parts, each marked by its own verses. First the contention is set out in verse 6 [...]. Then comes the sentence and his definite judgment, verse 7. In the contention [...] a comparison is made between the judgment and God's counsel, which is opposed to the counsels of men. In the judgment two things are set out: one concerning the workers, the other concerning their work. In the workers two advantages are chiefly observed. One is the agreement and conspiracy of minds in so great a crime, which God points out [...]: Behold, the people is one (in consent). The other is the sharing of one language, as a most necessary instrument for carrying the conspiracy through. God sets out the manner of the work in these words: and this is what they have begun to do. God's counsel is opposed to this evil through indignation. Therefore we take the second member of the verse also as words of indignation, with a question: now therefore (says God), that is, since these men at this time agree and conspire in mind, language and work against the will of God with a kind of giant audacity, now, I say, will not what they have thought to do be stopped for them? As if he were saying: they are certainly going to experience a hindrance. So in this part of the contention two things chiefly need to be noted. One is the impious presumption of men, who think it cannot happen that their carefully wrought plans should ever be overturned, not even by God. The other is that nothing stands in God's way of gathering in the very counsellors themselves when he sees fit (as the psalmist too has said), or even of cutting off their plans like the ropes of a cart by which sin is drawn, as they are called in Isaiah 5. The sentence by which God pronounces against their crime sets out first the divine judgment, then its end, in verse 7. The judgment of God is expressed in these words, spoken by God the Father, calling on the Son and the Holy Spirit to share in this judgment: come, let us go down, etc. For this work is undivided in the Holy Trinity. God did not descend in essence (for that is said in human terms), but as if he had descended, he who was already present bore witness to his presence by a singular work. That confusion of languages was brought about by the sudden introduction of a difference among them by God. For this reason Paul rightly confirmed from Isaiah, 1 Cor. 14, that tongues are a sign to unbelievers and not to believers, whether for punishment or for the training of those people, and that this training is common to believers and unbelievers. The end of this judgment was twofold. One is what Moses expresses, saying, that they may not understand one another's language. The other is what he passes over in the counsel, namely that by this ignorance of languages those who seemed to have risen up with one consent to one work should be scattered. But let the readers note here the brevity of Moses. In the counsel he passes over the first purpose, which he expresses in the narrative of the deed in what follows, verse 8. In the counsel he conceals the latter, which in the narrative of the deed he plainly sets out, so that the same thing need not be repeated again and again. From the counsel, therefore, the deed follows, verse 8: namely that God confounded their language, so that one should not understand another, as we have just said; and that he scattered them from there over the whole face of the earth, when they perceived themselves hindered by ignorance of languages. In this matter God's mercy was singular: he did not destroy men according to their merit, but withdrew the means of union for his own mercy's sake, so that they might desist from their impious counsel. This second deed is what verse 8 expresses. Thus they ceased to build that city which they had planned. The last point of the outcome is in verse 9. Moses sets out two outcomes: the first of these showed an example in the place, the second an example in the whole world, of God's justice opposing human impiety. In the place: the city was named Babel from the confusion that came upon it. In the world: from there Jehovah scattered them, etc. So far the first part of the narrative, or the history common to the whole human race from the flood onward. Now we must come to the particular history, which concerns the affairs of the Church of God and the elect seed, in which God willed the truth of his promises to continue. This narrative has a twofold manner: one cruder and not equally accurate, the other more accurate. With a softer, or as they say lighter, arm the narrative is woven of the heads which in this holy people ran from Noah down to Terah, as far as verse 25. More accurately, however, the history of the family of Terah is written out, to the end of the chapter. The common heading of these is given in these words, verse 10: these are the generations of Shem. Then the first part of the narrative concerning the posterity of Shem is set out, and the names of eight persons (as they say) are recounted in order in two verses. In the recounting of the individual heads, first the age at which each begot a son, in which the promises of God would be upheld, is set out in the first verse. Then the rest of the time of life is shown during which they lived after begetting their firstborn sons. From these numbers, gathered together, the whole span of each life can easily be established. The matter of time pertains to the certainty of the history, both for the world in general and for the Church in particular. One question arises here which might hold back a pious reader: namely, why the Septuagint translators, and all who have adhered to their translation, insert Kenan as the son of Arpachshad, when no mention of him can be confirmed from Moses or from any author of the Old Testament. To resolve this question, the following should be held in brief. The Septuagint translators were once indeed held in high esteem, especially since the commendation of a miracle is read of them in not a few authors. Yet even in former times the matter was not without cause in dispute, and Jerome in several places found it lacking. Although afterwards, when Rufinus rebuked him for this reason, he dissembled his opinion as far as he could, so as not to fall into hatred and the harassment of many (which he had already experienced more than enough). In this very argument there are chiefly two points where those Seventy departed from Moses. One is that they inserted Kenan. The other is that they wonderfully increased the years, as we also taught above in chapter 5. The cause of both acts seems to have been this: they thought they should not yield to the Egyptians or to that other nation in the most praiseworthy argument of antiquity, since the name of antiquity is wont to bring dignity to things worthy of reverence. For this reason they took pains (as we noted earlier elsewhere) to insert the names of persons into certain places of Scripture and to enlarge the reckoning of times. They did this not with the purpose of detracting from the truth, but rather to detract from the boasting of foreign nations, which they supported by the appearance of antiquity. This was especially so since they thought that in matters of this kind the faith of the pious, which is founded on the doctrines of piety and not on historical narratives, would not be weakened or harmed. We cannot indeed approve this reasoning, because without this art the truth and antiquity of sacred history cannot be defended. But Luke the Evangelist acted quite differently. In his genealogy he mentions Kenan, following that Septuagint authority, but with a most different purpose, since he saw that the salvation of the pious was not placed in this matter, but…

units.la: hac arte defendi veritas & antiquitas sacrae historiae poterit. Sed longe aliter Lucae Euangelistae accidit, qui in sua recensione Kenanis meminit sequutus illam LXX. fidem, sed consilio diuerfiffimo. cum enim videret non esse positam in hac re piorum salutem, sed errorem iam olim temere a maioribus inuectum, & apud omnes gentes aetate illa receptum non posse sine graui offensione tam repente conuelli extentibus & libris hominum, dedit Lucas charitati & pietati in Ecclesiam Dei quod temeritas ante inuexerat, ac proinde Kenanis appellationem eodem ordine in sua narratione inseri passus est, ne dum historiae veritas ageretur (in qua parum positum videbat esse) labefactaretur pietas infirmorum & dissueretur charitas, quae primis illis temporibus nascentis Ecclesiae omnibus modis fuit fulcienda. Quod modestum exemplum omnibus piis ante oculos versari cupiuerim, vt quaecumque pie tolerari possunt, ea propter pietatem in Deum & charitatem in proximum tolerentur. Alter narrationis locus, quem vnius familiae singularem diximus, primum vniuersae nomina filiorum Therachi edit v. 26. Deinde vero speciatim singulorum historiam pertexit, non quidem accurate, sed quantum visum est Spiritui sancto ad historiam populi Dei pertinere, reliquis versibus. Commune igitur illud est, quod Therach septuagenarius tres filios dicitur genuisse, quorum nomina non pro tempore genituraae ipsorum adferuntur; sed potius secundum dignitatem qua Abraham, quamuis natu inferior, aliis antestabat ex gratuita electione Dei. alioquin Haranem (qui postremus nominatur) natu fuisse maximum ex sequentibus eo colligitur, quod Lotum genuisset, quod Vre in conspectu patris sui obiit, & quod filiae ipsius fratribus datae sunt nuptui. Rationem dignitatis, ac non temporis fuisse habitam in hac liberorum enumeratione, demonstratur capite sequente ex annorum Therachi cum annis Abrahami comparatione. Nam cum Therach natus fuerit annos ducentos quinque quando Charane in Mesopotamia mortuus est, post cuius obitum statim Abram Charane profectus petiuit Cenahaneam ex mandato Dei agens annum septuagesimum quintum (vt capite sequente dicitur v. 4.) omnino necesse est Abramum ex Theracho fuisse genitum, cum Pater Therach annum ageret aetatis suae 135. Haranem vero natu maximum annis sexaginta Abramum praecessisse, quandoquidem Therach septuagenarius dicitur genuisse. Sic enim constabit sibi veritas historiae, si Haranem genitum esse patri septuagenario, Nachorem ampliusProuecto aetate, Abramum denique annum agenti 135. statuamus. Ac propterea cum Moses dicit, quando vixisset 70. annos, genuisse tres filios, hoc ita oportet accipi non eodem anno genuisse omnes; sed primum de filiis eo anno, reliquos suo tempore genuisse.
units.tr: This is the only way the truth and antiquity of the sacred history can be defended. But Luke the Evangelist acted quite differently. In his list he mentions Kenan, following that belief of the Seventy, but with a very different purpose. For when he saw that the salvation of the godly did not depend on this matter, and that the error had long since been rashly introduced by our forefathers and had been accepted among all nations in that age, he could not be uprooted so suddenly without serious offence to the minds of many. So he yielded to charity and piety towards the Church of God in what rashness had introduced earlier. Accordingly he allowed the name Kenan to be inserted in his narrative in the same order, so that while the truth of the history was being pursued (a matter he saw to be of little weight), the piety of the weak would not be shaken and charity, which in those first days of the infant Church had to be upheld in every way, would not be torn apart. I would wish this modest example to be kept before the eyes of all the godly, so that whatever can be tolerated with piety is tolerated for the sake of piety towards God and charity towards our neighbour. The second part of the narrative, which we said concerns one family alone, first gives the names of the sons of Terah in general, in verse 26. Then, in the remaining verses, it goes on to relate the history of each one individually, not with exact detail but as far as the Holy Spirit thought it pertinent to the history of the people of God. What is common to them, therefore, is that Terah, at seventy years of age, is said to have begotten three sons, whose names are not given in the order of their births, but rather according to the dignity by which Abraham, though younger by birth, stood above the others, through God's free election. Otherwise, that Haran (who is named last) was the eldest by birth is gathered from what follows, since he begot Lot, died in the sight of his father Ur, and his daughters were given in marriage to his brothers. That in this enumeration of the children the order of dignity and not of time was followed is shown in the next chapter, by comparing the years of Terah with the years of Abraham. For since Terah was two hundred and five years old when he died in Haran in Mesopotamia, and immediately after his death Abram departed from Haran and sought Canaan at the command of God, in his seventy-fifth year (as is said in verse 4 of the next chapter), it is altogether necessary that Abram was begotten by Terah when his father was 135 years of age. And Haran, the eldest by birth, must have been born sixty years before Abram, since Terah is said to have begotten him at seventy. For the truth of the history will thus be consistent with itself if we hold that Haran was born to a father of seventy, Nahor when his father was further advanced in age, and finally Abram when his father was 135. And therefore, when Moses says that Terah, having lived seventy years, begot three sons, this must be understood thus: not that he begot all of them in the same year, but that he begot the first in that year and the others at their own times.

units.la: Quamobrem non male interpretati sunt qui istud verbum Genuit hoc loco verterunt, coepit gignere, ne quis fortasse tergeminos eo anno fuisse natos arbitraretur. Huius autem familiae ratio minutatim insti-tuitur inde a v. 27. Vbi repetita trium genitura, postea singulariter primum de Harane v. 27. & sequente; tum de Abramo & Nachore reliquis versibus narratio instituta est. In Haranis historia ponuntur duo: primum quod Filium Lotum genuerit, quae res ad proxime fe-quentis historiae intelligentiam pertinet; Secundo quod in solo natali suo & ciuitate sua obierit in conspectu patris, id est, antequam singularis vocatio fuisset a Deo facta, de qua sequente capite. Fuit autem solum natale ipsius Chaldaea ciuitas Vr: quod nomen ignem, siue incen-dium, aut lucem significat. Geographis dicitur Orchoe, vt probabile est ab eo quod ignis iam olim illic coleretur: unde etiam tertia Chaldaeorum disciplina ignem pro Deo colentium Orchoena appellatur Plinio libr. 6. nat. historiae. Alter locus narrationis communis est Abrami & Nachoris: in quo primum de coniugio vtriusque dicitur, v. 29. & seq. Deinde vero de migratione, v. 31. & seq. Postremo autem de patris obitu, v. vltimo. De coniugio primum communiter hoc dicit Moses, assumpsit Abram & Nachor sibi vxores: Deinde speciatim vtramque circumscribit, nomine primum, Milcam & Sarain; deinde origine, quod Filia Haranis essent. Nam illud membrum, Filia Haranis [illegible, ~4 letters] ad vtramque vxorem cum Hebraeis statuo per-tinere. Quod autem postea adiicit, Filia Haranis patris Milcae & patris Iiscae, illud duabus quaestionibus agitari solet. Primum enim quaeritur, quae sit Iisca: deinde vero cur istud a Mose fuerit additum. Iiscam eamdem cum Sara esse Iudaeis statuentibus assentimur. Cum enim scriptura non soleat de nihilo eiusmodi membra historiae sacrae attingere: Iiscae vero (prout hic appellatur) nusquam extet mentio, omnino statuimus Iiscam hic eandem esse quae prius Sarai, post etiam Sara fuit appellata. Nam fuit binominis: quod non est in scripturis infrequens, praesertim si nomina ad eamdem pertineant si-gnificationem. Cuius rei exempla innumera ex comparatione locorum educi possunt. Sarain enim de eadem gente exstitisse, commu-nemque patrem habuisse, ipse Abram testatur infra 12. & 20. c. Nam qui pater fuit Abrami Therach, idem fuit auus Sarai, Haranis pater, ex quo Sarai est genita: quam etiam propterea Iiscam appellamus, quod Sarai & Iischa significatione concurrant. Est enim Sarai Domina: Iisca vero Chaldaeo sermone & Syro est spectata siue conspicua, vel clauum administrationis tenens. Cur autem hoc membrum fuerit additum, ratio est euidens: nempe quòd ita demonstratum volebat Moses non fuisse Harani liberos mares, ac proinde tum bonorum præsentium, tum primogenitorum ius optimè in Abramum translatum esse. Quod v.30. Sarai sterilis & improles fuisse dicitur, hoc ad historiam sequentem respicit cap.16. & seqq. Sequitur migrationis historia duobus membris distincta, narratione facti, & temporis. Historia facti, v.31. ostendit causam proximam, consilium factumq; migrationis. Causa proxima fuit Therach illius familiæ pater, qui Abramum filium, Lotum nepotem, vxoresque assumpsisse ad migrationem secum dicitur, non temerè, sed ex institutione Dei, de qua proximè dicturi sumus. Consilium fuit, quòd egrederentur Vre vt venirent in terram Cenahanis obsequentes mandato Dei. Factum, quòd peruenerunt Chananem vsque in Mesopotamia & ibi consederunt, detenti(o-pinor)senio & imbecillitate graui Therachi patris: quapropter etiam illius ætas secundo annotatur loco in versu vltimo.
units.tr: For this reason those were not wrong who translated the word Genuit in this place as began to beget, lest anyone perhaps suppose that triplets were born in that year. The account of this family, however, is set out in detail from verse 27 onwards. Here, after the birth of the three is repeated, the narrative is then carried on individually: first concerning Haran, in verse 27 and the following, then concerning Abram and Nahor in the remaining verses. Two things are put in the history of Haran: first, that he begot a son Lot, which matter pertains to the understanding of the history that immediately follows; second, that he died in his native land and in his own city, in the sight of his father, that is, before the singular calling was made by God, of which the next chapter speaks. The native place of Haran was the Chaldean city of Ur, a name which signifies fire, or conflagration, or light. Geographers call it Orchoe, as is probable from the fact that fire was worshipped there even in ancient times; hence also the third sect of the Chaldeans, those who worshipped fire as God, is called Orchoena by Pliny in book 6 of his Natural History. The second part of the narrative is common to Abram and Nahor. In it, first, their marriages are mentioned, in verse 29 and following; then their migration, in verse 31 and following; and finally the death of the father, in the last verse. Concerning the marriages, Moses first says in general: Abram and Nahor took wives for themselves; then he describes each one particularly: first by name, Milcah and Sarai; then by origin, that they were daughters of Haran. For I hold that the phrase daughters of Haran [illegible] pertains to each wife, according to the Hebrews. As for what he adds afterwards, daughter of Haran, father of Milcah and father of Iscah, this is usually debated on two questions. For first it is asked what Iscah is, and then why Moses added this. We agree with those who hold that Iscah is the same as Sarah. For since Scripture does not usually touch on such parts of sacred history without reason, and no mention of Iscah (as she is called here) is found anywhere else, we conclude that Iscah here is the same as she who was earlier called Sarai and afterwards Sarah. For she had two names, which is not infrequent in the Scriptures, especially when the names have the same meaning. Countless examples of this can be drawn from comparing passages. That Sarai was of the same family and had a common father, Abram himself testifies below, in chapters 12 and 20. For the father of Abram, Terah, was also the grandfather of Sarai, the daughter of Haran, from whom Sarai was born; and we call her Iscah for this reason also, that Sarai and Ischa coincide in meaning. For Sarai means mistress, while Iscah in the Chaldean and Syrian tongue means one who is looked upon or conspicuous, or one who holds the rudder of government. Why this clause was added is clear: namely, because Moses wished to show that Haran had no male children, and therefore the right of present goods and of the firstborn had been most properly transferred to Abram. As for verse 30, where Sarai is said to have been barren and without offspring, this looks forward to the history in chapter 16 and following. There follows the history of the migration, divided into two parts: the narration of the deed and of the time. The account of the deed, in verse 31, shows the immediate cause, the plan and the act of the migration. The immediate cause was Terah, the father of that family, who is said to have taken with him on the migration Abram his son, Lot his grandson, and their wives, not rashly, but by the instruction of God, which we shall shortly discuss. The plan was that they should go out from Ur to go into the land of Canaan, obeying the command of God. The deed was that they came as far as Haran in Mesopotamia and settled there, being detained (I think) by the old age and grave infirmity of their father Terah; for which reason his age is also noted a second time, in the last verse.

units.la: CAPITIS XII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 12.

units.la: Hic secundus historiæ locus de rebus à diluvio gestis (vt supra in cap.x. ostendimus.) Res Abrami continet prout à Deo procuratæ, & ab Abramo gestæ sunt secundum dispensationem gratiosam Dei. Hæc itaque historia eo consilio conscripta est, vt res prisicas illius Ecclesiæ quæ in familia Abrami constitit, veritatemque promissionū Dei ex eis cognoscamus. Summa est, Abramū singulari vocatione Dei electum, ex media idololatria sic à Deo gratiosè deductū & curatū esse, vt promissionibus instructus in terrā promissam deuenerit, tamquā hæreditatē sibi addictā à Domino: & de hæredibus fuisse signis ac sedere gratioso confirmatus, donec tandem adeptus filiū promissionis per Dei gratiā in cælestē hæreditatē assumptus esset. Partes itaq; huius historiæ duæ summatim possunt constitui, secundū tempora duo: vnū, promissionis, ad c.16.vsque: alterū sederis, sequentibus. Res historicæ promissionis tempore coprehensæ duæ sunt, quæ in prima illa vocatione Abrami simul cōtinentur; prior est, de promissa & adita hæreditate, tribus c.12. & 13. & 14. Posterior est, de promisso perceptoq; hærede, inde à c.15. Vtrūq; generatim primaDei vocatione fuit Abramo expositū, tribus versibus. Postea verò vterq; historiæ locus minutatim exponitur; quapropter etiā cum ille primus vocationis locus sit plane ἀπολογητικὸς[?] & causam exponens cur Therach cū familia Vre Chaldæorū discesserit, commodius ad historiæ intelligentiā videtur fore, si tres illi versus vocatione Abrami exponētes, ad fine præcedentis capitis attexantur. Nam facto migrationis institutæ
units.tr: Here is the second section of the history, concerning the events after the flood (as we showed above in chapter 10). It contains the affairs of Abram, as they were arranged by God and carried out by Abram, according to God's gracious dispensation. This history was written with the purpose that we might learn from it the early affairs of that Church which was established in Abram's family, and the truth of God's promises. The sum is this: Abram, chosen by God through a singular calling, was so graciously led out of the midst of idolatry and cared for by God that, furnished with promises, he arrived in the promised land, as an inheritance assigned to him by the Lord; and he was confirmed by signs and a gracious settlement for his heirs, until at last, having obtained the son of promise through the grace of God, he was taken up into the heavenly inheritance. The parts of this history can therefore be set out briefly as two, according to two periods: one of promise, up to chapter 16, and the other of the seed, which follows. The historical matters comprised in the period of promise are two, and they are contained together in that first calling of Abram. The first concerns the promised and entered inheritance, in chapters 12, 13 and 14. The second concerns the promised and received heir, from chapter 15 onward. Each was set out to Abram in general terms by God's first calling, in three verses. Afterwards each section of the history is expounded in detail. Therefore, since that first passage about the calling is plainly apologetic [ἀπολογητικὸς] and explains why Terah left Ur of the Chaldeans with his family, it seems more convenient for understanding the history if those three verses, which explain Abram's calling, are attached to the end of the preceding chapter.

units.la: (de quo in fine præcedetis capitis diximus)causa subiicitur,mandatū & vocatio Dei,cuius conscius Abrā patrē quoq; fecit participē, adeò vt tota illa familia Deo auctore & patre Theracho duce in Mesopota miā migrauerit Cenahanea petitura. Quòd si quis dixerit cōpendiū itineris futurū fuisse, si per montana Babyloniæ & Arabiā desertam Cenahanea rectà petiuissent,respōdeo Deū pro sua sapientia voluisse hos quoq; circūducere vt Israelitas fecit, & de cōmoditate viæ prospexisse; quæ per Arabiā deserta & periculosissima est,propter latrocinia,& impeditissima propter rerū omniū inopiā. In hac autē vocatione vel mandato Dei duæ partes,vt in omnib. Dei mādatis,obseruandæ sunt:nēpe vocatio siue mandatū vocationis,& promissio;nam nulla Dei vocatio promissō caret, adeò gratiosè Dominus solet cum reb.creatis omnibus,præsertim cū Ecclesia sua,agere.Mandatū vocationis est,v.1.promissum duob.seqq.Huius mandati partes duę sunt; vna excedēdi è præsente statione, quē locū Deus amplificauit ad probandā & demonstrandāAbrahami fidē cū diceret,è terra tua,&c. Altera pars est veniendi in locū alterū,vbi etiā est amplissima probatio vel experimentū, quōd Deus locū incertū Abramo imperat vt fides illius amplius illustraretur,dicendo,in terrā quā ostenda tibi.Mandato huic diuino suæ promissiones cōiunctæ sunt,non solū quōd ad hęreditatē adeundā,verūetiam quōd ad hęredes omnēsq; benedictiones quę ad Abrahamū & semē illius fuerūt peruenturę.Harū promissionū aliæ omniū omnib.tēporibus cōmunes sunt, aliæ proprię & peculiares Euangelij.Cōmunes sunt hæ, Gentis propagatio siue feminis,his verbis,Facia te in gente,&c. Benedictio & cōmunicatio bonorū præsentium,& benedicā tibi:Honoris & glorię accumulatio,Magnificabo nomē tuū:Deniq; vis & facultas præsentissima benedictionis tū in ipsis omnib. perstiturę, quēadmodū Abramo indicta est his verbis,Et esto benedictio, tū in alios dimanaturę qui Ecclesię Dei bene cupiuerint, Benedicā benedicentibus tibi,cui ex cōtrario opponitur facultas quædā maledictionis in obstirmatos Dei Ecclesiæq; hostes diffundēdæ,Maledicetem tibi exsecrabor.Hę cōmunes promissiones;quēadmodū extāt summatim cōprehensæ principio c.24. Particulares benedictiones,& ad tēpus prædicationis Euāgelij spēciatim pertinētes,proponūtur his verbis, benedictūrā sunt sibi in te omnes familiā terrā,i.omnes gētes quę per familias non ita pridem diffusæ sunt, quamuis à benedictionibus his alienissimæ,eas adipiscentur tamē,cōscientiāque earum sibi benedicēnt, nō in se aut propter se;sed in te,i.in semine tuo promissio, quod est(vt ita loquamur)in lumbis tuis(Heb.7.)Nam propterea Abrahā dicitur vidisse diē Domini,& gauisus esse. Hactenus de vocatione.Sequuntur deinceps historiæ de hæreditate,tribus cap.Tum de haerede, seqq. vt ante distinximus. Hæreditatem tota hæc historiæ narrat non fuisse ab Abrahamo possessam iure hæreditario ex facto; sed tantum fide promissionis Dei perceptam & oculis collustratam, quemadmodum Apostolus ad Hebr. 11. auctor est, non fuisse illis patribus vestigium proprietarium, eo quod meliorem ciuitatem exspectarent hac terrena hæreditate adumbratam. Quapropter his tribus historiis, quæ singulis capitibus exponuntur, duo summatim declarat Moses: Vnum, hæreditatem illam terrenam fuisse ab Abramo perlustratam religiofiffimè: Alterum, illud ipsum tempus perluftrationis fuisse conditum grauissimis & acerbissimis tentationibus quas Deus certo consilio immisit Abramo, cùm vt fidem probaret illius, tum vt hanc non esse veram hæreditatem, sed vmbraculum verę hæreditatis ostenderet, vt ex 11.Heb. modò dicebamus. Itaque in hoc capite narratur lustrantem Abramum Cenahanæam fame tentatum esse, eoque in Ægyptum abiisse; Sequente, altero luftrationis tempore rixam inter domesticos suos & Loti expertum esse, propter quam impulsi fuerint alter ab altero discedere. Decimoquarto denique, in eadem commoratione dolorem acerbissimum cepisse ex Loti agnati fui deportatione, ac propterea bellum humanitus periculosum suscepisse, cui Dominus benedixerit. Prior locus in hoc capite de luftratione hæreditatis continetur à v. 4. ad 10. vsque;posterior verò, de tentatione qua Deus probauit virum, à v.10. ad finem vsque capitis. Prior locus de facto Abrami, quo vocationi Dei obediuit; has partes continet: Profectionem Abrami in terram quam ostensurus ipsi erat Deus, v.4.&5. Deinde declarationem diuinam ex quo in terram illam aduenerat, v.6.& 7. Tum professionem indefinentem religiosámque illius Fidei, qua promissa Dei prehendebat, v.8: Postremo autem in his omnibus obsequium, v.9. In profectione hæc sunt obseruanda; Primùm causa profectionis, vocatio & mandatum Dei: deinde modus, nempe quod Abram Lotum affumpfit secum, id est, & suam familiam & agnati fui ex pietatis & charitatis officio in communionem eiusdem gratiæ. Tertio, circumstantia temporis, quod Abram iam senex effet, puta 75. annos natus, cum ex Dei mandato Charane discederet: qui annus cum fuerit 205. Therachi patris (vt in fine capitis præcedentis dictum est) sequitur Abramum non septuagesimo Therachi anno, sed cetefimo trigesimo procreatum esse. Declarationem diuinam sic exponit Moses, vt primum locum illius declarationis & tempus designet, v.6. deinde substantiam vel summam illius, v.7. locus & tempus expressa sunt his verbis, Cum Abram vsque ad locum vsque Schecemi dicitur peruenisse, id est, in medimeditullium ferme regionis,antequam consilium suum Deus exponeret. Amplificatur autem promissionis diuinæ admirabilitas & Abrami fides circūstantiis incolarum & vicinitatis illius, quod tum Cenahaneus in terra esset, quo obtinente ne spes quidem Abramo esse videbatur regionis illius possidendæ,nisi, ut de hærede postea, sic de hæreditate sub spe cōtra spem credidisset. Declarationis modus substantiáque priore parte 7. verf.exponuntur. Modus,visio,eáque diuina: substantia, quod Deus illam regionem femini eius daturus esset. Hinc sequitur professio religiosa Abrami, qui singulis stationib. per medios Cenahanæos etiam in angustiis altare Iehoua instituisse & invocasse nomen Dei,id est cultum Dei internum & externum sine metu spectatibus infidelibus statuisse dicitur:nam externus,altaris institutione,internus etiā inuocatione per synecdochen describitur. Ex his omnibus sequitur obsequiū,quod Abrā regione sibi promissam perlustrauit,fide,v.9. Huius autem fidei, qua Abramus credentiū pater acquieuit diuinis promissionibus,certissimum documentum est tentatio foris adueniens,& patientia in Abrahamo constans:quā ad rem pertinet secūdus historiæ locus à v.10.ad finem vsque capitis. In hac autem historia, ut ordinem seruemus quē ante instituimus, primum causa historię proponitur,verf.10:secundo consilium,tribus sequentibus: tertio factum,tribus alteris: postremo autem euentus,reliquo capite. Causa migrationis institutæ in Ægyptum fuisse dicitur fames infestans Cenahaneam:quam ob causam Abram siue monitus à Deo reuelatione singulari, siue præsente difficultate adductus in Ægyptum dicitur cogitauisse. Nam in eo nihil fuit reprehensione dignum, quod Abram præsenti fame pressus cessit ad tempus, non autem promissioni diuinæ renuntiauit. Consilium, quod Abram in Ægyptum aduentans cepit,tribus partibus continetur. Nam primū occasionem præsentem capiendi consilij narrat,formamSarai,v.11. Deinde metum quem præcepit de Ægyptiorum iniuria, fore ut illa rapiatur & ipse trucidetur,verf.12. Postremò summam consilij & finem illius:summam,ut Sarai sororem se Abrami prædicet:finem,ut ipsi bene sit,& anteuertatur malum. In hoc autem consilio quæruntur duo: unum, qua fide Abram se fratrem Sarai & illam sororē suam dici voluerit: sed hæc quæstio infrà cap. 20. verbis Abrami ipsius soluitur: Alterum, qua fide pudicitiam vxoris suæ,quantum in ipso erat, prostituerit,ut vitæ suæ prospiceret. Sed huic quæstioni responsio commoda hæc est, negari propositionem : nam neque Abram hoc pacto pudicitiam vxoris suæ pro[?]ituisse, neque mala fide egisse. non prostituisse constat, eo quòd sororem suam prædicaret, ac proinde illam suæ curæ commissam, quamuis dissimulato coniugali iure, ostende-ret. Ex quo consequebatur, si quispiam in Ægypto Sarain ambiturus esset, cum ordine legitimo Abramum esse aditurum. Sic autem Abramum secum statuisse, fore animis procantium efferuescentibus, si tamquā cum fratre acturi circumducerentur, vt interea animi eo-rum magis deseruerent, quàm si vno impetu abrepti forma Sarai sibi rem cum viro illius fore credidissent: constat enim, quod vulgò dici-tur, primos illos motus minimè omnium esse in hominum potesta-te. Quòd si itā cogitauit Abram, non mala fide cogitauit; sed infirma, qui prudentiam carnis ad cautionem vitę suæ huic actioni asperserit.
units.tr: Because the migration was undertaken (of which we spoke at the end of the preceding chapter), the cause is given: the command and calling of God, of which Abram was aware and which he also made known to his father, so that the whole family migrated to Mesopotamia under God's direction and with Terah as leader, intending to seek Canaan. But if someone says that the journey would have been shorter had they made straight for Canaan through the mountains of Babylonia and the desert of Arabia, I answer that God, in his wisdom, wished them to be led about in this way, as he did the Israelites, and he took care for the convenience of the way; for the route through the desert of Arabia is very dangerous because of robbers, and most difficult because of the lack of all things. In this calling, or command of God, two parts are to be observed, as in all God's commands: namely the calling, or command to be called, and the promise; for no calling of God is without a promise, so graciously does the Lord usually deal with all created things, and especially with his Church. The command of the calling is in verse 1, and the promise is in the two following verses. This command has two parts. One is going out from the present station, a place which God enlarged in order to test and demonstrate Abraham's faith when he said from your land, etc. The other part is going to another place, where there is also the fullest proof or trial, because God commands Abram to go to an uncertain place so that his faith might be more clearly illustrated, saying into the land which I will show you. To this divine command his promises are joined, not only as regards entering the inheritance, but also as regards the heirs and all the blessings which were to come to Abraham and his seed. Of these promises some are common to all peoples at all times, and others are proper and peculiar to the Gospel. These common ones are: the propagation of the nation or seed, in these words, I will make you into a nation, etc.; the blessing and sharing of present goods, and I will bless you; the accumulation of honour and glory, I will magnify your name; and finally the power and most present faculty of blessing, which is to remain in those very persons, just as it was declared to Abram in these words, and be a blessing, and which is to flow out to others who wish well to the Church of God, I will bless those who bless you. Against this is set a certain power of cursing to be poured out upon those who are obstinate and enemies of God and his Church, I will curse the one who curses you. These are the common promises, as they are briefly summed up at the beginning of chapter 24. The particular blessings, which pertain specifically to the time of the preaching of the Gospel, are set forth in these words, all the families of the land will be blessed in you, that is, all the nations, which have been spread out by families not long ago, although they are most alien to these blessings, will nevertheless obtain them, and they will bless themselves by their knowledge of them, not in themselves or on their own account, but in you, that is, in your seed, the promise which is (as we may so speak) in your loins (Heb. 7). For this reason Abraham is said to have seen the day of the Lord and to have rejoiced. Thus far concerning the calling. What follows is the history of the inheritance, in three chapters, and then of the heir, in the following chapters, as we distinguished before. This whole history relates that the inheritance was not possessed by Abraham by hereditary right in fact, but was received only by faith in God's promise and surveyed with the eyes, just as the Apostle, in Heb. 11, testifies that those fathers had no property of their own, because they were looking for a better city, shadowed forth by this earthly inheritance. Therefore, through these three histories, which are explained in the individual chapters, Moses sets out two things in summary. One: that Abram surveyed that earthly inheritance most devoutly. The other: that the very time of this surveying was marked by the most grievous and bitter temptations, which God sent upon Abram with a certain purpose, both to test his faith and to show that this was not the true inheritance but the shadow of the true inheritance, as we were just now saying from Heb. 11. Accordingly, in this chapter it is related that Abram, surveying Canaan, was tested by famine, and therefore went down into Egypt; in the following chapter, during the second period of his survey, he experienced a quarrel between his household servants and those of Lot, on account of which they were driven to separate from one another. Finally, in chapter 14, during the same sojourn, he was overwhelmed with the bitterest grief at the capture of his kinsman Lot, and therefore undertook a war, humanly speaking dangerous, to which the Lord gave his blessing. The first section of this chapter, concerning the survey of the inheritance, is contained from verse 4 to verse 10; the second section, concerning the temptation by which God tested the man, runs from verse 10 to the end of the chapter. The first section, concerning Abram's act by which he obeyed God's calling, contains these parts: Abram's departure into the land which God was about to show him, verses 4 and 5. Then the divine declaration from the time when he arrived in that land, verses 6 and 7. Then the unceasing and devout profession of his faith, by which he grasped God's promises, verse 8. Last, obedience in all these things, verse 9. In the departure these points are to be observed: first, the cause of the departure, namely the calling and command of God; then the manner, namely that Abram took Lot with him, that is, both his household and his kinsman, out of a duty of piety and charity, into fellowship of the same grace. Third, the circumstance of time: that Abram was already old, being 75 years old when he left Haran at God's command; and since this year was the 205th of Terah's life (as was said at the end of the preceding chapter), it follows that Abram was born not in Terah's seventieth year but in his hundred and thirtieth. Moses sets out the divine declaration in such a way that he marks first the place and time of that declaration, verse 6, and then its substance or sum, verse 7. The place and time are expressed in these words: when Abram is said to have come as far as the place of Shechem, that is, to about the middle of the region, before God set out his plan. The wonder of the divine promise and Abram's faith is further magnified by the circumstances of the inhabitants and neighbours of that place, because the Canaanite was then in the land; while he held it, Abram seemed to have no hope at all of possessing that region, unless, as he believed concerning the heir afterwards, so also concerning the inheritance he believed in hope against hope. The manner of the declaration and its substance are set out in the first part of verse 7. The manner is a vision, and a divine one; the substance is that God would give that region to his seed. From this follows Abram's devout profession, who, at each station, even in difficulties, among the Canaanites, is said to have built an altar to Jehovah and to have called upon the name of God, that is, to have set up, without fear before the unbelievers who were looking on, the inward and outward worship of God; for the outward is described by the building of the altar, and the inward by the invocation, through synecdoche. From all these things it follows that Abram, by faith, traversed the region promised to him as an act of obedience, verse 9. Now the most certain proof of this faith, by which Abram, the father of believers, assented to the divine promises, is the temptation that came from outside and the steadfast patience in Abraham; to this matter pertains the second section of the history, from verse 10 to the end of the chapter. In this history, to keep the order we set up before, first the cause of the story is put forward, verse 10; second the plan, in the three following verses; third the deed, in the three after that; and last the outcome, in the rest of the chapter. The cause of the migration undertaken into Egypt is said to be the famine afflicting Canaan; for this reason Abram, either warned by God through a singular revelation or led by the present difficulty, is said to have thought of going down to Egypt. For there was nothing blameworthy in this, that Abram, pressed by the present famine, gave way for a time and did not renounce God's promise. The plan which Abram formed on arriving in Egypt is contained in three parts. First he relates the present occasion for the plan, the beauty of Sarai, verse 11. Then the fear he conceived of injury from the Egyptians, that they would seize her and kill him, verse 12. Last, the sum of the plan and its aim: the sum, that he would declare Sarai to be his sister; the aim, that it might go well with him and the evil be averted. In this plan two questions arise. One: with what faith Abram wished himself and her to be called brother and sister. But this question is resolved below, in chapter 20, by Abram's own words. The other: with what faith he, so far as lay in him, prostituted his wife's chastity in order to provide for his own life. To this question the answer is convenient: the proposition is denied. For Abram did not in this way prostitute his wife's chastity, nor did he act in bad faith. That he did not prostitute her is evident, because he declared her to be his sister, and so showed that she was entrusted to his care, although the conjugal right was concealed. From this it followed that if anyone in Egypt wished to court Sarai, he would have to approach Abram according to proper order. And Abram reasoned thus: the minds of suitors would be inflamed if they were brought forward as though they were to deal with a brother, so that in the meantime their minds would cool more than if, carried off by a single impulse by the beauty of Sarai, they believed that they would have a matter with her husband. For it is certain, as is commonly said, that those first impulses are least of all in men's power. But if Abram thought in this way, he did not think in bad faith, but in weak faith, who mixed the prudence of the flesh into this action for the sake of safeguarding his life.

units.la: Ex antecedenti consilio sequitur facti narratio, v.15. nempe quod Principes Pharaonis formam Sarai obseruauerunt: quod vt assentato-res aulici eam laudauerunt apud Pharaonem suis lenociniis: postremò quod effecerunt vt raperetur & perduceretur in Pharaonis domum, vt impia & inhumana ipsorum officia iniustum adulterium sequeretur: cuius lenocinij & raptus humanam curationem Pharao sibi adhibitu-rus esse videbatur, si ob causam Sarai Abramo bene faceret, vt vers. 16. exponitur. Ex hoc autem facto triplex euentus consequutus esse di-citur ad finem vsque capitis. Primus, quòd Iehoua Pharaonem familiamque affecit plagis grauissimis, quæ facti conscientiam ipsis excita-rent; Pharaonem, quia adulterium moliebatur: domum, quia hi adul-terio ministrauerant, illi contagione eius inficiebantur, quâ rē impu-nè abire noluit iustitia Dei. Secundus euentus est, quòd ex facti con-scientia Pharao ad emendationem illius adductus est, & expostulauit cum Abramo velut teste resipiscentiæ; cuius expostulationis partes duæ sunt, excusatio, & conclusio. Ad excusationem hæc membra per-tinent; primùm, quòd nulla causa exstet propter quam sic fieri ab Abramo oportuerit: secundò, quòd etiam nulla de causa æquum fuerit dissimulare Abramum hanc vxorem ipsius esse; quod vinculum tan-tam habet necessitudinem vt eidem humana cætera æquum sit cede-re. Tertiò quòd sororem suam sit professus, ex quo legitimū fore con-iugium concubitúmque Pharao putauerit. Conclusio verò sub finem 19. versus, sententia est, qua Abram & vxor dimittuntur. Huius rei ex-sequutionem vlt. versu exponit Moses, cùm narrat primùm homines constitutos & mandata illis de Abramo fuisse data: secundò, eos ex mandato Abramum, Sarain, Lotū, & quicquid habebant ex Ægypto indemnes dedaxisse, comprehensis etiam donatiuis illis Pharaonis de quibus vers.16. dictum est, quia quod faciebat male Pharao, illud bene præstabat Deus, Abramum de bonis Ægypti locupletans, ex promissione supra principio cap. benedicam tibi.
units.tr: From the preceding counsel follows the narrative of the deed, v.15: namely, that the princes of Pharaoh observed the beauty of Sarai; that, like courtiers flattering, they praised her before Pharaoh with their enticements; and finally that they brought it about that she was taken and brought into Pharaoh's house, so that their impious and inhuman services would be followed by unjust adultery. By this enticement and abduction Pharaoh seemed about to apply a human remedy to himself, if for Sarai's sake he dealt well with Abram, as is set out in v.16. From this deed, it is said, a threefold outcome followed, to the end of the chapter. The first is that Jehovah afflicted Pharaoh and his household with very grievous plagues, which would stir in them a consciousness of the deed: Pharaoh, because he was plotting adultery; the household, because they had served the adultery, and they were infected by its contagion, which the justice of God was unwilling to let go unpunished. The second outcome is that, from the consciousness of the deed, Pharaoh was brought to amendment and expostulated with Abram as a witness of his repentance. This expostulation has two parts, excuse and conclusion. The following members pertain to the excuse: first, that there is no cause for which Abram ought to have acted thus; second, that there was no cause for which it was fair for Abram to conceal that she is his wife, a bond of such necessity that all other human ties ought fairly to yield to it; third, that he professed that she was his sister, from which Pharaoh thought a lawful marriage and cohabitation would follow. The conclusion, however, at the end of v.19, is the sentence by which Abram and his wife are dismissed. Moses sets out the execution of this in the last verse, when he narrates, first, that men were appointed and that commands concerning Abram were given to them; second, that they, by command, sent Abram, Sarai, Lot, and whatever they had from Egypt away unharmed, including also those gifts of Pharaoh of which it was said in v.16, because what Pharaoh did badly, God did well, enriching Abram from the goods of Egypt, in accordance with the promise above at the beginning of chapter 12, I will bless you.

units.la: CAPITIS XIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER XIII

units.la: HVIVS capitis summa est: Abramum fretum Dei promissionibus & vocatione, in cultu Dei vocantis se occupavisse, difficultates quib. premebatur pie & prudenter curavisse, denique singularibus Dei revelationibus consolationem in omni angustia sua percepisse. Tres itaque sunt partes huius capitis: Prima de officio praestito in cultu Dei & vocationis obsequio per fidem, quatuor verf. Secunda, de difficultatibus quas expertus est & curavit idem, inde ad v. usque 13. ultima vero de revelatione tertia, qua Deus Abramum consolatus est & confirmavit, usque ad finem cap. Officium fidei in vocatione persequenda & colendo Deo, principio designatur: Primum eo quod In Cena-haneam per meridianum tractum illius dicitur revenisse, v.1. & ita benedictionem Dei opum singulari accumulatione expertus esse, ex promissione supra cap. praeced. v. 16. Secundo quod in ea perlustratione terrae venit ad altare suum, & nomen Domini invocavit, v.3. & 4. Quae membra exposuimus supra cap. 12. v. 7. & 8. Secundus locus capitis ordinem historicum accuratius persequitur. Nam primum causa sive occasio difficultatum quas experiebatur Abram, exponitur vers.5. & duobus seqq. Secundo consilium, v.8. & 9. Tertio factum, v.10. & tribus seqq. Postremo autem eventus, cuius historiam tertio huius cap. loco deputabimus. Occasionum sive causarum quae Abramum pressisse dicuntur tria sunt genera: Primum est quod aeque Loto atque ipsi magnus erat numerus rei pecuariae, adeo ut simul eodem loco commode versari non possent, v.6. Secunda occasio fuit, quod ex illa incommoditate lites domesticae inter huius & illius pastores excitabantur, intestinaque odia. Tertia denique, quod foris peregrinabantur apud vicinos pecore item abundantes, impios & adversarios, a quibus illi amplius quotidie premebantur, v.7. Ex his incommodis consilium ortum est v.8. & 9. Cuius consilij partes duae sunt: Prima, deprecatio mali, v.8. Secunda, propositio modi quo curandum esse malum videbatur, vers.9. In mali urgentis deprecatione Abram duabus partibus usus est: primum enim deprecatur duplex malum: unum praevisum, alterum praesens: ex quo futurum fuisset ut alterum malum, nisi tempestivè prospiceretur, ipsos infestaret. Praevisum malum deprecatur his verbis, Ne quaso esto contentio, &c. Praesens malum deprecatur illis, Ne esto inter pastores. Nam providebat Abram facile ex domesticorũ rixis etiã dominorũ animos inflãmari, nisi prudẽtia & pietate caueatur. Deprecationis causa est, quia ⊃ iri fratres siue agnati fumus, quos neq; pietas, neq; ius naturæ, tum cōmune inter homines, tũ singulare necessitudinis, neq; infidelium vicinorū exemplū patiebatur inter se digladiari. Propositio consilij v.9. sapientissimè ab Abramo facta est, cū primum optione, quamuis ætate maior, attribuit Loto his verbis, Nonne tota terra tibi est expolita ? Nimirum à me, vel quantum ad me attinet : deinde cum seperationem consulit, separa te: Tertio quum spondet se acquieturum esse optioni Loti, & vtramuis partem agri elegerit Lotus, se in alteram vltro abiturum. Ex consilio sequitur factum. Nam & Lot elegisse dicitur, & seperatio facta esse, & Abram electioni Loti acquieuisse. In electione Loti proponuntur duo: Vnum, quòd oculos suos consuluisse dicitur, & ex eis de eligendo agro iudicasse, v. 10 : Alterum, quòd eo consilio planitiem illam secundum Iardenem elegit, quæ ad orientem spectabat, v.11. Electionis iudicio oculorum facţ causa adfertur agri commoditas, fertilitas, atque amœnitas. commoditas, quòd irriguus esset; fertilitas amœnitásque, quòd cum horto Iehouæ, de quo supra c.2. & cū Ægypto quam pinguefacit Nilus comparandus. Hinc sequitur seperatio, proficiscente versus orientem Loto. Abrami verò consensus atque facilitas in optione ista acquiescentis ostenditur v.12. Abram(inquit Moses) consedit in terra Cenahanei, Lot vero, annuente facile Abramo, incoluit ciuitates planiciei illius, &c. Hic verò est obseruadum propter historiam cap.19. non male notari siue auaritiam, siue imprudentiam dicamus, Loti, qui tanti fecit commoda rei familiaris, vt ingenium regionis solum, non autem incolarum respexerit cū ad Sedomum transmigraret : cum tamen viri pij officium sit illud, vt pium vicinum procuret : Boni officium, vt vicinum bonum. Hoc autem scriptura notat his verbis, Tentoria fixit Lot Sedomum vsque. Deinde v.13. Quamuis Sedomita mali & peccatores essent in Iehouam valde. De hac autem loquutione supra in cap. 10. satis diximus. Sequitur euentus, qui tertius est locus huius capitis : nempe tertia reuelatio, qua Deus Abramum coram ex istis difficultatibus consolatus est, & in fide promissionum Dei officioque confirmauit. Cuius rei circumstantia notanda est, Posteaquam Lot ab Abramo separatus esset, id est, ab eo in cuius consuetudine promissionibus Dei communicauerat. Huius reuelationis narratio, versibus quatuor; euentus vltimo proponitur. Reuelationis summa v.14. proponitur symbolicè his verbis, attolle oculos tuos & respice, &c. q.d. Oculis collustra & fide percipe, quamuis nondum in possessionem mittaris : deinde verò huius summæ reuelationis membra ponuntur duo ex ordine : promissio, v.15. & seq. mandatum, v.17. Promissionis loci duo sunt: prior, de hæreditaria promissione futura illius terræ, v.15: posterior de innumerabili hæredum propagatione, quam ex hypothesi ἀδωάτῳ[?] Deus amplificat v. 16. Mandati summa est, vt terram illam liberè obeat Abram ex fiducia percepta donationis diuinæ, v.17. Quam promissionem mandatúmque fide amplexus Abram dicitur, & regionem peruasisse certa fiducia fretus promissionum vocantis Dei; & cultum Dei professus esse, quæ professio synecdochicè institutione altaris figuratur.
units.tr: The sum of this chapter is that Abram, relying on the promises and the calling of God, occupied himself in the worship of God who called him, prudently and piously took care of the difficulties by which he was pressed, and finally received consolation in all his distress through singular revelations of God. There are therefore three parts of this chapter. The first, concerning the duty performed in the worship of God and obedience to the calling through faith, is vv.1–4. The second, concerning the difficulties which he experienced and which he also dealt with, runs from there to v.13. The last, concerning the third revelation, by which God consoled and confirmed Abram, runs to the end of the chapter. The duty of faith in pursuing the calling and in worshipping God is indicated at the beginning. First, in that he is said to have returned into Canaan, through the southern tract of it, v.1, and so to have experienced the blessing of God in his wealth with singular increase, from the promise in the preceding chapter, v.16. Second, that in that survey of the land he came to his altar and invoked the name of the Lord, vv.3 and 4. These members we have explained above in chapter 12, vv.7 and 8. The second part of the chapter follows the historical order more closely. For first the cause or occasion of the difficulties which Abram experienced is set out in v.5 and the two following verses; second, the counsel, vv.8 and 9; third, the deed, v.10 and the three following verses; last, the outcome, whose history we shall treat in the third place of this chapter. There are three kinds of occasions or causes which are said to have pressed upon Abram. The first is that the number of his livestock was as great as that of Lot, so that they could not conveniently dwell together in the same place, v.6. The second occasion was that from this inconvenience domestic quarrels arose between the shepherds of this one and of that one, and internal hatreds. The third, finally, was that they wandered abroad among neighbours who were likewise rich in flocks, impious and adversaries, by whom they were pressed more and more every day, v.7. From these inconveniences the counsel arose, vv.8 and 9. This counsel has two parts. The first is the deprecation of evil, v.8; the second is the proposal of the manner by which the evil seemed to be dealt with, v.9. In deprecating the pressing evil, Abram used two parts, for he deprecates a twofold evil: one foreseen, the other present. From the one, the other evil would have followed, which, unless it were timely foreseen, would have harassed them. He deprecates the foreseen evil in these words, Let there be, I pray, no contention, etc. He deprecates the present evil in these words, Let there be no strife between the shepherds. For Abram foresaw that from quarrels among household servants the minds of the masters too would easily be inflamed, unless it were guarded against by prudence and piety. The reason for the deprecation is that we are brothers or kinsmen, whom neither piety nor the law of nature, nor the common bond among men, nor the particular bond of kinship, nor the example of the neighbouring unbelievers, permitted to fight among themselves. The proposal of the counsel in v.9 was most wisely made by Abram, when first he gave Lot the choice, though he was older in age, in these words, Is not the whole land before you?, that is, by my own permission, or so far as it lies with me. Then he proposes separation, separate yourself. Third, he promises that he will acquiesce in Lot's choice, and that whichever part of the land Lot chooses, he himself will go willingly into the other. The deed follows the counsel. For Lot is said to have chosen, and the separation was made, and Abram acquiesced in Lot's choice. In Lot's choice two things are set forth. One is that he is said to have consulted his eyes and to have judged from them about which land to choose, v.10. The other is that by this counsel he chose that plain along the Jordan, which faced towards the east, v.11. The commodity of the land, its fertility and pleasantness, are brought forward as the cause of the judgement of the eyes in the choice: its commodity, because it was well watered; its fertility and pleasantness, because it was to be compared with the garden of Jehovah, of which above in chapter 2, and with Egypt, which the Nile makes fat. Hence follows the separation, Lot setting out towards the east. Abram's consent and ease in accepting this choice is shown in v.12: Abram, says Moses, settled in the land of Canaan, but Lot, Abram readily assenting, dwelt in the cities of that plain, etc. Here it must be observed, on account of the history in chapter 19, that we may fairly remark upon Lot, whether we call it avarice or imprudence, who valued the advantages of his household property so highly that, when he migrated to Sodom, he regarded the nature of the region and not the character of its inhabitants. Yet it is the duty of a pious man to provide for a pious neighbour, and of a good man to provide for a good neighbour. Scripture notes this in these words, Lot pitched his tents as far as Sodom. Then in v.13, although the men of Sodom were evil and great sinners against Jehovah. We have said enough about this manner of speaking above in chapter 10. There follows the outcome, which is the third part of this chapter: namely, the third revelation, by which God consoled Abram, now, out of these difficulties, and confirmed him in faith in the promises of God and in his duty. The circumstance of this matter is to be noted: after Lot had been separated from Abram, that is, from him with whom he had shared the promises of God. The narrative of this revelation is in four verses; the outcome is set forth last. The sum of the revelation is set forth symbolically in v.14 in these words, lift up your eyes and look, etc., as if to say: survey with your eyes and perceive by faith, although you are not yet put into possession. Then two members of this sum of the revelation are set down in order: the promise, v.15 and following, and the command, v.17. There are two parts of the promise: the first concerns the future hereditary promise of that land, v.15; the second concerns the innumerable propagation of his heirs, which God amplifies from a hypothesis (v.16), [ἀδωάτῳ?]. The sum of the command is that Abram should freely go through that land, trusting in the divine gift received, v.17. Abram is said to have embraced this promise and command in faith, and to have taken possession of the region, relying on the firm trust in the promises of the calling God, and to have professed the worship of God, which profession is figuratively expressed, by synecdoche, in the establishment of an altar.
