units.la: OTUM hoc caput est ad sequentem locum promissionum Dei μεταβατικόν, nempe de hæredibus quos gratiosè Deus Abramo erat suppeditaturus de semine ipsius. Nam re quidem ipsa ad argumentum antecedens promissionum pertinet, vt intelligamus hæreditatem Abramo promissam fuisse, iam tum fultam præsidio Dei, & ab aliena omni violentia vindicatam, quibus in rebus summa huius capitis posita est. Sed eo transitum parat ad sequentem locum, quòd occasionem ostendit Moses cur ad quartam reuelationem, quæ sequente capite exponitur, Deus transierit. Summa igitur est, hæreditatem quam Abramo Deus promiserat, quamuis ab impiis scelera-tisque incolis possessam & ab exteris oppressam, tum gratiosè à Deo vindicatam esse, & vires Abramo inditas, vt tum amicos hæreditatis eiusdem confortes; tum hæreditatem ipsam ab aliena iniuria vindicaret: quod beneficium Dei omnibus sanctificationis officiis religiosè Abram professus est. Itaq; duę sunt huius capitis partes: prior, qua narratur historia singularis illius liberationis, ad v.vsque 17: posterior, qua pietas iustitiáque Abrami minimè insolescentis ex parta victoria ostenditur, inde ad finem capitis. Liberationis quam Deus Loto & regioni attulit Abrami opera, primùm occasiones exponunrur ad v. vsque 13. deinde modus & argumentum liberationis exponitur, seqq. Occasiones quæ liberationis opus antecesserunt, narrantur tribus versibus: deinde verò speciatim exponuntur. Occasio enim proxima hæc fuisse dicitur, quòd Reges quatuor exteri, vers.1. bello petiuerunt regulos quinque in Cenahanea degentes, vers.2. Ac proinde conserendo prælio vltro citróque sese comparauerunt in loco, qui circumscribitur antiqua & noua ipsius appellatione, v.3. Loci antiquá fuit appellatio vallis Sidimorum, id est, arualis & abundans feracæ gleba, quam propter foli pingue densitatémque occari op-portebat diligentissimé. Noua appellatio est mare salis. Mare autem est quoduis amplū aquarum conceptaculum apud Hebræos, vt Mo-ses Gen. 1. demóstrauit. Salis siue salsum eo appellatur, quòd totus il-le lacus spatiúmque eius factum est infertile, tamquā si terra salsugi-nosa esset, ac nihil amplius præ maledictione Dei ferret. Nam solum infertile Hebrei salsum appellant. Lacum vero illum neque piscium, neque fructuum, neque rei vllius vtilis feracem esse præter quàm asphalti, omnes historiæ consentiunt: Et quamuis exstent arborum species in oculis omnium aspectabiles, tamen earum fructum ina-nem adeóque fœtidum existere, vtcumque aspectu speciosissimum. Hic lacus alioquin Asphaltites à Geographis, quia asphaltū gignit, aut etiam mare mortuum, quia nihil viuum ferre potest, appella-tur. Occasionum, quas summatim tribus versibus perstrinxit Mo-ses, duo sunt genera: nam aliæ sunt remotæ & ad exteros perti-nentes, aliæ vero propinquæ ad familiam sanctam: quarum prio-res ad vers. vsque 11. Posterior, vers. 11. & 12. proponitur. Prio-rum occasionum summa est, quòd Cedorlahomer Rex Assyrio-rum tractum illum ante subiugauisset & annos 12. obtinuisset; pro vt tyrannis nunquam satis esse potest, adeò inexplebilis est ambi-tio eorum & auaritia: tum quòd illi ex mollitie tyranni istius ani-mos sumentes anno 13. cum finitimis rebellassent, vers. 4. Tertio quòd rebellionis istius causa indignatus Cedorlahomer adiunctis federatorum copiis ad rebelles domandos reuertisset, prout vers. 5. & duobus seqq.exponitur: qua in reuersione siue expeditione obser-uandum illud est, tyrannum strategemate militari vsum, vt circum-stantes regiones omnes trans Iardenem sitas ante sibi adiungeret, quàm eum transmitteret Regulis istis quatuor debellandis. Quapro-pter ordine narratur illius expeditio in hunc modum: quòd primùm tractu Bascanis subiecit sibi, vbi erant Gigantes illi qui Aschtharotas incolebant, in quibus Iuppiter cornutus arietis specie (vt in Libya) colebatur: secundò, quòd inde petens Meridiem versus Suseos in Hamo, quę regio Hammonitarum est, profligauit: tertiò, quòd Emæos in planitie ad Kiriathajima, qui post Moabitarum ager fuit, subie-cit sibi, v. 5: quartò, quòd Choræos incolentes tractum Sehiris siue Edomeæ (vt postea dicta est) ad extremos vsque terminos illius, qui ad desertum Paranis mari rubro coniunctum pertinent, v. 6. Tum quòd à Meridiano tractu Aquilonem versus reflectentes Arabas illos subegerunt, qui inde ad Kadeschum habebant sedes: deinde, quòd omnes incolas perdiderunt montani illius tractus quem post obti-nuerunt. [?]uerunt Amalekitæ: Postremò, quòd etiam {?}Amorrhæos pessumde-derunt qui ad Engadda habitabant: quibus regionibus in ambitum occupatis fieri non poterat vt hi quatuor reguli commodè ex manibus tyranni illius effugerent, v. 7. Quartus occasionum locus est, quòd reguli isti quatuor locorum peritiæ confidentes, ad conferendum prælium sibi delegerunt campum, quem suis copiis vtilem propter peritiam, hostilibus damnosum propter imperitiam statuebant[?], vers. 8. & 9. Cuius loci opportunitas atque commoditas principio vers. 10. exponitur: nempe quòd campus ille siue conuallis fossis bituminis abundaret, id est, ex quibus effodiebatur bitumen; quarum commoditate tum sibi perfugium fore suisque considebant, tum hostibus siue victoribus siue victis periculum: victoribus quia ex illis ipsis fossis ferme ab inermibus poterant debellari: victis, quia in præcipite fuga erant eò turmatim corruituri: postremò quòd prælio commisso fugientes reguli in illud perfugium fossarum sese receperunt, reliquæ copiæ in montana, vers. 10. Hinc autem sequitur alter occasionum locus: nempe quòd Reges illi exteri victoria parta, depositá persequendi fugitiuos molestia, quæ cum periculo coniuncta foret, in prædam inuolauerunt, & tum facultates atque commeatum regulorum ceperunt sibi atque auexerunt, tum verò Lotum, agnatum Abrami, qui inter Sedomitas agebat in agro ipsorum, cum omnibus illius facultatibus, quasi mancipatum iure belli, abduxerunt, vers. 12. Sequuntur iam res Abrami gestæ: Quarum ordo à Mose hoc pacto instituitur: Primum, quòd ex profugo cognouit omnia diligentissime ipse cum sederatis suis, idest, tum cladem à Loto acceptam, tum iter à regibus institutum, vers. 13: Deinde quòd re optimè cognita informauit suos expeditionem duce Abramo suscepturos, primùm de officio pietatis in agnatum, iustitia causæ suæ, & fide certissima in promissiones Dei, eosdémque armis instruxit, & ordinem docuit in itinere & impressione obseruandum: Tertiò quòd sic instructis copiis persequuntur est Danem usque, qui locus dicebatur tum Leschen[?], post Cæsarea Paneadis: Quartò quòd explorata hostium statione copias suas de nocte aduersus inopinantes duxit, vt eos commodius opprimeret: qua arte cæsi hostes atque fugati sunt. Postremò quòd illos in fugam versos quàm longissimè est persequutus, nempe ad oppidum usque Chobam non procul Damasco, quod oppidum Syra adiectione facta post à Geographis Opotos dictum est. His rebus gestis subiicitur vsus victoriæ moderatissimus reliquo capite, index pietatis, humanitatis, iustitiæ, temperantiæ, & fortitudinis sanctissimæ,qua Abram in rebus prosperis ac adversis utebatur. Demonstrātur ista tribus historiis ex illa insigni victoria consequutis,quæ ad secundum capitis locum pertinent.Hic postremus locus ergo sequitur deinceps, ut ante distinximus, qui totus consumitur in narratione usus victoriæ ante à Deo acceptæ. Hac itaque narratione tria documenta usus illius adseruntur. Primum est, quòd Abram accepta victoria & receptis rebus omnibus quas Reges secum exportauerant, non in convivis aut festivitatibus res acceptas occupauit, sed pie & sanctè de omnibus eò reportandis unde ablata erant cogitauit, v.16: Secundum,quòd gratulationem,beneficium,benedictionemque sibi à Malcitzedeko oblatam sic accepit utDeo pro victoria parta oblatis decimis gratias ageret,inde à v.20 : Tertium documentum est quòd rem alienam iure belli à se receptam ne vltro quidem à Domino oblatam voluit sibi mancipare, sed Deo gloriam, sibi famam integram, restitutis rebus omnibus conseruare, v.21. ad finem. In primo documento duo sunt membra : Unum, quòd omnium possessiones ablatas dicitur reduxisse,v.16: Alterum , quòd speciatim Loti agnati sui, personarum, rerúmque ad eum pertinentium curam dicitur habuisse, ut nihil agnato suo,tamquam earumdem promissionem consorti,deperiret.Sic exemplo præstitit quod Paulus præcipit documento Gal. 6. omnibus benefacite, maximè verò iis qui domestici sunt fidei. Quod autem postea v.17. interseritur historia de Rege Sedomi obuiam Abramo præcedente,quæ historia postea intercisa videtur esse narratione nova de Malcitzedeko,deinde verò ad eam reuerti v.21.Id nō temere à Mose factum est.Nam propterea versum hunc anteponi oportuit, ut utrumque simul intelligeretur; tum Sedomi Regem eodem loci Abramo occurrisse ubi Malcitzedek conuivio Abramum erat excepturus , testémque fuisse totius huius historiæ: Tum verò rem illam ab Abramo gestam occasioni fuisse Regi Sedomi, ut cum Abramo pacisci quodammodo cuperet. Nam dicitur Rex Sedomi parta ab Abramo victoria obuiam ipsi occurrisse in conuallem Schaue , quæ iam dicitur conuallis Regis, Erat autem convallis Regis proxima Ieruschalaimis, ut ex 2. Sam. historia de Absalomo constat:ac proinde facilè ex eo colligitur Malcitzedekum, ut prudentem Regem, non intromisisse Abramum copiasq; ipsius in suum opidum, maximè parta victoria qua miles ferè insolescit ( id enim non fuisset hominis politici ) sed Abramo diem locúmque conuivio dixisse in eadem conualle; Quod ubi resciuit Rex Sedomi, eodem ad excipiendum salutatione Abramum convenisse. In secundo huius historiæ loco narrantur primùm officium Malcitzedeki in Abramum mum,quòd panem vinúmque protulerit,id est conuiuio regifico ipsum & copias ipsius exceperit, v.18. Secundò, quòd gratulatus Abramo ipsi benedixerit, tum quòd benedixit ei nomine Dei Opt. Max.v.19. Tum quòd Deo optimo Max. de ante attributa victoria solemniter gratias egit, v.20. Ad utrumque officium pertinent duo elogia, quæ de Malcitzedeko à Mose prædicantur: unum, quòd Rex Salemi esset, id est, Jeruschalimorum. (Sic enim prius appellata sunt) ac proinde commodis abundauit quibus Abramum regaliter exciperet. Alterum, quòd Sacerdos fuit Dei fortis excelsi,ac proinde, auctoritatem pro vocatione habuit benedicendi Abramo Dei ipsius verbis. Hinc autem tertius locus omnino sequitur, quòd Abram vicissim Deo & Malcitzedeko Regi gratias quas potuit, habuit decimis oblatis de o-mnibus, id est, de omnibus spoliis rebúsque bello captis decimas, quas sibi iure poterat vindicare, nulla re sibi iure mancipij conseruata, consecrauit Domino, dedítque sacerdoti illius. Atque hæc causa fuit, cur Rex Sedomi putans sibi mancipio vindicare omnia, pacisci cum eo voluit, ut post dicturi sumus. Antequam verò eò descendimus, de Malcitzedeko pauca dicenda sunt. Interpretatur copiosè historiam hanc auctor ad Heb. cap. 7. adductus auctoritate Dauidis Psalm. 110. Quæ autem eo loco ab Apostolo dicuntur nolumus adferre: tantum monebimus ad intelligentiam illius typi & accommodationis eius, duo maximè observanda esse: nempe tum in iis quæ dicuntur à Mose, tum verò in iis quæ reticentur constitui typum. In iis quæ dicuntur: ut cùm dicitur Malcitzedek, id est, Rex iustitiæ; Rex Salem, id est, pacis sacerdos fuisse Dei altissimi, benedixisse Abramo, & decimas accepisse, in quibus omnibus typus Christi expressus observandus est. In iis verò quæ reticentur: ut cum auctore Dei Spiritu neque parentum, neque principij vitæ, neque finis vitæ, neque genealogiæ vlla vsquam inuenitur mentio: qui narrationis modus eoipso typicus fuit per Spiritum Dei, ut Dominum nostrum & Seruatorem Christum idem Spiritus ostenderet sine Patre secundum humanitatem, sine matre secundum personam diuinam, & sine genealogia, & sine principio aut fine vitæ exstitisse. Atque hæc ratio est cur Psalm. 110. Deus iurat Christum sacerdotem esse in æternum Haldibrathi, id est, ad verbum, secundum narrationem meam Malcitzedeki, id est, de Malcitzedeko, siue [illegible, ~6 letters], id est, prout narratio fuit à Mose ordinata: ut ea loquutione psaltes demonstraret non solùm ea quæ dicuntur sed etiâ quæ reticentur de Malcitzedeko typum Christi iam olim habuisse. Tertium documentum est bimembre: nam primùm conditio à Rege Sedomi Abramo oblata ostenditur, verf. 21. Secundò religio summa Abrami, tum in rebus alienis Domino suo restituendis, tum in aliena opera ex æquo bono compensanda. Conditio oblata hæc fuisse dicitur, vt Abram Regi Sedomi animas, id est personas, redderet, possessiones reliquas receptas seruaret sibi: sic enim statuebat Rex Sedomi, iure gentium nihil sibi ab Abramo ereptum esse, sed ex eo iure Abramum Dominum factum esse rerum quas bello parauerat, ac proinde ex illo iure gentium cogitabat gratiam sibi facturum Abramum, fi vel personas solùm recuperaret beneficio eius. Itaque videmus aliud esse ius gentium à naturali, quod tamen interdum à Iurisconsultis confunditur. Abram verò non ex illo iure gentium, sed ex integro naturali iure statuebat, nihil alienum eo bello receptum ad fe pertinere, non magis quàm fiquis rem vi à prædone, aut clam à fure sublatam suam esse affirmaret, eo quòd eam prædoni aut furi extorsisset. Respondit itaque Abram conditioni illi à Rege Sedomi oblatæ, primùm religioso iureiurando, verf. 22. Secundò summa recusatione rei vel minimæ, ne Dei gloria aut existimatio Abrami hac specie minueretur, verf. 23. Tertiò prudenter & pie quæ ad victum mercedémque operarum pertinebant excipit, verf. vltimo. Quemadmodum æquum est, vt qui regioni seruiunt ex regione viuant: ac propterea de suis ostendit liberaliter fe acquiescere & solo victu contentum esse, de sederatis autem fe velle, vt illis sua merces præter victum ex spoliorum parte tribuatur. Vnum restat, quod imperiti fortasse speciem contradictionis habere cogitauerint, nisi commodè ex Mosis ipsius verbis & natura rei dissoluatur. Nam dicitur verf. 20. Abram decimas Malcitzedeko dedifle de omnibus, putà quæ recuperauerat cæsis bello regibus: sub finem verò Abram cum religione iurisiurandi testatur fe ne minimam quidem rem vllam, quæ aliena fit, in rem suam versurum esse, & concludens verf. vltimo ait, nihil penes me futurum est earum rerum. Nam fi religio fuit Abramo quicquam rei alienæ sibi vsurpare, non videtur fuisse æquius, vt de re quâ alienam agnoscit, decimas Deo traderet vel Malcitzedeko in manum. fi enim res aliena fuit, non potuit dare: sin ipsius, potuit & sibi mancipare. Refponfio est triplex ad dirimendam hanc contradictionis speciem adhibenda. Primùm enim soluitur ex facto; fecundò ex fine vel consilio Abrami: tertiò denique ex rei ipsius æquitate atque pietate. Ex facto, quia aliud est Abramum sibi aliquid de spoliis feruare fi dixeris (quod iure belli poterat.) Aliud, fi decimas Deo dare Eucharisticas, fiue opima (vt vocant) spolia. Ex fine, quia etsi iure sibi aliquid etiam prioribus Dominis annuentibus poterat retinere, tamen finis alius Abramo fuit, cum decimas consecraret Deo: quod humano iure ex illis spoliis potuit, & religione diuina debuit. Alius autem quòd sibi eo consilio nihil seruatum voluit, ne sanctum Dei nomen ab exteris blasphemaretur, aut ipsa Abrami existimatio laboraret, tamquam si ex alieno dispendio procurauisset sua compendia, quia sic voluit liberalitate exteris pietatem, iustitiam, veritatemque commendare. Ex pietatis denique officio, quia gentes ipsæ inde à principio naturalem hanc persuasionem habuerunt, ex amplissimis Dei beneficiis gratias Deo esse agendas, eucharisteriis. Quòd si Abram omnia, etiam non exceptis decimis, restituisset in manum priorum dominorum, illi infideles idolis suis sacrificauissent, & attribuissent eis beneficia quæ Deus in Abramum ex promissione, & in ipsos Abrami causa contulerat. Pie itaque & sancte Abram partem Deo dicatam excepit ipse, qui plura poterat excipere; Deúmque ex officio hac parte excepta muneratus est. Nam cum etiam iuste & honeste sibi suisque mercedem seruare potuisset, ea liberaliter cesserat: tantum quod Deo debebatur, de cuius pietate nihil voluit aut potuit cedere, illud ex pietatis & religionis officio prælibauit(siue præcerpsit.)
units.tr: This chapter is a transition to the following passage of God's promises, namely concerning the heirs whom God was graciously going to give Abram from his seed. In fact it belongs to the preceding argument about the promises, so that we understand that the inheritance promised to Abram was already then upheld by the protection of God and defended from every foreign violence; and this is the chief concern of this chapter. But it also prepares the transition to the next passage, since Moses shows the occasion for God's passing on to the fourth revelation, which is set out in the following chapter. The summary, then, is this: the inheritance which God had promised to Abram, although it was held by impious and wicked inhabitants and oppressed by foreigners, was then graciously vindicated by God, and strength was given to Abram both to protect his kinsmen, the companions of that inheritance, and to defend the inheritance itself against foreign injury. Abram devoutly acknowledged this benefit of God by all the duties of sanctification. There are therefore two parts of this chapter: the first, which narrates the history of that singular deliverance, runs to verse 17; the second, which shows the piety and righteousness of Abram, who was in no way made proud by the victory won, runs from there to the end of the chapter. Of the deliverance which God brought to Lot and to the region through Abram's work, the occasions are first set out, to verse 13; then the manner and the course of the deliverance are set out, from verse 14 onward. The occasions which preceded the deliverance are narrated in three verses, and then they are set out one by one. The proximate occasion is said to have been this: four foreign kings made war (verse 1) on five petty kings who dwelt in Canaan (verse 2), and so they prepared themselves for battle on both sides in a place which is marked by its old and new names (verse 3). The old name of the place was the vale of Siddim, that is, a level and abundant field of fertile soil, which had to be cultivated with the greatest care because of the richness and density of the soil. The new name is the Salt Sea. Among the Hebrews a sea is any large receptacle of waters, as Moses showed in Genesis 1. It is called salt, or salty, because that whole lake and its surroundings became barren, as if the land were full of salt, and bore nothing further under the curse of God. For the Hebrews call barren soil salty. All the histories agree that this lake produces no fish, no fruit, and nothing useful, except asphalt; and although there are kinds of trees visible to everyone's eyes, their fruit is nonetheless empty and even foul, however lovely it looks. This lake is otherwise called Asphaltites by the geographers, because it produces asphalt, or also the Dead Sea, because it can bear nothing living. There are two kinds of occasions, which Moses touched on briefly in three verses: some are remote and pertain to outsiders, others are near and pertain to the holy family. The former are set out up to verse 11; the latter are proposed in verses 11 and 12. The sum of the former occasions is this: Chedorlaomer, king of the Assyrians, had earlier subjugated that region and held it for twelve years. Such is the nature of tyranny: it is never satisfied, so insatiable are their ambition and avarice. Then, in the thirteenth year, the people, taking heart from the softness of that tyrant, rebelled together with their neighbours (verse 4). Third, Chedorlaomer, angered by this rebellion, returned with the forces of his confederates to subdue the rebels, as is set out in verse 5 and the two that follow. In this return, or expedition, it must be noted that the tyrant used a military stratagem: he first brought under his power all the surrounding regions beyond the Jordan, before sending his forces against those four kings. Accordingly, his expedition is narrated in this order: first, he subjected to himself the district of Bashan, where those giants lived who dwelt in Ashtaroth, among whom Jupiter Ammon was worshipped in the form of a horned ram, as in Libya; second, going from there towards the south, he struck down the Zuzim in Ham, which is the land of the Ammonites; third, he subjected to himself the Emim in the plain at Kiriathaim, which afterwards became the territory of the Moabites (verse 5); fourth, he subdued the Horites, who inhabited the region of Seir, or Edom, as it was later called, to its farthest limits, which lie toward the wilderness of Paran, joined to the Red Sea (verse 6). Then, turning from the southern region northward, they subdued those Arabs who had their dwellings from there at Kadesh; next, the mountain dwellers of that region, which they afterwards held, were all destroyed. The Amalekites were also... and finally they also destroyed the Amorites who dwelt at Hazezon-tamar, so that, with the regions thus occupied on every side, it was impossible for those four petty kings to escape easily from the hands of that tyrant (verse 7). The fourth occasion is this: these petty kings, trusting in their knowledge of the terrain, chose for themselves a field for the battle, which they judged useful to their own forces because of their skill, and damaging to the enemy because of their lack of skill (verses 8 and 9). The suitability and convenience of that place are set out at the beginning of verse 10: namely, that the plain, or valley, abounded in pits of bitumen, that is, pits from which bitumen was dug. They relied on these pits for their convenience, both as a refuge for themselves and their people, and as a danger to the enemy, whether victors or vanquished: to the victors, because from those very pits they could be overcome almost without arms; to the vanquished, because in headlong flight they would fall into them in droves. Lastly, when the battle was joined, the fleeing kings withdrew into that refuge of the pits, while the remaining forces fled to the mountains (verse 10). From this follows the second place of occasions: namely, that those foreign kings, having won the victory and set aside the trouble of pursuing the fugitives, which would have been attended with danger, rushed upon the spoil. They took and carried off the goods and provisions of the petty kings, and then they also carried away Lot, the kinsman of Abram, who lived among the Sodomites on their land, together with all his possessions, as if he had been seized by the right of war (verse 12). Now follow the deeds of Abram. Moses arranges their order in this way. First, he learned everything most carefully from the fugitive, namely, he himself with his confederates learned both the disaster which Lot had suffered and the route the kings had taken (verse 13). Then, having well understood the situation, he instructed his men that they would undertake the expedition under Abram as leader: first on account of the duty of piety towards their kinsman, the justice of their cause, and the most certain faith in God's promises; and he armed them and taught them the order to be observed on the march and in the attack. Third, with the forces thus equipped, they pursued as far as Dan, a place then called Laish, afterwards Caesarea Philippi. Fourth, when the enemy's position had been discovered, he led his forces by night against the unsuspecting enemy, so that he might more conveniently overwhelm them; by this stratagem the enemy were slain and put to flight. Last, he pursued them in flight as far as possible, namely as far as the town of Hobah, not far from Damascus, which town, with a Syrian addition, was afterwards called Oposto by the geographers. With these deeds done, there follows in the rest of the chapter the most moderate use of victory, a sign of the most holy piety, humanity, justice, temperance and fortitude, which Abram showed in both prosperous and adverse circumstances. This is shown by three episodes that followed from that notable victory, which belong to the second part of the chapter. This last part therefore follows next, as we distinguished before, and it is wholly taken up with the narrative of the use of the victory previously received from God. In this narrative three lessons about its use are asserted. The first is that Abram, having received the victory and recovered all the goods which the kings had carried away with them, did not seize the things he had received at banquets or festivities, but devoutly and holily considered how all of them might be brought back to where they had been taken from (verse 16). The second is that he received the congratulation, the kindness and the blessing offered to him by Melchizedek in such a way that he gave thanks to God for the victory won, offering tithes, from verse 20 onward. The third lesson is that he was unwilling to make his own property a thing which he had received by right of war, even when it was offered to him by the Lord, and that he preserved for God the glory, and for himself an unblemished reputation, by restoring all the goods (verse 21 to the end). There are two parts in the first lesson: one, that he is said to have brought back the possessions of everyone who had been robbed (verse 16); the other, that he is said to have taken particular care of his kinsman Lot, of his persons and goods pertaining to him, so that nothing might perish for his kinsman, as a partner in the same promise. Thus by his example he did what Paul enjoins in Galatians 6: "Do good to all men, but especially to those who are of the household of faith." But the fact that afterwards, at verse 17, the history of the king of Sodom coming to meet Abram before is interposed, a history which afterwards seems to have been interrupted by a new narrative about Melchizedek, and then to return to it at verse 21, was not done by Moses without reason. For this verse had to be placed first, so that both could be understood together: that the king of Sodom met Abram at the same place where Melchizedek was going to receive Abram at a banquet, and was a witness to the whole of this history. Then also, that deed done by Abram gave occasion to the king of Sodom to wish, in some way, to make a bargain with Abram. For it is said that the king of Sodom, after the victory won by Abram, went out to meet him in the Vale of Shaveh, which is now called the King's Vale. Now the King's Vale was near Jerusalem, as is clear from the history of Absalom in 2 Samuel; and so from this it is easily gathered that Melchizedek, as a prudent king, did not admit Abram and his forces into his own town, especially after a victory, when soldiers are almost always inclined to arrogance (for this would not have been the act of a prudent man), but appointed a day and a place for a banquet with Abram in that same vale. When the king of Sodom learned of this, he came to that same place to greet Abram and receive him. In the second part of this history, first the office of Melchizedek towards Abram is narrated: that he brought out bread and wine, that is, he received Abram and his forces with a royal banquet (verse 18). Second, that, having congratulated Abram, he blessed him, both because he blessed him in the name of God Most High (verse 19), and because he solemnly gave thanks to God Most High for the victory previously granted (verse 20). Two epithets which Moses attributes to Melchizedek belong to these two offices: one, that he was king of Salem, that is, of Jerusalem (for it was called so earlier), and therefore abounded in the resources with which he might receive Abram in royal fashion; the other, that he was priest of God Most High, and therefore had the authority, by his office, to bless Abram in God's own words. From this the third point follows at once: that Abram, in return, gave thanks as far as he could to God and to King Melchizedek, and gave tithes of all, that is, of all the spoils and goods taken in war, of which he could justly claim the tithes, keeping nothing for himself by right of ownership; he consecrated them to the Lord and gave them to his priest. And this was the reason why the king of Sodom, thinking that he could claim everything for himself by right of possession, wished to make a bargain with him, as we shall say below. But before we come to that, a few things must be said about Melchizedek. The author expounds this history at length in Hebrews chapter 7, relying on the authority of David in Psalm 110. We do not wish to bring forward what the Apostle says in that place; we will only remind readers that, to understand that type and its application, two things especially must be observed: namely, that the type is established both in what is said by Moses and in what is passed over in silence. In what is said: as when Melchizedek is called "king of righteousness", "king of Salem, that is, of peace", "priest of the Most High God", who blessed Abram and received tithes, in all of which the type of Christ is to be observed as expressed. In what is passed over in silence: as when, the Spirit of God being the author, no mention is found anywhere of his parents, or of the beginning of his life, or of the end of his life, or of any genealogy; this manner of narration was typical by the Spirit of God, so that the same Spirit might show that our Lord and Saviour Christ, according to his humanity, was without a father, according to his divine person without a mother, and without genealogy, and without beginning or end of life. And this is the reason why in Psalm 110 God swears that Christ is a priest for ever, after the manner of Melchizedek, that is, word for word, according to my narration of Melchizedek, that is, concerning Melchizedek, or in the manner in which the account was arranged by Moses; so that by this expression the psalmist might show that not only what is said but also what is passed over in silence about Melchizedek had long before been a type of Christ. The third lesson has two parts: first, the condition offered to Abram by the king of Sodom is set out (verse 21); second, the supreme piety of Abram, both in restoring what belonged to others to his Lord and in compensating the labour of others with fair reward. This condition is said to have been offered in this form: that Abram should return the souls, that is, the persons, to the king of Sodom, and keep for himself the other goods received. For the king of Sodom reasoned that by the law of nations nothing had been taken from him by Abram, but that by that law Abram had become lord of the goods which he had gained in war; and therefore, by that law of nations, he thought Abram would be doing him a favour if he recovered even the persons alone by his kindness. So we see that the law of nations is one thing and the natural law another, although the jurists sometimes confuse them. But Abram did not reason by that law of nations, but by the whole natural law: he held that nothing belonging to others that had been received in that war pertained to him, no more than if someone should claim that a thing seized by violence from a robber, or secretly stolen from a thief, was his own because he had wrested it from the robber or the thief. Abram therefore answered that condition offered by the king of Sodom, first, with a solemn oath in the sight of God (verse 22); second, with the utmost refusal of even the smallest thing, lest the glory of God or Abram's reputation should be diminished in this way (verse 23); third, he wisely and piously accepted what pertained to the sustenance and wages of the men (last verse). For it is fair that those who serve a region should live from that region; and so he shows that he is liberally content with his own portion and with food alone, but that he wishes his confederates to have their wages, beyond their food, from the share of the spoils. One point remains, which the unskilled may perhaps think shows a contradiction, unless it is easily resolved from the words of Moses himself and from the nature of the matter. For it is said in verse 20 that Abram gave Melchizedek tithes of everything, namely of what he had recovered after the kings were slain in battle; but near the end Abram, with a solemn oath, declares that he will not take for his own use even the smallest thing that belongs to others, and concluding in the last verse he says: nothing of those things shall be with me. For if it was a matter of conscience for Abram to appropriate anything belonging to others, it does not seem fairer that he should give tithes to God or into the hand of Melchizedek of that which he acknowledged to be another's. For if it was another's, he could not give it; but if it was his own, he could also have kept it for himself. The answer is that a threefold response must be applied to resolve this appearance of contradiction. For it is resolved first from the fact, second from the purpose or intention of Abram, and third from the very equity and piety of the matter. From the fact: because it is one thing for Abram to have kept something of the spoils for himself (which by the right of war he could have done), and another to give tithes to God as thanksgiving, or the choice spoils (as they are called). From the purpose: because although by right he could have kept something for himself, even with the consent of the former owners, yet Abram had a different aim when he consecrated the tithes to God: a purpose which he could have pursued by human right from those spoils, but which he owed by divine religion. And his other purpose, in that he wished to keep nothing for himself by that design, was that the holy name of God should not be blasphemed by outsiders, nor Abram's own reputation suffer, as if he had procured his own gain at another's loss; for he wished in this way, by his generosity, to commend piety, justice and truthfulness to outsiders. Finally, from the duty of piety, because the nations themselves from the beginning have held this natural conviction, that thanks must be given to God for his most ample benefits, by way of thanksgiving. But if Abram had restored everything, even without excepting the tithes, into the hand of the former lords, those unbelievers would have sacrificed to their idols and would have attributed to them the benefits which God had bestowed upon Abram by promise, and upon them for Abram's sake. Abram therefore piously and holily set aside for God the part dedicated to him, though he could have set aside more; and from a sense of duty he rewarded God for the part so set aside. For although he could justly and honourably have kept back a reward for himself and his men, he had generously given that up; but what was owed to God, of whose piety he was unwilling or unable to give anything up, that he offered first out of the duty of piety and religion (or, as it were, took in advance).

units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 15.

units.la: IXIMVS ante, promissionis illius quâ fecit Abramo Deus partes duas esse: vnam, de hæreditate; alteram, de hęredibus ad quos ex promisso peruentura fuerat hæreditas. De hæreditate diximus tribus antegressis capitibus, quorum vltimo docuimus comparari transitum ad secundum promissionis locum de hæredibus, qui locus hoc cap. & seqq. duobus maximè exponitur. Occasione igitur arrepta ex historia proximè præcedente Deus in hoc capite primùm confirmat & consolatur Abramum v. 1. Deinde Abramo in sermonem de altera promissionum parte vltro venienti Deus eandem partem confirmat: Primum quidem promissione simplice, ad v. vsque 7. deinde signo ad vers. vsque 17. Postremò autem sedere ad signum accedente, in fine cap. Primus ergo locus huius cap. ad confirmationem Abrami aduersus omnium hominum iniurias pertinens (prout extranei iniuriisferè sunt expositi) continetur vers. 1: quo ostenditur, primùm qua occasione Deus Abramum duxerit confirmandum esse, nimirum post gesta res illas de quibus cap. praecedente. Nam exterorum apud indigenas ea fere conditio est, ut de malis ipsorum laeti-tia percipiatur, de bonis, doleatur inuideatūrque, denique omni te-pore multi dent operam ut stantes deiiciantur, labentes propellan-tur, ruentibus insultetur, & fabula sint omnium ubi corruerint. Cum itaque Abramo extero impendere metus videretur, tum ab exteris, tū à vindicta Regum potentissimorum quos ceciderat, tum ab odio incolarum inimicitias in ipsum exercentium, tum etiam ab invidentia eorum qui se amicos Abramo simulabant: propterea commodissimo tempore dicitur Dominus ipsum compellasse, idque per modum visionis, quæ reliquo capite amplius describitur. Sermonis vero quo Deus Abramum confirmaturus utebatur, duæ sunt partes: una, hortationis; altera, promissionis. Hortationem Deus pronuntiavit his verbis, ne metuas Abram. Nam etsi in speciem videtur a metu de-hortari: id tamen omnino constat inesse his verbis hortationem contrariam, ut abiecto omni metu bono animo sit, fiduciamque sumat, quamvis multis gravibusque malis circumsidentibus ipsum, & fermè (ut videbatur) jamjam oppressuris. Huic vero hortationi promissio, tamquam hortationis causa, subnectitur, cuius promissionis membra sunt duo; Unum, quo Deus Abramo cavet ab omni malo ne metuat, dicens, ego sum[?] clypeus tibi. Alterum, quo ipsi cavet de omni bono, quamvis interuertentibus & impedientibus pro viri-li omnibus tum indigenis, tum alienigenis, dicens, merces tua am-pla est valde. Cautio defensioque ab omni malo, quam electis suis solet praebere Deus, exprimitur similitudine rei militaris, nimirum clypei, ut alibi in scripturis passim. Cautionis vero de bonorum amplitudine ad Abramum perventura, simile sumptum est a re sive forensi, sive communi omnium, quum Deus Abramo spondet, quamvis neque de inimicis victis commoda ulla perceperit, neque ab amicis oblata, neque ab indigenis debita, sed in his rebus omnibus sese quam liberalissime gesserit, atque regifice mercedem omnem con-temnendo, Deum tamen, qui justus est μισθαποδότης[?], non esse passurum, ut sine mercede tantum beneficium Abram in cognitionem suam & in gentem exteram contulerit. Atque hæc interpretatio mihi pluris est quam vulgata illa, ego sum merces tua &c. Nam si Deus ita dixisset, & Abram Dei sermonem accepisset, nunquam fuisset dicturus illico Abram, Domine Jehova, quid daturus es mihi? Sed pro pietate sapientiaque sua, acquievisset amplissimæ illi promissioni Dei; neque supra creatorem se ipsum dantem pro mercede ipsi, fuisset desideraturus quicquam. Contra vero ex eo quod Deus amplissimam mercedem hic futuram ipsi promittebat, respondet Abram nihil esse cur mercedem eiusmodi in hac vita promittat ipsi, aut ipse sibi desideret, cum careat iustis hæredibus ad quos merces illa trans-portari possit, vt ipse v. 2. & 3. conqueritur. Ex antecedente promis-sione Dei nascitur modesta illa recusatio, qua Abram visus est secun-doverfu, cuius recusationis partes duæ sunt; propositio, & causa illius. Recusatione enim proponit Abram his verbis: Domine Iehoui, quid daturus esses mihi? quasi dicat, plura non posco, sed rebus præsentibus facile acquiesco, vt inquit Apostolus, pietate cū [illegible, ~6 letters] magnū lucrum esse. Recusationis causam re quidem vnicam, ratione vero duplicem affert Abram, cum subiicit, nam ego abeo improles, id est, liberis carens, propriisq; hæredibus de hac vita decessurus sum. Deinde hæres futurus est Damascenus iste Eliezer, tamquam si diceret, promissionibus tuis & hæredem & hæredis commoda mihi pronuntiaueras: nunc vero quid opus est amplioribus commodis, cum illa promissio de hærede, meo peccato quasi extincta sit? Quapropter huic recusationi subiicitur expostulatio de eadem re in v.3, & eiusdē argumēti. Huic ergo modestæ recusationi & expostulationi Abrami, tribus modis respondet Deus, promissione, signo, & sedere, vt ante diximus. Promissio duobus modis à Deo facta est; Simplice enuntiatione, & simili. Simplex enuntiatio est v.4. Non hic hæres tuus futurus est, sed is qui prodibit, &c. Simili vero exponitur promissio v.5. cum dicitur Abramum foras eduxisse Deus & demonstratis stellis cælestibus eamdem innumerabilitatem seminis ei promisisse. Hanc promissionem diuinam, quamuis simplicem, iuramento & signo confirmauit Deus occasione noua per Abramum oblata, quæ indicatur v.6, his verbis, credidit Abram Iehouæ, & hoc illi imputatum est ad iustitiam. Occasio igitur hæc fuit, quod Abram fide simplicissima acquieuerit simplicibus illis Dei promissionibus, Iustitiamque Dei eadem fide prehenderit, prout à Deo non operantibus ad mercedem, sed credentibus ad iustitiam & vitam imputatur, quemadmodum Apostolus o-ptime interpretatur Rom. 4. Hac igitur occasione ad secundum narrationis locum deuenit Deus, nempe promissionem iuramento v.7. & signo confirmandam v.9. & seqq. Iuramentum est, quod Deus tum per seipsum iurat, tum antegressam Abrami vocationem Vrę recordatur, tum denique præsentes suas promissiones repetit de tradenda illi hæreditate: Quem sermonem etsi Abram importunius quodam-modo intercepit illa sua interfatione v. 8. testificationem aliquam à Deo postulans ad confirmandam ipsius fidem in hæreditatis expe-ctatione: Deus tamen hac infirmitate Abramo ignoscens studiumq; probans illius cui fidem in iustitiam imputauerat, pergit in sermone instituto, ac proinde Abramo signum imperat v. 9. deinde vero obsequenti promissiones suas amplius explicat, signumque tradit promissionum, vt Abrami fides confirmata esset. Itaque materia signi imperatur v.9. Obsequium Abrami & fidelis exspectatio narratur, v. 10. & duobus seqq. Communicatio vero diuina tum sermonis, v.13. & tribus seqq. tum signi v.17. proponitur. Materiæ ad signum imperatæ cum argumento promissionum optime conuenit. Nam quatuor ordines animantium, quatuor centuriæ sunt annorum. Tres ordines interserti, tres centurias ærumnosissimas significant: Vna centuria non est experta tam multas angustias. Hic vero non solum obsequium Abrami dignum est obseruatu, sed etiam constantia; quod inde ad tempus vsq; noctis exspectans quid sibi Deus vellet, in loco constitit Abrā, &volucres ad cadauera accéssuras diligenter religioseq; arcuit, v.11. vsq; dū Abramo ex indefinente illa obseruatione fatigato irrepsit al-tusopor, v.12. quo Deus metum grauissimum incussit Abramo, eòque religioso metu hominem comparauit ad sanctam perceptionem rerum sequentium, qua Dei sermones & signa commodiùs perciperet. Sermonum autem quos Deus habuit summa est, historia de Abramo & semine ipsius, cuius historiæ partes sunt hæ: Prima de peregrinatione & afflictionibus seminis Abrami quadringentos annos (nam tot anni præcise à nato Isaaco ad exitū ex Ægypto in sacra Scriptura numerantur) v. 13. Secunda, de iudiciis Dei contra inimicos exercendis, liberandóque semine v. 14. quæ tota historia in libro Exodi explicatur. Tertia, de particulari historia Abrami, tranquilla vita & vitæ exitu, v.15. Quarta de semine Abrami in possessionem terræ vel hæreditatis suę mittendo, cùm primùm absoluta foret Amorrę[?]orum iniquitas. vers. 16. His promissionibus signum Deus adiicit, vers. 17. fornacis fumantis & ardentis lampadis, quibus signis transiuit Deus inter illa segmenta quæ ab Abramo iusserat collocari. Nam hic transeundi inter segmenta ritus testificabatur contrahentes ita fidem suam obstringere, vt se dederent anathemati aut lacerationi, vt lacerata & dissecta erant animalia, nisi præstarent fidem. Simile est Iirme. 36. His modis fedus illud constitutum est quod Deus pronuntiat à v.18. ad finem vsque de hæreditate integra posteris Abrami tradenda beneficio eius.
units.tr: I have already treated the first part of God's promise to Abram, which had two parts: one concerning the inheritance and the other concerning the heirs to whom the inheritance was to come by the promise. I spoke about the inheritance in the three preceding chapters, and at the end of the last of them I showed that the transition is made to the second part of the promise, concerning the heirs, which is explained mainly in this chapter and the following ones. Taking his occasion from the history immediately preceding, God in this chapter first confirms and comforts Abram (v. 1). Then, when Abram has come of his own accord to speak about the second part of the promises, God confirms that same part: first by a simple promise, down to verse 7; then by a sign, to verse 17; and finally by sitting down, when the sign is brought near, at the end of the chapter. The first section of this chapter, which pertains to the confirmation of Abram against the injuries of all men (as foreigners are usually exposed to injuries), is contained in verse 1. In it is shown first on what occasion God had to confirm Abram, namely after the events described in the preceding chapter. For the usual condition of foreigners among the natives is that they rejoice at their misfortunes and grieve at and envy their good fortune; in short, at all times many take pains to knock down those who stand, to push back those who slip, to trample on those who fall, and to become the talk of everyone when they have fallen. So when danger seemed to hang over Abram as a foreigner, both from other foreigners and from the vengeance of the most powerful kings whom he had defeated, and from the hatred of the inhabitants who were directing enmity against him, and also from the envy of those who pretended to be his friends, the Lord is said to have addressed him at the most fitting time, and this by way of a vision, which is described more fully in the rest of the chapter. Now the speech by which God was about to confirm Abram has two parts: one of exhortation and one of promise. God pronounced the exhortation in these words: Fear not, Abram. For although on the surface it seems to dissuade from fear, it is entirely certain that these words contain a contrary exhortation: that, having cast off all fear, he should be of good courage and take hold of confidence, although he was beset on every side by many grave evils, which seemed almost ready to overwhelm him. To this exhortation a promise is attached, as the reason for the exhortation. This promise has two members. The first, by which God gives Abram security from every evil so that he need not fear, says: I am a shield to you. The second, by which he gives security concerning every good, even though all men, both natives and foreigners, would hinder and obstruct it as far as they could, says: Your reward is very great. The security and defence from every evil which God is accustomed to give his elect is expressed by the likeness of a military matter, namely the shield, as elsewhere in Scripture everywhere. The security concerning the abundance of goods that is to come to Abram is taken from a likeness either of the law courts or of common life, since God promises Abram this although he has gained no advantage from the enemies he defeated, none from the offers of friends, none from what the natives owed him; but in all these matters he has conducted himself most generously, and in a kingly way has despised every reward. Yet God, who is just, the rewarder [μισθαποδότης], will not allow Abram to have conferred so great a benefit on the knowledge of himself and on a foreign nation without reward. And this interpretation is worth more to me than that common one, I am your reward, etc. For if God had spoken thus, and Abram had received God's word, Abram would never have immediately said: Lord Jehovah, what will you give me? Rather, in keeping with his piety and wisdom, he would have acquiesced in that most ample promise of God, and would not have desired anything further beyond the Creator himself giving himself to him as a reward. On the contrary, from the fact that God here promised him a most ample reward, Abram answers that there is no reason why he should be promised, or desire for himself, such a reward in this life, since he lacks lawful heirs to whom that reward could be passed on, as he himself complains in verses 2 and 3. From God's preceding promise arises that modest refusal by which Abram seems, in the second verse, to have refused; and this refusal has two parts: a statement and its cause. For in the refusal Abram states it in these words: Lord Jehovah, what would you give me? as if to say: I do not ask for more, but I readily acquiesce in present things, as the Apostle says, that piety with contentment is great gain. Abram gives one cause for the refusal, but a twofold reason, when he adds: for I go childless, that is, lacking offspring, I shall depart from this life with no heirs of my own. Then: this Eliezer of Damascus will be my heir, as if he said: you had promised me both an heir and the advantages of an heir; but now what need is there for greater advantages, since that promise concerning an heir has been, as it were, extinguished by my sin? Therefore to this refusal is attached an expostulation about the same matter in verse 3, of the same argument. To this modest refusal and expostulation of Abram, God replies in three ways, as we said before: by promise, by sign, and by sitting down. The promise was made by God in two ways: by a simple statement and by a likeness. The simple statement is in verse 4: This one will not be your heir, but he who shall come forth, etc. The promise is set out by likeness in verse 5, where it is said that God led Abram forth outside and, pointing to the heavenly stars, promised him the same innumerable seed. This divine promise, though simple, God confirmed by an oath and a sign, on a new occasion offered by Abram, which is indicated in verse 6 in these words: Abram believed the Lord, and it was imputed to him for righteousness. The occasion, therefore, was that Abram with the simplest faith acquiesced in those simple promises of God, and laid hold of God's righteousness with the same faith; which, not to those who work for a reward but to those who believe, is imputed for righteousness and life, as the Apostle best explains in Romans 4. On this occasion, therefore, God comes to the second place of the narrative, namely that the promise is to be confirmed by an oath in verse 7 and by a sign in verses 9 and following. The oath is that which God swears both by himself and recalls Abram's earlier calling from Ur, and finally repeats his present promises of delivering the inheritance to him. Although Abram somewhat importunately interrupted this speech with his own interjection in verse 8, asking God for some testimony to confirm his faith in the expectation of the inheritance, God nevertheless, pardoning this weakness in Abram and approving the zeal of him whose faith he had imputed for righteousness, goes on with the subject of his speech; and accordingly he commands Abram to bring a sign in verse 9, then further explains his promises to him as he obeys, and delivers a sign of the promises, so that Abram's faith might be confirmed. Thus the matter of the sign is commanded in verse 9. Abram's obedience and faithful expectation are related in verse 10 and the two following. But the divine communication, both of the speech in verse 13 and the three following, and of the sign in verse 17, is set forth. The matter commanded for the sign agrees excellently with the subject of the promises. For the four orders of animals are four centuries of years. The three orders interposed signify three most troublesome centuries; one century did not experience so many distresses. Here, however, not only is Abram's obedience worthy of notice, but also his constancy: for waiting from then until the coming of night to see what God wished of him, he stood in place, and diligently and reverently drove away the birds that were coming down on the carcasses, verse 11, until a deep sleep fell upon Abram, verse 12, wearied by that unremitting watching. Into this sleep God struck the gravest fear into Abram, and by that reverent fear prepared the man for the holy perception of the things that follow, by which he might more readily perceive God's words and signs. The sum of the words God spoke is the history of Abram and his seed, whose parts are these: first, of the sojourning and afflictions of Abram's seed for four hundred years (for so many years exactly are counted in Holy Scripture from the birth of Isaac to the exodus from Egypt), verse 13. Second, of God's judgments to be executed against the enemies and of the liberation of the seed, verse 14, which whole history is explained in the book of Exodus. Third, of the particular history of Abram, his quiet life and the end of his life, verse 15. Fourth, of the sending of Abram's seed into possession of the land, or of its inheritance, when the iniquity of the Amorites should first be complete, verse 16. To these promises God adds a sign, verse 17: a smoking furnace and a burning lamp, by which signs God passed between those pieces which Abram had been ordered to place. For this rite of passing between the pieces testified that the contracting parties thus bound their faith, so that they gave themselves over to the anathema or to laceration, just as the animals were torn and cut in pieces, unless they kept their faith. There is a similar rite in Jeremiah 34. By these means that covenant was established, which God pronounces from verse 18 to the end, that the whole inheritance is to be given to Abram's posterity by his benefit.

units.la: CAPITIS XVI ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 16.

units.la: POSTQVAM Deus Abramo de haeredibus verbo promissionis signo & sedere singulari cauerat, vt proxima praecedeti cap. narrauit Moses; Sequitur historia infirmitatis fidei, qua nō solū Sarai, sed etiā Abrā pater credentiū ex illa fiducia in promissiones Dei, aberrarunt: vt eo pacto omnes intelligant non esse humani operis, vt promissiones Dei consequamur ipsi; sed potius Misericordiae Dei. Summa autem huius capitis est, Sarain & Abramum in fide tituban-tes, de haerede acquirendo modis illegitimis consilia iniuisse, secis-se, & multa mala sibi familiaeque accersiuisse, nisi Deus pro infinita sua gratia abiiciens peccati illius ex infirmitate fidei recordatione in veritate suarū promissionum perstitisset. Itaque huius capitis partes sunt hae: Primum narratio facti, inter Sarain & Abramum, ad ver. vsque 7. Secunda narratio sermonum inter Angelum & Hagaram habitorū ad v. vsque 12. Postremò autē euecta ex vtroque facto consequentia narrantur versibus vltimis. In primo historiae loco, quemadmodum ante obseruari docuimus in historiis oportere, primum causae narrantur in v.1. Deinde consilium, vers.2. Tertiò factum, in v.3. Postremò autem euentus, 4. & 5. Causarum duo sunt genera: Vnum impellens, cum dicitur Sarai vxor Abrami non peperisse illi, hoc est, liberis caruisse. Altera, non tam causa quàm occasio facti dicenda est, nempe quòd ancillam Aegyptiam nomine Hagaram haberet Sarai. Harum verò causarum neutra quicquam poterat ad defensionem aut probationem sequentis facti, praesertim cum recente memoria Deus promissiones suas antecedentes confirmasset, atque haec omnia ex sola fidei infirmitate profecta sint. Quemadmodum autem causa factum probare non potest, sic neque consilium, aut à Sarai datum, aut ab Abramo acceptum: quae duo distinctè 2. versu exponuntur. Nam in consilio Sarai tres sunt partes, quarum nulla ex diuino, aut naturae iure probari potest. Causa prima est, cum dicit, Ecce iam occlusit mihi Iehoua ne parerem.: nam his ipsis verbis se ipsam damnabat Sarai, quòd consilio Dei non acquiesceret. Nam si consilium Dei illud esse sensit, parendum fuit, ac non eludendum; Neque malum faciendum vt eueniret bonum. Hinc sequitur secunda pars consilij, congredere iam cum ancilla mea: Quod consilium iuri diuino & naturali aduersatur, de quo supra 2. capit. Nam etsi inter virum vxoremque mutua est obligatio,huius tum obligationis auctoritas non ex solo contrahentium consensu pendet; sed ex prima ordinatione Dei instituentis coniugium, & in natura hactenus conseruantis. Quod si ex mero contrahentium consensu penderet, eodem quoque modo legitime dissolui posset. Cum autem superior illa auctoritas e cælo hoc instituerit & consensionem inspirauerit,non possunt qui semel consenserunt iugum matrimonij abiicere sine grauissima in Deum auctorem contumelia.At non abiecit Sarai,dixerit quispiam.Respondetur non solum flexisse, sed etiam abrupisse iugum connubij, quisquis vel semel a iure illo discessit, quo per voluntatem Dei obstrictus est. Et vero tertia pars consilij, nimirum finis illius, docet euidentissime quicquid fecit Sarai, in fraudem fecisse naturalis illius legis, cū dicit, fortasse liberos consequar ab illa. hic enim qui ex coniunctione hac natus est, non fuit propterea filius Sarai, neque promissionis filius, ad quam oportuit illam respicere, sed tantum quadam imputatione & similitudine, cuius imputationis leuitatem & instabilitatem vel ipsa Sarai postea demonstrauit, cum infantem adhuc in vtero eiecta matre domo eiiceret. Quod autem de consilio Sarai diximus, cur improbari ipsum oporteat,idem iudicium de Abramo facimus: qui acquiescens consilio vxoris magis illius quam Dei rationem in facto, habuit, quod posteriore membro 2.v. ostendit Moses. Hinc sequitur factum consilio capto,in v.3; quod Abram duxit Hagaram rogatu vxoris Sarai:qua in re duo singulariter obseruauit Moses; primum tempus,secundo ius copulationis istius. Tempus,quod Abram duxit Hagaram decimo post anno quam in Cenahaneam aduenisseт. Ius vero, quod ipsa Sarai dedit ancillam suam viro suo in vxorem. Temporis obseruatio partim ad diuturnam expectationem illorum demonstrandam pertinet,qui ante annos quindecim promissionem de femine acceperant, eamque sæpius sibi renouari a Domino audiuerant. Sed è diuerso eadem temporis circumstantia demonstrat infirmitatem fidei & impatientiam Sarai,quam Abram sequutus est; tum quia amplius expectari promissionem Dei oportuit,tum quia recentem superiore capite promissionem de eodem argumento a Deo acceperant.Ius autem coniugationis istius duobus modis factum est tolerabilius: Primùm quia de consilio & consensu vxoris iustæ, Sarai facta est;tum quia non simplex aut vagus congressus, sed coniugium fuit secundo gradu,id est,non quidem a Deo probatum,sed tamen receptum & excusatum ciuili more. Hoc vero vt intelligamus, copulationem viri & fœminæ obseruandum est iustam, aut iniustam esse, aut mediam. Iusta copulatio duobus modis facta legitur in Testamenti menti Veteris. Nam primùm commune est omnium iustarum copulationum, quòd à Deo sint, & quòd ex consensu eorum, quorum interest. Sed harum vna habet consortium æquabile omnis diuini & humani iuris, si tamen ordinem maritalem exceperis. Altera verò consortium quidem habet omnis diuini iuris, sed humani ex parte, vt fit cùm vxores adiunguntur viris citra collationem bonorum omnium, & seruatis quibusdam exceptionibus. atque in hunc modum Abraham duxerat Keturam, Gen. 25. Iniusta coniugatio non eget definitione. Media coniugatio est, quæ ita fit inter contrahentes vt aliquid tamen essentiale iusti coniugij desideretur: vt fit si copulatio & fides inter partes seruatur, cùm tamen aut non fuerit instituta à Deo copulatio, aut ab iis probata quorum interest diuino & humano iure. Eiusmodi autem vxores concubinæ dicebantur, quæ aut contra institutionem Dei, aut contra voluntatem eorum quorum interfuit, aut denique contra legem publicam ducebantur. Verumtamen honestiore loco habebantur quàm fœminæ prostibulæ, quarum coniugatio semper iniusta est. Ex hoc Sarai & Abrami facto euenta consequuta sunt de quibus, vers. 4. & seqq. quorum euentorum vnum naturale est, quòd Hagar ex concubitu Abrami dicitur conseppisse: reliqua verò euenta infirmitati humanæ adscribi debent; primùm est Hagaræ, quæ vbi se grauidatam sensit, insolētior effecta est, reipsa confirmans quod sapiens dicit in Prouerbiis, nihil esse seruo insolentius vbi Dominus est factus. Alterum est infirmitatis Sarai, vers. 5. quod indignatione exardescens etiam in virum suum inuexit, Deúmque vindicem iniuriæ sibi factæ appellauit. Ac primùm quidem iniuriam sibi factam in virum insolenter cudit: deinde verò narrat illam iniuriam per comparationem, quòd benefica in Hagaram fuerit, extollens ipsam, & ipsa ex contrario ingrato contemptu Sarain profequuta sit: Postremò Deum appellat vindicem in virum, quem Deus ipsi caput præsecerat, hoc pacto & in Deum, & in virum, & in seipsam iniquissima. Tertius euentus infirmitatis est, quòd Abram pacis causa ancillam suam, quam duxerat coniugem, exponit voluntati Sarai; cùm tamen alia moderatiore via potuisset Hagaræ & vetri illius consulere. Ex his ergo infirmitatis humanæ exemplis id tandem consequuntum est, vt Hagar duriter à Sarai accepta domo illius profugerit, vers. 6. Sequitur itaque alter locus capitis de fuga Hagaræ & rebus in ea gestis. Res autè in hac fuga gestæ dialogisticè à Mose exponuntur, quia sermone Angelus cum illa cömunicauit: illius autem sermonis quem præcedit circumscriptio loci, vers. 7. partes omnino sunt tres: prima est parafcœue, præparatio ad sermonem necessariū habendum,
units.tr: After God had secured Abram's heirs for him by the word of promise, with a sign and a singular seal (as Moses related in the immediately preceding chapter), there follows the history of the weakness of faith, in which not only Sarai but also Abram, the father of believers, went astray from that trust in God's promises. In this way all may understand that it is not by human work that we ourselves obtain the promises of God, but rather by the mercy of God. The sum of this chapter is that Sarai and Abram, wavering in faith, devised and carried out plans to acquire an heir by illegitimate means, and drew many evils upon themselves and their household, unless God, by his infinite grace, had set aside the memory of that sin, which arose from weakness of faith, and had remained steadfast in the truth of his promises. Accordingly the parts of this chapter are these. First, the narrative of the deed between Sarai and Abram, to verse 7. Second, the narrative of the words exchanged between the Angel and Hagar, to verse 12. Last, the consequences drawn from both events are recounted in the final verses. In the first part of the history, as we have taught earlier that histories ought to be observed, the causes are narrated first, in verse 1; then the plan, verse 2; thirdly the deed, verse 3; and finally the outcome, verses 4 and 5. There are two kinds of causes. One is an impelling cause, when it is said that Sarai, Abram's wife, had not borne him children, that is, had been without children. The other is not so much a cause as an occasion of the deed, namely that Sarai had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar. Yet neither of these causes could contribute anything to the defence or proof of the deed that follows, especially since God had recently confirmed his earlier promises, and all these things proceeded from weakness of faith alone. But just as a cause cannot prove a deed, neither can the plan prove it, whether it was given by Sarai or accepted by Abram; these two are set out distinctly in verse 2. For in Sarai's plan there are three parts, none of which can be proved by divine law or by the law of nature. The first cause is when she says, Behold, now Jehovah has shut me up so that I cannot bear children. For by these very words Sarai condemned herself, because she did not submit to the counsel of God. If she perceived that this was the counsel of God, she ought to have obeyed it and not evaded it; nor should evil be done so that good may come of it. Hence follows the second part of the plan, go in now to my maidservant, a counsel which is contrary to divine and natural law, concerning which we spoke above, in chapter 2. For although there is a mutual obligation between husband and wife, the authority of this obligation does not depend on the consent of the contracting parties alone, but on God's first ordinance instituting marriage and preserving it in nature until now. If it depended on the mere consent of the contracting parties, it could be lawfully dissolved in the same way. But since that higher authority from heaven instituted marriage and inspired the consent, those who have once consented cannot cast off the yoke of marriage without the gravest insult to God, its author. Someone may say, "But Sarai did not cast it off." The answer is that whoever has departed from that law, by which he is bound through the will of God, has not merely bent the yoke of marriage but broken it, even if he did so only once. The third part of the plan, namely its purpose, shows most clearly that whatever Sarai did was a fraud against that natural law, when she says, perhaps I shall obtain children from her. For the child born of this union was not on that account the son of Sarai, nor a son of the promise, to which she ought to have looked; he was a son only by a certain imputation and resemblance. The lightness and instability of that imputation Sarai herself afterwards demonstrated, when she drove the mother out of the house while the infant was still in the womb. As for Sarai's plan, which we have said ought to be disapproved, the same judgment we pass on Abram, who, assenting to his wife's counsel, took more account of her reasoning than of God's in the deed, as Moses shows in the latter part of verse 2. Hence follows the deed, done in accordance with the plan, in verse 3: Abram took Hagar at the request of his wife Sarai. In this matter Moses has noted two things especially: first the time, and second the legal standing of that union. As to the time, Abram took Hagar ten years after he had come into the land of Canaan. As to the legal standing, Sarai herself gave her maidservant to her husband as a wife. The notice of time relates partly to showing how long the expectation was of those who, fifteen years earlier, had received the promise of a seed and had heard it repeatedly renewed by the Lord. But on the other hand the same circumstance of time demonstrates the weakness of faith and the impatience of Sarai, which Abram followed: both because God's promise ought to have been awaited longer, and because they had received from God, in the preceding chapter, a recent promise on the same subject. The legal standing of this union was made more tolerable in two ways. First, because it was done with the counsel and consent of Sarai, his lawful wife; and second, because it was not a casual or random intercourse, but a marriage of the second degree, that is, not indeed approved by God, yet received and excused by civil custom. In order to understand this, we must observe that the union of a man and a woman is either just, or unjust, or intermediate. A just union is recorded in two forms in the Old Testament. The first feature common to all just unions is that they are from God and are made by the consent of those concerned. Of these, one kind has an equal fellowship with all divine and human law, except for the marital order. The other kind, indeed, has fellowship with all divine law but with human law only in part, as when wives are joined to husbands without the transfer of all their goods, and with certain exceptions preserved. In this manner Abraham had taken Keturah, Gen. 25. An unjust union needs no definition. An intermediate union is one which is made between the contracting parties in such a way that something essential to a lawful marriage is still lacking, as happens when intercourse and faithfulness are kept between the parties, but the union was not instituted by God, or was not approved by those whose right it was, under divine and human law. Women of this kind were called concubines, who were taken either against the institution of God, or against the will of those whose interest was concerned, or finally against public law. Nevertheless they were held in higher regard than harlots, whose union is always unjust. From the deed of Sarai and Abram there followed the outcomes of which Moses speaks in verse 4 and following. Of these outcomes, one is natural: Hagar is said to have conceived from Abram's intercourse. The remaining outcomes must be ascribed to human weakness. The first is Hagar's: when she perceived that she had conceived, she became more insolent, actually confirming what the wise man says in Proverbs, that nothing is more insolent than a servant when he has become master. The second is Sarai's weakness, verse 5: she burst out in indignation, lashed out even at her husband, and called God the avenger of the wrong done to her. First she rashly accuses her husband of the wrong done to her; then she describes that wrong by comparison, saying that she had been kind to Hagar, exalting herself, while Hagar in return showed her ungrateful contempt. Last, she calls God the avenger against her husband, whom God had set over her as head, and in this way she was most unjust toward God, toward her husband, and toward herself. The third outcome of the weakness is that Abram, for the sake of peace, gave his maidservant, whom he had taken as wife, over to Sarai's will, although he could have looked after Hagar and his own son by some other, more moderate way. From these examples of human weakness, then, it finally followed that Hagar, harshly treated by Sarai, fled from her house, verse 6. Therefore there follows the second part of the chapter, concerning Hagar's flight and the events that took place in it. The events of this flight are related by Moses in dialogue form, because the Angel communicated with her in speech. Of that speech, which is preceded by the description of the place, verse 7, there are altogether three parts: the first is the preparation, parascue, for the necessary speech to be delivered; the second is the command, verse 9; the third is the promise, verse 10 and the two following verses. The outcome of this speech is set out in verses 13 and 14. The preparation for the speech in verse 8 is posed in a familiar question and answer, a kind of communication which God uses very much, so that whoever is held...

units.la: N. j. vers.8. Secunda est mandati, vers. 9. Tertia promissionis vers.10. & duobus seqq. Huius sermonis euentus, vers.13. & 14. exponitur. Præparatio ad sermonē v.8. in familiari quæstione & responsione posita est eiusmodi communicatione Deus plurimum vtitur, vt quicumque habetur sermo ex re præsente datus videatur, coque facilius insinuatur in hominum mentes. Mandati vers.9. partes duæ sunt: vna, reuer-sionis; altera, abiectionis, qua se iubetur Hagar dominio Sarai, quamuis aspero, subiicere. Promissionis locus, v. 10. duas partes habet: quarum prior de vniuerso semine Hagaræ in communi, illud nu-merosum fore, v.10. Posterior est, de filio proximè nascituro, vers.11. & conditionibus illius, vers.12. Priore loco filius futurus dicitur, & nomen illius indicitur ad beneficij præsentis à Deo accepti recordationem. Posteriore loco mores, actiones, & sedes filij exponuntur. Mores, agrestes, expressi onagri similitudine: actiones, militares vltro citroque. Habitatio amplissima, prout describitur infrà cap.25. Hinc sequitur euentus duplex: prior, quòd Hagar affecta Dei beneficio recordata est, & memoriam statuit illius, v.13: Posterior, quòd in posteritatem memoria illa fuit conseruata ex imposita per Hagaram putei siue fontis appellatione. Restat iam tertius locus, de genitura & appellatione Ischmaelis, v.15. qua ratione tum Hagaræ fides atque obsequium, tum etiam Abrami ostenditur, siue ex Hagara sermonem Dei cognouerit (quod credibile est) siue ipse quoque à Deo nominatim fuerit de re eadem compellatus. Quòd autem ætas Abrami per illud tempus exprimitur in vers. vltimo, id eò pertinet, tum vt veritatem antegressæ promissionis intelligamus; tum vero vt obseruemus conplemetum promissionum diuinarum plurimum in annos & tempora plurima, peccatis nostris, infirmitate, & impatientia nostra solere reiici iusto iudicio Dei. Nam Abram natus 86. annos genuit Ischmaelem; filium vero promissionis Isaacum centenarius demum adeptus est.
units.tr: Verse 8. The second part is the command, verse 9. The third is the promise, verse 10 and the two following verses. The outcome of this speech is set out in verses 13 and 14. The preparation for the speech, v. 8, is cast as a familiar question and answer. God makes much use of this kind of conversation, so that whatever speech arises from a present matter seems to be given on the spot, and so it is more easily insinuated into people's minds. The command, v. 9, has two parts: one of return, and the other of submission, by which Hagar is told to subject herself to the rule of Sarai, however harsh it may be. The promise, v. 10, has two parts. The first concerns Hagar's whole seed in general, that it would be numerous, v. 10. The second concerns the son who is about to be born, verse 11, and his conditions, verse 12. In the first part the son to come is named, and his name is given as a reminder of the present benefit received from God. In the second part his character, actions and dwelling are described. His character is wild, expressed by the likeness of the onager; his actions are warlike, raiding back and forth. His dwelling is very spacious, as it is described below in chapter 25. From this follow two outcomes. The first is that Hagar, moved by God's kindness, remembered it and established a memorial of it, v. 13. The second is that this memory was preserved for posterity through the name Hagar gave to the well or spring. There remains the third part, concerning the birth and naming of Ishmael, v. 15, by which both Hagar's faith and obedience, and also Abram's, are shown, whether Hagar had learned God's word (which is credible), or he himself was addressed by God by name about the same matter. As for the fact that Abram's age is stated at that time in the last verse, this pertains to two things: first, that we may understand the truth of the promise that went before; and second, that we may observe that the fulfilment of God's promises is very often deferred over many years and long periods of time, and that this is usually because of our sins, our weakness and our impatience, by the just judgment of God. For Abram, when he was eighty-six years old, begot Ishmael; but he obtained the son of promise, Isaac, only at the age of a hundred.

units.la: CAPITIS XVII. ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII. ANALYSIS.

units.la: [?]Istoriā Abrami in duas partes ante distinximus: vnam, ad promissionum tempus pertinentem; alteram, ad tempus sederis quo promissiones illæ mutua stipulatione & sponsione confirmatæ sunt. Hactenus de promissionibus, tum ad hæreditatem, tum ad hæredes respicientibus, quas duas partes distinctè adhuc percurrit Moses. Deinceps de tempore sederis & rebus per illud gestis dicendum est, ad c.25. víque.
units.tr: Above we divided the history of Abram into two parts: one concerning the time of the promises, and the other concerning the time of the covenant, by which those promises were confirmed through mutual stipulation and pledge. So far we have dealt with the promises, which bear both on the inheritance and on the heirs, and Moses still runs through these two parts separately. Next we must speak of the time of the covenant and the things done in it, down to chapter 25.

units.la: In hac secunda parte primùm substantia foederis ex cap. 17. deinde verò effecta veritatis Dei ex promissionibus & foedere ipsius, in cap. seqq. exponuntur. Ac primùm quidem illud tenendum est, promis- siones illas Dei gratiosas per se satis esse quibus homines aquiescant: sed tamen Deum singulari gratia fedus solemne ad promissiones ad- ieciisse vt eò amplius infirmitas hominū leuaretur, quemadmodum de iuramento scribit Apostolus Heb. 6. Etsi hoc amplius necesse est obseruari, fedus apud Hebraeos non simpliciter appellari, quicquid inter partes diuersas consensu mutuo ad vtriusque partis obligatio- nem contrahitur; verum etiam appellari vniuersè quicquid condi- tionibus obligat, etiâsi ex vnius tantū partis auctoritate positæ sint. Quapropter Hebraeorum appellatione Berith institutum quoduis conditiones lectissimas in se implexas habens, appellatur, vt etiam apud Latinos fedus Ennio, Lucretio, Virgilio, & aliis appellatur, & interpretatur Varro lib. 6. de ling. Lat. fedus à fidedo, quasi fidus no- minatum esse. Atque eo sensu in genere federum testamenta quoque continentur: quamobrem etiam commodè auctor ad Hebraeos eam- dèvocem apud Iirmeiā testamentū interpretatus est. Illa autè latiore significatione nomē foederis accipitur supra 9.9. & 15.18. vt illic oste- dimus: angustiore verò significatione in hoc cap. accipiendū est, vbi secūdum communem naturam contractuū quatuor sunt partes, quā- uis tacitè comprehensę, stipulatio, sponsio, restipulatio, atque respon sio. Hæc igitur huius capitis summa est, fedus à Deo cū Abrahamo in- itum & in omnem posteritatem conseruandum hoc cap. enarrari. Ac proinde huius cap. duas partes statui necesse est: Quarum prior est de sedere inter Deum & Abrahamum inito, ad v. vsque 22. Posterior de professione foederis iusto obsequio fidei per Abrahamū facta, inde ad finem cap. In priore loco & sedere tria sunt mēbra quæ Moses distin- guit cōmodissimè: Primum est de subsistantia foederis, ad v. vsq; 9: se- cundum est de signo permanente foederis, ad v. 16. vsq; tertium deniq; est de cōsequentibus foederis, inde ad 22. v. Ad subsistantiā foederis expo nendā venturus Moses prēmittit duo historicē; notatione temporis, & modum communicationis. v. 1. temporis notatio est, cum Abraham natus fuisse dicitur 99. annos: Modus communicationis est visio. Tēpus no tari maximè pertinuit ad nostram ædificationem, tum vt dilationem in præstandis promissionibus à nostra infirmitate & peccatis disca- mus oboriri, tum vt veritatē Dei propter solā ipsius gratiam, quāuis obnitente hominū infirmitate, sibi cōstare agnoscamus, & quāuis se- rō tamen certò promissarū rerū cōplementū exhibere. Modus reue- lationis ad rei auctoritatē facit. sederis autē substantia Deus declarat, primùm stipulatione, altera parte versus primi: deinde sponsione, v.2. quâ substantiam sederis generatim propositam post minutatim exponit Deus seqq. Summæ propositionis sederis præmittitur excr-dium quoddam tribus verbis, à natura Dei, qui auctor est sederis, cùm ait, ego sum Deus omnipotens: quo exordio Abramum docilem & attentum facit, vt potentiæ Dei credat atque obsequatur. Huic exordio subiungitur proximè stipulatio: primùm quidem sanctificationis, quæ in fide & obsequio posita est, Ambula coram me: deinde verò integritatis siue veritatis, id est, vt Apostolus exponit, conscientiæ bonæ, quam qui abiiciunt naufragium faciunt fidei, his verbis, esto integer[?]. Huic stipulationi accedit sponsio secundo versu: primùm de sedere, deinde verò de multiplicatione vel incremento ex sedere, quas duas partes signo probat Abram, tamquam vltro, cum Deo contrahens, beneficiùmque accipiens sederis, cùm dicit Moses versu tertio, tum Abramum in faciem suam procidisse. Atque hac ratione transitur ad expositionem sederis, dicente Mose, & loquutus est cum eo dicendo, &c.
units.tr: In this second part, the substance of the covenant is set out first, in chapter 17, and then the effect of God's truth, from the promises and his covenant, in the following chapters. In the first place we must hold that God's gracious promises are in themselves enough for people to rest in. Yet God, by singular grace, added a solemn covenant to the promises, so that people's weakness might be the more firmly supported, as the Apostle writes of the oath in Heb. 6. We must also observe that among the Hebrews a covenant (Berith [ברית]) is not simply whatever is agreed between different parties by mutual consent, binding both sides; rather, the word is used generally for any arrangement that binds by conditions, even if it is laid down by the authority of one party alone. Hence the Hebrew term Berith is applied to any arrangement having very choice conditions bound up within it, just as among the Latins the word fedus is used by Ennius, Lucretius, Virgil and others, and Varro, in book 6 of his work on the Latin language, derives fedus from fidedo, as if it were named from fidus.
