In this sense testaments too are included under the general heading of covenants; for this reason the author of the Epistle to the Hebrews fittingly translated the same word in Jeremiah as "testament." In its wider meaning the name of covenant is taken in 9:9 and 15:18, as we showed there; but in this chapter it must be taken in the narrower sense, where, according to the common nature of contracts, there are four parts, though tacitly included: stipulation, undertaking, counter-stipulation, and response. This, then, is the sum of this chapter: that the chapter sets out the covenant entered by God with Abraham and to be kept for all his posterity. Accordingly, we must divide this chapter into two parts. The first is about the covenant made between God and Abraham, down to verse 22; the second is about the profession of the covenant, made by Abraham through the righteous obedience of faith, from there to the end of the chapter. In the first part, the covenant has three members, which Moses distinguishes most conveniently: the first concerns the substance of the covenant, down to verse 9; the second concerns the permanent sign of the covenant, to verse 16; the third, finally, concerns the consequences of the covenant, from there to verse 22. To explain the substance of the covenant, Moses first sets out two things in narrative form: a notation of time, and the manner of communication. In verse 1 the notation of time is that Abraham is said to have been "ninety-nine years" old; the manner of communication is a vision. Marking the time pertains chiefly to our edification, so that we may learn that delay in fulfilling the promises arises from our weakness and sins, and so that we may acknowledge that God remains faithful to himself, purely by his own grace, even when human weakness resists, and that he nevertheless certainly exhibits the fulfilment of the promised things, though late. The manner of revelation serves to confirm the authority of the thing. God declares the substance of the covenant first by stipulation, in the other part of verse 1; then by undertaking in verse 2, in which God, after first setting out the substance of the covenant in general terms, explains it piece by piece in what follows. Before the summary of the covenant's proposition, God prefaces a kind of exordium in three words, drawn from his own nature, as the author of the covenant, when he says, "I am God Almighty"; by this exordium he makes Abram docile and attentive, so that he may believe in God's power and obey it. Next to this exordium comes the stipulation, first concerning sanctification, which consists in faith and obedience: "Walk before me"; and then concerning integrity or truth, that is, as the Apostle explains it, a good conscience, which those who cast off make shipwreck of faith; this is expressed in the words "be upright." To this stipulation is joined the undertaking in the second verse: first concerning the covenant, and then concerning the multiplication or increase arising from the covenant. Abram confirms these two parts by a sign, as one who, of his own accord, contracts with God and receives the benefit of the covenant, when Moses says in the third verse, "then Abram fell on his face." In this way the account passes to the exposition of the covenant, Moses saying, "and he spoke with him, saying," and so on.

units.la: Huius sederis explicatio singularis [illegible, ~8 letters] exponitur v. 4. & seqq. Nam primùm sponsio Dei vel promissio v.2. comprehensa versibus quinque exponitur: deinde verò stipulatio, v.9.[?] sponsionis siue promissionis quam Deus Abrahamo facit, partes hoc loco tres distinguendæ sunt: prima est de benedictione diuina in communicandis hæredibus, v.4. & duobus seqq. Secunda est de substantia ipsa æterni sederis, vnde aliæ omnes benedictiones tamquam ex fonte profluunt, v.7. Tertia deinde est promissio hæreditatis terrenæ, tamquam symboli hæreditatem cælestem nostram adumbrantis, v. 8. Quæ omnia initio proposita sunt, principio v. 4. his verbis, Ecce fœdus meum te-cum, postea verò speciatim exponuntur. Promissio hæredum facta est vniuersè sermone, & signo. Sermone, v.4. his verbis, Quod eris pa-ter multitudinis Gentium, id est, multarum Gentium, prout hanc hypallagen Paulus interpretatus est. Signo autem v.seq. quum Deus ait, Non vocabitur amplius nomen tuum Abram, sed erit, &c. Nam accessit nomini Abram libera He ex nomine Hebræo Hamon multitudo: ac proinde ex Abram, quod est pater excelsus, factum est Abraham corruptis duabus vocibus, quasi dicas patrem magnæ multitudinis. Nam corrumpi nomina inter componendum apud Hebræos exempla innumera docent euidentissimè. Postea verò modus istius posteritatis describitur in v. 6. Primùm quidem generatim, quòd Deus facturus est vt fœtificent posteri Abrahami quàm plurimum: postea verò sigillatim duobus modis: primùm dispositione multarum Gentum ex hac una radice: secundo dignitate atque maiestate, quod Reges ex Abrahamo proditurí effent, ut hoc pacto Abrahamo fore plurimos & summos ostenderet. Hoc promissionis loco exposito, quod ad Abrahamum & hæredes ipsius omnes substantia promissionum peructura esset, alterum locum continuo Deus subiicit v.7, De substantia fœderis ad Abrahamum hæredésque ipsius peruentura. De hoc autem fœdere circumstantiæ duæ proferuntur, antequam ad summam illius veniatur: nam hæc duæ sunt partes septimi huius versus, circumstantiæ, & summa fœderis circumstantiarum una est, quod fœdus instituit Deus communem cum Abrahamo & femine illius post venturo per generationes ipsorum, siue continuato, siue interrupto per infirmitatem humanam ordine: Altera, quod fœdus æternum futurum est, hoc est (ut cum scholasticis loquamur) interminabile. Summa fœderis est, Deum fore Deum Abrahamo & feminî eius post ipsum. Nam vox Deus in hac loquutione relatiua est, ut ex multis Mosis & Prophetarum locis constat & diuersis verbis Hoscheae 1. & 2. Relatio huius promissionis ostenditur, ubi Deus populi sui & populus Dei sui vicissim appellatur. In primis autem Hoscheae 1. c. ult. vers. Dicam ei qui non est populus meus, populus meus es, & ipse dicturus est, Deus mi. Nam hac loquutione omnino continetur quicquid ad iustam illius diuini fœderis naturam potest pertinere. His duabus partibus promissionum tertia subiicitur, de symbolo cælestis illius hereditatis ad filios Abrahami peruenturo, v.8. & dabo, inquit, &c. Sic hæ tres promissionum partes repetita earum summa concluduntur his verbis, Deniquefuturus sum ipsis Deus. Atque hæc quidem de promissionibus diuinis. Sequitur stipulatio, v.9. qua Deus Abramum appellat, ut ipse cum suis posteris illud fœdus gratiosè à Deo initum seruet obsequio fidei atque veritate, quemadmodum in v.1.exposuimus. Huic substantiæ diuini fœderis, quam primum esse huius capitis locum docuimus, subiicitur altera pars de signo ad fœdus accedente. Quod signum primum proponitur summatim v.10. deinde imperatur cum promissione singulari, v.11. Postremò autem singularia quædam præscribuntur ad observationem signi pertinentia, tribus versibus seqq. Signum est, circumcidendum esse omnem marem: huius signi obseruationi v.10 imperatæ sua promissio attexitur v.11. Illud signum coram Deo signum fore fœderis inter Deum & Abrahami posteros. Singularia vero ad obseruationem huius signi pertinentia præscribuntur ista: primum, qui, quando circumcidendi sint, v.12. Secundò quibus, & quando promissio competitura sit, v.13. Postremò, quid eis futurum sit qui circumcisionem & promissiones Dei coniunctas contempserint. Cir-
units.tr: The particular explanation of this covenant is set out from verse 4 onward. For first the undertaking, or promise, of God in verse 2 is explained in five verses; then the stipulation of verse 9. Here three parts of the undertaking or promise that God makes to Abraham must be distinguished. The first is about the divine blessing in bestowing heirs, verse 4 and the two following. The second is about the substance of the eternal covenant itself, from which all the other blessings flow as from a fountain, verse 7. The third is the promise of an earthly inheritance, as a symbol foreshadowing our heavenly inheritance, verse 8. All these things are set out at the beginning, at the start of verse 4, in the words "Behold my covenant is with you," and afterwards they are explained one by one. The promise of heirs is made in general terms, by word and by sign. By word, verse 4, in the words "you shall be a father of a multitude of nations," that is, of many nations, as Paul explained this hypallage. By sign, in the following verse, when God says, "Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but shall be..." and so on. For a free He was added to the name Abram from the Hebrew word hamon [המון], meaning multitude; and so from Abram, which means "high father," Abraham was made by two words being shortened, as if you said "father of a great multitude." Indeed, countless examples show quite clearly that names are shortened when they are compounded among the Hebrews. Afterwards the manner of this posterity is described in verse 6: first in general, that God will make Abraham's posterity increase as much as possible; then particularly, in two ways: first by the arrangement of many nations from this one root; and second by dignity and majesty, in that kings would come forth from Abraham, so that he might show that Abraham would have very many and very great descendants. Once this promise has been explained, namely that the substance of the promises would reach Abraham and all his heirs, God immediately adds a second point, verse 7, concerning the substance of the covenant that would come to Abraham and his heirs. Before we come to its summary, two circumstances are brought forward concerning this covenant; for these two are the parts of the seventh verse: the circumstances, and the summary of the covenant. There is one summary of the circumstances: that God established the covenant to be common with Abraham and his seed to come after him, through their generations, whether the order is continued or interrupted through human weakness. The other is that it will be an eternal covenant, that is, (to speak as the Schoolmen do) unending. The summary of the covenant is that God will be God to Abraham and his seed after him. For the word "God" in this expression is relative, as is clear from many passages of Moses and the Prophets, and from the different words in Hosea 1 and 2. The relation of this promise is shown where God is called the people of his people, and the people of his God, in turn. Above all, see Hosea 1, last chapter and verse: "I will say to him who is not my people, you are my people, and he shall say, my God." For in this speech is contained entirely whatever can pertain to the true nature of that divine covenant. To these two parts of the promises a third is added, concerning the symbol of that heavenly inheritance that would come to the sons of Abraham, verse 8: "and I will give," he says, and so on. Thus these three parts of the promises are concluded, with their summary repeated, in the words "Finally, I will be God to them." And these things concern the divine promises. Next comes the stipulation, verse 9, in which God addresses Abram, so that he, with his posterity, may keep that covenant graciously entered into by God, by the obedience of faith and truth, as we set out in verse 1. To this substance of the divine covenant, which we have shown to be the first place in this chapter, is added the second part, concerning the sign accompanying the covenant. This sign is first set forth in summary in verse 10, then commanded with a singular promise in verse 11. Finally, certain particular points pertaining to the observance of the sign are prescribed in the three following verses. The sign is: "every male shall be circumcised"; to the observance of this sign, commanded in verse 10, its promise is attached in verse 11, namely that this sign would be a sign of the covenant between God and the posterity of Abraham. The particular points pertaining to the observance of this sign are prescribed as follows: first, who is to be circumcised and when, verse 12; second, to whom and when the promise will belong, verse 13; and finally, what will happen to those who despise circumcision and the promises of God joined together. Accordingly, all males are said to be circumcised, of every age, from the time they are eight days old. God commanded the eighth day precisely, because until that day whatever is born is regarded as unclean in its own blood.

units.la: cumcidendi ergo dicuntur omnes mares, omnibus ætatibus, ex quo diem octauum agunt. His dies octauus præcise à Deo imperatus est, quia ad illum usque diem quæcumque nascuntur, impura habentur in suo sanguine. Quapropter etiam non homines solum, verum etiam pecudes ante illum diem nefas erat offerri Domino, Exodi 23. & 31. Leuitici 12. Sed quia hac eadem occasione fortasse Iudæi fuissent existimaturi, non ergo alios, nec alio tempore circumcidi oportere: propterea definiuit Deus, non solum eos qui de Gente sunt Iudæorum, sed & alienigenas circumcidendos esse qui in Israelitarum potestate forent, siue nascerentur domi, quos octauo die à natiuitate circumcidi oportuit; siue pecunia empti essent & mancipia Iudæorum effecti quocumque modo, qui similiter octauo die ex quo fuerant comparati, & in potestatem Iudæorum venerant circumcidebantur. Illius instituti sederis & signi eodem pertinentis communicatio præcise mandatur verf. 13. etiam cum alienigenis, si modo vlla ratione ad populum Dei pertinerent, siue natalibus, siue emptione. Ex quo sequitur multò magis in sederatis censeri oportere eos qui fide cum Abrahamo communicant.
units.tr: Those to be circumcised are therefore called all males, at every age, from the eighth day of life. God commanded the eighth day precisely, because until that day whatever is born is regarded as unclean in its blood. For this reason it was not lawful to offer to the Lord even animals before that day (Exodus 23 and 31; Leviticus 12). But because on this same occasion the Jews might have supposed that others were not to be circumcised, nor at any other time, God ordained that not only those who are of the nation of the Jews but also foreigners who were under the power of the Israelites should be circumcised. Those born in the household had to be circumcised on the eighth day after birth. Those bought with money and made slaves of the Jews by any means were likewise circumcised on the eighth day after they had been acquired and had come into the power of the Jews. The communication of this institution and of the covenant and sign belonging to it is commanded precisely in verse 13, even to foreigners, if in any way they belonged to the people of God, whether by birth or by purchase. From this it follows that much more should those be counted within the covenant who share in faith with Abraham.

units.la: Deinde verò mandato subnectitur sua promissio ad omnes pertinens natos in sedere, aut etiam aduenas, altera parte versus. Eritque foedus meum, id est, signum foederis, in carne vestra in fedus perpetuum. Ex hac promissione profluit tertius locus verf. 14: nempe denuntiatio in eos qui circumcisionis vsum sedere imperatum contempserint: nempe cum qui non fuerit circumcisus carne præputij sui, excisum iri. Hic autem obseruandum est retinendam esse propriam coniugationis passiuæ significationem: tamquam si dixisset Moses, Qui non circumciderit se carne præputij sui, id est circumcidendum se curauerit. Quapropter inanis est eorum quæstio qui de pueris incircumcisis disputant, atque hanc mortis denuntiationem ad illos statuunt pertinere. Non enim hic de infantibus qui nesciunt discernere dextram à sinistra (vt scriptura loquitur) sed de contemptoribus, qui circumcidi carnem suam in sese aut in suis certa malitia neglexerint. Atque hæc interpretatio ratione demonstratur posita in fine versus, Fedus meum irritum fecit, Nam actiones voluntatis sunt, quæ in pueris aut ignorantibus sederis eodem loco haberi non potuerant atque in iis qui voluntarie peccauerunt. Hic duæ quæstiones incidunt: Vna, cur ergo rebelles Israelitas illos qui proterue circumcisionem spreuerant, & quorum præputia circumcisa sunt in colle præputiatorum ad Gilgalem, Iosuæ 5, Moses non curauit è medio tolli, prout Deus hoc loco imperauerat: Altera, cur mares solum signum sederis habuerint. buerint. Ad priorem respondemus duobus modis. Primum enim impij illi qui nec se nec filios suos circumciderant, ij sunt quibus propter rebellionem perfidiamque Deus fore denuntiauerat ut ca-derent in deserto: atque ex eo casu tantum excipiebantur ij qui vi-gesimum annum minimè excellissent, Num. 14. Cùm itaque Deus illis suam poenam denuntiauisset, non potuit, nec debuit Moses tentare amplius quàm singulari sententia Deus pronuntiauerat. Deinde verò & hoc obseruandum est, politica ratione Deum Mosi consuluit se: id autem politici hominis est, ut in publico peccato parcatur publico: non autem omnia summo iure, pro ut singularia peccata merita sunt cruententur: quam legem natura ipsa gentes etiam infidelissimas docuit, adeò ut in confusionibus etiam militaribus, quæ remedia postulant acria & præsentissima, Romani centesimare, vicesimare, decimare cohortes maluerint, quàm omnia rigidè per omnes persequi. Atque ex hoc exemplo confirmatur magis illud quod ante dicebamus. nam patres rebelles, qui auctores erant liberis ne circumciderentur, multati sunt sententia Dei: liberi verò, quos patres sua rebellione detinuerant ne circumciderentur, nec eam docuerant, illi sunt excusati: & circumcisio demum in primo Cenahanæ aditu restituta, Iosue 5. De altera quæstione, Respondetur vulgò & verum est, mares propterea solùm circumcidi, quia illi soli præ-putium habent: Deinde, quia sunt auctores generationis. Sed tertium etiam subest quod à pleriisque interpretibus non fuit obser-vatum: nempe in maribus secundum ordinem, cuius meminit Apo-stolus 1. Corinth. 11. typum quemdam singularem esse & cæremo-nialem Christi, quapropter ad illos res ipsa circumcisionis cæremo-niáque pertinuit; ad fœminas, virtus solùm & efficacitas. Atque hanc quidem cæremonialem fuisse & typicam institutionem de-monstrat sanguinis effusio. Nam circumcisionem sine sanguine non fuisse factam scriptura & natura clamant. Sanguinis autem omnis effusio in Vetere Testamento, Typica fuit futuræ effusionis illius, quæ unica est efficax pro peccatis nostris. Quapropter in Sacra-mentis Testamenti Noui iublata est sanguinis effusio, eò quòd con-summata fuerit in Christo veritas: & tamen eadem sacramenta Noui Testamenti, tum circumcisionis ἀχειροποιήτου Coloss. 2. tum spiritualis Paschatis appellantur. Sequitur locus secundus capi-tis, in quo ostenditur fides Abrahami, & singularis locus ex-plicatur de semine eius. Ad hanc narrationem transitur occa-sione à Deo oblata, verf. 15. & 16. Deinde fides Abrahami narra-tur modestiáque, verf. 17. & 18. Postremò autem singulares Dei promissiones amplius exponuntur,inde ad 22. versum. Occasionem dicitur Deus attulisse ex nomine Sarai, eo quòd primum mutationem nominis illius imperat v. 15. deinde rationem mutationis adfert,v.16. Mutationem nominis varij interpretantur varie. Nobis sic videtur paucis. Nomen Sarai nõ fuisse formae Hebreae,sed Chaldaicę vnde migrauerat, ac proinde praecepisse Dominum vt ne nomine quidem cum vetere illo fermento Chaldaeorum communicaret. Mandato adiungitur promissio, v. 16. cuius membra duo sunt: prius singulare;posterius, commune: singulare est, benedicam ei, quia fons omnium bonorum est Dei benedictio, deinde ne forte promissum illud benedictionis aliter acciperetur quàm prout sentiebat Dominus,circumscribitur post, dabo tibi ex illa filium. Commune membrum est altera parte versus: quo primum benedictio, vt ante, deinde benedictionis huius circumscriptio adhibetur eadem quae supra v.6. Ex hac oblata diuinitus occasione dicitur Abraham primùm promissionem illam Dei grato animo accepisse in fide, v.17. deinde verò modestam postulationem huic postulationi diuinae subiecisse, v. 18. Prehensam fide promissionem Dei testatur Moses duobus modis: signis,priore membro versus: & admiratione cum animo suo,posteriore membro. Signa acquiescentis animi & promissa diuina percipientis duo sunt: proclinatio siue adoratio, & risus ex praecepta mentis laetitia proficiscens. Interna verò admiratio non ex diffidentia,sed ex reuerentia profecta est: quaAbraham non spectauit vires effaetas suas, aut Sarae corpus emortuum, vt loquitur Apostolus Rom. 4. sed sub spe contra spem credidit, sciens eum qui promiserat potentem esse, & acquieuit Dei promissionibus: quemadmodum etiam Onkelos paraphrastes Chaldęus hunc locum optime intellexit. Modesta petitio illius. verf. 18. ex argumento eodem proficiscitur. Nam videtur Abraham ex consequentibus ita percepisse promissionem Dei de filio ex Sara tolledo,vt sollicitudo de Ismaele animum eius incesserit. Quapropter Deum modeste orauit vt Ismael coram Domino viueret, id est,si Deus(vt promiserat)alterum filium daturus esset,ne hic propterea ex vita aut promissionibus excluderetur; quam sollicitudinem Abraham modestè per modum optati explicat, non recusans rei futurae promissum,sed praesens bonum insuper conseruari petens: quod postulatum Deus annuit sequentibus. Itaque responsionis Dei ad hoc postulatum duae sunt partes:propositio,v.18:& expositio, duobus sequentibus.Propositionis partes sunt duae: vna,Sara paritu-ram esse, & partui illius nomen fore Isaacum ex Abrahami risu. Altera, illud aeternum Dei fedus, de quo prima parte cap. huius dictum est, in Isaaco permansurum esse ac posteritate illius. Expositionis autem quæ fit per comparationem, partes sunt duæ: nam prius membrum comparationis de Ismaele, vers. 20. Posterius de Isaaco v. seq. legitur. Summa est, Deum utrique benedicturum; sed Isaaco maximè æterni sederis communicatione. Occasione Deus proponit, Abrahami preces: nam aures Dei inclinant ad preces invocantium se: benedictionum modus idem est cum antecedentibus, vt vers. 6. & 7. unde hæc omnia verba fermè petita sunt. Id unū singulare est, quod de Ismaele duodecim principes dicūtur exstituri, cuius rei complementum infra 25. v. 12. à Mose ostenditur: de Isaaco verò, quòd eadem tempestate anno proximo nascituri dicitur, vt etiam cap. seq. Cuius rei complementum exstat cap. 21. Sic concluduntur hæ duæ partes capitis v. 22, cùm Deus absoluto sermone ab Abrahamo dicitur discessisse. Restat iam tertius locus de obsequio fidei, quo Abraham de sedere diuino confirmatus signum illius sibi familiæque toti applicauit. Quæ res universè enuntiatur, 23. v. Deinde verò amplificatur certis circumstantiis, versibus reliquis. Ac primùm quidem illud est, vers. 23. quòd eo ipso die Abraham circumcisionem instituit prout Deus imperauerat; neque cōsilium ex carne aut sanguine petiit. Secunda circumstantia accedit vers. 24. quòd Abraham natus annos 99. se circumcidi non modò passus est, sed etiam curauit, vt Deo in fide obsequeretur, cū tamen illa ætas & huic actui ineptior & ad curationem incommodior, & persona in speciem grauior fuerit, quàm vt sese coram domesticis nudari pateretur. Tertia circumstantia est à persona Ismaelis, qui ex promissione Dei particeps benedictionum similiter fuit circumcisus. Quarta denique circumstantia est, quod omnes sine exceptione uno eodémque die fuerunt circumcisi, ac proinde omnes eodem tempore fuerunt in dolore, ita ut perincommodè sese omnes eodem tempore habuerint ad rerum domesticarum siue communium siue priuatarum & singularium procurationem.
units.tr: Then, after the command, God's promise is added, applying to all the males born in the house or even to strangers, in the second part of the verse: And my covenant shall be, that is, the sign of the covenant, in your flesh for an everlasting covenant. From this promise there follows the third point, in verse 14: a threat against those who despise the use of circumcision commanded for the covenant. The threat is that the uncircumcised male, whose flesh of the foreskin is not circumcised, shall be cut off. Here it must be observed that the passive sense of the verb must be kept, as if Moses had said, "He who has not circumcised himself in the flesh of his foreskin," that is, who has not seen to it that he is circumcised. Therefore the question of those who dispute about uncircumcised boys, and who hold that this threat of death applies to them, is pointless. For this does not concern infants, who do not know how to tell right from left (as Scripture puts it), but contemptuous people who, by deliberate malice, have neglected to circumcise their own flesh or that of their children. This interpretation is also shown by the reason given at the end of the verse: He has broken my covenant. For these are acts of the will, which could not be attributed to boys or to those ignorant of the covenant in the same way as to those who sinned wilfully. Two questions arise here. The first: why did Moses not, as God had commanded in this place, remove from among the people those rebellious Israelites who had insolently rejected circumcision, and whose foreskins were circumcised on the hill of foreskins at Gilgal (Joshua 5)? The second: why did only males have the sign of the covenant? To the first we reply in two ways. First, those impious men who circumcised neither themselves nor their sons are those whom God, because of their rebellion and faithlessness, had declared would fall in the wilderness. Only those who were not yet twenty years old were excepted from that fate (Numbers 14). Since God had pronounced his punishment on them, Moses could not, and ought not, to attempt more than God had decreed in his particular sentence. Second, this too must be observed: God consulted Moses on the basis of political prudence. It belongs to the political man that a public sin be spared by the public, and that not everything be punished with full rigour of law as individual sins deserve. Nature itself taught this law even to the most unfaithful nations, so that in military mutinies, where sharp and immediate remedies are needed, the Romans preferred to decimate, or to execute every twentieth or hundredth man of the cohorts, rather than to pursue everything rigidly against all. And from this example what we said before is confirmed more strongly. For the fathers, the rebels who were the instigators of their children's failure to be circumcised, were punished by God's sentence. But the children, whom their fathers' rebellion had kept from circumcision, and who had not been taught it, were excused. Circumcision was finally restored at the first entry into Canaan (Joshua 5). As to the second question, it is commonly answered, and it is true, that only males are circumcised because they alone have the foreskin, and also because they are the authors of generation. But there is also a third reason, which most interpreters have not observed: in males, according to the order of which the Apostle speaks (1 Corinthians 11), the act of circumcision and its ceremony pertained to a certain singular and ceremonial type of Christ, whereas for females there was only the virtue and efficacy. That this institution was ceremonial and typical is shown by the shedding of blood. For Scripture and nature alike declare that circumcision was not performed without blood. Moreover, every shedding of blood in the Old Testament was a type of that future shedding which alone is efficacious for our sins. Therefore in the sacraments of the New Testament the shedding of blood has been removed, because the truth has been accomplished in Christ. And yet these sacraments of the New Testament are called, both the circumcision made without hands [ἀχειροποιήτου] (Colossians 2) and the spiritual Passover. The second point of the chapter follows, in which Abraham's faith is shown and the singular passage concerning his seed is explained. The narrative passes to this occasion offered by God, in verses 15 and 16. Then Abraham's faith and modesty are related, in verses 17 and 18. Lastly, God's singular promises are further set out, from verse 19 onward. God is said to have provided the occasion from the name Sarai, since first he commands the change of her name (verse 15), and then gives the reason for the change (verse 16). Interpreters explain the change of name in various ways. To us it seems, in brief, as follows. The name Sarai was not in the Hebrew form but in the Chaldean, from which Abraham had migrated; and so the Lord commanded that she should not even share the name with that old leaven of the Chaldeans. The command is joined to a promise (verse 16), which has two parts: the first is particular, the second common. The particular part is I will bless her, because God's blessing is the source of all good things. Then, lest that promise of blessing be understood otherwise than the Lord intended, it is qualified: I will give you a son by her. The common part is in the second half of the verse, in which first the blessing, as before, and then the qualification of this blessing are applied, the same as those above in verse 6. From this occasion given divinely, Abraham is said first to have received that promise of God with a thankful heart, in faith (verse 17); and then to have added a modest request to this divine promise (verse 18). Moses bears witness that Abraham grasped God's promise by faith in two ways: by signs, in the first part of the verse, and by inward wonder, in the second part. The signs of a mind that acquiesces and receives the divine promise are two: prostration, or adoration, and laughter, arising from the joy of a mind that is exulting. The inward wonder, however, arose not from distrust but from reverence: for Abraham did not look at his own spent strength or at Sarah's dead body, as the Apostle says (Romans 4), but against hope, in hope believed, knowing that he who had promised was powerful, and he acquiesced in God's promises. Onkelos the Chaldee paraphrast also understood this passage very well. Abraham's modest request (verse 18) proceeds from the same argument. For Abraham seems to have understood God's promise of a son by Sarah in such a way, from what followed, that anxiety about Ishmael stole into his mind. Therefore he modestly prayed that Ishmael might live before the Lord, that is, that if God, as he had promised, was going to give another son, Ishmael should not for that reason be excluded from life or from the promises. Abraham explains this anxiety modestly, in the manner of a wish, not refusing the promise of the future thing but asking that the present good be preserved besides; and God granted this request in what follows. Thus God's response to this request has two parts: the proposition (verse 18) and the explanation in the two following verses. The proposition has two parts. One is that Sarah will bear a child, and that the child will be named Isaac from Abraham's laughter. The other is that that eternal covenant of God, of which the first part of this chapter spoke, will remain in Isaac and in his posterity. The explanation, which is given by way of comparison, has two parts: the first member of the comparison concerns Ishmael (verse 20), and the second concerns Isaac, read in the following verse. The sum is that God will bless both, but Isaac especially by the communication of the eternal covenant. God takes up the occasion from Abraham's prayers, for the ears of God incline to the prayers of those who call upon him. The manner of the blessings is the same as before, as in verses 6 and 7, from which nearly all these words are taken. The only singular thing is that of Ishmael it is said that twelve princes will arise, the fulfilment of which Moses shows below in 25:12. Of Isaac it is said that he will be born at this season in the next year, as also in the following chapter, whose fulfilment is found in chapter 21. Thus these two parts of the chapter are concluded in verse 22, when, the discourse having ended, God is said to have departed from Abraham. There remains the third point, concerning the obedience of faith, by which Abraham, confirmed by the divine covenant, applied its sign to himself and to his whole household. This is stated in general terms in verse 23, and then it is amplified by certain circumstances in the remaining verses. The first circumstance, in verse 23, is that on that very day Abraham instituted circumcision, as God had commanded, and did not seek counsel from flesh or blood. A second circumstance is added in verse 24: that Abraham, being ninety-nine years old, not only submitted to circumcision but also saw to it, so that he might obey God in faith, although that age was both less suited to this act and less fit for healing, and his person was more grave in appearance, than that he should allow himself to be stripped before his household. The third circumstance concerns the person of Ishmael, who, as a sharer in the blessings by God's promise, was likewise circumcised. The fourth circumstance, finally, is that all, without exception, were circumcised on one and the same day, and therefore all were in pain at the same time, so that they all were very much hindered at the same time in the management of household affairs, both common and private and particular.

units.la: CAPITIS XVIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVIII ANALYSIS.

units.la: Huius[?] capitis finis est, ut fidem veritatemque promissionum Dei videamus: summa, fidelibus suis & fidem suam instituto vitæ comprobantibus Deum vicissim probare fidem ac veritatem suam, tum erga ipsos, tum erga alios ipsorum causa. Itaque tres sunt huius capitis partes: quarum prima, fides & obsequium fidei in Abrahamo ostenditur ad vers. usque
units.tr: The purpose of this chapter[?] is that we may see the faithfulness and truth of God's promises. In sum: God, in turn, proves his own faithfulness and truth both towards his people, who confirm their faith by the course of their lives, and towards others for their sake. Accordingly, the chapter has three parts. The first, which runs as far as verse 8, shows the faith of Abraham and the obedience that flows from faith. The second, from there to verse 21, shows the truth of the promises and the communication of God's counsels. The last, which runs to the end of the chapter, shows God's most ready blessing towards strangers at the prayer of his household.

units.la: 8.Secúda,veritas promissionū,& consiliorū Dei communicatio,inde ad v.21. Postrema denique promptissima Dei benedictio erga extraneos ad domesticorum suorum preces, inde ad finem capitis.
units.tr: 8. The second part, the truth of the promises and the communication of God's counsels, runs from there to verse 21. The last part, God's most ready blessing towards strangers at the prayers of his household, runs from there to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Primi loci, quo fides Abrahami & obsequium fidei ostenditur, summa posita est in hospitalitatis officiis: quorum occasio, verf. 1. modus, sequentibus exponitur. Occasionem Deus obtulit: temporis opportunitatem Abraham obseruauit, vt peregrinis ex diei æstu laborantibus succurreret. Hospitalitatis officia deinceps exponuntur: primùm studio, quòd diligenter obseruaret si qui viatores aduentarent:tum blando occursu & salutatione, verf.2. Præterea ınuitatione officiosissima, qua tunc illos subsistere apud se petit,& prensat singulos, verf. 3. dum omnia hospitis officia spondet ad viatores recreandos, puta lotionis & vmbraculi, verf. 4. Prætereáque cibarij, & cautionis de mora non iniicienda facturis iter, verf.5. Quam conditionem illi dicuntur accepisse. Postremò quòd singula illa officia tum per se ipse, tum per vxorem,administrósque procurauit diligentissimè: vxori & gynæceo panes imperans, sibi hoc munus asseruans vt vitulum de armento deligeret,famulóque parare iuberet;interea butyrum & lac ad refrigerium afferens;conuiuas denique excipiens humanissimè. Ex hac occasione, quam Deus ipse obtulerat, idem nouam occasionem captauit conferendi cum Abrahamo. Huius autem sermonis duæ sunt partes; vna repetitio promissi de semine, ad verf. vsque 16. Altera, consilij de quinque ciuitatibus perdendis communicatio, inde ad verf. 21. Sermonem de promisso semine sic Deus ingreditur, verf. 9. vt se Deum esse non obscurè patefaciat, cùm dicit, vbi est Sara vxor tua? Atque hac occasione promissio de Isaaco post annum complenda repetitur verf. 10. & euentus quidam subnectitur, quo Deus amplius declarauit præsentiam maiestatis suæ: nempe quòd Sara audiuit, verf. 10. & risit, ac ludificata est,non habens fidem, verf. 12. Cuius infidelis risus, causa exponitur, [?]παρα̈θέσεως verf.11.pro vt ipsius Sarę verba demonstrant sequente versu.Hinc reprehensio facta diuinitus,verf.13.& 14. Et negatis Sarę ex metu iterata reprehensio,verf.15.cuius reprehensionis causa summa affertur,versu 14.Quòd Iehoua est qui promissiones istas eloquitur,cui neque est occultum quidquam quin sciat,neque [?]ἀδύνατον quin possit. His sermonibus habitis conuiuas discessuros Abraham dicitur prosequutus,versu 16. Quod officium noui sermonis cómunicatione Deus muneratus est,nempe de iudicio in vrbes proximas exsequendo. In hoc sermone duæ sunt partes. Vna est, [illegible, ~6 letters],qua disceptare videtur Deus vtrum hoc institutū sit cum Abrahamo cōmunicaturus, ad verf.vsq; 19:Altera est ipsa rei communicatio, verf. 20. & seq. Illius [illegible, ~5 letters] propositio fit ver. 17. Deinde causae adferuntur cur Deus communicandam rem cum Abrahamo statuat: nempe quod promissiones suas temporales & aeternas, corporales & spirituales iam cum eo communicauerit, v. 18. Secundò, quòd eum Deus agnoscat, qui fons omnium benedictionum est, & gratuito amore prosequatur. Tertiò, quòd hac via futurum est ut Abraham magis ac magis informetur ad docendam pietatem in Ecclesia Dei. Postremò, quòd hac eadem via Deus promissiones suas completurus est, v. 19. His igitur de causis ad propositionem instituti Deus venisse dicitur: cuius partes duae sunt; una, de causa instituti, nempe impietate & iniustitia Sedomitarum, verf. 20: Altera, de substantia instituti, quòd Deus velit cognoscere, & re cognita dispicere quae facto sint opus: quae omnia dicuntur humanitus, ut & studium suum erga creaturas testetur Deus, & nostrum informet: inprimis autem eorum quibus mandata est iuris dicundi auctoritas, nequid faciant temere.
units.tr: The summary of the first part, in which Abraham's faith and the obedience of faith are shown, lies in the duties of hospitality. The occasion is given in verse 1, and the manner is set out in what follows. God offered the occasion, and Abraham watched for the opportunity of helping travellers who were suffering from the heat of the day. The duties of hospitality are then set out. First, with eagerness, in that he carefully watched whether any travellers were approaching; then with a friendly meeting and greeting (verse 2). Besides this, with a most dutiful invitation, in which he asks them to stay with him and presses each of them (verse 3), while he promises every service of a host for refreshing the travellers, namely washing and shade (verse 4). Further, he offers food, and a guarantee that there will be no delay to those about to continue their journey (verse 5), which they are said to have accepted as a condition. Last, he himself and his wife and servants took care of each of these duties most diligently: he orders bread from his wife and the women's quarters, reserves for himself the task of choosing a calf from the herd and ordering a servant to prepare it, meanwhile bringing butter and milk for refreshment, and finally receiving the guests most kindly. From this occasion, which God himself had offered, the same God seized a new occasion of conferring with Abraham. This conversation has two parts. One is the repetition of the promise about the seed, up to verse 16. The other is the communication of the plan to destroy the five cities, from there to verse 21. God begins the discourse about the promised seed (verse 9) in such a way that he makes plain that he is God, when he says, "Where is Sarah your wife?" On this occasion the promise about Isaac, to be fulfilled after a year, is repeated (verse 10), and an incident is added by which God declared more fully the presence of his majesty: namely, that Sarah heard (verse 10), laughed and mocked, not having faith (verse 12). The cause of this faithless laughter is explained by a [parathesis: juxtaposition] in verse 11, as the words of Sarah herself show in the following verse. Hence a rebuke was given by God (verses 13 and 14). And when Sarah denied it out of fear, the rebuke was repeated (verse 15), and the chief reason for the rebuke is given in verse 14: because it is Jehovah who speaks these promises, to whom nothing is hidden that he does not know, and nothing [adynaton: impossible] that he cannot do. Having held these discourses, Abraham is said to have accompanied the guests as they set off (verse 16). God rewarded this duty with the communication of a new discourse, namely about the execution of judgement on the neighbouring cities. In this discourse there are two parts. One is [illegible], in which God seems to deliberate whether he is to communicate this plan to Abraham (up to verse 19). The other is the communication of the matter itself (verse 20 and following). The proposition of the former is made in verse 17. Then the reasons are given why God decides to share the matter with Abraham: namely, that he has already communicated to him his promises, temporal and eternal, bodily and spiritual (verse 18). Second, that God acknowledges him as the one who is the source of all blessings and loves him with free love. Third, that in this way Abraham will be more and more instructed to teach godliness in the Church of God. Last, that by this same way God is going to fulfil his promises (verse 19). For these reasons, then, God is said to have come to the proposition of the plan. It has two parts: one concerning the cause of the plan, namely the impiety and injustice of the Sodomites (verse 20); the other concerning the substance of the plan, that God wishes to know, and, having known the matter, to examine what needs to be done. All these things are said in human terms, so that God may both bear witness to his care for his creatures and instruct ours, especially of those to whom the authority of judging has been entrusted, lest they do anything rashly.

units.la: Tertius locus cap. effecta exponit promissionum Dei tum in piis & a piis ipsis proficiscentia, tum a Deo erga ipsos collata, & aliis ipsorum causa exhibita secundum promissionem Dei supra cap. undecimo sive duodecimo, ut vulgo distinguitur. Benedicam benedic. &c. In hac itaque parte duo observanda sunt: Unum, de piorum studio, officio, precibusque: Alterum de beneficio Dei ad piorum preces tum collato singulariter, tum communiter exhibito. Piorum studium est charitas, quam Abraham in animo sensit commotus antecedente illa Dei communicatione. Officiorum vero est genus duplex: unum intercessionis opere, alterum sermone. Opere intercessisse Abrahamum seorsim coram Domino, prout pietatis & charitatis lex flagitat, confirmat Moses his verbis vers. 12. Stetit Abraham adhuc coram Iehoua. Nam stare coram Iehoua Hebraeis est ministrare ipsi ex officio nostro, aut pro aliis intercedere, quaedam modo Sacerdotes, hac phrasi proprie denotatur Leuit. 4. Deut. 10. & alibi. Officium vero intercessionis quam diligenter fecit Abraham, cum narratione prima vers. 23. & duobus seqq. tum repetitionibus eiusdem narrationis inde ad vers. pen. ostenditur. Intercessionis loci duo sunt. Nam primum propositio argumenti ad intercessione pertinentis instituitur v. 23. his verbis, An etiam consumpturus esses &c. Quae argumentatio sumpta est a iustitia Dei. Deinde vero propositionis illius exornatio subiicitur duobus seqq. Cum ex hypothesi v. 24. quaestatuitur, si vel 50. iusti exstiterint in loco, alienum fore ut Dominus locum perdat, per deprecationem. Deinde vero deprecationis eiusdem argumentum affirmatur, v.25. Tum per figuram quam rhetores apo-copen vocant, tum verò per simplicem affirmationem sumptam ex natura Dei, nunquam futurum vt iudex totius terrae, qui incorruptus est, ius dicat aut exerceat iniuste. Huic pietati Abrahami annuit Dominus v.26. & gratiam se loco facturum spondet ex hypothesi quam Abraham attulerat. Quapropter miratus Abraham gradatim de hypothesi instituta minuit, vt gratiae diuinae documenta augeat, inde à v.27. praemissa tamen modesta excusatione & deprecatione infirmitatis suae, sed quia tota haec gradatio vnius est argumenti, fidele piorum officium in charitate & constantissimum Dei beneficium in faciendâ gratia explicans, non sumus in hoc argumento diutius immoraturi, tandem caput concluditur narratione discessus Dei ab Abrahamo, in versu vltimo.
units.tr: The third part of the chapter sets out the effects of God's promises, both those that proceed from the godly and from God through the godly, and those that were given by God to them and shown to others for their sake, according to the promise of God in chapter eleven or twelve, as it is commonly divided: I will bless those who bless you, etc. In this part two things are to be observed. One is the eagerness, duty and prayers of the godly; the other is the benefit of God, given to the prayers of the godly both singularly and in common. The eagerness of the godly is love, which Abraham felt in his mind, stirred by that earlier communication from God. There are two kinds of duty: one by the work of intercession, the other by speech. That Abraham interceded by work, alone before the Lord, as the law of godliness and charity demands, Moses confirms in these words, verse 22: Abraham still stood before Jehovah. For to stand before Jehovah, among the Hebrews, means to minister to him from our office, or to intercede for others, as the priests did; and this phrase properly denotes that (Lev. 4; Deut. 10; and elsewhere). How diligently Abraham performed the duty of intercession is shown first by the initial narrative in verse 23 and the two following verses, and then by the repetitions of the same narrative up to the penultimate verse. There are two places of intercession. For first the proposition of the argument pertaining to intercession is set out in verse 23, in these words: Will you indeed destroy, etc. This argument is taken from the justice of God. Then the embellishment of that proposition is added in the two following verses. For from a hypothesis (verse 24) he asks whether, if there should be even fifty righteous in the place, it would be inappropriate for the Lord to destroy the place, by way of entreaty. Then the argument of that entreaty is affirmed (verse 25), both by the figure which the rhetoricians call apocope, and by plain affirmation taken from the nature of God: that it will never happen that the judge of all the earth, who is incorrupt, should judge or act unjustly. The Lord assents to this piety of Abraham (verse 26) and promises to spare the place for the sake of the hypothesis Abraham had put forward. Wherefore Abraham, marvelling, gradually diminishes the hypothesis, so that he may increase the proofs of divine grace, from verse 27 onward, having first made a modest excuse and a plea for his own weakness. But since this whole gradation belongs to one argument, explaining the faithful duty of the godly in charity and the most constant benefit of God in granting grace, we are not going to dwell longer on this argument. At last the chapter is concluded with the narrative of God's departure from Abraham, in the last verse.

units.la: CAPITIS XIX ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 19.

units.la: ANTECEDENTI communicationi factę diuinitus cō-modè subiicitur in hoc capite narratio exsequutionis, qua Deus se veracem in minis & promissionibus demo-strauit. Summa igitur est, Deum misertum Loti propter fedus suum & promissiones sederis Abrahamo factas Lotum seruasse, & impios perdidisse: sed Lotum salute à Deo acceptâ turpissimè ex infirmitate abusum esse: cuius infirmitatis monimentum Deus exstare voluit ad aedificationem Ecclesiae suae. Partes itaque huius capitis sunt tres. Prima occasionem rerum à Deo gestarum continet, ad v. vsque 9: secunda res gestas, inde ad v.30: tertia denique indignum abusum ex infirmitate fidei proficiscentem, ad finē vsq; capitis. Occasionum, vt rerum gestarum, duo sunt loci. Nam primum narratur occasio salutis in Lotum collatae, tribus versibus: deinde verò subuersionis qua Deus Sedomū & ciuitates alias pessum-dedit, ad v.vsque 9. Occasio quam Lot obtulisse dicitur, est pietas in Deum, & pietatis fructus humanitas, ac hospitalitas persimilis illi quam principio capitis praecedens exposuimus. Nam & studium Loti v. 1. & officiū accursu, salutatione, inuitatione, v.2. Et hospitali impor-tunitate, conuiuioque, v.3. ostenditur. Vnica incidit quaestio, cur Angeli recusauerint, negauerintque id quod postea fecisse dicuntur. Resp. est, in hoc angelorum facto non esse mendacium, sed dissimulatio-nē: nam mendacium per se malum esse, sed dissimulationem mediam. Cū autem res mediae actionesq; in rebus moralibus formam suam ex intentione solet[?] accipere, tū demū dissimulationem fieri malam, cū malis mediis ad malā intentionē contenditur: alioqui bonā dissimu-lationem. lationé esse, si mediis non malis ad bonũ finem referatur. Hic autem neque mala sunt media, neque finis malus. Nam finis erat, vt tum Loti studium acuerent, tum etiam occasionem darent sciscitandæ causæ, cur in platea pernoctare ipsos oporteret. Postremò etiam prudentiæ fuit illud, ne qua Sedomitis exardescendi in peregrinum Lotum occasio præberetur. Modus verò non fuit malus, cum Lotho negarent: non enim simpliciter negabant se facturos esse; sed tantum negabant, se ea de causa aduenille; quin potius in eum finem, vt in platea pernoctarent. Aliud est autem siquis simpliciter se facturum negauerit, & consilio certo, quod tamen costituit facere; aliud autem si non simpliciter negauerit sed respectu consilij, cuius causa aduenerit: cuiusmodi responsiones aliquot à Christo in Testamento Nouo leguntur datæ, vt cum diceret matri, Ioh. 2: Quid mihi tecum, fœmina? nondum venit hora mea. Itémque fratribus Ioh. 7: Vos ite in festum &c. & aliis aliquot locis. Alter occasionis locus est, de Sedomitarum præsente impietate, inhumanitate & iniustitia, ob quam Deus executus est iudicia quæ in eos prænuntiauerat. Hoc autem crimen in eo positum est; primùm quòd hospites Loti ad nefariam suam libidinem explendam petiuerunt illi, v.4. & 5. Secundò quòd Loti verbis nulla ratione acquieuerunt; sed omnes conatus adhibuerunt vt optata perficerent, versibus seqq. In priore membro primùm circumstantiis quibusdam crimen amplificatur v.4. & quinti parte. Deinde scelerata illorum postulatio exponitur, reliquo v.5. In circumstantiis sunt hæc: tempus, cùm nondum cubuissent: modus, quòd domum circumdederunt & circumsederunt: numerus, quòd omnes omnis ætatis, ex omni vrbis parte accurrerunt, v.4. Postremò autem actio ipsa, quòd tamquam furibundi homines aut dementes Lotum inclamauerunt, vt voluntati ipsorum ministraret. Sermonis autem duæ sunt partes; quæstio, & mandatum: nam quæstione rogant vbi sunt Loti hospites: mandato verò tum eos coram se sisti iubent, tũ etiam horrendum suum consilium verbis minimè obscuris repetunt, dicentes, vt cognoscamus eos. nam cognoscendi verbo decore scriptura vtitur ad significandũ concubitum siue naturalem siue præter naturam, siue legitimum siue illegitimum: Hanc enim istorũ libidinè demonstrant verba deprecantis Loti in v. 7. cũ filias suas eorum loco spõdet se exhibiturum. Hanc impietatem & iniustitiam sequitur alter occasionis locus, quòd etiam in Lotum hospitalitatis iura colentem instituunt furere. Itaque tum Loti hospitalis verba v. 6. 7. & 8. tum impiorum furores v. 9. proponuntur: Lot enim primùm ad illos dicitur prodiuisse v.6. & ianuam pone se occlusisse, ne forte irrumperent dum ageret cum ipsis, v.6. Deinde vero deprecationis loci duo adferuntur: quam deprecationem vbi simpliciter proposuit, v.7. tandem membratim exponit, v.8. Nam primum filias suas spondet insano populo, & quidem abutendas; quarum conditionem commendat etiam eo nomine quod nondum cognouissent virum. Deinde vero hac succedanea sponsione proposita, deprecatur nequid suis hospitibus fiat, & causam obtendit hospitalitatis, quae apud omnes etiam infideles Gentes semper habita est religiosissima. His rebus a Loto gestis opponitur Sedomitarum proteruia in verf. 9. qui sermone & facto suam impietatem expresserunt: sermone, tum quia Lotum a domo abductum iusserunt secedere vt scelerate inter se consultarent: tum quia consilium iniquissimum iniuerunt, cuius consilij causam & substantiam Moses paucis explicauit. Causam, quod vnum toti populo aduenam & peregrinum, ac non indigenam cum in hoc facto, tum in aliis fere omnibus, praeter officium, sibi tamquam iudicis partes arrogare statuerent; perinde atque si hominis inquilini & aduenae officium esset omnibus assentari, aduersari nemini, & aequum bonum habere promercale, vel eo nomine quod peregrinus est: Substantiam vero vel summam consilij, quod grauiora Loto denuntiant, nisi a deprecando desisterit. Facto autem demonstrauerunt impietatem suam, quod & in personam Loti, & in ianuam domus illius vi publica institerunt. Hactenus occasiones. Secundus locus de exsequutione iudiciorum Dei similiter duobus membris concluditur; quorum vnum est de liberatione quam Deus Loto praestitit, ad v. vsque 22. Alterum membrum est de Sedomitarum, aliorumque peccatorum subuersione, ad v. vsque 29. Ad liberationem Loti tria pertinent: primum, quod e medio furentis populi receptus est ver. 10. & 11. Secundum, quod consilium ipsi discessus datum est, & causa exposita, ver. 12. & duobus seqq. Postremo quod consilium effectum per ipsos, inde a versum 15. Liberationis ex medio populi duae sunt partes: Vna, quod emittentes manum, Lotum introduxerunt domum, ianuamque firmauerunt aduersus populum, verf. 10: Altera, quod populum vniuersum caecitate animi & corporis percusserunt, adeo vt sese frustra in porta quaerenda fatigauerint, v. 11. Secundi loci de consilio partes duae sunt: Vna ipsorum, v.12.& seq. altera Loti, v. 14. Ipsorum, quia Lotum cum omnibus suis personis & rebus loco iusserunt cedere, v. 12. & causam attulerunt, subuersionem diuinitus mox futuram, duobus nominibus: nempe propter grauitatem peccatorum quibus Sedomitae tenebantur, & propter decretum Dei exardescentis in peccata illorum, v.13. Hinc Loti partes sequuntur v.14. Quod generos suos quibus filiis desponderat, ad salutis participationem accersiuit ex mandato Dei & charitatis officio: sed surdis canebat Lot, quia fascinati eodem furore, illudi sibi à Loto iudicabant. Huic consilio successit Angelorum factum, qui Lotum cunctantem vrgebant, vt saluti ipsius consulerent: quapropter primum sermone vrsisse dicuntur v. 15. deinde vero opere, vt qui cunctantem Lotum familiamque illius manu prehenderunt, & extra oppidum deduxerunt, v. 16. Denique etiam res singulares ad salutem illius pertinentes communicauerunt, v. 17. & seqq. Explicato liberationis mandato, cuius effectionem Angeli sermone & opere procurauerunt, exponitur modus quo illa Loti cum familia liberatio effecta est, v.17. & seqq. Nam primum modus effugij imperatur Loto ciuitate egresso, v.17. Deinde Loto expostulanti & gra-tè[?] fugæ conditionem accipienti v.18. & duobus seqq. Deus pro misericordia sua ad demonstrandam veritatem promissionum suarum postulatum Loti annuit, v. 21. & seq. In mandato modò duæ partes continentur: Nam primum ratio itineris; secūdò meta siue statio indicitur. Ad rationē itineris duo pertinent; vnum, vt tantum cogitent de vitæ suæ conseruatione; alterum, vt propter hunc ipsum finem ab aliis omnibus cogitationibus vel occupationibus abstineant credentes & obsequentes mandato Dei. Quo in genere duo interdicta sunt, vnū, ne quisquam aspiciat retrorsum, id est, se domum versus, vnde profecti erant, tamquam indignè ferens aut loci aut rerū quæ in loco erant iacturam: alterum, ne consisterent in itinere, sed vno quasi spiritu imperatum iter perficerent. Meta vel statio itineris indicatur his verbis, ad monte, &c. Huic mandato subiicitur postulatū Loti, continens primū deprecationem, v.18. deinde postulatum, duobus seqq. Nam postulati causæ v.19. summa illius v. 20. exponuntur. Causarū postulati tres sunt loci: primus ab antecedēte Dei gratia, quę est ἀμεταμέλητος[?]. Secundus, à præsente beneficio salutis. Tertius, ab infirmitate Loti, quem si gradum sic accelerare oporteat, metus erat ne in ipso itinere prægrauatus infirmitate occumberet. Itaque duæ postremæ causæ ad vnam argumentationem quæ à fine est pertinent. Postulatum est, vt commoditate exiguæ vrbis, quæ in proximo erat, liceret vti, v. 20. Hoc postulatum annuit Deus, v.21. Ac proinde alterum mandatum substituit, verf.22. vt in exiguum illud oppidum sese proripiat saluis interea de reliquo conditionibus: quo ex sermone ad perpetuam rei memoriam ciuitati nomen fuit impositum. Alter iudiciorum locus est de exitio Sedomi, aliarūmque ciuitatum, à v. 23. ad 29. vsque. In hoc exitio tria ponuntur membra: nam primùm subuersio declara-tur, tribus versibus; deinde metamorphosis vxoris Loti, v.26. Poftre-mò, religiosa Abrahami obseruatio, duobus versibus sequentibus. In subuersione notantur ista: tempus, modus & actus. Tempus, v.23. Modus, v.24. quòd ignis sulphureus cælitus demissus est per Iehovam à Iehova, id est, per filium à Patre, quemadmodum orthodoxi Patres optimè interpretati sunt. Actus denique exprimitur v.25. verbis cuidentissimis. Huic iudicio alterum coniunctum est in vxorem Loti, propter infidele & immorigerum factum ipsius, v.26. nam factum est quòd retrorsum aspexit, id est, Sedomum versus præter virum suum qui subfe-quebatur ipsam: Iudicium, quòd statua salis effecta est; nam historiam hanc ad verbum (vt scripsit Moses) accipimus. Restat religiosa Abrahami obseruatio, qui pridie illius iudicij prænmonitus obseruauit diligenter quid factum esset, & tum iustitiam Dei admiratus est aduersus Sedomitas, v.27. & seq. tum gratiam Dei erga Lotum propter fedus gratiæ & promissiones sibi factas v.29. Tertius locus est de abusu, in quem homines procliues sunt acceptis Dei beneficiis, inde à v.30. ad finem vsque. Ostenditur illud exemplo Loti & filiarum ipsius. Nam primùm infirmitas Loti ostenditur in fide, v.30. deinde infirmitas in moribus & ratione vitæ, versibus seqq. fidei infirmitas causa & facto ostenditur. Facto: quòd ascendit Tsoharam & se ad montem recepit cum familia sua, atque ibi iam habitauit, quem potius oportuerat ad Abrahamū (à quo priùs discesserat) referre pedem. Causa; quòd metu fecisse dicitur, nimirum metuens ibi habitare, quamuis promissionibus Dei confirmatus. Infirmitatem vitæ copiosius narrauit Moses; nam primùm occasionem, v.31. & seq. Secundò, factum inconsultum Loti, v.33. & duobus seqq. Postremò effectum, inde ad finem vsque, exponit Moses. Occasio à filiabus fuisse dicitur, quæ contra pietatem, naturam, humanitatem, honestatem, consilium iniuerunt fine & modo damnabile: finem, quia ex patre concubitu illicito cupiuerunt liberos tollere, v.32. Modo, quia patrem vino dementandum esse statuerunt, vt ipsum eò pellicerent, v.32. Huic consilio factum subiicitur, quod non habet opus interpretatione, tribus versibus seqq. Euentus autem fuit quòd vtraque grauidata est, & peperit ex patre: cuius rei perpetuum monimentum in appellatione Gentium, quæ inde fluxerunt, fuit constitutum. Atque hæc narratio non eo solum consilio ponitur vt Patrum infirmitates ante oculos habeamus, atque ex eis videamus nostras; sed etiam nominatim vt multorum sequentium iudiciorum ratio, & locorum scripturæ sententia aperta sit.
units.tr: Following on from the communication made by God just before, this chapter fittingly sets out the carrying out of what was promised, by which God showed himself true in his threats and in his promises. The sum, then, is this: God, mindful of Lot because of his covenant and of the promises of the covenant made to Abraham, preserved Lot and destroyed the wicked; but Lot, though he had received salvation from God, shamefully abused it through weakness, and God willed that this weakness should stand as a monument for the edification of his Church. The chapter therefore has three parts. The first contains the occasion of the things God did, to verse 9; the second the things done, from there to verse 30; the third the unworthy abuse arising from weakness of faith, to the end of the chapter. There are two places concerning the occasions, as there are concerning the deeds. First, the occasion of the salvation bestowed on Lot is related, in three verses; then the overthrow by which God destroyed Sodom and the other cities, to verse 9. The occasion which Lot is said to have offered was his piety towards God, and the fruit of his piety was humanity and hospitality, very like that which we set out at the beginning of the preceding chapter. For Lot's eagerness is shown in verse 1, and his service in the running to meet them, the greeting and the invitation, in verse 2, and his hospitable insistence and feast in verse 3. One question arises: why did the angels refuse and deny what they are afterwards said to have done? The answer is that in this act of the angels there was no lie but dissimulation. For a lie is evil in itself, but dissimulation is a middle thing. Moreover, since middle things and actions in moral matters usually receive their form from the intention, dissimulation becomes evil only when evil means are used for an evil intention; otherwise it is good dissimulation, if it is directed by means that are not evil to a good end. Here, however, the means are not evil, nor is the end evil. For the end was both to whet Lot's eagerness and also to give him occasion to ask why they had to spend the night in the square. Finally, it was also a matter of prudence, lest the Sodomites be given any occasion to inflame themselves against Lot the stranger. Nor was the manner evil in what they said to Lot. For they did not simply deny that they would do it; they only denied that they had come for that reason, but rather to the end that they might spend the night in the square. It is one thing if someone simply denies that he will do something which he has nonetheless firmly resolved to do; it is another if he does not deny it simply but with respect to the purpose for which he came. Replies of this kind are read in the New Testament as given by Christ, as when he said to his mother, "Woman, what have I to do with you? My hour is not yet come" (John 2), and likewise to his brothers, "You go up to the feast..." (John 7), and in several other places. The other place concerning the occasion is the present impiety, inhumanity and injustice of the Sodomites, on account of which God carried out the judgements he had foretold against them. This crime consists in this: first, that Lot's guests were asked for by the men, to satisfy their wicked lust (verses 4 and 5); second, that they paid no heed at all to Lot's words, but made every effort to accomplish what they desired, in the following verses. In the first member the crime is first magnified by certain circumstances (verse 4 and the first part of verse 5). Then their wicked demand is set out in the rest of verse 5. The circumstances are these: the time, when they had not yet gone to bed; the manner, that they surrounded and besieged the house; the number, that all, of every age, from every part of the city, ran together (verse 4). Finally, the act itself, that like madmen or lunatics they shouted for Lot to serve their will. The speech has two parts: a question and a command. For by the question they ask where Lot's guests are; by the command they bid them to be brought out before them, and then they repeat their horrible plan in words that are by no means obscure, saying, "that we may know them." For Scripture uses the word "to know" with decency to signify intercourse, whether natural or against nature, whether lawful or unlawful. This lust of theirs is shown by the words of Lot, who begs in verse 7, when he offers his own daughters in their place. This impiety and injustice is followed by the second place of the occasion, that they also rush madly against Lot, who observed the rights of hospitality. Thus both Lot's hospitable words (verses 6, 7 and 8) and the madness of the wicked (verse 9) are set forth. For Lot is said first to have gone out to them (verse 6) and to have shut the door behind him, lest by chance they should break in while he was dealing with them (verse 6). Then, indeed, two parts of his plea are brought forward: the plea he first proposed simply (verse 7), and then he sets it out part by part (verse 8). For first he offers his daughters to the mad crowd, to be abused, and he commends their condition on the ground that they had not yet known a man. Then, having put forward this substitute offer, he pleads that nothing be done to his guests, and he advances the reason of hospitality, which has always been held most sacred even among all the unbelieving nations. Against these deeds of Lot the Sodomites' insolence is set in verse 9, who expressed their impiety both in word and in deed: in word, because they ordered Lot, who had been brought out of the house, to stand aside, so that they might plot wickedly among themselves; and because they adopted a most iniquitous plan, the cause and substance of which Moses has explained in a few words. The cause was that they resolved to claim for themselves, as if they were judges, the office of judging one stranger and sojourner against the whole people, and not a native, both in this deed and in almost all others beyond their duty; just as if it were the office of a resident alien and a stranger to flatter everyone, to oppose no one, and to regard the goods of a stranger as fair game, for the reason that he is a foreigner. The substance, or sum, of their plan was that they threatened Lot with worse things unless he desisted from pleading. They showed their impiety by their deed, in that they pressed with public violence both upon Lot's person and upon the door of his house. So far the occasions. The second place, concerning the carrying out of God's judgements, is likewise concluded in two members: one is the deliverance which God granted to Lot, to verse 22; the other is the overthrow of the Sodomites and of the other sinners, to verse 29. Three things pertain to Lot's deliverance: first, that he was taken out from the midst of the raging people (verses 10 and 11); second, that the counsel of his departure was given him, with the cause set out (verse 12 and the two following); finally, that the counsel was carried out by the angels themselves, from verse 15. The deliverance from the midst of the people has two parts: one, that the angels, stretching out their hands, brought Lot into the house and made the door fast against the people (verse 10); the other, that they struck the whole people with blindness of mind and body, so that they wearied themselves in vain in seeking the door (verse 11). The counsel of the second place has two parts: one of the angels (verse 12 and following), the other of Lot (verse 14). The angels' part: they bade Lot leave with all his persons and goods (verse 12), and they gave a reason, the overthrow that would soon come from God, for two reasons: namely, on account of the gravity of the sins by which the Sodomites were bound, and on account of God's decree, flaring up against their sins (verse 13). Then follows Lot's part (verse 14): because his sons-in-law, to whom he had betrothed his daughters, he summoned to share in the salvation, by God's command and out of the duty of charity; but Lot was singing to deaf men, for they, bewitched by the same madness, judged that they were being mocked by Lot. The angels' deed followed this counsel: they urged Lot, who was hesitating, to look to his own safety. Therefore they first urged him in speech (verse 15), and then in deed, as they took hold of the hesitating Lot and his family by the hand and led them out of the town (verse 16). Finally they also communicated particular matters pertaining to his salvation (verse 17 and following). When the command of deliverance has been explained, whose carrying out the angels secured by speech and by deed, the manner in which that deliverance of Lot with his family was accomplished is set out (verse 17 and following). For first, the manner of escape is enjoined on Lot, when he has gone out of the city (verse 17). Then, when Lot pleads, and receives the condition of his flight (verse 18 and the two following), God, in his mercy, to show the truth of his promises, grants Lot's request (verses 21 and following). In the command itself two parts are contained: first, the reason for the journey; second, the goal or resting place is indicated. Two things pertain to the reason for the journey: one, that they think only of preserving their life; the other, that for this very end they abstain from all other thoughts and occupations, as believers obeying God's command. Under this heading two prohibitions are given: one, "that no one look back", that is, towards home, whence they had set out, as if grieving unworthily at the loss of the place or of the things that were in it; the other, "that they not stop on the way", but that they complete the journey commanded as if with one breath. The goal or resting place of the journey is indicated by the words "to the mountain", etc. To this command is added Lot's request, containing first a plea (verse 18), then the request itself (verses 19 and following). For the grounds of the request are set out in verse 19, and its substance in verse 20. The grounds of the request are three: the first from God's prior grace, which is immutable [ἀμεταμέλητος]; the second from the present benefit of salvation; the third from Lot's weakness, since, if he had to hasten his pace in this way, there was fear that he would die on the journey itself, overburdened by his infirmity. Therefore the last two grounds pertain to a single argument drawn from the end. The request was that, for the sake of the convenience of the small city which was near at hand, it might be lawful to use it (verse 20). God granted this request (verse 21), and accordingly he substituted another command (verse 22), that he should hasten into that small town, with the conditions for the time being preserved; from this saying the city was given its name, to keep the matter in perpetual memory. The second place, concerning the judgements, is about the destruction of Sodom and the other cities, from verse 23 to verse 29. Three parts are laid down in this destruction: first, the overthrow is declared, in three verses; then the transformation of Lot's wife (verse 26); finally, Abraham's devout observance, in the two following verses. In the overthrow the following are noted: the time, the manner and the act. The time, verse 23. The manner, verse 24, that "sulphurous fire was sent down from heaven by Jehovah from Jehovah", that is, by the Son from the Father, as the orthodox Fathers have rightly interpreted. Finally the act is expressed in verse 25 in the most evident words. To this judgement another is joined, concerning Lot's wife, on account of her unfaithful and disobedient deed (verse 26). For the deed was that "she looked back", that is, towards Sodom, "beyond her husband", who was following her. The judgement was that she was made a pillar of salt; for we take this history literally, as Moses has written it. There remains Abraham's devout observance, who, having been forewarned the day before that judgement, observed carefully what had happened, and then admired the justice of God against the Sodomites (verses 27 and following), and then the grace of God towards Lot, on account of the covenant of grace and the promises made to himself (verse 29). The third place concerns the abuse to which men are prone when they have received God's benefits, from verse 30 to the end. This is shown by the example of Lot and of his daughters. For first Lot's weakness is shown in faith (verse 30), then weakness in morals and way of life, in the following verses. The weakness of faith is shown both by deed and by cause. By deed: that he went up to Zoar and withdrew with his family to the mountain, and there dwelt, whereas he ought rather to have turned his step back to Abraham, from whom he had earlier departed. By cause: it is said that he did it from fear, namely "fearing to dwell there", although he had been confirmed by God's promises. Moses related the weakness of his life more fully; for first he gives the occasion (verses 31 and following); second, the ill-advised deed of Lot (verse 33 and the two following); finally, he sets out the outcome, from there to the end. The occasion is said to have come from the daughters, who, contrary to piety, nature, humanity and decency, adopted a plan that was damnable both in its end and in its manner: in its end, because they wished to bear children from their father by unlawful intercourse (verse 32); in its manner, because they decided that their father must be made drunk with wine, so that they might thereby entice him (verse 32). To this plan a deed is added, which needs no explanation, in the three following verses. The outcome was that both of them conceived and bore children by their father; and a perpetual monument of this matter was established in the names of the nations which sprang from them. And this narrative is set down not only with the aim that we should have the weaknesses of the Fathers before our eyes and see our own in them, but also so that the reason for many later judgements, and the plain sense of passages of Scripture, may be made clear.

units.la: CAPITIS XX ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER XX

units.la: VEritatem promissionum sederisque diuini quod pepi-git cum Abrahamo Deus, Moses duobus exemplis ha-ctenus confirmauit: gratiosa communicatione consi-liorum, cap. 18. & gratiosa liberatione propter diuinas promissiones Abrahamo factas. Sequitur deinceps alter locus ad veritatis eiusdem confirmationem, hoc & sequente capi-te: quo primum exponitur sanctorum infirmitas, qua ipsi suo facto a se abalienant promissiones Dei, nisi Deus propter veritatem suam gratiose eos conseruaret, hoc capite. Deinde vero ostenditur non eo minus veritatem promissionum sederis a Deo opere fuisse praesti-tam, cap. seq.
units.tr: So far Moses has confirmed the truth of the promises and of the covenant that God made with Abraham by two examples: the gracious communication of counsels in chapter 18, and the gracious deliverance made for the sake of the divine promises made to Abraham. Next follows a second passage confirming the same truth, in this chapter and the following one. In this chapter, first, the weakness of the saints is set out, by which, through their own deed, they estrange themselves from the promises of God, unless God for the sake of his truth graciously preserves them. Then, in the following chapter, it is shown that the truth of the promises and covenant was nonetheless carried out by God's work.

units.la: Summa itaque huius capitis est, pios, quamuis promissione & sedere diuino confirmatos; ex infirmitate naturali in ea vitia labascere, quae ipsos quidem per se indignos testantur illa Dei beneficetia, sed eo amplius commonstrant Dei virtutem in ipsorum infirmitate perfici. Itaque huius cap. partes duae sunt: quarum priore narratur Abrahami infirmitas ex ipso; posteriore, Dei veritas in ipsum. Prius membrum duobus versibus, posterius reliquo cap. proponitur. In narranda Abrahami infirmitate, primum occasio, verf. 1: deinde consilium factumque exponuntur, v. 2. Occasio est migratio Abrahami, cuius migrationis causa hic no exprimitur: siue ea fuerit horror iustissimus praesentium iudiciorum Dei in Sedomitas, & maleficiorum quae Lot perpetrauerat; siue (quod magis videtur probabile) incolarum iniquitas, qui eo amplius in sanctum virum exarserunt. Consilium Abrahami in principio 2. versus. in dissimulatione positum est. Cum autem dissimulatio generis sit medij, eaque omnino probetur a bonis quae sine iactura primum veritatis, secundo pietatis in Deum, charitatisq; in homines, & aedificationis etiam in rebus indifferentibus adhibetur, charitas autem ex vocatione aut communi aut particulari determinanda sit: in hoc Abrahami consilio & facto agnoscimus, neque contra veritatem Abrahamum peccauisse, neque contra pietatem in Deum simpliciter: neque etiam contra charitatem communem; sed contra singularem vocationem, qua ipse & vxor inter se constricti erant, ita peccauisse Abrahamum, vt ex eo peccato charitas publica periclitata sit. Sic ergo consilium fuit Abrahamo cum Sara, & ex consilio factum consequutum, priore membro 2. v. Atque hinc euentus ille quo Deus Abrahami dissimulationem quodammodo castigauit, quod mittens Abimelec Saram assumpsit domum. Hinc secundus locus capitis nascitur, quod periculo ex infirmitate nato, Deus medetur providentissime. Huius autem medicinae partes duae sunt: prior, qua Deus Abimeleco prospicit ne peccet, a vers. 3. ad 7. usque: Posterior, qua Abimelec a Deo reprehensus facile efficium ostendi-tur, inde ad finem capitis. Reprehensionis, qua Deus instituit Abimelecum, locus dialogisticus est: nam primum Deus sententiam fert mortis ex maleficio in Abimelecum, quod ius coniugale aboleret, vers. 3. Deinde Abimelec sibi non male conscius excipit, vers. 4. & 5. Cuius exceptionis argumenta sunt tria: primum a persona Dei, quod sit iustissimus, vers. 4: Secundum a persona Abrahami, quod dissimulata rei veritate uterque fuisset in causa cur Saram ad se perduci curauisset: postremo a persona Abimeleci, quod bona fide bonoque animo gessisset omnia, vers. 5. Hac exceptione audita Deus alteram dialogismi partem adhibet, vers. 6. & 7. in qua primum ostendit se bonae illius fidei conscium esse: praeterea bonam fidem integram a malo conseruauisse: tertio singulariter in hac ipsa causa prospexisse ne Sarae fieret iniuria: deinde vero praecipit quid sit facto opus adiunctis promissionibus, & minatur, mortemque denuntiat neglectis promissionibus, vers. 17. Atque hac ratione sententiam, quae absolute lata videbatur, demonstrat Deus fuisse hypotheticam, prout plerasque ipsius denuntiationes accipi oportere demonstratur lege. Sequitur locus alter de facto Abimeleci, quo res male gestas curare statuit secundum Deum. In hoc autem facto hi gradus distincte observandi sunt; primum con-filiorum, vers. 8. Deinde communicationis, a vers. 9. ad 13. Tum restitutionis & compensationis honestissimae, a vers. 14. ad 16. Postremo euentus, duobus ultimis. Consilia Abimeleci relata in melius ostendit Moses, tum in persona ipsius; cuius studium iu-rectione matutina; officium, servorum advocatione & communicatione rerum omnium exponitur: tum vero in persona servorum illius, quod diuino quodam metu perculsi sint ex quo mutatio consilij nata. Sic consilio habito, venitur ad secundam partem, de rebus cum Abrahamo gestis sermone & opere. Sermonis Abimeleci duae sunt partes: una, increpationis, vers. 9. tum eo quod veritatem dissimulauisset nulla occasione iusta, tum quod per ipsum non stetisset quo minus ruina gravissima superuenisset regi & populo eius: altera pars est scisscitatio causae, cur ita se Abraham gesserit, vers. 10. Huic sermoni respondens Abraham de periculo quidem obiecto dissimulat, de facto respondet duobus modis: excusans factum, primum ex præsumpto metu, quòd gentem illam reuerentia Dei carere putauisset, versu 11; quod factum infirmitatis est: deinde verò commoda suorum sermonum interpretatione, cùm ostendit Saram sibi vxorem & sanguine coniunctissimam esse: ac proinde nihil à se contra veritatem fuisse dictum, etsi veritatis partem dissimulauit quam dissimulari posse statuerat.
