Sed ne forte antecedentis illius sermonis grauior offensa esset, prudentissima ὑπόθεσι[?] adhibetur versu decimo tertio: Tamquam si Abraham dixisset, hoc consilium de vxore dissimulanda speciatim non fuisse à se captum quòd gentem istam præ aliis abundare impietate cogitasset; sed hanc fuisse communem inter coniuges conuentionem ex quo à solo natali discesserant, quod totum mundum reliquum iacere in impietate cernerent, vnde Abrahamum Deus gratiosè eduxerat. Alioquin enim contumeliosum illud in Geraritas fuisset visum, si de hac gente sola dictum hoc Abraham prædicauisse putaretur. Ex hoc sermone sequitur opus compensationis & restitutionis, versu 14. Qua ratione malum sublatum est, & Dei gratia reconciliata, vt ante promiserat. Huius verò restitutionis adiuncta duo sunt: vnum, quòd regionis fit Abrahamo copia, versu 15: alterum, quòd Sara officij sui admonetur, versu 16. Nam & munere dolorem leuat Abimelec & officium coniugale ipsius sermone explicat, nempe tum vt viro subsit, tum vt deinceps caueat nequando se viro subesse dissimulet. Restat euentus duobus versibus vltimis. Oratio Abrahami, & exoratio qua Abimelec curatus est, vt Deus ante promiserat.
units.tr: The sum of this chapter, then, is that the godly, although confirmed by promise and by the divine covenant, slip from natural weakness into those faults which indeed testify that they are unworthy of God's benefits, but which further show that God's power is made perfect in their weakness. The parts of this chapter are therefore two. In the first, Abraham's weakness is related on his own side; in the second, God's truth towards him. The first member is set out in two verses, the second in the rest of the chapter. In relating Abraham's weakness, first the occasion is set out (verse 1), then his counsel and deed (verse 2). The occasion is Abraham's migration, the cause of which is not expressed here: whether it was the most just horror at the present judgments of God against the Sodomites and at the crimes Lot had committed, or (which seems more probable) the wickedness of the inhabitants, who blazed up the more against the holy man. Abraham's counsel, at the beginning of verse 2, consists in dissimulation. Since dissimulation belongs to the middle kind of action, and is wholly approved by good people when it is used without loss of truth in the first place, without loss of piety towards God in the second, and without loss of charity towards men, and also for edification in matters indifferent; and since charity must be determined by vocation, whether general or particular: in this counsel and deed of Abraham we recognise that he did not sin against truth, nor simply against piety towards God, nor even against general charity. Rather, he sinned against the singular vocation by which he and his wife were bound to each other, so that through that sin public charity was endangered. So the counsel was Abraham's with Sarah, and the deed that followed from the counsel is set out in the first member of verse 2. Hence came that event by which God in some measure chastised Abraham's dissimulation, when Abimelech sent and took Sarah into his house. From this arises the second place of the chapter: that God most providently heals the danger born of weakness. The parts of this healing are two. The first, by which God provides that Abimelech should not sin, runs from verse 3 to verse 7. The second, by which Abimelech, rebuked by God, is shown to have performed an easy duty, runs from there to the end of the chapter. The rebuke by which God instructs Abimelech takes the form of a dialogue. For first God pronounces a sentence of death upon Abimelech for the wrong, which would abolish the marriage right (verse 3). Then Abimelech, not conscious of any wrong in himself, puts forward his objection (verses 4 and 5). The arguments of this objection are three: first from the person of God, that he is most just (verse 4); second from the person of Abraham, that both had concealed the truth of the matter and so were the cause why he had Sarah brought to him; last from the person of Abimelech, that he had acted in good faith and with a good conscience in everything (verse 5). This objection having been heard, God brings in the other part of the dialogue (verses 6 and 7), in which he first shows that he was aware of that good faith; further, that he had kept the good faith unharmed from evil; and third, that in this very matter he had specially provided that no injury should be done to Sarah. Then he commands what must be done, with the promises attached, and threatens, announcing death for neglecting the promises (verse 17). By this reasoning God shows that the sentence, which seemed to have been pronounced absolutely, was hypothetical, just as the law shows that most of his denunciations ought to be understood. There follows a second place concerning Abimelech's deed, in which he decides to set right the wrongs done, according to God. In this deed the following stages are to be distinctly observed: first, the counsels (verse 8); then the communication, from verse 9 to 13; next the restitution and most honourable compensation, from verse 14 to 16; last, the outcome, in the final two verses. Moses shows Abimelech's counsels changed for the better: first in his own person, whose zeal is set out in his early rising, and whose duty in calling his servants and sharing all things with them; and then in the person of his servants, who, struck by a certain divine fear, changed their counsel. With counsel taken in this way, we come to the second part, concerning the things done with Abraham in word and deed. Abimelech's speech has two parts: one of reproach (verse 9), in which he complains that Abraham dissembled the truth without any just occasion, and that by him it had not stood that a most grievous ruin did not come upon the king and his people; the other part is an inquiry into the cause of why Abraham had so behaved (verse 10). Answering this speech, Abraham does not deny the danger laid to him, but replies to the deed in two ways: excusing the deed, first from a presumed fear that he had thought that people lacked the reverence of God (verse 11), which is a deed of weakness; then, by a convenient interpretation of his own words, by showing that Sarah was his wife and closely related by blood, and that therefore he had said nothing against the truth, although he had concealed a part of the truth which he had decided could be concealed. But lest the graver offence of that earlier speech should perhaps remain, a most prudent supposition [ὑπόθεσις] is brought in at verse 13: as if Abraham had said that this counsel to conceal his wife had not been taken by him specifically because he had judged that this people abounded in impiety beyond others, but that this was a common agreement between spouses from the time they had left their native land, since they saw that the rest of the world lay in impiety, from which God had graciously led Abraham out. Otherwise that statement would have seemed insulting to the Gerarites, if it were thought that Abraham had spoken this of that people alone. From this speech follows the work of compensation and restitution (verse 14), by which the evil was removed and God's grace reconciled, as he had promised before. Two things are added to this restitution: one, that the region is made available to Abraham (verse 15); the other, that Sarah is reminded of her duty (verse 16). For Abimelech both alleviates the grief with a gift and explains her marital duty in his words, namely both that she should be subject to her husband and that from then on she should take care not to pretend that she is subject to him. The outcome remains in the final two verses: Abraham's prayer, and the prayer by which Abimelech was healed, as God had promised before.

units.la: EXEMPLVM infirmitatis humanæ, de quo præcedente capite, proximè adiunctum habet exemplum diuinæ benignitatis, vt eam sibi perpetuo constare sciamus. Huius autem diuinæ bonitatis in hoc 21. capite tria sunt documenta. Nam primùm prolem Abrahamo dedisse Deus dicitur, ad versque 6. Secundò non familiæ solùm Abrahami prospexisse, verùm etiam Ismaeli Abrahami causa, vt promissionibus ante fuerat significatum, indead versu 21. Postremò à Deo existimationem & gloriam fuisse Abrahamo attributam, vt Reges quoque amicitiam illius quæsiuerint, indeadfinem capitis.
units.tr: The example of human weakness, of which the preceding chapter speaks, is immediately followed by an example of divine kindness, so that we may know that this kindness is constant. In this 21st chapter there are three proofs of God's goodness. First, God is said to have given Abraham a son, up to verse 6. Second, He cared not only for Abraham's household but also for Ishmael, for Abraham's sake, as had been signified in the promises earlier, from verse 21 onward. Lastly, God bestowed esteem and glory on Abraham, so that even kings sought his friendship, to the end of the chapter.

units.la: Primus locus, de filio promissionis quē dedit Abrahamo Deus, primū generatim proponitur v.1.deinde speciatim seqq.exponitur.Ge-neralis propositio Dei factum cū promissione coparat, & tū figurate priore membro versus, tum etiam propriis verbis filium promissionis à Deo ostendit exhibitum.Specialis verò declaratio primum geniturarn Isaaci,2.v. Deinde professionem certam promissi diuini, v. 3. & 4. Postremo lætitiam ex complemento promissionum Dei v.6. & 7.narrat. Genituræ locus est apertus, & veritatem Dei asserit obseruato eodem tempore,quod Deus capit. 17. & 18. ante prædixerat. Agnitio verò promissionis à Deo præstitæ duobus modis facta ab Abrahamo prædicatur. Primum impositione nominis, quod Deus ibidem imperauerat: secundò circumcisione Isaaci secundum institutionem diuinam,cap.17.vt dicitur v.4. Quarum rerum prior,id est nominis impositio, singularis fuit personæ: posterior, circumcisionis applicatio, communis illius Ecclesiæ. His adiicitur notatio ætatis Abrahami v.5. ad amplificandam veritatem Dei,effœta corpora ad generationem vegetantis. Hinc sequitur hilaritas,lætitiaque ex complemento diuinæ promissionis percepta. Cuius loci duo sunt: primum testificatio lætitiæ singularis & publicæ,v.6.& Saræ admiratio, quòd ista veritas miraculo coniuncta effet, & supra humanam opinionem Abrahami familiæ contigisset,v.7. Secundus locus veritatem promissionum Dei asserit erga alienos piorum causa, quemadmodum Ismaeli propter Abrahamum benefecit Deus. In huius autem loci narratione tria membra distincte opus est obseruari: primum eiectionem Hagaræ cum filio,ad v.viique 14. Secundo afflictionem exsulantium,v.14. & sequentibus duobus. Postremo Dei misericordia in solandis & iuuandis illis propter Abrahamum, v. 17. & sequentibus. In eiectione primum occasio & causa,v.8.&9. deinde consilium, v.seq. postremo factum,v.11.& duobus seqq.exponitur. Occasio v.8. fuisse dicitur,quòd Isaac cum depelleretur à lacte, conuiuium hilare fecit Abraham pro vnigenito & promissionis filio. Causa v.9. fuisse dicitur,quòd Iischmael spectante Sara illusit Isaaco,id est,(vt Paulus ad Gal.interpretatur) cū atrocibus verbis persequutus est, atque infestauit: quod factum non fuit puerile; sed partim malo animo ab Iischmaele commissum,agete annum minimum xvi.aut etiam xvii. vt Iudæi putant, partim verò profectum videtur à matre, tamquam insaniente quòd rem filij sui quasi retrolabi propter Isaacum animaduerteret. Quapropter optimè Apostolus ad Galat. ex hoc typo communi statuit,Ecclesiam adulterinam solere persequutionibus filios promissionis infestare. Hac de causa sequutum est consilium v. decimi.nempe quòd Sara ægrè iniuriam feres,Abrahamū appellauit, siue priuato studio impulsa, siue singulari Spiritus Dei motu instiga-ta, siue utroque modo, ut matrem cum filio eiiceret domo: cuius sententiæ causam eiusmodi affert, quæ argumentum perseqvutionis videtur exponere, cùm ait, Nam nō est futurus hæres filius istius ancillæ, &c. Ex hoc consilio nascitur Abrahami factum: quòd naturæ sensu ductus, & Iischmaheli consulturus improbat asperitatem Saræ, v. 11. Deùmque consulens, oraculo confirmatur, & certior fit de voluntate diuina, v. 12. & 13. Oraculi partes duæ sunt: mandatum, & promissio. Mandatum duplex: unum, ut certo animo accipiat postulatum Saræ, tamquam diuinitus inspiratū: alterum, ut efficiat, nempe solum Isaacum retinens domi, & dimittens Iischmahelem. Promissionis mēbra duo sunt: unum, de Isaaco promissionum hæredē, v. 12: alterum de Iischmahele etiam propter Abrahamum benedicendo, prout c. 17. exposuimus. Ex hoc facto sequitur eiectio, v. 14. Abrahamum nempe sine mora mādato Dei paruisse, & Hagaram domo domini sui, Iischmahelem domo paterna exsulasse: quo in exilio afflictiones obortæ sunt, quæ v. 15. & 16. proponuntur: nempe primùm quòd in deserto versantes potu fuerunt destituti: secundò quòd inopia potus mater coacta est filium à se procul abiicere ne videret exitium illius: tertiò quòd illo eiecto nihil aliud potuit nisi miseram suam conditionē flebiliter libero cœlo coram Domino exponere, ut cui omnia præsentem mortem ostenderent. Sed Deus diues consolationibus huic malo dicitur prospexisse, v. 17. & seqq. cùm ad præsentem necessitatem ad v. usque 19. tum verò ad reliquum vitæ tempus, v. 20. & seq. Prospiciendi occasio fuit Hagaræ desperatio. Modus: primùm quòd Deus attendit ad vocem pueri, id est, ad puerum respexit secundum promissionem Abrahamo factam: deinde quòd per Angelum & Hagaram confirmauit, v. 17. & 18. & opere leuauit, v. 19. Confirmauit autem exordio per modum scitcitantis facto, primùm à metu reuocans fiducia benevolentiæ præsentiæque diuinæ: secundò ad officium maternum erga filium hortans fiducia earumdem promissionū, quas iam antea Hagar ab Angelo cap. 17. audiuerat. Facto autem leuauisse dicitur, tum quia occulos aperuit fœminæ, ut puteum aquis abundantem cerneret, v. 18. tum quia copiam fecit potus quæ præberet filio, v. 19. Atque hoc singulare beneficiū deinceps continuauisse Dominus dicitur, qui & incrementum, & habitationem, & occupationem Iischmaheli tribuisse dicitur v. 20: eūmque in sede sua usque adeò confirmauisse, ut auctore matre Ægyptia uxorem Ægyptiam duxerit v. 21. Tertius locus de amplitudine beneficiorum Dei erga Ecclesiam & pios quosque in Ecclesia eius continetur inde à v. 22. Eius historia primum occasionem & consilium Abimelechi proponit v.22.& 23.deinde sederis constitutionem,inde ad v.30. Postremo autem eucenta consequentia, ad finem capitis. Occasionem praebuisse dicitur Abimelec,qui proceribus suis comitatus accessit Abrahamum,& de ineundo sedere compellauit. Huic autem facto occasione dedit mirifica benedictio Dei erga Abrahamum, quam percipiens Abimelec partim opere testificatus est,partimq; sermone. Opere, quod rex cum suo comitatu in ditione sua non dubitauit eo se demittere, vt ad inquilinum & aduena veniret ipse, eumque de sedere pacis ineundo appellaret: Sermone,qui utroque versu exponitur,nam primum occasionem postulati narrat in fine v.22: Tum postulationem pacis iureiurando confirmandae, ver. 23. Cum autem pacis inter homines ciuiliter ineundae duo sint genera: prius, ne inter se offendant; posterius,vt etiam defensione inter se communicent: non est hic locus de secundo pacis genere accipiendus; sed tantum de priore illo, ne qua inuicem nascatur offensio,siue inter principes, siue inter populares qui principum iurisdictioni parent. quae duo diserte cauentur in fine v. 23. Hac propositione facta & occasione arrepta, pax inter has partes constituta dicitur volutate Abrahami iurantis, v.24.deinde vero prudentia eiusdem,vt pax iusta esset,duo accesserunt. Nam primum impedimenta pacis vt tollerentur prouidit v.25. & seq.dein de bona illius vt stabilirentur, v.27.& seqq. impedimentorum amolitio exemplo illius putei ostenditur, quem a suis fossum & vi ab indigenis ereptum queritur Abraham, v.25. Quae res cum a popularibus fuisset facta, (horum enim facta principibus attribui solent) merito apud Abimelecum conqueritur Abraham. Abimelec vero se defendit exceptione duplice, v. 26. Primum quod se conscio id factum negat,vt probet innocentiam suam: secundo, quod nullum ad se postulatum de ea re, siue per Abrahamum, siue per alium quemquam negat peruenisse: qua ratione probat euidentissime,neq; contra praesens institutum pacis,neque contra spem illius quidquam a se fuisse procuratum.Hoc impedimento sublato, sequitur stabilimentum pacis. Estque duum genera: commune, v. 27. & singulare, sequentibus:commune est,quod symbolum sederis & fedus constitutum est ab Abrahamo:singulare est, quod causa illius putei de quo expostulauerat,cum vt memoriam ante acceptae iniuriae ex animo delectam ostenderet, tum vt rem in posteritatem amplius confirmaret, symbola singularia adhibuit v. 28. de quibus roganti Abimeleco v., 29.Respondet Abraham 30. & facti singularis causam ficexplicat, vt Abimeleco satisfaciat.Sequuntur cuncta. Primum quod ex iurato illo sedere in causa communi atque singulari nomen loco fuit impositu, v. 31. Secundum, quod foedere constituto æquis conditionibus vtrinque discessum est, & vsus rerum suarum cuique sine alterius offensa permissus commodé. Quod de Abimeleco dictum, v. 32. de Abraha-mo amplius exponitur duobus vltimis: tum eo quod nemus potuit, tum maximé eo quod cultum Dei libertate sancta professus est, tamquam imperium in secula obtinentis, v. 33 : tum quod multos annos ibi commoratus est, puta quasi triginta annos : vt coniectura est ex natiuitatis Isaaci cum morte Sarae, capite vigesimo tertio, comparatione.
units.tr: The first place, concerning the son of promise whom God gave to Abraham, is first set out in general terms in verse 1 and then explained in particular in the verses that follow. The general proposition joins the fact to the promise, and shows, both figuratively in the first clause of the verse and in plain words, that the son of promise was given as God had said. The particular account first narrates the birth of Isaac (verse 2), then Abraham's sure profession of God's promise (verses 3 and 4), and lastly the joy at the fulfilment of God's promises (verses 6 and 7). The account of the birth is clear, and it asserts God's truthfulness, since the birth occurred at the time God had foretold in chapters 17 and 18. The acknowledgement of the promise that God had made is described as taking place in two ways on Abraham's part. The first was the giving of the name that God had commanded there; the second was the circumcision of Isaac according to God's institution in chapter 17, as is said in verse 4. Of these two things, the first, the giving of the name, belonged to the one person; the second, the application of circumcision, was common to that whole Church. To these is added the mention of Abraham's age (verse 5), to magnify God's truthfulness, since bodies worn out by age were made to bring forth new life. Hence follows the cheerfulness and joy received from the fulfilment of God's promise. This place has two parts: first, the testimony of a singular and public joy (verse 6), and Sarah's wonder that this truth, joined with a miracle, had come to Abraham's household beyond human expectation (verse 7). The second place asserts the truth of God's promises toward strangers for the sake of the godly, just as God did good to Ishmael on account of Abraham. In narrating this place three parts must be distinctly observed: first, the casting out of Hagar with her son (up to verse 14); second, the affliction of the exiles (verse 14 and the two following verses); and lastly, God's mercy in comforting and helping them for Abraham's sake (verse 17 and those following). In the casting out, the occasion and cause are set out first (verses 8 and 9), then the counsel (verse 10 and the following), and lastly the deed (verse 11 and the two following). The occasion is said to have been (verse 8) that when Isaac was weaned, Abraham made a joyful feast for his only son and the son of promise. The cause is said to have been (verse 9) that Ishmael, in Sarah's sight, mocked Isaac, that is (as Paul interprets it in Gal.), he persecuted and harassed him with savage words. This was not a childish act: it was committed partly with an evil mind by Ishmael, who was at least sixteen or even seventeen years old, as the Jews think, and partly it seems to have proceeded from his mother, who, as though frenzied, noticed that her son's inheritance was being snatched away, as it were, on account of Isaac. Therefore the Apostle rightly concludes from this common figure in Galatians that a spurious Church is wont to harass the sons of promise with persecutions. For this reason there followed the counsel of verse 10: Sarah, bearing the injury with difficulty, appealed to Abraham, whether driven by private zeal, or stirred by a singular movement of the Spirit of God, or by both, that he should cast out the mother with her son from the house. She gives for this judgement a reason of the kind that seems to set out the argument of persecution, when she says: For the son of this bondwoman shall not be heir, and so on. From this counsel arises Abraham's deed: led by natural feeling, and wishing to consult for Ishmael, he disapproves of Sarah's harshness (verse 11). Consulting God, he is confirmed by an oracle and is made more certain of the divine will (verses 12 and 13). The oracle has two parts: a command and a promise. The command is twofold: one, that he should accept with a steadfast mind Sarah's demand, as if divinely inspired; the other, that he should carry it out, namely keeping only Isaac at home and dismissing Ishmael. The promise has two members: one, that Isaac is the heir of the promises (verse 12); the other, that Ishmael too would be blessed for Abraham's sake, as we set out in chapter 17. From this deed follows the casting out (verse 14): Abraham, namely, without delay obeyed God's command, and Hagar departed from the house of her master, and Ishmael was exiled from his father's house. In this exile afflictions arose, which are set out in verses 15 and 16: first, that while they were in the desert they were deprived of water; second, that because of the lack of water the mother was compelled to cast her son far from herself, so that she would not see his death; third, that once he was cast off she could do nothing but tearfully lay out her wretched condition before the Lord under the open sky, since her circumstances showed her present death. But God, rich in consolations, is said to have provided for this evil (verse 17 and following), both for the present need (up to verse 19) and for the rest of life (verse 20 and following). The occasion of this provision was Hagar's despair. The manner was: first, that God "hearkened to the voice of the boy," that is, he regarded the boy according to the promise made to Abraham; then, that through the angel he confirmed Hagar, and by deed relieved her (verses 17 to 19). He confirmed her at the outset, by way of a question, first by calling her back from fear with the confidence of God's goodwill and presence, and second by exhorting her to her maternal duty toward her son, with the confidence of the same promises that Hagar had already heard from the angel in chapter 17. He is said to have relieved her by deed in two ways: because he opened her eyes, so that she might see a well abounding with water (verse 18), and because he provided a supply of water to give to her son (verse 19). The Lord is said to have continued this singular benefit thereafter, granting Ishmael growth, a dwelling place, and an occupation (verse 20); and he so established him in his seat that, at his mother's Egyptian urging, he took an Egyptian wife (verse 21). The third place, concerning the greatness of God's benefits toward the Church and toward all the godly in his Church, is contained from verse 22 onward. Its history first sets out the occasion and purpose of Abimelech (verses 22 and 23), then the making of the covenant, up to verse 30, and lastly the outcome and consequences, to the end of the chapter. Abimelech is said to have given the occasion: attended by his nobles he came to Abraham and urged him to make a covenant. But the occasion for this deed was the wonderful blessing of God upon Abraham, which Abimelech perceived and testified to partly by deed and partly by word. By deed: the king, with his retinue, did not hesitate to lower himself within his own realm, so that he himself came to a sojourner and alien and invited him to make a covenant of peace. By word: this is set out in each verse, for first he relates the occasion of the request at the end of verse 22, then the request that the peace be confirmed by oath (verse 23). Since there are two kinds of peace that men make civilly, the first to keep from offending one another, the second that they may also share in mutual defence, the second kind is not to be understood here; only the former is meant, that no offence may arise between them, whether between princes or between subjects who obey the jurisdiction of princes. These two things are expressly provided for at the end of verse 23. With this proposal made and the occasion seized, peace between these parties is said to have been established by the will of Abraham, who swore (verse 24). Then, by his prudence, two things were added so that the peace might be just. For first he took care that the hindrances to peace should be removed (verse 25 and following), and then that its benefits should be secured (verse 27 and following). The removal of hindrances is shown by the example of that well, which Abraham complains had been dug by his people and seized by force by the natives (verse 25). Since this had been done by his subjects (for their deeds are usually attributed to the princes), Abraham rightly complains to Abimelech. Abimelech defends himself with a twofold plea (verse 26). First, he denies that he knew of the deed, to prove his innocence; second, he denies that any request about this matter, whether through Abraham or through anyone else, had reached him. By this reasoning he proves most clearly that nothing had been done by him against the present purpose of peace or against Abraham's expectation. With this hindrance removed, the confirmation of the peace follows. It is of two kinds: a common one (verse 27) and a singular one (verses that follow). The common one is that the symbol of the covenant, and the treaty, was established by Abraham. The singular one is that, in the matter of that well about which he had complained, Abraham used special symbols (verse 28), both to show that the wrong received had been erased from his mind and to confirm the matter more firmly for posterity. When Abimelech asked about them (verse 29), Abraham answers (verse 30) and explains the cause of this particular deed, so as to satisfy Abimelech. Then come the concluding matters. First, that from the sworn covenant, both in the common and in the singular matter, a name was given to the place (verse 31). Second, that the treaty having been made on equal terms on both sides, they parted, and each was rightly permitted the use of his own goods without offence to the other. What is said of Abimelech (verse 32) is further set out for Abraham in the last two verses: both because he planted a grove there, and especially because he professed the worship of God with holy liberty, as one who holds dominion for ever (verse 33); and because he dwelt there for many years, about thirty years, as is conjectured by comparing the birth of Isaac with the death of Sarah in chapter 23.

units.la: Actenus exempla duo veritatis diuinæ in præstandis promissionibus & seruando foedere diuino audiuimus: deinceps vero visus veritatis illius ostenditur, tum obsequio fidei, in hoc capite; tum vero religioso humanitatis officio cap. seq. atque pietatis, cap. 24. Huius autem capitis duæ partes sunt in vniuersum: quarum prior exemplum sancti obsequij continet, ad v. vsque 19: Posterior est parascevastica ad capitis 24. historiam, à v. 20. ad finem cap. In illius fidelis obsequij quod Abraham præstitit historia, tria membra summatim opus est obseruari: primum causam, mandatum Dei, duobus primis versibus: secundo factum, puta obsequium Abrahami, inde ad v. 11. Postremo euentum à Domino, à v. 12. ad 19. vsque. In causæ explicatione narrantur duo: consilium Domini, & mandatum Abrahamo datum. Consilium v. 1. his verbis exponitur, Deus tentauit Abrahamum; mandatum, sequetibus. Vtrique præfigitur circumstantia obseruatu digna, cum hæc dicuntur fuisse post res illas gestas, i. post multiplicē declarationē promissionum fœderisque diuini, & post Isaacum natum atque educatum in familia à verna: qua circumstantia augetur plurimum grauitas mandati à Deo, & obsequij ab Abrahamo præstiti: qui æque in hac causa post Isaacü natü sub spe contra spē credidit, atq; præcedente tempore nodü nato illo crediderat, vt cap. 15. expositum. Quod autē Deus tentauisse dicitur consilio suo, id ΣΥΜΦΩΝΙΑ; oportet accipi. Non enim tentat Deus vt aliquid discat, cùm nihil fugiat scientiam ipsius, sed tentat, vt monstret siue discendū aliis proponat quod ipsi cognitum est penitissimè: aliis autē dico, siue iis ipsis qui tentantur, quorū interest maximè vt probent, & pernoscant seipsos, siue aliis quorum interest, vt cū exempla fidei & patientiæ sanctorū videat atq; in eis Deū glorificēt, tum vt sese ipsi comparent ad eorum imitationem. Alioquin illud certissimum est quod Iacobus ait cap.1, Neminem à Deo tentari ad malum, neque id pie ab vllo homine affirmari posse. In sermone Dei duæ sunt partes : vna, qua Abrahamum vocat : nam citra vocationem diuinam nihil instituitur à piis : altera, qua instruit de mandato suo, fecundo versu. Mandati summa est, vt Abraham Deo sacrificet Ifaacum: modus est ad probandam fidem & patientiam illius, vt non eodem loco sacrificet, sed potius triduale iter suscipiat ad locum sacrificio dictum. Sacrificij imperati grauitas singulis vocibus amplificatur:locus describitur communi descriptione quadam, cùm dicit Deus, Abi in regionem, &c. Definitionem vero singularis loci sibi reseruat Deus, vt ante in prima Abrahami vocatione factum c. 12.ad amplius probandum fidem & constantiam ipsius. Quod autem sacrificium cruentum à Deo imperatur, illud non rei atrocitatem ostendit, quam mutata reuelatione mutauit Deus ; sed maximum fuit ad probationem Abrahami argumentum : alioqui sanctè Deus consilij fui partem solet explicare, partémque dissimulare, vt est liberrimus.
units.tr: Thus far we have heard two examples of divine truth, in fulfilling promises and keeping the divine covenant. Now the image of that truth is shown: in this chapter, through the obedience of faith; in the following chapter, through the religious duty of kindness; and in chapter 24, through piety. This chapter has two parts in general. The first, up to verse 19, contains the example of holy obedience. The second, from verse 20 to the end of the chapter, is a supplement (parascevastica) to the history of chapter 24. In the history of Abraham's faithful obedience, three parts must be noted briefly: first the cause, God's command, in the first two verses; second the deed, Abraham's obedience, from there to verse 11; and last the outcome from the Lord, from verse 12 to 19. In explaining the cause, two things are related: the counsel of the Lord and the command given to Abraham. The counsel is expressed in verse 1 by the words God tested Abraham; the command follows. A circumstance worth noting is placed before each of them, since these things are said to have happened after those things, that is, after the many-sided declaration of the promises and the divine covenant, and after Isaac had been born and brought up in the household among the homeborn servants. This circumstance greatly increases the weight of the command from God and of the obedience Abraham rendered. In this case, after Isaac was born, he believed in hope against hope, just as in the earlier time, before the boy was born, he had believed, as explained in chapter 15. That God is said to have tested by his counsel, one must understand as [συμφωνία]. For God does not test in order to learn anything, since nothing escapes his knowledge; rather he tests in order to show what he knows most thoroughly, either to teach it to others, that is, either to those who are tested, for whom it matters most that they prove and know themselves, or to others, for whom it matters that, when they see the examples of the faith and patience of the saints, they glorify God in them and prepare themselves to imitate them. Otherwise it is most certain, as James says in chapter 1, that no one is tempted by God to evil, nor can anyone devoutly affirm this. In God's address there are two parts: one, by which he calls Abraham, for nothing is undertaken by the godly without a divine call; the other, by which he instructs him about his command, in the second verse. The sum of the command is that Abraham sacrifice Isaac to God. The manner, meant to prove his faith and patience, is that he should not sacrifice in the same place but rather undertake a three-day journey to the place named for the sacrifice. The gravity of the sacrifice commanded is increased by each word. The place is described by a general sort of description when God says Go into the land, and so on. But God reserves for himself the definition of the particular place, as he did earlier in Abraham's first call, chapter 12, to prove more fully his faith and constancy. As for the fact that a bloody sacrifice is commanded by God, this does not show the atrocity of the thing, which God changed by a later revelation; rather it was the greatest proof of Abraham. Otherwise God, as is entirely free, is accustomed to explain one part of his counsel and to conceal another part.

units.la: Est autem regio dicta Morija per anticipationem hic ab historia quę postea sequitur v.14. Regio ad Ierufchalajima montana, in qua mons Tzijonis, vel collis continebatur, vt aperte fecundi Schemuelis cap. vltimo, & 1.Chronic.libro oftéditur. Obsequium Abrahami accuratissimè perscribitur, vt fidem Abrahami videamus, & illius patris credentium exemplo conformemus nostram: nam primùm narratur Abrahamum omnia expediuisse eo ipso matutino quæ fuerant imperata, & iis instructum ad locum abiuisse, v.3. Secundò, perfecto tridui itinere ad locum respexisse quem ipsi demonstrauit Deus, v.4: Acceptáque reuelatione seruos iussisse ibi consistere, v.5: Ipsum vero cum rebus ad holocaustum necessarìis comitatum filio ad locum quem monstrabat Deus abiuisse, v. 6. Tertió neque adspectu filij, neque blandis sermonibus, v.7. & 8. fuisse deterritum, quo minùs locum peteret, altare exstrueret, ligna finderet, filiúmque obligatum imponeret & gladio iugulaturus peteret, v. 9. & 10. Sed in hoc facto duplex fidei locus notandus est piis pernecessarius : Vnus, quòd mandato Dei in simplicitate acquieuit Abraham, tamquam reuelatæ voluntati ipsius: Alter, quòd nihilominus ad prouidentiam respexit, in qua latet voluntas Dei homini incognita, fiduciáque voluntatis illius incognitę acerbitatem cognitæ voluntatis superauit, prout ab ipso cùm feruis, 5. v.tum filio ipsi, v.8. dictum est. Ex his sequitur euentus narratio, cuius partes duæ sunt: est enim euentus singularis, ad v. 14. vsque: Est euentus cōmunis, ad 19. In euētu singulari posita sunt : hæc primùm quòd Abraham ab Angelo Dei reuocatus est, v.11.ne filium iugularet, vers.12. Cuius rei causa exponitur cum vers.1. consentiens, quòd Deus probauerit Abrahami fidem, & foris opere cognouerit quod intus in mente viderat. Secundò, quòd aries Abrahamo submi-nistratus est sacrificandus Domino: atque hac ratione per quamdam similitudinem recepit filium, vt Apostolus Heb.11. scribit. Postremò, quòd perpetuum rei monimentū exstare voluit, imposita loco appellatione, quæ in Proverbium abierit, v.14.
units.tr: The region is called Moriah here by anticipation of the history that follows in verse 14. The region near Jerusalem was mountainous, containing Mount Zion or the hill, as is clearly shown in the last chapter of Second Samuel and in 1 Chronicles. Abraham's obedience is described with great care, so that we may see Abraham's faith and conform our own to the example of that father of believers. For first it is related that Abraham got everything ready on the very morning he was commanded, and set off to the place with these things, verse 3. Second, when the three-day journey was complete, he looked up at the place God showed him, verse 4; and having received the revelation, he told the servants to stay there, verse 5; but he himself, accompanied by the things needed for the burnt offering, went with his son to the place God pointed out, verse 6. Third, he was not turned aside, either by the sight of his son or by his gentle words, verses 7 and 8, from going to the place, building the altar, splitting the wood, and binding his son and laying him on it, intending to slay him with the sword, verses 9 and 10. But in this deed there is a twofold point of faith to be noted, most necessary for the godly. One is that Abraham yielded in simplicity to God's command, as to the revealed will of God. The other is that nevertheless he looked to providence, in which God's will, unknown to man, lies hidden; and by trust in that unknown will he overcame the bitterness of the known will, as he said to his servants (verse 5) and to his son himself (verse 8). From this follows the narrative of the outcome, which has two parts: there is a particular outcome, up to verse 14, and a common outcome, from 15 to 19. In the particular outcome, these things are set down: first, that Abraham was called back by the angel of God, verse 11, so that he would not slay his son, verse 12. The reason for this is stated, in agreement with verse 1, that God tested Abraham's faith and knew by outward work what he had seen inwardly in his mind. Second, that a ram was supplied to Abraham to be sacrificed to the Lord; and in this way, by a certain likeness, he received back his son, as the Apostle writes in Hebrews 11. Last, that God wished there to be a lasting memorial of the event, by giving the place a name which passed into a proverb, verse 14.

units.la: Secundi sermonis quem Deus per angelū habuit summa est, quòd promissiones antecedentes repetiuit & explicauit Deus; harum autem promissionum, cur repetitæ à Deo fuerint, occasio exponitur, v.16. argumentum verò v.17. & seq. Neque enim putandum est sanctarum promissionum Dei atque iuramenti causam 16.v. explicari, tamquam si promissionum causa meritum Abrahami esset, ac non gratiosa Dei benevolentia: sed hoc tantùm statuendum est, eas promissiones quas Dei gratia contulerat, occasione obsequij ab Abrahamo præstiti, cum iureiurando fuisse repetitas atque confirmatas. Promissionum verò summa duabus partibus continetur: nam primùm temporales promissiones exponuntur, vers.17. Deinde verò spirituales, v.18. in quibus consistit temporalium illarum fundamentum. Temporalium partes duæ sunt, vt in cap.12. antè ostendimus: quæ à Deo v.17. primùm contrahuntur proposita illa summa his verbis, Benedicendo benedicturus sum, &c. Deinde ex hac promissione duæ partes promissionum profluunt: vna, de semine, vt c.15. antè explicauimus; altera, de hæreditate vberrima, potentissimóque dominatu in hæreditatem illius. Harum verò promissionum veritas & fundamentum v.18. proponitur, cùm dicit Deus futurum vt benedicant sibi in semine Abrahami omnes gentes terræ. Nam primùm materia atque fundamentum benedictionum omnium proponitur, non semen illud commune & multiplicatum, cuius mentio est in fine præcedentis versus; sed singulare semen benedictionis, quod est Christus Iesus, vt exponit Apostolus Gal.3: deinde obiectum ad hoc semen pertinens disertè exponitur, omnes gentes terræ, vt hac quoque appellatione Deus ostenderet eamdem benedictionem à Iudæis ad gentes omnes peruenturam. Postremò autem actio feminis illius benedicti in gentes: nempe quòd benedictionem in ipsas est collaturus, eæq; benedictionem illam ab eo perceptam certa fide magis ac magis prehensuræ, de ea sibi gratulaturæ, & coram omnibus liberè professuræ. Neque verò cuiquam mirum videri debet quòd nomen seminis præcedenti versu collectiuè, singulariter verò v.18. accipimus, vt etiam accipi ostedimus supra cap. 4. & 15. Nam illud semper verum habendum est quod tradunt Logici, modum subiectorum ex praedicatis, & viciissim praedicatorum ex subiectis cognosci oportere. Cum autem praecedente versu dixerit, Multiplicabo multiplicabo semen tuum, &c. id vt collectiue accipiatur ipsa verba iubent euidentissimè: singulariter vero eadem voce seq. v. accipi oportere demonstrat, primùm Apostoli auctoritas Gal. 3. Secundo praedicatio, quòd in semine Abrahami omnes gentes sibi sint benedictae: id autem est, non in gente Iudaeorum, quae ipsa maledictionem Dei est experta, sed in vno aliquo semine, cuius immota est benedictio, & virtus benedictionis illius communicandae: id autem est Christus. Postremò quòd nomen feminis à Mose de inductria adhibetur, cuius loco fuisset proculdubio dicturus, & benedicent sibi in eo omnes gentes terrae, si de collectiuo femine illo, de quo praeced. v. sermonem habuisset. Ex his sequitur euentus tertius v. 19: quòd Abraham ad pueros suos reuersus est; quòd illi firmul venerut domum, & quòd in ea commodè habitauit percipiens veritatem benedictionum Dei. Sequitur locus alter de generatione Nachoris: cuius loci duae videntur causae: vna, vt ostendatur veritas promissionum Dei, qui nō solùm electis suis, sed propter eos amicis ipsorum benedicturum sese promiserat supra 11: Altera, quia hoc pacto gentem constare oportuit, cuius historia propter coniugium Isaaci 24. cap. exprimitur.
units.tr: The sum of the second address which God gave through the angel is that God repeated and explained the earlier promises. The occasion for the repeating of these promises is stated in verse 16, and the argument from verse 17 onward. For we must not think that the cause of God's holy promises and oath is explained in verse 16, as if the merit of Abraham were the cause of the promises, and not God's gracious goodwill. Rather this alone must be affirmed: that the promises which God's grace had bestowed were repeated and confirmed with an oath, on the occasion of the obedience rendered by Abraham. The sum of the promises is contained in two parts: first the temporal promises are set out, verse 17, and then the spiritual ones, verse 18, in which the foundation of those temporal promises consists. The temporal promises have two parts, as we showed earlier in chapter 12. Verse 17 first presents them, when God puts forward that summary in these words, Blessing I will bless, and so on. Then from this promise two parts of the promises flow: one concerning the seed, as we explained earlier in chapter 15; the other concerning a most abundant inheritance and the most powerful dominion over its inheritance. The truth and foundation of these promises is set forth in verse 18, when God says that it will come about that all the nations of the earth shall bless themselves in the seed of Abraham. For first the matter and foundation of all the blessings is set forth: not that common and multiplied seed, mentioned at the end of the preceding verse, but the singular seed of blessing, which is Christ Jesus, as the Apostle explains in Galatians 3. Then the object pertaining to this seed is clearly stated: all the nations of the earth, so that by this name too God might show that the same blessing would reach all nations from the Jews. Last, the action of that blessed seed towards the nations is stated: namely that he will bestow the blessing upon them, and that they, receiving that blessing from him, will lay hold of it ever more with certain faith, will rejoice over it, and will freely profess it before everyone. Nor ought it to seem strange to anyone that we take the word seed collectively in the preceding verse but in the singular in verse 18, as we showed above in chapters 4 and 15. For what the logicians teach must always be held true: that the manner of the subjects must be known from the predicates, and conversely the manner of the predicates from the subjects. Since in the preceding verse he said, I will multiply, I will multiply your seed, and so on, the words themselves most clearly direct that it be taken collectively. That the same word in the following verse must be taken in the singular is shown, first, by the authority of the Apostle in Galatians 3; second, by the predication that in the seed of Abraham all the nations shall be blessed to themselves, which means not in the nation of the Jews, which itself has experienced the curse of God, but in one singular seed, in which the blessing is fixed and the power of communicating that blessing; and this is Christ. Last, the word seed is used by Moses deliberately, for in its place he would undoubtedly have said, and all the nations of the earth shall bless themselves in him, had he been speaking of that collective seed of which the preceding verse spoke. From this follows the third outcome, verse 19: that Abraham returned to his servants; that they came together to the house; and that he lived there comfortably, perceiving the truth of God's blessings. Next follows another passage, on the genealogy of Nahor. Two reasons for this passage seem to exist: one, that the truth of God's promises may be shown, for he had promised, above in verse 11, to bless not only his chosen ones but also their friends for their sake; the other, because in this way it was necessary for the nation to be established, whose history, on account of Isaac's marriage, is set out in chapter 24.

units.la: CAPITIS XXIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 23.

units.la: ROPOSITO fidei pietatisque Abrahami exemplo, alterum quoque religionis exemplum hoc loco narratur, vt non solùm de haerede Abrahamo prospectum diuinitus praecedentibus capitibus, sed etiam de haereditate cognoscamus. Nam etsi Abrahamo nō fuit certa possessio vbi pedem iure mancipij vel proprietatis poneret, tamen proprietatem religiosam sepulcri Deus illi esse ac posteritati voluit, vt eo symbolo Deus veritatem suam confirmaret, & Patres ampliùs obstricti essent religione sepulcri in promissae illius terrae expectatione. Huius itaque capitis partes omnino tres sunt: quarum prima occasionem, duobus versibus; secunda factum Abrahami, seqq. ad v. 17. vsque; tertia euentum ex facto consequentem ostendit, ad finem vsque capitis. Occasio, fuit mors Sarae; factum, emptio religiosi loci, & sepultura mortui; euentus, ius proprietatis ad religiosum locū. Ad occasionem duo pertinent, aetas Sarae, v.1. & mors illius, quam luctus Abrahami confequutus est v. 2. In facto Abrahami duo ordine pro-ponuntur: postulatum commune ipsius, ad verf. vsque 8. & contra-dictus singularis, ad 17. vsque. Postulati communis duæ sunt partes, quod exponit Reip. Chitthæorum in loco agentium. Nam primum indefinitè religiosi sepulcri locum apud indigenas permitti sibi po-ftulat, v.3. & 4. Cui postulato dicuntur annuisse, v.5. & 6. Deinde ve-rò audito illorum consensu, postulat intercessionem ipsorum, vt sua causa agerent cum eo quem de nomine cognouerat, à quo sepulcri locum exoraret, ad v. vsque 8. Horum postulatorum exordium est ad benevolentiam, cùm fe inquilinum & peregrinum esse Abrahã prosi-tetur. Postulati prioris mebra duo; summa, vt sibi detur sepulcri lo-cus; & finis ex re præsente, vt mortuum suum ibi sepeliat; qua reli-gione semel in loco instituta, ex iure gentiu locus in perpetuitate fa-cer & religiosus habebatur. Admirabilis verò est Chittheorũ annuc-tium humanitas, v.6. qui pro eo quòd Abraham fe peregrinum agno-uerat, illi contra Abrahamum sibi & virum principem & diuinum quodammodo principem videri agnouerunt; ac proinde duobus membris ad postulatum ipsius responderunt; quorum priore copiam faciunt sepeliendi mortuum; posteriore, optionem faciunt. Ex poste-rioris responsi argumento transit Abraham ad postulatum alterum, v. 7. & 8. petens tum vt intercedant apud Hephronem Abrahamo ignotum, tum vt optima lege lectum ad religionem sepulcri locum ab eo obtinerent. Ex communi actione sequitur particularis. Nam & Hephron vltrò sese stitisse [?] dicitur, v.9. & Abrahamo etiam gratis ob-tulisse, v.10. Sed quia Abraham honestum ius possessionis, quàm gra-tuitum maluit, prout etiam quę donantur gratis ea(si quid acciderit) præstari à donatoribus non solent, instituit Abraham tum vt pretium cognosceret, v.13. & 14. Tum verò indicato per Hephronem pretio, v.15. illud præstitit optima fide, vt fide publica in possessionem agri mitteretur, v.16. Hinc euentus consequutus est, quòd Abrahamo & posteritati illius religiosus fuit sepulcri locus. Quapropter & idem ibi sepultus est, vt narratur c. 25. v. 9. & seq. & Isaac, sub finem c.35. & Iacob sub finem libri, itémque posteri ad eam familiam pertinen-tes quamplurimi: ac propterea Moses accuratissimè totam illam no-uam acquisitionem iuris verbis forensibus tamquam ex præscriptio-ne publica descriptis hoc capite complexus est, tum minutatim, v.17. & seq. tum verò generatim conclusionis loco, in versu vltimo.
units.tr: Having set out the faith and piety of Abraham as an example, this passage relates a second example of religion, so that from the preceding chapters we learn not only what God provided for Abraham's heir, but also about the inheritance. Although Abraham had no certain possession where he could set his foot by right of purchase or ownership, God wanted him and his posterity to have a sacred ownership of a burial place, so that by this sign God might confirm his truth, and the Fathers might be more firmly bound by reverence for the sepulchre while they awaited the promised land. The parts of this chapter are therefore three in number. The first, in two verses, sets out the occasion; the second, from verse 2 to verse 17, sets out Abraham's act; the third, to the end of the chapter, shows the outcome that follows from the act. The occasion was the death of Sarah; the act was the purchase of a sacred place and the burial of the dead; the outcome was the right of ownership of the sacred place. Two things belong to the occasion: Sarah's age (v. 1) and her death, which was followed by Abraham's mourning (v. 2). In Abraham's act two things are set out in order: his common request, to verse 8, and the individual dealing, to verse 17. The common request has two parts, which explains the position of the commonwealth of the Hittites in the matter. First he asks, in general terms, that he be allowed a sacred burial place among the natives (vv. 3–4), and they are said to have agreed to this (vv. 5–6). Then, having heard their consent, he asks for their intercession, that they should act on his behalf with the man whom he knew by name, so that he might obtain from him a place for a sepulchre (to v. 8). The beginning of these requests is aimed at goodwill, since he declares himself a sojourner and stranger. The first request has two members: the substance, that a place for a sepulchre be given to him; and the purpose, drawn from the present circumstance, that he might bury his dead there. Once such a rite had been established in a place, under the law of nations that place was regarded as fixed in perpetuity and sacred. Admirable, however, is the courtesy of the Hittites' reply (v. 6). Because they recognised that Abraham was a stranger, they acknowledged in turn that he seemed to them a prince and, in a sense, a prince of God; accordingly they answered his request in two parts: in the first they grant him the right to bury his dead, and in the second they give him a choice. From the argument of this second part of their reply, Abraham passes to his other request (vv. 7–8), asking them both to intercede with Ephron, who was unknown to him, and to obtain for him, on the best legal terms, the field for a sacred sepulchre. From the common action there follows the particular one. For Ephron is said to have offered himself freely (v. 9) and to have given the field to Abraham as a gift (v. 10). But since Abraham preferred a lawful right of possession to a gratuitous one, and since gifts, if anything should go wrong, are not usually guaranteed by the givers, Abraham insisted on knowing the price (vv. 13–14). Then, when the price had been named by Ephron (v. 15), he paid it in the best faith, so that he was put into possession of the field by public faith (v. 16). From this came the outcome, that the sepulchre became a sacred place for Abraham and his posterity. For this reason he himself was buried there, as is related in chapter 25, verse 9 and following; so too Isaac, at the end of chapter 35, and Jacob at the end of the book, and very many of their posterity who belonged to that family. Therefore Moses, with the greatest care, has comprised the whole of that new acquisition of right in this chapter, in forensic terms drawn as if from a public deed of purchase: partly in detail (v. 17 and following), and partly in general, as a conclusion, in the last verse.

units.la: CAPITIS XXIIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 24 ANALYSIS.

units.la: HUIUS[?] cap. consequutio cum praecedentibus (si bene obseruabitur) est μεταβατικὴ, nempe ut commode ab historia Abrahami (quae principio capitis sequenti terminatur) ad Isaaci historiam veniatur. summa est, Deum qui inde a principio coniugiorum auctor est (ut ante cap.2. ostendit Mosche[?]) Isaaco suo tempore prospexisse de iusta coniuge ad propagationem sancti generis legitime adiungenda. Itaque huius capitis partes omnino duae sunt. Nam cum legitima coniugiorum institutio (quae in relatione posita sunt) ad partium duarum inter se factum pertineat; propterea tum stipulantis factum seorsim opus est obseruari, id est, viri qui affectat coniugium, tum vero spondentis, id est, foeminae accipientis conditionem viri. Prior locus, de facto stipulantis, maxima parte huius capitis exponitur ad v. usque 49: Posterior de facto spondentis & conditionem accipientis, ad finem usque cap. In facto stipulantis tres partes obseruandae sunt: Primum Abrahami consilium atque auctoritas, versibus nouem: deinde factum serui ad perficiendum Abrahami consilium & mandatum pertinens secundum Deum, inde ad v.34. Postremo autem stipulatio ordine instituta, inde ad v. 49. Quemadmodum vicissim in futurae coniugis sponsione, primum nutus & testificatio eorum quorum interfuit v.50. & seq. deinde partium consensus integer & absoluta sponsio, inde ad v,58. Postremo autem sponsae in domum viri deductio, v. 59. & seqq. exponitur. His praemittitur narratio occasionum, quae Abrahamum ad consilium istud capessendum adduxerunt: nempe tum ratio aetatis, ante cuius exitum filio prospectum voluerat; tum ratio commoditatum & benedictionum acceptarum a Domino, quarum sibi conscius Abraham ex promissione & foedere Dei amplius obstringebatur, ut promissionem & fedus Dei seruandum proponeret. Atque haec causa est cur Abraham aetate vergens & fractus senio, cum per se praestare non posset, famulum praefectum domui suae mandatis instruxit quae ad coniugium filij pertinebant. In his mandatis partes duae sunt: Propositio, v.2.3. & 4. & enarratio, seqq. In mandatis spectatur forma, & substantia illorum. Forma, quod & signo, v.2. & sermone seruus obstringitur ad ea praestanda quae Deus per herum imperabat. Signum est, quod seruus manum subdere foemori Domini sui iubebatur: quod signum apud Indos sua memoria fuisse obseruatum Aben-Ezra testis est: & nos quoq; non in ciuilibus solum honoribus habendis, sed in feudalibus etiam (vt vocant) ritibus vidimus obseruari. Nam signum est quo inferiores apud superiores vtuntur ad summæ reuerentiæ testificationem: quemadmodum vbi reuerentia aliqua, sed non summa ostenditur, id est, qualis infimorum apud summos esse solet, osculum legimus adhiberi, siue ad os, vt Iosepho Gen.42. siue ad aliquas alias partes, exempli causa, ad genua, vt idolis factum esse ex lib. 1. Reg. & Prophetia Hosea didicimus. Materia mandatorum est per negatiuam (vt loquitur) v.3. & affirmatiuam, 4. nempe ne vxor Isaaco adhibeatur ex gente infideli alienaque à fede- re, sed ex gente fideli, aut saltem ad fedus pertinente ex vocatione Dei. Horum mandatorum explicatio sequitur occasionem habens ex postulato serui, v.5: qui prudenter sibi cauet nequid contra mentem Domini sui, aut fidem à se datam faciat; ac proinde ea petit sibi explicari in quibus facile labi potuisset. Itaque rogat ex euentu, siquidè ipsi non detur sponsa, vtrum Isaacum filium eo posset deducere. Interpretationis loci duo sunt: nam primum interdicitur, ne Isaac eo deducatur v.6. deinde euentus ostenditur ab Abrahamo duplex: vnus ex fide, v.7. Alter ex hypothesi famuli, v.8. Nam ex fide statuit Abraham fretus Dei promissionibus, fore vt succedat coniugium optatum v.7. ex hypothesi autem famuli, contra quam certus erat Abraham & Dei promissionibus confirmatus, si non successerit, pronuntiat fore vt ipse officio perfunctus sit famulus, ita vt Isaacum in Mesopotamia non teneatur abducere. sed obseruent studiosi locum priorem promissionum v.8. amplissimis verbis ab Abrahamo exornari, vt fidem suam ostenderet, eamdemque in famulo obsignaret. Hinc sequitur famuli consensus, & signo, & iuramento spondentis Domino obsequium, verf. 9.
units.tr: The sequence of this chapter with the preceding ones is, if it is carefully observed, transitional [μεταβατικὴ], so that one passes conveniently from the history of Abraham, which ends at the beginning of the next chapter, to the history of Isaac. The sum is this: God, who from the beginning has been the author of marriages (as Moses showed before chapter 2), provided for Isaac in his own time that he should be legitimately joined to a suitable wife, for the propagation of a holy race. Accordingly the chapter has altogether two parts. For since the lawful institution of marriage, which is set out in the narrative, concerns the deed of two parties towards each other, the deed of the one who stipulates must be observed separately, that is, of the man who seeks the marriage, and then the deed of the one who pledges, that is, of the woman who accepts the man's terms. The first part, concerning the deed of the one who stipulates, is set out for the greater part of the chapter, down to verse 49. The second, concerning the deed of the one who pledges and accepts the terms, runs to the end of the chapter. In the deed of the one who stipulates three parts are to be observed. First, Abraham's counsel and authority, in nine verses; then the servant's deed, pertaining to the carrying out of Abraham's counsel and command according to God, running on to verse 34; and lastly the stipulation arranged in order, running on to verse 49. Conversely, in the pledge of the future wife, there is first the nod and attestation of those whose concern it was (verse 50 and following); then the full consent of the parties and the complete and settled pledge, running to verse 58; and last the leading of the bride into the husband's house, verse 59 and following. Before these is placed a narrative of the occasions which led Abraham to undertake this counsel: namely, first the consideration of his age, before whose end he had wished provision to be made for his son; and then the consideration of the blessings received from the Lord, of which Abraham, being conscious, was bound all the more by God's promise and covenant, so that he should set before himself the promise and covenant of God to be kept. And this is the reason why Abraham, advanced in years and broken with age, since he could not himself attend to matters, instructed his servant, who was put in charge of his household, with commands concerning his son's marriage. In these commands there are two parts: the proposition (verses 2, 3 and 4) and the explanation that follows. In the commands we consider the form and the substance. As to form, the servant is bound both by a sign (verse 2) and by words to perform what God commanded through his master. The sign was that the servant was ordered to place his hand under the thigh of his lord. That this sign was observed among the Indians in his own time, Aben-Ezra bears witness; and we too have seen it observed not only in the rendering of civil honours but also in what are called feudal rites. For it is a sign by which inferiors use towards superiors to attest the highest reverence. Just as where some reverence is shown, though not the highest, such as is customary for the lowest towards the highest, we read that a kiss was applied, either to the mouth, as to Joseph (Gen. 42), or to other parts, for example the knees, as we learn was done to idols from 1 Kings and from the prophecy of Hosea. The matter of the commands is stated negatively (as it is put), in verse 3, and affirmatively, in verse 4: namely, that the wife should not be given to Isaac from an unbelieving nation alien from the covenant, but from a faithful nation, or at least one belonging to the covenant, by the calling of God. The explanation of these commands follows, having its occasion in the servant's request (verse 5), who prudently takes care that he does nothing contrary to the mind of his lord or to the faith he had given; and therefore he asks that the points on which he might easily go astray be explained to him. So he asks, in case the outcome should be that no bride is given to him, whether he could lead Isaac his son there. The interpretation of the place is twofold: for first it is forbidden that Isaac be led there (verse 6); then a twofold outcome is set forth by Abraham: one from faith (verse 7), the other from the supposition of the servant (verse 8). For from faith Abraham, relying on God's promises, decides that the desired marriage will follow (verse 7); but on the supposition of the servant, against which Abraham was confident and confirmed by God's promises, he declares that if it does not succeed, the servant will be discharged from his duty, so that he is not bound to lead Isaac away to Mesopotamia. But let the studious observe that the first part of the promises (verse 8) is adorned by Abraham with the fullest words, so that he might show his faith and seal the same in the servant. Hence follows the servant's consent, and his obedience to his lord by a sign and by an oath of pledge (verse 9).

units.la: Antecedentis facti quod stipulatione coniugij præcessit ex Abrahami mandato, membra tria à Mose ordine pertexuntur. Nam primum instrumentum itineris & ipsum iter exponitur v. 10. Secundo factum serui sese ad exsequendum mandatum comparantis, indeque v.vsque 28. Postremo autem ea quæ proximè antecesserunt stipulationem ab Abrahamo imperatam, fuerúntque illius parasceuastica. Instrumentum duplex ponitur; vnum ad iter, alterum ad sponsalia. Iter euntium, quod & redeuntium. Iter duobus modis circumscribitur, à termino ipsius communi, quòd in Mesopotamiam venerit, & à particulari, quòd in vrbem Nachoris. Ea autem videtur esse Padam, quam Ptolomæus Apadanam vocauit. Confecto itinere, de quo v.10. factum serui exponitur triplex. Vnum, quomodo suis camelis, dum constitutus in loco ad fontem erat, prospexerit, vt commodè quiefcerent, v.11. Secundū quo se modo erga Deum comparauerit, v.12. & duobus seqq. Tertium, quomodo se erga Ribkam gesserit inde ad v. 27. Quo se modo gesserit erga Deum coniugiorū auctorem, ostendit Moses exposita oratione illius. Huius orationis partes sunt exordiū a persona Dei secundum naturam, fedus, & experientiā antegressam veritatis ex sedere, v.12. deinde verò petitio signi ad certam demonstrationē diuini instituti in hoc coniugio. Qua in petitione, primum occasio proponitur, v.13. deinde verò substantia illius, i. tum notatio signi, tum rei significatæ ex signo declaratio, v. 14. Proximè antecedentia stipulationem imperatam, alia cum Ribka, alia cum parentibus sunt gesta. Cum Ribka, quorum tempus ponitur principio v.15. hæc sunt: primum occursus, v.15. Ribkæ, & famuli ad Rebecam v.16. Secundò complementum signi ante pronūtiati v.18. & duobus seqq. Tertiò, declaratio vel enuntiatio consilij & imperatæ postulationis, vel stipulationis ordine conueniente ac decoro facta. Est enim admiratio diuinæ prouidentiæ, v. 21. deinde humana confabulatio famuli cum Ribka, tum muneribus oblatis, quia rem diuinitus agi animaduertebat, v.22. tū sermone siue cum Ribka, v.23. & duobus seqq. siue ad Deum, ἀχχείσκ, v. 26. & seq. Hinc sequitur locus de rebus quæ proximè stipulationem antecesserunt, cum familia gestis. Non enim cum puella seorsim agit famulus, sed honesta grauitate & honestate procurat rem sibi imperatam. Huius membri sunt hæc: quòd Ribka excurrit ad suos, v.28. quòd ad famulum excurrit Laban, v. 29. visis muneribus & audito sermone sororis, v.30. quòd famulum aduocat domum humaniter, v.31. & cum camelis, tum ipsi, comitibusque prospicit ex humanitatis officio, v.32. & 33. His proximè subiicitur stipulatio, quem tertium esse locum ostendimus. Huius stipulationis partes duæ sunt; narratio, inde ad v.48. & conclusio per stipulationem ex antecedente narratione, v.49. Narrationis membra sunt hæc: primū, de personis stipulantibus, v.34. & duobus seqq. Secundum, de modo ad stipulationem pertinente, inde ad v.41. Tertium, de signo diuino stipulatione comprobante, inde ad v.48. Personæ tres distinctæ proponuntur: famuli, vt mandatarij, v.34. Abrahami, vt auctoris secundū Deum, v.35. Isaaci, vt acquiescentis iudicio patris, v.36. Modus positus est in adiuratione per Abrahamū facta, & hypothetica interpretatione illius, de quibus dictum est in principio cap. significatio diuina & illius complementum ex narratione proximè præcedente petita sunt. Restat igitur vt de stipulatione, v.49. Videamus. Stipulationis partes duæ sunt; vna, vt spondeant & annuant stipulanti: altera, vt siquidem aliter senserint, sine mora aperiant mentem suam. Nam ex signo famulus optimè concludebat diuinam vocationem esse: In rebus autem sanctis (vt Cyprianus loquitur) nō esse deliberationes necessarias. Hic tantum quæstio vna videtur incidere: An non factū fuerit audax istius famuli, quòd ipse quodāmodo signū dixerit Domino? Resp. Signorū quæ ab hominibus petūtur, alia temere peti, alia iudicio certo. Quæ iudicio certo postulātur, ea aut aperto Dei mandato aut occulto instinctu postulantur. Vtrumque autem à Spiritu Dei est: quēadmodū à Gedeone & Ionathane factum legimus. Fuit autē hoc ex instinctu Dei, nēpe recūbente famulo in promissiones illius, quas ipse tū fide perceperat; tū Abraham auctor itineris pronuntiauerat. Secundus locus capitis sponsione narrat, cōmunēmq; contractū, ad v.vsq; 53. deinde profectione ad Isaacū, inde ad v. 62. Postremò autē coniugij illius consummatione, inde ad fine cap. sponsione dicuntur facere pater & frater tū diuina auctoritate ducti, v. 50. tū propria voluntate, 51. & inde cōmunis cōtractus statuitur: primū gratiarū actione, v.52. dein muneratione, v.53. tamquā symbolo ad contractū stabiliendū pertinente. Profectionis postulatū, v.54. & consiliū per disceptationē proponitur v.55. & seq. Concluditur verò, puella cōsulta: v.57. & accipiente conditione oblatā v. 58. deinde consilij effectus traditur: primū honorifica profequutione cognatorū, v.59. Tū benedictione & precibus sanctis, v.60. Postremò discessu mutuo, 61. Consummationis, quam postremò narrari diximus, loci duo sunt: primus, quòd se coiugali modestia Ribka stitit Isaaco, ad v.vsq; 65. Posterior, quòd Isaac rebus omnibus auctis eam deducit domū, duobus versibus vltimis. Nam qui versus antecedūt, nempe v.62. de ambulatione Isaaci, v.63. de obseruatione aduentantiū, illi occasionem exponunt cur sese Ribka, re ex famulo cognita, tum de camelo deiecerit, v. 64. tum velo obduxerit, quòd peplum nuptarum prisci Latini appellarunt nubem, ex quo nubendi verbum.
units.tr: Of the deed that preceded the stipulation of the marriage, by Abraham's command, Moses sets out three members in order. For first he sets out the equipment for the journey and the journey itself (verse 10). Secondly, the servant's deed of preparing himself to carry out the command, and this runs on to verse 28. Lastly, those things which immediately preceded the stipulation required by Abraham, and which were its preparation. A twofold equipment is set down: one for the journey, the other for the betrothal. The journey, both going and returning, is circumscribed in two ways: by its general end, that he came into Mesopotamia, and by a particular one, that he came to the city of Nahor. This seems to be Padan, which Ptolemy called Apadana. When the journey, of which verse 10 speaks, was completed, the servant's deed is set out as threefold. First, how he provided for his camels, while he stood at the well, so that they might rest conveniently (verse 11). Second, how he conducted himself towards God (verse 12 and the two following). Third, how he behaved towards Rebekah, from there down to verse 27. How he behaved towards God, the author of marriages, Moses shows by setting out his prayer. The parts of this prayer are: a beginning from the person of God according to his nature, the covenant, and the truth of experience gone before, drawn from the covenant (verse 12); then the petition for a sign, for a certain demonstration of the divine ordinance in this marriage. In this petition, first the occasion is put forward (verse 13); then its substance, that is, both the notation of the sign and the explanation of the thing signified by the sign (verse 14). The things immediately preceding the required stipulation were done partly with Rebekah and partly with her parents. With Rebekah, whose time is given at the beginning of verse 15, these are: first, the meeting of Rebekah and the servant (verses 15 and 16); secondly, the fulfilment of the sign previously announced (verse 18 and the two following); thirdly, the declaration or announcement of the counsel and of the requested proposal, made in a fitting and seemly order of stipulation. For there is admiration of divine providence (verse 21); then the servant's human conversation with Rebekah, and the gifts offered, because he perceived that the thing was being done by divine guidance (verse 22); then speech with Rebekah (verse 23 and the two following), or towards God, [ἀχχείσκ] (verses 26 and 27). Hence follows the account of the matters immediately preceding the stipulation, transacted with the household. For the servant does not deal with the girl apart, but with honest gravity and decorum he carries out the business entrusted to him. Of this member these are the parts: that Rebekah runs to her own people (verse 28); that Laban runs out to the servant (verse 29), having seen the gifts and heard the words of his sister (verse 30); that he invites the servant into the house courteously (verse 31); and that he cares for the camels, and for the servant himself and his companions, as a duty of humanity (verses 32 and 33). Immediately after these comes the stipulation, which we have shown to be the third place. The parts of this stipulation are two: the narrative, running on to verse 48, and the conclusion through the stipulation arising from the preceding narrative (verse 49). The members of the narrative are these: first, concerning the persons who stipulate (verse 34 and the two following); second, concerning the manner pertaining to the stipulation, running on to verse 41; third, concerning the divine sign confirming the stipulation, running on to verse 48. Three distinct persons are set forth: the servant, as a mandatary (verse 34); Abraham, as author under God (verse 35); Isaac, as acquiescing in the judgment of his father (verse 36). The manner is laid down in the adjuration made by Abraham and in its hypothetical interpretation, of which mention was made at the beginning of the chapter. The divine sign and its fulfilment have been taken from the narrative immediately preceding. It remains, therefore, to look at the stipulation (verse 49). The parts of the stipulation are two: one, that they pledge and assent to the one who stipulates; the other, that if they think otherwise they should without delay declare their mind. For from the sign the servant rightly concluded that the calling was divine; for in holy matters (as Cyprian puts it) there ought to be no deliberation. Here only one question seems to arise: whether it was not bold of that servant to have, as it were, set a sign for the Lord? Answer: of the signs that are sought from men, some are sought rashly, others with sure judgment. Those sought with sure judgment are sought either by an open command of God or by a hidden prompting. Both, however, come from the Spirit of God, as we read was done by Gideon and by Jonathan. This was from the prompting of God, namely while the servant rested in God's promises, which he had himself received in faith, and which Abraham, the author of the journey, had announced. The second place of the chapter tells of the pledge and the common contract, to verse 53; then of the departure to Isaac, to verse 62; and lastly of the completion of that marriage, to the end of the chapter. The father and brother are said to make the pledge, led both by divine authority (verse 50) and by their own will (verse 51). And thus the common contract is settled: first by thanksgiving (verse 52), then by a gift (verse 53), as a token pertaining to the confirming of the contract. The request for departure is put forward (verse 54), and the counsel, by deliberation, is set forth (verse 55 and the following). It concludes with the girl having been consulted (verse 57), and accepting the offered terms (verse 58). Then the effect of the counsel is recorded: first, an honourable escort by her kinsmen (verse 59); then blessing and holy prayers (verse 60); lastly, a mutual parting (verse 61). Of the completion, which we said is narrated last, there are two places: the first, that Rebekah presented herself to Isaac with conjugal modesty, to verse 65; the second, that Isaac, with all things increased, led her home, in the last two verses. For the verses that precede, namely verse 62 on Isaac's walking and verse 63 on the observing of the arrivals, set out the occasion why Rebekah, having learned from the servant who the man was, both dismounted from the camel (verse 64) and covered herself with a veil, which the ancient Latins called the nuptial cloth (peplum nuptarum), from which comes the verb to marry (nubere).

units.la: CAPITIS XXV ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 25.

units.la: H[?]actenus historiam Abrahami Patris credentiū inde ab 11.cap. percurrimus. Sequitur historia Isaaci duobus capitibus; quorū priore genus, posteriore vitæ ratio & benedictionū diuinarū veritas erga ipsum in mediis angustiis præstita exponitur. Huius autem capitis tres omnino sunt partes: prima transfitiua ad Isaaci historiam, quæ est de hæreditate, morte & sepultura Abrahami, ad v. vsque 11. Secunda est [illegible, ~4 letters] de historia Iischmahelis, tum ad affirmandam veritatem promissionum Dei quę ante cap.16.& 17.precesserunt,tū ad sequentiū historiarū & Prophetiarum illustrationem, in quibus multa de Gente Iischmahelis inserta sunt. Tertia pars est de posteris Isaaco datis diuinitus, à v.19. ad finem vsque cap. Ad primum locum pertinent ista: primùm vt intelligatur qui posteri fuerint Abrahamo præter Iischmahelem, de quo supra cap.16. & Isaacum, de quo 21. c. propterea posteri Keturę hoc loco versibus quatuor exponuntur: deinde diuisio inter liberos ab Abrahamo facta exponitur v.5. & 6. tum mors & sepultura illius, ad v.10.postremò autem benedictionis diuinę in Isaacum translatio, v. 11. Liberorum aliorum generationi anteponitur locus de coniugio,v.1.cùm Abraham vxorem nomine Keturam duxisse dicitur.Hic verò quæstiones oriuntur duæ: vna, vtrum post obitum Sarę duxerit eam,necne;ac proinde vxor iusta,an concubina illius fuerit: altera, vtrum credibile sit Abrahamum post natum Isaacum & mortuam Saram liberos sustulisse.Ad priorem quæstionem respondemus hoc modo, vt Augustinus & alij censuerunt: Abrahamum post Sarę obitum Keturam iustam vxorem duxisse:quæ res tum sanctimonia & exemplo Abrahami, tum verbis Mosis confirmatur. Sanctimonia, quia Abraham non erat nescius naturalis de coniugio iuris,ac proinde polygamiam fugiebat. Exemplo, quia ne de Hagarę quidem ducendæ consilio cogitasset, nisi Sara importunius fecisset, supra 16. Verbis denique Mosis, quia dicitur adiecijse siue perrexisse vxorem ducere. Adiecisse autem non superstiti Sarę,sed defunctę; quia superstes Sara,neque coniugium ante oculos suos, neque liberorum procreationem fuisset perlatura, quod argumento c.16.& 21. quo ancilla cum filio eiecta est,confirmatur. Altera quæstio,qui fieri potuerit vt Abraham liberos procreauerit,postquā annos 137. superauerit,optimè ab August. quæst.in hunc locum soluitur:nempe diuinam benedictionem in corpus effœtum illius non solùm ad momentum generationis Isaaci pertinuisse; sed reliquo tempore vitę perdurasse, ex quo vegetum illius corpus effectum est. Quò pertinet promissio supra cap.15. & complementum illius iisdem verbis enuntiatum infrà v. 8. mortuum esse Abrahamum in canicie bona senem & saturum diebus. Ex hac igitur vxore qui liberi nati sunt,nominantur v.2.3. & 4. Hinc secūdus locus de bonorū diuisione,v. 5.& 6.qua in diuisione duplex inæqualitas statuitur: vna, quòd Isaac hæres dicitur, alij verò filij potiùs donatarij: deinde quòd hæreditas bonorum omnium illi, his particula bonorum aspersa est, & aliæ sedes attributæ. Hic verò altera quæstio est,quo iure Abraham vnicum hæredem dixerit, reliquos donatarios; cum omnes æquè fuerint ipsius filij. Soluitur hęc quæstio tribus modis:primùm religioso vel ceremonia-li iure: secundò,iure ciuili: postremò, priuato iure, vel conuentionis modo.Ius religiosum coniunctum ceremonia fuit, quòd Deus Isaa-cum hæredem dixerat, non tantùm ad hæreditatem hanc terrenam respiciens ; verumetiam ad symbolum cælestis illius hæreditatis quâ Deus promissionibus ostenderat, & cuius causa symbolum hoc san-ctificauerat,supra 12,13. & 15.& 17. & 18.& 21. & 22.capp. Iuris ciuilis fuit,quòd Isaac omnia bona obtinuit, quia plurimùm constate con-iugio cum Sara vxore comparauerat, provt iure ciuili cautum est, & ratione certa. Iuris denique priuati vel conuentionis fuit hoc, quòd ita nominatim cauit Abraham, cùm Keturam ducturus esset:quapro-pter Ketura quoque in v. 6. nomine concubinæ vxoris designatur, quamuis respectu consortij iusta fuerit Abrahami vxor.De variis au-tem vxorum generibus & iure illarum iam ante diximus in c. 16. His occasionibus factum est vt Isaaco cederet hæreditas, v. 5. aliis verò dona & sedes exteræ attribueretur,v.6. tempus vitæ & mortis Abra-hami v.7.perspicuè definitur,& 8.vbi complemetum promissionum diuinarum, quæ cap. 16.fuerant factæ, perspicuè ostenditur. Restat sepultura,vers.9. & 10. quæ quia religionem & ceremoniam impera-tam à Deo habuit,ex cap. 23. argumento, quemadmodum etiam Ia-cob cauisse legitur infrà 48. & 49. propterea eò diligentiùs à Mose annotatur. His expositis, vers. 11. de rebus Isaaci vniuersè subiici-tur, vt transitio ad sequentem historiam comparetur, in quo bene-dictiones diuinæ erga Isaacum & sedes ipsius exponuntur. Sic au-tem de industria fecit Moses, vt innueret versum hunc per prole-psin hoc loco positum (licet narratione altera intercurrente versuum aliquot) per ἐπανάληψιν[?] cum ea narratione coniungi oportere quæ se-quitur, inde à vers. 19. Sic ergo interseritur Iischmahelis historia παραφρασις[?], vers. 12. & sequentibus. in qua pars secunda capitis con-sumitur. Narrantur autem primùm liberi Iischmahelis, vers. 13. & duobus sequentibus: secundò dignitas ipsorum, vers.16. prout Deus nominatim promiserat supra 17. cap. Tertiò tempus vitæ & mor-tis Iischmahelis, vers. 17. Postremò autem sedes illorum amplissi-ma, vers. 18. cuius spem angelus fecerat matri supra 16. cap. vers. 12. Sic constat Dei veritas ex promissionum & complementi com-paratione.
