Tertia pars capitis ad historiam Isaaci pertinens, expo-nit primùm genus illius proximum, id est, liberos ab eo genitos ad vers. vsque 25. Deinde verò singularium illorum historiam prædi-ctioni diuinæ conformatam, à vers. 27. ad finem vsque capitis. In recensione liberorum primùm ponuntur antecedentia genituræ & conceptus ipsorum, ad vers. vsque 21. Deinde antecedentia partus, quæ gestationis tempore euenerunt, vers. 22. & 23. Tertio autem modus partus, vers. 24. & sequentibus. Postremo historia singularis ad conditionem fratrum demonstrandam pertinens, à vers.29.ad finem vsque. His anteponitur versus μεταβατικὸς[?], siue transitionem à præcedentibus faciens ad historiam Isaaci: is versus est 19. Deinde vero antecedentia conceptus ponuntur duo: primum enim coniugii ratio exponitur summatim, quæ copiose narrata fuit cap.24. Tandem notatur Isaaci ætas, quòd quadragenarius fuerit cùm vxorem duceret; quod eo consilio fit, tum vt sequentis versus causa ostendatur, tum verò vt illustretur Dei veritas in præstãdis promissionibus, cum sexagenarius demum genuerit, vt v.26. diserte ponitur. Alterum antecedens est, quòd Isaacus precibus Deum exorauit, cùm sterilem esse vxorem diuturna exspectatione animaduertisset; quo pacto ostenditur & patientia Isaaci, & fides in promissiones Dei, & efficacia orationum fidei (vt vocat Iacobus) cùm Deum exorauerit, & vxor illius conceperit. Antecedentia partum siue gestationis tempore accidentia ponuntur duo: vnum, certaminis & conflictus grauis inter liberos in matris vtero, vers. 22. alterum, Dei reuelatio consulenti de conflictu isto Ribkæ respondentis. In conflictu duo obseruanda sunt; actus, & effectus: actus, quòd liberi inter se in vtero quassauerunt. Esse-ctus, quòd mater tam graui agitatione commota per se animum ab-iectura videbatur, & quod propterea ad consulendum Iehouam abiit, cum nihil exstaret in rebus humanis quo erigeretur. Hic autem conflictus fuit particularis: nã neque liberis in vtero fuit conscientia de sui prædestinatione, aut conditione alterius, neq; corporibus facultas ita dimicandi; sed singularis fuit & supra naturã motus, cuius occasione Dominus parentes instituit de futuro voluit. Matris abiectus animus his verbis ostenditur, si ita est, quasi dicat, Si me oportet his agitationibus rupi, quid restat quàm vt iam vitã abdicë? Statuebat enim illa cau sam aliquã naturale istius agitationis esse, provt fœminis interdum solet accidere aliquo vitio vteri. Aditus ad Deum consulendum narratur verbis euidentibus. Reuelationis diuinæ vers.23. partes sunt duæ. Vna, de personis priore membro versus: altera, de euentu illarum, posteriore membro. De personis, exponit Deus duo esse capita in vtero illius, ex quibus nationes duæ profluxuræ sint, prout sequentibus historiis demonstratur. De historia illorum prædicitur minoris imperiū & maioris seruitus. Atque hæc prædictio. In tertio autem loco primum historia partus, duobus versibus proximè sequentibus: deinde historia filiorum cùm adoleuissent ostenditur: nam in partus historia primum dicitur, deprehensi gemelli, v.24. deinde singularis gemellorū ratio cum prędictione diuina concueniens demonstratur, uersibus duobus seqq. Nam primùm maioris, siue illius qui prior natus est, ratio seruilis demonstratur habitu corporis, quòd rufus & pilosus, id est, præceps ad iram & viribus corporis præualens; non autem animi, quas vires denotat plurimùm villosa corporis constitutio, verf. 25. Ex qua nomen dicitur habuisse Esau, tamquam si perfectum dixeris: aut ( si magis placet) hominem agendis rebus potiùs virtute quadam naturali quàm contemplandis natum. Minoris verò constitutio verf. 26. actione ipsius designata est, ex qua nomen habuit: quòd calcaneo teneret fratrem ex vtero prodeuntem: quo signo reuelationem antecedentem confirmabat Deus, fore vt maiorem minor superaret. Altera historia eamdem reuelationem confirmans, transitionem habet v.27. deinde narrationem facti singularis reuelationi diuinæ conuenientis. Transitione narratur primùm incrementum filiorum, deinde occupatio, ex quo increuerant. In occupatione vtriusque duplex gradus obseruandus est: habitus, & actus. Habitus, quòd Esau fuit sciens venationis, id est, instructus omnibus artibus, fraudibus, & dolis, quæ ad venationem sunt opus. Nam reuera iusta venatio est omnium artium militarium præexercitatio. Iacob verò integer & simplex vocatur. Actus verò maioris dicitur fuisse in percurrendis agris: minoris in procuranda domo, quæ ex variis tentoriis in familiis quibusque amplis erat constituta. Atque hinc parergas obseruauit Moses verf. 28. differentia fuisse parentum in liberos studia: nam Isaaco gratam fuisse venationem, ac proinde venatorem: vxori verò curæ rem domesticam fuisse, ac proinde Iacobum fuisse pluris apud matrem, non naturæ ordine fretam, vt erat Isaac; sed auctoritate reuelationis diuinæ. Hinc sequitur singularis horum fratrum historia: in qua primùm occasio verf. 29. secundò factum, verf. 30. & tribus seqq. postremò euentus, v.vltimo exponitur. Occasio duplex: Iacob coquens pultem, & esuries Esau ex agris reuertentis: factum, quo Esau pultem stipulatus est, ex qua nomen habuit, v.30. Quòd Iacob spopondit venditionis lege, si venderet fratri primogenita, & contractus Esaui cedentis hac lege primogenitis, v.32. quem contractum iuramento firmari oportuit, vt rata venditio haberetur, v.33. Horum euentus, quòd comedit quidem & bibit Esau, sed pretio grauissimo, & animo præfracto abiciens primogenita, diuturno silentio profanum animum suum plus satis confirmauit. Ex huius autem loci argumento, & Pauli affirmatione pauca de prædestinatione videamus. Primùm, esse prædestinationem docemur auctoritate diuina, communi ratione, & exemplis plurimis. Auctoritate diuina, atque ratione docemur in scripturis, non solùm à posteriore, argumentis ἀπ, verumetiam à priore, id est demonstratione ἀπόδ. Tertiò exemplis docemur per demonstrationem κατ᾽ ἐκ. Nam exempla illius respectu vario particularia & communia dicenda sunt: Particularia, quia effecta sunt totius diuinæ prædestinationis illius in particularibus aut singularibus indiuiduis; communia verò, qua signa sunt totius prædestinationis, & quidem essentialia: quemadmodum siquis ex pede aut manu hominem totum animaduerteret. Huius generis sunt illa signa quæ in hoc cap. de Iacobo & Esauo enuntiantur: nempe quòd maior minori seruiuisse dicitur, primogenitâque sua eidem vendidisse. Prædestinatio pars est prouidentiæ Dei, qua rerum ad imaginem suam creatarum finem ordinauit in Christo, ad bonitatis gloriæque suæ declarationem. Vt autem prouidentia est ratio ordinis rerum ad finem ipsarum perducens, quæ absolutè exstit in mente prouidentis: sic etiam prædestinationem statuimus tantum in mente prædestinantis rationem totam prædestinationis prædestinatorumque ponere. Nam id nisi de Deo crederetur, sapiens homo secundum modum prouidentiæ suæ esset Deo ipso perfectior. Cum enim sapientis sit primùm intentione finem ordinare, deinde prudentia certa prospicere de mediis ad finem asequendum pertinentibus: omnino Deus sapiente inferior futurus esset, nisi de fine & de mediis perfectissimè perfectus opifex prouidisset. Atque hæc de genere, & causa efficiente. Materia prædestinationis est res creatæ ad imaginem Dei, quibuscum Deus vt imaginem suam in creatione, sic gloriam suam in confirmatione communicatam voluit. Eæ res sunt aliæ cœlestes, Angeli; aliæ terrestres, nimirum homines. Forma prædestinationis est ordinatio rerum istarum ad finem suum in Christo Iesu, cui suos dedit ab æterno Pater: nam in eo omnes ordinantur ad suum finem caulaliter; pij ad suum finem formaliter; impij effectiuè. Finis autem creaturarum est duplex: vnus proportionatus, vt loquuntur, secundùm conditionem ipsarum; alter excedens proportionem ipsarū, ad quē finem aliena vi, nō sua transmittuntur; vt sagitta verbi gratia à iaculatore. Hīc autē de fine posteriore agitur, cū prædestinatio sit prædestinantis actus, & in prædestinatis effectus. Qui ergo secundum prædestinationis actum transmittit, Deus est; proximè verò Christus, vt sapientia Dei & potentia Dei ad hoc singulare opus à Deo Patre instituta: qui transmittuntur, sunt creaturæ ad imaginem Dei: transmissio autem duplex; vna ad vitam, altera ad mortem. Finis prædestinantis est duplex; nempe declaratio bonitatis, & gloriæ ipsius. Voluit enim Deus in iis quos prædestinat ad salutem declarare bonitatem suam misericorditer confuledo & parcendo. In iis verò quos reprobat iustè puniendo, vt diserte Apostolus Rom. 9. & 2. Tim. 2. docet. Tota itaq; prædestinationis ordinatio paucis hoc modo perscribenda est, quo & bonitas & gloria Dei in misericordia iustitiáq; ipsius ostendatur. Primum fons prædestinationis; secundò, media intercurrētia; postremò effecta distingui necesse est. Quę tria scholasticè si placet appellare, dicemus, actum causantem, accidentia & effectū. Fons Deus est absolutè, relatè verò Pater in Filio per Spiritum; nam Patris actus est tradere Filio quos elegit feruados, è diuersò autem præterire, i. non tradere Filio eos quos sibi ipsis voluit relinquere perituros. Accidentium locus duplex instituendus est: nam alia est ratio Angelorum, alia hominum. Angelorum, quia electi angeli perseuerant, vindicati à mutabilitate sua in Christo Iesu, cui sunt traditi per gratiā sustentandi: præteriti (angeli) verò mutabilitate sua corruerunt, vt qui in Christo non subsisterent subsistentia gratiæ secundùm electionem Dei. Hominū verò accidentia duūm sunt generum: vnum, commune omnium, & à nobis, quòd omnes peccauerunt; alterum, particulare à Domino, quòd eos qui ab æterno electi fuerant & sibi traditi, Christus vocat, iustificat, sanctificat, &c. Alterum, quòd eos qui præteriti sunt ab æterno, Christus finit in impuritate ipsorum, indurat, impellit, & si qua sunt alia ad eius iustitiam pertinentia. Effectus horum est, quòd electi glorificantur à Deo sola misericordia propter solam eius bonitatem; præteriti damnantur ab eodem iustitia eius propter peccata ipsorum, ad gloriam ipsius sempiternam.
units.tr: Thus far we have run through the history of Abraham, the father of believers, from chapter 11. There follows the history of Isaac in two chapters: the first sets out his lineage, the second his manner of life and the truth of God's blessings toward him, shown in the midst of straits. This chapter has altogether three parts. The first passes over to Isaac's history: it concerns the inheritance, death and burial of Abraham, to verse 11. The second concerns the history of Ishmael, both to affirm the truth of God's promises that went before in chapters 16 and 17, and to illustrate the histories and prophecies that follow, in which much about the nation of Ishmael is inserted. The third part concerns the posterity given to Isaac by God, from verse 19 to the end of the chapter. To the first place belong these matters: first, that it may be understood who were the posterity of Abraham besides Ishmael, of whom above in chapter 16, and Isaac, of whom in chapter 21; for which reason the posterity of Keturah is set out in this place in four verses. Then the division of the property made by Abraham among his sons is set out in verses 5 and 6; then his death and burial, to verse 10; and finally the transfer of the divine blessing to Isaac, verse 11. Before the account of his other children's descent comes the passage on marriage, verse 1, where Abraham is said to have taken a wife named Keturah. Here two questions arise. One: whether he took her after Sarah's death or not, and therefore whether she was a lawful wife or his concubine. The other: whether it is credible that Abraham begot children after the birth of Isaac and the death of Sarah. To the first question we reply in the manner that Augustine and others have judged: that Abraham, after Sarah's death, took Keturah as his lawful wife. This is confirmed both by the holiness and example of Abraham and by the words of Moses. By holiness, because Abraham was not ignorant of the natural law of marriage, and therefore he avoided polygamy. By example, because he would not even have thought of taking Hagar, had not Sarah urged him more insistently, as above in chapter 16. Finally by the words of Moses, because it is said that he added, or went on, to take a wife. Moreover, he added her not while Sarah was still alive but after she had died; because while Sarah survived she would not have endured a marriage before her eyes, nor the procreation of children, which is confirmed by the argument of chapters 16 and 21, where the maidservant was cast out with her son. The second question, how it could come about that Abraham begot children after he had passed 137 years, is very well resolved by Augustine in his Questions on this passage: namely, that the divine blessing was not only operative at the moment of Isaac's conception, but endured for the rest of his life, from the time his body had been made vigorous. To this belongs the promise in chapter 15, and its fulfilment, expressed in the same words below in verse 8: that Abraham died in a good old age, an old man and full of days. From this wife, then, the children who were born are named in verses 2, 3 and 4. Hence the second point, on the division of the goods, verses 5 and 6. In this division two inequalities are established: one, that Isaac is called the heir, while the other sons are rather called recipients of gifts; and then that the inheritance of all the goods was given to him, while to the others only a small portion of the goods was sprinkled, and other dwelling-places were assigned. Here arises the other question: by what right Abraham called the one son his sole heir and the rest recipients of gifts, when all were equally his sons. This question is answered in three ways: first by the religious or ceremonial right; second, by the civil right; finally, by private right, or by the mode of agreement. The religious right was joined to the ceremony, because God had named Isaac the heir, looking not only to this earthly inheritance but also to the symbol of that heavenly inheritance which God had shown by his promises, and for whose sake he had consecrated this symbol, as above in chapters 12, 13, 15, 17, 18, 21 and 22. The civil right was that Isaac obtained all the goods, because he had acquired them chiefly by his marriage with Sarah his wife, as civil law provides and sound reason. Finally, the private right, or right of agreement, was this: that Abraham expressly stipulated it when he was about to take Keturah; for which reason Keturah too is designated in verse 6 by the name of concubine, although with respect to the partnership of marriage she was Abraham's lawful wife. We have already spoken before about the various kinds of wives and their rights, in chapter 16. By these circumstances it came about that the inheritance fell to Isaac, verse 5, while gifts and foreign dwelling-places were assigned to the others, verse 6. The span of Abraham's life and death is clearly defined in verse 7, and in verse 8 the fulfilment of the divine promises made in chapter 16 is clearly shown. There remains the burial, verses 9 and 10, which, because it had the religious observance and ceremony enjoined by God, as is shown by the argument of chapter 23, and as is also read that Jacob made provision below in chapters 48 and 49, is therefore recorded by Moses with greater care. With these matters set out, verse 11 describes in general the affairs of Isaac, so that the transition to the following history may be made; in it the divine blessings toward Isaac and his dwelling-places are set out. Moses did this deliberately, so as to signal that this verse, placed here by way of prolepsis (although one narrative of several verses intervenes), must be joined by recapitulation [ἐπανάληψιν] to the narrative that follows, from verse 19 onward. So the history of Ishmael is inserted by way of paraphrase [παράφρασις], verse 12 and following, in which the second part of the chapter is occupied. First the children of Ishmael are recounted, verse 13 and the two following; second, their dignity, verse 16, as God had named expressly in chapter 17; third, the span of Ishmael's life and death, verse 17; and finally his very ample dwelling-places, verse 18, the hope of which the angel had given to his mother above in chapter 16, verse 12. Thus the truth of God is established by comparing the promises with their fulfilment. The third part of the chapter, pertaining to the history of Isaac, first sets out his immediate posterity, that is, the children born of him, down to verse 25. Then, however, it sets out the history of those individuals, conformed to the divine prediction, from verse 27 to the end of the chapter. In the enumeration of the children, first are set out the circumstances preceding their begetting and conception, to verse 21. Then the circumstances preceding the birth, which occurred during the time of pregnancy, verses 22 and 23. Third, the manner of the birth, verse 24 and following. Finally, the particular history bearing on the demonstration of the brothers' condition, from verse 29 to the end. Before these stands verse 19, a transitional verse [μεταβατικὸς], or one making the transition from what precedes to the history of Isaac. Then two circumstances preceding the conception are set out: for first the manner of the marriage is set out in summary, which was narrated at length in chapter 24. Finally Isaac's age is noted, that he was forty years old when he took a wife; this is done both so that the cause of the following verse may be shown, and so that the truth of God in fulfilling his promises may be illustrated, since he begot children only at sixty, as is stated plainly in verse 26. The other preceding circumstance is that Isaac entreated God with prayers when he perceived that his wife was barren through long waiting; by this is shown both the patience of Isaac, and his faith in God's promises, and the efficacy of the prayers of faith (as James calls them), since he entreated God and his wife conceived. Two circumstances occurring before the birth, or during the time of pregnancy, are set out: one, the severe struggle and conflict between the children in the mother's womb, verse 22; the other, God's revelation answering Rebekah when she consulted him about that conflict. In the conflict two things are to be observed: the act and the effect. The act: that the children "struggled with one another in the womb." The effect: that the mother, moved by so grave an agitation, seemed about to abandon her spirit, and therefore "went to consult Jehovah," since nothing existed in human affairs by which she might be raised up. This conflict, however, was a particular one: for the children in the womb had no awareness of their own predestination or of each other's condition, nor did their bodies have the capacity to fight in such a way; but it was singular and beyond nature, and on its occasion the Lord chose to instruct the parents concerning the future. The downcast spirit of the mother is shown by these words, "If it is so," as if she said: If I must be torn by these agitations, what remains but to renounce life? For she thought that some natural cause of this agitation existed, as women sometimes suffer from some defect of the womb. The approach to God for consultation is narrated in clear words. The divine revelation in verse 23 has two parts. One concerns the persons, in the first member of the verse; the other concerns their outcome, in the second member. Concerning the persons, God declares that there are two heads in her womb, from which two nations will proceed, as the following histories demonstrate. Concerning their history, there is foretold the rule of the younger and the servitude of the elder. And this is the prediction. In the third place, first the history of the birth, in the two verses immediately following, and then the history of the sons when they had grown up is shown: for in the history of the birth it is first said, "twins were found," verse 24; then the particular nature of the twins, agreeing with the divine prediction, is demonstrated in the two following verses. For first the condition of the elder, or of him who was born first, is shown as servile by his bodily habit, that he was red and hairy, that is, headlong to anger and prevailing by bodily strength, but not by strength of mind; which strength a very hairy bodily constitution chiefly signifies, verse 25. From this he is said to have had the name Esau, as if you were to say "perfected," or (if you prefer) a man born to act by a certain natural strength rather than to contemplate. The constitution of the younger, however, is indicated in verse 26 by his action, from which he had his name: that he held his brother by the heel as he came forth from the womb; by this sign God confirmed the preceding revelation, that the younger would overcome the elder. The second history, confirming the same revelation, has its transition in verse 27, and then the narration of a particular event agreeing with the divine revelation. By the transition are narrated first the growth of the sons, and then their occupations, as they grew. In the occupation of each a twofold stage is to be observed: disposition and action. The disposition: Esau was "skilled in hunting," that is, trained in all the arts, stratagems and wiles which are the business of hunting. For indeed true hunting is a preliminary exercise in all the military arts. Jacob, however, is called "blameless and simple." The action of the elder is said to have been in roaming the fields; of the younger, in managing the house, which in large families was made up of various tents. And hence Moses observed, as an incidental matter, in verse 28, that there was a difference in the parents' affections toward the children: for Isaac liked hunting, and therefore loved the hunter; but the mother's care was for domestic affairs, and therefore Jacob was dearer to his mother, relying not on the order of nature, as Isaac did, but on the authority of the divine revelation. Hence follows the particular history of these brothers: in which first the occasion is set out, verse 29; second, the deed, verse 30 and the three following; finally the outcome, in the last verse. The occasion is twofold: Jacob cooking a pottage, and the hunger of Esau returning from the fields. The deed: Esau begged for the pottage, from which he had his name, verse 30. That Jacob made a bargain, under the terms of a sale, that if Esau sold him his birthright, and the agreement of Esau yielding his birthright on these terms, verse 32; which agreement had to be confirmed by an oath, so that the sale might be held valid, verse 33. Its outcome: that "Esau indeed ate and drank," but at a most grievous price; and by casting away his birthright with a stubborn spirit, through long silence he confirmed his profane mind more than enough. From the argument of this passage, and from Paul's affirmation, let us look briefly at predestination. First, we are taught that there is predestination by divine authority, by common reason, and by very many examples. We are taught by divine authority and reason in the Scriptures, not only from the effect, by arguments from the posterior [ἀπ], but also from the cause, that is, by demonstration from the prior [ἀπόδ]. Third, we are taught by examples, by demonstration from the particular to the general [κατ᾽ ἐκ]. For these examples, in their various respects, are to be called particular and common: particular, because they are effects of the whole of that divine predestination in particular or singular individuals; common, however, because they are signs of the whole predestination, and indeed essential signs, just as if someone were to perceive a whole man from his foot or hand. Of this kind are those signs which are stated in this chapter concerning Jacob and Esau: namely, that the elder is said to have served the younger, and to have sold his birthright to him. Predestination is a part of the providence of God, by which he ordained the end of things created in his own image, in Christ, for the declaration of his goodness and glory. Now, as providence is the plan of the order of things leading them to their end, which exists absolutely in the mind of the one who provides, so also we hold that predestination places the whole plan of predestination, and of the predestined, only in the mind of the one who predestines. For if this were not believed of God, a wise man, according to the measure of his providence, would be more perfect than God himself. For since it is the mark of a wise man first to set the end by intention, and then with sure prudence to foresee the means pertaining to attaining the end, God would certainly be inferior to a wise man, unless the most perfectly perfect Maker had foreseen both the end and the means. So much concerning the genus and the efficient cause. The matter of predestination is the created things made in the image of God, with which God willed to share, as in creation his image, so in confirmation his glory. These things are some celestial, the angels; others terrestrial, namely men. The form of predestination is the ordering of these things to their end in Christ Jesus, to whom the Father gave his own from eternity: for in him all are ordered to their end causally; the godly to their end formally; the ungodly effectively. The end of creatures, however, is twofold: one proportionate, as they say, according to their own condition; the other exceeding their proportion, to which end they are sent not by their own power but by a foreign force; as an arrow, for instance, by the archer. Here, however, the latter end is treated of, since predestination is an act of the one who predestines and an effect in the predestined. Therefore he who sends them according to the act of predestination is God; and most immediately Christ, as the wisdom and power of God, instituted by God the Father for this singular work; those who are sent are creatures made in the image of God. The sending is twofold: one to life, the other to death. The end of the one who predestines is twofold, namely the declaration of his goodness and of his glory. For God willed, in those whom he predestines to salvation, to declare his goodness by showing mercy and pardoning; and in those whom he reprobates, by punishing justly, as the Apostle teaches plainly in Romans 9 and 2 Timothy 2. So the whole ordering of predestination is to be described briefly in this way, so that both the goodness and the glory of God may be shown in his mercy and justice. First, the source of predestination must be distinguished; second, the intervening means; finally, the effects. If it pleases, we may call these three, in the scholastic manner, the causing act, the accidents, and the effect. The source is God absolutely, but relatively the Father in the Son through the Spirit; for the act of the Father is to hand over to the Son those whom he has chosen to be saved, and on the other hand to pass by, that is, not to hand over to the Son those whom he willed to leave to perish. The place of the accidents must be set up in a twofold way, for the account of angels is one thing, that of men another. Of angels: because the elect angels persevere, preserved from their mutability in Christ Jesus, to whom they have been delivered to be sustained by grace; but the passed-over angels, through their mutability, fell, since they did not subsist in Christ, who subsists by grace according to the election of God. The accidents of men are of two kinds: one, common to all and on our side, that all have sinned; the other, particular and from the Lord, that Christ calls, justifies, sanctifies, and so on, those whom he has elected from eternity and delivered to himself. And the other, that Christ leaves those who have been passed over from eternity in their own impurity, hardens, impels, and whatever other things pertain to his justice. The effect of these is that the elect are glorified by God by mercy alone, on account of his goodness alone; the passed-over are condemned by the same God by his justice, on account of their sins, to his everlasting glory.

units.tr: CHAPTER 26 ANALYSIS.

units.la: HUIUS cap. summa est, Deum pro infinita sua misericordia, promissionúmque veritate Isaaco prospexisse in omnibus rerum angustiis, per quas oportet nos ad regnum cælorum contendere. Huius autem documenti exempla in hoc cap. afferuntur tria, prout sementis afflictionum ex tribus fontibus oriri solet, àDeo, à nobis ipsis, & ab aliis; quibus singulis afflictionibus suæ liberationes diuinitus allatæ narrantur. Nam afflictionum à Deo locus est versibus 5. Earū quas homo sibi ipse seuit, locus est ad v. vsque 11. Earum denique quas piis alij dferunt, ad finem vsque capitis. Afflictionum diuinitus oblatarum exemplum est fames, verf. 1. quam Moses de industria distinaguit à famis illius historia, de qua supra cap. duodecimo. Huius famis occasione afflictus Isaac, Gerarum profectus dicitur, non quidem animo ibi commorandi, sed vlterius abeundi, nempe in Ægyptum, prout Dei monitio ostendit v. 2. Sic ergo factum Isaaci probatur v. 1. consilium habetur 2. cùm afflictioni isti & consilio ex afflictione sumpto Deus dicitur prospexisse. Liberatur autem Isaac, tum Dei sermone ad v. 5. vsque: tum opere, v. 6. & seqq. Sermonis diuini partes duae sunt, vt alibi passim; mandatum v. 2. & promissio mandato accedens, v. seqq. Mandato Deus interdicit profectionem in Ægyptum, & commorationem in loco imperat, vt principio v. 3. diserte dicitur. Promissionis loci sunt duo, communis, & speciaIis. In communi promissiones duae sunt; praesentia Dei assistentis gratiose, & benedictionis ex praesentia. Loci speciales duo sunt, vnus haereditatis ex sedere, iuramentoque, prima parte v. 3. altera haeredum, v. 4. tum ex Iudaeis, deinde ex gentibus, in communione Christi, vt in fine versus dicitur, quemadmodum bene opponit Apostolus Gal. 3. nam locis antecedentibus nomen feminibus collectiuum est, postremò verò hoc loco indiuiduale. His subiungitur causa, nimirum gratiosum Dei fedus cum Abrahamo initum, & perceptum fide; obedientiáque fidei comprobatum, verf. 5. Huic mandato Dei Isaac obsequutus dicitur, verf. 6. Atque haec commoratio secundae afflictioni occasionem praebuit, per infirmitatem Isaaci metum praesumentis vbi non erat metus. Nam Isaac de vxore percepto metu, mentitus dicitur verf. 7. magno periculo suo. Deinde verò Deo auctore per Abimelecum reprehensus, ad v. 10. & regifice seu regaliter defensus verf. 11. Istius autem metus atque mendacij exempla duo consimilia iam ante vidimus cap. 12. & 20. Reprehensionis verò primùm occasio, verf. 8, quòd Isaacum colludentem cum vxore familiarius vidisset Abimelec: deinde modus ostenditur verf. 9. & 10. nam primùm cognoscit de re Abimelec, & Isaacum cognituraus interrogat de causa, vbi cognouit factum, verf. 9. qui ordo in rebus omnibus apprimè est necessarius. Deinde verò reprehendit eum Rex, & periculi futuri grauitatem obiicit, verf. 10. postremò autem illi à periculo consulit, mandato publico, vt pium & bonum Magistratum decet, verf. 11. Sequitur tertius locus, in quo primùm afflictiones Isaaci narrantur, ad v. vsque 21. deinde libeliberatio ab afflictionibus, & rerum commoditas à Deo procurata, reliquo cap. Narrationi afflictionum duæ occasiones præmittuntur: vna,messis copiosissimæ per benedictionem Dei, v.12. altera incrementum in rebus omnibus, v. 13. Huius incrementi circumscriptio duabus rebus ostenditur: sequente nimirum pecore & famulitio. Ex his occasionibus afflictiones Isaaco ortæ dicuntur: primò inuidentia incolarum, verf. 14. deinde puteorum quos à patre habebat obthuratio, verf. 15. Tum discedendi mandatum per regem v. 16. Hinc secundum genus afflictionum præterea natum: quòd etiam tum cùm extra terminos, sed proximis sedibus Isaac habitaret, v. 17. etiam extra terminum ditionis suæ Phelistæi [?] mouerunt Isaaco litem; & tum puteos ante fossos à patre obstruxerunt, verf. 18. tum recens à famulis curatos v. 19. excitatis nouis litibus eidem eripuerunt verf. 20. & seq. Donec tamdem Isaac longius concessisset, vbi commodiorem ab hominum inuidia habitationem nactus est beneficio Dei, vt ipse profitetur v. 22. Atque hoc principium fuit commodorum, quibus liberatum ex afflictionibus Isaacum instruxit Deus. Horum itaque commodorum genera hoc ordine recensentur, postquam Isaac in stationem sibi attributam extremo termino Cenahaneæ deuenisset, verf. 23: Primùm quòd de sedere promissionibusque sederis ampliùs à Deo confirmatus est, v. 24. Secundò quòd commoditatem ibi sortitus est, tum Dei colendi & inuocandi ex sedere, tum figendæ sedis, verf. 25. tertiò quòd ipsi quoque exteri, quos ante inuidentia excitarat, rapti admiratione benedictionum Dei, etiam Rex ipse Abimelec Isaacum accedunt, v.26. Expostulantem mitigant, v. 27. testantur agnitionem earum benedictionum quas Deus in ipsum contulerit, eoque nomine fedus pangi cum ipso petunt, verf. 28. Cuius sederis circumscriptio, verf. 29. proponitur, nempe fedus pacis ab illis ambiri, ne alter noceat alteri, tamquam metuentibus sibi à potentia illius. Huiusmodi enim fedus Isaac inire potuit integra fide & conscientia: prout conuiuio iuramentóque confirmauit, verf. 30. & 31. postremum genus commodorum est, aquæ ad rem familiarem & pecoris vsum opportunitas: cui propter iuramentum pacis inter ipsos factum nomen iuramenti fuit impositum, v.32. & 33. vt hoc monimentum in posteritatem ad Dei gloriam constitutum esset.
units.tr: The summary of this chapter is that God, in his infinite mercy and the faithfulness of his promises, watched over Isaac in all the straits through which we must press on towards the kingdom of heaven. Three examples of this teaching are set out in this chapter, corresponding to the three sources from which afflictions usually spring: from God, from ourselves, and from others. For each kind of affliction, the deliverance granted by God is related. The afflictions sent by God are described in verses 1 to 5. Those which a man inflicts on himself are dealt with from verse 6 to verse 11. Finally, those which others bring upon the godly fill the rest of the chapter. The example of an affliction sent by God is the famine (verse 1), which Moses deliberately distinguishes from the famine of that earlier story, discussed above in chapter 12. Because of this famine Isaac is said to have set out for Gerar, not with the intention of staying there, but of going further, namely into Egypt, as God's warning shows (verse 2). So Isaac's action is approved in verse 1, and his plan is noted in verse 2, since God is said to have watched over both the affliction and the plan that Isaac adopted because of it. Isaac is delivered, first by the word of God as far as verse 5, and then by action, from verse 6 onwards. The word of God has two parts, as is common everywhere else: a command (verse 2) and a promise added to the command (verses following). By the command God forbids the journey into Egypt and orders him to remain in the land, as is plainly said at the beginning of verse 3. The promises are of two kinds, general and special. There are two general promises: the gracious presence of God who helps, and the blessing that comes from his presence. There are two special promises: one of the inheritance, arising from the land and the oath, given in the first part of verse 3; the other of the heirs, in verse 4, first from the Jews and then from the Gentiles, in communion with Christ, as the end of the verse says, just as the Apostle rightly sets out in Galatians 3. For in the preceding passages the word "seed" is a collective noun, but here at last it is used of an individual. To this is added the cause, namely the gracious covenant of God made with Abraham, received by faith and confirmed by the obedience of faith (verse 5). Isaac is said to have obeyed this command of God (verse 6). And this stay in the land gave occasion for the second affliction, when Isaac, through weakness, feared where there was no fear. For Isaac, out of fear for his wife, is said to have lied, at great risk to himself (verse 7). Then, at the instigation of God, he was rebuked by Abimelech (as far as verse 10), and was defended in a royal and kingly manner (verse 11). Examples of this fear and this lie, very like one another, we have already seen before, in chapters 12 and 20. The occasion of the rebuke is first given (verse 8): Abimelech had seen Isaac playing more familiarly with his wife. Then the manner of it is shown (verses 9 and 10): first Abimelech learns the matter and, wishing to know it, asks Isaac the reason; when he learns the fact (verse 9), an order which is especially necessary in all such matters. Then the king rebukes him and sets before him the gravity of the danger to come (verse 10); and finally he gives him counsel to escape the danger by a public command, as befits a pious and good magistrate (verse 11). There follows the third part, in which first the afflictions of Isaac are related, as far as verse 21, and then his deliverance from afflictions, and the advantages of his situation procured by God, in the rest of the chapter. Two occasions are set before the narrative of the afflictions: one, a most abundant harvest through the blessing of God (verse 12); the other, increase in all things (verse 13). The limit of this increase is shown by two things: namely, the flock and the household servants that followed. From these occasions the afflictions of Isaac are said to have arisen: first, the envy of the inhabitants (verse 14); then the stopping up of the wells which he had from his father (verse 15); and then the command from the king to depart (verse 16). Hence a second kind of affliction arose besides: even when Isaac dwelt outside the borders, but in neighbouring places (verse 17), the Philistines, even outside the bounds of their own territory, stirred up a quarrel against Isaac, and they stopped up the wells which had been dug by his father (verse 18); then, after the servants had newly cleared them (verse 19), they seized them from him again by stirring up fresh quarrels (verses 20 and following). Until at last Isaac withdrew further, and, by the favour of God, found a dwelling more suitable and free from the envy of men, as he himself declares (verse 22). And this was the beginning of the advantages with which God furnished Isaac, delivered from his afflictions. The kinds of these advantages are therefore recounted in this order, after Isaac had come to the place assigned to him at the furthest border of Canaan (verse 23): first, that he was further confirmed by God concerning the land and the promises of the land (verse 24); secondly, that he obtained a convenient place there, both for worshipping and calling upon God in the land and for fixing his dwelling (verse 25); thirdly, that even the strangers, whom envy had earlier stirred up, struck with admiration at the blessings of God, even King Abimelech himself came to Isaac (verse 26). Isaac, complaining, they appease (verse 27); they bear witness to their acknowledgement of the blessings which God had bestowed upon him, and on that account they ask to make a covenant with him (verse 28). The terms of this covenant are set out (verse 29): namely, that they seek a covenant of peace, so that neither harms the other, as though fearing his power. For Isaac was able to enter into such a covenant with a whole faith and a clear conscience, as he confirmed it with a feast and an oath (verses 30 and 31). The last kind of advantage is the convenience of water for the household and for the use of the flock; and on account of the oath of peace made between them, the name of "oath" was given to it (verses 32 and 33), so that this memorial might be established for posterity to the glory of God.

units.la: HVIVS capitis argumentum vnum est; quo & narratio de Isaaci rebus absoluitur, & transitio paratur ad Iacobi historiam, tamquam si ablegatione ad quaerendam coniugem emancipatus fuisset e patria potestate. In hac autem historia tres summatim partes constitui necesse est. Nam primum antecedentia narrantur illius colloquij, quo benedictio per Isaacum in Iacobum collata est, ad versum vsque 17. deinde modus colloquij & benedictio ipsa proponitur ad v. vsque 29. postremo autem res quae ex eo consequutae sunt, inde vsque ad finem capitis. His autem omnibus duo versus praefiguntur de coniugiis Esaui, pertinentes ad declarationem historiae, quae postea vers. vltimo huius ipsius capitis & v.6. sequentis capitis proponitur. Quia dicuntur illae coniuges indigenae, dolorem animo Isaaci & Ribkę indidisse. In rebus colloquium antecedentibus, partes duę sunt obseruandę: mandatum Isaaci, consilio ipsius coniunctū, versibus 4. deinde vero fraudes quaesitę aduersus mandatum & consilium senis, versibus seqq. Mandato praefigitur sua occasio, quod senuisset Isaac, adeo vt oculi eius caligarent. Quod tempus deficientis naturę parentes nō obscurè cōmonefacit tempus esse vt prouideant domi suę, & liberis suis exponant vltimam voluntatem suam: quę res ad sanctimoniam familię & pacem pernecessaria est. Hac igitur occasione Isaac maiorem filium accersiuisse dicitur, v.1. dein accersito, primùm hanc ipsam occasionem v.2. tum mandatum v.3. & seq. parte, postremò consilium, altera ver. 4. parte indicasse. Mandatum est de venatione quaerenda & paranda, quam pater noverat: Consilium est de benedictione in maiorem filium, tamquam diuina auctoritate conferenda. Quaestio vna incidit, qui fieri potuerit vt senex Isaac timens Dei de filio natu maiore verbis Dei benedicendo, contra quam reuelatum fuerat, cogitaret. Nam Deus iam olim antequam infantes nati essent exposuit voluntatem suam, supra c.25. Sic enim quis argumentari posset: Diuinę reuelationis istius Isaac aut conscius fuit, aut non fuit. Non fuisse, quì potest? cùm iam diu voluntatem suam Deus explicauisset Ribkę, & multis ex eo tempore testimoniis confirmasset? Si fuit; qua fide obniti potuit voluntati Dei? Resp. Reuelationem quidem àDeo Ribkę iam diu fuisse factam, siue immediatè, vt illam Deus consolaretur per Spiritum, siue mediatè per Abrahamum, qui adhuc viuebat per illud tempus, & nepotes suos annum fermè decimum sextum agentes viderat. Nam hic uterque modus à Deo fuit observatus, sive ut ipse immediatè per Spiritum suos consulentes privatim institue-ret, sive ut adhiberet primogenitorum, tamquam sacerdotū suorum, operam in revelanda voluntate sua. Abraham autem tantisperdum vixit, fuit primogenitus in familia sua, & primogenitorum ex se de-scendentium caput, tamquam sacerdos summus, per quem Deus consulentibus respoderet. Cum autè haec revelatio utrouis modo Ribkae privatim fuerit exposita, ac non Isaaco; utrumque verè potest de Isaa-co praedicari, illum revelatione divinam inaudivisse quidem ex uxore sua, sed non pro divina agnovisse: ut autè demus Isaacum ex Ribka revelationem divinam inaudivisse, id tamen credibile est, si audivit, certis causis adductum esse ut illi plane non haberet fidem. Causarum una communis est, altera particularis. Communis est, ius naturae. Nam cum Esau prior sit editus, ad ipsum naturali iure primogenita pertinebant. Particularis, quia videtur fuisse singulare matris studium & inclinatio in Iacobum, & ante c.25, Moses confirmavit. Hanc autem inclinationem cum iam diu Ribka sermone & factis ostēdisset[?], prudentiae suae Isaac putavit esse, ut ordine potius naturae quàm sermonem coiugis sequeretur: huic causae tertia quoq; si placet addere, per me licet: quòd dicitur Isaac similiter in Esau studio & amore inclinavisse, idque eo nomine quòd venatio gratia esset ori ipsius, ut ante c.25. exposuit Moses. Secundum duas priores causas excusabile est Isaaci factu, cui de revelatione Dei non idem constabat; de ordine verò naturae & matris in filiū animo optimè noverat. Quapropter naturae potius obsequendum, quà humano studio parentum iudicabat. Alter antecedetiū locus duas fraudes continet: unam matris, alteram filij. Harum fraudum, quae interse coniunctae sunt: primò occasiones, v.5: tum consilia, à v.6. ad 14: Postremò autem facta, consilio capto informata, seqq. v. exponuntur, occasiones duae; una, ad causam pertinens, quòd Ribka audivisset; altera ad rei gerendae opportunitatem, quòd Esau ad venationem abiisset. His occasionibus consilium capitur; cuius partes duae sunt: una, rei agendae, à v.6. ad 11: Altera, modi ad rem conficiendam necessarij, v.11. & sequentibus. In priori parte consilij, Ribka primum occasiones narrat ex re gestā quam inaudiverat, versu 6. & 7. deinde consilium proponit, tum generatim v.8. tum verò speciatim, de haedis substituendis in venationis locum, condimentoque parando, vers.9. iisque Isaaco exhibendis, ut Iacob hac via benedictionem paternam interciperet, v.10. Hinc altera pars consiliorum sequitur de modo rei istius perficiendae: cuius occasionem attulit Iacob, v.10. & 11. Ribka dissoluit dubitationem illius, v.13. occasionem Iacob asseri[?] ex personarum comparatione, suæ nimirum & fratris, cum ille cutę læui,hic villosâ esset: qua ex conditione personarum ostendit duplicem euentum facile consequuturum,contra quàm spondebat mater. nempe vt & fraudem ipsius pater retegeret, & ipse maledictione pro benedictione sperata & affectata consequeretur, v. 12. Quæ res vnico iudicio tactus patri, quamuis cæcucenti, poterat innotescere. Huic dubitationi respondet mater, certa fiducia euentus præsumpta ex reuelatione Dei, quam supra cap.25.audiuimus. Hinc ergo sequitur factum:nempe quòd Iacob matri obsequitur, hœdósque adducit illi,& illa edulium Isaaco parat, v. 14. deinde quòd filium tum vestibus Esaui,v.15, tum pellibus hœdulorum,vt villosus videretur, v.16. Tum edulio instruit patri apportando, v.17. Hic verò quæstio incidit,vtrum fraus vtriusque iure excusari possit. Excusationis duo sunt loci:vnus à patribus plurimùm adductus,quòd hæc sint ἀντίτυπα[?], vt loquitur Apostolus ad Gal.& typum quemdam contineat cuius causa sic geri oportuit: alter, quòd vterque certus fuit de consilio Dei ex reuelatione Spiritus:ac propterea dedit vterque operam vt effectu suum sortiretur Dei reuelatio. sed neutra harum excusationum factum omnino probat.Primùm enim,vt demus rem fuisse typicam,id tamè certum est vbi aliquid humanæ infirmitatis in typum incidit, non eò minùs reprehendi factum oportere quâ vitiosum est. Nam eatenus purus est à vitio typus,quatenus imperio Dei nititur. Hic autem nihil de imperio,aut singulari mandato Dei ad hanc fraudem nectendam afferri potest.Deinde cùm typus hic non fuerit imperatus, nec disertis verbis ex scriptura probari possit, typus communis, non autem proprius & destinatus est. Ad typos autem communes tam exempla mala quàm bona pertinent: mala autè eo quòd typi sunt,fieri bona non possunt.Secundus excusationis locus plus habet ponderis:nēpe Ribkæ & Iacobo de reuelatione & ordinatione Dei constitisse[?].Sed hic rursum distingui est necesse vtriusq; factum. Nam finis vtriusque ad complemetum reuelationis diuinæ[?] pertinebat. Bonus igitur.Modus autem quem fraude tenuerunt, nihil ad reuelationem diuinam pertinet.Id autem inter bonos constat,quod dicit Apostolus, nō esse facienda mala vt eueniant bona. Ergo intentionis bonæ mala actio fuisse dicenda est. quemadmodum autem intentio bona non purgat aut probam efficit actionem malam, sic de Ribkæ & Iacobi facto iudicium fieri necesse est. Dixerit fortasse quispiam, atqui absque hoc facto, fuisset diuina benedictio per Isaacum in Esaum translata. Responsum est,negari propositionem.Nam Deus qui finem constituerat, idem quoque modum multiplicem iustitia coniunctum habebat ad manum, vt finem consilij sui reuelationisque assequeretur. Sapien-tiæ diuinæ est boni finis bona media semper ordinare. Sapientia hu-mana quum ad finem quem proposuit Deus contendit, non potest bonis mediis quæ à Deo sunt acquiescere; quia non fidem colit, sed ex infirmitate fidei Deum sibi anteuertendum putat, & media adhi-benda, quæcumque tandem illa sint, citra prudentiæ Dei iustissimæ contemplationem. Secunda pars capitis, nempe colloquium Iacobi cum Isaaco patre, duabus partibus continetur: primum antecedenti-bus rebus benedictionem paternam, indead verf.vsque 25: deinde ve-rò benedictionis illius pronuntiationem ad versum vsque 30. In re-bus autem antecedentibus numerantur istæ; Primum fraudulenta Patris appellatio, qua Iacob ementito nomine, & fratris nomine af-sumpto, Patrem appellauit, vt benedictionem illius perciperet, v.18. & 19. Huic fraudi ab Isaaco tamquam minus habente fidem, probatio triplex vel exploratio apponitur, ne sese temere circuueniri patere-tur, & benedictionem per imprudentiam transportari. Prima proba-tio est facti, quòd miratur Isaac tam breui tempore capturam vena-tionis successisse. Hanc vero dubitationem dissoluit Iacob, mentiens prouidentia Dei, & indigne abutes Dei federisq; gratiosi nomine, vt circumueniret patre; quod secundum est mendacii illius, & priore gra-uius, prout peccata necti alia ex aliis solent, v.20. Secunda probatio est signi, quia (vt s.cap.25. & hoc ipso cap. didicimus) Esau fuit vir villo-sus, quo signo Isaac cogitauit filium præsentem internosci oportere, v.21. Sed hoc signum Iacob eluserat, hœdulorū pellibus appositis: ex quo facto est vt Iacob (quauis ex significatione vocis sibi fraudis ali-quid visus esset animaduertere,) tamen acquieuerit ad manuū cotre-ctationem, v.22. & 23. Tertia denique probatio fuit blāda interroga-tio filij, vt bona fide Patri quis esset exponeret; quia pietate Iacobi confirmatus putabat fore vt a mendacio apud patre & fraude caueret sibi; præsertim rogatus patria auctoritate, quæ secundum Deum pluri-mum potest, & in re diuina, quæ alias omnes dignitate superat: graue e-nim est mentiri pareti, Deo metiri grauissimū: sed tamen hunc scru-pulum quarto mendacio Iacob dicitur exemisse, cum eū ipsum esse se affirmaret, quem volebat pater, v.24. Hinc sequitur antecedentiū argumentorū clausula, euentúsque quòd Isaac Iacobo iusso propiús accedere, cibúmque apponere, de manu eius cibum sumens conuiua-tus est, v.25. Atque hinc alter locus consequuturus est, nempe benedi-ctionū diuinarum pronuntiatio: cuius pronuntiationis adiuncta po-nuntur duo, osculum à Patre imperatum, verf. 26. & odoratio filij, verf. 27. cum iam oculorum acie [?]præsenio filium non posset discernere. His ergo adiuncta fuit benedictio, ut generatim docet Moses priore membro verf.27.Deinde vero minutatim benedictionis argu-mentū exponitur,altero mēbro versus,& duobus sequentibus.Huius ergo benedictionis loci duo sunt: Unus,benedictionis præsentis con-scientia, secūdo membro versus:alter,futuræ prophetia,duobus seqq. In benedictione præsente spectatur duo per hypotypofin quandam, effectus,& causa illius. Effectus, quod filius promissionis est εὐωδία[?], id est bonus odor, vel vera fragantia apud omnes qui aguntur Spiritu Dei; causa,quod huius εὐωδίας[?], qua ij cum agris uberibus & odoratissi-mis comparantur, auctor est publicus Iehoua per benedictionem suam.Prophetia vero futuræ benedictionis tribus membris compre-hensa est:quæ singula,non tantum carnali(vt loquuntur) modo, ve-rum etiam spirituali intelligenda sunt: primum membrum est bene-dictionum secundum hæreditatem,v.28:secundum membrum, be-nedictionum in hæredes,priore membro v.29:tertium communica-tionis benedictionum diuinarum vel maledictionum in alios pro-pter hæredes Dei,quem ordinem in suis promissionibus idem ser-uauerat Deus,cum eas primum Abrahamo supra c.12. faceret. Harum autem benedictionum duo priores loci in iure primogenitorum sunt insiti; tertius vero ascitus est tamquam effectus ex prioribus conse-quens.Nam primogenitis duo iura supra alios liberos competebant: dupla hæreditas,& ampla dignitas siue auctoritas : quæ duæ res pro-pterea (postquam Reuben incesto cocubitu amisit primogenita, Si-meon vero & Leui, qui Reubeni fuerat successuri,atroci in Sechemi-tas cæde indignos se hac successione reddiderunt) translatæ fuerunt in duos tamquam primogenitos Iacobi filios;in Ichudam, tamquam primogenitum ex Lea filium,dignitas ; in Iofephum , tamquam pri-mogenitum ex Rachela filium, dupla hæreditas; quam rationem Ia-cob ipse obscurius pronūtiauerat,Gen.49. Sed Spiritus sanctus eui-denter expressit 1.Chron.5.v.1.& 2.Atque hæc paucis de benedictio-ne in Iacobum pronūtiata.Hic vero incidit quæ[?] io, quo iure inter-cepta per fraudem benedictio neque à patre reuocari potuerit,neque ex facto reuocata fuerit,sed rata permanserit,cùm irrita sint quæ per-fraude fiunt, & præter consilium donantium. Cur rata fuerit hęc be-nedictio in Iacobum, nec irrita fieri potuerit, si causam efficientem istius benedictionis animaduertamus , rationem facilè assequemur.
units.tr: The argument of this chapter is one thing: it completes the account of Isaac's affairs and prepares the transition to the history of Jacob, as if Jacob, having been sent away to seek a wife, had been released from his father's authority. In this history three main parts must be distinguished. First, the events preceding the conversation in which the blessing was conferred by Isaac on Jacob are related, up to verse 17. Then the manner of the conversation and the blessing itself are set forth, to verse 29. Finally, the consequences that followed are told, from there to the end of the chapter. Before all of these, two verses are placed concerning the marriages of Esau, which relate to the explanation of the history and which are later set out at the last verse of this chapter and at verse 6 of the next. For these wives are said to be native women, and they had caused grief to the minds of Isaac and Rebekah. In the events preceding the conversation, two parts are to be observed: Isaac's command, joined with his plan, in verse 4, and then the deceits devised against the old man's command and plan, in the verses that follow. The command is preceded by its occasion: Isaac had grown old, so that his eyes were dim. This time of failing nature plainly warns parents that it is time to provide for their household and to make known their last wishes to their children, a thing most necessary for the holiness and peace of the family. On this occasion, then, Isaac is said to have summoned his elder son (verse 1), and after he had come, first to have given the occasion itself (verse 2), then the command (verses 3 and following), and last, in the fourth verse, his plan. The command concerns the seeking and preparing of game, which his father knew how to do; the plan concerns conferring the blessing on the elder son as if by divine authority. One question arises: how could old Isaac, who feared God, have thought of blessing his elder son in words of God, contrary to what had been revealed? For God had already, long before the boys were born, made known his will (above, chapter 25). Someone might argue thus: either Isaac knew of this divine revelation or he did not. How could he not have known, since God had long since declared his will to Rebekah and had confirmed it by many testimonies from that time? And if he knew, with what faith could he resist the will of God? I answer: the revelation had indeed been made by God to Rebekah long before, either immediately, so that God consoled her through the Spirit, or mediately, through Abraham, who was still living at that time and had seen his grandsons nearly sixteen years old. For God observed both modes: either he himself instructed his consulting people privately through the Spirit, or he employed the firstborn, as his priests, in making known his will. Now, as long as Abraham lived, he was the firstborn in his family and the head of the firstborn descended from him, as a high priest through whom God answered those who consulted him. Since this revelation was in either mode made known privately to Rebekah and not to Isaac, it can truly be said of Isaac that he indeed heard the divine revelation from his wife, but did not acknowledge it as divine. But even if we grant that Isaac heard the divine revelation from Rebekah, it is nonetheless credible that, if he heard it, he was led by certain causes to have no faith in it at all. Of these causes one is common, the other particular. The common cause is the law of nature: since Esau was born first, the rights of the firstborn belonged to him by natural law. The particular cause is that the mother seems to have had a singular zeal and inclination toward Jacob, as Moses also confirmed before chapter 25. Since Rebekah had long shown this inclination by her words and deeds, Isaac thought it prudent to follow the order of nature rather than the words of his wife. If it pleases, I am willing to add a third cause to these: that Isaac is said to have been similarly inclined in affection and love toward Esau, and that for this reason, because the game was pleasing to his palate, as Moses set out before chapter 25. According to the two former causes, Isaac's action is excusable, since he did not have the same certainty about God's revelation; but about the order of nature and the mother's feeling toward her son he knew very well. Therefore he judged that he should obey nature rather than the human zeal of the parents. The other part of the preceding events contains two deceits, one of the mother and one of the son. Of these deceits, which are joined together: first the occasions are given (verse 5), then the plans (from verse 6 to 14), and last the deeds, carried out in accordance with the plan that had been adopted, are set forth in the verses that follow. There are two occasions: one, pertaining to the cause, that Rebekah had overheard; the other, pertaining to the opportunity for acting, that Esau had gone off to hunt. From these occasions the plan is adopted, and it has two parts: one concerning the thing to be done (verses 6 to 11), the other concerning the means necessary to carry it out (verse 11 and following). In the first part of the plan, Rebekah first relates the occasions from what she had overheard (verses 6 and 7), then proposes the plan: first in general (verse 8), and then specifically, about substituting kids for the game and preparing a dish, in verse 9, and presenting it to Isaac, so that Jacob might intercept the paternal blessing in this way (verse 10). Hence the second part of the plans follows, concerning the manner of accomplishing the matter, whose occasion Jacob raised (verses 10 and 11). Rebekah dissolves his hesitation (verse 13). Jacob's objection arose from a comparison of the persons, namely his own and his brother's: the one had smooth skin, the other was hairy. From this difference of persons she showed that a double outcome would easily follow, contrary to what the mother had promised: namely, that the father would uncover the fraud, and that he himself would obtain the curse instead of the blessing he hoped for and sought (verse 12). This matter could become known to the father, even though he was blind, by a single judgment, by touch. The mother answers this doubt with a firm confidence in the outcome, presumed from the revelation of God that we heard above, in chapter 25. Hence the deed follows: namely, that Jacob obeys his mother, fetches the kids to her, and she prepares the food for Isaac (verse 14); then that she clothes her son with Esau's garments (verse 15), and with the skins of the kids, so that he would appear hairy (verse 16); then she equips him with the food to bring to his father (verse 17). Here the question arises whether the deceit of each may be excused by right. There are two grounds for excusing it. The first, very much urged by the Fathers, is that these things are antitypes [ἀντίτυπα], as the Apostle speaks in Gal., and contain a certain type, for which cause they had to be done thus. The second is that both were certain of God's counsel from the revelation of the Spirit, and therefore each took pains that God's revelation should obtain its effect. But neither of these excuses wholly justifies the deed. For first, even if we grant that the thing was typical, it is certain that wherever something of human weakness falls into a type, the deed must nonetheless be blamed insofar as it is faulty. For a type is free from fault only so far as it rests upon the command of God. But here nothing can be cited about a command, or a particular mandate of God, for weaving this fraud. Next, since this type was not commanded, and cannot be proved from Scripture in express words, it is a common type and not a proper and designated one. Now both bad and good examples belong to common types; but bad examples, because they are types, cannot become good. The second ground of excuse carries more weight: namely, that it was agreed between Rebekah and Jacob that this was the revelation and ordination of God. But here again it is necessary to distinguish the deed of each. For the end of each pertained to the fulfilment of the divine revelation, and so that end was good. But the means they employed by fraud has nothing to do with the divine revelation. Now it is agreed among good people what the Apostle says: that evil things are not to be done so that good may come of them. Therefore an evil action must be called an action done with a good intention. But just as a good intention does not cleanse or make an evil action good, so the judgment on the deed of Rebekah and Jacob must be made. Perhaps someone will say: but without this deed the divine blessing would have been transferred to Esau through Isaac. The answer is that the proposition is denied. For God, who had set the end, also had at hand, joined with his justice, many means to attain the end of his plan and revelation. It belongs to divine wisdom always to order good means for a good end. Human wisdom, when it strives toward the end which God has proposed, cannot rest in the good means that come from God, because it does not cultivate faith, but, from the weakness of faith, thinks that it must get ahead of God and adopt means, whatever they may be, without regard for the contemplation of God's most just prudence. The second part of the chapter, namely the conversation of Jacob with his father Isaac, is contained in two parts: first, the events preceding the paternal blessing, up to verse 25; then the pronouncement of that blessing, up to verse 30. Among the preceding events these are counted: first, the fraudulent address to the father, by which Jacob, under a false name and having assumed his brother's name, addressed his father so that he might obtain his blessing (verses 18 and 19). To this fraud, Isaac, as one with less faith, applied a threefold proof or test, lest he should allow himself to be rashly circumvented and the blessing transferred through carelessness. The first proof is by the fact: he wonders that the catching of the game had succeeded in so short a time. Jacob dissolved this doubt by lying, claiming the providence of God, and unworthily abusing the name of God and of the gracious covenant, so that he might circumvent his father. This is the second of his lies, and graver than the first, as sins are usually linked one to another (verse 20). The second proof is by a sign: for (as we learned above, in chapter 25, and in this very chapter) Esau was a hairy man, and by this sign Isaac thought that the son present ought to be recognized (verse 21). But Jacob had eluded this sign by placing the skins of the kids upon himself. As a result of this, although from the sound of the voice Jacob seemed to have perceived something of the fraud, nevertheless he yielded to the touching of his hands (verses 22 and 23). The third proof, finally, was a gentle question from the son, so that he might in good faith declare to his father who he was. For Isaac, confirmed by Jacob's piety, thought that he would be kept from lying and fraud before his father; especially since he was questioned by paternal authority, which, under God, has the greatest power, and in divine matters surpasses all others in dignity. For it is a grave thing to lie to a parent, and to lie to God is the gravest of all. Yet Jacob is said to have removed this scruple by a fourth lie, when he affirmed that he was the very one whom his father wished (verse 24). From this follows the conclusion of the preceding arguments and the outcome: Isaac, having ordered Jacob to come nearer, to set out the food, and to take the food from his hand, ate and was refreshed (verse 25). Hence the second matter will follow, namely the pronouncement of the divine blessings. Two things are added to this pronouncement: the kiss commanded by the father (verse 26), and the smelling of the son (verse 27), since Isaac, now unable to distinguish the son by the sharpness of his eyes, could not recognize him. To these was added the blessing, as Moses teaches in general in the first member of verse 27. Then the content of the blessing is set out in detail, in the second member of the verse and the two that follow. There are therefore two parts of this blessing: one, the consciousness of the present blessing, in the second member of the verse; the other, the prophecy of the future, in the two following verses. In the present blessing two things are considered, by a certain hypotyposis: its effect and its cause. The effect is that the son of promise is an aroma [εὐωδία], that is, a good odour, or true fragrance, before all who are moved by the Spirit of God. The cause is that the Author of this aroma, by which they are compared to fields that are fruitful and most fragrant, is publicly Jehovah, through his blessing. The prophecy of the future blessing is comprehended in three members, each of which must be understood not only in a carnal (as they say) sense, but also in a spiritual one. The first member is the blessing according to the inheritance (verse 28); the second member is the blessing upon the heirs, in the first member of verse 29; the third is the communication of the divine blessings, or the curses, upon others on account of the heirs of God. This is the order which God himself had kept in his promises, when he first made them to Abraham, above, in chapter 12. Now of these blessings the first two places are implanted in the right of the firstborn; the third is taken up as an effect following from the former. For two rights belonged to the firstborn above the other children: a double inheritance and ample dignity or authority. These two things, after Reuben lost the rights of the firstborn by incestuous intercourse, and Simeon and Levi, who were to succeed Reuben, rendered themselves unworthy of this succession by their savage slaughter of the Shechemites, were transferred to two sons of Jacob as firstborn: dignity to Judah, as the firstborn son of Leah; the double inheritance to Joseph, as the firstborn son of Rachel. Jacob himself had declared this arrangement more obscurely, in Gen. 49. But the Holy Spirit expressed it clearly in 1 Chron. 5, verses 1 and 2. These things, briefly, concerning the blessing pronounced upon Jacob. Here arises the question by what right the blessing, obtained by fraud, could neither be revoked by the father nor in fact was revoked, but remained valid, since things done by fraud and contrary to the intention of those who give are void. Why this blessing upon Jacob remained valid and could not be made void, we shall easily grasp if we consider the efficient cause of this blessing.

units.la: Queadmodū efficientes causæ hæ principales sunt,illæ instrumetales: ita in illa Isaaci actione Iacobo benedicentis statuendum est, causam utrăque concurrisse; quarū principalis est Deus,ut communis pater prin-cipiumque[?] omnium;instrumentalis vero Isaac, ut particularis Iacobi pater,& Dei in actione hac,vt in aliis,administer.Cùm itaq;benedi-ctionem ab vtroq; simul pronuntiatá constet:vis autem actionum omniū,ad quas efficiendas causæ plures convenerunt, ita se habeat, vt principalis causa non cedat inferiori vim& auctoritate suâ;ex eo planè consequitur, vim veritatémque huius benedictionis non ab Isaaco (instrumentum enim fuit,quod principalis causa non necessitate, sed bonitate & gratia sibi adoptauit seu adiunxit) sed à Deo esse, qui est ipsa per se efficiens causa,vimque benedictionis contulit. Itaque personam quidem Isaaci & vocationem patriam ipsius Deus hoc ministerio honorauit;sed neque cæcitas ipsius,neque consilium, neque imprudens factum Isaaci opus illud diuinum potuit vitiare. Cùm itaque Deus omnia quæ gerebantur viderit,sciuerítque; & cō-silium suum hoc pacto sine vlla imprudentia exsequi voluerit: ex eo necesse fuit vt benedictio maneret rata, quam principalis causa effi-ciebat,neque vitio instrumentalis causæ fieret irrita,ac propterea videmus Deum imprudentibus tum seruis suis, tum etiam exteris iñ voluntatis suæ consiliorúmque explicatione tam sapienter fuisse v-sum , vt illi aut nihil, aut aliquid cogitantes volentésque,tamen Dei consilium & voluntatem expresserint; contrà in ea ipsa actione imprudentes sæpe impegerint, vt tota laus penes Dominum vt auctorem suum,permaneret.Sic Samuel in filiis Isai fallebatur ; sic Natan Davidi pronuntians,vt quicquid in animo erat exsequeretur:sic contrà in exteris & infidelibus Bilean expressit voluntatem Dei; Caiphas consilium, Pilatus sententiam, & siqua sunt eiusmodi. Sic ergo vtrumque nobis est evidens,tum cur imprudentiâ vel infirmitate in-strumentorum huiusmodi opus minimè vitietur:tum verò ex conse-quente cur benedictio rata permanserit. Tertia pars cap.duo conse-quentiû genera exponit:vnum, quid superveniens Esau & infans apud Patrem fuerit assequutus, ad v.vsque 40. deinde quid postea ex his rebus gestis fuerit consequutum , vsque ad finem capitis. Nam primùm narratur factum Esau ad patrem accedentis, benedictionem flagitantis versibus 9. deinde benedictio ab Isaaco pronuntiata, vel potius Prophetia de rebus Esaui & familiæ eius v.39.& 40. Hæc au-tem eo ordine quo gesta fuerunt narrantur. Primùm aduentus Esaui eodem ferme momento quo Iacob discedebat à patre,v.30.tum edu-lij præparatio & oblatio ex mandato, v. 31: deinde verò dialogismus siue colloquium inter vtrumque. Huius autem colloquij argumenta sunt tria : primum de persona, v. 32. secundum de benedictione ab Isaaco frequentiùs recusata, deinde ab Esauo flagitata, v.33. & seqq. postremò autem de argumento benedictionis, quam Isaac collatam in Iacobum confirmabat, v.37. recusatæ benedictionis, nempe ad primogenitum peruenturæ, causa narratur v.33. eaque duplex: primum, quod Deus Israel repente pauore affecit nequid, puta priuato studio reuocaret, quod Dei prouidentia per cũ effecisset; quapropter hunc pauorem Græci per ἐκστάσεως nomen expresserunt. Altera causa est, quod benedictio in eum ante collata fuerat: quam communicationem Deus auctoritate sua vsque adeò comprobarit, vt Isaac dixerit; benedixi eum, etiā benedictus est futurus. Sequitur flagitatio contraria, clamoribus & sermonibus, v.34. cum subiecta causa recusationis, v.35. deinde inuectio in Iacobum impotens, cum elegante paronomasia, & repetita flagitatio, v.36. cui subnectitur repetita excusatio ab argumento benedictionis in Iacobum collatæ, v.37. postremo tertia flagitatio Esaui, ius patrium implorantis, v.38. cui tandem Isaac certum benedictionis modum pronuntiat, quæ antecedenti diuinitus pronuntiatæ non aduersaretur, nimirum actus spiritu prophetico, v.39. & seq. Nam primum conditionem hæreditatis & possessionis illius exprimit v.39. prout Edomæa siue Idumea partem regionis feracem habuit, quamuis montosam: deinde vero historiam posterorum suæ hæreditatem pronuntiat, v.40. nempe cum bellis conflicturos, Iudeæ seruituros, tum præ grauitate iugi & afflictionum ingemituros, vt narratur 2. Reg. 3. postremo tandem de collo suo Iudæorum iugum decussuros, vt narratur 2. Reg. 8. & seqq. Reliquentia alia: nempe de consiliis primum Esaui v.41. tum Ribkæ, verbus 4. seqq. & tandem Isaaci, v.vlt. De Esau duo enuntiantur carnis opera grauissima; odium intestinum propter interceptam benedictionem, & consilium interimendi fratris: quod tamen consilium Esau suspensum dicitur tenuisse reuerentia patris: quamuis non semper dissimulare potuerit quin Ribkæ matri innotesceret. Hoc consilium Ribka primum Iacobo, deinde Isaaco significauit. Iacobo mater significat causam, verf. 42. deinde modum fugiendi odium & insidias fratris, tribus seqq. Isaaco vero consilium idem; sed prudenter dissimulata causa, & altera quam speciosissima adhibita; nempe quod tæderet ipsos consortij cum fœminis alienigenis, ac proinde de commodiore coniugio prospici oportere: etsi hæc causa quoque vera fuit; sed alteram, quæ maxime vrgebat, dissimulare fuit prudentiæ.
units.tr: Just as the principal causes are efficient causes and those others are instrumental, so in Isaac's act of blessing Jacob we must hold that both causes concurred. The principal cause is God, as the common Father and beginning of all things; the instrumental cause is Isaac, as Jacob's particular father and God's minister in this action, as in others. Since it is established that the blessing was pronounced by both together, and since the force of all actions to which several causes contribute is such that the principal cause does not yield its power and authority to the lesser one, it clearly follows that the force and truth of this blessing come not from Isaac (for he was an instrument, which the principal cause adopted or joined to itself not out of necessity but out of goodness and grace) but from God, who is the efficient cause in himself and conferred the power of the blessing. God therefore honoured Isaac's person and his paternal calling by this ministry, but neither Isaac's blindness, nor his intention, nor his unwitting deed could spoil that divine work. Since God saw and knew all that was happening, and wished to carry out his purpose in this way without any imprudence, it was necessary that the blessing, which the principal cause was effecting, should remain valid and not be made void by a fault of the instrumental cause. Accordingly we see that God used his servants, and even foreigners, who were unwitting, so wisely in setting forth his will and counsels that, although they thought or wished something or nothing, they nevertheless expressed the counsel and will of God; and on the other hand, he often caused them, though unwitting, to stumble in that very action, so that all the praise might remain with the Lord as its author. Thus Samuel was deceived about the sons of Jesse; thus Nathan, pronouncing to David, carried out whatever was in his mind; thus, on the other hand, among foreigners and unbelievers, Balaam expressed the will of God, Caiaphas the counsel, Pilate the sentence, and whatever other things there are of this kind. So both points are evident to us: why the work is in no way vitiated by the imprudence or weakness of such instruments, and also, from the consequence, why the blessing remained valid. The third part of chapter 27 sets out two kinds of consequences: the first, what the coming Esau and the child obtained from their father, to verse 40; then what followed afterwards from these events, to the end of the chapter. For first is related the deed of Esau approaching his father and demanding the blessing, verses 30 to 39; then the blessing pronounced by Isaac, or rather the prophecy about the affairs of Esau and his family, verses 39 and 40. These things are narrated in the order in which they were done. First, Esau's arrival at almost the same moment that Jacob was leaving his father, verse 30; then the preparation and offering of the food according to the command, verse 31; then the dialogue or conversation between the two. The subjects of this conversation are three: first, concerning the person, verse 32; second, concerning the blessing, which Isaac had repeatedly refused and Esau now demanded, verse 33 and following; lastly, concerning the subject of the blessing, which Isaac confirmed as conferred upon Jacob, verse 37. The cause of the refused blessing, namely that it was to come to the firstborn, is given at verse 33, and it is twofold: first, that God suddenly struck Isaac with a trembling amazement [ἐκστάσεως], lest he should, as it were, revoke by private zeal what God's providence had brought about through him; for this reason the Greeks expressed this trembling by the word ecstasy. The other cause is that the blessing had been conferred upon Jacob earlier; God so confirmed this transfer by his own authority that Isaac said: I have blessed him, and he shall indeed be blessed. Then follows Esau's contrary entreaty, with cries and words, verse 34, together with the cause for the refusal, verse 35; then an unrestrained invective against Jacob, with an elegant paronomasia, and a repeated entreaty, verse 36; to this is joined the repeated excuse drawn from the subject of the blessing conferred upon Jacob, verse 37; finally the third entreaty of Esau, imploring his paternal right, verse 38. To this Isaac at last pronounces a certain measure of the blessing, which would not be contrary to the earlier blessing pronounced divinely, namely one uttered by the Spirit of prophecy, verses 39 and following. For first he sets out the condition of that inheritance and possession, verse 39, namely that Edom or Idumea had a fertile part of the region, though mountainous; then he pronounces the history of his descendants and their inheritance, verse 40, namely that they would wage wars, serve Judah, and groan under the heavy yoke and afflictions, as is related in 2 Kings 3; lastly, that they would shake the yoke of the Jews from their neck, as is related in 2 Kings 8 and following. The remaining matters are other things: namely, the counsels first of Esau, verse 41, then of Rebekah, verses 42 and following, and finally of Isaac, the last verse. Concerning Esau two most grievous works of the flesh are declared: inward hatred on account of the blessing he had lost, and the plan of killing his brother; yet Esau is said to have kept this plan suspended out of reverence for his father, although he could not always hide it from his mother Rebekah. Rebekah first signified this plan to Jacob, then to Isaac. To Jacob the mother signifies the cause, verse 42, then the manner of fleeing the hatred and snares of his brother, in the three following verses. To Isaac, however, she signified the same plan, but with the true cause prudently concealed and another, most specious one put forward, namely that they were disgusted with association with foreign women, and therefore a more suitable marriage ought to be provided for; although this cause also was true, it was a matter of prudence to conceal the other, which pressed most of all.

units.la: CAPITIS XXVIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: Analysis of Chapter 28.

units.la: ISToriam Isaaci & Abrahami sequitur suo ordine Iacobi historia: quæ inde ab hoc capite ad finem vsque huius libri pertinet, hanc vero Iacobi historiam pro ratione temporum, stationumque in tres partes commodè diuidemus.
units.tr: Jacob's history follows the history of Isaac and Abraham in its order. It runs from this chapter to the end of this book. For the sake of the times and the stages of the narrative, we will conveniently divide this history of Jacob into three parts.

units.la: Nam primum exponit Moses historiam peregrinationis in Mesopotamiam, ad caput vsque 32. Deinde vero historiam rerum in Cenahanea gestarum, ad caput vsque 42. Postremo autem rerum Ægyptiacarum, & quæ tum in Ægypto ipsi, tum etiam liberis acciderunt, inde ad finem vsque libri. Primus locus tria membra continet: primum, profectionis in Mesopotamiam, hoc capite: secundum, de coiugiis & liberis quos inde sustulit, duobus sequentibus: postremum de profectione ex Mesopotamia, & redditu in Cenahaneam, capite 31. In hac profectionis historia, tres perspicuæ habentur huius capitis partes. Nam primum narratur causa profectionis ad verf. vsque 10.
