Secundò narratur modus profectionis & præsentiæ Dei ad profectionem adstituri, inde ad 20. Postremo pium Iacobi votum reliquis versibus.
units.tr: Moses first sets out the history of Jacob's journey into Mesopotamia, up to chapter 32. Then he sets out the events in Canaan, up to chapter 42. Lastly, he gives the events in Egypt, and what happened to Jacob and his children there, from that point to the end of the book. The first part has three members: first, the departure for Mesopotamia, in this chapter; second, the marriages and the children he had there, in the two following chapters; last, the departure from Mesopotamia and the return to Canaan, in chapter 31. In this account of the departure there are three clear parts of this chapter. First, the cause of the departure is narrated, to verse 10. Second, the manner of the departure, and God's presence assisting him on the journey, is narrated, up to verse 20. Lastly, Jacob's pious vow, in the remaining verses.

units.la: Primus locus causam profectionis in Mesopotamiam explicans ad verf. vsque 9. pertenditur, & duas partes distinctas habet; vnam propriam, alteram, Proprię narrationis locus est versibus 5. versibus seqq. Propria narrationis summa est Isaacum in causa fuisse cur Iacob peteret Mesopotamiam: alteram causam incidentem expo- suit Moses sup. c. 26. 41. occasionem vero versu vltimo. Huius autem causæ loci duo sunt, mandatum & missio: mandatum versibus 4. missio versu 5. exponitur. Mandati duo sunt antecedentia: vnum, quòd Isaac Iacobum accersit ad se; alterum, quòd ei benedicit, i. benedictione ante collatam in ipsum confirmat sciens prudens. In mandato duo sunt: primum substantia mandati, duobus versibus 1. & 2: deinde promissio, duobus alteris. Mandatum est bimembre. Nam prius contrariū prohibetur, Ne Cenahaneā ducat, v.1: deinde res sancta imperatur, vt petat Mesopotamiam & agnatam ducat de gente sua; cuius mandati causa est gentis illius electio & sanctificatio à Domino; vt cui coniugium placet, non tamen promiscuum, sed in Domino, vt loquitur Apostolus 1. Corinth. 7. promissionis, quæ diuinitus cum hoc mandato coniuncta est, generalis enuntiatio principio verf. 31. continetur: post singularis interpretatio, primum de hæredibus & Ecclesia Dei, deinde vero de hæreditate tum vniuersa, quamcumque
units.tr: The first part, which explains the cause of the departure to Mesopotamia, extends to verse 9, and has two distinct parts: one proper, the other incidental. The place of the proper narrative is verse 5 and the verses that follow. The summary of the proper narrative is that Isaac was the reason Jacob sought Mesopotamia. Moses set out the incidental cause above, in chapter 26, verse 41, and the occasion in the last verse. This cause has two parts: a command and a sending. The command is explained in verse 4, the sending in verse 5. The command has two preceding elements: first, that Isaac summons Jacob to himself; second, that he blesses him, that is, confirms in him, knowingly and prudently, the blessing conferred before. The command has two parts: first the substance of the command, in verses 1 and 2; then the promise, in the two verses that follow. The command has two members. For the first, the contrary is forbidden: he must not take a wife from the Canaanites (v. 1). Then the holy thing is commanded: he is to go to Mesopotamia and take a kinswoman from his own people. The cause of this command is the election and sanctification of that nation by the Lord, so that marriage is pleasing, yet not promiscuous but "in the Lord", as the Apostle puts it in 1 Corinthians 7. The general statement of the promise, which is joined divinely to this command, is contained at the beginning of verse 3. After it comes the particular interpretation: first concerning the heirs and the Church of God, then concerning the inheritance, both the whole of what God had promised to Abraham and his seed by his blessing, and specifically the blessing of that symbolic or sacramental inheritance, that is, Canaan, which God wished to give to the Jewish nation as confirmation of the spiritual promises.

units.la: Deus Abrahamo promiserat benedictione sua & semini illius, tum speciatim benedictione hæreditatis illius symbolicę vel sacramentalis, idest, Cenahanæ quam Deus Iudæorum genti ad confirmationem promissionum spiritualium donatam voluit. Mandatum sequitur exsequutio, v.5. Quod Iacob instructus hoc mandato promissionibúsque à patre in Mesopotamiam dimissus est. Sequitur locus πρόθεσις, nempe de Esaui nouo coniugio: quod ex æmulatione fratris cogitauit, sed non propterea iniuit sanctè; tum quia sine non sancto ad coniugium illud trāsiliuit, tum quia modus non fuit sanctus, cùm duas vxores iam ante ductas haberet, ac proinde fuit πολυγαμίας. Huiųs mali causæ tribus versibus exponuntur: factum v.9. Causæ duæ; vna, scientia mandati paterni, benedictione coniuncti, v. 6. & obsequija Iacobo præstiti, v. 7. altera conscientia tædij quod pater Isaac de Cenahaneis fœminis conceperat, v.8. Quibus occasionibus adductus est, vt fœminam de gente sua, sed non sancta superduceret, nempe ex posteris Iischmahelis. Secúda pars capitis profectionem Iacobi continet, & confirmationem illius. Profectio v. 10. & 11: confirmatio versibus seqq. exponitur. Profectionis termini pronuntur v. 10. nam profectus est Beerschebahe è domo paterna, & contendit in Mesopotamicam Charanē, id est, (vt vocant Geographi) Carras Crassi clade nobilitatas. In itinere autem ad stationem nocturnam, Bethelem dicitur peruenire, v.11. & ibi quieuisse facto ex strue lapidum cerui- cali: tum vt rigidam simplicitatem illius ætatis ac minimè mollem videamus; tum vero vt via sternatur ad narrationem illam de conse- cratione lapidis, quæ habetur sub finem capitis. In hoc loco & sta- tione hæc confirmatio dicitur obuenisse Iacobo: primùm quidem ty- po, deinde sermone & declaratione singulari. Typus v.12; declaratio seqq. versibus continetur. Typus hic in somnis dicitur obuenisse; scala maxima, ima parte sua incumbens terræ, & summa cælum pertingens; qua significabatur tota ratio itineris à Iacobo suscepti: dein- de Angeli Dei ascendentes & descendentes per scalam: quibus significabatur singularis dūctus & assistentia Dei Iacobum agentis toto hoc itinere, v.12. Postremò Iehoua stans ad scalam, idest, ipse non solùm per angelos, sed sua ipsius præsentia & virtute totum iter moderans. Quòd enim vulgò à Patribus & hominibus nostris altera huius loci allata est interpretatio, id totū est allegoricum; & documentum per se quidem verum, sed non huius loci proprium. Sequitur declaratio verbis facta: cuius exordium priore membro v.13. est petitum ab affirmatione sederis, quod Deus cum Abrahamo initum, cap. 17. continuauerat cū Isaaco patre, & per illum Iacobo trās̄ederat. Hinc sequunsequuntur promissiones: primum de haereditate, reliquo v.13. secun-dò de haeredibus, tum ex Judaeis tum ex gentibus adjungendis, v.14. in quibus observandum nomen feminis non esse collectivum, sed proprie ad Christum respicere, ut monet Apostolus Galat. 3. tertiò spondet singularem assistentiam in toto hoc itinere, & deductionem domum; & veritatem suarum promissionum tantae curae sibi esse praedicat, ut non sit hominem desertûrus quin omnia promissa faciat. Quod autem dicit, non d feram te usque dum fecero,non est illud perinde accipiendum ac si postmodum desertus fuisset Deus Jacobum; sed intelligendum hanc loquutionem interdum(ut ita loquamur) terminalem esse, interdum verò non esse terminalem simpliciter, sed tantum secundum quid continuationem rei promissae ad complementum ipsius usque,aut etiam rei enuntiatae tantum disser-minare. Restat locus ultimus, de agnitione & voto Jacobi: nam agnitio ad verf. 19 : votum ad finem usque exponitur. Tertius ergo locus capitis duobus membris describitur, agnitione, & professione. In agnitione sunt ista: primum quòd expergefactus Jacob sensit duo cum animo suo quae ad initiandam religionem plurimum faciunt: unum, Deum adesse singulari praesentiae modo: alterum, se tamen eam praesentiam, dum vigilavit, non animadvertisse, ac proinde illam conscientiam praesentiae Dei non esse à sensu ipsius; sed à singulari instinctu & inspiratione Dei, quam etiam gentes agnoverunt. Deinde ex hac conscientia sequitur religio, v. 17. qua religione tactus Jahakob profitetur ista: primùm reverentiam loci non per se; sed ex Dei praesentis majestate: secundò singularem illius loci sanctificationem ex Dei praesentia, ut Deus dicebat Mosi, Exodi 3. & Josue 6. Postremò usum praestantiae illius, quòd illa porta caelorum esset[?]. Hac autem loquutione varij varia intelligunt: nos simpliciter ductu administrationemque caelestè intelligimus. Nam respiciens Jacob ad singulares Dei promissiones, signaque promissionibus conjuncta, ita statuit; se jam vere animadvertere quàm certo receptus sit in domum Dei, & quàm fideliter circumseptus administratione, gubernatione, & procuratione divina ipsius: quae gubernatio in rebus humanis synecdochicè declarari solet portarum appellatione. Ex his autem sequitur professio Jacobi, qui manè surgens non potuit non testificari palam, pro sua pietate, quàm singulare Dei beneficium accepisset. Itaque primùm ex lapidibus, quos sibi ad ceruical substraverat, statuam erexisse dici-tur, eámque oleo perfudisse ad signum sanctificationis & gratiarum actionis, versu 18. Secundò locum illum religioso nomine appellasse, versu 19. Postremò autem votum singulare vouisse Deo, versu 20. & sequentibus. Voti autem partes sunt duæ: vna suppositi, (vt ita loquamur) verf. 20. & 21. Altera propositi, quod spondet Domino, verf. 22. Suppositum siue hypothesin appello summam illam repetitionem promissorum quæ Deus ipsi tum per Isaacum versu 3. & sequentibus; tum per seipsum versu 13. & sequentibus fecerat: tam totum promissionum illarum argumentum duobus his versibus continetur, adiecta singulari determinatione, vel circumscriptione temporis, cum ait, cum adfuerit Deus mihi, vt promissum est versu 15. Et seruauerit me in via, &c. vt promissum est ibidem: cum & dederit mihi cibum ad comedendum & vestem ad vestiendum, quod membrum illo benedictionis genere comprehenditur versu 3. Deinde versu 21. & reuersus fuero cum pace domum Patris mei, vt promiserat Deus versu 15. Denique fuerit mihi Iehoua Deus, id est, præstiterit promissiones Abrahamo & semini ipsius factas, vt versu 4. Atque hoc suppositum. Sequitur propositum votum versu vltimo; in quo Iacob pro ratione ceremoniali illorum temporum duo spondet; primum se in eo loco eoque signo agnituram præsentiam Dei, vt quem locum Deus sanctificasset; deinde vero se, vt gratum animum suum testificetur, eorum omnium quæ a Deo accepit decimas daturum esse ad professionem religiosi & grati animi sui, & conseruationem diuini cultus. De ritibus autem istis ceremonialibus, qui per tempus illud ante legem diuinitus inspirati, post legem instituti sunt, vt rerum futurarum in Christo essent umbracula: quia corpus earum Christus est (vt inquit Apostolus ad Colossenses 2.) nihil necesse est a nobis hoc loco dici.
units.tr: The command is followed by its execution, in verse 5: Jacob, instructed by this command and by the promises of his father, was sent away into Mesopotamia. Next comes the purpose [πρόθεσις], namely Esau's new marriage. He conceived this out of rivalry with his brother, but did not on that account enter into it piously: partly because he leapt into that marriage without a holy purpose, and partly because the manner of it was not holy, since he already had two wives, and so it was polygamy. The cause of this evil is set out in three verses: the deed in verse 9. There are two causes: one, the knowledge of the father's command, joined with the blessing, in verse 6, and the obedience Jacob rendered in verse 7; the other, the consciousness of the displeasure which his father Isaac had conceived against the Canaanite women, in verse 8. Moved by these occasions, he took a woman from his own people, but not a holy one, namely from the descendants of Ishmael, as a second wife. The second part of the chapter contains Jacob's departure and its confirmation. The departure is in verses 10 and 11; the confirmation is explained in the verses that follow. The termini of the departure are stated in verse 10: for he set out from Beersheba, from his father's house, and made for Haran in Mesopotamia, that is (as the geographers call it) Carrhae, made famous by the defeat of Crassus. On the way, at his night's halt, he is said to have arrived at Bethel (v. 11), and there to have rested, having made a bed of a heap of stones for a pillow. This shows us the rough simplicity of that age, which was by no means soft; and it also prepares the way for the narrative about the consecration of the stone, which is found near the end of the chapter. At this place and this halt, the confirmation is said to have come to Jacob: first by a type, then by a word and a particular declaration. The type is in verse 12; the declaration is contained in the verses that follow. This type is said to have come to him in dreams: a very great ladder, resting on the earth with its lower end and reaching the heavens with its top, by which the whole plan of the journey undertaken by Jacob was signified; then the angels of God ascending and descending by the ladder, by which the singular guidance and the assistance of God, guiding Jacob throughout this journey, were signified (v. 12). Lastly, Jehovah standing by the ladder, that is, himself moderating the whole journey not only through angels, but by his own presence and power. For the other interpretation of this place, which is commonly offered by our Fathers and our own people, is wholly allegorical: it is a lesson true in itself, but not proper to this passage. The declaration in words follows. Its beginning, in the first member (v. 13), is taken from the affirmation of the covenant which God made with Abraham in chapter 17, and which he had renewed with Isaac, the father, and through him had handed on to Jacob. Then the promises follow: first concerning the inheritance, in the rest of verse 13; second concerning the heirs, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles who are to be joined to them (v. 14). In these verses we should observe that the word "seed" is not collective, but properly refers to Christ, as the Apostle reminds us in Galatians 3. Third, he promises his singular assistance throughout this whole journey and his leading home, and he declares that the truth of his promises is so dear to him that he will not forsake the man without fulfilling all that was promised. As for his saying, "I will not leave you until I have done", this is not to be taken as if God had afterwards forsaken Jacob; rather, this phrase is to be understood as sometimes terminal, so to speak, and sometimes not terminal absolutely, but only in a certain respect, extending the continuation of the promised thing to its completion, or merely spreading abroad the thing declared. The last place remains, concerning Jacob's recognition and his vow. The recognition is explained up to verse 19, and the vow from there to the end. The third part of the chapter is therefore described in two members: recognition and profession. In the recognition there are these points. First, that when Jacob woke from sleep he perceived two things in his mind which contribute greatly to beginning religion: one, that God was present in a singular manner; the other, that he had not noticed that presence while he was awake, and so the consciousness of God's presence did not come from his own sense, but from a singular instinct and inspiration of God, which even the Gentiles have recognised. From this consciousness religion follows (v. 17). Moved by this religion, Jacob professes the following: first, the reverence of the place is not in itself, but arises from the majesty of God's presence; second, the singular sanctification of that place arises from God's presence, just as God spoke to Moses in Exodus 3 and to Joshua in Joshua 6; lastly, the use of that dignity, namely that this place was the gate of heaven. Various people understand this expression in various ways. We understand it simply as the heavenly guidance and administration. For Jacob, looking back on God's singular promises and the signs joined to them, judged thus: he now truly perceives how surely he has been received into the house of God, and how faithfully he has been protected by the administration, government and providence of God. Such government in human affairs is commonly described, by synecdoche, under the name of gates. From these things follows Jacob's profession. Rising in the morning, he could not fail to bear witness openly, as befitted his piety, to the singular benefit of God that he had received. Accordingly, first, he is said to have set up a pillar from the stones he had placed under his head as a pillow, and to have poured oil on it as a sign of consecration and thanksgiving (v. 18). Second, he called that place by a religious name (v. 19). Lastly, he made a singular vow to God (v. 20 and following). The vow has two parts: one of the supposition, so to speak, in verses 20 and 21; the other of the proposal, which he pledges to the Lord, in verse 22. I call the supposition or hypothesis the summary repetition of the promises which God had made to him, both through Isaac (v. 3 and following) and through himself (v. 13 and following). The whole argument of those promises is contained in these two verses, with a particular specification or limitation of time added, when he says: "if God shall be with me, as he has promised" (v. 15); "and shall keep me in the way", etc., as promised in the same place; "and shall give me bread to eat and clothing to wear", a clause comprehended under that kind of blessing in verse 3; then, in verse 21: "and I shall return in peace to my father's house", as God promised in verse 15; lastly, "Jehovah shall be my God", that is, he shall perform the promises made to Abraham and his seed, as in verse 4. This is the supposition. The proposed vow follows in the last verse. In it Jacob, according to the ceremonial custom of those times, pledges two things: first, that in that place and by that sign he will acknowledge the presence of God, since God has sanctified the place; second, that, to bear witness to his grateful mind, he will give a tenth of all that he has received from God, as a profession of his religious and thankful spirit and for the preservation of the divine worship. Concerning those ceremonial rites, which were divinely inspired in that period before the law and were instituted after the law, so that they might be shadows of things to come in Christ (for "the body of them is Christ", as the Apostle says to the Colossians 2), there is no need for us to say anything about them in this place.

units.la: CAPITIS XXIX ANALYSIS
units.tr: CHAPTER XXIX: ANALYSIS

units.la: EX profectione, de qua cap. præcedente narratio a Mose fuit instituta, sequitur historia aduentus in Mesopotamiam, rerumque in ea gestarum. Sunt autem hæ res ordine a Mose descriptæ: primùm factum coniugale, idque duplex, ad versum vsque 30. huius capitis: deinde liberorum procreatio ex coniugiis, ad verf. vsque 25. sequentis capitis: postremò autem mercedis ratio quam in Mesopotamia Iacob consequutus est, inde ad finem vsque. Itaque huius cap. summæ partes sunt duæ: prior de coniugiis; posterior de liberis, quos ex priore coniugio sustulit Iacob. In coniugiorum historia duo ordine oportet obseruari: primùm quàm rationem Deus exhi-buerit buerit Iacobo vt coniugium in Labanis familia assequeretur, ad versum vsque 14. secundò qui contractus & euentus coniugij, ad vers. 30. Rationi quam Deus Iacobo obtulit ad coniugium Rachelæ obtinendum præcedit conclusio capitis 28. nempe quòd Iacob mandato patris & promissionibus Dei confirmatus regionem illam petiuit, vers. 1. Post aduentum eius hæc narrantur sponsaliorum & coniugij antecedentia: primùm quòd Iacob imprudens Rachelæ occurrit, ad vers. vsque 9. Deinde quòd singulari officio studium & amorem illius promeritus est, vers. 10. Tum quòd sanctis documentis studij & necessitudinis inter ipsos Rachelam certiorem fecit de conditione sua, vers.11. & 12. Postremò quod notitia inita in domum Labanis, vt necessarius, exceptus est, vers. 12. & duobus sequentibus. Primi loci facilis est historia: quòd gregibus ad puteum recubantibus, in quo pastorum opera aquarentur, vers.2. & 3. Iacob pastores compellauit, vers. quarto, & rogauit de cognatione sua, versu 5. & 6. Ex quibus cùm de cognatæ suæ aduentu audiuisset, consilium dedisse commodum omnibus dicitur, vt deuoluto puteali aquarent pecudes, & amplius pascerent, vers. septimo, quam rem illis abnuentibus propter lapidis grauitatem, vers. octauo, ad Rachelæ aduentum, vers. nono, dicitur communi opera cum aliis pastoribus puteal deuoluisse. Atque hæc omnia humanitatis honestatisque officia Iacobum commendabiliorem omnibus, in primis autem Rachelæ, reddiderunt. Notitiæ verò argumenta fuerunt hæc: osculum sanctum, fletúsque, vers. 11. & generis explicatio, vers. 12. Ex quo factum est, vt Rachel ad suos domum cucurrerit, & Laban vicissim re audita accurrens, amplexu, osculo, domo exceperit, & res suas narrantem amicè audiuerit. Etsi autem non videtur Moses diserte exponere rerum quas Iacob narrabat argumentum, tamen tum ex conditione rerum illarum, tum ex Labanis responso facile potest colligi quid narrationis Iacob adhibuerit: primùm enim dicit Moses eum narrauisse omnes res istas, putà quæ inde à capite 26. fuerunt expositæ. Deinde conditio præsens Iacobi desiderare illud videbatur, cum nudus à rebus omnibus in Mesopotamiam aduentaret, pro eo quod paternus famulus ante annos multos instrumentissimus auro, argento, muneribúsque venerat, supra cap. 24. Postremò autem Labanis responsio, quasi interrumpentis sermonem illius. Idem videtur confirmare vers. 14. tamquam si diceret, Quid multis opus est? etiam si horum nihil effet quæ à te adducuntur, cum tamen mihi ita sis propinquus sanguine, vt vix propinquior mihi quisquam esse possit, & (quod prouerbiali loquutione dicitur) os meum & caro mea fis; ego aliis omnibus rebus missis cupio te de meo studio confirmatum esse, & morari apud me. Quapropter sequitur illud Mosis dictum, consedisse apud illum mensem integrum, nempe vt alter alterum exploraret & videret vtrum conditio vtrinque esset placitura. sic antecedetia sponsaliorum sunt haec: occasio, congressus, notitia ex congressu, & familiaris conuersatio. Iam sequitur locus alter de sponsalibus & nuptiis. Qui locus bipertitus est, quia bina fuerunt sponsalia, binaeque nuptiae: prior locus sponsaliorum & nuptiarum cum Lea, ad verf. vsque 24. Posterior cum Rachela ad verf.29. vsque protenditur. In priore parte historiae contractus narratur ad verf. vsque 20. Nuptiae vero & deductio in domum viri, sequentibus. Contractui occasionem dedit Labanis stipulatio, verf. 15. cum sibi mercedem a Iacobo pro seruitute indici postularet. Huic stipulationi sponsio & restipulatio subiicitur, verf. 18. Duo intercurrentes versus ad ἀρμοδιώτερον restipulationis factae a Iacobo pertinent, vt intelligamus quid causae Iacob habuerit vt ita restipularetur, nempe optione Rachelę prę Lea, propter huius inualetudinem & illius formam. Restipulationis argumentum est, Iacobum sibi Rachelam coniugem deposcere: sponsionis, eum pretio coniugis illius seruiturum: quam restipulatione sponsionemque auarus Laban obuiis vlnis dicitur accepisse, verf.19. Perplacebat enim conditio homini auaro, quod filiam sine pretio ita elocaret, vt etiam ex genero filiaque diuturna commoda esset percepturus. Qua in re etsi oculis suis iniquè consulebat, honestati tamen & paci iniquius: prout filiarum quaerelae aperte ostendunt infra 31.cap.verf.14.& sequentib. Atque haec quidem de sponsalitio cōtractu inter Iacobum & Rachelam: cum autem sponsalia de bonorum omnium sententia inter bonę fidei contractus numerentur, nihil ex eo contractu sequi aliud oportuit, quàm vt Rachel (de qua contractus fuerat initus) bona fide Iacobo dederetur: sed Laban prout fide non bona contractum iniuerat, ita etiam dicitur praestitisse, versibus seq. Antequā autem de praestatione dicatur, Moses de inductria versum 20.interposuit, in quo hi storiam promissae seruitutis pro Rachela cum historia contractus copulauit ad commoditatem historiae; nempe ne postea diuisionibus & distinctionibus historia obscuraretur. Non enim scriptura sacra tantopere solet de distinctione temporum laborare, quā de argumetorum perspicuitate, quia in his plus multo positum est. Atque hinc natū est illud Iudaeorum dictū in commentariis ipsorum, non esse prius aut posterius in scriptura; pro eo quod est, nō accurate ratione temporū & distinctē obseruari. Nā alioquin narratio huius versus 20, narratione sequentium sequentiū omniū in hoc cap.non plane quidem sequuta est,sed tamē coniunctā habet tēpore. Huius autē narrationis interductæ duo sunt membra: vnum,quod Iacobus sponsionem suam præstiterit,quamuis Laban non peræque seruasset fidem : alterum , quod alacerrimo animo præstiterit,eo quod amata potiretur,quamuis Laban acerbitate quadam lętitiam illius condiuisset mutata perfida sponsione sua. Itaque duæ rationes adferuntur, cur Iacob iniquitatem hominis æquo animo pertulerit:vna,quod fide sua vincere voluit perfidiam illius,id est, bono malum , quod Christianum est:altera, quod amore in Rachelam omnis memoria iniquitatis deleta est,quod humanum. Sequitur ergo præstatio infida, quæ narratur versibus 4. seq. Nam primùm postulatum Iacobi ponitur v.21. secundò simulatio Labanis facto solemni conuiuio,v.22.ac postremò fraus effecta, duobus seqq. Postulatum Iacobi de habenda vxore duobus argumentis nititur:iure communi,&singulari ratione ipsius. Iure communi enim Rachel fuit Iacobi vxor,quia nuptias consensus non concubitus facit;quapropter sponsæ in scripturis sacris, quamuis nondum innupserint, vxores appellantur,vt Num.30. Deut.22.Matt.1. Singulari ratione, quia iam ad ætatem plus satis iustam peruenerat, quod enuntiat his verbis, nam completi sunt dies mei, nempe non seruitutis (quod multi imprudenter existimauerunt) sed ætatis ad coniugium ineundum commodæ, atque adeo iam ingrauescentis: agebat enim Iacob hoc tempore annum ferme 75.provt ex comparatione ætatis facilè potest colligi qua in Ægyptum legitur migrauisse, cap.46. Quo tempore Ioseph annum ferme agebat 40.& Iacob 137.vt ipse Parhoni rogan- ti narrat.
units.tr: After the departure, which the preceding chapter recounts, Moses goes on to the history of the arrival in Mesopotamia and of what was done there. Moses describes these matters in order: first the marriage affair, and that a double one, down to verse 30 of this chapter; then the begetting of children from those marriages, down to verse 25 of the following chapter; and lastly the account of the wages Jacob earned in Mesopotamia, from there to the end. So the chapter has two main parts: the first on the marriages, the second on the children whom Jacob had by his first marriage. In the history of the marriages two things must be observed in order. First, the plan God set before Jacob so that he might obtain a marriage in Laban's family, down to verse 14. Second, the agreement and outcome of the marriage, to verse 30. The plan God offered Jacob for obtaining Rachel is preceded by the conclusion of chapter 28, namely that Jacob, confirmed by his father's command and God's promises, sought that region (verse 1). After his arrival, the following things are narrated as preliminaries to the betrothal and marriage: first, that Jacob met Rachel by chance, down to verse 9; then that by a singular service he earned her attention and affection (verse 10); then that by holy words of kinship and familiarity he made Rachel aware of his circumstances (verses 11 and 12); and lastly that, having come to Laban's house as a kinsman, he was received (verse 12 and the two following). The first episode is simple. While the flocks lay resting by the well, where the shepherds watered them (verses 2 and 3), Jacob addressed the shepherds (verse 4) and asked about his kinsfolk (verses 5 and 6). When he heard of the arrival of his cousin, he is said to have proposed a plan that suited everyone: that they should roll away the stone from the well, water the flocks and pasture them longer (verse 7). When they refused, because the stone was heavy (verse 8), then at Rachel's arrival (verse 9) he is said to have rolled the stone away from the well with the other shepherds' joint labour. All these acts of courtesy and honour made Jacob more commendable to everyone, and above all to Rachel. The tokens of acquaintance were these: a holy kiss and tears (verse 11), and the explanation of kinship (verse 12). As a result Rachel ran home to her people, and Laban, on hearing the news, ran in turn, embraced and kissed him, took him into his house, and listened kindly while he told his story. Although Moses does not expressly set out the content of what Jacob related, it can easily be gathered both from the circumstances and from Laban's reply. Moses first says that Jacob narrated all those things, that is, the things set out from chapter 26 onward. Then Jacob's present condition seemed to call for it, since he arrived in Mesopotamia naked of all possessions, whereas his father's servant, many years before, had come laden with gold, silver and gifts (chapter 24 above). Lastly, Laban's reply seems to break in upon his speech. Verse 14 seems to confirm this, as if Laban were saying: "Why need there be many words? Even if none of these things you bring were here, since you are so near to me in blood that hardly anyone could be nearer, and (as the proverb says) you are my bone and my flesh, I wish, setting aside all other matters, that you be secured in my affection and stay with me." Hence follows Moses' statement that Jacob stayed with him a whole month, namely so that each might test the other and see whether the terms were acceptable on both sides. Thus the preliminaries of the betrothal are these: the opportunity, the meeting, the acquaintance formed from the meeting, and familiar conversation. Next follows the second place, concerning the betrothal and the marriages. This place is in two parts, because there were two betrothals and two marriages. The first part, on the betrothal and marriage with Leah, extends to verse 24; the second, with Rachel, runs from there to verse 29. In the first part the agreement is narrated down to verse 20, and the marriage and the bride's leading into her husband's house follow. Laban's stipulation gave occasion for the agreement (verse 15), when he demanded that Jacob name his wages for his service. To this stipulation is added the promise and counter-stipulation (verse 18). The two intervening verses relate to the counter-stipulation Jacob made, so that we understand why he had such a reason for making it, namely his choice of Rachel rather than Leah, because of the weakness of the one and the beauty of the other. The substance of the counter-stipulation is that Jacob demanded Rachel as his wife; that of the promise, that he would serve for the price of her as a wife. Greedy Laban is said to have accepted this counter-stipulation and promise with open arms (verse 19). For the terms pleased a greedy man, that he would give his daughter without a price, and would gain lasting advantages both from his son-in-law and from his daughter. In this matter, though he consulted his own eyes unjustly, he consulted honour and peace even more unjustly, as the complaints of his daughters clearly show below, chapter 31, verses 14 and following. So much for the betrothal agreement between Jacob and Rachel. Since, by the judgement of all, betrothals are counted among contracts of good faith, nothing else could follow from that agreement than that Rachel, to whom the contract had been made, should be given to Jacob in good faith. But Laban, who had entered the contract in bad faith, is said in the following verses to have performed it accordingly. Before Moses tells of the performance, he has inserted in verse 20 a note of the diligence of Jacob, in which he joined the history of the promised service for Rachel to the history of the agreement, for the convenience of the narrative, so that later the history would not be obscured by divisions and distinctions. For Holy Scripture does not usually labour so much over the distinction of times as over the clarity of the matters, since far more is at stake in those. From this comes the saying of the Jews in their commentaries that there is no before or after in Scripture, because it is not always observed in exact order of times and in distinct sequence. For otherwise the narrative of this verse 20 does not follow in full the narrative of all the things that follow in this chapter, yet it is joined to them in time. Two parts make up this inserted narrative: first, that Jacob performed his promise, although Laban had not kept his faith equally; second, that he performed it with the utmost eagerness, because he would obtain the one he loved, although Laban, having changed his perfidious promise, had mixed some bitterness into his joy. Thus two reasons are given why Jacob bore the man's injustice with an even mind: one, that he wished to overcome his treachery by his own good faith, that is, to overcome evil with good, which is Christian; the other, that from his love for Rachel all memory of the injustice was blotted out, which is human. Next comes the faithless performance, which is narrated in verses 4 and following. For first Jacob's demand is set out (verse 21); second, Laban's pretence, when a solemn banquet was made (verse 22); and lastly the fraud, carried out in the two following verses. Jacob's demand to have his wife rests on two grounds: common law, and his own particular circumstance. By common law Rachel was already Jacob's wife, since consent, not intercourse, makes a marriage; for this reason in the Scriptures betrothed women are called wives even before they have married, as in Numbers 30, Deuteronomy 22 and Matthew 1. The particular circumstance is that she had already reached a more than sufficiently just age, which he expresses in these words, for my days are fulfilled. This refers not to the time of service, as many have imprudently supposed, but to the age suitable for entering marriage, and one already advancing. For at this time Jacob was about seventy-five years old, as can easily be gathered from a comparison of ages, at which he is read to have migrated into Egypt (chapter 46). At that time Joseph was about forty years old, and Jacob 130 and 7, as he himself tells Pharaoh when asked.

units.la: Iosephautem natus est 14.huius seruitutis anno,vt seq. capite di- stertis verbis ostenditur.Traditio vero ex contractu primùm simula- ta conuiuio dicitur,v.22.Deinde vero fraudata seqq.hæc autem factū iniquè fuisse factum nemo bonus dubitauerit.quo modo factum fue- rit,quæritur,vt Iacobo ea noctę,altera submissa sit in locum alterius.
units.tr: Joseph, however, was born in the fourteenth year of this servitude, as the following chapter shows in plain words. But the handing over is said, at verse 22, to have been first feigned by a contract for a feast, and then carried out by fraud, in the verses that follow. Nobody who is good will doubt that this was done unjustly. The question is how it was done: that on that night another woman was sent in to Jacob in place of the one he expected.

units.la: Hic vero ritus prisci obseruandi sunt ad fraudis istius intelligetiam: nam primùm intempesta noctę in thalamum deducebantur : dein sponsus prior intromittebatur, post adducebatur sponsa cum luce quidem ad thalami usque aditum,sed ita velata vt à nemine in os videri posset. Postremò intrudebatur sine luce in thalamum, & tradebatur viro ad pudoris muliebris & honestatis significatione. Atque hinc factum est vt apud Græcos quoque ipsos, alioqui malos honestatis & pudicitiæ custodes, posterus à nuptiis dies ἀναχαλυπτήρια[?] dicebatur, quia tum nubes, id est,peplum aut caliptra qua obnubebatur sponsa eximebatur, & revelata prodibat in virorum cospectum. Huius fraudis occasione Iacob ad nuptias alteras deductus est, ut narratur v.25. & seqq. Nam primum occasio exponitur, v.25. deinde contractus novus novarum nuptiarum, v.26. postremo autem praestatio contractus, versibus seqq. occasio fuit; primum quod Iacob matutino animadvertit fraudem, deinde quod de fraude cum socero expostulavit. Hanc fraudem ut levaret Laban, & ne Lea maiori filiq[?] fraudi esset; primum excusat factum a consuetudine, v.26. deinde vero levationem fraudis offert oblato coniugio quod Iacob ambiverat, iteratāque conditione antecedentis contractus. Quapropter dicit, compleseptimanam huius, non servitutis; sed festivitatis nuptialis, quae apud illos septem dialis erat ut exemplo Schimschonis discimus in libro Iudicum. Deinde sponsionem facit amatæ filiæ, ut v.19. Quam sponsionem Iacob accepisse dicitur, & Rachelam sororem Leæ superduxisse v.28. & 29. Hic vero quaeritur, utrum iusta fuerit haec polygamia. Resp. Quod iuri naturali repugnat, id nulla ratione iustum dici posse: ac propterea in omnibus exemplis polygamiæ quæ hactenus legimus, illud observatu dignum est, aut impios homines auctores fuisse polygamiq[?], aut pios infirmitate fidei lapsos:impios, ut Lemech, Gen. 4. Esau, 26. & 27, & Laba, hoc loco. Pios, ut Sara, Gen. 16. & Iacobum hoc loco. Hoc autem naturale ius a Mose descriptum Gen. 2. accuratissime persequitur Prophetam Malach. 2. c. Sequitur iam de usu coniugij & benedictione divina, qui postremus est cap. huius locus. In usu notat Moses inaequalitatem amoris atque consuetudinis consortij v.30. deinde vero iudicium Dei, res pro sua providentia, non autem pro studiis nostris administrantis sapientissime ad afflictorum consolationem, quod Lea exosa effet, i.no aeque amata: nam haec dicuntur comparate. Quapropter generis propagatio Iacobo divinitus per Leam primo attributa est. Ex hac benedictione Dei quatuor filij ordine ex Lea dicuntur nati; in quibus, primum benedictionis divinae efficacitas observanda est; secundo matrum in liberos auctoritas nomen indentium, sed viris annuentibus: postremo autem praedicatio illius divinae benedictionis quae in singulorum nominibus est evidens: id tantum ratione linguae Hebraeae observandum est, plurimum voces in nominibus imponendis corruptas esse, adiectis, detractis, aut mutatis literis vocalibusque ad commoditatem pronunciationis.
units.tr: Here, however, the ancient customs must be observed if we are to understand this fraud. For first, in the dead of night, the bride was led into the bridal chamber. Then the bridegroom was admitted first, and afterwards the bride was brought up with a light as far as the entrance of the chamber, but so veiled that no one could see her face. Last, she was pushed into the chamber without light and handed over to her husband, as a sign of womanly modesty and honour. From this it came about that among the Greeks themselves, who were otherwise poor guardians of honour and chastity, the day after the wedding was called the day of unveiling [ἀναχαλυπτήρια], because then the cloud, that is, the veil or head-covering with which the bride had been shrouded, was removed, and she came forth unveiled into the sight of men. It was on the occasion of this fraud that Jacob was brought to a second marriage, as is narrated at verse 25 and following. For first the occasion is set out, at verse 25; then the new contract of the new marriage, at verse 26; and finally the performance of the contract, in the verses that follow. The occasion was this: first, that Jacob noticed the fraud in the morning; then, that he complained to his father-in-law about the fraud. To lessen this fraud, and so that Leah should not be a burden to her elder daughter, Laban first excuses the deed by custom, at verse 26; then he offers a remedy for the fraud, by offering the marriage that Jacob had sought, and by repeating the condition of the earlier contract. Therefore he says, fulfil this week, not of servitude but of nuptial festivity, which among them lasted seven days, as we learn from the example of Samson in the book of Judges. Then he makes the promise of his beloved daughter, as at verse 19. Jacob is said to have accepted this promise, and to have taken Rachel, the sister of Leah, as a second wife, at verses 28 and 29. Here, however, the question is whether this polygamy was lawful. Answer: what is contrary to the natural law can by no means be called lawful. Therefore, in all the examples of polygamy that we have read of so far, this is worth noting: that either impious men were the authors of polygamy, or pious men fell into it through weakness of faith. Impious men, such as Lamech, Genesis 4; Esau, Genesis 26 and 27; and Laban, in this place. Pious men, such as Sarah, Genesis 16, and Jacob in this place. Moses described this natural law in Genesis 2, and the prophet Malachi, in chapter 2, follows it very precisely. Next comes the use of marriage and the divine blessing, which is the last part of this chapter. In the use of marriage, Moses notes the inequality of love and of the companionship of living together, at verse 30; then the judgment of God, who in his providence, and not according to our wishes, arranges things most wisely, for the comfort of the afflicted, that Leah was hated, that is, not equally loved, for these things are said by way of comparison. Therefore the propagation of offspring was first given to Jacob by God through Leah. By this blessing of God four sons are said to have been born to Leah, in order. In these, first, the efficacy of the divine blessing is to be observed; second, the authority of the mothers over their children in naming them, though with the consent of the husbands; last, the proclamation of that divine blessing, which is plain in the meaning of each name. Only this must be observed, in view of the Hebrew language: in imposing names, the words are very often corrupted, with letters added, removed or changed, both consonants and vowels, for the sake of ease of pronunciation.

units.la: CAPITIS XXX. ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXX. ANALYSIS.

units.la: ENEDICTIONEM diuinam, de qua sub finem cap. præced. cœpit Moses dicere, pergit in hoc capite explicare. Huius autē benedictionis duo sunt genera: vnum est liberorum procreatio, alterum, bonorum temporalium siue commodorum multiplicatio; quorum prius ad verf. vsque 24. posterius ad finem vsque cap. exponitur. In liberorum procreatione exponenda singulares quædam historiæ intercidunt, ex quibus summatim ista cognoscimus: primùm polygamiæ incommoda; secundò sanctorum in grauibus incomodis patientiam: postremò autem Dei misericordiam, quæ vitiositate hominum non potest intercipi quin benefaciat suis. Inter polygamiæ incommoda, primum hoc loco ponitur zelotypia, verf. 1. quæ Rachelæ animum sic dicitur accendisse, vt stultè virum de liberorum procreatione appellauerit, & ille cum indignatione animi respondērit, 2. versu; reuocans illa ad cogitationē iustitiæ Dei, cuius voluntas nobis summa est necessitas. Alterum polygamiæ incommodum ex eo sequitur, quòd zelotypa Rachel amplius per imprudentiam accedens ignem zelotypiæ ancillam suam vxorem Iacobo dedit: cuius rei consilium, verf. 3. pactum, 4; euentus, 5. & seqq. exponitur, nempe ancillam peperisse, verf. 5. quo nomine Rachel gloriatur, verf. 6. & stultitiæ suæ monimentum statuit in Filij sui nomine: tū quod eadem iterū parit v. 7. eiusdémque stultæ gloriationis argumentū Rachelæ exhibet, v. 8. Tertiū incommodum est, quòd illud stultè ab vna factū ab altera in exēplum trahitur, quæ tamē liberorum numero, & quidem ex se superabat, v. 9. Ac proinde ex ancilla altera dedita partus item duplex, & eiusdem modi gloriatio consequuta est, v. 10, & duobus seqq. Tertius infirmitatis locus ex eodem fonte zelotypiæ ductus demonstratur v. 14. & seq. quòd fororcs de rebus etiam leuiculis concitæ zelotypia inter se dimicauerunt: etsi ex hac ipsa concertatione gratiosus Dominus occasionem cepit amplius benedicendi familiæ Iacobi, vt verf. 16. & seqq. ostenditur. Occasio fuisse puerilis dicitur, flores à puero inuenti & matri traditi, quos soror Rachel appetiuerit, versu. 14. Atque hinc sordida concubitus cum viro nundinatio, v. 15. Ex hoc tamen infirmitatis exemplo, Deus sapientissimus id elicuit boni, quod ex vendito illo viri cocubitu & cosensione illius confirmato, v. 16. Deus Iahakobū ex Lea voluit gignere, v. 17. cuius genituræ ad testificationē grati animi documētū exstitit in nomine Filij. v. 18. Et ita ordine benedictio Dei perrexisse, tū in Lea v. 19. & duobus seq. tū verò tandē in Rachelā quam Deus ex sterili effecit matrem ad tollendum probrum illius, prout hoc beneficium misericordiae Dei adscribitur a Mose v.22. & a Rachela ipsa tum agnoscitur, v. 23. tum vero impositio nomine amplius exoptatur, v.24. Sequitur deinceps alter locus capitis v. 25. quo modo & quantopere Deus Iacobo in re familiari benedixerit. Itaque primum occasio v.25. & seq. Deinde modus, quo Iacobo benedixit Deus, a v.27. ad 40. Postremo, amplitudo benedictionis, indead finem capitis exponitur. Occasio fuit elapsum tempus seruitutis promissae, quo tempore praecise Ioseph Iacobo natus est: hac enim occasione Iacob auctam suam familiam videns, primum a Labane dimitti petit se, v. 25. & uxores liberosque suos, quia seruitutem suam praestitisset Labani & probauisset satis, v.26. Ex hac vero petitione, primum adversa petitio Labanis v.27. deinde contractus nouus sequutus est, versibus seqq. ad 35. usque. Postremo pactum, & euentus ex contractu, inde ad 40. in petitione Labani primum blanditur Iacobo, ut maneat. Homo avarus ad sua commoda per fas & nefas respiciens: deinde agnoscit iustam Iacobi seruitutem, eamque praedicat ut amplius eum demereatur sibi: hoc facto stipulatur, v. 28. ut seruitutem sibi Iacob spondeat pretio, quod ille vicissim se numeraturum spondet. Hanc stipulationem recusat Iacob, v.29. & seq. Tum fructus seruitutis suae satis a Labane perceptos docens, tum aequum esse ut deinceps a familia sua percipiantur. Atque haec praedicat Iacob, non exprobrandi animo; sed tantum demonstrandi aequitatem recusationis suae. Ad hanc recusationem instat Laban: instanti modestus Iacob non potest diutius recusare. Itaque praecavens sibi a Labanis soceri avaritia, non indicit mercedem ullam pecuniariam; sed ex diuina relatione, prout sequente cap. ostenditur, nouum genus mercedis petit a socero, quod ex sola Dei benedictione pendeat, quia vix Iacobo de iusta mercede cum avaro socero conuenisset. Sic ille spondet, primum se greges curaturum conditione certa, v. 31. deinde conditionem explicat, duobus seqq.: conditio haec fuit, ut ex gregibus suis Laban omnes pecudes varias educat; postea vero quicquid varium in gregibus Iacobo commissis nascetur, id cedat in mercedem ipsi. Hanc conditionem Iacob duobus nominibus commendat v. 33. tum quia nihil in hac re humani operis futurum esset, sed potius Deus mercedem assignaturus ipsi, quam iuste a socero esset percepturus: tum altera cautione, quod spoponderit se omnes varias pecudes quae nascerentur, semper a grege suo sepositurum ea lege, ut siquid varium penes ipsum deprehenderetur, id deputaretur furto & malae fidei. Hanc conditionem avarus Laban primum expendit apud se: deinde probat optato: postremò confirmat, vt ratus inter ipsos contractus, haberetur. Contractû sequitur factum, & euentus illius. Factum; pri-mùm quidem Labanis, quòd seposuit procul varias pecudes à reliquo grege vnicolore, quem Iacobo pascendum committebat, verf. 35. & 36. Deinde verò Iacobi. Huius factum duplex ponitur: vnum, quòd virgas versicolores subiecit in aqualiculos, vbi cùm aquarentur pecudes incalescebant, v.37. & 38. & incalescétes ad aspectum virgarum versicolorum, varios & versicolores edebant foetus, verf.39. Alterum, quòd qui foetus varij fuerant editi: ij ex contractu ita seponebantur à Iacobo, vt semper versarentur ante oculos gregis quem seruabat sibi; ac proinde ex vnicoloribus varij & versicolores foetus itidé ederen-tur. Accessit ars altera, v.41. & seqq. quòd copactas pecudes & vege-tas, cùm incalesceret, sic informabat Iacob: alias autem serotinas mi-nimè:atque hinc benedictio diuina, qua Iacob sexennio plurimum fuit cumulatus. Hic duplex incidit quæstio; vna facti, vtrum fieri hoc pos-sit: altera iuris, vtrum iustè Iacob has artes occupauerit. Fieri posse, tum ex natura, tum ex Dei instituto ad naturam accedente constat. Ex natura: nam maxima est vis phantasiæ, quæ obiectis mouetur e-iusmodi, vt Medici & Physici de hac re tradunt. Cùm verò ad na-turam singularis Dei reuelatio accesserit, id eò amplius fieri potuit, ad Iacobi commodum dispensante diuina prouidentia. Vtrum iu-re hanc artem Iacob occupauerit, grauior est quæstio. Nam vide-tur Iacob secundum communem vsum à fraude & dolo malo pla-nè excusari non posse, quum arte eiusmodi rei alienæ commoda in-teruerterit,eáque verterit in suam rem. Responsio est, Dolus, vt na-tura & attributum docent, apud homines duplex est; bonus, & ma-lus. Vtriusque circumscriptio partim ex consilio & fine, partim-que ex modo sumenda est. Ex consiio, quia in rebus moralibus consilium vel finis dat formam actionibus: modus mediaque sunt quasi materia illarum.
units.tr: Moses goes on in this chapter to explain the divine blessing, of which he began to speak at the end of the preceding chapter. This blessing is of two kinds: one is the procreation of children, the other the multiplication of temporal goods or advantages. The former is explained up to verse 24, the latter from there to the end of the chapter. In explaining the procreation of children, certain particular histories intervene, from which we learn the following in summary: first, the disadvantages of polygamy; second, the patience of the saints under grave hardships; and last, the mercy of God, which the wickedness of men cannot prevent from doing good to his own. Among the disadvantages of polygamy, the first placed here is jealousy (verse 1), which is said to have so inflamed Rachel's mind that she foolishly appealed to her husband about the procreation of children. He answered with indignation (verse 2), recalling her to the thought of the justice of God, whose will is for us the highest necessity. The second disadvantage of polygamy follows from this: Rachel, jealous and too rash, gave her maidservant to Jacob as a wife, a fire of jealousy kindled by her own imprudence. The plan of this is set out in verse 3, the agreement in verse 4, and the outcome in verse 5 and following: namely, that the maidservant bore a child (verse 5). Rachel boasts of this name (verse 6) and sets up a memorial of her folly in the name of her son, both because the same woman bore again (verse 7), and because she provides evidence of the same foolish boasting (verse 8). The third disadvantage is that what one woman did foolishly is taken by the other as an example, though she was already ahead in the number of children (verse 9). Accordingly, from the second maidservant given over, there was likewise a double birth and the same kind of boasting followed (verse 10, and the two following verses). The third instance of human weakness, drawn from the same source of jealousy, is shown in verses 14 and following: the sisters, stirred up over even trivial matters, fought with one another out of jealousy. Yet from this very contention the gracious Lord took occasion to bless the family of Jacob more abundantly, as is shown in verse 16 and following. The occasion is said to have been a childish one: flowers found by a boy and brought to his mother, which Rachel's sister (Leah) sought (verse 14). From this came the shameful bargain over lying with the husband (verse 15). Yet from this example of weakness God, most wise, brought out a good: from that lying with the husband which had been bargained for, and confirmed by her consent (verse 16), God willed to beget through Leah a son of Jacob (verse 17). This birth became, as a token of a grateful mind, a testimony in the name of the son (verse 18). And so the blessing of God proceeded in order: first in Leah (verse 19 and the two following), and then at last in Rachel, whom God made a mother from being barren, to take away her reproach. This favour of God's mercy is ascribed by Moses to God (verse 22), and Rachel herself acknowledges it (verse 23), and then, by the naming of the son, desires more (verse 24). Next follows the second part of the chapter (verse 25), in which it is told how and how greatly God blessed Jacob in his household affairs. First, then, the occasion is given (verse 25 and following); then the manner in which God blessed Jacob, from verse 27 to 40; lastly, the extent of the blessing, which is set out to the end of the chapter. The occasion was the lapse of the period of promised servitude, at the very time when Joseph was born to Jacob. For Jacob, seeing his family enlarged by this occasion, first asks Laban to dismiss him, with his wives and children, since he had rendered his service to Laban and had sufficiently proved it (verse 26). From this request, first Laban's answer, which was adverse (verse 27), and then a new contract followed, in the verses that follow as far as verse 35. Lastly come the agreement and its outcome, which arise from the contract, up to verse 40. In answer to the request, Laban first flatters Jacob that he should stay: a covetous man, looking to his own advantage by right or wrong. Then he acknowledges Jacob's just service and praises it, so that he may win him more closely to himself. Having done this, he stipulates (verse 28) that Jacob should set a price on his service, which Laban in turn promises to pay. Jacob refuses this stipulation (verses 29 and following), showing that the profits of his service had already been sufficiently received by Laban, and that it was fair that from now on they should be received by his own household. Jacob says these things not in a spirit of reproach but only to show the justice of his refusal. Laban presses him against this refusal, and the modest Jacob cannot refuse for longer. So, guarding himself against the covetousness of his father-in-law Laban, he names no monetary wage at all. Instead, by divine revelation, as the following chapter shows, he asks his father-in-law for a new kind of wage, one that depends on God's blessing alone, since he could hardly have come to terms with a covetous father-in-law about a fair wage. So Laban agrees: first, that he will look after the flocks on a fixed condition (verse 31); then he explains the condition in the two following verses. The condition was this: Laban was to take out of the flocks all the speckled and varied animals; afterwards, whatever speckled or varied animal was born in the flocks entrusted to Jacob was to go to him as his wage. Jacob commends this condition on two grounds (verse 33): first, because in this matter nothing of human work would be involved, but rather God would assign him a wage which he would justly receive from his father-in-law; second, as a further safeguard, he promised that he would always keep apart from his flock whatever speckled animals were born, on the understanding that if anything speckled were found in his possession, it would be counted as theft and bad faith. Laban, the covetous man, first weighed this condition within himself, then approved it as he wished, and finally confirmed it, so that it might count as a binding part of their contract. The contract is followed by the act and its outcome. First, Laban's act: he set apart far from the rest of the flock the varied animals, and the single-coloured flock that he entrusted to Jacob to pasture (verses 35 and 36). Then Jacob's act, which is given in two parts. One: he placed striped rods in the watering troughs, where the animals, when they came to drink, grew hot (verses 37 and 38), and, growing hot at the sight of the striped rods, they bore varied and speckled young (verse 39). The other: the varied young that were born were separated by Jacob, in accordance with the contract, so that they were always kept before the eyes of the flock he kept for himself; and so from the single-coloured animals came forth varied and speckled young in the same way. Another device was added (verses 41 and following): when the strong and vigorous animals grew hot, Jacob set the rods before them, but not for the late and weaker ones. From this came the divine blessing, by which Jacob was greatly enriched over six years. Two questions arise here: one of fact, whether this could happen; the other of right, whether Jacob justly employed these arts. That it could happen is clear, both from nature and from God's ordinance, which comes in addition to nature. From nature: for the power of the imagination is very great, being moved by such objects, as physicians and natural philosophers teach on this subject. And when a singular revelation of God was added to nature, it could happen all the more, God's providence dispensing it for Jacob's advantage. Whether Jacob employed this art justly is a more serious question. For it seems that Jacob, according to common practice, cannot be wholly excused from fraud and wicked deceit, since by such an art he diverted the advantages of another's property and turned them to his own. The answer is that deceit, as both nature and the attributes of God show, is of two kinds among men: good and bad. The distinction between the two must be taken partly from purpose and end, and partly from manner. From purpose, because in moral matters the purpose or end gives form to actions; the manner and the means are, as it were, their matter.

units.la: Hic verò consilium Iacobi obseruandum est, non fuisse humanum, siue ad consilij auctorem respexeris, siue ad propositum vel substantiam ipsius. Nam Deus fuit auctor consilij: propositum verò & substantia illius non fuit vt rem alienam interciperet, sed vt tantum perciperet quantum sua benedictio-ne Deus esset largiturus. Quapropter Iacob, quamuis (vt credi-bile est) nondum ea media nouisset quæ post imperauit ipsi Deus, certa fiducia promissionum Dei in contractu ineundo dicebat La-bani, ita attestabitur mihi iustitia mea. Quibus verbis, si fraudem cogitauisset Iacob, impiè nomine Dei & iustitiæ abusus esset. Media verò in actionibus humanis ea reprehensione digna sunt, quæ aut naturæ, aut institutioni iustæ aducerfantur. Hæc media non aducerfantur naturæ; sed ex natura sunt. Restat ergo, vt qui factū Iacobi damnat, aducerfari institutioni criminentur. Si autem institutioni, certe aut publicæ, aut priuatæ: non publicæ, priuatæ igitur, dicturi sunt, nimirum conuentioni inter Labanem & Iacobum, quia contractus est bonæ fidei. Nos autem negamus priuatæ institutioni contractus factum Iacobi aduersari. Nam cum bona fide Labani dixerit se ab ipso non petere quicquam, sed à Domino expectare, qui sua administratione fit effecturus vt ipsius iustitia attestetur ipsi: hac vnica exceptione probatur bona fides Iacobi, quia totam actionem subiecit voluntati Dei. Deus autem volutate sua ad iuste dispensandam mercedem Iacobo media imperauit, quæ Iacob bona fide fecundum Deum, non mala fide fecundum homines exfequutus est.
units.tr: Here, however, we must notice that Jacob's plan was not a human one, whether we look to the author of the plan or to its purpose and substance. For God was the author of the plan, and its purpose and substance was not to seize another's property but only to receive as much as God would give by his blessing. Therefore Jacob, although (as is credible) he did not yet know the means that God later commanded him, confidently relying on God's promises when he made the bargain, said to Laban: so will my righteousness testify for me. If Jacob had intended fraud by these words, he would have abused the name of God and of righteousness impiously. But in human actions, the means deserve blame only when they are contrary to nature or to lawful institution. These means are not contrary to nature; they arise from nature. It remains, then, that those who condemn Jacob's act must charge it with being contrary to institution. If it is contrary to institution, it is surely either public or private. They will say it is not public but private, namely the agreement between Laban and Jacob, since it is a contract of good faith. But we deny that Jacob's act in the contract is contrary to private institution. For when Laban in good faith said that he did not ask anything of Jacob, but expected it from the Lord, who by his governance would bring it about that his righteousness would testify to him, Jacob's good faith is proved by this one exception: that he committed the whole transaction to the will of God. And God, by his will, commanded Jacob the means by which to distribute the wages justly; and Jacob carried them out in good faith before God, not in bad faith before men.

units.tr: CHAPTER 31 ANALYSIS.

units.la: ic principium statuimus secundi loci, qui est de Iacobi reuersione in Cenahaneam, & rebus quæ ibi acciderunt Iacobo & familiæ illius. Huius autem loci duæ partes omnino tenendæ sunt: prior de reuersione quæ hoc capite exponitur. Posterior vero de iis rebus quæ in Cenahanea euenerunt, inde ad cap. 38. vsque. Reuersionis autem historia tribus partibus conclusa est; prima est narratio consilij de reuersione, ad verf. 16. vsque. Secunda est narratio facti, id est, itineris suscepti post consilium captum, inde ad v. 21. Tertia est narratio euentorum, quæ ex illo Iacobi discessu & reuersione in ipso reuersionis tempore confequuta sunt, inde ad finę capitis. Ad narrationę consilij tria ordine à Mose proponuntur: primum occasiones, tribus versibus: deinde comunicatio, inde ad v.14. Postremo autę deliberatio & determinatio, vt vulgo dicitur, consilij, ad v.16. vsque. Occasionum tria genera afferuntur, singulis verfib. Primum genus est inuidentia nō obscura affinium Iacobi, quā ex sermonibus ipsorū & aliorū cognouerat, v.1. Secundum genus est mutatio vultus Labanis, dolorem animi fui non valentis dissimulare; sed filiorū suorum inuidentiam mœsto animo suo confirmantis, v.2. Quā imprudentia & filiorū inuidiam & dolorem generi confirmauit. Tertiū genus est mandatū & promissio Dei, Iacobū ex consortio eorū hominum, quibus propter felicitatem illius dolebat oculi, prouidetiffimę liberantis. Consilij comunicationę primū antecedit vxorū aduocatio, v.4, quas Iacob velut confortes diuini & humani iuris in confiliū adhibuit, de re totą fecundū Deum fufcipiendaʒ suscipienda;non pro auctoritate tyrannica vxoribus,velut instrumen-tis,pecudibus,aut mancipiis imperas; sed ex coiugali officio in com-municatione consilij eas adiungens sibi. Hoc facto sequitur communi-catio, qua in communicatione primum occasione proponit cosilij Iacob,v.5. deinde res anteactas narrat, ad v. vsque 13. Postremo autem propositione consilij adfert ex mandato & auctoritate Dei,v.14. Occasiones ponuntur duae:vna,quod animum Labanis recognoscat; altera quod Deus habeat auctore consilij. Nam prima & secunda occasio vnius habetur loco. Narrationis partes duae sunt:prior,qua Iacob probat vxoribus officium suum, & Labanis soceri indignum factum exponit ipsis,ad v.9.vsq;.Posterior,quo omnia a se ex Dei reuelatione & mandato gesta pronuntiat:atque haec eo consilio facit,vt vxores(a quibus metuebat ne forte familia paterna amplius obseruaret) ad sequendum consilium ipsius flecteret potentius atq; adduceret:facta sua probat Iacob v.6. Labanis facta improbat, & mala fide improbat illius, tribus versq.feqq.Primum a re ipsa v.7.&8. Deinde ab euentu diuinitus consequuto,v.9.Re quā in Labane improbat primum generatim proponit, ostendens eum sibi illusisse & egisse mala fide,v.7. Cuius malae fidei incomoda Deus sua prouidetia in amplissima comoda Iacobi cōuerte-rit. Deinde haec duo speciatim explicat,opus malę fidei,v.8.ab exem-plis singularibus:& singulare Dei prouidentia malū commutatis bono, v.9.& Iacobo benedicentis,perfidiamque Labani punietis,v.9. Etsi hoc obseruandum est, perfidiam illa & frequente mutatione mercedis iniuste a Labane facta hactenus a Mose non fuisse narratam,quia satis habuit Moses ab vno exemplo ostendisse iniqua Labanis administratione,& summa Iacobi patientia. Altera narrationis pars eo pertinebat, vt doceret vxores Iacob nihil a se mala fide,vt a socero gestum;sed ex singulari Dei reuelatione & mandato omnia,reuelatione duplice:quarum priore Deus in somnio Iacobo dicitur ostendisse quid effecturus esset ad benedictiones ipsius,v.10.Posteriore imperauisse ea ipsa quae a Iacobo gesta sunt v.11.&12.prout capite praecedente exposuit Moses. Huic autem mandato Moses elleiptic[?]s postremum mandatum coniungit, ne saepius eadem verba repeterentur. Na v.13. desiderantur haec verba, Postremo dixit Iehoua mihi,quae verba,quia praecedetibus versib. fuerunt posita,velut continete narratione proponuntur,cum tame visionis sint alterius. Atq; hoc mandato continetur propositio illius consilij, quod cum vxoribus communicatum Iacob voluerat, & cuius causa tum occasionis, tum narrationis antecedetis partes duas praemiserat. In huius autem consilij propositione Iacob narrat duas illius reuelationis partes:vnam,qua Deus Iacobum confirmat recordatione sederis, promissionū, beneficiorumque ante collocatorū ipsius in Iacobum, & Iacobi gratiis,& voto singulari Bethele facto,vt sup.28.c.narrauit Moses.Deinde vero propositionem mandati adfert, discedendi de loco, & Cenahaneam repetendi. Huic communicationi subiicitur constitutio & deliberatio certa per consensum vxorum,tribus versi-bus, quę primum iniquitatem patris sui incusant grauiter, vers.14.& seq. Secundo æquitatem suam & iustitiam in rebus possidendis con-firmant: postremo concludunt Dei mandato parendum esse, v. 16. Iniquitatem patris tribus nominibus exagitant:primum, quòd cùm ius filiarū sit vt dotem a parentibus accipiant & hæreditatem conse-quantur,ipsæ indotatæ ac velut exhæredes fuerint elocatæ.Secundo, quòd non solum filiarum iure priuatæ,verùm etiam (quod iniquius) quasi extera mancipia venditæ sint a patre,& a viro emptæ seruitutis pretio : postremò, quòd etiam post tantam indignitatem siquid ha-bent peculij,id tamquam suum non dubitat pater consumere. Huic ergo iniquitati iustitiam & ius possessionū suarum opponunt, v.16.& concludunt ex Dei mandato abeundū esse. Quæstio est,reŏténe sece-rint vxores Iacobi,cùm patris sui administrationem ita traducerent. Resp.est, tria in hac quæstione spectari oportere: rei veritate,loquē-tiū affectū, & rationem eorū ad quos sermo est habitus. Rei verita-tem ita se vt loquūtur habuisse,Moses & Iacob ante sunt testati:asse-ctum,aut simpliciter spectari necesse est,aut secundum quid. Simpli-citer hoc fuit fœminarum studium , vt consilio viri sui rationibus e-tiam adductis subscriberent: secundum quid vero spectatur hoc stu-dium,si animo perturbatiore studium per se non malum exponitur. Ratio eorum ad quos habetur sermo aperta est, cùm illæ virum suū alloquantur istarum rerum scientissimum diuturna experientia. Ex his autem illud sequitur,cùm rei veritas,deliberationis & consilij ca-piendi ratio, & viri auctoritas conscientiáque fœminas obstrinxerit vt bona fide in argumento hoc loquerentur, non posse hoc illarum factum simpliciter improbari,sed tātùm si quid (vt credibile est) fer-uidè perturbatiore animo in parentem suum cogitauerint aut effuti-uerint. Historiam facti in duas partes distinguimus:vnam,quo modo se cum suis Iacob ad profectionem comparauerit; alteram,quo modo profectus fit.Quo se modo comparauerit,v.17. & 18. exponitur:libe-ros fœminasque iumentis instruxisse, & possessionem totam com-modead profectionem instituisse. In profectione vero narrantur, primùm occasio & opportunitas temporis, quòd Laban ad tonden-dum oues peregrè abiisset, vers.19.qua ratione furtim se surripuit Ia-cob,& facilè curauit nequid Laban de consilio rescisceret,v.20.dein-de prode profectionis modus,& terminus indicatur v.21.[?]nempe quòd fuga discesserit trans Euphratem, deinde Gileadem versus tetenderit. Sed huic narrationi παρέργως[?] altera interseritur, quòd Rachel viro inscio imagines siue idola patris sui furata est, quæ secum exportauit. Hæc autem particula historiæ propterea accessit, quòd & amplioré causam accelerationis, eo habuisse Laban videbatur, & iurgij materiam exponi oportuit, de quo v.30.& seqq. Atque hinc confirmatur illud quod ex Iosue vltimo & Esaiæ 41. aliisque scripturæ locis didicimus; nempe idololatriam in cognatione Abrahami, vt in aliis, obtinuisse, antequam à Deo vocaretur, supra 11. & 12. Quæritur de Rachela, vtrum rectè fecerit, nec ne idola surripiens patris, & quo consilio fecerit. De consilio non satis ex scriptura constat: alij studium idololatriæ fuisse in illa putauerunt, alij studium pietatis, vt patris familiam imaginibus destitueret. Non defuerunt etiam, qui materiam imaginum istarum preciosam fuisse crediderint, & Rachelam pretio illectam voluisse in rem suam imagines illas vertere. Primùm responsi genus probare non possum. Mihi enim non videtur esse probabile, Rachelam (quæ iam cum Iacobo viginti annos amplius vixerat) adhuc hæsisse in luto Idololatriæ, etsi putant illi hanc suam affirmationem cap.35.v.2. confirmari, vbi Iacob familiæ & omnibus qui sibi aderant imperauisse dicitur, vt omnes Deos alienigenarum è medio sui amoueret: sed non videtur locus ille ad hanc causam pertinere, quia respiciebat tu Iacob ad spolia Sichemitarum, quæ filij ipsius expilauerant, c.34. Nam cum ex ea præda maximam impuritate familia tota Iacobi contraxisset, discessuros mandauit sanctificare sese, & vestes etiam ipsas, quæ madebant sanguine, deponere. Nihil ergo ille locus ad hanc quæstionem facit. Tertium responsum mihi non probatur magis, quòd pretio imaginum Rachel ad furtum allecta sit. Nam imagines illas, præsertim verò familiares, tanti pretij non fuisse constat; prout etiam exemplo Micalæ confirmatur, 1. Sam. 19. Restat itaque responsum illud secundum, pio studio à Rachela fuisse factum. Verùtamen vt pio studio fecerit, manet adhuc quæstio, vtrum rectè fecerit, an secus? Responsio est: Vt demus bonum fuisse finem quem illa proposuit sibi, tamen factum eo probari non posse; primùm quia modus iniquus est; secundò, quia ne hoc quidem pacto fine propositum est assecuta: fit enim potius vt idololatriæ his occasionibus inardescant, & furentius ruant in idololatriam, quàm vt hoc argumento respicant; maximè cùm argumento furti aut vis publicæ in hoc casu soleat confirmari. Sequitur locus tertius, quid ex ea fuga fuerit consecutum in ipso itinere. Huius narrationis partes summæ sunt tres: prima, de eo quòd Laban Iacobum persequutus est, ad v. vsque 25. Secunda, de rixa inter Iacobū & Labanem, ad v. vsque 42. tertia, de conciliatione & sedere, inde ad finem capitis. Narrationi iurgij per singularem Dei prouidentiam antecessit nocturnum monitum, quo Deus æstuantem Labanis animum repressit, & ad mitigationem iurgij facilitatemque cociliationis comparauit, v. 24. maximè quia ad violentiā potiùs quā ad amicam actionem colleētis amicorum copiis se composuisse Laban videbatur, v. 22. & 23. Hac igitur diuina monitione præparatus Laban, Iacobum accessisse, v. 25. & cum eo iurgatus esse dicitur seqq.
units.tr: Here we set down the principle of the second section, which concerns Jacob's return to Canaan and the things that happened there to Jacob and his household. Two parts of this section must be kept in view. The first is the return, which is set out in this chapter. The second is the events that took place in Canaan, from here to chapter 38. The account of the return is divided into three parts. The first is the narrative of the decision to return, up to verse 16. The second is the narrative of the deed, that is, of the journey undertaken after the decision was made, up to verse 21. The third is the narrative of the events that followed Jacob's departure and his return, and that occurred at the time of the return itself, from there to the end of the chapter. In the narrative of the decision, Moses sets out three things in order. First come the occasions, in three verses. Next comes the communication, up to verse 14. Last comes the deliberation and determination of the decision, as it is commonly called, up to verse 16. Three kinds of occasion are given, each in its own verse. The first is the open ill will of Jacob's kinsmen, which he had learned of from their own words and from the words of others (verse 1). The second is the change in Laban's countenance, which showed that he could not hide his resentment, and which confirmed his sons' ill will with a gloomy mind (verse 2). Jacob's own imprudence had strengthened both the sons' ill will and their father's resentment. The third is the command and promise of God, who most providently freed Jacob from the company of those men, whose good fortune made their eyes ache (verse 3). The communication of the decision is preceded first by the summoning of his wives (verse 4). Jacob brought them into the counsel as partners in divine and human law, in a matter that was to be undertaken entirely according to God's will. He did not command them with tyrannical authority, as one would command tools, cattle, or slaves. Rather, out of the duty of marriage, he joined them to himself in taking counsel. After this comes the communication itself. In it Jacob first gives the occasion for the decision (verse 5), then relates the past events, up to verse 13. Last, in setting out the proposal of the decision, he brings it forward on the command and authority of God (verse 14). Two occasions are given. One is that he recognised Laban's mind; the other is that God is the author of the decision. For the first and second occasions make up one point. The narrative has two parts. The first, in which Jacob shows his wives that he has done his duty and sets out to them the unworthy conduct of their father Laban, runs up to verse 9. The second, in which he declares that everything he has done was done by God's revelation and command, is told with this purpose: that he might more powerfully bend his wives (who feared that perhaps their father's household would keep them in its power) to follow his counsel. Jacob justifies his own conduct in verse 6. He condemns Laban's conduct and his bad faith in three verses that follow. First he condemns it from the deed itself (verses 7 and 8). Then from the outcome brought about by God (verse 9). Concerning Laban's conduct, he first condemns it in general terms, showing that Laban had mocked him and had acted in bad faith (verse 7). God, by his providence, turned the harms of that bad faith into the greatest benefits for Jacob. Then he explains these two points in particular: the deed of bad faith (verse 8), with individual examples; and God's singular providence, which changed the evil into good and blessed Jacob, and punished Laban's treachery (verse 9). Yet it must be noted that this treachery and the frequent alteration of wages done unjustly by Laban has not so far been related by Moses, because Moses thought it enough to show from one example Laban's unjust management and Jacob's great patience. The second part of the narrative served this purpose: to teach Jacob's wives that he had done nothing in bad faith toward their father, but that everything had been done by a singular revelation and command of God. The revelation was twofold. In the first, God is said to have shown Jacob in a dream what he would bring about for Jacob's blessings (verse 10). In the second, God commanded the very things that Jacob did (verses 11 and 12), as Moses set out in the preceding chapter. Moses joins to this command a final command, and does so elliptically, so that the same words would not be repeated. For in verse 13 these words are missing: Finally the LORD said to me, which, because they had been put in the preceding verses, are set forth as if they belonged to the continuing narrative, although they belong to a different vision. In this command is contained the proposal of that decision which Jacob had wished to share with his wives, and for whose sake he had put forward the two parts of the occasion and the narrative above. In the proposal of this decision, Jacob relates two parts of that revelation. One part is that God confirmed him by recalling the covenant, the promises, and the benefits previously bestowed on Jacob, and Jacob's vows and his special vow made at Bethel, as Moses related in chapter 28. Then he brings forward the proposal of the command to depart from that place and return to Canaan. To this communication is added the settled resolution and deliberation, by the agreement of the wives, in three verses. These first sharply accuse their father of injustice (verse 14 and following). Second, they affirm their own fairness and right in the possession of goods. Last, they conclude that the command of God must be obeyed (verse 16). They denounce their father's injustice under three heads. First, although it is a daughter's right to receive a dowry from her parents and to inherit, they were given in marriage without dowry, as if they had been disinherited. Second, not only were they deprived of the rights of daughters, but (what is more unjust) they were sold by their father as if they were foreign slaves, and bought by their husband for the price of their servitude. Last, even after such great indignity, if they have any property at all, their father does not hesitate to consume it as if it were his own. To this injustice they oppose their right and the title to their own possessions (verse 16), and they conclude that they must depart by God's command. The question is whether Jacob's wives acted rightly when they spoke about their father's management in this way. The answer is that three things must be considered in this question: the truth of the matter, the feelings of the speakers, and the position of those to whom the speech was addressed. Moses and Jacob have already testified that the truth of the matter was as they spoke. The feeling must be judged either absolutely or in relation to circumstances. Absolutely, it was the women's eagerness to agree with their husband's counsel, even with reasons added. In relation to circumstances, this eagerness is judged if it is set forth as a feeling not in itself wrong, but expressed with a rather disturbed mind. The position of those to whom the speech was addressed is plain, since they were speaking to a husband who was most experienced in these matters through long experience. From these points it follows that, since the truth of the matter, the manner of taking counsel and deliberating, and the authority of the husband and their own conscience bound the women to speak in good faith on this subject, their deed cannot be simply condemned. Only if (as is credible) they thought or said something against their father in a more heated and disturbed spirit might it be found fault with. We divide the history of the deed into two parts: one, how Jacob prepared himself and his people for the departure; the other, how the departure itself took place. How he prepared himself is set out in verses 17 and 18: he loaded his children and women on beasts, and arranged his whole property for the journey. In the departure itself, there are narrated first the occasion and the opportunity of the time, namely that Laban had gone away to shear his sheep in another place (verse 19), and by what means Jacob slipped away secretly and easily ensured that Laban should learn nothing of the plan (verse 20). Next, the manner and the goal of the departure are shown in verse 21: that he fled across the Euphrates and then set his course toward Gilead. But into this narrative another element is inserted in passing [παρέργως]: that Rachel, without her husband's knowledge, stole her father's images or household gods, and carried them away with her.
