This part of the history was added because Laban seemed to have a larger reason for hastening, and because it was necessary to set out the cause of the quarrel, which is dealt with in verse 30 and following. From this it is confirmed what we have learned from the last chapter of Joshua, from Isaiah 41, and from other passages of Scripture: that idolatry prevailed among Abraham's kindred, as among other peoples, before he was called by God (see chapters 11 and 12). A question arises about Rachel: whether she acted rightly or not in stealing her father's idols, and with what intention she did it. Scripture does not fully establish her intention. Some have thought that she was moved by a zeal for idolatry; others by a zeal for piety, to strip her father's household of its images. There have also been those who believed that these images were of precious material, and that Rachel, enticed by their price, wished to turn them to her own profit. I cannot accept the first answer. For it does not seem probable to me that Rachel, who had by then lived with Jacob more than twenty years, still stuck in the mire of idolatry. Although some think that this is confirmed by what is said in chapter 35, verse 2, where Jacob is said to have commanded his household and all who were with him to remove the gods of foreigners from among them, that passage does not seem to bear on this question. For Jacob was then looking at the spoils of the Shechemites, which his sons had plundered (chapter 34). For when the whole household of Jacob had contracted the greatest uncleanness from that booty, he commanded them to sanctify themselves before they departed, and to put off even the garments themselves, which were stained with blood. That passage therefore has nothing to do with this question. I do not approve the third answer any more, that Rachel was enticed to theft by the price of the images. For it is clear that those images, especially household ones, were not of such great price, as is also confirmed by the example of Micah (1 Sam. 19). There remains, then, that second answer, that Rachel acted from a pious zeal. Yet even if she acted from pious zeal, the question remains whether she acted rightly or not. The answer is this. Even granting that the end she proposed to herself was good, the deed cannot be justified by it. First, because the means is wrong. Second, because she did not even attain the purpose by this method. For these occasions rather inflame idolatry, and make people rush into idolatry more furiously, instead of turning them back by this argument. This is especially so since, in such a case, the charge of theft or of public violence is usually brought forward. The third place now follows: what came of that flight on the journey itself. This narrative has three main parts. The first concerns Laban's pursuit of Jacob, up to verse 25. The second concerns the quarrel between Jacob and Laban, up to verse 42. The third concerns the reconciliation and peace, from there to the end of the chapter. Before the narrative of the quarrel, through God's singular providence, there came a warning by night, by which God restrained Laban's raging mind and prepared it for the easing of the quarrel and for an easy reconciliation (verse 24). This was especially so because Laban seemed to have prepared himself, by gathering his kinsmen, for violence rather than for a friendly action (verses 22 and 23). Laban, therefore, prepared by this divine warning, is said to have come up to Jacob (verse 25), and to have quarrelled with him in the verses that follow.

units.la: Quòd autem impios etiam homines suæ Ecclesiæ suorúmq; causa cõpellarit Deus, iam ante demonstrauimus in cap. 20, Abimeleci exemplo. Iurgij partes duæ sunt; vna, Labanis increpantis Iacobum ad v. vsque. 30. Altera Iacobi probantis factū suū, v. 31. & seqq. 4. In Labanis iurgio argumentū duplex: vnum, de fuga, versibus 4. alterū de furto imaginum, v. 30. O biurgationis de fuga partes sunt hę: prima, simplex reprehēsio factì, tamquam indigni facta multis nominibus, v. 26. Secunda, causarum inuestigatio, quibus ad eam fugam commotus est Iacob. v. 27. & seq. Quibus ostendit Laba nullâ fuisse tam graue causam cur se gereret in hunc modum Iacob; sed stultum factum ipsius esse, sine modo, sine causa. Postrema pars iurgij, vltionis ad quam se Laban comparauerat, tamquam iniuria accepta, remissio; non quidē ex nutu consilioque proprio ipsius, sed ex diuina reuelatione quam sibi proxima nocte testatur factam, v. 29. Huic parti subiungitur altera, v. 30. in qua primùm honesta concessione Laban vtitur, tamquā reperiens inhonestum genēri discessum, deinde furti exprobratione, Cur furatus es? Huic iurgio modeste respōdisse Iacob dicitur; ad priore quidem partem illius, v. 31. exponens causam cur clàm discesserit; nēpe quòd socero suo propter duritiem spectatam hominis dissideret, vt qui detentis filiabus generum fuisset apud se detēturus. Ad posteriorem, v. 32. nam furtū à se, aut ab vllo suorum se cōscio negat fuisse factum. Confirmat Iacob primùm deditione noxæ, cùm dicit, Apud quemcumque, &c. Deinde copia facta peruestigationis in tota familia v. 32. postremò verò exsequutione, v. 33. 34. & 35. Nam pro ea conditione quàm Iacob obtulerat, Laban omnia tentasse in familia Iacobi dicitur, v. 33. sed Rachel furti conscia patrem fefellisse: primùm quòd imagines abdidisset loco opportuno cui insideret, v. 34. deinde quòd honestam specie excusationis attulisset patri, ne cogeretur ipsi assurgere: qua ratione factum est vt idola sua Laban non reciperet. Sic Rachel peccatum ex peccato nectebat, cùm furtum illud suum furtiuis artibus & mendacio cumularet. Hinc sequitur alter obiurgationis locus: in quo Laban à Iacobo reprehenditur propter iniuriam illatã. Causa fuit ira qua Iacob fuit percitus, propterea quòd soçer illũ tam infeste persequutus esset & incusauisset furti. Huius itaque obiurgationis partes duæ sunt: nam primùm à iustitia sua argumentatur Iacob Labanem imprecans, deinde Deo gratias agit, ac non socero, quòd iustitia sua attestaretur ipsi, vers. 3. Iustitiæ suæ nomine primùm præsentis Labanem increpat, v. 30. & 37. Deinde verò totius præteritæ administrationis, vers. 38. & tribus sequentibus. Præsentem iustitiam obiicit; primùm quòd nullo peccato suo feruenter ipsum persequatur Laban: deinde quòd purgauerit se ab iniqua illa furti accusatione, de qua præsentes amicos cupit cognoscere vers. 37. Hanc probationem sui amplificat Iacob ab anteacta 20. amplius annorum administratione. Nam se res Labanis optimè procurauisse, vers.38, amissas, raptas, furto sublatas de suo præstitisse, vers.39, omnia labore incredibili & fide summa perfecisse, ver.40. à socero nihil nisi persidiam in tanta fide & constantia sua expertum esse: denique malum semper vicisse bono, vers. 41. Ex his concludit Iacob non esse cur gratias agat socero, vers. 42. sed Dei prouidentiam paternam in se agnoscere, ex sedere & promissionibus Abrahamo & Isaaco factis: Labanis verò iniquitatem, qua in se fuisset vsurus nisi prospexisset Dominus, se iam ex facto peruidere. Hinc sequitur conciliatio & fœdus inter partes: cuius auctor fuisse dicitur Laban blanda quadam deprecatione, vers. 33. Cùm testatur non fuisse sibi animum, aut in præsentia esse, vt noceat suis: itaque proponit conditionem sederis inter ipsos pangendi vers. 44. In hoc autem sedere primùm spectantur signa, de quibus ad vers. vsque 51. Deinde spectatur substantia sederis, vers. 51. & sequentibus. Postremò confirmatio, vers. 53. & sequentibus. Federis signa ponuntur ista; primùm quòd Iacob ex sua parte disposuit statuam, vers.45. deinde quòd Laban ex altera parte, monente Iacobo, aceruum instituit: quibus signis alia accesserunt duo transeuntia; conuiuium super aceruo factum, vers.45. & appellationes vtrinque impositę, vers.47. & tribus sequentibus. Nam aceruus fuit appellatus nomine Hebræo & Syro, aceruum testimonij significante, vers. 47. Cuius causa habetur vers.48. Statua verò appellata est nomine speculam significante, vt v.49. & seq. proponitur. Nam hoc signo Dei oculum testem & vindicem actionum inter se appellauerunt. Ex his sequitur fœdus v.51. & seq. de communi officio in posterum exhibendo: quod fœdus confirmatur primùm religione iuramenti, v. 53. deinde conuiuio vltro citróque exhibito. In iuramento hoc est singulare, quòd Laban iurauit per Deos suos, Iacob vero per verū Deum, qui Isaacum expauefecerat ne benedictionem illam Iacobo pronuntiatam reuocare, supra cap. 27. Deinde obseruanda est superstitiosorum hominum consuetudo qui religionem ab antiquitate & successione à patribus accepta solum probari putant.
units.tr: Moreover, that God has compelled even impious men for the sake of his Church and his people, we have already shown in chapter 20, by the example of Abimelech. The quarrel has two parts: one is Laban's rebuke of Jacob, up to verse 30; the other is Jacob's defence of his deed, verse 31 and following. In Laban's rebuke there is a double argument: one concerning the flight, verses 26–30, and the other concerning the theft of the images, verse 30. The rebuke about the flight has these parts: first, a plain reproof of the deed, as one unworthy of it in many respects, verse 26. Second, an inquiry into the causes that moved Jacob to that flight, verse 27 and following. In these Laban shows that there was no grave cause why Jacob should behave in this manner, and that his act was foolish, without measure and without reason. The last part of the rebuke is the abandonment of the vengeance for which Laban had prepared himself, as if he had received an injury. He did this not by his own will and counsel, but by a divine revelation, which he testifies was made to him the night before, verse 29. To this part another is joined, verse 30, in which Laban first makes a courteous concession, as if he found the departure to be a dishonourable kind of leaving, and then reproaches Jacob with theft: "Why did you steal?" Jacob is said to have answered this rebuke modestly. To the first part of it, verse 31, he gives the cause of his secret departure, namely that he disagreed with his father-in-law because of the man's harshness, which he had observed, since he would have kept the son-in-law with him by keeping the daughters. To the second part, verse 32, he denies that the theft was committed by himself or by anyone of his household who was aware of it. Jacob confirms this first by the surrender of the guilty party, when he says, "With whomever, &c." Then he confirms it by granting a search through the whole household, verse 32; and finally by the carrying out of the search, verses 33, 34 and 35. For under the condition Jacob had offered, Laban is said to have tried everything in Jacob's household, verse 33. But Rachel, knowing of the theft, deceived her father: first, because she had hidden the images in a suitable place on which she sat, verse 34; then, because she offered her father a plausible excuse, so that he would not be forced to rise before her. By this device it came about that Laban did not recover his idols. Thus Rachel linked sin to sin, when she heaped her own theft with stealthy arts and lying. Hence follows the second place of the rebuke, in which Jacob reproves Laban for the injury done to him. The cause was the anger with which Jacob was stirred, because his father-in-law had pursued him so bitterly and accused him of theft. The parts of this reproof are therefore two. For first Jacob argues from his own righteousness, calling down curses on Laban; then he gives thanks to God, and not to his father-in-law, that his righteousness was attested to him, vers. 3. On the ground of his righteousness Jacob first rebukes Laban in the present, verses 30 and 37. Then he rebukes him for the whole past administration, verse 38 and the three following. He sets against Laban his present innocence: first, that Laban pursues him so fiercely although he has committed no sin; then, that he has cleared himself of that unjust accusation of theft, about which he wishes his present friends to know, verse 37. Jacob amplifies this proof from the administration of more than twenty years past. For he had managed Laban's affairs very well, verse 38; the losses, the things seized and the things stolen he had made good from his own resources, verse 39; he had accomplished everything with incredible labour and the greatest fidelity, verse 40; and from his father-in-law he had experienced nothing but treachery, despite such great faithfulness and constancy on his own part; finally, evil has always been overcome by good, verse 41. From these things Jacob concludes that there is no reason for him to thank his father-in-law, verse 42, but that he recognises in himself the fatherly providence of God, shown in the seed and the promises made to Abraham and Isaac; and he recognises from what has already happened the iniquity of Laban, which would have been used against him had the Lord not looked out for him. Hence follows the reconciliation and the covenant between the parties. Its author is said to have been Laban, by a certain flattering entreaty, verse 43, when he testifies that he had no intention, nor is it in his present power, to harm his own people; and so he proposes the terms of the covenant to be made between them, verse 44. In this covenant the signs are considered first, up to verse 51; then the substance of the covenant is considered, verse 51 and following; lastly, its confirmation, verse 53 and following. The signs of the covenant are these: first, Jacob set up a pillar on his side, verse 45; then Laban, at Jacob's urging, set up a heap on the other side, verse 46. To these signs two others were added: a meal eaten upon the heap, verse 46; and names imposed on both sides, verse 47 and the three following. For the heap was named with a Hebrew and a Syriac name, meaning the heap of witness, verse 47; its cause is given in verse 48. The pillar, however, was named with a name signifying a watch-tower, as set out in verse 49 and following. For by this sign they called God's eye the witness and avenger of their actions towards one another. From these things follows the covenant, verse 51 and following, concerning mutual duty to be performed in future. This covenant is confirmed first by the sanctity of an oath, verse 53, and then by a meal offered on both sides. In this oath there is something singular: Laban swore by his gods, but Jacob by the true God, who had struck Isaac with fear lest he revoke the blessing pronounced on Jacob, see above chapter 27. Then the custom of superstitious men is to be noted, who think that religion is to be approved only because of its antiquity and the succession received from the fathers.

units.la: CAPITIS XXXII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXII ANALYSIS.

units.la: Secundum locum historiæ Iacobi in duas partes distinximus[?]: quorum vnum de reuersione eius in Cenahaneam 31. ca. exposuimus. Alterum, de commoratione in Cenahanea rebusq; in eagestis a 32. ad 39. usque, deinceps exponemus. Huius autem partis historiæ summatim hæ sunt: prima, de congressu Iacobi cum Esauo fratre, hoc, & seq. cap. Secunda, de Schecemitarum cæde, c. 34. Tertia, de Iacobi progressu, cap. 35. Quarta, de Iosephi venditione, cap. 37. Vltima, de Iudæ historia, 38. Reliqua cum historia Ægypti proprie coniungenda sunt. Historia congressus Iacobi cum Esau fratre duobus membris concluditur: præparatione, hoc cap. & facto siue congressu ipso, seq. cap. Præparationis duę sunt in vniuersum partes: vna, qua seipsum Iacob; altera, qua Deus Iacobum comparauit. Prius membrum ad v. usque 23. protenditur. Posterius reliquo capite conclusum est. In priore membro, quo præparationem à Iacob factam diximus, duo ordine exponuntur: primum, amica apud fratrem de aduentu fratris pronunciatio, versibus quinque: deinde vero singularis & curiosa rerum omnium præparatio in aduentum fratris ex percepto metu, versibus seqq. prior locus facilis est: ad quem tamen diuinitus Iacob confirmatus fuisse dicitur, conspectis angelorum Dei copiis ipsi assistentibus, ex promissione supra cap. 28. quam visionem oblatam vers.1. Iacob percepisse, agnouisse, & grato animo nomen loco in memoriam rei imposuisse dicitur, vers. 2. Hac testificatione diuina confirmatus Iacob homines ad Esauum misisse dicitur aduentum prænuntiaturos, v.3. & summa nuntij exponitur vers. 4.& 5. Primum, res præteritas in Mesopotamia narrantis: deinde benedictionem præsentem, & animum fraternum, studiumque fratris conciliandi quem ante offensum cognouerat. Hic quæritur, primum quæ causa fuerit legationis; secundò, rustūmne modum Iacob tenuerit, cū se seruum Esau, & fratrem suum Esau Dominum suum appellaret. Prioris dubitationem mouet, quod Esau iam à Cenahanea & conspectu patris in Edomeam ad cogitationem vxorum suarum migrauerat, vbi esse-
units.tr: Having divided the second place of Jacob's history into two parts, we have already expounded the first, concerning his return to Canaan, in chapter 31. The other, concerning his sojourn in Canaan and the events there, from chapter 32 to 39, we shall expound in turn. The main points of this part of the history are these: first, Jacob's meeting with his brother Esau, in this chapter and the next; second, the slaughter of the Shechemites, chapter 34; third, Jacob's journey, chapter 35; fourth, the sale of Joseph, chapter 37; last, the history of Judah, chapter 38. The rest must be joined with the history of Egypt proper. The history of Jacob's meeting with his brother Esau is concluded in two parts: the preparation, in this chapter, and the deed or the meeting itself, in the following chapter. The preparation has two parts in general: one by which Jacob prepared himself, the other by which God prepared Jacob. The first part extends to verse 23; the latter is concluded in the rest of the chapter. In the former part, in which we said Jacob made the preparation, two things are set out in order: first, a friendly announcement to his brother of his brother's coming, in five verses; then a singular and careful preparation of all things for the brother's coming, arising from the fear he had conceived, in the following verses. The first point is easy. Jacob is said to have been strengthened for it by God, when he saw the hosts of God's angels standing by him, in accordance with the promise above in chapter 28. He is said to have perceived and recognised the vision offered, verse 1, and with a grateful mind to have given the place a name in memory of the event, verse 2. Strengthened by this divine testimony, Jacob is said to have sent men to Esau to announce his coming, verse 3, and the substance of the message is set out in verses 4 and 5: first, recounting past events in Mesopotamia; then the present blessing, together with his fraternal disposition and his eagerness to win over the brother whom he knew to have been offended before. Here two questions arise: first, what was the reason for the embassy; second, whether Jacob kept the proper measure when he called himself your servant and called his brother Esau my lord. The first question is raised because Esau had already migrated from Canaan and from his father's sight into Edom, to the household of his wives, where he had

units.la: vbi effectus iam erat amplissimus: proinde non videtur causa fuisse Iacobo Cenahaneam petenti cur fratrem in regione extera agentem tanto studio compellaret. Respondeo, in causa fuisse charitatē. Nam primùm inter fratres charitatem esse natura iubet; itaq;, vel ex charitatis officio, Iacobum necesse fuit salutare fratre. Præterea antecedentium offensorum necessaria fuit obliteratio: præsertim cùm Iacob non esset ignarus quomodo frater ex antecedentibus offensis de nece ipsius cogitauisset, vt narratum est supra cap.27.sub finem. Postremò fuisse etiam futurum metum à noua offensione, si Iacob patrem patriámque promissam, tamquam iustus hæres, virtute antecedentium promissionum quas subripuerat quodámodo fratri sine hac cautione adiuisset. His igitur de causis tum communibus charitatis, tum singularibus, quas modo diximus Iacob nuncios ad fratrem ablegauit.
units.tr: where his household had already grown very large. Therefore it does not seem to have been a reason for Jacob, who was seeking Canaan, why he should address his brother with such eagerness while he was living in a foreign region. I answer that the reason was charity. For first, nature bids brothers to have charity; and so, even from the duty of charity, Jacob had to greet his brother. Besides, the obliteration of the earlier offences was necessary, especially since Jacob was not unaware how his brother, because of the earlier offences, had thought about his death, as was related above in chapter 27 near the end. Lastly, there would also be fear of a fresh offence in the future, if Jacob had approached his brother without this caution, as a just heir, by virtue of the earlier promises which he had in some way snatched from him, concerning his father and the promised land. For these reasons, both the common ones of charity and the particular ones just mentioned, Jacob sent messengers to his brother.

units.la: Altera quæstio, cur fratrem Dominum suum: se, seruum illius appellarit, facilè soluitur, si ad duo respiciamus; nempe ad naturam, & ordinem rerum agendarum. Nam natura prior erat frater; ergo secun dum naturam anteuerti omni honore fratrem à Iacobo oportuit: non solùm propter vrbanitatem aut ciuilem honestatem, vt vulgus putat; sed etiam propter conscientiam naturæ lege obligatam: sed quia hîc forte obiiceretur, huic naturæ legi singulare institutû & declaratione Dei aduersari, cui naturâ oportet cedere omnibus in rebus; propterea altera causa adiiciêda est, nempe ordo in rebus agendis: nā vsque dum ordo ad res agêdas necessarius perfectus sit, statur in naturæ lege: perfecto ordine, tũ naturæ ius illud deponitur. Ac proinde in hoc facto accidit quod in iure dici solet, potiorem esse causam possidentiû. Sic Esau à natura primogenitus, primas tenuit ex natura, vsque dum ordo à Deo institutus perfectus esset, id est, non solû reuelata Dei volûtas & cognita, non solùm iudicata, sed etiam effecta esset reddita. Effecta autem cùm fuit, tum primæ simpliciter ad Iacobum pertinuerût. Itaque primùm natura ad Esauû; deinde post reuelationem diuinam & declarationem ex facto ad Esauû, iure ad Iacobum; postremò autem ordine perfecto ex iure & facto simul ad Iacobum pertinuit benedictio. Posita ergo, sed nondum effecta illa actione diuina, non modò similiter verè, sed etiam secundum conscientiam Iacob fratrem Dominum suû appellauit, vt Dauid Saulem, vt legimus 1.Sam.24, & 25, cap.Ex legatione reuersi dicuntur nuncij, v.6. officium Esau renuntiantes. Sed illud officiû occasione Iacobo attulit, primùm diffidendi rebus suis v.7. deinde prospiciendi, seqq. Prospiciêdi autê modus & præparandi res suas ponitur à Mose triplex: primus, consultationis, v.7.&8. secundus, orationis v.9.& seqq. Tertius, ordinationis rerum omnium, v.14. & seqq. Primus locus consultationi datur. Nam omne inconsultū temerarium. Huius cōsultationis modus ponitur duplex; vnus quōd res omnes suas ante oculos suos disposuit in duos ordines, vt ex re praesente amplius consilium inire possit, v.7. Secundus, quōd hanc distributionem in omnem euentum seruari statuit oportere, vt si forte frater in vnam seuituru̇s esset, saluti partis alterius cōsuleret, verf.8. Orationis partes sunt tres; exordium v.9. Propositio, duobus seqq. & confirmatio, v.12. Exordium, quo Deum appellat Iacob, tribus argumentis captat Dei beneuolentiam, & fidem Iacobi testatur: nempe duobus communibus, à natura Dei, & sedere communi cum maioribus Ecclesiaque ipsius: vnum singulare est, nepe à promissionibus priuatim Iacobo factis, vt cap. 28. exposuit Moses. Itemque cap.31. verf. 12.13. Propositionis loci duo sunt, professio singularis benedictionis diuinae, & indignitatis humanae, qua Iacob vtitur verf. 10. Deinde petitio liberationis à manu Esau fratris, quem sibi infenfiffimum cum tantis copiis aduenire metuebat: ac proinde de sua suorumque salute, nisi praesidio Dei caueretur, actum putabat fore, verf. 11. Propterea lamentabiliter euentum illum describit Iacob à quo metuebat. Confirmatio petitionis sumpta est à singulari Dei promissione, tum de bonis, siue haereditate, tum de liberis, siue haeredibus: quae duo se praestiturum amplissime Deus promiserat, verf.12. In narratione facti duplex est ordinatio à Iacobo factaṙ rerum, & sermonum: nam & res ordinauit, disposuitque fratri praemittendas, & composuit suas. Rerum fratri praemittendarum muneris nomine, vt dicitur verf.13. numerus describitur verf.14. & 15. Ex quo facile colligitur, quam opulentus diuina benedictione Iacob effectus esset. Deinde vero ordinatio tum rerum, tum sermonum, quibus seruos instruxit, describitur; primum quidem generatim, verf. 16. deinde speciatim, sequentibus. Nam primi serui primum gregem agentis caprarum, modus actionis verf. 17. & sermonis, verf. 18. exponitur: deinde vero eadem ratio caeteris imperatur verf. 19. & seq. Nempe vt eadem ratione secundus, qui opilio fuit, tertius qui camelarius, quartus qui bubulcus, quintus denique asinarius omnino vterentur, cùm in Esauum inciderent. Huius ordinationis causam consilio suo exponit Iacob, verf. 20. quōd ita & concilationem cum fratre redempturus esset, & placide cum eo congressurus. Atque haec quidem muneris praemissi constitutio. Sequitur altera dispositio rerum quas sibi seruabat Iacob ver.21. & seqq.cùm enim pernoctasset v.21.in suis illis castris, dicitur postridie personas primùm transmisisse, verf. 22. deinde vero res, verf. 23. Atque hac occasione alter praeparationis locus sequutus est, de quo verf.24. & seqq. Nam cùm Iacob trans-missis trans torrētem rebus omnibus de integro reuertisset, ut bonus pater familias agmen claudens recognoscit siquid fortasse per obli-uionem aut negligentiam famulitij intercidit: hac igitur occasione cum solum Deus humana specie aggressus est, v.24. & lucta diu exer-cens firmè colluctantem ita cōpressit lacertis, ut claudum Iacobum effecerit, verf.25. Atque hinc occasio primum colloquij, v. sequentib. Deinde publicæ gratiarum actionis & solemnis testificationis, ad finem vsque capitis. Colloquij partes duæ sunt. Nam priore Iacob benedictionem adipiscitur, v.26. & duobus seqq. Posteriore, rogans de nomine repulsam patitur, v.29. Benedictionis adipiscendæ antecedentia sunt hæc; postulatio Angeli, ut se dimittat Iacob, & postulatio Iacobi claudicantis, ut sibi Deus benedicat antequam dimittat, quam postulationem fuisse fletu coniunctam scribitur Oseæ 12. Hac postulatione Angelus adductus primum de nomine Iacobi quærit, ut viam benedictioni futuræ sterneret, verf.27. Deinde benedictionem pronuntiat, verf. 28. mutato nomine Iacobi & eo diuinitus confirmato. Cùm autem benedictionem Iacob adeptus esset, vici-ssim nomen angeli quæsiuisse dicitur, verf.29. sed Deum recusa-uisse, ut qui suorum bono,non vanitati curiosæ solet consulere.Hinc sequitur gratiarum actio, & solemnis testificatio duplex: vna Iacobi, qui loco impositum nomen de hac visione, verf.30. Altera fami-liæ, quæ propter claudicationem hanc in perpetuam rei memoriam a membro illo abstinuit quod Angelus in Iacobo contuderat, verf. 31. & 32. Hic autem quæritur primùm quæ causa huius certaminis: secundò, quis luctator iste: postremò, quo iure posteritas a vescendo membro illo abstinuerit. Causa huius visionis & luctæ fuit, primùm ut Iacob a metu concepto confirmaretur; deinde ut viribus nouis instrueretur in Domino, quibus se aduersus omnes tempestates & procellas circummunitum a Domino esse confide-ret. Luctator fuit Deus: nam ipse Iacob agnoscit, dicens, Vidi Deum, &c. verf. trigesimo. Fuit autem humana specie, & humana ratione cum Iacobo egit secundum dispensationem, qua Deus inaniens se ipsum conditioni filiorum suorum accommodat, ut indulgentes patres faciunt interdum liberis. Interea verò exercita-tione hac suum seruum instituit ad certamina euctura. Nobis itaque non est dubium quin hæc fuerit persona Christi, cuius personæ illud maximè proprium est ut se inaniat propter suorum salutem: & ita senserunt orthodoxi patres. Quòd ad ritum in cibis obser-uatum à Iudæorum gente, non fuit inutilis, dum seruata est pia illius operis divini commemoratio: ac proinde justa fuit observatio apud eos quorum animus vacabat superstitione. Nam res est per se indifferens,instituto bona,si Dei beneficium commemoretur; sed usu mala,si in superstitionem abiverit.
units.tr: The second question, why he called his brother his lord and himself his servant, is easily resolved if we look at two things: nature and the order of the things to be done. For by nature the brother was prior; therefore, according to nature, Jacob ought to have given every honour to his brother, not only on account of courtesy or civil propriety, as the common people think, but also on account of the conscience bound by the law of nature. But because here it might perhaps be objected that a singular institution and declaration of God opposes this law of nature, to which nature must yield in all things, a second cause must be added, namely the order in the things to be done. For as long as the order needed for doing things is not complete, one stands by the law of nature; once the order is complete, that right of nature is laid aside. And so in this deed what is commonly said in law happens, that the cause of those in possession is stronger. Thus Esau, by nature the firstborn, held the first place by nature until the order instituted by God was complete, that is, until God's will was not only revealed and known, not only judged, but also made effective and delivered in fact. When it was made effective, then the firsts simply pertained to Jacob. Thus first the natural right was Esau's; then, after the divine revelation and declaration, Esau's by fact and Jacob's by right; lastly, when the order was complete, the blessing pertained to Jacob both by right and by fact together. Therefore, while that divine action was posited but not yet effected, Jacob called his brother his lord not only truly in the same way but also according to his conscience, as David called Saul his lord, as we read in 1 Sam. 24 and 25. The messengers, returned from the embassy, are said (v. 6) to have reported Esau's response. But that report gave Jacob occasion first for distrust of his own affairs (v. 7), and then for taking precautions in the following verses. The mode of taking precautions and preparing his affairs is set out by Moses as threefold: first, of deliberation, vv. 7 and 8; second, of prayer, v. 9 and following; third, of arranging all things, v. 14 and following. The first is given to deliberation, for everything undertaken without deliberation is rash. The mode of this deliberation is twofold: one, that he arranged all his goods before his eyes into two groups, so that he could take counsel further from the present situation (v. 7); the other, that he decided this distribution must be kept against every outcome, so that if perchance his brother fell upon one group, he would provide for the safety of the other (v. 8). The parts of the prayer are three: the exordium (v. 9), the proposition in the two following verses, and the confirmation (v. 12). In the exordium, by which Jacob calls upon God, he wins God's goodwill by three arguments and attests his own faith: two common ones, from the nature of God and from the common ancestry with the fathers and the Church itself; and one singular, namely from the promises privately made to Jacob, as Moses set out in chapter 28, and likewise in chapter 31, verses 12 and 13. The proposition has two points: a profession of the singular divine blessing and of human unworthiness, which Jacob uses in v. 10; then a petition for deliverance from the hand of his brother Esau, whom he feared would come with such great forces, most hostile to him, so that he thought the matter of his own and his people's safety would be lost unless it were guarded by God's protection (v. 11). Therefore Jacob describes pitifully that event which he feared. The confirmation of the petition is taken from God's singular promise, both concerning goods or inheritance and concerning children or heirs, which two things God had promised most amply (v. 12). In the narration of the deed there is a twofold arrangement by Jacob, of things and of words: for he both arranged and disposed the things to be sent ahead to his brother, and composed his own. Of the things sent ahead to his brother, under the name of a gift, as it says in v. 13, the number is described in vv. 14 and 15, from which it is easily gathered how wealthy Jacob had become by divine blessing. Then the arrangement, both of things and of words, with which he instructed his servants, is described: first in general (v. 16), then in particular in the following verses. For the first servant, who drove the flock of goats, the manner of action (v. 17) and of speech (v. 18) is set out; then the same method is commanded to the others (v. 19 and following): that the second, who was a shepherd, the third, who was a camel-driver, the fourth, a herdsman, and the fifth, finally, a donkey-driver, should all use the same method when they met Esau. Jacob explains the cause of this arrangement in his plan (v. 20): that he would thus win back reconciliation with his brother and meet him calmly. And this is the arrangement of the gift sent ahead. There follows the second disposition, of the things Jacob kept for himself (v. 21 and following). For when he had spent the night in that camp (v. 21), it is said that the next day he first sent the persons across (v. 22), and then the goods (v. 23). On this occasion the second point of the preparation follows, concerning which v. 24 and following speak. For when Jacob, having sent everything across the torrent, returned alone, as a good father of a household bringing up the rear, to review whether anything had perhaps been lost through the forgetfulness or negligence of his household, then, on this occasion, God alone attacked him in human form (v. 24), and wrestling long, firmly pressed the wrestler with his arms, so that he made Jacob lame (v. 25). Thence comes the occasion for the first conversation, in the verses following, and then public thanksgiving and solemn attestation, to the end of the chapter. The conversation has two parts. In the first, Jacob obtains the blessing (v. 26 and the two following); in the latter, when he asks about the name, he suffers rejection (v. 29). The preconditions of obtaining the blessing are these: the angel's request that Jacob let him go, and Jacob's request, though lame, that God bless him before he let him go, which request is written to have been joined with weeping, Hosea 12. By this request the angel, moved, first asks about Jacob's name, so as to pave the way for the future blessing (v. 27); then he pronounces the blessing (v. 28), the name of Jacob having been changed and divinely confirmed. But when Jacob had obtained the blessing, in turn he is said to have asked the angel's name (v. 29), but God refused, as one who is wont to consult the good of his own rather than curious vanity. Hence follow the thanksgiving and a twofold solemn attestation: one by Jacob, who gave the place a name from this vision (v. 30); the other by the family, which, on account of this lameness, in perpetual memory of the thing, abstained from that limb which the angel had struck in Jacob (vv. 31 and 32). Here, moreover, the questions are: first, what was the cause of this struggle; second, who this wrestler was; last, by what right posterity abstained from eating that limb. The cause of this vision and wrestling was, first, that Jacob might be confirmed against the fear he had conceived, and then that he might be furnished in the Lord with new strength, so that he might be confident that he was fortified by the Lord against all storms and tempests. The wrestler was God, for Jacob himself acknowledges it, saying, I have seen God, etc., verse 30. He appeared in human form and dealt with Jacob in human fashion, according to that dispensation by which God, emptying himself, accommodates himself to the condition of his children, as indulgent fathers sometimes do with their children. Meanwhile, by this exercise he trained his servant for the contests yet to come. Therefore there is no doubt for us that this person was Christ, to whose person it is most proper that he empties himself for the salvation of his own; and so the orthodox Fathers have judged. As to the rite observed by the Jewish nation in regard to foods, it was not useless, as long as the pious commemoration of that divine work was kept; and so the observance was just among those whose minds were free of superstition. For the thing is in itself indifferent: good in its institution if the benefit of God is commemorated, but bad in use if it has turned into superstition.

units.la: CAPITIS XXXIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 33.

units.la: Ic demum alter locus est ad congressum Esaui cum Iacobo pertinens, cuius praeparatio antecedente capite fuit expo-sita.Huius autem cap.partes duae ponendae sunt;una,de congressu fratrum ad vers. usque 15. Altera, de stationibus Iacobi post discessum fratris,reliquo capite. Ad congressum fratrum, tria haec pertinent: primum concursus mutuus & salutatio, ad vers. usque 7. secundum muneratio a Iacobo facta, ad vers. usque 12. tertium officiosa Esaui erga fratrem suum oblatio; qua facta inter se di-scesserunt, ad vers. usque 16. In congressu narrantur ista: primum ordo, secundum quem visum est Iacobo familiam suam disponere E-sauo occursuram, duobus versibus. deinde factum ipsum congressus secundum ordinem a Iacobo institutum. Quo in congressu haec observanda sunt; Iacobum praefuisse omnibus suis ordinis causa, & fratrem suum honorifice salutavisse ut primogenitum, vers.3. ea ratio-ne quam in caput praecedens annotavimus: deinde Esauum vicissim accurrisse, amplexatum esse, ruisse in collum eius, & fuisse osculatum, ut studium suum fraternum in fratrem ostenderet: tertio utrumque fleuisse ad animi mutui testificationem & commotionis vehementif-simæ,v.4. Postremo Esauum rogavisse tum de uxoribus & liberis Iacobi, vers.5. quae omnes suo ordine dicuntur processisse, vers.6.& 7. Tum vero quaesivisse de illis rebus quas Iacob praemiserat, v.8. Qua quaestione via strata est ad secundum locu de muneribus a Iacobo oblatis. Nam proponit Iacob consilium suum munerandi fratrem, v.8. Hic honeste recusat, v.9. Iacob instat adductis rationib.tum ab officio suo in fratrem, v.10. tum ab amplissimo quod senserat Dei beneficio, v.11. Quapropter recusantem dicitur ursisse[?] donec accepisset. Hanc humanitatem Iacobi, altera excipit humanitas Esaui in ipsum. Nam primum fratrem deducere cupit Esau, v.12. Excusantem Iacobum, vers.13. & modeste recusantem etiam spe facta ipsum ad fratrem in Schicem venturum (quod tamen nusquam fecisse legitur) saltem id officium offert Esau, vt partem sui comitatus relinquat apud fratrem, vers.15. Hoc officio recusato disceditur, vers.15. Hinc ad stationes Iacobi venitur, (atque hic secundus capitis est locus) quarum prior trans Iardenem fuit, & cui nomen ex statione Iacobi inditum, v. 17. posterior verò cis Iardenem, v. 18. & seqq. De hac autem statione tria sunt à Mose obseruata: primum, quòd eò venit incolumis, id est, confirmatus ex eo claudicationis incommodo quod luctans senserat, c. 32. Secundum, quòd portionem agri emit, in quo tenderet tentoria sua: qua ratione possessionem habere, & non habere se profitebatur: habere, ex empto; non habere, eò quòd non ædificaret, sed tentoria duntaxat poneret, tamquam propediem migraturus: quemadmodum ex Apostoli ad Heb. 11. intelligendum est. Tertium, ibi exstruxisse altare Deo potius, quàm sibi domum, quod est summę pietatis in Iacobo argumentum, magis de cultu Dei quàm de familia sua laborante. Totum autem hoc caput eò spectat, vt cùm veritatem promissionum omnium Dei antecedentium ex hac historia cognoscamus, tum verò singularem effectum proximè præcedentis luctæ, qua Iacob aduersus metum à fratre omniaque alia incommoda diuinitus fuerat confirmatus.
units.tr: The last of the passages that concern the meeting of Esau with Jacob was set out in the preceding chapter as preparation. Two parts of this chapter must be set down: the first, on the meeting of the brothers, to verse 15; the second, on Jacob's stopping-places after his brother had departed, for the rest of the chapter. Three things belong to the meeting of the brothers: first, their mutual running together and greeting, to verse 7; second, the gift made by Jacob, to verse 12; third, Esau's kindly offer to his brother, after which they parted from each other, to verse 16. In the meeting these things are related: first, the order in which Jacob decided to arrange his household to meet Esau, in two verses; then the meeting itself, carried out in the order Jacob had set. In this meeting the following should be noted. Jacob went before all his people, for the sake of order, and greeted his brother with honour as the firstborn, verse 3, for the reason we noted in the previous chapter. Then Esau in turn ran to him, embraced him, fell on his neck and kissed him, to show his brotherly affection, and thirdly both of them wept, to attest their mutual feeling and their very great emotion, verse 4. Finally Esau asked about Jacob's wives and children, verse 5, who are all said to have come forward in their order, verses 6 and 7. Then indeed he asked about those things which Jacob had sent ahead, verse 8. This question paved the way for the second passage, on the gifts offered by Jacob. For Jacob sets out his plan of presenting a gift to his brother, verse 8. Esau honourably refuses, verse 9. Jacob presses him, with reasons drawn both from his duty towards his brother, verse 10, and from the very great kindness of God which he had experienced, verse 11. Because Esau refused, it is said that he urged him until he accepted. This kindness of Jacob is met by a second kindness of Esau towards him. For Esau first wishes to escort his brother, verse 12. Jacob makes excuses, verse 13, and Esau, with the hope of Jacob's coming to him at Seir (which, however, is nowhere read as having been done), offers at least this service, that he leave part of his company with his brother, verse 15, while Jacob modestly refuses him. When this offer was refused they parted, verse 15. From this we come to Jacob's stopping-places (and here is the second place of the chapter), of which the first was beyond the Jordan, and from which the name was given to the place after Jacob's stay, verse 17, and the later one on this side of the Jordan, verse 18 and following. Three things about this stopping-place are noted by Moses. First, that he came there safe, that is, strengthened after the injury of the limp which he had felt from wrestling, chapter 32. Second, that he bought a parcel of land on which he pitched his tents; by which means he declared that he both had and did not have a possession: he had it by purchase, and did not have it, because he did not build but only pitched tents, as one about to move on shortly, as is to be understood from the Apostle, Heb. 11. Third, that there he built an altar to God rather than a house for himself, which is a proof of Jacob's supreme piety, being more concerned about the worship of God than about his own household. Now this whole chapter aims at this: that, while we learn from this history the truth of all the earlier promises of God, we may also learn the singular effect of the wrestling immediately preceding, by which Jacob had been divinely strengthened against his fear of his brother and all other troubles.

units.la: CAPITIS XXXIV ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 34 ANALYSIS.

units.la: HÆc secunda historia de Iacobo in Cenahaneam reuer-so: cuius finis duplex, communis, & particularis. Finis communis huius historiæ & sequentium omnium est, vt vitam Iacobi afflictionibus conditam agnoscamus, pro-ut pios per afflictiones multas ad Dei regnum oportet contendere. Particularis est, vt occasionem intelligamus, ex qua factum est, vt Simeon aut Leui non successerint in primogenita, postquam Ruben incesto suo crimine ea amisisset: nempe quòd maleficio suo ipsi se indignos ea prærogatiua effecerint. Quapropter primogenita ad Iehudam ex filiis Leæ, & ad Iosephum ex filiis Rachelæ translata sunt, vt Gen. 49. ostendit Iacob, & aperte 1. Chro. 5. in principio scriptum est. Summa est, Dinam Iacobi puellam à Schecemo fuisse compressam; hinc contractum initum, & seruatum ab alienigenis, à filiis Iacobi fuisse ruptum. Tres itaque sunt huius cap. partes: prima, de vitio oblato puellæ, v. 1. & 2. secunda, de contractu inito, inde ad v. 18. tertia, de contractus præstatione & violatione, ad finem vsq; cap. Ad primum locum duo pertinent, occasio, & factum Schecemi. Occasionem fuisse vanitatem adolescentulæ, temere ad inuisendas puellas regionis domo prodeuntis ostendit Moses, v. 1. facti narratio est euidens, v. 2. quòd rapta & compressa à Schecemo fuit, reportans prætium vanitatis suæ. Ad secundum locum pertinent ista; primum antecedentia contractus ineundi, ad v. vsque 7. deinde contractus in vtramque partem conciliatio, inde ad v.18. Antecedentia contractus haec sunt: amor conflans iuuenis in adolescentulam, v.3. tum communicatio cum patre, v. 4. tertio Iacobi dissimulatio & silentium vsque dum aduenissent liberi, v.5. postremo congressus omnium vtrinque partium, v.6. & 7. Amorem adolescentis ex malo principio & instituto conciliatum, nemo bonus excusare potest: quod autem commissio maleficio in amore constanter perstitit, puellam consolatus est, & ambiuit coniugium ipsius, vt pudendum antecedens factum quasi corrigeret, id per se est laudabile & iuri naturae consentiens, si modo consensus earum partium, quarum interest accesserit. Sunt autem partes duae cum vterq; sub patria potestate fuerit. Quapropter legitime adolescens dicitur vtriusq; partis consensum procurauisse: primum quidem patris sui, v.4. deinde vero patris puellae, v.5. Quaeritur vtrum recte fecerit Iacob, an secus, quod coniugium ambienti primo non responderit. Solutio est, non Iacobi solum, sed etiam fratrum puellae, qui maiores annis erant interfuisse, vt consensum in commune afferrent. Cum itaque communem consensionem esse oportuerit, Iacobu bona fide sententiam suam dissimulauisse, & in communi causa commoditatem communis iudicij habendi exspectauisse. Ad congressum quod attinet, quod Schecemitae pater & filius aduenerunt, & Iacob filiique cum illis conuenerunt, actus fuit legitimus: neq; illegitimum fuit per se, quod indoluerunt fratres, & ira exarserunt propter indignitatem flagitij & contumeliae generi suo illatae: sed in eo solum reprehendi sunt, quod non tenuerunt iustum doloris modum, prout ex sequente narratione a Mose confirmatur. Secundus locus de contractu tribus partibus continetur: quarum prima est stipulatio coniugij, ad v.12. vsque. Secunda, restipulatio conditionis ad coniugium (vt illi fingebant) necessarie, inde ad v.vsque 18. Tertia, consensus in conditiones vtrinque allatas, v.18. Stipulationis duo sunt membra; vnum a patre, tribus verbis; alterum, ab adolescente, v.10. & 12. Paternae stipulationis loci sunt tres. Nam primum adfertur causa, amor filij: deinde stipulatio coniugij, vt Dina vxor detur ipsi, v.8. tertia sponsio omnis communicationis aequabilis inter ciues, quae Iacobo & filiis eius como do futura sit, v.9. & 10. Nam in hoc argumento amplius commoratus est Chamor, vt coniugium eo persuaderet. Vtrum autem bona fide haec a Chamore dicta sint, necne, non est facile iudicare. Tantu illud obseruandum est: si haec bona fide Iacobo dixerit, no satis bona fide ciues suos spe commodorum amplissima ad hunc contractum publice confirmandum pellexisse, prout verba ipsius v.23. aperte ostendunt. Itaque neccesse est ut in partem alterutram oratorie, vel potius vete-ratorie egisse dicatur.
units.tr: This second history concerns Jacob's return into Canaan. Its end is twofold, general and particular. The general end of this history and of all those that follow is that we should recognize Jacob's life as seasoned with afflictions, just as it behoves the godly to strive toward the kingdom of God through many afflictions. The particular end is that we understand the occasion from which it came about that Simeon or Levi did not succeed to the firstborn right after Reuben had lost it by his incestuous crime. Namely, by their wickedness they made themselves unworthy of that prerogative. Therefore the firstborn rights were transferred to Judah among the sons of Leah, and to Joseph among the sons of Rachel, as Jacob shows in Gen. 49, and as is plainly written at the beginning of 1 Chron. 5. The summary is this: Dinah, Jacob's daughter, was violated by Shechem; a contract was entered into and kept by the foreigners, but it was broken by Jacob's sons. There are therefore three parts to this chapter: the first, on the wrong done to the girl, vv. 1 and 2; the second, on the contract entered into, from there to v. 18; the third, on the performance and violation of the contract, to the end of the chapter. To the first place two things belong: the occasion and the deed of Shechem. Moses shows that the occasion was the vanity of the young girl, who rashly went out of the house to visit the girls of the region (v. 1). The narrative of the deed is plain (v. 2): she was seized and violated by Shechem, and paid the price of her vanity. To the second place the following belong: first, the things that preceded the making of the contract, to v. 7; then the reconciliation of the contract on both sides, from there to v. 18. The things that preceded the contract are these: the young man's burning love for the girl (v. 3); then his conference with the father (v. 4); third, Jacob's dissimulation and silence until the sons had arrived (v. 5); finally, the meeting of all parties on both sides (vv. 6 and 7). No good man can excuse the young man's love, which arose from an evil beginning and purpose. But that, having committed the wrong, he persisted constantly in his love, comforted the girl, and sought her in marriage, as if to correct the shameful deed that had gone before, is in itself praiseworthy and agrees with the law of nature, provided the consent of those whose concern it is has been obtained. There are, however, two parties, since each of them was under the power of a father. Therefore the young man is rightly said to have procured the consent of both parties: first indeed that of his own father (v. 4), then that of the girl's father (v. 5). It is asked whether Jacob acted rightly, or otherwise, in not answering at once the man seeking the marriage. The answer is that not only Jacob but also the girl's brothers, who were older, were present, so that they might bring a common consent. Since a common consent had to be given, Jacob in good faith kept his opinion to himself and waited for the opportunity of holding a common judgment in a common matter. As for the meeting, in that Shechem's father and son came, and Jacob and his sons met with them, the act was lawful. Nor was it in itself unlawful that the brothers were grieved and flared up in anger because of the indignity of the crime and the insult offered to their family. But they are blamed only in that they did not keep the just measure of their grief, as the following narrative of Moses confirms. The second place, concerning the contract, is contained in three parts: the first is the stipulation of marriage, to v. 12; the second is the counter-stipulation of the condition which they pretended was necessary for the marriage, from there to v. 18; the third is the consent to the conditions put forward on both sides (v. 18). The stipulation has two members: one from the father, in three words; the other from the young man (vv. 10 and 12). The places of the paternal stipulation are three. First, the cause is put forward, the son's love; then the stipulation of marriage, that Dinah be given to him as wife (v. 8); third, the promise of all equal sharing between the citizens, which will be common to Jacob and his sons (vv. 9 and 10). For Hamor lingered longer on this argument, so as to persuade them to the marriage. Whether these things were said by Hamor in good faith or not, it is not easy to judge. This only must be observed: if he spoke these things to Jacob in good faith, he did not in good faith entice his citizens, with the hope of very great advantages, to confirm this contract publicly, as his own words in v. 23 clearly show. It must therefore be said that he acted either rhetorically or, rather, craftily, one way or the other.

units.la: Alter stipulationis locus a filio, animum adolescentis declarat euidentissime, cum puellam quasi supplex sibi nuptum dari postulat, v. 11. deinde quamuis conditionem vel gravissimam sibi imperata spon det se præstituturum, v.12. Hæc omnia legitime. Sequitur iam restipulatio, quam non Iacob quidem; sed filij eius tamquam seni patri & gra-vi ætate consulentes dicuntur respondisse; sed respondisse per fraudē v.13.qua unica voce visum est S. Spiritui peccatum istorum notare graviter, prout a Iacobo hæc omnia distincte notantur, & illi propterea castigati sunt c. 49.v.5.& seq. Responsionis autem partes sunt omnino duæ: prior est thesis, v.14. posterior, hypothecsis & accommodatio ad præsentem causam, tribus seqq. Thesis est, Nõpossumus facere rem istam, &c. Cum autem sit duplex posse: unum facti, cum quis ex facto præstare non potest præ impotentia: alterum iuris, cum quis iure potest, aut non potest; non est dubium quin hoc loco filij Iacobi ad potestatem iustam respexerint. Potestas autem iuris, aut ex iure divino & religioso, aut ex humano est. Iure humano, non impediebantur quominus sororem suam elocarent: sed divinum obtendunt, ut religionis specie commodius fallerent, quod homines politici hoc tempore (si umquam) solent occupare: atque eò gravior & iniquior fuit fraus istorum, nomine Dei & religione ad scelerata sua consilia perficienda abutentium. Ex hac igitur thesi sequitur hypothecsis dilemmatica. Nam primùm ostendunt qua conditione acquieturi sint coniugio, & in societatem coniugiorum venturi: denique civitatis commune ius accepturi, versÄ. 15. & 16. deinde ostendunt nisi expleatur conditio ab ipsis dicta, rem non esse processuram; sed ipsos recepta sorore abituros loco, vers. 17. Atque hac denuntiatione amplius adolescentis animum, quem flagrantem amore animaduerterant, accendebant, ut eo maiore cæcitate in pedicas ipsorum irrueret. Hanc conditionem accepisse dicuntur illi, & contractum firmavisse v. 18.
units.tr: The second place of the stipulation, from the son, most clearly declares the young man's mind, when like a suppliant he asks that the girl be given to him in marriage (v. 11), and then promises that he will perform even the most burdensome condition imposed on him (v. 12). All of this is lawful. Now follows the counter-stipulation, to which it is said that not Jacob himself but his sons replied, consulting their aged father and his advanced years. But they replied by fraud (v. 13). In this single word the Holy Spirit seems to mark gravely the sin of these men, just as Jacob distinctly notes all these things, and they were therefore rebuked by him (ch. 49, vv. 5 ff.). There are altogether two parts to the reply: the first is the thesis (v. 14); the second is the hypothesis and its application to the present case, in the three following verses. The thesis is We cannot do this thing, etc. Since "can" is twofold, one of fact, when someone cannot perform a thing from impotence, the other of right, when someone may or may not do it by right, there is no doubt that the sons of Jacob here had regard to a just power. The power of right is either from divine and religious law or from human law. By human law they were not prevented from giving their sister in marriage. But they put forward the divine law, so that they might deceive more conveniently under the appearance of religion, which political men at this time (if ever) are wont to do. The fraud of these men was all the graver and more unjust, since they abused the name of God and religion to carry out their wicked plans. From this thesis therefore follows a dilemmatic hypothesis. For first they show on what condition they will agree to the marriage and enter into the fellowship of marriages, and finally receive the common right of the citizens (vv. 15 and 16). Then they show that unless the condition they state is fulfilled, the matter will not proceed, but they will depart with their sister taken back (v. 17). By this threat they further inflamed the mind of the young man, whom they had seen burning with love, so that he might rush into their snares with the greater blindness. They are said to have accepted this condition and confirmed the contract (v. 18).

units.la: Tertia pars capitis in præstatione contractus narranda consu-mitur[?]. Itaque duo sunt huius narrationis loci: unus, quomodo Schecemitæ bona fide contractum præstiterint, ad vers. usque 24. Alter, quomodo filij Iacobi perfidè contra omnes leges contra-ctus venerint, ad vers. usque 29. Unde eventus ille, qui duobus ultimis versibus exponitur; ad narrationem sequentem μεταβατικός. In præstatione à Schecemitis ponuntur ista; primùm quòd adolescens ipse, familiaque Chamoris omnem diligentiam adhibuerunt in conditione præstanda, verf. 19. Secundò, quòd non familiæ solum, sed toti ciuitati eandem conditionem persuaserunt, verf. 20. & feqq. Postremò quòd persuasi ciues cum suis principibus se circumcidi passi sunt, verf. 24. Persuasionis quam instituit Chamor v. 20. loci duo sunt; propositio, v. 21. & 22. & confirmatio propositionis, v.23.Propositionis partes duæ: primùm ciuitatem & coniugia cum istis aduenis communicari oportere, duobus argumentis:à persona ipsorum, quòd viri boni sint & colentes pacis; & à regionis commoditate, quòd sit amplißima. Altera pars est propositio cõditionis oblatæ de circumcidendis masculis, v. 22. confirmatur propositio ab vtili, v.23.quòd ita Schecemitæ dominium suum amplificaturi sunt.Hoc autem quomodo sit accipiendum,supra in v.9.&10. ostendimus.Huic contraćtui acquiescentes ciues dicuntur circumcisi fuisse.v.24.Sequitur locus alter,de non præstito, sed rupto perfidè contraćtu à filiis Iacobi;cuius perfidiæ gradus ponuntur duo. Nam primùm dicuntur duo filij vrbem inuasisse, mares trucidauisse, & sororem domum reduxisse, v. 25. & feq. deinde verò omnes simul coniuncta opera expilasse & diripuisse omnia, etiam fœminas & paruulos velut mancipia in seruitutem abduxisse.
units.tr: The third part of the chapter is taken up with narrating the performance of the contract[?]. There are therefore two places in this narrative: one, how the Shechemites performed the contract in good faith, to v. 24; the other, how the sons of Jacob came treacherously against all the laws of the contract, to v. 29. Hence that event which is set out in the last two verses leads to the following narrative, a metabasis [μεταβατικός]. In the performance by the Shechemites the following are set down: first, that the young man himself and the household of Hamor applied all diligence in performing the condition (v. 19). Second, that they persuaded not only the household but the whole city to the same condition (v. 20 and following). Lastly, that the persuaded citizens allowed themselves to be circumcised together with their princes (v. 24). The persuasion which Hamor undertook (v. 20) has two places: the proposition (vv. 21 and 22) and the confirmation of the proposition (v. 23). The proposition has two parts. First, the city and its marriages must be shared with these strangers, on two arguments: from their persons, that they are good men and peace-loving; and from the advantage of the region, that it is very spacious. The other part is the proposition of the condition offered, concerning the circumcision of the males (v. 22). The proposition is confirmed from utility (v. 23): thus the Shechemites will enlarge their dominion. How this is to be understood we showed above on vv. 9 and 10. The citizens, consenting to this contract, are said to have been circumcised (v. 24). There follows the second place, concerning a contract not performed but treacherously broken by the sons of Jacob. Two degrees of this treachery are set down. For first the two sons are said to have invaded the city, slain the males, and led their sister back home (vv. 25 and following); then indeed all together, by joint effort, to have plundered and looted everything, even leading away the women and little ones as slaves into bondage.

units.la: In maleficio duorum filiorũ Iacobi,qui ianuam primùm huic perfidiæ aperuerunt,primò notatur tempus & occasio temporis: deinde factum.Tempus est dies tertius à circumcisione Schecemitarum: Occasio, quòd eo die in dolore essent, & tamquam si omnia in vado fuissent,operam dabant valetudini: vnde consequuntum est illud maleficium,quòd vrbem securam,& nihil hostile à nouis aduenis sibi suisque ex recenti contraćtu ciuibus metuentem, indignè inuaserunt. Et tum omnes mares promiscuè, v. 25.tum principes ciuitatis trucidarunt,itáque recepta sorore sua abiuerunt, v.26. omnia præter ius naturæ & contraćtus fidem, quem contraćtum cum Schecemitis pepigerant.Hic autem quæritur,vtrum hi soli inter se communicato cõsilio facinus istud aggressi sint,an verò consciis fratribus, velut communes emissarij. Responsio est, hos duos principes consilij & exsequutionis fuisse:nam eo nomine singularem pœnam ipsis fuisse à Iacobo impositam, quam non fuisset in hos solùm denunciaturus, si commune fuisset consilium factum omnium.Commune maleficium fuit, quod tribus versibus describitur: ex euentu singularis facti omnes Iacobi filios in communionem maleficij abreptos fuisse, ac proinde in confossos cucurrisse, eósq; spoliasse,ciuitatem diripuisse, omne pecus, omnémque pecuniam domo & rure abstulisse, omnes opes sibi vendicasse, & capita ingenua puerorum fœminarúmque manmancipauisse: denique omnia in re suam perfide vertisse. quae omnia praeter ius naturae & contractum bonae fidei (vt ante diximus) Schecemitis euenerunt: ac proinde sunt nobis documento, quibus perturbationibus, & quibus sceleribus etiam dilecti Dei infesti sint, nisi virtute Spiritus etiā agātur in rebus singulis, & ipsi à Deo pedere discat: vt e diuerso ostendunt sequetia quibus afflictionibus pij affligat sese, tū iniustitiae odio,tū etiā contagionis metu, ex quo fugere etiā veste quae à carne contaminata sit (vt Iudas loquitur) didicerūt. Atque hic euetus est, qui postea describitur duobus verfib. vltimis, increpāte & lamentante patre, filiisque insolenter respondentibus tamquam elatis ex prospero consiliorum suorum successu. Sermonem Iacobi in duas partes distinguimus: in detestationem sceleris, & mali propediem futuri metu. Detestationis duo sunt loci; vnus, à persona Iacobi, quod totum se perturbatum in animo suo sentiat ex filiorum maleficio: Alter, à persona incolarum siue popularium, quod hoc facino re con-tra communia contractuū [?] iura perpetrato, tamquam periurus & religionis expers sit habendus apud vicinos, & nomen suum futurum odiosum, vt res foetidae sunt odiosae. Metus argumenta duo sunt, paucitas familiae Iacobi, & omnium vicinorum maximo numero in familiam ipsius, quasi perfidam incursantium furor iustus, à quo nihil nisi internecio exspectanda sit. Huic graui increpationi subiungitur im-potens & thrasonica filiorum responsatio, sub iuris communis specie suum facinus excusantium: quasi dicant quod vulgo respondentes solent, cur illi primo nobis dederunt causam? Caetera quae interuenerūt ad corrigendum factum, & contractum inter ipsos initum, denique perfidiam suam dissimulantes & tegentes primi actus criminatione.
units.tr: In the crime of the two sons of Jacob, who first opened the door to this treachery, the time is noted first, and the occasion of the time, and then the deed. The time is the third day after the circumcision of the Shechemites. The occasion is that on that day they were in pain, and, as if everything were in the shallows, they were tending to their health. From this circumstance came that wicked act: they attacked the city without justification, while it was secure and feared nothing hostile from the new arrivals, the citizens who, by their recent covenant, were bound to them and their people. Then they slaughtered all the males indiscriminately (v. 25), and they slew the chief men of the city; and so, having recovered their sister, they departed (v. 26), doing everything outside the law of nature and the faith of the covenant which they had made with the Shechemites. Here, however, it is asked whether these two alone undertook that crime among themselves, after communal deliberation, or whether the brothers too were privy to it, like common agents. The answer is that these two were the leaders of the plan and of its execution, for on that account a singular punishment was laid upon them by Jacob, which he would not have pronounced against these two alone if the plan had been the common decision of all. The crime was common, as the three verses describe it: from the outcome of the single deed, all the sons of Jacob were drawn into the common guilt, and accordingly they rushed upon the slain, stripped them, plundered the city, carried off all the livestock and all the money from house and farm, claimed all the wealth for themselves, and reduced to slavery the free-born boys and women. Finally, they turned everything to their own treachery. All these things befell the Shechemites outside the law of nature and the contract of good faith (as we said before), and so they are a lesson to us: with what disturbances and what crimes even the beloved of God are troubled, unless they are also governed in each single matter by the power of the Spirit, and learn to depend on God himself. Conversely, the following verses show with what afflictions the godly afflict themselves, both from hatred of injustice and also from fear of contagion, from which they learned to flee even the garment that has been defiled by the flesh (as Jude speaks). And this is the outcome which is described afterwards in the last two verses, with the father rebuking and lamenting, and the sons answering insolently, as if elated by the favourable success of their plans. We divide Jacob's speech into two parts: a detestation of the crime, and a fear of the evil soon to come. There are two places of detestation: one, from the person of Jacob, that he feels himself wholly disturbed in his mind by the sons' crime; the other, from the person of the inhabitants or neighbours, that this deed, committed against the common laws of contracts, is to be held among the neighbours as perjured and void of religion, and that his name will be hateful, as foul things are hateful. There are two grounds for fear: the small number of Jacob's household, and the greatest number of all the neighbours, who, as if they were attacking the household treacherously, will bring a just fury, from which nothing but total destruction is to be expected. To this grave rebuke is added the impotent and boastful reply of the sons, excusing their deed under the appearance of common right, as if they said what people commonly answer: why did they give us the first cause? The rest that intervened was to make amends for the deed and for the contract entered between them, and finally to conceal their treachery and cover it by accusing the first act.

units.la: CAPITIS XXXV ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 35 ANALYSIS.

units.la: Hæc secunda narratio est rerum à Iacobo in Cena-hanea gestarum. Hanc narrationē instituit Moses, vt aduentum Iacobi ad Isaacum patrem, & aditum ad hæreditatem illius ostenderet. Summa, Iacobū à Schecemo ad habitationem paternā certis stationibus contendisse, quae hoc capite sigillatim describūtur. Itaque huius capitis secundū stationes par-tes sunt quatuor: Prima, migratio Iacobi in Bethelem, ad v. vsque 15. Secūda, migratio in Bethlechemum, ad v. 19. vsque. Tertia, ad turrim gregis, quae inter Bethechem & Hebronem sita fuit, ad v. vsque 26. quarta denique, aduentus in domum paternam Hebronem. Singulis autem stationibus, singulæ historiæ coniunguntur, quas deinceps paucis percurremus. In historia primæ stationis tria ordine narrantur. Primùm causa migrationis à Schecemo, verf.1. Deinde modus præ-parationis ad migrationem, tribus sequentibus. Postremò autem ipsa migratio, & adiuncta eius, versibus reliquis. Causa migrationis fuit mandatum Dei: nam Deus revocans in memoriam Iacobo antece-dentes promissiones iubet ipsum à Schecemo discedere, & eodem re-gredi quò Iacob ex voto facto sup. cap.28. tenebatur. Modus insti-tuendi itineris in præparatione personarum & rerum positus est. Præ-paratio autem potentissima est sanctificationis; quia Deus seruos suos ad opus suum vocatos præparari sanctificatione iubet, & imparatos arcet à potiundis suis promissionibus: prout exemplo Mosis est eui-dens, qui iter in Ægyptum instituens nondum circumciso filio, ab angelo Dei fuit impeditus, donec familia purgata esset. Itaque Iacob primum duo denuntiat; deinde exsequitur. Denuntiat primum san-ctificationem toti familiæ suæ & reipsa, & significatione: reipsa, sub-mouendis idolis: significatione, mutandis vestibus, verf.2. Deinde professionem denuntiat, & consilium cultus Dei grato animo exer-cendi, verf.3. Prioris partis exsequutio verf. quarto ostenditur, cum dicuntur omnes idola sua & res ad idololatriam pertinentes Iacobo tradidisse, & ille sub quercu condidisse. Hic quæruntur duo: primum unde illa idola in familia Iacobi fuerint: secundò cur illa non verte-rit potius in rem suam, aut igni etiam tradiderit, quàm humo condi-derit. Idola fuerunt non ea solùm, quæ Rachel ex domo paterna ex-portauerat sup. cap. 31. sed etiam quæcunque Schecemi expilauerant filij in vrbe & in agro, ac proinde ista in familia Iacobi duobus mo-dis offensioni erant; primùm causa religionis veræ, cui idola aduer-santur: deinde causa latrocinij publici, quia ad ipsos res quamuis pre-tiosæ nullo iure pertinebant; cuiusmodi fuerunt inaures, de auribus ipsorum dependentes. Noluit autem Iacob ista in rem suam vertere, tum propter ius, tum propter significationem: propter ius, quia con-scius erat res illas ad se minimè pertinere: propter significationem, quia interest piorum, vt publicis etiam signis testatum faciant quan-tum ab impietate & iniustitia, adeoque ab specie impietatis, abhor-reant. Secundò, cur non igitur combussit potius, quàm vt terra con-deret? Quia vstionis ipsius & reliquiæ in materia, & vestigia in solo remansissent, ac proinde aut materiam reliquam velut sacram, aut etiä cineres ipsos pro sacris habuissent vicini & incolæ: propterea visum est potius sic humi defodere omnia, vt nemini homini costaret, vn-de recipi ista idololatriæ monumenta possent. Sequitur iam, quòd prosectus est Iacob Schecemo, fretus præsidio Dei, timorem incolis inii-cientis, nequid in Iacobum & familiam eius instituerent, v.5. & ad-uentus in Bethel, v.6. Cui narrationi subiungitur postea narratio ge-stariim in ea statione. Est autem narratio duplex; vna, diuini cultus a Iacobo instituti, v.7. altera, mortis Deboræ, quæ nutrix fuerat Rib-kæ, v.8. Hunc autem cultum religiosum Deus reuelatione diuina confirmauisse dicitur à v.9. ad 13. & Iacob confirmatus ampliora cul-tus diuini monumenta in loco statuisse, v.13. & duobus seqq. Reuela-tionis summa est, Deum Iacobo benedixisse, v.9. singularis verò in-terpretatio, tribus seqq. Nam primùm Iacobo benedicitur in signo, repetitione nominis ante impositi, v.10. Secundò promissione hære-dum, maximo numero & amplitudine, v.11. Tertiò promissione hæ-reditatis, v.12. Hinc sequitur cultus illius diuini amplior testificatio in eodem ipso loco edita vbi Deus ante Iacobo apparuerat. Itaque primùm circumstantia illa loci, verf.13. exponitur: deinde testificatio diuini cultus, tum religiosis actionibus, verf. 14. & ceremonialibus ad tempus illud præsignificando Christo pertinentibus; tum nomi-nis impositione, cùm locus Bethel fuit appellatus, verf. 15. Secun-da pars capitis profectionem Iacobi Bethele narrat Bethlechemum, & quid incommodi in ea profectione acciderit: quæ res summatim proponuntur verf. decimosexto. Deinde verò exponitur singula-riter mors Rachelæ, & adiuncta ipsius. Atque hæc illa sunt: primùm grauitas partus & consolatio de filio nascente ab obstetrice pronun-tiatia verf. decimoseptimo. Deinde nomen triste filio à matre mo-riente impositum, & iucundiore à patre commutatum; verf. deci-mooctauo. Tum mors Rachelæ, verf. decimonono. Postremò, sta-tua monumento illius impositat ad perpetuam rei memoriam & spei de futura resurrectione documentum, verf. vigesimo. Tertia pars capitis, profectionem Iacobi narrat Bethlechemo ad turrim gre-gis, verf. vigesimoprimo. & funestam historiam quæ ibi gesta est: Quòd Ruben primogenitus incesto concubitu vxorem concubinam patris compresserit; quo ex facto duo consequuta sunt: vnum, quòd Iacob de re audita cognouit, & grauissime affectus est; Alterum, quòd hoc impio facto, Ruben excidit ex primogenitorum iu-re ad ipsum pertinente: quapropter eodem loco, noua instituitur filiorum Iacobi enumeratio: cùm & Biniamin iam recens ad numerum accessisset, & Ruben de suo ordine flagitio suo de-cidisset.
units.tr: This is the second narrative of the things Jacob did in Canaan. Moses set out this narrative to show Jacob's coming to his father Isaac and his entry into the inheritance. In summary, Jacob travelled from Shechem to his father's home by definite stages, which are described one by one in this chapter. Accordingly, the chapter has four parts, divided by these stages. The first is Jacob's journey to Bethel, to v. 15. The second is the journey to Bethlehem, to v. 19. The third is the stage at the tower of the flock, which lay between Bethlehem and Hebron, to v. 26. The fourth, finally, is his arrival at his father's house in Hebron. Each stage has its own story attached, which we shall now briefly run through. In the story of the first stage, three things are narrated in order. First, the cause of the departure from Shechem, v. 1. Second, the manner of preparing for the journey, in the following three verses. Last, the journey itself and its circumstances, in the remaining verses. The cause of the departure was God's command. For God, bringing to Jacob's memory the earlier promises, orders him to leave Shechem and return to the place where Jacob was bound by the vow he had made (above, ch. 28). The manner of setting out lies in the preparation of persons and goods. Now preparation is chiefly a matter of sanctification, because God orders his servants who are called to his work to be prepared by sanctification, and keeps back the unprepared from obtaining his promises. The example of Moses makes this plain: when he set out for Egypt without having circumcised his son, he was hindered by the angel of God until the household was cleansed. So Jacob first gives two orders and then carries them out. He first orders the sanctification of his whole household, both in fact and in sign. In fact, by removing the idols; in sign, by changing their clothes, v. 2. Then he declares his profession and his resolve to worship God with a grateful heart, v. 3. The carrying out of the first part is shown in v. 4, where it is said that they gave Jacob all their idols and the things that pertained to idolatry, and that he buried them under an oak. Two questions arise here: first, where those idols in Jacob's household came from; second, why he did not rather turn them to his own use, or hand them over to the fire, instead of burying them in the ground. The idols were not only those which Rachel had carried off from her father's house (above, ch. 31), but also whatever the sons of Shechem had plundered in the city and in the countryside. Thus these things were an offence in Jacob's household in two ways. First, because of the true religion, to which idols are opposed. Second, because of public robbery, since those goods, however valuable, did not rightfully belong to them at all; such were the earrings hanging from their ears. Jacob, however, was unwilling to turn these things to his own use, both on account of right and on account of the signification. On account of right, because he knew that those things did not belong to him in any way. On account of the signification, because it concerns the pious to show by public signs how far they shrink from impiety and injustice, and so from the very appearance of impiety. Secondly, why then did he not burn them rather than bury them in the earth? Because the burning itself would have left remains in the material and traces on the ground, and so the neighbours and inhabitants would have held either the remaining material or even the ashes themselves as sacred. It was therefore thought better to bury everything in the ground in such a way that no man could learn from where those monuments of idolatry might be recovered. Next follows the departure of Jacob from Shechem, relying on the protection of God, who put fear into the inhabitants so that they did nothing against Jacob and his household, v. 5, and his arrival at Bethel, v. 6. After this account there follows a narrative of what happened at that stage. There is a twofold narrative: one of the worship of God established by Jacob, v. 7; the other of the death of Deborah, who had been Rebekah's nurse, v. 8. It is said that God confirmed this religious worship by a divine revelation, from v. 9 to 13, and that Jacob, once confirmed, set up more ample memorials of divine worship in the place, v. 13 and the two following. The sum of the revelation is that God blessed Jacob, v. 9; the particular explanation is in the three following verses. For first, Jacob is blessed by a sign, the repetition of the name formerly given, v. 10. Second, by the promise of heirs, in the greatest number and abundance, v. 11. Third, by the promise of the inheritance, v. 12. Hence follows a fuller testimony of this divine worship, given in the same place where God had earlier appeared to Jacob. First, then, the circumstance of the place is set out, v. 13. Then the testimony of the divine worship: partly by religious acts, v. 14, and by ceremonies pertaining to the foreshadowing of Christ at that time; partly by the giving of a name, when the place was called Bethel, v. 15. The second part of the chapter narrates Jacob's journey from Bethel to Bethlehem, and what misfortune befell him on that journey; these matters are set out briefly in v. 16. Then, however, the death of Rachel and the circumstances attached to it are explained one by one. These are the following: first, the hardship of the birth, and the comfort concerning the son about to be born, pronounced by the midwife, v. 17. Then the sad name given to the son by his dying mother, and its change to a happier one by the father, v. 18. Then the death of Rachel, v. 19. Last, the pillar set up over her tomb, as a lasting memorial of the matter and as a token of the hope of the future resurrection, v. 20. The third part of the chapter narrates Jacob's journey from Bethlehem to the tower of the flock, v. 21, and the sorrowful history that took place there: that Reuben, the firstborn, lay with his father's concubine in an incestuous union. Two things followed from this deed. One: Jacob learned of the matter when he heard of it and was most grievously affected. The other: by this impious act Reuben fell from the rights of the firstborn which belonged to him. For this reason, in the same place, a new enumeration of Jacob's sons is set down, since Benjamin had by now recently been added to the number, and Reuben had by his shameful deed lost his place in the order.
