units.la: Restat postremo statio, quòd Iacob ad Isaacum patrem, redit, ver. antepenultimo. Cui argumento certo consilio adiungitur historia de patris vita, & obitu, atque sepultura, v. ultimo. Fit autem illud ad commoditatem historiæ, quamuis non obseruata ratione temporis, quia argumenta in scripturis plurimum pro natura ipsorum, non pro ratione temporum describuntur. Nam alioquin certissimum illud est ex ætate Isaaci ante fuisse gestam historiam c.37. quàm Isaac vita defunctus esset. Hanc autem rationem historiarum sacrarum copiose in finem capitis quarti exposuimus.
units.tr: There remains, last of all, the stage in which Jacob returns to his father Isaac, v. penultimate. To this matter, in a fixed order, is joined the story of the father's life, death and burial, v. last. This is done for the convenience of the narrative, although the order of time is not observed, because in the Scriptures the matters are described chiefly according to their nature and not according to the order of times. For otherwise it is most certain that the history of Isaac's age, Genesis 37, took place before Isaac died. We have set out this principle of sacred histories at length at the end of chapter 4.

units.la: CAPITIS XXXVI ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 36 ANALYSIS.

units.la: Finis propter quem hoc caput à Mose descriptum est videtur fuisse, non tam ut Iudæi cognationem suam & ius illius cum Edomæis discerent, quàm ut descriptione & recensione hac via sterneretur ad sacræ historiæ de populo Dei intelligentiam, & iustitiæ Dei declarationem. Summa igitur est, populum regionis quæ Edomæa appellatur, & rationem totius administrationis in eo populo hoc capite explicari, ut exstaret in Ecclesia Dei perpetuum patientiæ diuinæ in omnes, iustitiæ in exteros atque infideles, & misericordiæ in suos argumentum. Duæ itaque sunt huius capitis partes summæ: quarum priore familiarum recensio; posteriore autem regum & principum qui obtinuerunt imperium describitur, prior locus ad vers. usque 30. Posterior ad finem capitis pertenditur. In recensione familiarum partes duæ sunt; nam primum familiæ Esau siue Edomi, ad vers. usque 19. deinde vero diuerso temporum ordine familiæ Sehiris siue Choreorum, qui agrum illum prius incoluerant, habetur recensio, inde ad vers. 30. In familia Esaui recensenda, primum liberorum qui proximè ex uxoribus & concubina sunt editi Esauo, nomina describuntur, ad vers. usque quintum; deinde, migratio Esaui, cum familia tota, & migrationis causa exponitur vers. 6.7.8. His velut capitibus gentis à Mose expositis, sequitur demum minuta gentis illius descriptio, secundùm familias imperiáque ipsorum, inde à versu nono. Posteà Moses ad gentem Choreorum describendam transit, cuius gentis studia & occupationes unius Chanæ exemplo demonstrantur, vers. 24. Quòd admissuram equorum cum asinabus, id est, mixta iumentorum generä dicitur in deserto excogitauisse: ac proinde illum præter naturam voluptati atque nouitati curiosæ studuisse, quo in genere luxuriatur infidelium animus. In secunda parte capitis ordo regum atque principum in Edomæa osteditur[?], qui annos amplius ducetos perdurauit; fortasse etiam annos ducentos quinquaginta. Nā cùm statio Israelitarũ in Ægypto fuerit annorum ducentorum decem,& annos minimùm triginta ante illud tempus Esau in regionem illam se receperit; omnino terminus istius historiæ ab eo tempore petendus est, quo Esau se in Edomæam contulit, antequam Iacob ex Mesopotamia reuersus esset; & definiendus illo ipso tempore quo Moses dux populo à Deo, datus est, & populus ex seruitute Ægypti liberatus: quo tempore ex ordine duplex fuit administratio; prior ducum, quæ posteriore loco exponitur à v.40.ad finem vsque; posterior regum,qui multorum ducum imperium assumpserunt, & suo ordine tenuerunt vsque ad Mosis aduentũ,v.31.& seqq.Vna hic incidit quæstio,quo iure Edom cum posteris regionis illius imperium obtinuerit? Resp. Videri iure sanguinis ex affinitate imperium ditionis illius ad Esauum peruenisse. Nam cùm hoc loco duxisse filiam Hanā, filiam Sibbonis legatur,qui principatum in ea gente tenuerunt; videtur Esau saltem dominij illius partem iure affinitatis adiuisse. Quòd si post aditam illam hæreditatem, siue pretio,siue fraude, siue armis(quibus modis possessiones à potentioribus acquiruntur) posteri Esaui aliud comparauerunt,aut nouis(quod magis probabile est) affinitatibus, ex ea recensione regum quæ fit inde à v.31.omnino tamen,ex locorum huius capitis comparatione, constat iustum fuisse primum aditum possessionis illius. Quam possessionem iam satis amplam fuisse penes Esauum ex historia 32. & 33 capitis est manifestum.
units.tr: The purpose for which Moses wrote this chapter seems to have been less that the Jews might learn their kinship with the Edomites and their rights against them, and more that, by this kind of description and enumeration, the way might be prepared for understanding the sacred history of God's people and for declaring God's justice. The sum, then, is that the people of the region called Edom, and the manner of God's whole administration among that people, are set forth in this chapter, so that there might stand in the Church of God a lasting proof of the divine patience towards all, of justice towards outsiders and unbelievers, and of mercy towards his own. There are therefore two main parts to this chapter. In the first, the families are enumerated; in the second, the kings and princes who held power are described. The first part runs to verse 30, and the second extends to the end of the chapter. In the enumeration of families there are two parts. First, the family of Esau, or of Edom, is listed down to verse 19. Then, in a different temporal order, the family of Seir, or of the Horites, who had earlier inhabited that land, is listed, from there to verse 30. In recounting the family of Esau, first the names of the children born to Esau from his wives and his concubine are given, down to the fifth verse. Then Esau's migration, with his whole household, and the cause of that migration, are set out in verses 6, 7 and 8. After Moses has set out these, as it were, headings of the nation, there follows at last a detailed description of the nation, according to its families and their rulers, from verse 9 onward. Afterwards Moses turns to describe the Horite people, whose habits and occupations are shown by the single example of Anah, verse 24. The text says that he invented in the desert the mixing of horses with asses, that is, the crossing of kinds of beasts of burden. Accordingly, he pursued a novelty against nature for the sake of pleasure and curiosity, which is the kind of luxury in which the minds of unbelievers delight. In the second part of the chapter, the order of kings and princes in Edom is shown, which lasted for more than four hundred years, perhaps even two hundred and fifty years. For since the sojourn of the Israelites in Egypt lasted two hundred and ten years, and Esau had withdrawn into that region at least thirty years before that time, the limit of this history must be taken from the time when Esau moved into Edom, before Jacob returned from Mesopotamia. It is to be defined by that very time when Moses was given by God as leader to the people, and the people were freed from the bondage of Egypt. At that time the administration was twofold: the first was of leaders, which is set out in the later place from verse 40 to the end; the second was of kings, who took up the rule of many leaders and held it in their order down to the coming of Moses, verse 31 and following. One question arises here: by what right did Edom, with the descendants of that region, hold dominion? I answer that the rule of that territory seems to have come to Esau by right of blood, through kinship by marriage. For since it is read in this place that he had taken to wife Hanah, the daughter of Sibbon, who held the leadership among that people, it seems that Esau at least acquired a share of that lordship by right of marriage. But if afterwards the descendants of Esau, either by price, by fraud or by arms (the ways by which possessions are acquired from the more powerful), or (what is more probable) by new marriages, obtained more, this may be gathered from the list of kings that begins at verse 31. Nevertheless, from a comparison of the places in this chapter, it is established beyond doubt that the first entry into that possession was just. That this possession was already quite large in Esau's hands is clear from the history in chapters 32 and 33.

units.la: CAPITIS XXXVII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XXXVII ANALYSIS.

units.la: AFFLICTIONIBVS antecedentibus Iacobi, alia superuenisse dicitur in hoc cap. post annum decimum, quàm Iacob ex Mesopotamia reuerterat. Summa igitur est, Iacobum filij Iosephi amantissimum, certis de causis & occasione imprudenter oblata, filio Iosepho per maleficium fratrum eius priuatum esse; sed qui beneficio diuinæ prouidentiæ in Ægyptum salutari consilio fuerit deportatus. Quatuor igitur sunt huius capitis partes: nam primum causæ exponuntur instituti à fratribus maleficij, ad v.vsque 17. Secundò consilia à fratribus inita,ad v.vsque 29. Tertiò maleficium fratrum scelerate Iosephum exteris vendentium,ad v. vsque 33[?]. Postremò autem euenta narrantur breuiter ex ea alienatione consequuta, sub finem capitis. Ad hanc narrationem transitio fit in v.1.per antithesin habitationis, qua Iacob vsus est, cum habitatione Edomi de qua præcedente capite mentio. Atque in hac Iacobi commoratione, cùm in terra peregrinationum patris sui sedem dicitur habuisse, fides & pietas illius a Mose comendatur, prout copiosè Apostolus ad Heb. xi. c. explicauit. Primus locus de causis bipertitus est: nam primùm veræ causæ adducuntur, cur Ioseph à fratribus fuerit venditus, ad v. vsque 12. deinde verò occasio exponitur, sequentibus. Narrationi causarum anteit breuis illius temporis circumscriptio, quo hæc dicuntur gesta: nempe quòd Ioseph tum ageret annum 17. ætatis suæ. Deinde verò tres causæ illius maleficij fratrum ordine proponuntur; prima, quòd Ioseph cum fratribus pascens, & administrum agens inter pastores grandiores, malam famam suorum fratrum ad patrem detulisset, verf. 2. siue puerili imprudentia, siue pietatis in Deum & existimationis publicæ studio, siue utraque causa ad hoc iudicium excitatus; secunda, quòd dilectus esset patris præ aliis fratribus, verf. 3. Cuius dilectionis causam, modum, euentum paucis exponit Moses: causam, quòd filius senectutis esset, constat enim tum parentum animos, quo magis considerescunt eò magis studio posteritatis affici, tum liberos quò teneriores ætate sunt, eò tenerius hærere parentum animis. Modum, quòd Iacob tenerum illum amorem suum non potuit dissimulare; quin Iosepho etiam externis signis aliquid amplius indulgeret; vt cùm induit ei versicolorem tunicam, quæ amoris significatio facile labitur in damnosam aliquam imprudentiam, vbi plures liberi sunt. Euentus amoris istius in verf. 4. triplex ostenditur; primus, quòd viderunt alij, & non obscurè perceperunt imprudente Iacobi facto; deinde quòd inuiderunt & oderunt fratrem: postremò, quòd bona verba cum ipso commutare minimè potuerunt, ex quo inuidentiæ & odio illi dederunt locum. Tertia demum causa est somniorum ratio, quæ diuinitus oblata sibi puer Ioseph fratribus indicabat, ac proinde imprudens & opus diuinum agens, flammam illam inuidentiæ & odij in suis fratribus accendebat, v. 5. Hæ autem causæ summatim positæ per se euidentes sunt: sed postremà necesse fuit minutatim à Mose explicari propter reliquam historiam cap. 43. & seqq. Itaque Moses somnia illa Iosephi diuinitus oblata duobus exemplis adductis narrat, ad v. vsque 11. Prius exemplum est mergitum, ad v. vsque 8. posterius, Solis, Lunæ, stellarumque, ad v. 11. Vtriusque exempli narratio tripertita est: nam primùm propositio somnij, secundò imprecatio siue reprehensio, deniq; euentus ostenditur. Sic prioris somnij propositio est (vt exordium omittamus in v. 6.) breuiter contexta v. 7. imprecatio à fratribus, priore parte 8. v. Euentus autem nempe odij incrementum, altera parte eiusdem versus. Posterioris verò somnij propositio positio habetur v. 9. qua summatim apud patrem & fratres iterata, increpatio a patre ponitur, in v.20, postremo autem eventus duplex, v.11.nempe fratrum invidentia, & attenta patris observatio, aliquid divinum in hac re quasi recognoscentis. Occasio vero (quam non proprie causam, sed accidentarie solum appellamus) narratur versibus seqq. Nempe quod pascentibus fratribus ad Schecemum, v.12. imprudens Jacob & nihil tale a filiis suis expectans, quamvis non inscius odij & invidentiae illorum, Josephum ad eos misit, prout a patre accersitus dicitur, v.12. & missus, v.13. Hic vero per occasionem narratio interseritur de evagatione fratrum sine patris conscientia; quod factum laudari non poterat: deinde vero Josephi diligentia in perquisitandis fratribus, postquam inscio patre migravissent. Lubenter enim Josephi statuebat, praestare ut ipse molestiam perquisitionis subiret, quam ut duplici molestia patrem afficeret: quemadmodum fuisset facturus, si non perquisitis & inventis fratribus domum reversset. Atque haec Josephi prudentia tum in quaerendo per errores, tum in rogando, v.35. & seq. tum in perquisitando, v.17. exponitur. Sequitur jam secundus locus de consiliis, quae in Josephum captae sunt, quorum consiliorum duo sunt genera, quae summatim in v.18. proponit Moses dicens, cum nondum appropinquavissent ad eos, ma-chinati sunt, &c. Hanc summam Moses sequentibus minutatim explicat, nam primum contemptum fratrum in Josephum μιμνηκῶς[?] demonstrat illorum verbis, v.19. deinde consilia duo ad mortem proponit sequentibus.
units.tr: It is said in this chapter that after the earlier afflictions of Jacob, other ones came upon him, in the tenth year after he had returned from Mesopotamia. The summary, then, is this: Jacob's most beloved son Joseph, for certain reasons and through an unwisely offered occasion, was deprived of his son by the wickedness of his brothers, but by the benefit of divine providence he was carried off into Egypt by a saving plan. There are therefore four parts to this chapter. First, the causes of the brothers' wickedness are set out, to v. 17. Secondly, the plans the brothers made, to v. 29. Thirdly, the brothers' wicked sale of Joseph to foreigners, to v. 33[?]. Lastly, the events that followed from this estrangement are briefly narrated, toward the end of the chapter. The transition to this narrative is made in v. 1, by way of an antithesis between the dwelling Jacob occupied and the dwelling of Edom mentioned in the preceding chapter. And in this sojourn of Jacob, where it is said that he had his home in the land of his father's pilgrimages, his faith and piety are commended by Moses, as the Apostle explains at length in Heb. xi. The first part, on causes, is in two sections: first the true causes are adduced, why Joseph was sold by his brothers, to v. 12; then the occasion is set out in what follows. Before the narrative of the causes comes a brief specification of the time in which these things are said to have happened, namely that Joseph was then seventeen years of age. Then three causes of the brothers' wickedness are put forward in order. The first is that Joseph, while pasturing the flocks with his brothers and acting as their assistant among the older shepherds, brought a bad report of his brothers to their father, v. 2, whether he was roused to this judgement by childish imprudence, by zeal for piety toward God and for public reputation, or by both causes together. The second is that he was loved by his father more than his other brothers, v. 3. Moses briefly sets out the cause, the manner and the outcome of this love. The cause was that he was a son of old age, for it is plain that parents' affections, the older they grow, are the more strongly moved by concern for posterity, and that children, the younger they are, cling the more tenderly to their parents' hearts. The manner was that Jacob could not conceal his tender love, but even indulged Joseph with outward signs beyond the rest, as when he made him a coat of many colours, a token of love which easily slips into some harmful imprudence where there are several children. The outcome of this love is shown threefold in v. 4. First, the others saw, and did not fail to perceive Jacob's imprudent act; then that they envied and hated their brother; lastly, that they could not speak kindly with him, which gave occasion to envy and hatred. The third and final cause is the matter of the dreams, which the boy Joseph, having been given them by God, reported to his brothers; and so, acting unwisely yet as an instrument of the divine work, he kindled that flame of envy and hatred in his brothers, v. 5. These causes, set down briefly, are plain in themselves; but the last one needed to be explained by Moses in more detail, on account of the rest of the history in chapter 43 and following. So Moses narrates those dreams of Joseph, given by God, by means of two examples, to v. 11. The first example is the sheaves, to v. 8; the second, of the sun, moon and stars, to v. 11. The narrative of each example has three parts: first the dream is proposed, secondly the curse or rebuke is shown, and lastly the outcome. Thus the proposal of the first dream (leaving aside the introduction in v. 6) is briefly woven together in v. 7; the curse from the brothers is in the first part of v. 8; and the outcome, namely the increase of hatred, is in the second part of the same verse. The proposal of the second dream is given in v. 9, and when it is briefly repeated before the father and brothers, the rebuke from the father is set down in v. 10. Lastly there is a twofold outcome, v. 11: the brothers' envy, and the father's attentive watching, as one who in this matter somehow recognised something divine. The occasion (which we call not strictly a cause but only incidental) is related in the verses that follow. Namely, while the brothers were pasturing at Shechem, v. 12, Jacob, unsuspecting and expecting nothing of the kind from his sons, although not unaware of their hatred and envy, sent Joseph to them, as he is said to have been summoned by his father, v. 12, and was sent, v. 13. Here, by way of occasion, the narrative is interrupted with an account of the brothers' wandering away without their father's knowledge, which deed could not be praised; then of Joseph's diligence in searching for his brothers after they had departed without his father's knowing. For Joseph judged it better to undergo the trouble of searching himself than to put his father to a double trouble, as he would have done had he not, after searching and finding his brothers, returned home. And this prudence of Joseph is set out both in his seeking through the wanderings, and in his asking, v. 15 and following, and in his searching, v. 17. Now follows the second part, on the plans that were laid against Joseph, of which there are two kinds, which Moses sets out in summary in v. 18, saying: when they had not yet come near them, they plotted, etc. Moses explains this summary in detail in what follows. For first he shows the brothers' contempt for Joseph by their own words, v. 19; then he sets out two plans for his death in what follows.

units.la: Prior consiliorum locus est de Josepho interficiendo, corpore illius in fovea deiiciendo, mendacioque comminiscendo ut patri illuderet; quae omnia inhumana consilia sunt & somniis divinis ludificandis, quod impium, v.20. Sed huic consilio mutatione dicitur attulisse Ruben frater maximus, qui partim vi necessitudinis, partimque metu offensionis paternae, quae in ipsum velut natu maximum gravior erat recursura, maxime anteacti sui facinoris conscientia. Hunc ergo verisimile est de infringendo fratrum consilio moderandoque cogitasse. Mutandi igitur consilii rationem dicitur Ruben obtulisse consilio certo, dehortantem a fraterna caede, v.21. tum humanius consilium adferentem, ut in fovea deserti fratres cum proicerent; quod consilium eo fine dicitur propositi esse ut servaret fratrem. v.22. His consiliis subiicitur narratio factorum. Primum quod fratres fratrem nudaverunt, v.23. & in foveam coniecerunt, v.24. secundo, quod ex tam inhumano impioque facto, ad cibum capiendum, quasi re bene gesta, extortaque vi conscientiae, transfuerunt, v.25. Tum quod occasione per mercatores exteros oblata, consilióque per Judam dato (qui inhumanum factum novo inhumanitatis exemplo videbatur sibi elucere, puta venditione fratris) eum mercatoribus vendiderunt, in longinquam regionem exteram deportandum loco mancipij: adeo se ipsi peccatis mancipauerat, v.26. & 27. Quo facto Josephin Ægyptum translatus est, prout summatim dicitur v. 28. & amplius exponitur v.ultimo huius capitis. Restat postremus locus eventorum: quorum alia sunt domestica, & alia extera. In eventis domesticis sunt hęc: primùm quòd Ruben non comperto fratre retexit lugens inhumanū consilium, & fratres obiurgavit. vers.29. & 30. Secundò, quòd fratres maleficium suum novo commento obvelantes, & summo vitæ paternæ discrimine fingentes eadem Josephi, v .32. luctum parenti attulerunt, v. 33. quem symbolis lugubribus vehementissime diutissimeque testatus est, v.24. Postremò quod isti in mendacio suo strenuè pergentes visi sunt studere consolationi paternæ, tu patris, tu avi, qui adhuc superstes erat; sed hanc consolationem fuit inefficacem, tum quia gravis erat luctus, tum quia ex hypocrisi simulatoq; animo profecta consolatio, non potuit eas vices obtinere quas vera habere solet. Eventus extraneus est, v.ultimo; quòd Josephab exteris emptoribus venditus est, & in Ægyptum deportatus, mancipium fuit Potifaris.
units.tr: The first of these plans is about killing Joseph, throwing his body into a pit, and inventing a lie to deceive the father; all of which are inhuman plans, and an impious mockery of the divine dreams, v. 20. But Reuben, the eldest brother, is said to have brought a change to this plan, partly by the force of kinship, partly from fear of their father's displeasure, which would fall more heavily upon him as the firstborn, and above all from his awareness of his own recent crime. It is therefore likely that he considered breaking up the brothers' plan and moderating it. Reuben is said, then, to have offered a reason for changing the plan, dissuading them from fraternal murder with a sure argument, v. 21, and to have proposed a more humane course, that they should cast the brother into the pit alive and leave him there; this plan is said to have been proposed for the purpose of saving him, v. 22. To these plans the narrative of deeds is joined. First, that the brothers stripped their brother, v. 23, and cast him into the pit, v. 24. Secondly, that after so inhuman and impious a deed, as if it were well done and as if their conscience had been stilled by force, they sat down to eat, v. 25. Then, when an occasion was offered by foreign merchants, and at the advice of Judah (who seemed to himself to shine out in a new example of inhumanity by the sale of his brother), they sold him to the merchants, to be carried off into a distant foreign land as a slave. So completely had they handed themselves over to sin, v. 26 and 27. By this deed Joseph was carried into Egypt, as is briefly said in v. 28 and more fully set out in the last verse of this chapter. There remains the last part, on the outcomes, some of which are domestic and some foreign. Among the domestic outcomes are these. First, that Reuben, not finding his brother, tore his clothes in grief at the inhuman plan, and rebuked the brothers, vv. 29 and 30. Secondly, that the brothers, veiling their wickedness with a new contrivance, and at grave risk to their father's life, pretended the same thing about Joseph, v. 32, and brought grief to their father, v. 33, which he attested most vehemently and most lastingly with mourning tokens, v. 34. Lastly, that these men, persisting vigorously in their lie, seemed to be eager to console their father, and also their grandfather, who was still alive; but this consolation was ineffective, both because the grief was heavy and because a consolation born of hypocrisy and feigned feeling could not hold the place that true consolation usually holds. The foreign outcome is in the last verse: that Joseph was sold by foreign buyers and carried into Egypt, where he became the slave of Potiphar.

units.la: In hac autem historia tota, res humanitus gestæ narrantur quàm simplicissimè: ut ex toto earū contextu plus habeat admirabilitatis sanctissima illa certissimaque Dei providentia, qua Joseph patri totíque familiæ ereptus, in Ægyptum abreptus, & ad divinum illud & salutare opus translatus est, quod Deus providentissimè post annos aliquot perfecit, cùm juvenis illius pietatem, patientiam, & fidem in rebus adversis, patris verò constantiam, & fratrum conscientiam tamdiu probavisset.
units.tr: In this whole history, the events of human affairs are narrated as simply as possible, so that from the entire sequence of them the most holy and most certain providence of God shines forth the more admirably: by which Joseph, snatched from his father and the whole household, carried off into Egypt, was brought to that divine and saving work which God most providentially accomplished after some years, when he had tested the piety, patience and faith of the young man in adversity, the constancy of the father, and the conscience of the brothers for so long.

units.la: CAPITIS XXXVIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 38.

units.la: HUIUS capitis fines duos opus est observari: unum communem, alterum singularem: communis, est causa Ecclesiæ, quod totum pertinet ad sequentium historiarum intelligentiam: singularis, est causa Gentis ex qua processit Christus, ut seriem & contextum certum, illius haberemus. Summa itaque est, hic aliam novam calamitatem Jacobo in Cenahanæa oblatam narrari: qua in calamitate, prout Jacobi fides & patientia fuit explorata; sic etiam in narratione illius, Ecclesiæ toti perpetuus afflictionum cursus quibus exercetur, & remedii ac sanctifificatio earum ostenditur in Christo Iesu, qui suo ipsius facto (cum his parentibus ita inquinatis & turpibus progigni voluit) aperte demonstravit se nostra causa supra quam victorem omnium infirmitatum & vitiorum esse, ut quisquis gloriatur glorietur in Domino. Commo-dè autem calamitosa hæc historia & Iacobo adversa, postremo loco exponitur, sive ad ordinem antecedentium historiarum, sive ad rationem temporum respexeris. Nam postquam Iacob reversus in Cenahaneam filiorum suorum Simeonis & Leui maleficio, filiæ stupro, uxoris obitu, incesto Rubenis concubitu, ac postremo Iosephi venditione probatus fuisse dicitur; quorum criminum alia priores natu qui Iudam ætate superabant, alia omnes attingebant: nunc demum vitium Iehudæ in hoc cap. recensetur, in quo primogenita substite-runt, quæ Ruben incestu, Simeon & Leui cædibus amiserant. Ratione vero temporum hanc historiam postremo loco huius partis locari opportuit, quia narratio huius capitis a primo anno adventus in Cenahaneam ad annum usque migrationis in Ægyptum pertinet: quemadmodum ex recensione animarum, quæ in Ægyptum migraverunt cum Iacobo, cap. 46. colligitur. Nam cum Iosephi sexennis aut quasi septennis in Cenahaneam migraverit, Iacob vero Ægyptum adiverit quo tempore Iosephi fuit fermè quadragenarius, totum hunc historiæ contextum necesse est breui curriculo annorum quasi triginta trium aut summum quatuor fuisse gestum: puta, Iehudam familiaritate cum Adullamæo inita filiam Schichæ duxisse, liberos ternos genuisse, de coniugio duobus prospexisse, tertij coniugium distulisse, Thamaram gravidasse, binósque liberos genuisse, qui cum ipso in Ægyptum discesserint. Partes autem huius capitis certæ vix dari possunt, quia totum consumitur in narratione Chroni-ca, vel secundum temporis seriem earum rerum quas ante perstrin-ximus, verùtamen evidentiæ causa tres ordine constitui possunt: quarum prima est de coniugio Iudæ, & liberorum ipsius, ad ver. usque 10. secunda de incesto concubitu eius cum Thamara, inde ad v. 23. postrema autem de rebus ex illegitimo concubitu illo consequutis, inde ad finem capitis. Ac primam partem quod attinet, tria distinctè in ea exponuntur: inde coniugium, duobus versibus; liberorum ex coniugio procreatio, inde ad v. 6. Postremò autem illorum quoque coniugatio, sequentibus. Ad coniugium Iudæ pertinent, primum occasio imprudenti oblata v. 1. Quod Iehuda imprudens abscessit a suis fratribus quibuscum pascebat, & sese dedit in Hadallamitæ consuetudinem: deinde quod visam filiam Cenahanæi deperierit, eámque uxorem duxit. Omnia vi-tiosè; & secundum licentiam quam in Mesopotamia hauserat apud Laban ē auum:nam[?] siue inscio & imprudente patre, siue inuito hæc gesta fue-rint, non potest Iuda excusari, quin grauiter contra Dei mandatum & patriam auctoritatem venerit. Nam neque à fratribus suis ipsis di-scedere (quibus ipsum pater coniunxerat) imprudete pater licuit, neque sine offensione Dei se dare in Adolamitæ consuetudinem, aut (quod grauius est) Cenahanea coniugem sibi adiungere, quasi à fœdere peculiari gentis cum Deo inito discedendo, neque impios illos amores æstumque iuuenilem nexu coniugij confirmare, qui nexus ubi est initus, non ita facile disrumpi potest; ex quo peccatum hominis antecedens hoc singulari nexu Deus obligauit. In procreatione li-berorum speciatim spectatur primum benedictio Dei, res male & iniuste coeptas sanctificantis, omniaque in bonum conuertentis suis. Deinde speciatim spectatur liberorum ordo, ad sequentis historiæ commo-dam intelligentiam pertinens. Restat coniugium quod Iuda patrio iure liberis suis procurauit, non imprudente (ut credibile est) patre, sed habenas administrationis filio (ut qui sese ex facto emancipauisset) permittente. Ac primum quidè de coniugio nihil est quod speciatim dicamus, quia de Thamara, quæ aut cuius fuerit scriptura reticet: sed in priorum liberorum coniugio utroque duo observanda sunt; illorum iniquitas exosa Domino, & iusta perditio. Ac prioris quidem iniquitatem non circumscribit Moses : posterioris vero flagitiū v.9. euidenter ostenditur, quod ultro se ipsum corrumperet, ne seme[?] ex Thramara coniuge procrearet. Fuit autem corruptio hæc (prout ex verbis Mosis possumus coniicere) quam poetæ impuri apud Latinos masturbationem vocant. Hic vero incidit quæstio, unde Juda;il-lud hauserit de filij defuncti coniuge filio alteri clocanda[?], & quo iure fecerit:nam hanc legem videtur primum tulisse Dominus in libro Deuteronomij.Resp.Quam legem Deus in libro Deuteronomij sanciuit, de uxore fratris defuncti posteriori fratri clocanda[?], ea lex tum quidem primum de scripto tradita est; sed iam ante divina quadam reuelatione apud populum Dei obtinebat: quapropter lex illa Deuteronomij non recens institutio est, sed antiquæ observationis confirmatio & obsignatio. Huius autem observationis auctor idem qui confirmator dicendus est. Causa vero instituendæ illius fuit benedictionis divinæ in familiam continuatio, secundum quam benedictionem ad primogenitos quosque prærogativæ duæ pertinebant; una sacerdotij ad cultum Domini, altera vero potentiæ ad benedictionem terrenæ pertinentis. Nam primogeniti & sacerdotes erant in familia universa, & hæredes duplicarij: quæ res etsi multis scripturæ locis confirmari potest, quia tamen infra cap. 49. ite Exodi 19.&24.& Num.3. & 4.commodior locus ad dicendum futurus est, hic ab eo labore supersedebimus. Atque hæc quidem res ceremonialis fuit, qua inde à conditu orbis dignitas Christi(qui primogenitus est inter multos fratres) fuit adumbrata: sed quemadmodum benedictionis illius ratio ceremonialis fuit, ita etiam continuatio illius: secundū quam factum est, primum vt primogenitus ex primogenito primogenita obtineret; deinde vt exstincto fine liberis primogenito, & fine vxore, secundus filius diuinitus in locum primogeniti adrogatus fuisse videretur; po-stremo vt si quis primogenitus sine liberis occideret, sed relicta vxo-re, hanc eandem vxorem sequens frater vna cum benedictione à pri-mogenito defuncto transfusa sibi assumeret. Atque hæc res alioqui non fuit licita ex lege, sed excepta solum huius benedictionis causa.
units.tr: Two limits of this chapter must be observed: one common, the other particular. The common limit concerns the cause of the Church, and it bears entirely on the understanding of the histories that follow. The particular limit concerns the cause of the people from whom Christ came, so that we may have a fixed sequence and context for it. The summary, then, is that here another new calamity is related as having befallen Jacob in Canaan. In this calamity, just as Jacob's faith and patience were tested, so in the narrative of it is shown the perpetual course of afflictions with which the whole Church is exercised, and their remedy and sanctification in Jesus Christ. By his own deed (in being willing to be born of such defiled and shameful parents) Christ clearly showed that he is for our sake the victor over all weakness and sin, so that whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord. This calamitous history, adverse to Jacob, is set out fittingly in the last place, whether you look to the order of the preceding histories or to the reckoning of the times. For after Jacob returned to Canaan, he is said to have been tested by the wickedness of his sons Simeon and Levi, by the rape of his daughter, by the death of his wife, by the incest of Reuben with a concubine, and finally by the sale of Joseph. Of these crimes, some touched the older sons who were senior to Judah, and others touched them all. Now at last the sin of Judah is recounted in this chapter, in which the rights of the firstborn remained, which Reuben had lost through incest and Simeon and Levi through murder. As for the order of time, this history had to be placed last in this part, because the narrative of this chapter extends from the first year of arrival in Canaan to the year of migration into Egypt, as is gathered from the list of the souls who migrated into Egypt with Jacob, in chapter 46. For since Joseph went into Canaan at about six or seven years old, and Jacob came to Egypt when Joseph was about forty, the whole context of this history must necessarily have been carried out in a short course of about thirty-three years, or at most four: namely, Judah, having formed a friendship with the Adullamite, took a wife, the daughter of Shua; he had three children, provided wives for two of them, deferred the marriage of the third; he was made pregnant Tamar, and begot two children, who left Egypt with him. The parts of this chapter can scarcely be fixed with certainty, because the whole is taken up with a chronicle narrative, or with the sequence of time of the matters we have just touched upon. Nevertheless, for the sake of clarity, three parts may be set out in order: the first concerns Judah's marriage and his children, down to verse 10; the second concerns his incestuous intercourse with Tamar, from there to verse 23; the last concerns the things that followed from that illegitimate intercourse, from there to the end of the chapter. As for the first part, three things are set out distinctly in it: first the marriage, in two verses; then the begetting of children from the marriage, down to verse 6; last, the marriage of those children, in what follows. To Judah's marriage belong, first, the occasion, offered inconsiderately, in verse 1: Judah, thoughtlessly, departed from his brothers with whom he was tending the flock, and gave himself up to the company of the Adullamite; then that he saw and loved the daughter of a Canaanite, and took her as his wife. All of this was done sinfully, and in keeping with the licence he had absorbed in Mesopotamia from Laban his uncle. For whether these things were done with his father unaware and inconsiderate, or against his will, Judah cannot be excused from having grievously transgressed against God's command and paternal authority. For it was not lawful for him, however thoughtlessly, to depart from his brothers, with whom his father had joined him; nor to give himself to the company of the Adullamite without offence to God; or (what is more grievous) to join himself in marriage to a Canaanite woman, as though departing from the special covenant of the people made with God; nor to confirm by the bond of marriage those impious loves and youthful ardour, a bond which, once entered, cannot easily be broken. By this singular bond God bound the sin of the man that went before. In the begetting of children, two things are chiefly to be noted: first, the blessing of God, which sanctifies things begun badly and unjustly and turns all things to good; second, specifically, the order of the children, which pertains to the proper understanding of the history that follows. There remains the marriage which Judah procured for his sons by paternal right, not with the father imprudent (as is credible), but with the father permitting the reins of management to his son, who (as one who had emancipated himself by his deed) had done so. Now, as for the marriage itself, there is nothing particular we need say, since Scripture is silent about Tamar, whether or whose she was. But in the marriages of the two older sons two things are to be observed: their iniquity, hateful to the Lord, and their just destruction. Moses does not describe the iniquity of the former, but the crime of the latter is plainly shown in verse 9: that he corrupted himself of his own accord, so that he would not beget seed from his wife Tamar. This corruption (as we may conjecture from the words of Moses) is what the impure poets among the Latins call masturbation. Here the question arises, from where Judah drew the custom of giving a dead son's wife to another son, and by what right he did so; for the Lord seems first to have laid down this law in the book of Deuteronomy. Answer: the law which God enacted in the book of Deuteronomy, that the wife of a dead brother should be given to the younger brother, was then indeed first handed down in writing; but it already prevailed among the people of God before, by some divine revelation. Therefore that law of Deuteronomy is not a new institution, but a confirmation and sealing of an ancient observance. The author of this observance is to be called the same as the one who confirmed it. The cause of its institution was the continuation of the divine blessing in the family, according to which blessing two prerogatives belonged to each firstborn: one of priesthood, for the worship of the Lord; the other of power, pertaining to the earthly blessing. For the firstborn were the priests in the whole family and double heirs. Although this matter can be confirmed by many passages of Scripture, since it will be more fittingly discussed in its proper place below, in chapter 49, and at Exodus 19 and 24, and Numbers 3 and 4, we shall here refrain from that labour. This indeed was a ceremonial matter, by which from the foundation of the world the dignity of Christ (who is the firstborn among many brethren) was foreshadowed. But just as the reason for that blessing was ceremonial, so also its continuation: according to which it came about, first, that a firstborn son should obtain the firstborn right from a firstborn; second, that when a firstborn died without children and without a wife, a second son should seem to have been adopted by divine decree into the place of the firstborn; last, that if a firstborn died without children, but leaving a wife, the following brother should take this same wife to himself, together with the blessing transferred to him from the deceased firstborn. This practice, moreover, was not otherwise lawful under the law, but was excepted solely for the cause of this blessing.

units.la: In secunda parte tria membra commodè distinguenda sunt: nam pri-mò occasiones adulterij traduntur à Mose ad v. vsque 14. deinde modus adulterij describitur, ad 19. vsque. postremo cōditionis à Thama-ra dictæ præstatio, verf. seqq. Occasionum quas enarrat Moses vna est à Iehuda, quòd coniugium cum Sela filio minimo subdole differebat, tamquam si Thamaræ facto antecedentes mariti periissent, v. 11. Altera, quòd Thamar indignum rata se viro legitimo frustratam esse, oc-casionem arripuit circumueniendi Iudam, v. 12. cū ad tondendas oues discederet, eáque occasione vsa est cùm primùm ipsi significata est, v. 13. Quapropter illa mutatis vestibus, ornatū, & locum, & tegmē quę-siuit quo scortum se esse confingeret; ornatum, quòd peplo obuelauit & obtexit vultum: locū, quòd in biuio viatores præstolata est: tegmē denique, quòd obtexit vultum: quæ notæ de meretrice leguntur, Prouerb. lib. Atque hæc v. 14, & 15. His positis occasionibus, sequitur narratio contractus ad maleficium: quo & precium promittit, & arrabone tradit Iehuda cum Thamara cōgressurus, v. 16. & seq. Vnde postremò incestus ille concubitus, de quo v. 18. Hic autem incertum est vtrum fraudem Iehudæ, an vero Thamaræ magis reprehendas: nam in vtro-que vitium fuit, & quidem grauissimū, cùm alter alterū indignissimè fefellerit contra voluntatē Dei & bonos mores, sed nimirū hoc pacto significauit Dominus, quod in principij c. dicebamus: maximas quidē & indignissimas esse iniquitates nostras; attamē earū turpitudine non solū obtegi, sed (quod amplius est) aboleri plane per sanctificatione nostrā in Christo Iesu. Quod ad pstatione rerū quas Iuda promiserat, narratio eius plana est: sed prudentia Thamarę, vel potius astū eo animaduertimus, quòd arrhabone, tamquā caues de sponsionū veritate, postulās, sibi de euētu cauit; vt Iudā facti euinceret, si forte ex eo cōce[?]ptura esset. Restat postremus locus, de euētu ex incesto illo adulterio. Euētus hic est, ꝙ[?] incestꝰ primò innotescit grauiditate Thamarę, v. 24. Secundo quod Iuda illa supplicium irrogat adulteris constitutum, ibid. v. 24. tertio quod Iuda euincit facti sui indiciis, v. 25. quarto quod Iudas agnoscit crimen suum, & de officio suo melius cogitat, v. 26. postremo quod gemelli ex eo fuerunt geniti, v. 27. & seqq. Hic autem incidunt quaestiones quaedam. Primum utrum Iuda haec verba, Educte illa ut coburatur, tanquam iudex enuntiet, aut tanquam accusator. Qui iudicis verba esse putant, sic interpretatur, Educite illa in loco supplicij ut coburatur. Qui accusatoris verba esse putant, interpretatur hoc modo: Educite illa in loco iudicij; ut quaestione habita & re coperta coburatur, me irrogate, ut accusatore, & iudicibus ex lege decernetibus. Prior interpretationem non possim admittere: cum enim ipsius interfuerit ut de crimine Thamarae cognosceretur, non potuit idem cuius interfuit & iudex & accusator esse: quin etiam si filius ipsius Schela Thamara adulteri j insimulasset, non potuisset Iuda huic iudicio praeficere: cum iuris naturalis sit, ut in necessitudinibus & propinquitatibus eiusmodi iudicia aliis permittantur. Statuimus itaque illa Iudae verba accusatoris irrogantis esse: atque in eam sententiam accipimus illa verba, v. 25. illa educebatur, puta ad iudicium, ut de crimine ipsius cognosceretur legitime: atque hac ratione factum est, ut Iuda recipiens indicia quae pro arrhabone in manus Thamarae dederat, ea commode agnouerit, & ex iis crimen suum senserit, Thamaramque purgauerit, cum se auctorem & caput huic malo fuisse animaduerteret: nam propterea dicebat Iuda, Iustior est me, quandoquidem non dedi illam uxorem Schelae filio meo. Hic vero altera quaestio incidit, utrum simpliciter verum sit illud Iudae dictum, iustiorem Thamaram esse, ac proinde, plus iniustitiae in ipso quam in illa deprehendi. Resp. Hunc sermonem a Iuda non simpliciter dici, sed potius (ut loquuntur) secundum quid, nam ut simpliciter crimina obseruemus, maius crimen si incestum sciens commiseris, quasi frau de coniugium aliquod distuleris. Deinde gravius est crimen incestus in sciente, quam in ignorate: sciuit autem Thamar & affectauit vltro. Sed respicit Iuda his verbis ad causam maleficij: hoc statues, qui prior causam dederit maleficio, cum hoc respectu iniustiore esse: sic vtrumque verum est, & iniustiorem fuisse Thamaram si genus facti respexeris, & iniustiorem Iuda, si causam & principium facti: alioquin incestum esse nouit concubitum, & ex facto demostrauit postea, cum ipsi religio fuerit amplius eam cognoscere. Quod ad gemellorum partu historia singularis est, singularem quendam instinctum ac motum comprehendes, quale supra sub fine ca. 25. audiuimus de Ribka Iacobi & Esau gestante. Na in vtraque historia pariter Deus sancti semel & ius primogenitorum contra quae natura ordo videbatur ferre demostrauit.
units.tr: In the second part three points are conveniently distinguished. First, Moses sets out the occasions of the adultery, to verse 14. Then the manner of the adultery is described, to verse 19. Last, the fulfilment of the condition mentioned by Tamar, from verse 20 onward. One of the occasions Moses relates is that Judah deceitfully put off the marriage with his youngest son Shelah, as if the earlier husbands had died because of Tamar's act (v. 11). The other is that Tamar, thinking herself cheated of a lawful husband and unworthily so, seized the opportunity to get round Judah (v. 12). When he set off to shear the sheep, she used the occasion as soon as it was reported to her (v. 13). Therefore she changed her clothes, looked for a dress and a place, and a veil with which she might pass herself off as a harlot: her dress, because she covered herself with a cloak; her place, because she waited for travellers at the crossroads; and finally her veil, because she covered her face. These are the marks by which a harlot is described in Proverbs (Prov. 7). All this is in verses 14 and 15. With the occasions set out, the narrative of the agreement to the wrongdoing follows: Judah promises a price and gives a pledge, to go in to Tamar (v. 16 and following). Hence comes that incestuous intercourse, of which verse 18 speaks. It is uncertain, however, whether you should blame Judah's deceit more, or Tamar's. For both were at fault, and indeed gravely, since each deceived the other most unworthily, against the will of God and good morals. But the Lord thereby showed, as we said at the beginning of the chapter, that our iniquities are very great and most unworthy; yet their foulness is not only covered over but, what is more, completely blotted out through our sanctification in Christ Jesus. As for the performance of what Judah had promised, the account of it is plain. But we notice Tamar's prudence, or rather her cunning, in that, asking for a pledge as if she were cautious about the truth of his promise, she made provision for herself against the outcome, so that she could prove Judah's deed if perhaps a child should be conceived from it. There remains the last point, the outcome of that incestuous adultery. The outcome is this: first, the incest becomes known through Tamar's pregnancy (v. 24); second, Judah orders the punishment laid down for adulterers against her (ibid., v. 24); third, Judah is convicted by the evidence of his own deed (v. 25); fourth, Judah acknowledges his crime and thinks more rightly about his duty (v. 26); last, twins were born from it (v. 27 and following). Here, however, certain questions arise. First, whether Judah's words, Bring her out, that she may be burned, are spoken as a judge or as an accuser. Those who think they are the words of a judge interpret them thus: Bring her out to the place of punishment, that she may be burned. Those who think they are the words of an accuser interpret them in this way: Bring her out to the place of judgement, so that, after an inquiry has been held and the matter uncovered, she may be burned, as I, the accuser, demand, and the judges decide according to the law. I cannot admit the former interpretation. For since it was in his own interest that the matter of Tamar's crime be investigated, he who had that interest could not also be both judge and accuser. Indeed, if his son Shelah had accused Tamar of adultery, Judah could not have been put in charge of that trial, since it is a principle of natural law that judgements of this kind in cases of such close kinship and relationship are left to others. We therefore decide that those words of Judah are the words of an accuser demanding punishment. And in this sense we take the words of verse 25, she was brought out, that is, to judgement, so that her crime might be lawfully examined. In this way it came about that Judah, receiving the pledges which he had given into Tamar's hands, recognised them properly, and from them perceived his own crime, and cleared Tamar, since he realised that he was the author and head of this evil. For this reason Judah said, She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah as a wife. Here, however, a second question arises: whether Judah's saying, that Tamar is more righteous, is simply true, and so that more injustice is found in himself than in her. Answer: this statement is not made by Judah simply, but rather, as they say, in a certain respect. For if we look at crimes absolutely, the greater crime is yours if you commit incest knowingly, as if you had deferred a marriage by fraud. Further, the crime of incest is graver in one who knows than in one who is ignorant, and she knew and willingly desired it. But by these words Judah looks to the cause of the wrongdoing: he who first gave the cause of the wrongdoing is, in this respect, the more unrighteous. So both are true: Tamar was more unrighteous if you look at the kind of act, and Judah more unrighteous if you look at its cause and origin. Otherwise, he knew the intercourse to be incestuous, and afterwards he showed this by his deed, since he scrupled to know her again. As for the birth of the twins, the story is singular, and you will perceive a singular impulse and movement of the kind we heard above, at the end of chapter 25, concerning Rebekah, Jacob and Esau, while she was carrying them. For in both stories God equally showed his sovereign choice and the right of the firstborn against the order which nature seemed to require.
