units.tr: CHAPTER 39 ANALYSIS.

units.la: SEQVITVR deinceps postrema pars historiae Genefeos, earumque rerum quae de Iacobo narrantur: nam vniuersam Iacobi historiam in tria summa capita distinximus: primum, rerum ante gestarum quam in Mesopotamiam proficisceretur; secundum, rerum in Mesopotamia; postremum autem in Ægypto confectarum. Hinc postremi loci initium in hoc cap. statuimus. Huius postremi loci quatuor sunt in vniuersum partes: nam primo exponuntur [illegible, ~8 letters] sive historiae quae antecesserunt profectionem Iacobi in Ægyptum, ad cap. usque 45. tum narratur profectio Iacobi familiaeque vniuersae, cap. 46. tertio res in Ægypto gestae describuntur Iacobo superstite, ad cap. 49. postremo autem quae proxime Iacobi mortem consecuta sunt, cap. ult. In [illegible, ~8 letters] rursum duae partes sunt observatu dignae, nam primo ostenditur quemadmodum Deus adhibuerit ut Ioseph innotesceret ad cap. usque 44. Deinde quem modum Ioseph adhibuerit ut paternam familiam accerseret c. 45. Innotuit autem Ioseph per varios gradus, primum quidem Ægyptiis tribus capitibus, deinde vero domesticis, fratribusque suis tribus seqq. Notus autem fuit exteris tum in carcere c. 39. & 40. tum in regno, c. 41. In carcere primum, custodi carceris, hoc cap. dein captiuis aliis, c. seq. Itaque huius cap. summa est, Iosephum indignae servituti mancipatum occasione tentatae pudicitiae in carcerem coniectum innotuisse, & gratiam iniuisse custodis, ut aliquo facto levaretur iniqua ipsius calamitas per benedictionem Dei. Finis ut providentiae & veritatis divinae admirabilitas in hoc exemplo piis omnibus sit exposita, ut ab hoc exemplo discant se providentiae & fidei divinae sine ulla haesitatione committere. Partes cap. duae sunt: nam primo occasio carceris; secundo benedictio Dei, ex qua innotuit in carcere exponitur. Occasionis duplex argumentum ordine proponitur: prius est, diuturnae fidei & probationis qua Ioseph probauit se ipsum in sua administratione: cui adiuncta fuit Dei benedictio, sex primis versibus. Posterius est sollicitati ipsius ad scelus animi per heram, v. 7. & seqq. ad v. 18. & 19. usque. Ad hanc enarrationem transitur per ἐπανάληψιν[?] v. 1. nam historiam proxime praecedente ad commoditatem Moses interiecerat. Quapropter ver. 1. finem cap. 37. repetit quodammodo, ad continuationem historiae ostendendam: postea vero Iosephi in servitute agentis duo ponuntur encomia: Administrationis coniunctæ benedictioni Dei,& firmæ in administratione fidei cùm Iosephi seruientis, tum Dei benedicentis: quæ res eo oftendun-tur, quòd Ioseph propter illam fidem & benedictionem paulatim à gradu infimo ad summum vsque per voluntatem heri eueƈtus est: qui primùm vile mancipium fuit rusticis & seruilibus operis mancipatum : inde ad ministerium domesticum vocatus est, v.2. & procedente benedictione,verf. 3. ad ministerium heri fui; tum à ministerio corporis eius ad præfecturam domus:postremò autem à præfectura domus ad vniuersalem (vt vocant) œconomiam , verf. 4. cui œconomiæ Deus domi & rure ita benedixit, verf. 5. vt omnia plane ipsius fidei herus commiserit, verf. 6. & in maxima eius gratia fuerit. Huic verò gratiæ altera accedebat; formæ, ad quam hera oculos coniecerat, verf. 6. Atque hinc proximus occasionum locus cur in carcerem coniiceretur Iofeph, nempe quòd sollicitata est per heram pudicitia illius;tum sermonibus,v.7. & duobus feqq.tum facto,verf. 10. & duobus feqq. Vnde creatum est Iofepho periculum accusationis v.13.& feqq. Nam ad vtrumque sollicitationis modum excusationem Iofeph adhibuerat; sermones herae impudicos verf. 7. modedeftiffimis sermonibus refellens,v.8.& 9. ab heri fui beneficio & fide in ipsum,à persona vxoris,& à perfonaDei peccatû aduersantis,& in quem peccat quisquis adulteratur. Facto autem impudico , quod foemina illa aggressa est , cùm sermonibus nihil videret effici,verf. 20.& neminem adefle testem, verf. 11. restitit Ioseph tum missa veste,tum fuga capta, verf. 12. Ex hac occasione accusatio oborta est, cùm à fraudulenta foemina res optima fide per Iofephum gestæ, occupantur in perfidiæ suæ prætextum , & argumentum vindictæ capiendæ impotentiffimé. Nam Iofephum accusauisse dicitur, & veste tamquam signo abusa esse, verf. 13. primùm apud domesticos, absente viro , verf. 14. & feq. deinde apud virum suum,v.16. & feq. His igitur occasionibus Iofeph mandato indignabundi Domini v.18.in carcerem coniectus est, eumque fontium , vbi captiui regis constricti arctissimè tenebantur , vt ex cap. feq. & Pfal. 105. maximè colligitur. Hanc autem afflictionem nouam Deus aliquo pacto dicitur fubleuaffe,sub finem cap.cùm in gratia custodis fuisse dicitur per singularem benedictionem Dei , v.21. cuius gratiæ hic fuit effectus,quòd custos ille; tum omnes captiuos Iofepho credidit versanti in carcere,tum verò res omnes gerendas,fiue à captiuis v.32.fiue à custode,v.23.ita gessit & procurauit Iofeph, vt fatis omnibus faceret prolixissimè.
units.tr: Next follows the last part of the history of Genesis, and of the things narrated about Jacob. For we have divided the whole history of Jacob into three main chapters: the first concerns the events before he set out for Mesopotamia; the second, the events in Mesopotamia; the last, the events carried out in Egypt. Hence we have placed the beginning of this last section in this chapter. This last section has four parts in all. First, [illegible] or the histories that preceded Jacob's journey into Egypt are set out, up to chapter 45. Then the journey of Jacob and his whole family is narrated, chapter 46. Third, the events in Egypt during Jacob's lifetime are described, up to chapter 49. Last, chapter 50 covers what followed closely after Jacob's death. Within [illegible] again there are two parts worth noting. First, it is shown how God arranged for Joseph to be made known, up to chapter 44. Then, in chapter 45, how Joseph arranged to summon his father's family. Joseph became known by various stages: first to the Egyptians, by three means, and then to his household and his brothers, by the three that follow. He was known to strangers both in prison, chapters 39 and 40, and in the kingdom, chapter 41. He became known first in prison, to the jailer in this chapter, and then to the other prisoners in the next. So the sum of this chapter is that Joseph, handed over to an unworthy servitude, was thrown into prison because of an attempt on his chastity, and that he won the favour of the jailer, so that by God's blessing his unjust misfortune might be eased by some act. The purpose is that the wonder of God's providence and truth in this example be set before all the godly, so that from this example they learn to commit themselves to divine providence and faith without any hesitation. The chapter has two parts: first the occasion of the imprisonment, and second the blessing of God, from which he became known in prison, is set out. The occasion is presented in a twofold argument, in order. The first is the long proof of faith and integrity by which Joseph proved himself in his administration, to which God's blessing was joined, in the first six verses. The second is the solicitation of his mind to crime by the mistress, verse 7 and following, down to verses 18 and 19. Moses passes to this narrative by an [epanalepsin] (verse 1), for he had inserted the preceding history for convenience. So in verse 1 he repeats the end of chapter 37 in a way, to show the continuity of the history. Then two commendations of Joseph while he was in servitude are given: his administration joined with God's blessing, and his steadfast faithfulness in administration, both of Joseph serving and of God blessing. These things are shown by this: that because of that faith and blessing Joseph was gradually raised by his master's will from the lowest rank to the highest. He was at first a worthless slave, assigned to rustic and menial labour; then he was called to domestic service, verse 2, and as the blessing advanced, verse 3, to the service of his master himself; then from personal attendance to the command of the household; and finally from the command of the household to the general (as they call it) management of all affairs, verse 4. God blessed this management at home and in the field, verse 5, so that the master entrusted to him absolutely everything he had, verse 6, and held him in the greatest favour. To this favour another was added: his beauty, on which the mistress had set her eyes, verse 6. And hence comes the next occasion why Joseph was thrown into prison: namely, that his chastity was solicited by the mistress, both by words, verse 7 and the two following, and by deed, verse 10 and the two following. From this arose the danger of accusation for Joseph, verse 13 and following. For against each kind of solicitation Joseph had made his defence: refuting the mistress's shameless words in verse 7, he answered with most serious words, verses 8 and 9, from his master's kindness and trust in him, from the person of the wife, and from the person of God, who opposes sin, and against whom every adulterer sins. But against the shameless deed, which the woman attempted when she saw nothing achieved by words, verse 10, and since no witness was present, verse 11, Joseph resisted both by leaving his cloak behind and by taking flight, verse 12. From this occasion an accusation arose, when the most honest deeds done by Joseph were seized upon by the fraudulent woman as a pretext for her treachery, and as an occasion for taking the most unrestrained revenge. For she is said to have accused Joseph, and to have misused his cloak as evidence, verse 13, first before the servants, her husband being absent, verse 14 and following, and then before her husband, verse 16 and following. By these occasions, then, Joseph, at the command of his indignant master, verse 18, was thrown into prison, the place where the king's prisoners were held most closely confined, as is chiefly gathered from the next chapter and from Psalm 105. Yet God is said in some way to have relieved this new affliction at the end of the chapter, when Joseph is said to have found favour with the jailer through God's singular blessing, verse 21. The effect of this favour was that the jailer entrusted to Joseph, while he was in prison, both all the prisoners, and all the matters to be done, whether by the prisoners, verse 22, or by the jailer himself, verse 23. Joseph so conducted and managed these things that he gave full satisfaction to all, in the most ample way.

units.la: CAPITIS XL ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER XL.

units.la: PRIMVM notitiæ in quam Iosephdeuenit gradum Moses praecedente capite demonstrauit: nempe quòd Io-seph tum in domo domini sui, tum verò apud custo-dem carceris iustitiam & fidem suam probauit reli-giosissimè. Nunc secundus notitiæ gradus in hoc cap. adiicitur: quòd Deus Iosephum non modò virum bonum esse, verùm etiam Spiritu Prophetico vel diuinationis præditum esse ostenderit: qua ratione tum antegressa criminatio falsi euicta est, tum ianua patefacta ad ampliorem illam notitiam, quę seq.cap.exponitur. Summa igitur est, Iosephum vinctum corpore, fuisse præditum spiritu liber-tatis, quo res obscuras solueret & explicaret, quia verbumDei non est vinctū, vt Paulus loquitur. Hoc demonstraturus Moses primò occa-sionem proponit, qua Deus visus est vt notum faceret Iosephū, ver-sibus quinque: deinde modū, quo gratia Dei innotuit Iosepho assiste-tis [?], ad v.vsq; 19. Postremò euentum, inde ad finem cap. In occasioni-bus sunt hæc: duos illos aulicos Pharaonē offendisse, v.1. Hunc ex offensa exacerba-tū, v.2. in eundē carcerem illos coniici curauisse, v.3. & illis curandis Iosephum à præfecto fuisse constitutum, v.4. Huic humano occasionū generi alterū subiicitur: nēpe occasio à Deo oblata ad testificandam singularē prouidentiā ipsius: vtriq; somniū diuinitus obtigisse eadē nocte, v.5. postridie mane Iosephū ex officio vin-ctos inuisente, animaduerso mœrore ex vultu ipsorū, v.6. eos de causa scisitatum [?] esse, v.7. cui illi neglectim responderint, v.8. donec à Iosepho fuerunt excitati, vt prout à Deo somniū, ita interpretatione à Deo expectarent, cuius se administrum fore Iosephpromittebat, cū diceret, None Dei sunt interpretationes? Narrate iam mihi somnia, reti-cet autē promissionis genus, tamquā si diceret, mihi futuro somniorū vestrorū à Deo interpreti. Atq; hoc pacto, sequitur narratio facti: nēpe quòd illi ordine somniū narrantes enarrationem à Iosepho acceperunt: primum quidem præfectus à cyathis, à v. 9. ad 13. dein verò præfectus coquis, à v.16. ad 19. Tātum illud obseruandū est, quòd hac quoq; occasione prudēter Iosepho vsus est, vt se suámq; causam commendaret, se quidē, rogās vt liberatus à cyathis memor esset Iosephi, benignitatemq; in eum exerceret, in duobus his rebus positam, vt recordaretur ipsius apud Pharaonē, & eum ex carcere vt curaret eximi, v.14. causam verò quia summa iniuria & mācipatuserat indignæ seruituti, & vinculis deditus, v.15. His somniis eorūq; interpretationibus euentus post triduū dicitur respondisse, si ad Iosephi verba respiciamus. Est autē euentus duplex: nā primū narratur euentus somniorum interpretationum quas Ioseph attulerat, v.20. & seqq. duobus. deinde vero alter euetus subiicitur ingrati aut certè immemoris animi; quòd ille à cyathis non est recordatus Iosephi apud Pharaonem, sed ipse oblitus est: quam culpam non obscurè agnouit idem capit. seq. cùm rem narraturus Pharaoni diceret, Peccata mea ego recordor hodie.
units.tr: In the previous chapter Moses showed the first degree of acquaintance by which Joseph became known: namely, that Joseph proved his righteousness and faithfulness most scrupulously both in his master's house and before the keeper of the prison. In this chapter a second degree of acquaintance is added: God showed that Joseph was not only a good man but was also endowed with a prophetic spirit, or the gift of interpretation. By this means the earlier charge of falsehood was refuted, and a door was opened to that fuller acquaintance which is set out in the following chapter. The sum, then, is that Joseph, though bound in body, was endowed with a spirit of freedom, by which he could solve and explain obscure things, because the Word of God is not bound, as Paul says. To demonstrate this, Moses first sets out the occasion on which God was seen to make Joseph known, in five verses; then the manner in which the grace of God became known to Joseph, as he attended them [?], down to verse 19; and finally the outcome, from there to the end of the chapter. The occasions are these: the two courtiers offended Pharaoh (v. 1); angered by the offence, he had them thrown into the same prison (v. 3), and Joseph was appointed by the keeper to look after them (v. 4). To this human kind of occasion another is added, an occasion offered by God to attest his singular providence: both men had dreams divinely given on the same night (v. 5). The next morning Joseph, in the course of his duty, visited the prisoners and noticed sadness in their faces (v. 6); he asked them the reason (v. 7), and they answered him carelessly (v. 8), until Joseph roused them, so that they should await from God the interpretation just as they had received the dream from God. Joseph promised to be the minister of this, when he said: Are not interpretations God's? Tell me the dreams now. He keeps silent about the kind of promise, as if he were saying: to me, who will interpret your dreams from God. And in this way follows the account of what happened: namely, that the two men recounted their dreams in order and received the interpretation from Joseph. First the chief cupbearer (vv. 9–13), then the chief baker (vv. 16–19). This only must be observed: on this occasion too Joseph prudently used the opportunity to commend himself and his cause. He asked the cupbearer, once freed, to remember Joseph and to show kindness to him, which consisted in two things: that he should recall him to Pharaoh and see that he was taken out of the prison (v. 14). His cause, however, was that he had been unjustly carried off and sold into an unworthy servitude, and had been given over to chains (v. 15). Following these dreams and their interpretations, the outcome is said to have corresponded after three days, if we attend to Joseph's words. The outcome is twofold: first the result of the dreams is related, as Joseph had interpreted them (v. 20 and following). Then a second outcome is added, of an ungrateful or at least forgetful mind: the cupbearer did not remember Joseph before Pharaoh, but forgot him himself. This fault the same chapter following acknowledges not obscurely, when the man, about to tell Pharaoh the matter, said: I remember my faults today.

units.la: CAPITIS XLI ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 41.

units.la: ANTE diximus maxima Dei prouidentia factum, ut Ioseph primum Ægyptiis, deinde vero domesticis suis innotesceret, eamque notitiam ipsius certis gradibus prouexisse, ut omnia prouidentiæ ipsius ferrentur accepta. Postquam itaque Iosephum in carcere & domi innotuisse ostendit Moses capit. 39. itemque duobus aulicis qui in vinculis agebant, c. 40. Nunc demum hoc cap. ostenditur quomo-do in notitiam Regis & regni totius peruenerit, atque adeo finiti-marum Gentium, quæ causa commeatus Ægyptij commoditate utebantur. Ad huius notitiæ in quam Ioseph cuectus est intelligentiam, duo distincte in hoc cap. exponuntur; primùm, ut Regi & proceribus innotuerit sermone suo, ad v. usque 39. deinde vero ut innotuerit omnibus communiter facto & administratione sua, reliquo capite. Ad priorem locum pertinent tum causa notitiæ, tum modus quo Deus usus est ut notum ipsum efficeret. Causa est, somnii duplex Pharaoni oblatum diuinitus, ad v. usque 7. & laboriosa inuestigatio Pharaonis ad consequendam somnii intelligentiam, v.8. postremò autem sermo præfecti à cyathis, qui recordatus historiæ quam fuerat expertus in carcere, Pharaoni indicauit de Iosepho, & dono interpretationis quod à Deo acceperat, prout ipse posito breui exordio in v.9. summatim narrat Pharaoni proximè præcedentis capitis historiam quatuor versibus seqq. Ex his causis inter se coniunctis modus amplioris notitiæ adipiscendæ est consequutus: nam primum Iosephum ad se Pharao adduci curat, v.14. quem (ut in transcursu dicamus) Regis administri summa diligentia & religione præparant, ut honestè regem adire posset, quia homines in luctu & squalore positi de more non comparebant in conspectu regum. Deinde Pharao somnia sua proponit, postquam Iosephum tentauisset utrum spem faceret interpretationis nec-ne. Nam tentat Pharao Iosephum utrum aliquid spondere possit in ea causa, v.15. & Ioseph nihil de se, sed omnia de gratia Dei sibi assistentis spondet magis specie voti, ut Pharaonis animum sibi adiugeret, quàm praesidente promissione: quod genus audaciae canina impudentia plurimum adhibet in magnatū congressibus. Somnia i-taque sua deinde narrat Pharao ad v. usque 24. & clausulam adhibet suis sapientibus turpe, sed Deo viuenti gloriosam: qui hac ratione te-statū faciebat neminē nouisse quæ sit mens Dei præter SpiritūDei,1. Cor.2. Itaque narrationi regis subiicitur Iosephi sermo, qui duabus partibus concluditur: enarratione, ad v. usque 32. & cosilio, inde ad v. 37. in enarratione primum summatim respondet Ioseph v.25. deinde vero minutatim partes somnij partibus interpretationis accomodas v.26. & 27. rei veritatem pro interpretatione somniorum pronunciat: ostendens primum septennii fore uberrimum, v.29. deinde alterum egentissimum, duobus seqq. Postremo autem causam adfert, cur somnium Deus iterauerit, nempe ut praedictionis huius veritatem & complementi acceleratione hoc pacto demonstraret: quemadmodum etiā in scripturis usu venit, ut repetitiones his duabus de causis adhi-beantur.Interpretationem illā sequitur consilium politicum, v.33. & seqq.Quo tria Pharaoni praecipiuntur: primum ut prospiciat de hominibus ad curationē hanc comodis, idest, tū de principe curatorum, v.38. tum de aliis curationis administris, & regionatim praefectis in Aegypto, v.39. secundo de modo triplici coaceruandi, nempe ut binas decumas Rex in horrea & apothecas iubeat comportari, quarum unę ad regem antiquo iure pertinebant, alterae commodo pretio per eum redimebantur toto septennio illo fertili, quo comeatus numo (ut ita dicamus) addicebatur. Atque hac narratione nihil tyrannicū aut iniustum praecepit Iosephū, sed viam strauit qua rex sine vlla iniuria popularium suorum praedia & facultates omnes sibi copararet, ut postea 45.cap. ostenditur. Postremo praecipit de asseruatione & usu comeatus, v.36. Hic igitur modus, quo Iosephū Deus voluit innotescere. I-taque Pharao agnoscit eum, proceresque ipsius, tum mete, v.37. tum sermone, v.38. Atque hinc sequitur alter locus, quo modo Ioseph toti regno innotuerit: nempe tū Pharaonis facto, ad v. usque 46. tū suo ipsius, reliquis. Pharaonis sunt haec: quòd Iosephi sapientia praedicat, v.39. eūmque tū domui, tū regno praeficit, duobus seq. tum signis ostendit quanti homine æstimaret, anuli, vestium, catenæ aureæ traditione, honorario curru, praeconū anteeuntiū significatione, honorifica appellatione & procuratione coniugij: ex quibus Ioseph executus in administratione sibi comissa occupauit sese quàm fidelissimè. His signis alia officia a Pharaone adiuncta sunt: quale illud est de coiugio. De hoc aute coiugio quisfpiā fortasse quæsiuerit, quo iure Ioseph cōiugem alienam à Dei sedere sibi adiunxerit. Atque hoc quidem coniugium vt simpliciter probemus, non puto laborádum esse: nam certum est illum & patrum suorum institutiones & Dei mádato iam ante cognouisse coniugiû huiusmodi non posse probari Domino, prout Apostolus priore Corinth. 7. ostendit: sed tamen multa sunt quæ leuare aliquo pacto factum Iofephi possunt: vt sunt tenera ætas qua in Ægyptum exportatus est, educatio, modus, quod conditionem à rege oblatam, eoque bene sentiente de viro Dei, & comparato ad benefaciendum populo Dei non potuit commodè recusare. Denique quid fi eodem spiritu auctore fecifle dicamus, quo spiritu somnia interpretatus erat & regi regnóque consuluerat? Hoc ego quidem malim. Nam hac ratione fit vt quæ simpliciter sancta dici non possunt, propter extraordinariam sanctificationem sancta habeantur. Sic ergo Iofeph per regem regno patefactus coepit partibus defungi quas sibi rex imperauerat verf. 47. & duobus sequentibus. Restant euenta, quorum vnum positum est in benedictione singulari Dei, quod cum liberis auxerit, & Iofeph eo argumento benedictionem diuinam imponendis nominibus prædicauerit, verf. 50. & duobus fequetibus. Alterum quòd res ita acciderunt vt Iofeph prænuntiauerat. Nam feptennium copiæ extitisse verf. 53. & alterum feptennium inopiæ fucceffiffe verf. 24. Vnde fames primum apud finitimos, deinde apud Ægyptios orta, cui prospectum est Iofephi opera ad mandatum Pharaonis v. 55. & feqq.
units.tr: Earlier we said that it was brought about by the greatest providence of God that Joseph should become known first to the Egyptians and then to his own household, and that he advanced this knowledge of himself by certain steps, so that all of it should be credited to God's providence. Having shown that Moses, in chapter 39, makes Joseph known in prison and in the house, and likewise to the two courtiers who were in chains in chapter 40, this chapter now shows how he came to the knowledge of the King and of the whole kingdom, and so of the neighbouring nations, by whose cause the Egyptians enjoyed the convenience of the grain supply. To understand this knowledge into which Joseph was brought, two things are set out distinctly in this chapter: first, how he became known to the King and the nobles through his speech, to verse 39; then, how he became known to all in common through his deed and his administration, in the rest of the chapter. To the former place belong both the cause of the knowledge and the means by which God used to make him known. The cause is the double dream divinely presented to Pharaoh, to verse 7, and Pharaoh's laborious inquiry to attain the understanding of the dream, verse 8; finally, the speech of the chief cupbearer, who, recalling what he had experienced in prison, told Pharaoh about Joseph and the gift of interpretation he had received from God. After a brief preface in verse 9, he summarily narrates to Pharaoh the history of the preceding chapter in the four verses that follow. From these causes, combined together, the means of wider knowledge followed. For first Pharaoh has Joseph brought to him, verse 14; the king's attendants prepare him with the greatest diligence and care (to mention this in passing), so that he might approach the king honourably, since men in mourning and squalor did not customarily appear before kings. Then Pharaoh sets out his dreams, after testing whether Joseph would hold out any hope of interpretation. For Pharaoh tests Joseph to see whether he can promise anything in this matter, verse 15, and Joseph promises nothing of himself but everything from the grace of God standing by him. He speaks more in the manner of a vow, so as to bind Pharaoh's mind to himself, than by a promise he could fulfil; a kind of bold impudence that is much employed in the gatherings of the great. Pharaoh then narrates his dreams to verse 24, and adds a closing remark, shameful to his wise men but glorious to the living God, by which he testified that no one knows the mind of God except the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2). Thus Joseph's speech follows the king's narrative, and it is concluded in two parts: the explanation, to verse 32, and the counsel, from there to verse 37. In the explanation, Joseph first answers briefly in verse 25, then matches the parts of the dream to the parts of the interpretation in detail, in verses 26 and 27, and pronounces the truth of the matter as the interpretation of the dreams: showing first that there will be seven years of great abundance, verse 29, and then the other, most destitute, in the two verses that follow. Lastly he gives the reason why God repeated the dream, namely, to demonstrate in this way the truth of the prediction and the speed of its fulfilment; just as also in the Scriptures it happens that repetitions are employed for these two reasons. The interpretation is followed by political counsel, verse 33 and following. In it three things are enjoined on Pharaoh: first, that he provide men suited to this care, both a chief overseer, verse 38, and other ministers of the care, and prefects by region in Egypt, verse 39; second, concerning a threefold way of gathering the store, namely that the King order two tithes to be carried into granaries and storehouses, of which one belonged to the king by ancient right, while the other was bought by him at a fair price throughout those seven fertile years, during which the grain was, so to speak, assigned to the coinage. In this account he commands nothing tyrannical or unjust, but paves the way by which the king could acquire for himself, without any injury to his subjects, all their estates and goods, as is shown afterwards in chapter 47. Third, he gives instructions about the keeping and use of the grain, verse 36. This, then, is the manner by which God willed Joseph to become known. Thus Pharaoh acknowledges him, and his nobles, both by his deed, verse 37, and by his word, verse 38. From this follows the second place, the manner in which Joseph became known to the whole kingdom: first by Pharaoh's act, to verse 46, and then by Joseph's own, in the rest. Pharaoh's acts are these: he proclaims Joseph's wisdom, verse 39, and sets him over both house and kingdom in the two verses that follow; then he shows by signs how highly he valued the man: the handing over of a ring, clothing and a gold chain, an honorary chariot, the announcement of the heralds going before him, an honourable title, and the arrangement of a marriage. In these honours Joseph, in the administration committed to him, busied himself as faithfully as possible. Other offices were added by Pharaoh to these signs, such as the matter of the marriage. About this marriage someone might perhaps ask by what right Joseph joined to himself a wife alien from the seat of God. Now, to prove this marriage simply lawful, I do not think we need to labour: for it is certain that he had already known, from the instruction of his fathers and from God's command, that a marriage of this kind could not be approved by the Lord, as the Apostle shows in 1 Cor. 7. Yet there are many things which can somehow lighten Joseph's act: such as the tender age at which he was carried into Egypt, his upbringing, and the fact that he could not conveniently refuse the condition offered by the king, who thought well of the man of God and was disposed to do good to God's people. Finally, why should we not say that he acted under the same Spirit by whom he had interpreted the dreams and counselled the king and kingdom? For my part I would prefer this view. For in this way things which cannot simply be called holy are held holy because of an extraordinary sanctification. So Joseph, made known to the kingdom by the king, began to discharge the duties which the king had laid upon him, verse 47 and the two following. There remain the events, one of which lies in the singular blessing of God, who increased him with children; and by this argument Joseph proclaimed the divine blessing in the names he gave them, verse 50 and the two following. The other is that things turned out just as Joseph had foretold: seven years of plenty came to pass, verse 53, and the other seven years of want followed, verse 54. Whence famine first arose among the neighbouring peoples and then among the Egyptians, for which provision was made through Joseph's work at Pharaoh's command, verse 55 and following.

units.tr: CHAPTER 42 ANALYSIS.

units.la: DIximus in capite 39. duplicem historiam de notitia Iofephi à Mose ordine narrari; vnam qua exteris innotuerit, putà Ægyptiis: alteră, qua suis, fiue domesticis. Priorem locum, nempe quo modo Iofeph in notitiam exterorum venerit, exposuit Moses tribus capitibus; nunc ad posteriorem locum transimus, quomodo suis innotuerit Iofeph; quam historiam Moses quatuor capitibus pertexit. Sunt autem huius loci partes duæ. Vna est historia aduentus prioris filiorum Iacobi in Ægyptum, hoc capite; altera posterioris aduentus fiue reuersionis, tribus sequentibus. Cùm autem Iofeph natus fuerit xxx. annos, cùm primus è septem annis saturitatis effet, fup. 41. 46. credibile est hanc historiam priorem anno demum trigefimooctauo fuisse gestam, posteriore vero fequentiû capitum anno trigefimonono. In hac autem historia duæ summatim partes obseruandæ sunt. Nam primò narratur aduentus filiorum Iacobi, & res cum illis gestæ in Ægypto, ad v. vsque 25. Deinde verò reditus illorum domum, ad finem capitis. In historia aduentus illorum in Ægyptum, primò ratio itineris, quatuor versibus: deinde rerum gestarum exponitur, a versu 6. ad 25. vsque. Ad rationem itineris pertinent ista; causa consilij de profectione suscipienda, nempe commeatus ex Ægypto apportandi, & summa illius consilium fuit nihil cunctandum esse, vers. 1. sed tempestiuè proficiscendum in Ægyptum, vt saluti familiarum consulatur, versu 2. In ratione itineris duo exponuntur; qui fecerint iter, nempe decem filij Iacobi, vers. tertio. excepto Beniamine per voluntatem patris apud ipsum commorante, vers. quarto. Deinde quibuscum, nempe cum aliis promiscuè accurrentibus in Ægyptum commeatus exportandi causa, vers. quinto. Rerum quæ illis in Ægypto obuenerunt Iosephi opera, si salutationem prætereamus, vers. sexto. loci tres summatim constituendi sunt. Primus locus est examinis duri, ad v. vsque 14. Secundus locus est probationis triduanæ in carcere, ad v. vsque 18. Postremus, dimissionis, ad v. vsque 26. Examinis occasio exponitur vers. 7. & sequente; quòd Iosephi illos agnouerit: hunc illi minimè. Atque hac fiducia Iosephi, omnes occasiones & commoditates occupauit, vt tum animos ipsorum, tum constitutionem paternæ familiæ totam cognosceret: quare alienum sese finxit, & pactionibus, & sermonibus suis, & duriter cum illis loquutus est: quemadmodum sapiens in Prouerbiis dicit verissime, diuitem cum paupere loqui duriter. Tota autem duritia in sermonibus examinis fuit, primùm in specie, quòd tamquam ignotus ignotos compellaret, rogans unde, quinam, & quorsum venirent: sed duritiei successit postea reipsa, cum Iosephi recordatus somniorum quibus Deus hanc historiam præfigurauerat, v. nono. coegit fratres suos vt se modis omnibus coram ipso abiicerent. Nam primò exploratores appellauit, ver. 9. Deinde verò negantibus, & tum causam aduentus sui, vers. decimonono: tum fidem suam à vitæ genere & instituto, affirmantibus, vers. 11. amplius vrsit, eiusdem criminis eos insimulans, vers. duodecimo. Et postremò amplius se purgantes vers. decimotertio. tamquam si ex sermonibus ipsorum mendacia euinceret, grauiùs instititit, vers. decimoquarto. Instititit autem grauiùs, cùm durum illum probationis modo imperauit, puta carcere omnibus, v. 15. iubens vt vnus solum reuerteretur domum, fratre minorem adducturus, v. 16. eòsque in custodia relinquens biduum, v. 17. Hic autem quæstiones duæ incidunt; vna de dissimulatione Iosephi: altera, de iuramento siue affirmatione qua vtitur, dicens.
units.tr: We said in chapter 39 that Moses narrates a twofold history of how Joseph became known: one by which he became known to outsiders, such as the Egyptians, and another by which he became known to his own people, that is, his household. Moses set out the first part, how Joseph came to the knowledge of outsiders, in three chapters. Now we turn to the second part, how Joseph became known to his own, which Moses continues over four chapters. This part has two sections. The first is the history of the first arrival of Jacob's sons in Egypt, in this chapter. The second is the history of their later arrival, or return, in the three following chapters. Since Joseph was thirty years old when the first of the seven years of plenty began (above, 41:46), it is credible that the first of these histories took place in the thirty-eighth year of his life, and the later one in the thirty-ninth year. In this history two main parts should be noted. First, the arrival of Jacob's sons and what happened to them in Egypt is narrated, to verse 25. Then comes their return home, to the end of the chapter. In the history of their arrival in Egypt, first the reason for the journey is given, in four verses, and then the events are set out, from verse 6 to verse 25. The reason for the journey involves the following: the purpose for undertaking it, namely to bring back food from Egypt, and the sum of the plan was that they should not delay but set out in good time for Egypt, so that the safety of their families would be provided for (verse 2). Two things are set out concerning the journey: who made it, namely the ten sons of Jacob (verse 3), with the exception of Benjamin, who remained with his father by his wish (verse 4); and then with whom they travelled, namely with others who ran together to Egypt to carry off food (verse 5). Of the things that befell them in Egypt through Joseph's work, leaving aside the greeting (verse 6), three places must be briefly distinguished. The first is the hard examination, to verse 14. The second is the three-day test in prison, to verse 18. The last is the dismissal, to verse 26. The occasion of the examination is set out in verse 7 and the following: Joseph recognised them, but they did not recognise him. Relying on this, Joseph seized every opportunity and advantage, so that he might learn both their dispositions and the whole state of his father's household. Therefore he made himself appear a stranger, and spoke to them harshly, both in his dealings and in his words, just as the wise man in Proverbs very truly says, that the rich man speaks harshly to the poor. The whole harshness of the examination lay first in appearance, in that, as a stranger, he addressed strangers, asking whence they came, who they were, and where they were going. But the harshness was afterwards followed in fact, when Joseph, recalling the dreams by which God had foreshadowed this history (verse 9), compelled his brothers to cast themselves down before him in every way. For first he called them spies (verse 9). Then, when they denied it and asserted both the reason for their coming (verse 19) and their honesty from their way of life and manner (verse 11), he pressed them further, accusing them of the same crime (verse 12). And finally, when they defended themselves more fully (verse 13), as if he would refute their lies from their own words, he insisted more severely (verse 14). He insisted more severely when he imposed the harsh form of testing, namely that they all be put in prison (verse 15), ordering that only one should return home to bring the younger brother (verse 16), and leaving the others in custody for three days (verse 17). Here two questions arise: one concerning Joseph's dissimulation, and the other concerning the oath or affirmation he uses, saying:

units.la: Vt viuit Pharao.De dissimulatione quæruntur duo; cur vsus fit, &, an iuste vsus fit. Cur vsus fit, scriptura indicat: nam primùm visum est Iofepho, explorare veritatem & coplementum somniorum, quæ diuinitus ante ipsi obuenerat; deinde visum est eadé ratione explorare fratrü animos: postremò, tota familię paternæ ratione immutatam ex sermonibus eorü cognoscere. Grauior questio est, an iuste vsus fit. De hac ita paucis statuimus. Dissimulatio res media est, siue indifferens, modò bonis & certis rationibus bona, modò mala aliis. Vtrumq; duobus modis dignoscitur, nimirû modo dissimulationis, & fine. Nam si modus & finis bonus est, per se nō potest dici mala dissimulatio; cōtrà si malus sit, nō potest dici bona: modus autem dissimulationis duplex est: nā aut dissimulatur falsum aut verū. Verū cū dissimulatur, tolerabilius est vulgò, quā si falsū dicitur, sed tamen in vtroque obferuādū illud est: primùm vtrum ferió dicitur, an non ferió: deinde si non ferió, vtrum ioco, an alia specie: si serió adhibetur dissimulatio, videndum vtrum dissimuletur verū, aut simuletur falsum in præiudicium, (vt loquuntur) id est, in fraudem veritatis ipsius aut personarū. Nam si alterutrum fit sine damno veritatis aut personæ illius, nō potest ea dissimulatio damnari. Verbi gratia, Deus dissimulat multa cōsilia sua hominibus; & cùm retegit, parte dicit, parte apud se cōtinet clausam.
units.tr: As Pharaoh lives. Two questions are raised about the dissimulation: why he used it, and whether he used it justly. Why he used it, Scripture indicates. For first it seemed good to Joseph to test the truth and fulfilment of the dreams which had come to him from God beforehand; then it seemed good, by the same method, to test his brothers' minds; and lastly, to learn from their words how the whole state of his father's household had changed. The graver question is whether he used it justly. On this we set out briefly the following. Dissimulation is a thing indifferent, or neutral: it may be good through good and certain reasons, and bad through other reasons. Its character is determined in two ways, namely by the manner of the dissimulation and by its end. For if both the manner and the end are good, dissimulation cannot in itself be called bad; on the contrary, if they are bad, it cannot be called good. Now the manner of dissimulation is twofold: for either what is false or what is true is dissimulated. When what is true is dissimulated, it is generally more tolerable than when what is false is spoken; yet in either case this must be observed: first, whether it is said in earnest or not in earnest; then, if not in earnest, whether it is said in jest or in some other form; if dissimulation is employed in earnest, we must consider whether the truth is dissimulated, or falsehood is feigned, to the prejudice (as they say) of the truth or of persons, that is, to the defrauding of the truth itself or of the persons. For if either happens without harm to that truth or that person, such dissimulation cannot be condemned. For example, God dissimulates many of his counsels to men, and when he reveals them, he tells part and keeps part hidden within himself.

units.la: Dissimulat bono nostro, quod alioquin plenè dicturus esset. Eadémque ratione parentes liberis, & alij similiter dissimulant, quæ opus est dissimulari, non malo, sed bono eorum quibuscum agitur; atque hæc quidem dissimulatio & simulatio iuris & libertatis est, qua pro suo iure & Deus & parentes & alij vtuntur in causis cōsimilibus. Sed quia sæpe accidit vt res per se liberæ tamen extra libertatem nostram positę sint, propterea veniendum est in causis veri & falsi ad leges illas duas, nequid in fraudem veritatis aut charitatis fiat; in causis verò iusti & iniusti, nequid in fraudem iustitiæ, vel vocationis eorum qui has artes occupandas putant: ídque tribus modis, sermone, opere, aut specie. Nunc exempla adferamus. Gen. 19. dissimulatio & simulatio non falsa, sed honesta atque ciuilis est, cùm angeli comparent humana specie, recusant commoditatem à loco sibi oblato, & se pernoctaturos facile in platea prædicat. Alterum exemplum est o 1. Reg. 18. & 22. vbi Elias Propheta pseudoprophetas Baalicos subsannat multis, & Micha similiter regi respondet ironicè: quorum exemplorū primum feriùm est exemplum ciuilis modestiæ; posteriora duo non feriū sermonem, sed sarcasmum acerbissimum continent, nulla fraude veritatis, & nulla charitatis; quia populi præsentis intererat vt virtutem Dei præsentissimā certissimámque Prophetæ fiducia agnosceret. Ex
units.tr: He dissimulates for our good what he would otherwise have declared fully. By the same reasoning parents dissimulate towards their children, and others likewise dissimulate things which need to be dissimulated, not for harm but for the good of those with whom they deal. This dissimulation and simulation is an exercise of right and of liberty, which God, parents, and others use by their own right in similar cases. But because it often happens that things which are free in themselves nevertheless lie outside our liberty, therefore in matters of true and false we must have recourse to those two laws, that nothing be done to the defrauding of truth or charity; and in matters of just and unjust, that nothing be done to the defrauding of justice, or of the calling of those who think they ought to take up these arts. This happens in three ways: by speech, by deed, or by appearance. Now let us bring forward examples. In Genesis 19, the dissimulation and simulation is not false but honest and civil, when the angels appear in human form, refuse the lodging offered to them in the place, and say they will readily spend the night in the street. Another example is in 1 Kings 18 and 22, where the prophet Elijah mocks the false prophets of Baal with many taunts, and Micaiah likewise answers the king ironically. Of these examples, the first is not a serious speech but an example of civil modesty; the latter two contain not serious speech but the most bitter sarcasm, with no fraud to the truth and no lack of charity, since it was the concern of the people present that they should recognise, by the prophet's confident trust, the most present and most certain power of God. From

units.la: Nouò Testamento exempla similiter afferemus tria. Primũ est ciuilis modestiæ atque prudentiæ, qua Christus erga suos agnatos vtebatur, Ioh. 7. Nã illis vrgentibus vt abiret Hierosolyma, & sese daret in coronam populi, respondit Christus, suum tempus non a duenisse; ipsi eant sanè, se autem non ire ad festum. &c. Nam hæc negatio, quæ simplex videtur esse, tamen secundum quid dicitur, & implexam habet dissimulationem, simulationemque per illud tempus ex causa necessaria. Reliqua duo exempla sunt Pauli: quæ à multis in controuersiam liberius vocatur, cùm tamen à Spiritu Dei testimonium habere videantur. Vnum est Act. 21. cùm vno codémque facto Paulus suam conditionem dissimulat, & se voti Nazireatus tenerì simulat. Hanc simulationem sanctam esse, nec vllo pacto damnari à piis oportere duobus argumentis demonstramus. Vnum est, quòd certo consilio Apostolorum qui aderant, & Ecclesiæ Dei res illa gesta est: alterum est, quòd si vllum ea in re peccatū extitisset, plurimū causæ Paulus habuisset agnoscendi & desendi peccatum suū in singulis suis defensionibus; sed de ea re verbū nullum. Obiicitur votū Nazireatus cæremoniale fuisse; cæremoniarū corpus fuisse in Christo: Ergo cæremonia post complementū à Christo exhibitū non fuisse obseruanda: Paulū itaq; à religione aberrasse: Resp. Nō omnes cæremonias fuisse typos Christi, & corpus veritatémq; suá in Christo habuisse; sed cæremonias imperatas lege & ad eū sinem prouidentia diuina imperatas. Nazireatus verò non est eiusmodi: nã, neq; cæremonia est impe rata, sed votiua & voluntaria; neq; ad præfigurandū Christum aut beneficia eius, sed tantū ad domituram carnis, & exercitatione piâ qua se fideles exercebāt: ac proinde Paulus votū Nazireatus simulans, neq; in Christū comisit quidquā, neq; inEcclesiā eius. Quod siquis adferat exēpla Nazireorū quos imperabat Deus; solutio facilisest, exēpla hæc Nazireorū singularia esse & extraordinaria: quæ autē singularia, perso nalia, & extraordinaria sunt, ea trahi in exemplū nequeunt. Nazireatus autē quem Paulus professus est, fuit secundum viam ordinariam, quā Moses præscripserat Num. 6. Addatur exemplū Act. 23. cùm Paulus prudentissimè cōmittit inter se Pharisæos & Saducæos, dicens se accusatum esse propter spē resurrectionis ex mortuis: verū dicit, sed multū veri dissimulat, & facit sine fraude veritatis. Nam vt in eo côsessu Paulus multū de charitate erga istos homines côiuratos in Christum cogitaret, tamquam ad pietatē reuocaturus ipsos, nō fuit locus. Ex his igitur exemplis cõficimus, simulationē & dissimulationē, modò citra fraudē veritatis & charitatis, itēmq; iustitię & vocationis adhibeatur, in homine Christiano minimè damnandam esse: maximè si obseruatio illa accesserit, vt videant pij, quotiescumq; de dissimulatione cogitant, apud quos adhibeant ipsam. Nā alia est simulationis ratio apud ignorantes, quàm apud scientes: alia apud infirmos, quàm apud firmos; alia apud amicos, quàm inimicos: alia apud simplices quàm apud malitiosos: alia apud eos de quorū salute spes est, alia apud desperatos. De fine, qui secūdus locus est in dissimulatione obseruandus, plura non dicemus, quia res per se est euidens. Secundus locus desumitur ab interpretibus: quorum hi reprehendunt, illi defendūt factū, quod Ioseph toties vitā Pharaonis nominauerit. Qui reprehendunt, iuramentum esse putant, ac proinde culpandum duobus nominibus: primùm quia temerarium, ac non necessarium; secundò quia obliquum. Nam cūm iuramentum sit religiosa affirmatio, religio autem ad Deum proprie spectet, non aliud iuramentum quàm Dei inuocatione adhibita probari oportere. Qui defendunt, negant iuramentum esse, sed tantùm affirmationem. Iuramentum autem eo differre ab affirmatione, quòd iuramentum affirmatio religiosa est: hîc autem nihil religiosi à Iosepho adhiberi. Mihi via quædam inter vtrumque placet: nam neque religiosam affirmationem à Iosepho putem adhibitam, qui fuit religiosissimus; neque affirmationem illius plane vacare aliqua religione. Nam quod Iosepho non erat religiosum, cùm vitam Pharaonis appellaret, illud religiosum apud Ægyptios habebatur: ergo non religiose affirmabat Ioseph, sed apud Ægyptios visus fuisset affirmare: specie tamen, cum religiose non affirmaret, affirmare religiose fratribus videbatur. Sic iudicio meo Ioseph à religione minimè discessit, sed nō satis sibi temperauit à specie mali, cùm fratres ita compellaret sui magis dissimulandi animo. Probationem, siue examen à Iosepho factum sermonibus, sequitur locus alter, de tentamento, quo Ioseph fratres suos probauit opere. Nam primùm carcerem imperauit illis ad triduum v.17. deinde quasi mitigatus nouo consilio tentauit illos, quod v. 18. & duobus seqq. exponitur. Causa illius consilij, verf.18. ostenditur his verbis, Deum ipsum ego timeo: tamquam si diceret, se Dei metu religioso distineri, ne quam vim aut iniuriā faciat exteris: deinde verò nouam rationem imperat, qua in specie quidem probaret illos, sed re & veritate alterum fratrem suum ad se adduci procuraret. Itaque huius tentamenti partes duæ sunt: vna vt vnus de numero fratrum quasi pignoris loco detineatur, dum alij domum reuersuri sunt, v.19. Altera, vt liberaturi fratrem suum adducant alterum illum minimum, v.20. Huius consilij exsequutio v.24. exponitur, sed antequam ad eam veniatur, Moses duo adfert testimonia scientiæ, homines siue de facto eorum, siue de naturali iure appellan-tis. Conscientia fratres Iosephi appellauit de facto ipsorum, cuius se agnoscunt reos, cum fratrem suum Iosephum deprecantem audiuissent, & tam duriter deprecationes eius depulissent: quam impietate & inhumanitatem nunc vlcisfcatur Deus, v. 21. & Ruben frater natu maximus hoc argento increpationem subiicit, verf.22. Conscietiam vero Iosephi ius naturæ excitauisse dicitur, v.23. & seq. cùm Iosephi & sermonibus illorum inter se conquerentium libere (quia non putarunt se ab ipso intelligi) & vi necessitudinis eò adductus est, vt secedes loco in fletum erumperet, v.24. ita subiicitur demum exequutio antecedentis consilij Simone vinco, & dimissis cæteris. Quàm liberaliter autem dimissi sint, narratur v.25. Sequitur locus de profectione, v.26. qua in profectione factū narratur, vt fratrum vnus promens pabulum, pecuniâ suam in ore manticæ inuenerit, v.27. unde omnes corripuit primò consternatio, ac postremò vbi recollegissent animos, admiratio tamquam diuini beneficij, v.28. Restat postremus locus de aduentu ipsorum domum & reditus, consequentibus. Ac primùm quidem aduentus ad patrem narratur, v.29. deinde narrantur facta & cuenta ipsorum. Factorum duo sunt genera: nam primò res in Ægypto gestas narrant, duritiem Iosephi, v. 30. defensionem suam, v.31. & seq. mandatum illius de vinciendo vno fratre, & minimo adducendo, v.33. & 34. deinde verò saccorum & onerum suorum deoneratio exponitur v.35. Atque hinc locus euentorum incidit: quòd primùm pecuniam suam singuli quasi receptam habuerunt: unde metus peruasit omnes, & parentem ipsorum: deinde quòd Iacob in illos inuexit acerbissimè, tamquam si ab ipsis proderetur, v. 36. tum quòd Ruben fide iubet, & filios suos dedit noxæ, nisi fidem præstiterit, v.34. Postremò quòd Iacob constanter denegat, donec ingrauescete fame (vt versu postremo dicitur) ad consensionem inuitus compulsus est. Hæc autem exempla sunt omnia humani studij & infirmitatis, in quam subinde prolabimur, donec in prouidentia Dei discamus conquiescere.
units.tr: We shall also give three examples from the New Testament. The first is of civil moderation and prudence, which Christ showed toward his kinsmen, John 7. When they urged him to go up to Jerusalem and present himself to the crowd, Christ replied that his time had not yet come; they should go on ahead, but he would not go up to the feast, etc. For although this refusal seems plain, it is nevertheless spoken in a qualified sense, and it contains a complex dissimulation and pretence for that time, from a necessary cause. The other two examples are from Paul, and many dispute them more freely, although they seem to have the testimony of the Spirit of God. One is Acts 21, where, by one and the same act, Paul conceals his own position and pretends to be bound by a Nazirite vow. We demonstrate by two arguments that this pretence was holy and that the pious ought by no means to condemn it. The first is that the thing was done by the settled counsel of the apostles who were present and of the Church of God. The second is that if any sin had existed in that matter, Paul would have had the strongest reason to acknowledge and defend his sin in each of his defences; but there is no word about that matter. It is objected that the Nazirite vow was ceremonial, that the body of the ceremonies was in Christ; therefore ceremonies were not to be observed after the fulfilment exhibited by Christ; so Paul had strayed from the religion. Answer: not all ceremonies were types of Christ, having their body and truth in Christ, but only those ceremonies commanded by the Law and commanded by divine providence for that end. The Nazirite vow, however, is not of that kind: for it is not a commanded ceremony but a votive and voluntary one, and it was not for prefiguring Christ or his benefits, but only for subduing the flesh and for the pious exercise by which the faithful trained themselves. Accordingly Paul, in pretending the Nazirite vow, committed nothing against Christ or against his Church. If anyone should bring forward the examples of Nazirites whom God commanded, the solution is easy: these examples of Nazirites were singular and extraordinary; and what is singular, personal and extraordinary cannot be drawn into an example. Moreover, the Nazirite vow which Paul professed was according to the ordinary way which Moses prescribed, Num. 6. Let the example of Acts 23 be added, where Paul very prudently sets the Pharisees and Sadducees against each other, saying that he was accused because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead: this is true, but he conceals much of the truth, and he does so without any fraud against the truth. For in that assembly there was no room for Paul to dwell at length on love toward those men who were sworn against Christ, as if he were about to call them back to piety. From these examples, therefore, we conclude that dissimulation and pretence, provided they are used without fraud against truth and charity, and likewise against justice and vocation, are by no means to be condemned in a Christian man, especially if that caution is added, so that the pious, whenever they think of dissimulation, may see before whom they employ it. For the manner of pretending is one thing before the ignorant, another before the knowing; one thing before the weak, another before the strong; one thing before friends, another before enemies; one thing before the simple, another before the malicious; one thing before those for whose salvation there is hope, another before the desperate. As to the end, which is the second point to be observed in dissimulation, we shall not say more, because the matter is evident in itself. The second example is drawn from the interpreters, some of whom blame and others defend the deed, namely that Joseph so often named the life of Pharaoh. Those who blame it think it is an oath, and therefore to be condemned on two counts: first because it is rash and unnecessary; second because it is indirect. For since an oath is a religious affirmation, and religion properly looks to God, an oath must be proved to be nothing other than one made with the invocation of God. Those who defend it deny that it is an oath but only an affirmation. An oath, moreover, differs from an affirmation in that an oath is a religious affirmation; but here nothing religious was employed by Joseph. To me a certain middle way between the two pleases: for I would not think that Joseph, who was most religious, employed a religious affirmation, nor that his affirmation was altogether void of any religion. For what was not religious to Joseph when he called it the life of Pharaoh was regarded as religious among the Egyptians; therefore Joseph was not affirming religiously, but he would have seemed to the Egyptians to be affirming; yet, although he was not affirming religiously, in appearance he seemed to his brothers to be affirming religiously. Thus in my judgment Joseph did not depart at all from religion, but he did not sufficiently restrain himself from the appearance of evil, since with that purpose of dissembling he thus addressed his brothers. The examination, or test, which Joseph made by words is followed by another point, concerning the trial by which Joseph proved his brothers by deed. For first he ordered them to be put in prison for three days, v. 17; then, as if softened, he tried them by a new plan, which is set out in v. 18 and the two following verses. The cause of that plan is shown in v. 18 by these words, "I fear God himself": as if he said that he is restrained by the religious fear of God from doing any violence or wrong to strangers; then he gives a new order, by which in appearance indeed he would test them, but in reality and truth he would bring about that another of his brothers should be brought to him. So there are two parts to this trial: one, that one of the number of the brothers should be kept as a kind of pledge while the others were to return home, v. 19; the other, that they should bring the other, the youngest, to set free their brother, v. 20. The carrying out of this plan is set out in v. 24, but before we come to it, Moses brings forward two testimonies of conscience, from men who speak either about their own deed or about natural right. The conscience of Joseph's brothers spoke about their own deed, of which they acknowledge themselves guilty, since they had heard their brother Joseph pleading and had so harshly rejected his entreaties; the impiety and inhumanity for which God now takes vengeance, v. 21. And Reuben, the eldest brother, adds this rebuke, v. 22. The conscience of Joseph, however, is said to have stirred up the law of nature, v. 23 and following, when, from their words in which they freely complained among themselves (because they did not think they were understood by him), and by the force of kinship, he was led to withdraw from the place and burst into tears, v. 24. Finally, the carrying out of the preceding plan is subjoined: Simeon is bound, and the others dismissed. How generously they were dismissed is related in v. 25. There follows the place about the departure, v. 26, in which departure an event is related: one of the brothers, opening his sack to give fodder, found his money in the mouth of the sack, v. 27; whence at first consternation seized them all, and at last, when they had gathered their spirits, admiration as at a divine benefit, v. 28. There remains the final point, about their arrival at home and their return, with what follows. First, indeed, their arrival at their father is related, v. 29; then their deeds and accounts are narrated. There are two kinds of deeds: for first they relate the things done in Egypt, Joseph's harshness, v. 30, their own defence, v. 31 and following, his command about binding one brother and bringing the youngest, vv. 33 and 34; then the unloading of their sacks and burdens is set out, v. 35. Hence the point about events arises: first, that each of them found his money as if it had been received back, whence fear seized them all and their father; then that Jacob railed at them most bitterly, as if they had betrayed him, v. 36; then that Reuben pledges his faith and gives his sons as a forfeit, unless he should keep faith, v. 37 (the Latin says 34); finally, that Jacob firmly refuses until, as the last verse says, the famine grew severe, and he was compelled against his will to consent. Now all these examples are of human zeal and weakness, into which we slip again and again, until we learn to rest in the providence of God.

units.la: CAPITIS XLIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 43 ANALYSIS.

units.la: [?]Riorf aduentu fratres à Iosepho fuisse cognitos, nō autē Iosephū ab illis cap. præcedente docebat Moses. Nūc sequitur historia aduentus posterioris, tribus capitibus; in qua historia hic ordo tenedus est, vt primū res gestas ante Iosephū agnitum obseruemus, c.43. & seq. deinde verò, quæ post iudiciū Iosephi sequuta sint, cū alij alios cognoscerent, cap. 45. Rerum antecedentium loci sunt duo: nam primum exponit Moses quid hoc aduentu sit gestum cap. 43. deinde quid proxime successerit, cum ex instituto discessu reuocati sunt, cap.44. Prioris loci membra sunt tria: primum est de consilio habito, & rebus ad discessum in Ægyptum comparatis, ad verf. vsque 13. secundum est de modo quo noui aduenæ à praefecto domus Iosephi excepti sunt, mandato illius, ad verf. vsque 24. postremum, quo modo Ioseph illos exceperit, ad finem vsque cap. In primo loco narrantur consilium habitum, atque profectio. In habendo consilio ordine narrantur ista; propositio Iacobi Patris de petenda Ægypto ad commeatum, versu primo. Responsio Iudæ ad propositionem Patris de conditione à praeposito Ægypti imperata, versu secundo. Quam conditionem in omnem euentum ostendit Iuda seruari oportere dilemmaticè, verf.3. & 4. Huic responsioni subiicitur Patris mœrentis obiurgatio, verf.5. De qua purgant se omnes ab humana inscientia, v.6. deinde Iuda consilium de conditione oblata repetit, adducens primum vtilitatem, v.7. deinde fidem suam, qua se obstringit patri, v. 8. postremò damnosum cunctationis euentum obiicit, v. 9. His occasionibus pater deliberat & consilium claudit, v.10. & seqq. ex communicatione consiliorum sequitur deliberatio, v. 10. cuius partes duæ sunt: propositio deliberationis, tribus versibus, & precatio, v.13. deliberationis membra sunt tria: nam primum de honorario ad Iosephum mittendo statuitur, v.10. tum de pecunia dupla, v.11. postremò de Biniamine, v. 12. Hæc autem sancta precatione gratiæ & pacis concluduntur, v.13. etsi Iacob tamquam de euentu diffidens, vel potius iudicio meo tamquam se ad lugubrem euentū comparās, omnia claudit tristi prædicatione calamitatis suæ, si ita Deo videbitur; quemadmodum ab Estera quoque factum est, quum aleę iudicij humani, sed tamen duce prouidentia Dei, salutem suam exponere videretur. Hinc sequitur profectio in Ægyptum, verf. 14. vbi cùm se Iosepho stitissent omnes, mandatur praefecto vt deducantur domum, & prandium comparetur, verf.15. Secundùm hoc Iosephi mandatum praefectus illos dicitur excepisse, verf. 16. sed aliquid interuenisse quod excipiendi modum imperatum paulisper retardauerit. Itaque duo narrantur: primùm quomodo morati sint, & purgationem sui instituerint Iosephi fratres, antequam ingrederentur domum, ad v.vsque 22. dein quomodo excepti sint, v.23. & seq. cunctationis causa fuit metus; metus verò causa, occasio oblata; nempe quòd deducerentur Iosephi domum, vbi vinciri Simeonem fratrem viderant; vnde primùm inter ipsos formidolosę querimoniæ, v. 17. deinde verò purgatio apud praefectum: quem adeuntes v. 18. docent de eo quòd priore aduentu pecuniam numerauissent, v. 19. Redeuntes in tes in suis manticis refusam inuenissent,v.20. quapropter se & illam & alteram attulisse v.21. Hanc purgationem præsectus accipiens eos tum metu liberat,tum prosequitur humanitatis officiis,sermone confirmando, & Dei prouidentiam prædicando,& satis sibi factū agnoscendo,Simeonémque liberū adducendo,v.22.tum ipsos & iumenta ipsorum excipiendo, vt Joseph mandauerat, v. 23. qua commoditavsi sunt, vt munera per singulos in aduentum Josephi pararent exhibenda,v. 24. Restat locus tertius, quomodo Joseph exceperit primùm munera, v.25. deinde personas, tum humanitate sermonis, tum vero officiis. Humanitatem sermonis ostendit Joseph rogando de valetudine primùm ipsorum,secundò patris, ver. 26. cui respondent, ver.27. Postremò Beniaminis,cui bene precatur Joseph,vers. 24.Humanitas verò facti fuit vna latens,altera euidens: latens, quòd animus Josephi ita commotus est vt latebras ad flendum quæsiuerit, victus sanguinis necessitudine,v.29.cuidens,quòd eos exceperit con uiuio humanissimo, prout mandatur v.30. In excipiendo autem fuit humanitas partim communis in omnes,partímque singularis in Biniaminem fratrem.Communis, quòd secum seruato decoro eos iussit accumbere;nō cū Ægyptiis,quibus Hebræi erant abominationi, non propter gentem proprie, sed propter institutum vitæ, quòd pastores essent:vt postea in hoc ipso libro & in Exodo ( si Deus volet ) videbimus, testis Berofus apud Josephum libro 1.contra Apionem Alexandrinum.
units.tr: Moses taught in the previous chapter that the brothers were recognised by Joseph at their first coming, but that Joseph was not recognised by them. Now follows the account of the second coming, which takes three chapters. In this account the order to be observed is this: first we note what was done before Joseph was recognised (chapter 43 and following), and then what followed Joseph's judgement, when they recognised one another in turn (chapter 45). The events before recognition fall into two parts. First Moses describes what was done on this coming (chapter 43), and then what happened next, when the brothers were called back after their planned departure (chapter 44). The first part has three members. The first, up to verse 13, concerns the deliberation held and the preparations made for the journey to Egypt. The second, up to verse 24, tells how the new arrivals were received by the steward of Joseph's house, on Joseph's orders. The last, from there to the end of the chapter, tells how Joseph himself received them. In the first part, the deliberation and departure are narrated. In the deliberation, the following is related: the proposal of their father Jacob that they should go back to Egypt for food, in verse 1; the answer of Judah to his father's proposal about the condition laid down by the governor of Egypt, in verse 2; and Judah's argument, in the form of a dilemma, that this condition must be kept in every outcome, in verses 3 and 4. To this answer is added the grieving father's rebuke, in verse 5. All of them clear themselves of human ignorance in this matter, in verse 6. Then Judah repeats his advice about the condition offered, first setting out its usefulness, in verse 7, then his own pledge, by which he binds himself to his father, in verse 8, and finally the harmful consequence of delay, in verse 9. Prompted by these considerations, the father deliberates and closes the counsel, in verse 10 and following. From the sharing of counsel follows the deliberation itself, in verses 10 to 13, which has two parts: the proposal of the plan, in three verses, and a prayer, in verse 13. The members of the plan are three. First it is decided what gift is to be sent to Joseph, in verse 10; then concerning the double money, in verse 11; and last concerning Benjamin, in verse 12. These matters are concluded with a holy prayer for grace and peace, in verse 13. Jacob, distrusting the outcome, or rather, in my judgement, preparing himself for a sorrowful end, closes everything with a sad declaration of his calamity, saying "if it shall so seem good to God." Esther likewise did the same, when she seemed to expose her life to the chances of human judgement, yet under the guidance of God's providence. Next follows the journey into Egypt, in verse 14. When all had presented themselves before Joseph, the steward is ordered to take them home and prepare a meal, in verse 15. In accordance with this command of Joseph, the steward is said to have received them, in verse 16, but something intervened which for a while delayed the carrying out of the order for their reception. Two things are therefore narrated: first how Joseph's brothers delayed and undertook to clear themselves before they entered the house, up to verse 22; then how they were received, in verse 23 and following. The cause of the delay was fear, and the cause of fear was the opportunity offered, namely that they were being taken to Joseph's house, where they had seen their brother Simeon kept in chains. Hence there first arose among themselves anxious complaints, in verse 17, and then their self-justification before the steward, whom they approached, in verse 18, and told him about the money they had paid on their first visit, in verse 19. On returning, they had found the money put back in their sacks, in verse 20, and so they had brought both that money and the other, in verse 21. The steward accepted this justification, and relieved their fear, and treated them with kindness, confirming his words, proclaiming God's providence, acknowledging that satisfaction had been made to him, and bringing Simeon out free, in verse 22. Then he received them and their animals, as Joseph had commanded, in verse 23. Having been given this favour, they were enabled to prepare the gifts to be presented, man by man, at Joseph's arrival, in verse 24. The third place remains: how Joseph received, first, the gifts, in verse 25, and then the men themselves, with kindness of speech and with acts of service. Joseph showed kindness of speech by asking first about their health, and second about their father's, in verse 26, to which they reply, in verse 27. Last, he asks about Benjamin, and blesses him, in verse 29. Joseph's kindness in action was of two kinds, one hidden and one plain. The hidden kindness was that Joseph was so moved that he sought a hiding place in which to weep, overcome by the bond of blood, in verse 29. The plain kindness was that he received them with a most generous feast, as he had ordered, in verse 30. In receiving them, his kindness was partly shared by all and partly special to his brother Benjamin. It was shared, in that he ordered them to recline together, keeping due order, not with the Egyptians, to whom the Hebrews were an abomination; not on account of the nation itself, but on account of their manner of life, because they were shepherds. We shall see this later in this same book and in Exodus, God willing. Berosus, cited by Josephus in the first book against Apion the Alexandrian, bears witness to this.

units.la: Tum communis fuit humanitas quòd omnes assidere iussit, sed seruato ordine quem Joseph nominatim imperabat: & illi admirati sunt,v.33. postremò quòd ferculis de suo missu fratres honorabat. Singularis verò fuit humanitas, quòd Beniaminem præ cæteris,vt germanum fratrem affecit honoribus. Quod autem bibisse & inebriati fuisse dicuntur,vt vulgus interpretum exposuit,id commodè opus est intelligi. Sic enim scriptura designare solet liberale & lautum conuiuium, non autem abusum ad ebrietatem: quia familiaria conuiuia, non vino sed aqua instructa erant ; festiuis autem & lautis vinum accedebat: propterea conuiuia lauta hac descriptione Hebræis designantur.
units.tr: The kindness was shared also in that he ordered them all to sit down, yet in the order which Joseph appointed by name; and they were amazed, in verse 33. Last, it was shared in that he honoured the brothers by sending them dishes from his own table. The kindness special to Benjamin was that he favoured him above the rest with honours, as a full brother. As for the statement that they drank and became drunk, as the common run of interpreters have explained it, this must be understood in a fitting way. For Scripture is accustomed to designate in this manner a generous and sumptuous feast, not drunkenness as an abuse; because ordinary meals were served with water rather than wine, whereas wine was added at festive and lavish occasions. For this reason the Hebrews use this description to denote splendid banquets.

units.la: CAPITIS XLIIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 44.

units.la: HVius capitis, quo res traduntur proximè gestæ antequam Joseph fratribus innotesceret,partes omnino tres sunt. Nā primò occasio reuocādorum fratrum exponitur à Josepho instituta, versibus 5. dein reuocatio ipsa, ad v.vsque 17.ac
units.tr: The parts of this chapter, which narrates the events immediately before Joseph made himself known to his brothers, are altogether three. First, the occasion for recalling the brothers, arranged by Joseph, is set out in verses 1 to 5. Next comes the recall itself, to verse 17. Last comes Judah's entreaty, from there to the end of the chapter.

units.la: postremò Iudæ deprecatio, inde ad finem capitis. Ad occasionem reuocationis, quam certo consilio quæsiuit Ioseph, pertinent mandatum ipsius, vers.1. & 2. præfecti obsequium, fratrumque disccessus, v. 3. Tum mandatum de reuocandis illis specie criminationis de obiecto furto, vers.4. & 5. Hic vero duo in Iosepho reprehenduntur vulgò:vnum, quòd fratres ita perculerit, & nimium furti insimulauerit. Sed aliud est re, aliud specie accusare; aliud bono consilio, aliud malo: aliud apud eos quorum res non agitur, aliud vero apud eos ipsos qui insimulantur facti. Nam si apud ipsos egeris, de facto cognoscitur ho neste; si apud alios, res quasi facta inhoneste traducitur: quamobrem prius illud factum Iosephi mihi quidem non potest improbari. Alterum quod reprehenditur, Act.vers.5. quod Ioseph vulgò creditur fratribus suis indicauisse diuinationes hasce ex poculo illo exercitas. sed re bene excussa videtur hæc accusatio ex vocis homonymia profluxisse: nam diuinatio si proprie accipiatur, prædictio est non ex causis naturalibus proficiscens, sed ex diuina communicatione: verumtamen per abusionem, diuinatio pro eo quod est quasi diuina quædam siue coniiciendi, siue probandi ratio nō raro accipitur. Verbum autem Hebræum mediam habet significationem, abs qua etiam serpentes propter astutiam quandam naturale suam appellantur Nechaschim. Atque hac ratione non potest damnari prudens ratio quæ tentandis, probandis, & cognoscendis hominibus adhiberi potest: alioquin cum in malam partem accipitur, videtur proprie & singulariter ex hydromantia vel Chiromantia deductum esse; cuius rei exemplum est in historia Nebucadnezaris, apud Ezech.ca.22. Ad reuersionem fratrum pertinet, primò factum præfecti, secundò illorum. In facto præfecti sunt ista: quòd assequutus est illos, v.6. & quòd illos modeste sese excusantes sermone quidem perculit, sed euicit peruerstigatione. Itaque sermones vltro citroque habentur ad vers. vsque 10. Deinde peruerstigatio facta dicitur, vers.11. & 12. Excusant autem se Iosephi fratres, primò modesta negatione, deinde animi sui affirmatione, ver. 7. Tertiò confirmatione, tum ab exemplo anteacto, vers.8. tum deditione noxæ, vers.9. quam voluntariam deditionem præfectus honeste mitigat, ver.10. Ita sequitur peruerstigatio duobus seqq. Re peruerstigata narratur reuersi o lacerantium vestes, sarcinas suas reportantium, & ad Iosephum redeuntium, v.14. Hinc sequitur increpatio à Iosepho, v.15. & fratrum deditio in noxam voluntariam, vt ante, v. 16. Sed quam Ioseph repudiat, v.17. Ita demum transitur ad locū tertium, id est deprecationem Iudæ: cuius deprecationis partes sunt hæ: exordium, v.18. narratio inde ad v.vsque 30. & deprecationis loci, inde ad dead finem vsque. In exordio & narratione plana sunt omnia. In deprecatione loci sunt tres: à persona patris, cui vita adimitur adempto filio, v.30. secundus à persona piorum omnium, quod ipsi futuri sint rei paternæ mortis, v.31. Tertius à persona Iudæ, quòd ipse fidem apud patrē interposuisset[?], v.32. Quapropter ex hac deprecatione assurgit conclusio, vt sistatur ipse & detineatur minimi fratris loco, ver.33. cui subiicitur pathetica confirmatio in v. vltimo, cuius πάθος[?] procul-dubio plurimum Iosephum affecit habentem rationem patris & fratrum omnium, vt cap.seq. exponitur.
units.tr: To the occasion of the recall, which Joseph sought by a deliberate plan, belong his command and the steward's compliance in verses 1 and 2, and the brothers' departure in verse 3. Then comes the command to recall them, under the pretext of the charge of the stolen cup, in verses 4 and 5. Here two things in Joseph are usually found fault with. The first is that he so alarmed his brothers and accused them too severely of theft. But it is one thing to accuse in appearance and another in fact; one thing to do so with a good purpose and another with a bad; one thing before those whose affair it is not, and another before the very men who are accused. For if you deal with them directly, the deed is known to be honest; if before others, the matter is presented as though it had been done dishonestly. Therefore that first act of Joseph's cannot, for my part, be condemned. The second thing blamed is in verse 5: that Joseph is commonly believed to have told his brothers that he practised divination with that cup. But when the matter is carefully examined, this accusation seems to have arisen from an ambiguity of the word. For if divination is taken properly, it is a prediction arising not from natural causes but from divine communication. Yet by an extended use, "divination" often means a kind of wise method of conjecturing or testing, as if it were a sort of divine art. The Hebrew word, moreover, has a neutral sense, from which serpents too are named Nechaschim for a certain cunning. In this way the prudent method which can be used for testing, proving and discerning men cannot be condemned. Otherwise, when the word is taken in a bad sense, it seems to have been derived specifically and exclusively from hydromancy or chiromancy. An example of this is in the story of Nebuchadnezzar, in Ezekiel chapter 22. To the return of the brothers belong, first, the steward's action and, second, theirs. In the steward's action are these: that he overtook them, verse 6; and that, when they excused themselves modestly, he struck them with his words but overcame them by searching. So speeches pass back and forth as far as verse 10. Then the searching is said to have been done, verses 11 and 12. The brothers excuse themselves first by a modest denial, then by affirming their own innocence, verse 7; third, by a confirmation, first from an example of the past, verse 8, and then by surrendering the guilty party, verse 9. The steward gently softens this voluntary surrender, verse 10. So the searching follows in the two verses after. When the search is over, the return is narrated: they tear their clothes, carry back their baggage, and come to Joseph, verse 14. Hence follows the rebuke from Joseph, verse 15, and the brothers' voluntary surrender to punishment, as before, verse 16. But Joseph rejects this, verse 17. So at last the narrative passes to the third part, that is, Judah's entreaty. The parts of this entreaty are these: the exordium, verse 18; the narration from there to verse 30; and then the parts of the entreaty, from there to the end. In the exordium and the narration everything is plain. In the entreaty there are three parts. The first is from the person of the father, to whom life is taken away once his son is taken, verse 30. The second is from the person of all the godly, who will be party to their father's death, verse 31. The third is from the person of Judah, who had given his pledge to the father, verse 32. From this entreaty therefore arises the conclusion, that he himself be kept and detained in place of the youngest brother, verse 33. To this is added a pathetic confirmation in the last verse, whose emotion without doubt moved Joseph very greatly, since he had regard for his father and all his brothers, as is explained in the following chapter.
