units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER 45.

units.la: Hactenus præparatio tribus capitibus, quam Ioseph præ-misit antequam suis fratribus innotesceret: hoc autem capite duo summatim ad terminandum hunc locum posita sunt: vnum, de notitia inter fratres conciliata, ad v. vsque 15. alterum de consilio deuehendæ totius familiæ Iacobi in Ægyptum: quod consilium est μεταβατικὸν[?] ad postremum locum huius historiæ. Quòd ad notitiam conciliatam inter fratres attinet, primum occasio ponitur vers.1. Deinde modus, sequentibus. Occasio fuit, quòd Ioseph non potuit amplius sibi vim facere ad dissimulationem institutam. Modus in his rebus positus est: primò quòd semotis omnibus testibus, v.1. tanta vehementia exclamauit Ioseph præ animi commotione, vt circumstantes etiá longinqui audiuerint, ver.2. deinde quòd fratribus suis gradatim sese patefecerit, cùm res à Iosepho affirmata omnem fidem superare illis videretur; quapropter primò se Iosephum esse prædicat, & rogat de patre, ver.3. Deinde rei nouitate consternatis, mandat vt se accedant & recognoscat propius, nomen suum affirmans, & historiam narrans venditionis suæ, v.4. Quia vero hanc historiam forte per modum exprobationis adduci putauissent, elegante epitherapeia vtitur: quum monet primùm neque molestia, neque tædio illos propterea affici oportere; nam in illa venditionis historia duo à se coniunctim obseruari, factum imprudens fratrum & Dei prouidentissimum, quam prouidentiam sigillatim explicat, v.6. & 7. Proinde concludit se in hoc facto non ad fratrum suorum culpa, sed ad Dei gratia quæ ipsum euexit respicere, verf.8. Quapropter e illis auctorem esse vt patri consilium suum significent: nempe vt cum eo diuinitus sit coniunctus, ver.9. se patri auctorem esse vt in Ægyptum veniat, cōmodè tum habitaturus verf.10. tum victurus, verf.11. Hac [illegible, ~6 letters] positâ, ad institutum sermone Ioseph reuertitur v.12. appellans oculos. ipsorum,testes quorum fiducia patre confirmaturi sint,v.13. Quarto osculis & amplexibus fraternis tum Beniaminis, v.14. tum reliquo-rum fratrum,v.15.confirmat.Secundus locus de consilio quodIoseph ante perstrinxera[?]t,duas partes habet.Nam primo consilium in Ægypto datum proponitur: deinde consilium captum in Cenahanea, ad finem vsque cap.In Ægypto dandi consilij occasio fuit, quod sermo percrebruisset apud Ægyptios & regem ipsum, v.16. Vnde sequuta est Pharaonis sententia ad Iosephum, qua consulit & mandat primo vt illis commeatus subministretur ad discessum,v.17. secundo vt pater adducatur, familiaque tota, cum amplissimis promissionibus a rege,v.18. tertio, vt auctoritate regis commoda omnia subministrentur[?] ad familias exportandas v.19. Quarum rerum fiduciam promis-sione gratiosissima a Rege,& a se omnium filialium fraternorumque officiorum confirmat dicens, oculus vester, &c. pro eo quod est,non esse cur solliciti sint de suppellectile: nam regis auctoritate regifi-ce ipsis prospectum iri. & his subiiciuntur quaedam signa ad confirmationem Patris pertinentia, cum plaustra & commeatus ad iter, v.21. & vestes fratribus, v.22. ac postremo munera amplissima patri transmissa sunt: quas res omnes auctario consilij sui pernecessario locupletauit Ioseph, cum fratribus suis Ioseph interdixit ne commo-uerentur inter se in via: cuius commotionis femina non obscura ani-maduerterat,cum fratres captiuos detenturus esset,sup.c.43.His rebus positis, sequitur narratio consilij in Cenahanæa facta, cuius consilij causæ antecedentes hæ fuerunt,aduentus filiorum Iacobi,narratio de vita & auctoritate Ioseph, Iacobi fidem superan[?], animumque assi-ciens vchementissime, verf.66. tum sermones Iosephi, & commoda transmissa ad deportatione familiarum,verf.27.Quibus rebus singu-lis obseruatis concludit Iacob se in Ægyptum migraturum esse,v.vlt.
units.tr: Thus far the preparation in three chapters, which Joseph sent before he made himself known to his brothers. In this chapter, however, two things are set down briefly to bring this section to a close: first, the recognition brought about between the brothers, to verse 15; second, the plan for bringing the whole family of Jacob into Egypt, which plan is the transition to the final section of this history. As to the recognition brought about between the brothers, first the occasion is given in verse 1, and then the manner, in what follows. The occasion was that Joseph could no longer force himself to keep up the pretence he had begun. The manner in these matters is this: first, that with all witnesses removed, verse 1, Joseph cried out with such vehemence, from the stirring of his feelings, that even those standing around, and those at a distance, heard him, verse 2; then that he revealed himself to his brothers gradually, since the matter, affirmed by Joseph, seemed to them to exceed all belief. So first he declares that he is Joseph, and asks about his father, verse 3. Then, with them dismayed by the novelty of the thing, he bids them come near and recognise him more closely, affirming his name and relating the story of his sale, verse 4. But because they might have supposed that this story was brought up by way of reproach, he uses an elegant epitherapeia: he first warns them that they ought not to be vexed or wearied on that account; for in that story of the sale two things were observed by him together, the thoughtless act of the brothers and the most provident purpose of God, which providence he explains point by point, verses 6 and 7. Therefore he concludes that in this matter he looks not to the guilt of his brothers but to the grace of God, which raised him up, verse 8. Accordingly he is the one who advises them to tell their father his plan, namely that he is joined with him by divine appointment, verse 9; he himself is the one who advises his father to come into Egypt, where he will dwell conveniently, verse 10, and live, verse 11. With this said, Joseph returns to his purpose in speech, verse 12, calling their eyes to witness, whose trust they would use to confirm their father, verse 13. Fourthly, he confirms it with fraternal kisses and embraces, first of Benjamin, verse 14, then of the rest of the brothers, verse 15. The second section, on the plan which Joseph had earlier outlined, has two parts. First, the plan made in Egypt is set forth; then the plan adopted in Canaan, to the end of the chapter. The occasion for the plan in Egypt was that the matter had spread abroad among the Egyptians and the king himself, verse 16. From this followed Pharaoh's decision, sent to Joseph, by which he advises and commands first that provisions for the journey be supplied to them for their departure, verse 17; second, that the father be brought, with the whole household, with the most generous promises from the king, verse 18; third, that by the king's authority all conveniences be supplied for carrying the households out, verse 19. Joseph confirms their trust in these matters with a most gracious promise from the king, and with his own assurance of all filial and fraternal duties, saying, "Your eye," etc., meaning that they need not be anxious about their goods, since by the king's authority provision would be made for them in a royal manner. And to these are added certain signs pertaining to the confirmation of the father: wagons and provisions for the journey, verse 21, and garments for the brothers, verse 22; and finally the most generous gifts were sent to the father. Joseph enriched all these things, as a most necessary addition to his plan, when he forbade his brothers to quarrel among themselves on the way; for he had noticed a not obscure sign of such quarrelling, when he was about to keep the brothers captive, as in chapter 43 above. With these things set down follows the narration of the plan made in Canaan. The preceding causes of this plan were these: the arrival of the sons of Jacob; the account of Joseph's life and authority, which overcame Jacob's belief and affected his spirit most vehemently, verse 26; then Joseph's words, and the gifts sent for the transport of the households, verse 27. Observing each of these things, Jacob concludes that he will migrate into Egypt, last verse.

units.la: CAPITIS XLVI ANALYSIS.
units.tr: ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER XLVI.

units.la: HISTORIAM Iacobi (quam vltimam esse hoc libro di-ximus) in tres summas partes ante distribuimus: qua-rum prima est de profectione in Mesopotamia & rebus in ea gestis: altera,de reuersione in Cenahanæa variis-que casibus qui Iacobo & familiæ illic obuenerunt.Restat deinceps vltimus locus ad finem vsque libri, de profectione ipsius & commoratione in Ægypto. Huius itaque partis duo membra vni-uersè constituimus: quorum prius est de profectione in Ægyptum, hoc cap. posterius de commoratione & iis rebus quæ in Ægypto acciderunt, quatuor seqq. Huius ergo capitis, quo narratur profectio, partes sunt tres à Mose commodissimè distinctę. Nam primùm narratur ipsa profectio Iacob familiæque ex Cenahanea discedentis, septem versibus, deinde recensentur distinctè tum qui in Ægyptum cum Iacobo profecti sunt, tum omnes posteri qui cum ipso versati sunt in Ægypto, ad v. vsque 27. Tertia pars est de aduentu ipsius & consiliis ad commorationem pertinentibus, à v.28. ad finem cap. vsque. In profectione autem duo membra commodè distingui necesse est: vnum religionis, alterum facti. Religionem Iacobi in suscipienda hac expeditione demonstrat Moses versibus quatuor: nam primùm ille Deo inconsulto noluisse dicitur ex Cenahanea excedere v.1. dein de verò illi Dominus respondisse, versibus sequentibus. In religioso Iacobi facto duæ circumstantiæ sunt obseruandæ: vna, quòd in eum locum venit dominum consulturus, vbi frequentibus signis præsentiam suam fuerat testificatus: altera, quòd sacrificia obtulit Deo in Bearschebah, id est, non sui fiducia, sed eius quem sacrificia figurabat, accessit Dominum. Huic ergo respondisse dicitur Deus versibus seqq. ad responsum præparatio est secundo versu. Responsi verò argumentum v.3. & 4. Hoc autem responso tria continentur: primùm loco exordij confirmat Deus Iacobum de præsentia sua: secundò, probatur instituta in Ægyptum profectio; postremò autem mandato huic promissiones annectuntur. Harum promissionum loci duo sunt, communis & singularis, in communi loco promissionum duo sunt distin guenda. Nam primùm promissio hæredum in numerum maximum à Deo fit, v.3. deinde promissio ductus diuini petentibus Ægyptum & reuertentibus ad possessionem promissæ terræ, v.4. Singularis promissionum locus est, cùm Deus Iacobo futurum spondet vt Iosephū[?] videat, & Ioseph occludat oculos morienti: quòd religiosum fuit apud veteres, & honoris causa obseruatum. Sequitur profectio tum personarum, v.5. tum rerum, v.6. postea autem per ἐπανάληψιν[?] reditur ad historiam de personis, in fine v.6. & v.7. vt fit commoda transitio ad secundam partem capitis. In recensione personarum, qui est secundus locus, primùm capita familiarum summatim proponuntur, v.8. deinde familiæ ipsæ ex capitum ordine recensentur secundùm vxores ex quibus fuerant editę: postremò autem singulæ recensiones capitum in certum numerum referuntur: tum distinctum, puta, posteri Iacobi ex Lea xxxii. Et comprehenso Iacobo xxxiii. Posteri ex Zilpa xvi. ex Rachela xiv. ex Bilha vii. qui numerus non comprehenso Iacobo præcisè efficit lxix. aut coprehenso Iacobo lxx. ex his assurgit summa duplex, v.26. & 27. nam primù v.6. numeratur qui cū Iacobo descenderunt in Ægyptū LXVI. nam ex hoc numero excludūtur Iacob, Iosephus, & duo filij illius. Deinde uero v.27. comprehēsō Iacobo, Iosepho, & filiis, omissa ratione uxorū quas filij Iacobi circūducebāt dicūtur LXX.v.26. Hic uero obiicitur locus Act.7. ubi Stephanus dicit descendisse Iacobum in Ægyptum & familiam eius cum ipso, animarum LXXV. Huic autem supputationi cū illa optime conuenit, si quis hoc statuerit: primum numero illo LXXV. Iacobū minimè comprehendi, quia ante fuit nominatus tamquam familiæ princeps: ad illos autem LXIX. reliquos, sex à Stephano adiungi nominatim ad familiam Iacobi pertinentes, quorum nomina hoc loco expressa sunt. Nempe uxores quatuor, & duos illos Iehudæ filios, Her & Onan, qui in Cenahanea ante decesserant (c. 38.) Rem ita se habere vidit Epiphanius in Panario, qui illa Stephani verba, [?]τῷ ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε[?] suppleuit addens [?]συγγενεσι μυριλω συγκεκιμένων[?], familiam conscriptam à Mose, aut constitutam ex animabus LXXV. Non enim respexit Stephanus ad numerum eorum capitum quæ in Ægyptum descenderunt, sed eorum potius quæ suis nominibus à Mose in hunc locum referuntur. Sunt autem omnino LXXV. non comprehenso Iacobo; aut (si comprehēditur) LXXVI. Hunc autem numerum adhibuit Stephanus ut Iudæos euinceret quàm bene teneret legem, quam illi impudenter affirmabat à Stephano oppugnari. Restat postremus locus de aduetu in Ægyptū. In hoc aduentu duplex historia ordine proponitur: una, quòd Iacob Iehudā præmiserit, ut de statione prospiceretur seni antequam ingrederetur Ægyptum, v.28. Altera, Iosephum obuiam uenisse patri, eoque salutato v.29. & gratulatione ultro citróque facta, v.30. Iosephum consilio suo legitimè Patri familiæq; toti prospexisse, postquam cum illis (ut par erat) communicauisset. Communicationis autem partes duæ sunt, priore ostendit Iosephus quid sibi facto sit opus, ut consciō & consentiente Rege illis non solum habitatio in Ægypto permittatur, v.31. uerum etiam pro ratione & conditione ipsorum detur habitatio commoda, v.32. Alter communicationis locus est de officio fratrum, ut accedentes Pharaonem, v.33. & rogati de sua conditione aperte ostendant se pecuariam semper fecisse. Nam hoc pacto fore ut commodam habitationem impetrent, duabus de causis: una, quòd regionem pascuam habituri sint, eò quòd pastores essent, proinde ab Ægyptiis habitationem seorsim habituri, propter antiquam illam Ægyptiorum superstitionem, qui à pastoritia uita pastoribusque plurimum abhorrebant, ut ex Iosepho lib. 1. contra Apionem Alexandrin. & ex Diodoro Siculo libro 1. Bibliothecæ constat.
units.tr: We have said that the history of Jacob, which is the last in this book, falls into three main parts. The first concerns his departure into Mesopotamia and what happened there. The second concerns his return to Canaan and the various misfortunes that befell Jacob and his family there. There remains the last section, from here to the end of the book, concerning his own departure and his sojourn in Egypt. We divide this part into two members as a whole. The first is his departure into Egypt, which is this chapter. The second, in the following four chapters, is his stay and the things that happened in Egypt. The parts of this chapter, which narrates the departure, are three, and Moses distinguishes them very conveniently. First, the departure itself of Jacob and his family from Canaan is narrated in seven verses. Then those who went down into Egypt with Jacob are listed separately, as are all the descendants who lived with him in Egypt, down to verse 27. The third part concerns his arrival and the plans that pertain to his settlement, from verse 28 to the end of the chapter. In the departure, two members must be distinguished conveniently: one of religion, the other of action. Moses shows Jacob's religious conduct in undertaking this journey in four verses. First he says that Jacob, without consulting God, was unwilling to leave Canaan (v. 1). Then, in the following verses, the Lord answers him. In Jacob's religious act two circumstances are to be noted. One is that he came to the place to consult the Lord, where the Lord had attested his presence by frequent signs. The other is that he offered sacrifices to God at Beersheba, that is, he approached the Lord not in reliance on himself but on him whom the sacrifices foreshadowed. God is said to have answered him in the following verses, and the preparation for the answer is in the second verse. The content of the answer is in verses 3 and 4. This answer contains three things. First, by way of introduction, God assures Jacob of his presence. Second, the journey into Egypt is approved. Last, promises are attached to this command. There are two places of these promises, the general and the particular. In the general place of promises two things are to be distinguished. First, God promises that his heirs will become a very great number (v. 3). Then comes the promise of divine guidance to those who go to Egypt and return to the possession of the promised land (v. 4). The particular place of promises is where God pledges to Jacob that he will see Joseph, and that Joseph will close his eyes as he dies. This was a religious custom among the ancients and was observed as a mark of honour. Then follow the departure of the persons (v. 5) and of the goods (v. 6). Afterwards, by epanalepsis [ἐπανάληψις], he returns to the history of the persons, at the end of verse 6 and in verse 7, so that there is a fitting transition to the second part of the chapter. In the listing of the persons, which is the second place, first the heads of the families are briefly set out (v. 8). Then the families themselves are listed in the order of their heads, according to the wives from whom they were born. Last, the individual lists of the heads are brought to a definite number. Thus, the descendants of Jacob by Leah are thirty-two, and with Jacob included thirty-three; the descendants by Zilpah sixteen; by Rachel fourteen; by Bilhah seven. This number, without Jacob included, comes exactly to sixty-nine, and with Jacob included to seventy. From these figures arises a twofold sum (vv. 26 and 27). For first, in verse 26, it is counted that those who went down into Egypt with Jacob were sixty-six, since Jacob, Joseph and his two sons are excluded from this number. Then, in verse 27, with Jacob, Joseph and the sons included, and the wives whom the sons of Jacob led about omitted from the reckoning, they are said to be seventy (v. 26). Here, however, the passage of Acts 7 is objected, where Stephen says that Jacob went down into Egypt with his family, seventy-five souls [ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε]. This sum agrees very well with that reckoning if one holds the following: first, that Jacob is by no means included in the number seventy-five, since he was named earlier as the head of the family; and second, that to the remaining sixty-nine Stephen adds by name six persons belonging to Jacob's family, whose names are expressed in this place. These are, namely, four wives, and the two sons of Judah, Er and Onan, who had died earlier in Canaan (ch. 38). Epiphanius, in the Panarion, saw that this was the case. He supplied the words of Stephen, [ἐν ψυχαῖς ἑβδομήκοντα πέντε], adding [συγγενέσι ... συγκεκιμένων] in kinship ... composed, and so the family, as written down by Moses, or constituted of seventy-five souls. For Stephen did not look to the number of those who went down into Egypt, but rather to those whom Moses names in this place by their own names. In all there are seventy-five, without Jacob included; or, if he is included, seventy-six. Stephen used this number in order to convince the Jews how well they kept the law, which they shamelessly claimed was being attacked by Stephen. The last place is the arrival in Egypt. In this arrival a twofold history is set out in order. One is that Jacob sent Judah ahead, so that a place to stay might be sought for the old man before he entered Egypt (v. 28). The other is that Joseph came to meet his father, and after greeting him (v. 29) and exchanging greetings on both sides (v. 30), Joseph, after communicating with them (as was fitting), provided lawfully for his father and the whole family by his own counsel. There are two parts to this communication. In the first, Joseph shows what must be done for them, so that with the consent and approval of the king they may be allowed not only to dwell in Egypt (v. 31), but also be given a convenient dwelling suited to their circumstances and condition (v. 32). The other part of the communication concerns the duty of the brothers: when they approach Pharaoh (v. 33) and are asked about their condition, they are to show openly that they have always kept livestock. For in this way they would obtain a suitable dwelling, for two reasons. One is that they would have pasture land, since they were shepherds, and so would have a dwelling apart from the Egyptians, on account of that ancient superstition of the Egyptians, who greatly abhorred the pastoral life and shepherds. This is clear from Josephus, book 1 against Apion the Alexandrian, and from Diodorus Siculus, book 1 of his Library.

units.la: CAPITIS XLVII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER XLVII ANALYSIS.

units.la: EXposita profectione & aduentu Iacobi familiæq; in Ægypto, sequitur historia rerum in Ægypto gesta-rum,quatuor capitibus.Earum autem hic ordo a Mose constitutus est,ut primum res communes & aliquo tempore ante obitum Iacobi gestæ describantur, cap. 47. Deinde res proximè antegressæ mortem illius,v.48.& 49. Postremo autem res post mortem consequutæ,cap.ult. Huius cap. partes statui oportet has tres summas:primam,de conditione Iacobi & familiæ eius,ad v.vsque 12.secundam, de conditione totius Ægypti per annos illos famis,ad v.vsque 27.Tertiam denique de religiosa cautione Iacobi, qua diu ante sibi de sepultura prospectum voluit quam de hac vita decederet, sub finem capitis. In singulari historia ad Iacobum familiamque eius pertinente hæc tria ordine proponuntur: primum aditus ad regem, ut toti familiæ statio ex auctoritate illius attributa esset,ad v.vsque 6. secundum; salutatio ciuilis & honorifica a Iacobo facta,ad v.vsque 20. postremum vero,Iosephi erga patrem familiamque totam eius sanctissimum officium,verf. 11. & 12. In aditu ad Regem hæc ordine obseruanda sunt;primum quod Icseph[?] primus seor-sim accessit ad Regem viam reliquæ actioni muniturus, verf.1. deinde quod fratres aliquot nomine communi ad Regem admissi, ver.2. qui Pharaoni roganti de conditione ipsorum, responderunt se pecuariam fecisse inde a maioribus, verf. 3. prout sub finem præcedentis capitis Iosephi respondendum esse docuerat: atque hac occasione tum necessitatem aduentus sui, tum postulationem de fede futura exponunt v. 4. tum Pharaonem nec ipsis coram nec ex tempore respondisse, sed communicato nimirum consilio Iosephum instru-xisse mandatis & auctoritate,ut illis cum stationem attribueret quam postulauerant, tum curam regij pecoris (si consultum putaret fore) committeret, v. 5. & 6. Iacobi vero aditus, tamquam gratias acturi Regi pro tanto beneficio, has partes complectitur: primum quod per Iosephum admittitur: deinde quod Regem salutat sine munere solum, siue adiuncto, ut plurimum fiebat, honorario, verf.7. Dein quod rogatus a Pharaone de annis vitæ suæ, verf.8. tum annorum numerum explicat, tum vitæ modum: nempe vitam suam ut maiorum, peregrinationem esse, prout omnes pij agnoscunt, quorum ius ciuitatis est in cælis: deinde illius temporis dies, id est, etiam minutas partes fuisse malas, & calamitatibus plurimis abundauisse, ut hanc vitam Deus sui contemperat afflictionibus, per quas ad regnum cælorum oportet contendere: postremum est, quod his sermonibus cum Pharaone habitis, Iacob eo salutato dimissus se ad suos recepit, v.10. restat officium religiosum Iosephi duplex: quod patri, familiaeque toti de rebus omnibus ad vitam hanc necessariis prospexerit. Sunt autem duæ(ut Iacob ostendit supra c. 28. & Apo-stolus 1.Tim.4.) tegmen & victus. De tegmine & habitatione pro-spectum dicitur v.11. de victu atque commeatu, v.12. Caveant autem lectores ne vocem Rahemses confundant cum altera illa voce, Ra-hamses, quae Exodi 1.nominatur. Hoc enim regionis nome, illud munitionis est. Sequitur communis historia: quid factum Ægyptiis, reliquis annis urgente fame: nam hæc tertio contigisse constat quæ modò diximus. Persequitur ergo Moses historiam Aegyptiorum inde ab anno quarto famis, quo anno furebat populus urgente fame, v.13. & Iosephi omnem pecuniam Ægypti collectam in Regis ærarium importaverat, v.14. Sequete igitur anno, absumta pecunia dicuntur Iosephum accessisse pro commeatu habendo, v. 15. Iosephum pecora exegisse v.16. & illos omnia ut commeatus haberent satis, in annum Iosepho in manus tradidisse, v.17. iterum vero alienatis pecoribus revertisse dicuntur ad Iosephum, & ostendisse nihil sibi factum esse reliqui quàm corpora & prædia sua, v. 18. se ea mancipij lege dedere in potestatem Regis, modò sibi de commeatu sit prospectum, v.19. Itaque probato hoc contractu tum prædia regi comparata esse, v.20. tum incolas in novas sedes ablegatos & colonias factas, v. 21. excipi tantum eos qui regi ministrabant, & quibus alimenta sumtibus Regis subministrabantur, v.22. Postremò exponit Moses ex hoc contractu & beneficio regis, quid Iosephi tum in sequentem annum, tum in ætates venturas constituerit. Nam in sequentem annum Ægyptiis tantum frumenti dedit quantum ad victum & ad sementem necesse videbatur, v.23. & pretium loco istius beneficij refundendum imperavit, quintam redituum pendendam regi, i. binas decimas, quarum unā ante fuerant ordinarii, alterq; ex hoc casu fuerunt impositæ, atque hanc conditionem Ægyptij cum gratiarum actione dicuntur accepisse v.25. Ex his initiis statutum perpetuum in Ægypto fuisse ut binæ decimæ quotannis penderentur Regi, exceptis tantum prædiis quæ ab eo tempore immunitatem habuerunt, eò quòd illorum Domini sumtibus Regis alerentur, v. 26. Restat iam postremus locus capitis; ad quem transiturus Moses primùm ostendit Israelitas commodè illic habitavisse, rerumque suarum sategisse[?], v.27. deinde venit ad religiosam illam cautionem Iacobi de sepultura, quam tertio loco posuiposuimus: ac primùm quidem [illegible, ~9 letters] spatium vitæ Iacobi ponitur, v. 28. deinde factum illius religiosum narratur, quòd filium suum rogauerit, ut corpus suum efferri curaret in Cenahaneam, v.29. & spondentem illud, v.30. fidem dare iussit, v.31. Hic duæ quæstiones oboriuntur, una, de religioso illo studio Iacobi ad locum sepulturæ spectante: altera, de adoratione ipsius. Religiosum illud studium quidam superstitiosum putant, nempe quia nec tempora, nec loca, institutione Dei omnino distincta nouerunt distinguere: quod enim hoc tempore superstitiosum esset futurum, id eo tempore & de eo loco quem Deus promissione sanctificauerat non potuit superstitiosum appellari: utrumque autem sanctificauerat Deus, & tempus ceremonialibus illis observationibus, & locum promissionibus figurandis. Non est autem superstitiosum quod à Deo instituitur, & promissiones coniunctas habet: religiosum igitur ac non superstitiosum Iacobi factum cesendū est. Dixerit quispiā, Atqui hoc Deus nō imperauerat. Respondetur. Qui de specie imperat, eū de indiuiduo quoque imperare. Deū autem regionem Cenahaneæ fedi Israelitarum sanctificauisse, Ergo Iacobum religiosè fecisse qui vel corpori suo sedem illam attribui cauerit. Itaque duplex causa Iacobo fuit cur hac religiosa cautione uteretur: una, quia hoc pertinuit ad præsentem consolationem feminis: altera, quia pertinuit ad posteritatis exemplum, quo Israelitæ monerentur, & hortationem publicam haberent ad persequendum idem, & consolationem in suis difficultatibus diuturnáque peregrinatione obtinendam. Atque hæc causa fuit cur Iacob iuramento filij confirmatus adorauerit ad ceruical lecti sui: i. Deū precatus est ut iuramentum filij suúmque optatum effectum redderet, egitque gratias de præsente consolatione. Restat altera quæstio, cur quū hoc loco dicatur à Mose Iacob adorauisse incumbés ceruicali cubilis sui, diuersum dicat Apostolus ad Hebræos, nempe illum adorauisse incumbentem summitati virgæ suæ. Responsio est, hæc non pugnare: verum utrumque verum esse, quòd Iacob senex, & infirmus lumbis à tergo ceruicali cubilis sui, à fronte summitate virgæ nixus fuerit: prout faciunt infirmi senes atque decrepiti, & fracti laboribus ac ætate mala. Ergo cùm utrumque verum sit, alterum altero non euertitur: nec refert quod LXX interpretes dicuntur vertisse, in summitate virgæ, quæ interpretatio mutatis punctis conuenire postremæ voci huius capitis potest. Nā ut demus ita esse, tamē cū utrūque simul sit verū, etiā utrūque simul, aut alterutrū seperatim potest affirmari sine offensa veritatis: & verè Apostolus respiciēs ad translationem iam eo tempore peruulgatissimam voces illius potius adhibuit, ut imperitiorum offensam caueret (quod charitatis est) quam vt mordicus has voces retineret, quod pertinaciae fuisset futurum ad offensionem multorum.
units.tr: Having described Jacob's departure and his arrival with his household in Egypt, Moses goes on to the history of what was done in Egypt, in four chapters. He arranged them in this order: first, the common events that took place some time before Jacob's death are described, in chapter 47; then the events immediately preceding his death, in vv. 48 and 49; and finally the events that followed his death, in the last chapter. For this chapter I think three main parts should be set out. The first, concerning the condition of Jacob and his household, runs to v. 12. The second, concerning the condition of all Egypt during those years of famine, runs to v. 27. The third, concerning Jacob's religious precaution, by which long before his death he provided for his burial, comes at the end of the chapter. In the particular history concerning Jacob and his household, these three things are set out in order. First comes the approach to the king, so that a place for the whole household might be assigned by his authority, to v. 6. Second comes the civil and respectful greeting Jacob gave, to v. 20. Last comes Joseph's most sacred duty toward his father and his whole household, vv. 11 and 12. In the approach to the king the following should be noted. First, Joseph alone went in to the king, to prepare the way for the rest of the business (v. 1). Then several brothers were admitted to the king in a common name (v. 2). When Pharaoh asked about their condition, they answered that they had kept livestock from their forefathers onward (v. 3), just as Joseph had taught them at the end of the preceding chapter that they should answer. On this occasion they set out both the necessity of their coming and their request for a dwelling in the future (v. 4). Then Pharaoh did not answer them in person or on the spot. Rather, having evidently taken counsel, he instructed Joseph with commands and authority, so that he might assign them the place they had asked for and, if he thought it advisable, put them in charge of the royal herds (vv. 5 and 6). Jacob's approach, as one about to thank the king for so great a benefit, has these parts. First, he is admitted through Joseph. Then he greets the king with nothing but a blessing, or with one accompanied, as usually happened, by an honorary gift (v. 7). Then, asked by Pharaoh about the years of his life (v. 8), he explains both the number of his years and the manner of his life. His life, like that of his forefathers, is a pilgrimage, as all the godly acknowledge, whose citizenship is in heaven. Moreover, those days, that is, even the smallest parts of them, were evil and abounded in many calamities, so that God tempers this life with afflictions, through which one must strive toward the kingdom of heaven. Finally, after these words with Pharaoh, Jacob, having blessed him, was dismissed and returned to his own people (v. 10). There remains Joseph's twofold religious duty: that he provided for his father and his whole household in all the matters necessary for this life. There are two such matters, as Jacob showed above in chapter 28 and the Apostle in 1 Tim. 4: clothing and food. Provision for clothing and dwelling is mentioned in v. 11, and for food and supplies in v. 12. Readers should take care not to confuse the word Rahemses with the other word, Ra-hamses, which is named in Exodus 1. The former is the name of a region, the latter of a fortress. Next follows the common history: what happened to the Egyptians in the remaining years, while the famine pressed. For the things just mentioned are known to have happened in the third year. Moses therefore follows the history of the Egyptians from the fourth year of the famine, in which the people were raging under the pressure of hunger (v. 13), and in which all the money of Egypt had been collected and brought into the king's treasury by Joseph (v. 14). Then in the following year, when the money was used up, they are said to have come to Joseph to obtain supplies (v. 15). Joseph is said to have taken their livestock (v. 16), and, so that they might have enough supplies, to have handed them over to him for the year in return for food (v. 17). Then, once their livestock was disposed of, they are said to have returned to Joseph and shown that nothing was left to them except their bodies and their lands (v. 18). They gave themselves up into the king's power on the terms of a bond of servitude, provided that provision was made for their food (v. 19). So, when this contract was approved, the lands were acquired for the king (v. 20), and the inhabitants were sent away to new settlements and made into colonists (v. 21). Only those who ministered to the king, and whose food was supplied at the king's expense, were excepted (v. 22). Lastly, Moses sets out from this contract and the king's kindness what Joseph established both for the following year and for the ages to come. For in the following year he gave the Egyptians as much grain as seemed necessary for food and for seed (v. 23). And in return for this benefit he ordered that a price be repaid, namely a fifth of the produce to be paid to the king, that is, two tenths, of which one had been an ordinary due before and the other was imposed from this emergency. The Egyptians are said to have accepted this condition with thanksgiving (v. 25). From these beginnings a perpetual rule was established in Egypt that two tenths should be paid to the king each year, except for those lands which from that time enjoyed immunity, because their owners were maintained at the king's expense (v. 26). There now remains the last part of the chapter. Moses, about to turn to it, first shows that the Israelites lived there comfortably and attended to their own affairs (v. 27). Then he comes to that religious precaution of Jacob concerning burial, which I have placed third. First the span of Jacob's life is given (v. 28). Then his religious act is related: that he asked his son to see that his body was carried up to Canaan (v. 29), and when Joseph promised this (v. 30), he bade him give his oath (v. 31). Here two questions arise. One concerns that religious zeal of Jacob with respect to the place of burial; the other concerns his worship. Some think that zeal superstitious, because they do not know how to distinguish times and places that God has not at all set apart by his institution. For what would be superstitious at a later time could not be called superstitious at that time, and concerning that place which God had consecrated by promise. God had consecrated both: the time, by those ceremonial observances, and the place, by promises that were to be figures. Now what God institutes and attaches promises to is not superstitious. Therefore Jacob's act must be judged religious and not superstitious. Someone may say: "But God had not commanded this." The answer is that whoever commands a kind commands its individuals as well. God has consecrated the region of Canaan as the seat of the Israelites. Therefore Jacob acted religiously who took care that his own body should be assigned that seat. Thus Jacob had a twofold reason for using this religious precaution: one, because it served present comfort for his family; the other, because it served as an example for posterity, by which the Israelites would be admonished, and would have a public exhortation to pursue the same, and would obtain consolation in their difficulties and their long pilgrimage. And this was the reason why Jacob, confirmed by his son's oath, worshipped toward the head of his bed. That is, he prayed to God that the oath of his son and his own desire might bring about their effect, and he gave thanks for the present consolation. There remains another question: why, when Moses here says that Jacob worshipped leaning on the head of his bed, the Apostle to the Hebrews says otherwise, namely that he worshipped leaning on the top of his staff. The answer is that these do not conflict. Both are true: Jacob, an old man, weak in his loins, leaned from behind on the head of his bed and from the front on the top of his staff, as weak old men and the decrepit, broken by labours and by bad age, commonly do. Therefore, since both are true, one is not overturned by the other. Nor does it matter that the Seventy are said to have translated "on the top of the staff," since by changing the vowel points that reading can agree with the last word of this verse. For even granting that it is so, since both are true at once, both, or either one separately, can be affirmed at once without any offence to the truth. And the Apostle, looking to the translation already very widely circulated at that time, rightly used its words, so as to avoid offence to the unlearned (which belongs to charity), rather than obstinately retaining these words in a way that would have been a matter of stubbornness and would have given offence to many.

units.la: CAPITIS XLVIII ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER 48 ANALYSIS.

units.la: Sequitur deinceps secundum caput de rebus à Iacobo gestis paulò ante mortem, quarum prius historiā singularem de bonis in Iosephum collatis, posterius vero historiam communem ac propheticam de futura filiorum omnium conditione complectitur, in hoc igitur ca. narratur summatim Iacobum primogenita (vt vocant) temporaria & ad hæreditatem terrenam pertinentia à Reubene in Iosephum transtulisse, duósque Iosephi filios ex æquo instituisse hæredes cum suis patruis & Iosephi fratribus, tanquam si Iacob eos proximè genuisset. De translatione autem primogenitorum à Reubene in Iosephū & Iudam à Iacobo factā propter maleficiū eius, supra sententiam nostrā ostendimus. In hoc autem c. pars hæc trāslati primogenitorū iuris tribus modis exponitur. Nā primū Iosephi filij ex æquo hæredes cum fratribus illius instituuntur communiter, ad v. vsque 7. deinde signum propheticè adhibetur benedictionis illius, ad v. vsque 20. postremò hæreditatis prærogatiua circumscribitur à Iacobo, duobus versibus vltimis. His præmittuntur quædam antecedentia, ex quibus occasio huius historiæ oblata est. Primò quòd Iosepho indicatū est de morbo ingrauescēte patris, & ille comitatus filiis ad ipsum venit, v. 1. deinde quòd Iacobo decumbenti nunciatum est, & ille intromitti iussit: postremò quòd Iacob non humanitus, sed diuinitus institutionem sanctam filiorū Iosephi enunciaturus se ipsum confirmauit, vt cubili insidere posset, quamuis exhausto corpore: videlicet quia stare propter infirmitatem nō poterat. Stabant autē qui verbū Dei propheticū aut enuntiabant ipsi, aut ab enuntiātibus accipiebant. His positis transfit Iacob ad propositione sua de instituendis hæredibus. ac primùm quidē auctoritate suam in instituendo asserit, v. 3. 4. deinde institutione hæredū pronuntiat v. 5. & 6. postremò sermonē de hæreditate attribuenda incipit, v. 7. quem occasione interruptū perficit tandē sub finem capitis. Auctoritatem suā in instituendis hæredibus demōstrat Iacob à persona Dei, qui primum apparuit ipsi, & copiosè benedixit, v. 3. deinde promissionibus instruxit de hæredibus & hæreditate iporū à Iacobo, velut communi parente, diuidunda, v. 4. Hac itaque auctoritate Dei fretus hæredes vncię singulos Iosephi filios pronūtiat, v. 5. & quia fortasse erat futurū vt plures adhuc liberos gigneret Iosephus, Iacob in futurum prospicit, v. 6. si forte plures sustulerit, ut illi fratribus suis accensentur, non autem singulæ tribus habeantur. His positis instituit Iahakob sermonem de hæreditate Iosepho attribuenda sigillatim, v. 7. nēpe in eo termino ubi Rachel, veniente in Cenahanea Iacobo, sepulta est. Nā locus ille præcise fuit Ephraimi & Iudæ conterminus: sed hunc sermonem interrūpit Iacob, & suspensum relinquit ad finem usque capitis, cū per occasionem filios Iosephi adesse animadverteret. Atque hoc pacto transitur ad secundum locum huius capitis, de signis quibus Iacob Iosephū filiosque eius de benedictione & institutione antegressa confirmauit, quam secundam capitis esse partem docuimus. In hac autem parte primo occasio illius narratur v.8. & 9. deinde signa ad eā rem pertinentia v.10. & seqq. Antecedentia sunt hæc filios Iosephi a Iacobo visos, quorum occasione, tū antecedēs sermo interruptus, tū sequēs institutus est: deinde Iosephum de illis rogatum quinā essent, v.8. tū hac re ex Iosepho cognita iussos esse ad avum Iacobū accedere, ut benedictionem ipsius perciperent, v.9. Atque hoc summum est argumentum totius huius loci. Nam benedictione in filios Iosephi contulit Iacob cœcutiens oculis, sed videns animo, primo communiter, deinde singulariter: communiter benedixit Iacob illis osculo, amplexu, vers.10. & sotu (ut ita loquamur) ad genua, ut ex v.12. intelligitur: itémque sermone, quo beneficiū Dei ergā se extollit Iacob, v.11. dicens, videre faciem, &c. singulariter vero benedicit Iacob sequentibus. Benedicit autem & signa exhibet propheticè, in quibus Iosephⁱ insciusactione Iacobi divinam aliquoties interturbat. Nam primo videns Iosephfilios[?] suos diverso ordine ad patris genua consistentes, eximit illos: id, cum bona Patris venia facturus se inclinauisse dicitur, ne pater facto ipsius offenderetur, versu duodecimo: deinde ordine diverso collocatis illis ut primogenitus ad dextram Iacobi sisteretur, eos de integro admovet patri, versu decimo tertio, nempe ut manus dextra maiori natu imposita esset, maioris benedictionis index. hoc humanum Iosephi iudicium testimonio Dei refellens signo Iacob manus decussauisse Spiritu Dei dicitur, versu decimo quarto.
units.tr: There follows next the second chapter, concerning the things Jacob did shortly before his death. Of these, the first is a special history of the blessings conferred on Joseph, and the second is a general and prophetic history of the future condition of all his sons. In this chapter it is related in summary that Jacob transferred the firstborn rights (as they are called), which are temporary and pertain to earthly inheritance, from Reuben to Joseph. He appointed Joseph's two sons as heirs equally with their uncles, Joseph's brothers, as if Jacob had only just begotten them. We have shown above, in our own note, the transfer of the firstborn rights from Reuben to Joseph and Judah, made by Jacob on account of Reuben's wrongdoing. In this chapter this part concerning the transfer of the firstborn's rights is set out in three ways. First, Joseph's sons are appointed heirs jointly with his brothers, to v. 7. Then the sign of that blessing is applied prophetically, to v. 20. Finally, the prerogative of the inheritance is limited by Jacob, in the last two verses. Some preceding matters come before these, from which the occasion of this history arose. First, Joseph was told of his father's worsening illness, and he came to him accompanied by his sons, v. 1. Then, when Jacob was lying ill, it was announced to him, and he ordered them to be admitted. Lastly, Jacob, about to declare the holy appointment of Joseph's sons not by human means but by divine, strengthened himself so that he could sit on the bed, though his body was spent. He did this because he could not stand on account of his weakness. Those standing by were either themselves declaring the prophetic word of God or receiving it from those who declared it. With these things laid down, Jacob passes to his proposition about appointing the heirs. First he asserts his authority in the appointing, vv. 3, 4. Then he pronounces the appointment of the heirs, vv. 5, 6. Lastly he begins his discourse on the attribution of the inheritance, v. 7. This he interrupts because of the occasion, and at the end of the chapter he finally completes it. Jacob shows his authority in appointing the heirs from the person of God, who first appeared to him and blessed him abundantly, v. 3. Then God furnished him with promises about the heirs, and about the inheritance to be divided among them by Jacob as their common parent, v. 4. Trusting in this authority of God, he pronounces each of Joseph's sons to be an heir, v. 5. And because Joseph might perhaps beget more children, Jacob looks ahead to the future, v. 6: if he should have more, they are to be counted among his other sons, and not each regarded as a single tribe. With these things laid down, Jacob begins to speak of the inheritance to be given to Joseph separately, v. 7, namely at the place where Rachel was buried when Jacob was coming into Canaan. That place lay exactly on the border of Ephraim and Judah. But Jacob interrupted this discourse and left it suspended until the end of the chapter, because he noticed by the way that Joseph's sons were present. And in this way one passes to the second place in this chapter, concerning the signs by which Jacob confirmed Joseph and his sons in the blessing and appointment just described. We have taught that this is the second part of the chapter. In this part, the occasion is first narrated, vv. 8, 9, and then the signs pertaining to the matter, v. 10 and following. The antecedents are these: Jacob saw Joseph's sons, and on account of this the preceding discourse was interrupted and the following one begun. Then Joseph was asked who they were, v. 8; and when this was learned from Joseph, they were ordered to approach their grandfather Jacob, to receive his blessing, v. 9. This is the chief argument of the whole passage. For Jacob, dim of eye but seeing in mind, conferred his blessing on Joseph's sons, first in common and then individually. In common he blessed them with a kiss and an embrace, v. 10, and with a sort of prostration (so to speak) at the knees, as is understood from v. 12; likewise with a speech in which Jacob extols God's goodness toward himself, v. 11, saying, "to see your face," etc. Individually, Jacob blesses them as follows. He also displays the signs prophetically, in which Joseph, unaware of Jacob's purpose, several times disturbs the divine act. For first, seeing his sons standing at their father's knees in a different order, he removes them, saying that he had bowed down, intending to do so with his father's good permission, lest the father be offended by his act, v. 12. Then, having arranged them in a different order so that the firstborn stood at Jacob's right hand, he again brings them near to the father, v. 13, namely so that the right hand should be laid upon the elder, as a sign of the greater blessing. Refuting this human judgment of Joseph by the testimony of God, Jacob is said, by the Spirit of God, to have crossed his hands in the sign, v. 14.

units.la: Atque hæc secunda est significatio, qua Iacob hæredum institutio nem ordine distinctam singulari Dei revelatione ostendebat; dextra minori impositá, & alteri siniistra. Huic signo aliud accessit, nimirum sermo divinus, quem Iacob per modum orationis & cōmendationis enunciabat benedicens Iosephi filiis, v.15. & seqq. Huius autem benedictionis partes duæ sunt: una, qua postulatur universe omne genus benedictionis spiritualis in sedere; altera, qua postulatur generis multiplicatio ꝑ ratione signi.i.minori maior, & maiori minor. Huius autem benedictionis assequendæ modus ab hominibus unus est, nimirū oratio fidei: fundamentum verò totum ac principiū æternū Deus est, qui fœdus suū cū patribus cōmunicauit & cū posteris spopondit cōmu-nicaturū, & qui ex fœdere omni officio veritatē fidémq;sua testatur in pascedis & curandis suis, v.15. Postremò autē modus àDeo est mediator Christus, qui per voluntariā dispensationem vel œconomiam, vt sermo est æternus Patris in se, ita nobis angelus Patris factus est, siue (vt appellatur à Malachia Propheta) Angelus fœderis, idémque liberator & seruator nostēr sacerdotio & regno æterno suo, vers.16. Nam vt hæc de aliquo Angelo creato accipiantur, religio vetat: cùm hic Angelus ex æquo oretur cum Deo, & opus diuinum, id est, vindicias nostras dicatur assequi: denique alij Scripturæ loci in quibus vel ipse Iacob hunc Angelum Deum fortem appellauit. Huius benedictionis à Iacobo pronuntiatæ deinceps confirmatio traditur, cùm tertia intercessione sua Iacobum Ioseph impediret. Intercessit autem Io-seph opere & verbo; opere, nam vt vidit dextram patris minori impositam, admouit manum ipse velut correcturus factum imprudentis patris, vers.decimoseptimo. & verbo etiam monuit, vers.decimooctauo. Hac igitur occasione amplius benedictionum suorum veritatem exponit Iacob, vers.19. & 20. cùm ostendit primum nihil à se imprudenter gestum: deinde singulariter modum benedictionum in utrumque definit, vt quo minores in maiorem natu, & minores in maiorem futuræ essent, v.19. postremò, dicto confirmat in posteritatem duraturo, vt Ephraim nomen ad amplas benedictiones significandas adhiberetur, & præponeretur nomini Menassis. Restat tertius locus, quem per occasionem Iacob interruperat de hæreditate filiis Iosephi attributa, duobus versibus vltimis. In hac autem attributione primum generalis promissio præsentiæ diuinæ & reuersionis in Cenahaneam proponitur, v.21. deinde singularis hæreditas attribuitur Iosepho, v.vlt. Nam cùm ex primogenitorum iure duplex hæreditas ad ipsum pertineret, simplam hæreditatem siue unciam, quæ ad Iosephum fuerat peruentura, reticet Iacob: sed alteram, quæ insuper erat addenda ipsi supra quam ipsius fratribus circumscribit, dicens, Ego dedero tibi portionem unam supra quam fratribus tuis, quam cepero, &c. Sic Iacob duo demonstrat ad circumscriptionem hæreditatis pertinentia: nā primùm singulari hypænixi fortem Ephraimi notat, cùm nominat Sechem: fuit enim Seche metropolis Ephraimi: deinde parandæ illius fortis modum, gladio & arcu, id est, virtute bellica, de manu Amoræorum, qui illam partem obtinebant: vt ex historia Iosuæ & iudicum manifesto constat.
units.tr: This is the second indication by which Jacob showed the appointment of the heirs, distinguished in order by a special revelation of God: the right hand laid on the younger, and the left on the other. To this sign another was added, namely the divine word, which Jacob uttered in the form of a prayer and commendation as he blessed Joseph's sons, v. 15 and following. This blessing has two parts. In one, every kind of spiritual blessing is asked for them in general; in the other, the multiplication of their stock is asked for, by way of the sign, that is, the younger being made greater and the greater made less. Men have one way of obtaining this blessing, namely the prayer of faith. But the whole foundation and the eternal beginning is God, who communicated his covenant with the fathers and promised to communicate it with their descendants, and who, from the covenant, testifies his truth and faithfulness in every office of feeding and caring for his people, v. 15. Finally, the mediator Christ is the way from God. By his voluntary dispensation, or economy, he is the eternal Word of the Father in himself, and so he has become the angel of the Father for us; or, as the prophet Malachi calls him, the Angel of the covenant, and the same is our deliverer and saviour by his priesthood and his eternal kingdom, v. 16. For religion forbids that these things be understood of some created angel, since this Angel is prayed to on equal terms with God, and is said to accomplish a divine work, that is, to vindicate us. Lastly, there are other passages of Scripture in which Jacob himself calls this Angel "God, strong". The confirmation of this blessing, pronounced by Jacob, is then handed down, since by his third intercession Joseph hindered Jacob. Joseph interceded both by deed and by word. By deed, for when he saw his father's right hand laid on the younger, he himself moved his hand, as if about to correct the act of his unwitting father, v. 17. And he also admonished him by word, v. 18. On this occasion Jacob further sets out the truth of his blessings, vv. 19 and 20. First he shows that nothing was done by him imprudently. Then he specifically defines the manner of the blessings for each of the two, so that the younger would be greater than the elder, and the younger would be greater in future, v. 19. Lastly, he confirms the saying with a lasting effect for posterity, so that the name of Ephraim would be used to signify great blessings, and would be put before the name of Manasseh. There remains the third place, which Jacob had interrupted for the sake of the occasion, concerning the inheritance attributed to Joseph's sons: the last two verses. In this attribution, first a general promise is set forth, of the divine presence and of return to Canaan, v. 21. Then a particular inheritance is given to Joseph, v. 22. For since a double inheritance would come to him by the right of the firstborn, Jacob passes over the simple inheritance, or one share, which would have come to Joseph, but he defines the additional portion which was to be added to him above his brothers, saying, "I have given you one portion above your brothers, which I took," etc. Thus Jacob sets out two things that pertain to the limitation of the inheritance. First, by a singular allusion he marks out the lot of Ephraim, when he names Shechem, for Shechem was the metropolis of Ephraim. Then he states the manner of acquiring that lot, "with the sword and the bow", that is, by warlike valour, from the hand of the Amorites, who held that part, as is clear from the history of Joshua and the Judges.
