units.la: XPOSITA praerogatiua, qua Ioseph secundum ius primogenitorum in ipsum diuinitus ex parte translatum fuit auctus de sententia patris, capite praecedente, sequitur capite 49. alter historiae locus: nempe communiter ad totam familiam, singulosque Iacobi liberos, & posteritatem illorum pertinens. Huius itaque capitis partes in vniuersum duae sunt: quarum priore Iacob Prophetico Spiritu denuntiat res singulis ipsius filiis posteriq; illorum cuenturas, qua haeredibus, qua haereditati a Deo attributae, inde ad v.29. Posteriore vero, narrat mandatum Iacobi de sepultura sua, quod mandatum iam diu ante Iosepho dederat in antecessum, siue (ut loquuntur vulgo) per prouisionem, sub finem c. 47. Atque hoc mandatum reliquo cap. inde a v.29. proponitur coniuncta historia mortis, quae est ad argumentum capitis sequentis μετάβασις. Ad priorem locum pertinent duo, aut (si magis placet) tria. Primum est exordium a Iacobo positum, v.1. & 2. secundum, narratio Prophetica ad haeredes haereditatemque illorum pertinens, & per singula capita descripta acuratissime, a v. 3. ad 27. vsque: tertia denique futura & conclusio totius sermonis huius, v.28. Ad sanctissimam actionem hanc liberos suos Iacob praeparauit convocatione, v. 1. deinde sermonibus ad audientiam & docilitatem ipsorum pertinetibus. Primum argumentum est quo audientiam facit a substantia rerum quas enuntiaturus est, quod & Prophetice sunt, & singulos attingunt ipsorum, itemque posteros, v.1. deinde vero a persona, tum sua, tum vero ipsorum, cum se patrem & illos filios: ie Israelem, id est, foederatum Deo & auctoritate Dei filios suos docentem appellauit, v.2. In Prophetica narratione, quae tota & argumento & loquutionum modo stylum Propheticum grauissime repraesentat, totidem sunt partes, quot fuerunt capita liberorum Iacobi: si hoc exceperis, quod Simeonis & Leui vna est communis praedictio. Alioquin siquis breuiorem diuinationem desiderauerit, tres partes commode statui possunt: quarum prima respicit filios Lea, ad v.vsque 16. secunda ancillarum filios ad v.vsque 21. tertia denique filios Rachelis, inde ad 37. Quo in ordine duo illi ad quos primogenita fuerunt a Reubene translata principalem locum obtinent & ampliorem narrationem, nimirum Iuda, v.8. & seqq. & Iosephi, v.22. & seqq. Primus ergo locus huius narrationis respicit eum qui naturae ordine fuerat primogenitus, v. 3. & 4. Huic autem primum dignitas quam
units.tr: Having set out the prerogative by which Joseph, by his father's sentence in the preceding chapter, was increased with the right of the firstborn that had been transferred to him from Reuben by divine decree, the second historical passage follows in chapter 49. It pertains in general to the whole family and to each of Jacob's sons and their posterity. The parts of this chapter, taken as a whole, are two. In the first, Jacob, by prophetic Spirit, foretells what will befall each of his sons and their descendants, both the heirs and the inheritance assigned to them by God, down to v. 29. In the second, he gives the command concerning his burial, which he had already given to Joseph long before, in advance, or (as they commonly say) by provision, at the end of chap. 47. After this command, in the rest of the chapter from v. 29 onward, the connected account of his death is set out, which is the transition [μετάβασις] to the subject of the following chapter. Two, or if you prefer, three parts belong to the first passage. The first is the exordium placed by Jacob at vv. 1 and 2; the second is the prophetic narration concerning the heirs and their inheritance, described most carefully part by part from v. 3 to v. 27; the third, finally, is the future events and the conclusion of the whole discourse, v. 28. For this most sacred act Jacob prepared his sons by summoning them, v. 1, and then by speeches aimed at their attention and docility. The first argument by which he wins their attention is drawn from the substance of what he is about to declare, which is prophetic and touches each of them and likewise their posterity, v. 1. Then it is drawn from the persons, both his own and theirs, when he calls himself the father and them the sons, and calls them Israel, that is, one bound in covenant with God and teaching his sons by God's authority, v. 2. In the prophetic narration, which in its whole subject and manner of speaking most gravely represents the prophetic style, there are as many parts as there were sons of Jacob, with the exception that the prediction for Simeon and Levi is one common prediction. Otherwise, if someone wants a briefer division, three parts can conveniently be distinguished: the first concerns the sons of Leah, to v. 16; the second the sons of the handmaids, to v. 21; the third, finally, the sons of Rachel, from there to v. 37. In this order, the two to whom the firstborn rights were transferred from Reuben hold the principal place and the fuller account, namely Judah, v. 8 and following, and Joseph, v. 22 and following. The first place of this narration therefore concerns him who by the order of nature had been the firstborn, vv. 3 and 4. To this one, first, the dignity which

units.la: ante habuerat exponitur, exprobratúrque, v.3. deinde amissio dignitatis illius, adducta causa iusta necessariáque, ostenditur, v.4. In dignitate tria considerantur: primùm naturæ ordo, velut causa dignitatis: deinde personæ conditio ex naturæ ordine in se, nempe quòd virtus fuit principiúmque virium paternarum; postremò autem dignitas in res alias omnes & præ omnibus, cùm dicitur Reuben excellentia dignitatis siue elationis, & excellentia roboris valuisse. Quibus verbis duo illa singularia Dei in primogenitos beneficia demonstrantur, quòd & honore ac dignitate antecellunt, & robore atque auctoritate imperium in alios obtinent. Atque hæc duo beneficia fuerunt in duos distributa; nam excellentia elationis siue dignitatis Iudæ, secundùm res spirituales & corporales; excellentia verò roboris in rebus temporalibus Iofepho obtigit, vt ante ex principio cap.5. in 1. Chron. demonstrauimus. Huic exprobrationi dignitatis subnectitur Prophetia de priuatione Reubenis, continens tamen sententiam priuationis his verbis, Rapiditate velut aquarum ruat, ac non excellat: quasi dicat dicto citius vt aqua non potest deorsum non ferri, ita ruat iste deorsum præceps, & de sua illa excellentia deturbatus: sententiæ causa est incestus ille concubitus, cuius ante Moses meminerat c.33. Hunc incestum in causa esse priuationis ostendit Iacob tum sermone ad Reubenem habito, tum verò communiter ad filios omnes verso, vt contestaretur iustitiam diuini iudicij. Nam Reubeni in hoc facto duo maleficia exprobrat: vnum incesti concubitus, in patrem contumeliosissimi: alterum, impietatis in seipsum & ius primogenitorum, ex quo sacratus erat Domino, tu(inquit)impurauisti: nimiru & te & primogenita, ac proinde abalienauisti te ab illa sanctitate quam in primogenitis impressit Deus, atque imperauit. Sequitur postea anastrophe siue sermonis conuersio ad fratres, Stratu meum ascendit, quasi dicat, Vos omnes appello iudices, vtrū bona fide necne, reum impietatis istius dissimulare possim, & sinere vt impunè abeat qui nec sui ipsius, nec mei, nec Dei rationem habuit. Secundus locus prophetiæ ad duos pertinet, quia communis maleficij non plane communem, sed tamen bona ex parte conuenientem pœnam Iacob vaticinatus est. Ij sunt Simeon & Leui, ad quos prophetia pertinet v.5. & duobus seqq. Prophetiæ autem ad ambos pertinentis membra sunt tria; nam primùm communiter enuntiatur argumentum totum, cùm appellantur fratres: non eò quòd germani essent fratres, sed quòd velut gemini essent, & pares inter se tum crimine, tum supplicio eius. Atq; hoc generatim dictum postea speciatim exponitur, duobus membris; nam primùm commune crimè altera parte quinti versus, deinde communes munes pœnæ duobus seq. exponûtur. Cômunis criminis cbicêtio: his verbis constat, instrumenta violentiæ sunt conuentiones illorum, i. optime conuenit inter illos vt instrumento violetię ad federatos Sechemitas perdendos per fraudē vteretur, c. 34. Quòd si cui altera interpretatio magis placuerit, In instrumentis violentiæ conuentiones eorum consistunt, suum cuiq; liberum erit iudicium: nam vtrouis sensu interpreteris, eadem manet sententia. Restat locus de suppliciis. Maleficium igitur istorum à Iacobo describitur his verbis, instrumenta violentiæ sunt conuentiones eorum: nam illi consilio inter se inito ex compacto in Sechemitas irruerunt, vt c. 34. exposuit Moses: quod maleficium quantopere Deo & Iacobo displicuerit, non solum ex historia illius & seq. cap. verumetiam ex sequentibus duobus versibus videmus luculentissime. In quibus tertia pars huius loci consistit: nam v. 6. detestatio & horror facinoris, v. 7. maledictio in auctores illius supplicium umque diuinum pronuntiatur. Ad detestationem facinoris demonstrandam, Iacob tum sensum suæ ipsius conscientiæ, tum atrocitatem facinoris obiicit: sensum conscientiæ suæ his verbis enuntiat, In arcanum eorum ne veniat, &c. Quibus verbis ostendit se tum à consilio, tum à conuentu quem habuerunt consilio capto, tum à facinore ita abhorrere, vt nec anima sua, id est, consilio atque voluntate intus, nec lingua sua, id est, professione foris possit cum eo facto communicare, siue probando, siue tolerado & dissimulando. Nam his modis qui in auctoritate sunt, cum aliorum peccatis communi facto, aut cótagione aliqua, aut etiam specie, factum ipsorum quàm sit indignum duobus modis ostenditur: primùm quia quicquid compromiserint aduersus Sechemitas, non ex iure, sed ex ira & perturbatione animi, adeoque libidine animi profectum est: ira autem (vt ait sapiens) ignorat iustitiam Dei. Deinde verò indignitas facinoris eò ostenditur, quòd promiscuè sæuierunt in fontes & insontes, mares & fœminas, grandæuos & pueros, homines & pecora: tanta fuit animorum in perpetrando hoc violento facinore perturbatio. Ex horrore isto consequuntur duo, verf. 7. maledictio communis verbis Dei in violentiæ auctores pronuntiata; & singularis in istas duas tribus, quæ maiorum suorum violentiæ perpetuam notam in populum Iudæorum circumferre coactæ sunt ex sententia Dei. Prius enuntiatur his verbis, Maledicta ira eorum, &c. posterius enuntiatur illis, dispertiam eos in Iacobo, &c. Huic autem maledictioni euentum respondisse testatur sacra historia in libro Iosue & Iudicum: nam hæc vtraq; tribus respectu hæredū & hereditatis aliquâ maledictionem experta est: hæredum, quia numquam in tantum numerum excreuerunt atque tribus aliæ:& ipsa tribus Simeonis cùm excreuisset, maximam demi-nutionem propter suum scelus iudicio Dei est experta, Num. 25. Ita vt longè minore hæreditate quàm aliæ tribus opus habuerit.Respe-ctu vero hæreditatis verissima est denuntiatio: nam Simeonis tribus (vt erat exigua) per tribum Iehudæ quæ fuit populofiffima dispersa est,Iofuæ.19.Tribus vero Leuitica,nec fortem habuit ipsam,nec co-tinentes habitationes; sed per totâ terram fuit dissipata, sedibus hic illic per tribus singulas dispositis,Iofuæ 22.& 1.Chron.6. Tertius locus omnium amplissimus ad tribum Iehudæ pertinet, versibus quin-que conclusus.De hac autem tribu primùm dignitas enûtiatur atque auctoritas versibus tribus;deinde commoditas habitationis vel fedis attributæ, v. 11. & 12.Dignitatem & auctoritatem tribus Iacob Dei Spiritu actus prædicauit:primùm quidem vniuerse, v.8.deinde verò distinctè duobus sequentibus. Vniuerse prædicatur Iehudæ dignitas ab euentis tribus:primum est quòd omnes fratres hanc primùm laudaturi ac prædicaturi sunt: fecundum, quòd omnes hostes manum ipsius & potentiam experturi,qua ceruices hostium prehensurus dicitur Iehuda tamquam Leo in prædam irruens, quamuis velocissimè fuga contendentem:postremum est,quòd etiam regnum in fratres fit habiturus: atque hæc dignitas vniuerse proposita fpeciatim postea distinguitur,v.9.& 10.quorum priore dignitas temporalis, pofterio-re dignitas æterna demonstratur in Christo Iesu. Temporariam di-gnitatem potentiámque summam Iacob enuntiat leonis iuuenis fi-militudine; quam similitudinem leonis amplificat duobus modis; primùm quòd vt leo prædainftructus redit, ficribus Iehudæ vi-ctricem de prædahoftium triumphaturam esse pronuntiat,v.9.dein-de quòd fruentem prædacommodè, nemointerturbaturus est, ac proinde quemcunque aggreditur superat, ipsum vero aggredi audet nemo.Huius vero dignitatis temporariæ,quæ velut auctarium fuit & fignû æternæ dignitatis in Christo, fundamentum ostenditur v. 10. cùm & dignitatis illius perduratio & in omnes gentes propagatio per Christum Iesum prædicitur. Perdurationem tum gentis tùm re-gni hæc verba significant,Non absistet sceptrum à Iehuda, & legislator a pedibus eius vsque dum veniet Siloh, id est, Filius fecundarum eius; propagatio verò istius regni pronuntiatur illis, & ad eum futura est expectatio Gentium. Prioris loci sententia est euidens, fi duo exceperis:nam primum vocisSchebet homonymia varias interpretationes attulit; deinde quæstio oritur de vsu particulæ illius vsque. Nomen Schebet proprie est ramus. Quia autem dominationis signum apud veteres virga fuit, & singulæ tribus singulis dominationibus erant tonoadscriptæ : ex eo factum est vt Hebræum istud vocabulum siue metonymicè;siue synecdochicè,tum dominatione imperiumque significet, tum verò gentem dominationi & imperio subditam, ac veluti virgæ pastoris sui. Itaque huius membri duplex affertur interpretatio: Non abstiet virga.i. sceptrum,ac proinde regnum siue dominatio, & non abstiet virga.i.tribus, ac proinde certa populi recensio gentisque descriptio. Priorem interpretationem videtur cofirmare membrum sequens, & Legislator à pedibus eius: posteriorem videtur cofirmare vsus nominis Schebet, quod nomen perraro apud Mosen pro regno, sed pro tribu plurimum legitur. Mihi placet vtrumque simul coniungi: etsi priorem interpretationem propter sequentia magis esse istius loci iudico. Altera quæstio respiciens ad vocem vsque non ita grauis est, quia communis est harum particularum vsus in linguis fermè omnibus: nâ, Had apud Hebræos, & Græcos, & apud Latinos vsque, duobus modis accipitur: exclusiuè, vt loquuntur vulgò, & inclusiuè. Ex clusiuè accipitur, quum tempus de reliquo sequuturû excluditur: inclusiue autem cùm tempus aut spatium vlterius propterea non excluditur, sed tantû dictum eo vsque affirmatur citra exclusionem sequentiû. quod fiquisLogicus ista amplius explicare volet, ita potest res exponi: Cum Vsque dicimus exclusiuè, esse dictû simpliciter, quum autè inclusiuè, esse dictum secundùm quid, nimirum respectu eius rei de qua agitur. Hoc autem loco vtrouis modo accipiamus, semper integra futura est rei interpretatio. Nam si particulam vsque exclusiuè placet accipere, hic sensus futurus est, non destiturum illud ius aut v-sum iuris illius ex facto secundùm temporalem auctoritatem familiæ huic attributæ, quàm cùm venerit Christus: cuius rei complementum Orthodoxi patres multis locis demonstrauerût, inter cæteros autem Eusebius de Demonst. Euangel. Quod si inclusiuè placuerit accipere, hic sensus futurus est, Regnû dignitatémque tribus Iehudæ, neque tum destituram, neque in æternum, quia regnum illud ex temporali Christus spirituale æternúmque fuit effecturus. Hactenus de regni perduratione, cuius non erit finis. Propagationes verò illius in omnes gentes ac coagmentationem Ecclesiæ Catholicæ demonstrat Iacob his verbis, In eo futura est expectatio populorum. Hactenus de rebus ad tribum Iuda pertinentibus: post de hæreditate Iacob agit, quam ostendit fore vberrimam hyperbolicis loquutionibus, v. 11. & 12. Nam primæ illius loquutionis, alligans ad vitem asellum suum, & ad generosam vitem pullum asinæ suæ, sensus est, fore vt ita abundent vitibus, iisque firmissimis, vt vix locum vacuum cultura inuenturi sint, vbi pecora sua alligent. Similiter cùm dicitur, lauat vino vestimentum suum,
units.tr: is first explained and its guilt charged, v.3. Then the loss of that dignity is shown, with a just and necessary cause assigned, v.4. Three things are considered in the dignity: first, the order of nature, as the ground of the dignity; second, the person's standing arising from that order in himself, namely that he was the firstfruits and the beginning of his father's strength; and last, the dignity over all other things and above all others, when it is said that Reuben excelled in dignity or pride and was strong in power. By these words two special benefits of God toward the firstborn are shown: that they surpass others in honour and dignity, and that they hold rule over others by strength and authority. These two benefits were divided between two sons. For the excellence of pride or dignity fell to Judah, in spiritual and bodily things, while the excellence of strength in temporal things fell to Joseph, as we showed earlier from the beginning of chapter 5 in 1 Chronicles. To this reproach of dignity is joined the prophecy about Reuben's deprivation, which nevertheless states the sentence of deprivation in these words: He shall rush on like waters, and shall not excel. It is as if he said: as water, faster than any word, cannot fail to be carried downward, so he shall rush headlong downward, cast out from that excellence of his. The cause of the sentence is that incestuous intercourse, which Moses had mentioned earlier in chapter 33. That Jacob shows this incest to be the cause of the deprivation, both in the speech addressed to Reuben and in the words turned to all the sons in common, so that he might attest the justice of God's judgment. For in this deed he charges Reuben with two wrongs: one, the incestuous intercourse, most insulting to his father; the other, impiety against himself and the right of the firstborn, by which he had been consecrated to the Lord. You, he says, have defiled: that is, you have defiled both yourself and the firstborn, and so you have alienated yourself from that holiness which God impressed upon and commanded for the firstborn. Next follows an anastrophe, or turning of the speech, to the brothers: He went up to my bed. It is as if he said: I call you all as judges, whether in good faith I can overlook the guilt of this impiety and allow him to go unpunished, who had regard neither for himself, nor for me, nor for God. The second part of the prophecy concerns two sons, because Jacob foretold for a common wrong a punishment not wholly common, yet in good part fitting. These are Simeon and Levi, to whom the prophecy applies in verse 5 and the two following verses. The prophecy addressed to both has three parts. First the whole argument is stated in common, when they are called brothers: not because they were brothers by the same parents, but because they were as twins, and alike in their crime and in their punishment. This general statement is afterwards set out in particular, in two parts: first the common crime, in the latter part of verse 5, and then the common punishments are set out in the two following verses. The common crime is indicated in these words: Instruments of violence are their covenants; that is, they agreed well among themselves to use the instrument of violence, by fraud, to destroy the Shechemites who were bound to them by treaty, Gen. 34. But if someone prefers the other interpretation, In their instruments of violence their covenants stand, each may judge as he pleases; for whichever sense you adopt, the meaning remains the same. There remains the passage on punishments. Jacob therefore describes their crime in these words: Instruments of violence are their covenants. For, having taken counsel among themselves, they rushed upon the Shechemites by agreement, as Moses set out in Genesis 34. How greatly this crime displeased God and Jacob we see most clearly not only from the story itself and the following chapter, but also from the two following verses. In these lies the third part of this passage: in verse 6 the detestation and horror of the deed, and in verse 7 the curse on its authors and the divine punishment are declared. To show his detestation of the deed, Jacob sets before them both the feeling of his own conscience and the atrocity of the deed. He expresses the feeling of his conscience in these words: Let not my soul come into their secret, and so on. By these words he shows that he so abhors the counsel, the gathering they made when they had taken counsel, and the deed, that neither his soul, that is his inward counsel and will, nor his tongue, that is his outward profession, can have fellowship with that deed, whether by approving it or by tolerating and overlooking it. For in these ways, when those in authority share in the sins of others by a common deed, or by some contagion, or even by appearance, the unworthiness of their act is shown in two ways. First, because whatever they undertook against the Shechemites did not proceed from right but from anger and disturbance of mind, and so from the lust of the mind; for anger, as the wise man says, does not know the justice of God. Then the unworthiness of the deed is shown further in this, that they raged promiscuously against the guilty and the innocent, males and females, the old and the children, men and cattle: so great was the disturbance of their minds in carrying out this violent deed. From this horror two things follow. In verse 7 a common curse is pronounced by the word of God upon the authors of the violence; and a particular curse upon those two tribes, which were compelled by God's sentence to carry the perpetual mark of their forefathers' violence among the Jewish people. The first is stated in these words: Cursed be their anger, and so on. The second is stated in these: I will divide them in Jacob, and so on. That this curse found its outcome, sacred history bears witness in the books of Joshua and Judges. For both tribes suffered some curse with respect to their heirs and their inheritance. With respect to their heirs, because they never grew to so great a number as the other tribes; and the tribe of Simeon itself, when it had grown, suffered a very great diminution by God's judgment on account of its wickedness, Num. 25., so that it needed a far smaller inheritance than the other tribes. With respect to the inheritance the declaration is most true: for the tribe of Simeon, being small, was scattered within the tribe of Judah, which was most populous, Joshua 19. The Levitical tribe had neither its own lot nor continuous dwellings, but was dispersed through the whole land, with dwellings set here and there in individual tribes, Joshua 22. and 1 Chron. 6. The third part, the most ample of all, concerns the tribe of Judah and is contained in five verses. Concerning this tribe, dignity and authority are first declared in three verses; then the convenience of its dwelling, or of the seat assigned to it, in verses 11 and 12. Jacob, moved by the Spirit of God, proclaimed the dignity and authority of the tribe: first in general, in verse 8, and then particularly in the two following verses. In general, Judah's dignity is proclaimed from the outcomes for the tribe. First, all the brothers shall praise and extol him first; second, all enemies shall experience his hand and power, for Judah is said to seize the necks of his enemies like a lion rushing on its prey, even though they flee most swiftly; last, he shall also have dominion over his brothers. This dignity, set forth in general, is afterwards distinguished in particular in verses 9 and 10: in the former, a temporal dignity is shown, and in the latter an eternal dignity in Christ Jesus. Jacob states the temporary dignity and supreme power by the likeness of a young lion. He amplifies this likeness of the lion in two ways: first, because like a lion returning equipped with prey, he declares that the tribe of Judah shall triumph as victor over the prey of its enemies, verse 9; then, because no one will disturb it while it is enjoying its prey conveniently, and so whomever it attacks it overcomes, while no one dares to attack it. The foundation of this temporary dignity, which was as an addition and a sign of the eternal dignity in Christ, is shown in verse 10, where both the perpetuity of that dignity and its propagation among all nations through Christ Jesus are foretold. The perpetuity both of the people and of the kingdom is signified by these words: The sceptre shall not depart from Judah, nor the lawgiver from between his feet, until Shiloh comes, that is, the son of his offspring. The propagation of that kingdom is declared in those words: and to him shall be the expectation of the nations. The sense of the first part is clear, if you except two things. First, the word shebet, being ambiguous, has given rise to various interpretations; second, a question arises about the use of that particle until. The noun shebet properly means a rod or branch. Since among the ancients the rod was the sign of rule, and each tribe had its own rod written with its own ruler's name, it came about that this Hebrew word, whether by metonymy or synecdoche, signifies both rule and dominion, and also the people subject to rule and dominion, as it were the rod of their shepherd. Hence a double interpretation of this clause is offered: The rod shall not depart, that is, the sceptre, and so the kingdom or dominion; and the rod shall not depart, that is, the tribe, and so the certain enrolment of the people and description of the nation. The first interpretation seems to be confirmed by the following clause, nor the lawgiver from between his feet; the second seems to be confirmed by the use of the name shebet, which is very rarely read in Moses for kingdom but very often for tribe. I am pleased to join both together, although on account of what follows I judge the first interpretation to be the more suitable to this passage. The second question, concerning the word until, is less serious, because the use of these particles is common in almost all languages. For the Hebrew 'ad, and the Greek and Latin until, are taken in two ways: exclusively, as people commonly speak, and inclusively. It is taken exclusively when the time that follows is excluded; but inclusively when a time or space beyond is not thereby excluded, but only the thing said up to that point is affirmed, without excluding what follows. If a logician wishes to explain these matters further, the matter can be put thus: when we say until exclusively, it is said absolutely; when inclusively, it is said with respect to something, namely with respect to the thing under discussion. But in this passage, whichever way we take it, the interpretation of the matter will always remain whole. For if it pleases us to take the particle until exclusively, the sense will be that this right, or the exercise of that right, by the fact itself, according to the temporal authority granted to this family, will not cease until Christ comes; the fulfilment of this the orthodox Fathers have shown in many places, among others Eusebius in his Demonstration of the Gospel. But if it pleases us to take it inclusively, the sense will be that the kingdom and dignity of the tribe of Judah will not then cease, nor will it cease forever, because Christ was to make that temporal kingdom spiritual and eternal. So far concerning the perpetuity of the kingdom, which shall have no end. But Jacob shows its propagation among all nations and the joining together of the Catholic Church in these words: To him shall be the expectation of the peoples. So far concerning matters pertaining to the tribe of Judah. Afterwards he treats of Jacob's inheritance, which he shows will be most abundant, by hyperbolical expressions, verses 11 and 12. For the sense of the first expression, binding his donkey to the vine, and his donkey's colt to the choice vine, is that they will so abound in vines, and very firm ones, that they will hardly find an empty place in the cultivated land where they may tie their animals. Similarly, when it is said, he washes his garment in wine,

units.la: { } — & sanguine uvarum tegmen suum, i. ut vitibus, sic vino abundaturum esse, adeo ut vino circumfluat tanquam si aqua esset, v.11. Eadem versus duodecimi ratio: nempe vino & lacte abundaturos; vino abundaturos, his verbis, Rubicundus oculos ex vino: Lacte illis, albus dentes ex lacte.
units.tr: — and the blood of grapes his garment: that as he will abound in vines, so also in wine, to such a degree that he will flow with wine as if it were water, v.11. The reasoning of verse twelve is the same: namely that they will abound in wine and in milk. That they will abound in wine is shown by these words: Ruddy are his eyes with wine. That they will abound in milk is shown by: white are his teeth with milk.

units.la: Ac proinde hoc pacto maxima hereditatis commoditas Poeticis loquutionibus, quibus prophetiae exornantur, luculentissime demonstratur. Sequitur locus quartus de Zebulune, de quo Iacob distincte pronunciat, primum qualem haereditatem sit habiturus, tum quibus in rebus se occupaturus, postremo qua in parte Cenahaneæ; qualem, docet his verbis, Zebulluna ad portum, &c. Quam occupatione exercitur illis, ipse ad nauale asiduus futurus est. Postremo ubi futura sit haereditas determinat illis, & latus eius ad Sidonem. Quintus locus de Isaacare haec ordine pronuntiat; primum obscuram & segnem potentiam illius, asini robusti similitudine: tum sedem, quod procubiturus est: id est sedem habiturus inter duas sarcinas, prout ab una parte Pelistaeis, ab altera Ammonitis & Syris erat conterminus: tertio studium ipsius, quod ad quietem spectabit & a negotiis plurimum abstinebit, v. 15. Postremo quod ab occupationibus molestis abstinebit, & potius onera subiturus est, tributaque soluturus ad redimendam quietem, quam ut in se grauius negotium aliquod suscipiat, atque haec a Zebulune fuisse facta ex libro Iudicum cognoscimus. Hactenus de filiis Leae.
units.tr: In this way the greatest advantage of the inheritance is most clearly shown by the poetic expressions with which the prophecies are adorned. Next comes the fourth place, concerning Zebulun, about whom Jacob speaks distinctly: first what kind of inheritance he will have, then with what occupations he will be busied, and last in what part of Canaan. What kind he teaches in these words: Zebulun shall dwell at the haven, and so on. The occupation with which he will be busied is given in these words: he himself will be constant at the shipping. Last, he determines where the inheritance will lie: and his border is unto Sidon. The fifth place, concerning Issachar, he sets out in this order: first, his obscure and sluggish power, by the likeness of a strong ass; then his seat, in that he will couch down, that is, he will have his seat between two burdens, since on one side he bordered the Philistines and on the other the Ammonites and Syrians; third, his disposition, which will look to quiet and keep himself much from business, v.15. Last, that he will keep himself from troublesome occupations and will rather take up burdens and pay tribute to buy his quiet, than undertake some heavier business on his own account. We learn from the book of Judges that these things were done by Zebulun. So far concerning the sons of Leah.

units.la: Sequitur iam pars altera de filiis ancillarum, quorum primus erat Dan. Itaque argumento Danis ad reliquos ancillarum filios transfituros Iacob, primum communem prophetiam omnium enuntiat, versu decimosexto: deinde singulare de Dane, duobus seq.
units.tr: Now follows the second part, concerning the sons of the handmaids, of whom the first was Dan. Therefore, with the argument that Jacob passes from Dan to the rest of the sons of the handmaids, he first announces the prophecy common to all of them, in verse sixteen; then the singular prophecy concerning Dan, in the two following verses.

units.la: Commune est illud: Dan iudicaturus est populi sui, sicut una tribus Israelis: Nam quod speciatim de Dane dicitur, quia primus est in eo numero, id communiter de reliquis intelligitur, quia iuris communis est. Itaque sensus est singulariter de Dane; Etsi Dan filius ancillae est, cum non propterea ex iure tribulitio exclusum iri, sed commune exaequo cum uxorum filiis ius ipsi adiudicatu esse. Cum autem institutu hoc commune habeat ratione cum aliis filiis quos Iacob ex ancillis suscitulerat, ex eo sequitur communiter ius illud ad alios cum ipso pertinere; quapropter postea suo ordine Gad, Asher, & Nephtali recensentur, ut suum illud commune ius cum Dane obtinentes. Singularis vero de Dane prophetia primum situ haereditatis & occupationes illius oftedit, v.17, deinde vero cuentu, v. 18. situs haereditatis est secundu viam & semita, i. in extimis finibus Cenahaneç. Occupatio est, quod propter incommoditate suæ habitationis ex improuiso in finitimos inuolaturus est, eosq; perditurus in modu serpentis, etiamque potentissimos qui extra periculum sibi videantur versari adorietur vehementissime: quapropter vtitur serpentium similitudine,tum humilis qui admordet equi calcaneum,tum acontię fiue iaculi,qui ex ramis arborum quibus insidet & viatores obseruat,tâquam sagitta in eos irruit,vnde nomen habet. Euentus verò demonstratur miser & deploratus istis tribus, v.18. cū Iacob fe ad Deum cõuertit,orans vt saluti Danis consulat. Nam hæc tribus miserè defecit prima,& in defectione permansit,adeò vt tempore reuersionis ex Babylonia nihil de Dane exstet, Chron.1. & Sanctus Ioânes,in Apocal.cap.7.nomen Danis plane reticeat. Septimus locus de Gade est v.19. in quo sedes Gaditarum innuitur, & historia subditur. Historia est,quòd finitimorum prædationibus infestus futurus est,& ille finitimos infestaturus & superaturus:quemadmodum tribum Gaditarum cõstat trans Iordanem in finibus Arabum, & Syrorum habitasse: quapropter ex historia sedes intelligenda est. Octauus locus est tribus Ascheris,vers.vigesimo. cuius habitatio commemoratur duobus nominibus: primò copia commeatus & soli vbertate: secundò rerum metallicarum atque fossiliū, vt exponit Moses Deut. 33. quibus reges & principes militiæ studentes delectantur. Nonus locus de tribu Nephtalitarum,vers.21.duo similiter enunciat. Primò lasciuiam & petulantiam illius tribus ex luxu: quæ res similitudine e-missæ ceruæ atque exsultantis, siue exsilientis ex viuario aut secluso-rio suo enuntiatur. Secundò studium elegantiæ in sermonibus,& vrbanitatis præotij abundantia. Decimus locus & vndecimus ad filios Rachelæ pertinent. Nam ad Josephū spectant versus 5. inde à v.22.ad Beniaminē,v.27.De Josepho primū generalis ppositio est,v.22. De ipso &tribu tota cõmuniter,priore mébro versus;de filiis verò duob. in duas tribus distinctis,posteriore. deinde verò minutatim illa enarrantur quatuor versibus. Vtrumque vesu v.22.allegoricè enûtiatur. Nam Iacob cum trûco,Joseph cum ramo ex trunco Iacobi prodeunte, sedes ipsius, cum agro irriguo & abundante frûctibus compa-ratur: ac proinde Joseph futurus dicitur numero gentis suæ copio-sissimus,vt arbor abûdat fructui, cuius radices nûquam humore necessario destituûtur. Ex hoc ramo duo velut brachia diffundi dicuntur,&ad muros vsque finitimorū propagari & lōgè lateque syluefcere vt ostendatur frequëtia duarum tribuum ex Josepho prognatarū, Ephraimi &Manassis. Atque hæc de hæredibus & hæreditate cõmuniter dicta sequentibus exponuntur, hoc modo: primò robur & potentia tanquam ad primogenitū pertinens demonstratur v.23. & seq. secundò benedictiones in hæreditatẽ à Deo profusæ, duobus alteris. Benedictionū ad hæredes pertinētiū,per prolepsim amplificatio po-
units.tr: This is common: Dan shall judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel. For what is said specifically of Dan, because he is first in that number, is understood commonly of the rest, because it is of common right. The sense, then, is that it is said singularly of Dan: although Dan is a son of a handmaid, he is not on that account to be excluded from tribal right, but an equal common right is adjudged to him along with the sons of the wives. Since this arrangement has a common reason in the case of the other sons whom Jacob raised up from the handmaids, it follows that that right pertains commonly to the others along with him. Therefore afterwards Gad, Asher and Naphtali are recounted in their order, as obtaining that common right along with Dan. The singular prophecy concerning Dan shows first the situation of his inheritance and his occupations, v.17, and then its outcome, v.18. The situation of the inheritance is by the way and the path, that is, on the outermost borders of Canaan. The occupation is that, because of the inconvenience of his dwelling, he will suddenly sally out against his neighbours and destroy them in the manner of a serpent, and will attack most vehemently even the most powerful who seem to themselves to live out of danger. Therefore he uses the likeness of serpents: the small snake that bites the horse's heel, and the acontius or javelin, which lies in wait from the branches of trees and watches travellers, and rushes at them like an arrow, whence it has its name. The outcome is shown to be wretched and desperate for these three, v.18, when Jacob turns himself to God, praying that he consult the safety of Dan. For this tribe failed first and remained in its failure, so that at the time of the return from Babylon nothing of Dan is found, 1 Chron. And St John, in Apocalypse chapter 7, plainly passes over the name of Dan in silence. The seventh place, concerning Gad, is v.19, in which the seat of the Gadites is indicated, and a history is added. The history is that he will be troubled by the raids of neighbours, and he will trouble and overcome those neighbours, just as it is established that the tribe of Gad dwelt beyond the Jordan on the borders of the Arabs and Syrians. Therefore the seat is to be understood from the history. The eighth place is the tribe of Asher, verse twenty. Its habitation is recalled under two heads: first, abundance of provisions and richness of soil; second, metals and fossil things, as Moses sets out in Deut. 33, in which kings and princes devoted to warfare delight. The ninth place, concerning the tribe of Naphtali, v.21, similarly states two things. First, the wantonness and petulance of that tribe from luxury, which is expressed by the likeness of a hind let loose and leaping, or springing out from its enclosure or pen. Second, zeal for elegance in speech and an abundance of refined expression. The tenth and eleventh places pertain to the sons of Rachel. For verses 22 to 26 relate to Joseph, and from v.22 onwards to Benjamin, v.27. Concerning Joseph there is first a general proposition, v.22: concerning him and his whole tribe in common, in the first member of the verse; concerning the two sons, divided into two tribes, in the latter member. Then these things are narrated one by one in four verses. Both are announced allegorically in v.22. Jacob is compared with the trunk, Joseph with the branch springing from the trunk of Jacob, and his seat with a well-watered field abundant in fruits. Accordingly Joseph is said to be going to be most numerous in his nation, as a tree abounds in fruit, whose roots never lack moisture. From this branch two arms, as it were, are said to spread out, and to extend even to the walls of the neighbours and to grow far and wide, so that the multitude of the two tribes descended from Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, may be shown. And these things, said in common about the heirs and the inheritance, are expounded in the following way: first, strength and power as belonging to the firstborn is shown, v.23 and following; second, the blessings poured out by God upon the inheritance, in two further parts. The amplification of the blessings pertaining to the heirs is set forth by prolepsis

units.la: DD. ij. nitur v. 23. cp & Iofcphū aduersarij petiuerint,& posteros eius petituri sunt multis modis:prout exponitur sagittariorū similitudine,modus vero potentiæ v.24.tribus argumentis ostenditur: primò quòd potétia ascita abundaturus est, vt sagittarius instructus arcu valente: secundò quòd potentia innata ei adfutura est, vt sunt lacerti valentes & rigidi sagittario : postremò, quòd ex causa inuicta, ac pro-inde diutissime hæc habiturusest, nempe à Deo forti Iacobi, provt exemplo antecedente Iacob confirmatus erat, cū singulari Dei pro-uidentia pastor getis suæ,& lapis siue perfugium à Deo effectus esset.
units.tr: in v.23, where Joseph's adversaries have assailed him, and will assail his posterity in many ways. The manner of his power is set out by the likeness of archers, and is shown by three arguments in v.24: first, that he will abound in power acquired, like an archer equipped with a strong bow; second, that innate power will be his, as strong and firm arms belong to an archer; last, that he will have this from an unconquered cause, and therefore for a very long time, namely from God, the Strong One of Jacob, just as Jacob had been confirmed by the preceding example, when, by the singular providence of God, he had been made a shepherd of his flock and a stone, or refuge, by God.

units.la: Ex quo signo & principio reliqua quæ sequuntur Iacob intelligi monet oportere : benedictiones enim in hæreditatem ab ope ac bene-dictione Dei eiusdem prouenturas Iacob pronuntiat v.25.& seq.tum exteras tum foris aduenturas e cœlo,terra,mari,tum intus sese exertu-ras ab vberibus & vtero,v.25. Deniq; copiosissimas & gloriosissimas in eam familiam,velut primogeniti & præcellétis suis fratribus,v.26.
units.tr: From this sign and principle Jacob bids us understand the things that follow: for Jacob pronounces that the blessings upon the inheritance will come from the help and blessing of God, v.25 and following; both foreign ones, coming from heaven, earth and sea, and those that will spring forth within from the breasts and the womb, v.25. Finally, most abundant and glorious ones into that family, as to the firstborn and one preeminent above his brothers, v.26.

units.la: Locus vndecimus de Beniamine facta eius prænuntiat, sedémque ex factis innuit. Facta, quòd omni tempore prædæ & rei militari operâ daturus est:ex quo sedes illius intelligitur,nepe quòd in finibus bello expositis quamuis in meditullio Cenahanæ sit habitaturus.Nã pri-mò temporibusIudicum vsque ad Dauidis tempora fuit res huic tri-bui cum Iebusæis:Salomonis verò exitu gens Israelitarum in duo re-gna discepta est,& ipsa tribus Beniamin lacerata, ita vt perpetuis bellis, dum alterum regnorum stetit, infesti Beniaminitæ fuerint. Hæc de priore parte huius capitis, cuius conclusio est vers.vigesimosexto.
units.tr: The eleventh place, concerning Benjamin, foretells his deeds and indicates his seat from those deeds. The deeds: that at all times he will give himself to booty and to military work. From this his seat is understood, namely that although he will dwell in the middle of Canaan, yet he will be on borders exposed to war. For from the times of the Judges down to the time of David, this tribe had war with the Jebusites; and at the departure of Solomon the nation of the Israelites was split into two kingdoms, and the tribe of Benjamin itself was torn apart, so that in perpetual wars, while one of the kingdoms stood, the Benjamites were hostile. So much concerning the first part of this chapter, whose conclusion is v.26.

units.la: In qua veritatem prædictionum Iacobi confirmat Moses: veritatem verò scripturæ à Mose exaratæ complemento Deus obsignauit. Sequitur locus alter duabus partibus comprehensus. Nam primo Ia-cob dat præcepta de sua sepultura, ad versum vsque penultimum: deinde moritur, versu vltimo. Causam præcepti de sepultura ante exposuimus capite quadragesimo septimo. Locum verò sepulturæ imperat versu vigesimonono. Circumscribit sequentibus: primò, emptione Abrahami & religioso iure sepulturæ, versu trigesimo: deinde vsu communi familiæ; quòd auus,auia,Pater,mater, cum Lea vxore ibi sepulti fuerint, versu trigesimo primo & sequente. Versu autem vltimo Iacobi mors exponitur. Quod verò narratur recepisse in lectum pedes suos postquam mandata dedisset liberis, non est cursim prætereundum ; sed reuocanda sunt illa ad huius loci in-telligentiam, quæ supra annotauimus in finem capitis quadragesi-miseptimi. Nempe ad signum reuerentiæ Iacobum, dum verbum Dei annunciaret, stetisse, aut certè sedisse[?] infirmitate pressum : post hoc diuino opere absoluto effœti sui corporis commodo consuluisse.
units.tr: In it Moses confirms the truth of Jacob's predictions, and God by the completion sealed the truth of the Scripture written by Moses. Follows the second place, comprised in two parts. For first Jacob gives commands about his burial, up to the penultimate verse; then he dies, in the last verse. We set out the cause of the command about burial before, in chapter forty-seven. He orders the place of burial in v.29. He circumscribes it in what follows: first, by the purchase of Abraham and the religious right of burial, v.30; then by the common use of the family, that grandfather, grandmother, father and mother, with Leah his wife, were buried there, v.31 and following. In the last verse Jacob's death is set forth. As for what is narrated, that he drew his feet into the bed after he had given commands to his sons, it must not be passed over hastily; but those things we noted above at the end of chapter forty-seven must be recalled for the understanding of this place: namely, that Jacob stood, or certainly sat [?], pressed by infirmity, as a sign of reverence while he announced the word of God; and after this divine work was finished, he took thought for the comfort of his weakened body.

units.la: CAPITIS L ANALYSIS.
units.tr: CHAPTER L ANALYSIS.

units.la: HIc demum postremus locus est ad sepulturam Iacobi pertinens: quam ipse aliquoties religiosissimè filiis mandauerat cap. 47. & 49. Huius autem capitis partes duæ sunt: prior ad sepulturam Iacobi pertinens, versibus 14. posterior, velut auctarium libri est de singulari filiorum Iacobi ac nominatim Iosephi historia, reliquo capite. Prioris loci partes sunt hæ: præparatio ad sepulturam: versibus sex; actus sepulturæ, ad versum usque 13. ac postremò reditus in Ægyptum, v.14. In præparatione duo posita sunt; conditura vel pollinctura corporis Iacobi, tribus versibus; & commeatus regis ad profectionem religiosæ sepulturæ causa, tribus alteris. Pollincturæ luctus coniunctus est, & alter locus ad præparationem sepulturæ pertinens, nempe quòd Ioseph commeatum ab Ægypti Rege exorauit. In hoc autem exorando primùm modus ad exorandum adhibitus, v.4. & 5. deinde euentus v.6. tenendus est. Ad modum exorationis pertinent duo; nam interuentores dicitur Ioseph adhibuisse, qui Pharaonem verbis ipsius compellarent, v.4. deinde iustis sermonibus instruxisse, quos ad exorandum commeatum sine offensa iudicauit pertinere. Vtrumque autem fuit necessarium, vt sibi ab offensa Regis Ægyptiorumque præcaueret: nam cùm pullati non possent ex lege & consuetudine coram Rege comparere, quòd inauspicatum factum vulgò haberetur, prudenter Ioseph interuentoribus vsus est. Deinde verò cùm nihil tantopere animos abalienet quàm si contemptum in alios ostenderis, prudenter Ioseph non causam religionis & sanctitatis simpliciter, sed causam communem sepulcri religiosi & familiaris, itémque adiurationis coniunctæ ostendebat, nequid esset quo Pharaonis aut Ægyptiorum animi in postulatione hac offenderentur. Itaque prudentem hanc postulationem euentus commodus sequutus est; nempe consensio Regis, v.6. Secundus locus de profectione sepulturaque exponit primo, profectionem, secundò luctum, postremò sepulturam corporis Iacobi. Profectio narratur primùm Iosephi procerúmq; omnium Ægypti, v.7. deinde totius familiæ Iacobi, eorum certè qui iustam ætatem attigerant, v.8. Postremò volutas[?] eorum omnium, qui hoc funus honorificè prosecuti sunt, verf. 9. Luctus ceremonia primùm exponitur verf. 10. qua ex ritu suo dies septem occupabantur. Deinde monimentum perpetuum illius luctus testimonio incolarum in posteritatem constitutum, verf. 11. Sepulturæ verò historia primum generatim proponitur, v.12. deinde specialius, v.13. sed singularia hæc omnia iam ante in mandatis Iacobi exposita sunt, cap. 47. & 49. Postremus locus de reuersione v.14. est euidens. Posterior pars capitis de rebus ex sepultura Iacobi consequutis duobus argumentis concluditur: vno communi omnibus Iosephi fratribus, ad verf. vsque 21. altero singulari ad Iosephum & familiam eius pertinente, inde ad finem capitis. Communis narratio est de fratrum submissione & deprecatione peccati sui apud Iosephum: cuius historiæ membra sunt duo, deprecatio ipsorum, & blanda Iosephi condonatio sponsióque[?]. Deprecationis ipsorum argumentum fuit mala conscientia rerum in fratrem gestarum, verf. 15. Hinc deprecatio facta legitur, primum per intercessores ad Iosephum ablegatos, verf. 16. & seq. deinde per ipsos, vbi intercessorum opera fuerunt confirmati de fratris erga se beneuolentia. Intercessorum memi-nit verf. 16. argumentorum ad conciliationem fratris pertinentium meminit verf. 17. quorum auctoritas amplificatur à patris defuncti reuerentia; quam mendaciter obtendebant, vt fratris animum amplius flecterent. Alioquin argumenta sunt hæc, primum à natura patris deprecantis, & fratrum agnoscentium crimen suum, & deprecantium: secundum à gratia, quòd eiusdem gratiæ ex sedere Dei essent participes, & vocati ad cultum eiusdem Domini. His Iosephi fletu magis quàm sermone dicitur respondisse, ne forte crimen suorum fratrum in se retegeret. Hinc sequitur fratrum aduentus verf. 18. deprecantium culpam, & se dedentium noxæ: quibus respondisse dicitur Iosephi primò per consolationem & confirmationem, cum fratribus suis testaretur se, officium Dei (cuius est vindicta) in ipsos assumere numquam cogitasse, verf. 19. Secundò, refert maleficium ipsorum ad singulare beneficium prouidentiæ Dei malo ventis bene, verf. 20. Non vt maleficium ipsorum transfundat in Deum, qui nullius mali affinis esse potest, sed vt eos à tristi recordatione maleficiorum suorum ad prouidentiæ illius sapientissimæ admirationem traduceret. Postremò consolatur sponsione in futurum, & blandè omnia de se fraterna officia pollicetur, verf. 21. Particularis historiæ ad Iosephum spectantis loci sunt hi; primò tranquilla ipsius in medio gentis suæ habitatio: deinde longævitas, verf. 22. tum familiæ propagatio in oculis ipsius, verf. 23. Postremò religiosum studium sepulturæ ad promissiones de hæreditate sancta in fratribus suis confirmandas : qua causa primùm promissionem Dei de Cenahanea possidenda repetit, vers. vigesimo quarto. Deinde adiurat ipsos de corpore suo illuc efferendo, ut eodem corpore suo illos edoceret promissiones Dei, & obstringerentur illi ad reversio-nem, versu 25. Quas res fuisse à posteris illius observa-tas narratur à Mose in versu ul-timo.
units.tr: Here at last comes the final passage concerning the burial of Jacob, which he himself had several times, most devoutly, commanded his sons to carry out (chap. 47 and 49). This chapter has two parts. The first, concerning Jacob's burial, runs to verse 14; the second, which serves as an appendix to the book, deals with the particular history of the sons of Jacob, and especially of Joseph, and fills the rest of the chapter. The first part has these divisions: the preparation for the burial, verses 1 to 6; the act of burial, to verse 13; and finally the return to Egypt, verse 14. The preparation contains two things: the embalming or preparing of Jacob's body, in three verses; and the king's leave to depart for the sake of the religious burial, in three further verses. The mourning is joined to the embalming, and the other element belonging to the preparation of the burial is that Joseph asked leave of the king of Egypt. In this request we must note first the means used to make the request, verses 4 and 5, and then the outcome, verse 6. Two things pertain to the means: first, that Joseph is said to have used intercessors, who were to address Pharaoh in his name, verse 4; and second, that he prepared his words with fitting speech, which he judged suitable for requesting leave without giving offence. Both were necessary, so that he might guard himself against the displeasure of the king and the Egyptians. For since those in mourning garments could not, by law and custom, appear before the king, a thing commonly thought ill-omened, Joseph wisely made use of intercessors. Further, since nothing alienates minds so much as showing contempt for others, Joseph wisely did not present the cause simply as one of religion and holiness, but also as the common cause of a religious and family tomb, together with the oath that was bound up with it, lest there be anything by which the mind of Pharaoh or of the Egyptians might be offended by the request. Accordingly, this prudent request was followed by a favourable outcome, namely the king's consent, verse 6. The second part, concerning the journey and the burial, sets out first the journey, then the mourning, and lastly the burial of Jacob's body. The journey is recounted first as that of Joseph and all the chief men of Egypt, verse 7, then that of the whole household of Jacob, at least of those who had reached the proper age, verse 8. Finally, the consent of all those who honoured this funeral with their presence, verse 9. The ceremony of mourning is set out first, verse 10, by which seven days were spent according to their custom. Then the lasting memorial of that mourning, established for posterity by the testimony of the inhabitants, verse 11. The history of the burial is first proposed in general terms, verse 12, and then more particularly, verse 13; but all these particulars had already been set out in Jacob's instructions, chap. 47 and 49. The final division, the return, verse 14, is plain. The second part of the chapter, concerning the things that followed upon Jacob's burial, is concluded by two arguments: the first common to all of Joseph's brothers, up to verse 21; the second peculiar to Joseph and his family, from there to the end of the chapter. The common narrative concerns the brothers' submission and their entreaty for pardon of their sin before Joseph. This history has two members: their entreaty, and Joseph's gentle forgiveness and promise. The ground of their entreaty was the guilty conscience for what they had done to their brother, verse 15. Hence it is recorded that the entreaty was made, first through intercessors sent to Joseph, verse 16 and following, and then by the brothers themselves, when through the intercessors' work they were assured of their brother's goodwill towards them. The intercessors are mentioned in verse 16, and the arguments belonging to the reconciliation of the brother are mentioned in verse 17. Their authority is magnified by the reverence due to their deceased father, which they falsely put forward, so that they might bend their brother's mind further. Otherwise the arguments are these: first, from the nature of the father who entreats, and from the brothers who acknowledge their crime and entreat; second, from grace, since they were partakers of the same grace from the same God and called to the worship of the same Lord. It is said that Joseph replied to these arguments more with weeping than with speech, lest he should perhaps reveal the crime of his brothers against himself. Hence follows the arrival of the brothers, verse 18, who confess their fault and give themselves up to punishment. To them Joseph is said to have replied, first by consolation and reassurance, testifying to his brothers that he had never thought of taking upon himself the office of God, whose is vengeance, verse 19. Secondly, he refers their wrongdoing to the singular benefit of God's providence, which turned evil into good, verse 20. Not that he transfers their wrongdoing to God, who can have no connection with any evil, but that he might lead them away from the sad remembrance of their misdeeds to wonder at that most wise providence. Finally, he comforts them with a promise for the future, and gently pledges all fraternal services on his part, verse 21. The passages concerning Joseph's particular history are these: first, his peaceful dwelling in the midst of his own people; then his long life, verse 22; then the increase of his family within his sight, verse 23. Lastly, the pious concern for the burial, bound up with the confirmation to his brothers of the promises of the holy inheritance. For this reason he first repeats God's promise concerning the possession of Canaan, verse 24. Then he binds them by oath to carry his body thither, so that by that same body of his he might teach them God's promises and they might be bound to return, verse 25. That these things were observed by their posterity is recounted by Moses in the last verse.
